HOUSE OF COMMONS.

---

Tuesday, 27th February, 1923.
The Third Session of the First Parliament
of Northern Ireland, appointed to meet 27th
February, 1923, in the thirteenth year of the
Reign of King George V., was opened by the
Governor (His Grace the Duke of Abercorn,
K.P.) in person.
The House met at a Quarter before Twelve
of the Clock, Mr. Speaker (Right Hon. Hugh
O'Neill, D.L., M.P.) in the Chair.
The Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod
(Major T. D. H. Hackett, D.S.O.)
announced.
was
Addressing Mr. Speaker, the Gentleman
Usher said: His Grace the Governor of
Northern Ireland commands this Honourable
House to attend immediately in the Senate.
Mr. Speaker, accompanied by the Prime
Minister (Right Hon. Sir James Craig), and
other Members went to the Senate.
On their return, the Sitting was suspended
until Three of the Clock, and then resumed.

SESSIONAL ORDERS.
ELECTIONS.
(3),
(By
Ordered. That all Members, who are returned for two or more places in any part of
Northern Ireland do make their Election for
which of the places they will serve, within
one week after it shall appear that there is
no question upon the Return for that place;
and if anything shall come in question
touching the Return or Election of any
Member, he is to withdraw during the time
the matter is in debate; and that all Members returned upon double Returns do withdraw till the Returns are determined.
Resolved: That if it shall appear that any
person hath been elected or returned a Member of this House or endeavoured so to be,
by Bribery, or any other corrupt practices,
this House will proceed with the utmost
severity against all such
persons as shall
have been wilfully concerned in such Bribery
or other corrupt practices.
WITNESSES.
Resolved: That if it shall appear that any
person hath been tampering with any
Witness, in respect of his evidence to be
given to this House, or any Committee
thereof, or directly or indirectly hath endeavoured to deter or hinder any person from
appearing or giving evidence, the same is
declared to be a high crime or misdemeanour; and this House will proceed
with the utmost severity against such
offender.
Resolved: That if it shall appear that any
person hath given false evidence in any case
before this House, or any Committee thereof this House will proceed with the utmost
severity against such offender.
ROYAL ULSTER CONSTABULARY.
Ordered: That the Commissioner of the
Royal Ulster Constabulary do take care that,
during the Session of Parliament, the passages through the streets leading to this
House be kept free and open, and that no
obstruction be permitted to hinder the passage of Members to and from this House,
and that no disorder be allowed in the precincts of or in the passages leading to this
House, during the Sitting of Parliament,
and that there be no annoyance therein, or
thereabouts; and that the Serjeant at Arms
attending this House do communicate this
Order to the Commissioner of the Royal
Ulster Constabulary aforesaid,
VOTES, PROCEEDINGS, AND RECORDS.
Ordered: That the Votes, Proceedings, and
Records of this House be printed, being first
perused by Mr. Speaker; and that he do
appoint the printing thereof; and that no
person but such as he shall appoint do presume to print the same.
PRIVILEGES.
Ordered: That a Committee of Privileges
be appointed.
OUTLAWRIES BILL,
"for the more effectual preventing
Clandestine Outlawries" read the first time,
and ordered to be read a second time.
KING'S SPEECH.
Mr. SPEAKER: I have to report that the
House has this day attended in the Senate
to hear his Grace's Speech, on behalf of the
Crown, to both Houses of Parliament; of
which I have for greater accuracy obtained
a copy. The Speech is as follows:
Members of the Senate and of the
House of Commons.
On this the first occasion on which 1
have the privilege to address you in my
present capacity, I desire to express my
appreciation of the high honour conferred
upon me by our Sovereign, and my sense of
humble duty to Him and His Loyal subjects
throughout Northern Ireland, and my congratulations to all concerned that this, the
third Session of your Parliament, opens
under brighter auspices than might have
been hoped for even six months ago.
Hitherto you have been mainly occupied
with matters incidental to the setting up
of your Parliament and Government Departments, and with measures necessary
for safeguarding life and property. Owing
to wise administration, and with a Judiciary
of which any State might be proud,
strengthened by Acts passed for the specia!
purpose, order has been restored and repect for the Law established. For this satisfactory condition I feel a tribute should
be paid to the Inspector-General and the
officers and men of the Royal Ulster Con-
The King's Speech.
The King's Speech.
27 FEBRUARY 1923.
stabulary, and of the Special Constabulary
in which Forces discipline and a high
sense of duty throughout all ranks have
called forth universal and well-merited
praise, which is also due to officers and
men in your Prison service.
The time has now happily arrived when
you are in a position to enter upon the
consideration of affairs of a more domestic
and remedial nature.
The Principal Bills of the new Session
will deal with Education and Temperance
Reform. The first of these, which will be
laid before you at an early date, will be
framed to co-ordinate and reform the several services of public education and to premote the general welfare of children and
young persons. The latter cannot be dealt
with, at the earliest until after Easter,
owing to complicated financial and other
questions involved. I earnestly trust that
the discussion on these two primary
measures will be conducted with a spirit of
helpfulness, toleration and goodwill, to the
end that there may be placed upon the
Statute Book Acts conferring lasting benefits
upon the people as a whole.
an
Other important measures which will engage your attention will include the application to Northern Ireland of the Criminal
Evidence Act, 1898, which enables
accused person to give evidence in his own
defence, and a Bill dealing with the Amendment of Criminal Law in the interests of
young persons. Bills to amend the Trade
Boards Acts, the Unemployment Insurance
Acts, and the Petty Sessions Acts will be
introduced, and also legislation having for
its object the reconstruction of records of
Joint Stock Companies whose registered
offices are situate in Northern Ireland. A
Bill will be introduced making it obligatory
upon all Civil Servants and other persons
employed by the Government of Northern
Ireland to take the Oath of Allegiance to
His Majesty the King and His Government
of Northern Ireland.
There are in addition, a certain number
of other administrative measures which will
claim your attention.
It is intended at an early date to appoint
a Royal Commission-
To consider and report as to how the
natural and industrial resources of Northern Ireland can be best developed, with
a view to increasing general prosperity
and reducing the extent of unemployment."
The Government proposes to set up a Committee to consider the form legislation should
take to deal with the question of Rent Restriction, in view of the expiry of control in
June next.
A Committee has been appointed to inquire
into Reformatory and Industrial Schools,
and steps have been taken to appoint a
Committee to investigate the Jury system.
I am particularly gratified to learn that
voluntary machinery for negotiation is being
set up by the Railway Companies and the
Railway Trade Unions, the result of which,
I trust, will be that a larger measure of
harmony will in future prevail throughout
the railway systems of Northern Ireland.
in
The problem of unemployment is still
serious, and I appreciate the patient way
in which the people have borne the trials
which they have been called upon to endure
common with their fellow subjects
throughout the United Kingdom. The prevailing indication of a revival of trade and
shipbuilding encouraged in certain directions by the operation of the Loans
Guarantee Act of last Session causes me
great satisfaction; my Ministers are giving
their most anxious consideration to the
many problems inseparable from such a
revival, so that as quickly as possible steady
employment may be provided as a natural
consequence of trade prosperity, and local
authorities and other public bodies throughout the country are heartily co-operating
with the Government in the promotion of
Telief schemes, many of lasting utility,
providing much-needed employment and
absorbing over £1,500,000. Work on the
preparation of the site for permanent
Parliamentary and Ministerial Buildings
has been begun, and I am assured that there
will be no interruption until the whole
undertaking is completed.
Members of the House of Commons.
By agreement with the British Government a Special Committee has been
established under the Chairmanship of

The estimates of expenditure on the

Members of the Senate and of the

His Gracious Majesty, when he addressed
you in Person on the 22nd June, 1921, said,
"I am confident that the important

And I pray that Almighty God may bestow His abundant blessing upon your
deliberations.
Debate on the Address.
Mr. JOHNSTONE (in morning dress): I beg
to move:
"That an humble Address be presented to
His Grace the Governor of Northern
Ireland, as followeth :
Your Grace,
We, His Majesty's most dutiful and loyal
subjects, the Commons of Northern Ireland,
in Parliament assembled, beg leave to offer
our humble thanks to your Grace for the
Speech which your Grace has addressed
to both Houses of Parliament."
I am sure that I should very ill represent the
feelings of this House if I did not take this
opportunity of conveying to his Grace the
Governor of Northern Ireland our most
sincere and respectful congratulations on the
honour which the King has done him. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) His Grace the Duke
of Abercorn comes of a family which has
been long connected with Northern Ireland.
His Grace himself has long been prominent
both in the political and in the social life
of our Province. That he possessed the confidence of this House was shown when we
elected him unanimously as one of the first
Members of our first Senate, and, if
there was any proof required that the choice
of His Majesty was a popular one, we have
only to call to witness the demonstration of
yesterday, when he made his State entry,
and of to-day when he came to open Parliament. We anticipate for his Grace a
most prosperous and a most successful term
of office, and we are sure that not the least
of the factors which will contribute to that
success is the personality of her Grace the
Duchess. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
When I turn to the King's Speech I see
that a very considerable programme is to
be put before us in the coming Session.
Among the various measures which we will be
asked to consider, two important measures
are singled out by his Grace for special
attention. One is the Education Bill, and
the other is the Bill for Temperance Reform.
I am sure the House will bear with me if
I say something in regard to the Education
Bill. I do not think I am giving away any
State secret when I say that I understand
the Bill will be based mainly on the lines
of the Lynn Report, and as I am a member
of the Lynn Committee and took a considerable share in drafting that Report, I am
sure the House will bear with me if I make
a few remarks on the subject of education.
I should like, first of all, to say this, I have
heard some criticisms to the effect that the
Bill to be introduced in this House-I do
not know where the information comes from
-will differ in many material points from
the Lynn Report. The Lynn Committee do
not consider that their Report is direct inspiration from heaven, and they are very far
indeed from claiming even verbal inspiration
for it, so that I do not think they will feel
in the slightest degree annoyed or upset if
the Bill is improved or is rather different
from the conclusions that they put before
the public generally. But there are one or
two points I should like to mention, because
I became a member of this Committee with
an absolutely unbiassed mind and really
knowing very little of a definite nature about
the problem, especially as regards primary
education. One of the very first things
with which I was impressed during the
sittings of the Committee was the fact that
there was an urgent need for better primary
education in Northern Ireland. I had, of
course, heard a good many complaints about
primary education, that it was not so good
as it used to be, that the boys were not so
well taught now as they formerly were. On
that point I do not think we came to any
conclusion. I do not know whether primary

concerning agriculture. Mr. Gordon caid,
"The best way in which you can improve
agriculture in Northern Ireland is to give
these boys a better primary education." When
we have both technical schools and schools of
agriculture telling us that the only way in
which we can improve these technical crafts
is by giving a better primary education, I
say the time has come when this House must
seriously consider this question and be pre
pared to deal with it in no niggardly spirit.
education is better or worse than it was
thirty, forty or fifty years ago, but I do know
it is evidently not good enough for the needs
of the moment. The reason I say so is
that in the course of our investigations we
had to discuss the question of technical
education. Technical education is remarkably well done in Northern Ireland, but
we found that one of the great drawbacks of
technical education was the fact that the
young men and the young women who may
be coming forward to join the technical
schools had not received a good enough primary education to benefit by the instruction
which was to be given to them. So much
is that the case that in our largest technical
school like the Municipal Institute in Belfast
space and time have to be given to teaching
young boys and girls English, elementary
mathematics, and simple matters of that
sort which they ought to have learned in
their primary schools. That is a thing that
should not be.
One criticism which I have heard with
regard to our Report is that this may be
all very well for a great centre of industry
where boys require to be exceedingly
well trained and exceedingly well educated
in order to take up the various forms
of handicraft, but that So far as the
country is concerned the education is perfectly good enough for them to become farm
labourers or farmers. If this House is content, as I personally am not content, that the
population of Ulster should be simply hewers
of wood and drawers of water, I say well
and good. Then, from that point of view,
we had evidence before us to show that the
primary education which is given in Ulster
is not good enough even to make a good farm
labourer, still less a good farmer. We had
before us Mr. Gordon, who is attached to
the Agricultural Department of Northern
Ireland, and who is responsible for the
classes of instruction in agriculture which
have been held throughout Northern Ireland
for some time past. They have been very
popular and, I believe, have done a great deal
of good. Mr. Gordon told us that one of the
great obstacles to the extension of these
classes, one of the great obstacles to the
utility of these classes, was that the young
farmers and the young men who came in to
attend them had not got a good enough primary education to understand anything more
than the mere rudiments of scientific agriculture. Some of the Members on the
Committee interested in agriculture asked
Mr. Gordon if he thought something ought
to be done in the primary schools to teach
the boys and girls something about agriculture. There were suggestions with regard to
teaching these boys in regard to the chemistry
of soils, in regard to the germination of seeds,
and in regard to a number of other matters
When one comes to consider the reason
why the results of primary education are so
poor, the next most striking thing to my
mind in the evidence that we had before us
was that the school attendance in Northern
Ireland was exceedingly bad. Whether the
teaching is good or bad, boys and girls cannot
learn the subjects in primary education without attending school, and the standard of
attendance in Northern Ireland is very much
below what one should expect in a community
like ours and very much below what is found
in neighbouring countries. There were two
reasons put forward for that. One
of those reasons applies to some centres
---I am sorry to say that it applies to Belfast
--that you cannot enforce compulsory school
attendance because there are not enough
schools for the children to go to. The second
reason is even less creditable to our Northern
community and that is the fact that a large
number of parents find that a sturdy lad, or
a sturdy lass for the matter of that, is of
some monetary value, and they prefer to reap
a fleeting advantage from the labours of their
boy or their girl rather than put that boy
or that girl in the way of bettering himself
or herself by getting a good primary education. That is the reason why we have
proposed that the penalties for not sending a
child to school should be very largely increased in the case of a parent, be it the
father or mother, who keeps his or her child
at home and prevents him from attaining the
education which is so necessary for his advancement in life.
The third point which I would like to
touch on is the question of what I may call
the whole system of education in the North
of Ireland. Up to the present time, as this
House knows, primary education in Northern
Ireland, and in Ireland generally, has been
completely centralised: it has been run from
a centre. There has been no local control,
or practically no local control. Now, we of
the Lynn Committee considered there was far
too little interest being taken in education
in Northern Ireland, and until a much wider,
much more extended interest was taken in
education we would not get a real advance
in education. So for that reason, in order to
foster local interest in education, we have
suggested the setting up of Local Committees.
This system is working exceedingly well both
Debate on the Address. 12
Debate on the Address.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Mr. Johnstone]
in England and in Scotland There is no
question that in England and in Scotland
vastly more interest is taken in education
than anywhere in Ireland. Those Local
Committees carry another point that is not
perhaps so pleasant, inasmuch as you have
to pay for it. We suggest that in order that
this local interest might really touch the
people in a very tender spot a local rate
should be imposed to assist in paying for
education. The main reason why we ask
for a local rate to pay for part of educationand remember this local rate only pays for
a very small part; it only pays for
a mere tithe of the local expenses because for
every shilling paid by the Local Authority
the Government will pay 9s or 10s, and more
in some cases--one of the reasons for a local
rate is that if the people are paying for a
thing they appreciate it better than if they
were not paying for it. A man in general,
and a North of Ireland man in particular,
never thinks anything he gets for nothing
is worth very much, but if he feels he is
paying for his education be will take a very
much greater interest in it and will appreciate
it very much more. The other reason is this,
that we want that local patrictism in which
Ballymena is fighting Antrim as to which
of them is going to have the better school,
and Omagh is holding up the flag of defiance
to Dungannon, and towns in Armagh will
be contesting with one another as to which
offers the best educational facilities. They
will be able to improve their educational
facilities by increasing their rates and they
will be able to spend money on education, a
thing which at present they have no power to
do.
The next point which I would like to touch
on very briefly is the question of the teachers.
I think I need not preach to this House in
regard to the disabilities of secondary
teachers. Everybody admits that the secondary teachers are wretchedly paid, and
also that their present position is a standing
disgrace to Northern Ireland. It is more
than that, it is a standing menace to Northern Ireland. The evidence which we had
before us, not merely in the Lynn Committee
but elsewhere is this, that unless very
speedy relief is granted to give a living wage
to the secondary teachers there will be no
secondary teachers to support in Northern
Ireland. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) It
is simply a question of supply and demand.
A number of these men have undertaken a
long and in many cases on expensive training.
they are possessors of University Degrces
and have had much experience. At the preent time they are rece ving wages much less
than those they w uld earn by labour, manual
unskilled labour, and these men :ould o' tain,
and they are chlaining, posts across the
water. In England and in Setland there is
a stage of secondary teachers, and unless
we offer these men some inducement to remain here, unless we offer them wages something approximating to what they could get
across the water we shall lose our secondary
teachers and we shall lose our secondary
schools too. A great many Members of this
House may consider that this is a thing
that we can contemplate with equanimity.
I differ entirely from that point of view. I
do not want to see a situation forced on
Northern Ireland where secondary education
is going to be the privilege of the rich man's
son, and that is what is going to happen if
you lose your present secondary teachers and
if you have to close a number of your secondary schools. Then we come to the
question of the primary school teachers. The
Lynn Committee have been rather blamed
because they considered the primary teachers
should retain the salaries which they have
at present. They are looked on as bloated
plutocrats who do a few hours' very easy work
for a very considerable wage. I sometimes
wish that the people who think these teachers
carn their money so easily were put in charge
of a score of sturdy boys from 9 o'clock till
12 and from half-past 12 till 3 to keep those
boys in order and teach them at the same
time.
Mr. McGUFFIN: Would it be harder than
riveting iron?
Mr. JOHNSTONE: I do not think it would
be physically harder than riveting iron but I
believe the mental toil and strain would be
considerably more. Another point wh
struck me in the course of the investigations
of the Lynn Committee was that these teachers-I do not say that they are too well
paid, that is a matter for this House to consider are expected to be men of various parts.
In the course of the investigations of the
Lynn Committee we found that in primary
schools the clergy expected that religion
should be taught by the teacher; then the
medical men came forward and said that a
child in a primary school should get instruction in hygiene, and they laid it down that
the teacher should give that instruction also;
then we had another band of theorists who
thought that children, especially in the country, should learn something about agriculture
and horticulture, and that the teacher should
teach that as well. For so many-sided
a man I say a fairly reasonable salary
ought to be paid. There is another point
quite apart from that and that is, no matter
what system this House may succeed in setting up, no matter how good the administrative machinery may be, in the long run
for the success of primary education in
Ireland you must depend upon the teacher.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) Unless you
give conditions of work which are attractive,
Debate on the Address.
Debate on the Address.
27 FEBRUARY 1923.
unless you give a salary that is sufficient to
maintain a man in reasonable respectability.
you are not going to attract into the service
of your schools young men and young women
of ability and of the right stamp; You are
going to get a discontented service, and you
have not provided for the carrying on of the
work of the general community. I think
that is the real reason why we should, if
anything, err on the side of generosity towards the school teacher.
Now, I should like, in conclusion, just to
say that in the Speech of his Grace this
morning he expressed the hope that the discussion on these Measures, including this
Education Bill, will be conducted in a spirit
of helpfulness and tolerance and good-will.
I am sure that that hope will be fully realised
in this House. If I may say so, I should like
one other thing to be added. I should like
that this House should approach this question
in a spirit of liberality, and the reason
I say
so is this. Modern life is becoming very complex, and the race for success, and even the mere struggle for
existence, gets more and more strenuous,
individual,
for the
for the community
and for the nation. The problems that are
presenting themselves can be solved by brains,
and can only be solved by educative brains.
We are about to set up in this Bill, which
I hope will be found on the Statute Book
and in force during the coming session, a
monument to the first Parliament of Northern
Ireland, a monument which will probably
last for some time. I hope it will be a
monument of statesmanship and foresight,
and I hope it will also be a monument of
liberality.
I know that the greatest things in this
world cannot be bought with money, neither
can they be bought at a price nor sold. They
are the things of the spirit, and in those
things Ulster is reasonably rich, but there
are some things which can be purchased with
money, and of those which can be purchased
with money, education, and an opportunity
for education, to my mind are pre-eminently
well worth buying. I beg to move.
Members: Hear, hear.)
(Hon.
Mr. MARK (in morning dress): It
is with great pleasure I rise to second
the motion for the Address of Thanks,
so ably moved by the Hon. Member
for the University (Mr. Johnstone). I
should also like to take the opportunity
of joining with him in offering my sincere
congratulations on behalf of this House to
His Grace the Duke of Abercorn on his
appointment to the high office of Governor
of Northern Ireland. Coming as I do from
the Maiden City, which constituency his
race so long and honourably represented
in the Imperial Parliament, it is to me a
matter of great personal delight and satisfaction that his Grace has been pleased to
accept this responsible office, all the duties
of which we know he will discharge with becoming dignity and efficiency, and in such
an acceptable manner as will give universal
satisfaction to everyone within the boundaries of Northern Ireland. I am also
assured that the traditions in which he has
been nurtured, the prestige which he universally enjoys and his manifest desire to
discharge impartially all the functions pertaining to his office, will, if possible, increase
that general confidence and esteem in which
he is already held. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.)
We offer to His Majesty our humble thanks
for his gracious appreciation of the administration by the Northern Government since
its inauguration. and it greatly pleases us
to know that the faith entertained by His
Majesty when he addressed this House in
person on 22nd June, 1921, has been abundantly justified. It is the unanimous opinion
of this House and of the people in Northern
Ireland that the present satisfactory condition which has merited His Majesty's
gracious appreciation is due to the unfailing
loyalty, energy and ability of our Prime
Minister, his Cabinet, the officers and men
of the Royal Ulster Constabulary and
the Special Constabulary, coupled with
the firm determination of the people to
make Ulster a peaceable, prosperous and
contented area. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
May we respectfully assure His Majesty
that the Bills and other important matters
mentioned in his gracious Speech will receive
our most careful attention, whether regarded
from the financial, industrial or social standpoint, to the ultimate end that they may
benefit all classes and creeds in Northern
Ireland.
The Government is to be congratulated
upon the fact that it is intended at an early
date to appoint a Royal Commission to consider and report as to how our natural and
industrial resources can be best developed
with a view to increasing the general prosperity and reducing the extent of unemployment. I feel sure that this House will
approve of this appointment, and that all
our people will rejoice to know that it is
the Government's intention to do everything
in its power for the material benefit of the
community; for, notwithstanding the magnificent progress that we have made in the
past. I firmly believe that there are many
sources of development still remaining untapped, and it will be our duty, as it is
our privilege, to strive until by every legi
timate means of enterprise and co-ordination
of effort we have laid an enduring basis for
an industrial prosperity and a social standard
unexcelled by any other people within the
confines of our great Empire. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.)
Debate on the Address. 16
Debate on the Address.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Mr. Mark]
We all realise that the one great factor
which is dominating the industrial situation,
and which will dominate it, to a greater or
lesser extent for years to come is the War
aftermath on the Continent. The chaos in
Europe has necessarily re-acted with great
severity upon Northern Ireland, and the rebuilding of our economic life will not only
require wise administration and sympathetic
legislation, but also, as his Grace has said,
a spirit of helpfulness, toleration and goodwill from all classes of the community.
The Government is also to be congratulated
upon its intention of introducing at an early
date Bills dealing with Education and Temperance Reform. The commendably prompt
manner in which it has kept its pledges by
framing Bills to deal with these very important and controversial matters should give
satisfaction to the great majority of our
people, and should assure them-if assurance
is required that their general welfare is
being carefully and assiduously looked after
by the Government.
The House will be pleased to hear that it
is the intention of the Government to set up
a Committee to consider the form legislation
should take to deal with the subject of Rent
Restriction in view of decontrol in June next.
I feel certain that the House will approve of
the course adopted by the Government as
the only fair way of dealing with this very
important and complicated question.
Before I close I should like on this the
opening of the third Session of our Parlia-
Iment to express, and to have placed on
record, the sincere thanks of our people,
which most assuredly are due, to the Members
of our Cabinet for the very successful way
in which all difficulties and obstacles that
had to be surmounted have been overcome.
It surely must be most gratifying that during
such a short period of time since our Parliament was born we can to-day survey with
justifiable pride and great satisfaction the
machinery of Government functioning in
every Department, and in this connection
may I also be permitted to bear tribute to
the universal courtesy and ability that is
being shown by our officials.
Having succeeded in bringing about security
for the lives and property of our people by
unflinching determination and the most
scrupulous and rigid impartiality of
the administration of the law we can
indeed truthfully and joyfully assent
to the gracious words of the Speech
that this the third Session of our Parliament
opens under brighter auspices than might
have been hoped for even six months ago.
To restore law and order, to give absolute
security to the lives and property of a people
is the fundamental duty of all democratic
and constitutional Government, and having
done this we now stand on the threshold
of what I trust and hope will be a new era
in our history, when we can devote our time
and attention to those great constructive
measures which are so necessary to give effect
to the thoughts and aspirations, ambitions
and hopes of our people. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.)
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: May I at the
outset be permitted to offer my congratulations to the learned Member for the
University (Mr. Johnstone) who has so very
effectively and efficiently performed the duty
entrusted to him. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) And may I at the same time offer my
very sincere congratulations to my colleague
in the representation of Derry (Mr. Mark)
for the very forcible speech he has made in
seconding the Address. I am sure we have
listened to both speeches with the greatest
pleasure, and I hope profit. I have no
intention this afternoon, indeed I think it
would be out of place, of going into any
detail whatever in regard to the various
matters contained in the Speech delivered
to-day by his Grace the Governor of Northern
Ireland. There are, however, a few thingsoutstanding things-to which I would like to
make a passing reference. May I be permitted to say-I hope it will not be considered
out of place, but I think for obvious reasons
I am well qualified to do so-with what real
pleasure, what peculiar pleasure, coming from
Derry that I listened to the Speech read by
his Grace the Governor this morning. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) I think this Parliament and the people of Ulster are to be congratulated on the choice made in the selection
of his Grace as the Governor of Northern
Ireland, and may I associate with him his
gracious Consort the Duchess of Abercorn.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
The first outstanding thing in the Speech
was the reference to the condition of things
in Northern Ireland. Since we last met in
this House we have had peace and order restored throughout the country. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) I think it is only right
that acknowledgment should be made of the
splendid services of the officers of the Crown,
in co-operation, may I add, with the Minister
of Home Affairs (Sir Dawson Bates). (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) It is a pleasure to us
in Northern Ireland that we are living in
peace and tranquillity. I hope with the cooperation of the people of all classes that
the conditions of peace and good order which
have now been established will long continue
so that the basis of prosperity may be firmly
laid. May I add that I hope we will have
the co-operation in securing a continuation
of that peace of all that is best in the community and of all creeds and classes. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) There is one thing
in connection with this matter that should
17 Debate on the Address.

Debate on the Address.
not be lost sight of. We have had peace for
the last six or eight months, and one of the
ways to secure peace in the future is to be
prepared for any contingency that may arise.
I hope we will have no trouble from any
internal opponents, and I hope we will have
no trouble from any external opponents
whatever. But in this connection I have been
somewhat concerned by the fact that I have
noticed there has been a gradual withdrawal
of the Imperial forces from the province.
Now, I am sure that withdrawal has been
made for very good and sufficient reasons,
and I am certain that the Members of the
Government are in close touch with what
is going on. I am hopeful that while this
withdrawal may be for good and sound
reasons, and that while the representatives
of the Imperial authority do not continue
to be as strong as they have hitherto been,
there will be no further disbanding of the
Constabulary Force on which we have to
depend to protect us and preserve peace and
order throughout the Province. Now if
there is going to be a diminished number
of the Forces of the Crown from the Imperial
standpoint, and if there is going to be a
redistribution of the numbers which are going
to remain in Northern Ireland, may I press
on the Government the necessity of seeing
that those forces are placed as close to the
boundary lines as possible. And here may
I put in a claim for such places as Enniskillen and Londonderry, where there are
Constabulary barracks accommodation, and
where you have people willing and anxious
to show their goodwill and give a loyal welcome to the Forces of the Crown, that they
may be provided with adequate garrisons.
I need not enlarge upon the necessity for
following this course, and I hope the Government to-day will be able to assure this House
and to assure the people outside that a matter of this kind is receiving their best and
fullest consideration, and that in due course,
if necessary, they will impress upon the Imperial authority the necessity of these outposts of the Six Counties so that they may
be provided with sufficient garrisons.
When I come to the question of the legislation mentioned in the gracious Speech delivered this morning there are just a few
things that call for observation. First of all
there is the Education Bill. Various aspects
of it have been dealt with by the hon. and
learned Member for the University (Mr.
Johnstone), and I need only say a few words
in the way of laying down the general principles, which, I hope, will be carried out by
the Government when this Bill is being
placed before us. I am sure the Bill will be
designed to meet the conditions which exist
in Northern Ireland, whether in the rural
districts or in the city districts, and the
problem in the one is somewhat different
ir m the problem in the other. I hope
that to a large extent this Measure will be
framed on the lines laid down in the report
known as the Lynn Report. With most of
the conclusions in that Report I can agree;
with some of them I cannot agree, but I
believe that, taken as a whole, they are such
as should commend themselves to the judgment of this House and to the judgment of
the country as a whole. The only observation
I would like to add further in this espect
is that I hope the Government will in their
Bill see to it that we are going to have an
amalgamation of small schools. (Hon. Meinbers: Hear, hear.) Let me further hopealthough I may be considered an extreme
optimist-that the Bill will not establish itself as absolutely denominational in
character. While I consider it is not possible
at the moment to get away from demominational education-
HON. MEMBERS: Why not?
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: I hope the Bill
will be built up on such lines that eventually
we can have a system of education under
which the youth of this country can be
educated together, irrespective of creed, or
class, or party. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
We are going to have. I understand, popular
control. I hope that is going to be real
and genuine, and that the people are going
to be allowed to participate in the education
of their children, and that they are going
to be made feel that they are going to contribute something, in any case, towards that
education. I want to say to the Government
that they will have to move 'cautiously in
regard to an education rate. I do not want
any parsimony at all in regard to the education rate, but from what I know of he
sentiments of a great many people they are
not, some of them, prepared, perhaps, to face
a large education rate, and the amount that
will be fixed will. I hope, be an extremely
moderate item. The only thing I would like
to add further in regard to this matter is
that the Government in placing education
in the forefront of their programme have
done the right thing, because the best investment any State can make is by giving a
good education to the young people in that
State, and I believe the best investment even
a parent can make is by trying to co-operate
with the State in seeing that the children
get every facility for having that asset, which
is the greatest asset any person could have
going out into the world, education based
upon good lines, and an education strengthened further by good moral character.
Now I come to the next subject, and that
is the question of Temperance Reform. I am
delighted that the Government have placed
this in the forefront of their programme.
The Prime Minister intimated that this was
a subject upon which the Government in
due course would legislate, and I did not

HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Sir Robert Anderson]
expect anything else than to see this question
mentioned in the Speech to-day. Reform in
this direction is long overdue. We are to a
large extent behind Great Britain in this
matter, but I am hopeful that the Measure
when submitted to the House will be such
that it will meet with the approval of the
majority of the House, and the majority of
the people outside, and do something to make
Ulster a cleaner, happier, and better place
to live in.
Next I come to another question-that of
unemployment. We are all delighted to know
that there is an improvement in this direction, and may I offer my congratulations to
the Minister of Labour (Mr. Andrews) and
those associated with him on the splendid
efforts they have made during the past six
or twelve months to grapple with this the
most difficult of all questions? (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) Nothing has appealed
to the masses of our people more than the
kindly thought and the sympathetic interest
taken by the Minister of Labour and his
entire staff in trying to help those who at
the moment cannot help themselves, and enable them to tide over one of the most difficult periods we have passed through from a
commercial standpoint. I hope the Minister
of Labour will not hesitate, if unemployment
continues, and there is no improvemnt in
many directions, to press upon the Cabinet
that another grant of, say, £20,000 should
be given to help forward these very desirable
improvement schemes that have been adopted
throughout the country. The Imperial
Government dealt very fairly with the condition of affairs existing in Belfast, which was
very peculiar, but I am glad that this Government, considering its resources, dealt equally
well with those outside the City of Belfast.
and I am perfectly sure they will consider
with feelings of sympathy-if the conditions
exist the necessity of still further helping
in the direction I have indicated.
I am also delighted to know that a Commission is to be set up to consider the
resources of Ulster and see if there may be
any developments so that employment may
be increased. I look upon that paragraph
in the Speech with the greatest interest and
the greatest possible pleasure. I do not intend to enlarge upon it except to say just in a
sentence or two that the position of affairs
in Ulster from an economic standpoint can
be improved, and it is the duty of the
Government to see how they can create, or
sympathise with, or in what direction they
can assist in the creation of new industry.
The problem of the statesman, whether in
other countries or in Ulster, seems to me for
the future to be how you are to deal with the
decrease in the population in rural districts
and the increase of the population in the
towns and cities. I am hopeful that this
Commission will be enabled to suggest certain
lines on which, perhaps, industries can be
started to give employment in the small
towns and villages, and thus retain the people
in their respective districts rather than see
them going to the larger towns or, perhaps,
emigrating to other countries. The
Ministry of Commerce has done a great deal,
but in this connection let me throw out to
them a suggestion which I have seen. working in other countries. I hope the Ministry
of Commerce will establish in the city of
Belfast as early as possible, and impress
upon the Ministry of Finance the necessity
for money with which to do it, a permanent
exhibition of all the industries of Ulster,
what Ulster can produce, where buyers from
the overseas Dominions, and from America,
and elsewhere, in passing through the city of
Belfast-which is going to be the capital of
this Northern area, with its Parliamentary
buildings, and to which people from all parts
of the world will come-may see what we can
produce. Why should we not have an exhibition where these men can see what Ulster
can produce, and what Ulster can do, and
from which the officials of the Ministry of
Commerce would be able to send these men
on to the manufacturers and the people who
could properly meet their needs? I throw
out that suggestion to the Ministry of Commerce, and I think it might be utilised in
a very practical way.
The last thing to which I want to refer is
the fact that there is a clause in the Speech
dealing with the special Committee which is
presided over by Lord Colwyn to fix up
certain matters due to the establishment of
the Free State. We have an interest undoubtedly in certain buildings and other
things outside the Six Counties, and I hope
satisfactory conclusions will be arrived at
there; but I would like to know from the
Minister of Finance--I do not wish to press
this point if he does not consider it advsable
to give the information for which I am asking-if the Government have arrived at any
arrangement with the British Treasury in
regard to our future financial relationships.
if any fixed basis has been secured in regard
to what our contributions shall be? I may
be considered very pressing in this matter.
because on the last occasion I mentioned it
too, but when the Bill establishing this
Parliament was passed through the British
House of Commons, the Minister in charge
told the House that Ulster was to have a

above what her contributions to meet

of Finance tell us if the present Government
is going to honour that promise, if they have
told what they are going to do, if the matter
has been pressed upon the British Treasury
and the British Chancellor of the Exchequer,
because undoubtedly Ulster has a claim to

I do not
be recognised in that respect?
grumble for a moment at the treatment that
has been meted out by the British Treasury
to this Government since it was started.
They have in many matters dealt with us in
the most handsome and generous manner
possible, but I really do want to see the time

-that we were to have a free gift of the

I have nothing further to add to the remarks I have just made. I think the Address
as a whole is a somewhat remarkable document. A great deal of legislation will have
to be passed to bring into effect all these
things that have been promised.
We are
evidently going to have a busy Session, and
I sincerely hope that, in conformity with the
wish expressed by His Grace the Governor,
our deliberations will be carried on in the
best of spirit and goodwill, and that we shall
all be animated with the one honest and
sincere desire to do the very best we can for

The PRIME MINISTER (Sir James Craig):
I think perhaps it will be for the convenience of the Members of the House if I
adopt the custom which long usage at Westminster has almost sanctified, and rise after
the mover and seconder and one other
speaker from some other part of the House.
In the first instance, I would like to join
with my hon. Friend who has just sat down
(Sir Robert Anderson) in paying a high
tribute to the mover and to the seconder of
the Motion which is now before us. I have
heard a good many speeches in my time in
reply to the Gracious Message from the
Throne, and I can only say that the
eloquence and the tact with which the
various subjects were dealt with have reached
the high level which I anticipated
would be the case when we got our Parliament established for a year or two. I congratulate them both most heartily on my
own behalf, and on behalf of the House,
because they have added to the dignity of
this assembly.
In the second place, I would like to say
with what great joy we all welcomed our new
Governor to our midst on his first State
entry to the City of Belfast and to Ulster,
and how glad we all were to see him in such
good health and accompanied by the Duchess.
I can only believe that as time goes on, and
we have our own Governor, our own Parliament, and our own institutions of every kind,
Ulster, feeling so safe and so secure with her
institutions, will rise to be a great State
within the Empire. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.)
Then it would certainly be the desire of
us all to tender to the Royal Family our
respectful greetings on the joyful news of a
two-fold character that reached the country
a short time ago. I refer in the first instance
to the event with regard to Princess Mary,
and in the second place to the announcement
(Hon.
with regard to the Duke of York.
Members: Hear, hear.)
May I go on to the pith, if I may say so,
of the Speech to which we listened this morning in another place? First of all, of
course, without a doubt we have to congratulate ourselves upon the restoration of
law and order, and when we are doing that
we must pay a tribute to those on whom
rested the honour and duty of maintaining
law and order, that is, to our Royal Ulster
Constabulary and to our Special Constabulary, assisted by the Forces of the Crown,
the military, where necessary. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) I can only state that the
relationship between the military forces and
ourselves has been most cordial throughout
somewhat trying times, and to-day is on a
better foundation than ever before.
It would, perhaps, be convenient for
the House if I say at once that the British
Government have treated us so generously
and fairly with regard to the coming
financial year that there will be no necessity
whatever to change the general scheme of
our Special Constabulary, to reduce in any
way their numbers, or to alter their pay.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) Consequently,
for another thirteen months we may relieve
our minds of the anxious question of ways
and means to meet that charge either upon
this Exchequer or the British Exchequer, as
it has now been settled definitely that the
British Exchequer will meet the cost of our
Specials for another twelve months. This is
the generous way they are treating us. Some
may say it is our right, but I would rather
say that the right is recognised by them so
generously that we look upon it rather as a
matter of the head of a family being kind
and good to one of his own children. Therefore, with that particular matter, one of
great anxiety to myself and to my colleagues,
set aside, we may look forward, I think, to
the coming year with the feeling that, while
the organisation if it requires improvement
will be improved, and if it requires tightening
up it will be tightened up, the general scheme
which was outlined by us two years ago, and
approved of by Field-Marshal Sir Henry
Wilson, still holds the ground. Therefore it
is possible, as I say, to give praise to those
men who have done such good work in the

Had we
I would like in this connection just to
couple up for a moment a remark that fell

I wish to pass from that to another point
to which my hon. Friend referred, and that
is the safety of the Border. There is nothing
so precious to us as the safety of the Border,
and he may rest assured that no alteration
in the number of troops in a certain locality,
or even their withdrawal from the Ulster
area, is done without-I will not say the
sanction of the Cabinet and myself, but
certainly it is never done without consultation and advice being given. There are, of
course, very many reasons why troops should
not be kept in Ulster more than is absolutely
necessary. As I have indicated on a former
occasion, we have now arranged a system
whereby the Borderland is absolutely safe
and secure, and the Imperial Government is
pledged to us that at a moment's notice, as
quickly as they produced the artillery on the
last occasion when it was required, any
troops that are necessary to take action upon
the Borderland will be offered to the Northern
Government as and when they are required.
I know well, of course, the disappointment
that is created when regiments are taken
away from localities within the Ulster Border.
The reason of that is all to the credit of the
Ulster people, because they love the troops,
and they like to see His Majesty's uniform
in their midst. (Hon. Members: "Hear,
hear."). But I have an assurance that every
attempt will be made to keep up the depots,
even of those specific regiments that are
taken away, that is to say, even if they
reduce the number of Imperial battalions
inside our area, the old depots will be
occupied and revived for the regiments which
they serve. I am at present in negotiation
with Lord Derby and the War Office on that
particular point, and I can only say that
they are most sympathetic, and are endeavouring to do their very best in this matter.
I have also, of course, as every member is
aware, a promise from Lord Derby that he
will come over here in April in order to
study this and many other problems on the
spot, and while he is here-and we can assure him of a right hearty welcome-we will
be able to go further into that matter and
others which are engaging the attention of
my colleagues and myself. But, as I say,
the safety of the Borderland is our first
thought. Without that nothing else can
proceed satisfactorily, and I am sure it was
with great pleasure that we all heard the
ringing cheers in the Ulster Hall yesterday--
spontaneous, not in any way organised; not
from one person, but from the whole body of
the people who were in the hall-when those
deputations came up from the outer parts
of our territory. (Hon. Members: liear,
hear). I think it was a great eye-opener if
I may say so to some members of the deputations, and it showed them that Ulster
was not that cold and selfish centre that
some of them were led to believe.
They went back satisfied with the
spontaneity of the audience that carried
comfort to their hearts in the outlying parts,
that if ever the necessity arose the great city
of Belfast and its loyal population were at
the beck and call of Clogher, Augher, or any
other of the outside parts of our dominions.
That is all part of the Ulster spirit-we are
one and undivided where the protection of
our territory is concerned. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.)

never heard the suggestion mentioned by anyone. After all. we have our own Ulster

praise a Bill which we have not yet read.
There is one factor, to me it is the greatest
factor, which I should like to point out to
the Government, if they wish to bring in
a Bill which is going to meet with the
greatest measure of approbation in this
democratic and intensely liberty-loving Ulster.
They ought to bring in a Bill that will cut
out all sectarian education whatever. They
ought to bring in a truly national system
of education. Let them bring in some
formula that will honour God and
acknowledge God in the school. Have
God acknowledged by the little children.
If any Church wishes to teach a dogma
let there be some facility by which that
Church may each that dogma, but the
teachers should not be made the servants
of any particular Church. We want a
system of education in Ulster that will be
truly national and truly democratic. I want
to suggest to the Prime Minister that the
great self-governing Colonies are looking on
Ulster to-day, and they believe that Ulster
is going to bring in the finest system of
education to be found in the United Kingdom. They have said so. They have been so
informed from the Old Country. I want you
to realise that the whole English speaking
world is looking on. The United States of
America are looking on. It is a fact that the
United States of America have a truly national system of education. They provide
only one school, and that school has the
American flag flying over it while in session.
In that way they have preserved the national spirit in America, but when we come
to this country what do we see? What has
been the curse of this country? It is because
you allow clerical dictation in education. You
segregate the children of one denomination
and keep them from sitting beside the children of another denomination. The little
tots dare not sit beside each other to be
taught the rudiments of education as little
neighbours together. If they cannot be
taught and brought up in the same schools
-itting at the same seats together, how will
they be good citizens together?
We have made Sinn Feiners in this
country. We have destroyed this country,
at least, Great Britain has, by the way she
has allowed this country to be run in the
matter of the control of education. I hope
the Government will not fall into the same
pit. I do not know what is in their Bill.
I am awaiting it with very great interest.
I did not get time to read the Lynn interim
report, but from what I hear of some things
in it I would not personally agree with them.
I hope these are being remedied in the Bill,
and that they are being remedied in the
right direction. We are awaiting a Bill
that will not satisfy any particular denomination, but will be truly national in all its
aspirations, and truly British in all its
history and outlook. That is what we want
here in Northern Ireland.

There is another matter I wish to deal with,

I regret that there is no mention in His

relegated to the position of being a mere
colony in the Six Counties. Imagine, Imperial Ulster a little bit of a colony, shown

it was exceedingly unfortunate when this

away our case. It was impossible then to

the House at the last meeting just prior to

British House of Commons.

such thing as the putting of Southern Ireland on a par with England and Scotland
after they had selected a form of Colonial
administration. These are matters which
have not been dealt with in the Gracious
Speech we have heard to-day. I regret it
very much, and the country will regret it.
There are other matters which have not
been mentioned, such as land purchase-the
remaining tenants and landlords. Will the
time never come when we will have this
matter cleared up once and for all, when
the pledges given by the late Government
will be given effect to, when the tenants will
not have a penalising rent charged, and the

Dr. MORRISON: I would like to say a
word or two with reference to the remarks
which have fallen from my hon. Friend tho
Member for Fermanagh and Tyrone (Mr.
Coote), with whom I must say I am very
often in agreement. I think in this case he
is rather rough on the Government, and that
he forgets that there are other people in this
House who are responsible for looking after
the interests of the farmers as well as the
Government. I think the Government may
have been a little remiss in connection with
this matter, but I am convinced that in
looking after the interests of Ulster they
were perfectly prepared and did everything
they thought possibly could be done. I think
also that the hon. Members who represent agricultural districts in this House, if they
thought that anything could be done to
strengthen the hands of the Government,
could easily have brought forward a motion,
or could have had a discussion in this House
on the motion for adjournment-(hon. Members: Hear, hear)-and that, in the first
place, before a man begins to find fault with
the Government he should say to himself,
"What have I done? Have I done
share? Have I pushed on the Government?
I regret to say that while I represent the
University I am also interested in agriculture,
and if I had thought that raising a discussion
in this House on the motion for adjournment
would have helped to prevent the gross injustice which has been inflicted upon the
farmers of Ulster by including them with
the Free State in this matter of the cattle
embargo I certainly would have done it, and
used all the forms of this House, and I
imagine I would have got the support of
every Member of this House in that matter.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) The hon.
Member for Fermanagh and Tyrone (Mr.
Coote) said some very hard things, but I
confess that I did not take them too
seriously, because I have found by coming
in contact with him, not in a public capacity,
but in a private capacity, that he is bubbling
over with the milk of human kindness. I,
therefore, beg that no one, particularly the
Minister of Agriculture, will feel hurt by
these somewhat severe references to the way
in which he discharged his duties. I think
it is extraordinary that we as a part of the
British Empire should have to submit to
be treated in the same way as the Free
State. I think on reconsideration the Imperial authorities will certainly remove that
grievance, and that the Prime Minister, who
has shown such admirable wisdom, discretion
and tact. will do all that is necessary to
have this injustice remedied for the farmers
of Ulster.
I want to raise one or two points in connection with some of the matters mentioned
in his Grace the Governor's Speech. I think
37 Debate on the Address.

27 FEBRUARY 1923.

the Prime Minister has not his opinion fully
consolidated as regards the form these Bills
are going to take. I would not say that his
opinions are altogether negative, but I think
they are not so solid that they might not
be influenced by the expressions of opinions
by Members of this House. There are some
points in connection with education which
I would lie to press, and which I hope will
not be overlooked in the Bill. The first is
one on which I have heard general agreement
during discussions in this House, and upon
which I have acted on deputations to the
Prime Minister, and that is the question
of the salaries of secondary teachers. An
interim grant was given to meet the desperate
condition in which they found themselves,
and I hope that beyond all controversy the
Bill will embody in clear and definite terms
a living wage for secondary teachers. With
regard to primary teachers, everybody, at
least a large number of people, are of opinion
that their salaries are too high. I think in
the present conditions that exist in Northern
Ireland they are possibly too high, but I think
that could be counteracted if we bring about
the amalgamation of schools and wipe out
a number of the unnecessary schools that
exist and which at present require the services of a highly paid teacher. I think if
reasonable steps are taken to get rid of these
unnecessary schools there will be no need to
reduce the salaries of our teachers. Again,
with regard to the matter of compulsory
attendance, I think it is vital. I had
experience as a dispensary doctor of these
people coming in for medical certicates. I had experience also as a member of a School Attendance Committee,
I know that as at present constituted the
School Attendance Committee in the Coleraine district, of which I am a member, is
an absolute fraud, and I say this, that if
you do not specify definitely and clearly the
fine that you are going to inflict upon parents
for neglecting this matter of attendance, the
whole thing will work out as a sham, and
a serious injustice will be done to the
children.
With regard to temperance reform, we
have three distinct pledges from the Government, and it is a curious thing-I always
thought it was a curious thing-that the
leader of the trade, in the many speeches
that he has made with regard to the position
that this Parliament has taken up in the
matter, says that no pledges were ever given
that temperance reform would be introduced
here during this first Parliament. I represent the University, and there are four
Members in that representation. I want
to say that those four Members are pledged
to support the three items in the programme
that the temperance party have put forward
here. Some of us would go further, but at
any rate we are thoroughly pledged to support those three items. Many other Members
are pledged-I think the great bulk of this
House is pledged--to temperance reform, and
I am glad to know that the Government are
going to introduce a Bill. I hope they will
fulfil all the pledges and promises that have
been made. I would go a little further.
Anybody who knows anything about the
conditions that prevail in this country at
present knows that poteen is being manufactured very largely all Over the Six
Counties. What happens is this: a case is
brought before the magistrates. There is
a statutory fine of £100 for breaches of the
law in this respect. The Bench fall in with
that. They inflict a fine of £100, and they
make a recommendation that the penalty
should be reduced to £15, £10 or £5. The whole
thing is a farce, and I do not see why the
Government should not introduce a clause
dealing with all breaches of the Licensing
Acts, and especially with the manufacture of
poteen. The Government should bring in a
clause that would compel these cases to be
tried by the resident magistrate and by him
alone.
There is one matter in connection with this
Speech that I regret exceedingly, and that
is that no attempt is being made to deal
with the very serious question of illegitimacy. Fifty years ago the British people had
some protection from the monstrous injustice
that was done to the morals of our Province.
The Prime Minister has always insisted that
we should go breast to breast with English
legislation, and that our people should have
all the advantages that they would have
possessed under the English law. It is two
years since this Parliament was established,
and I pointed out to the Government that
there are 3,000 illegitimate births in ireland
every year. I take it that 600 of these illegitimate births take place in Ulster, so that
in the two years we have had 1,200 girls who
have given birth to 1,200 children, and you
may take it from me that all the suffering,
all the pain, all the shame, and all the
pecuniary loss and trouble that this involves
are borne by the girls alone. The Government here have allowed two years to pass.
They are sitting twiddling their thumbs and
doing nothing, although the Minister of
Home Affairs promised in this House that the
matter would be seen to without delay. In
the interest of the girls of our land I protest against this unnecessary delay, and I
hope that the Government will take steps at
an early date to introduce a Bill similar to
the English Act, which gives protection to
girls who suffer in this way from the unprincipled blackguards who are going about
even in our rural districts.
That is all I have to say. I think that as
a House we should congratulate ourselves on
the peaceful state of the country, the orderly
progress that is being made, and on the skill,
management, prudence and discretion which

THE GOVERNOR'S ANSWER TO THE
ADDRESS.
The PRIME MINISTER (at the Bar)
reported the Answer to the Address from his
Grace the Governor of Northern Ireland as
followeth :
I have received with great satisfaction
the expression of your thanks for the
Speech with which I have opened the
present Session of Parliament.
The Orders of the Day were read and
postponed.
Motion for Adjournment.

two suggestions, not arising out of the Bills

House, but in view of the fact that it is

Session as a time of reconstruction. From
what I can gather the Government contemplate taking up schemes with a view to
relieving unemployment as far as possible.
I do not wish to go into the details of that

that the Government should consicer the
question of bringing into operation the Unemployment Relief Works Act of 1920.

LOCAL GOVERNMENT INSPECTORS.
Dr. MORRISON: There is one thing to
which I wish to direct attention. Perhaps
it is unreasonable to take up the time of
Ministers with regard to it, but it is an
important matter from my standpoint, and
from the standpoint of many other people,
and it has been before this House for fifteen
months. I have been doing what I can to
remedy a very serious grievance from my
viewpoint. The medical profession has been
agitating over this matter, they have passed
resolutions, they have appointed deputations,
they have petitioned, they have remonstrated
and supplicated, and at the end of fifteen
months we are no nearer a settlement. The
Minister of Home Affairs, I understand, has
to go away to attend to some function, and
I should be very reluctant to take up his
time. I could allow him to go with an
easy mind, because he is entirely of my way
of thinking, so far as I know, and in his
case it would be only forcing an open door.
If the Prime Minister feels called upon to
go to this function I would not ask even
him to wait because he is so broad, and
generous. Although I have never gone to
him I know that when he has this thing
brought before his notice he will say so and
so. The man I want to get at is the right
hon. the Minister of Finance (Mr. Pollock).
I do not know if I were approaching this
question and wanted a level-headed, clear
thinking and clear-seeing man, and a man
who would weigh the matter justly and
strictly. I could select a man in whom I
would have more confidence than the Minister of Finance, but in a curious way in this
matter he seems to have hardened his heart.
I am told this matter is under discussion.
but what I am afraid of is that you will
discuss the thing and that my right hon.
Friend the Minister of Home Affairs (Sir
Dawson Bates) wil! be over-ruled, and that
owing to the magnitude of the thing you
are about to decide you will give a decision
which you will find it hard to go back
That is why I raise the question
upon.

pay of the Local Government Inspectors.
You are starting two highly-qualified men
who should be, and who in this case are,
the pick of the medical profession in Belfast
at salaries of £500 a year.
Mr. McGUFFIN: Full time?
Dr. MORRISON: Full time at £500 a year

Dr. MORRISON: The pick of the medical
profession, men who have powers put into
their hands to deal with the most important
questions that can affect the whole community. They have control of the work-houses,
of all the dispensary districts, of the public
health in the urban and rural council areas,
and in connection indeed with all the public
health schemes, with schemes for venereal
diseases, with tuberculosis, with maternity.
with child-welfare, and with everything that
affects the public health in the Six Counties.
You start men on such important business,
with such very delicate matters in their
hands, picked men, at a salary of £500 a
year rising to £700. The Minister of Home
Affairs gave me an assurance that this
matter was under his consideration about a
year ago, and it has been under his consideration since, and we are no nearer
settlement. I have gone with deputations
representing the University to the Minister
of Home Affairs, and we have urged upon
him the necessity of increasing, and very
materially increasing, this salary. The
medical profession have been called together
and they have put a resolution on their
books specifying clearly and distinctly what
they think is due to these two Local Government Inspectors. It is a curious thing that
when you come to deal with the scale under
which these men are paid that the Scotch
scale has been chosen and not the English
scale. You adopt the English scale for all
indoor officers, which includes 90 per cent. of
your staffs, and these two men are paid under
the Scotch system, which is much lower.
Why is this distinction made? This matter
is going before the Minister of Finance, and
I think it is perhaps going to be discussed
by the Cabinet. It is a very small thing,
the difference between what is paid these
men and what the medical profession and the
medical representatives in this House think
is sufficient. It is a very small thing,
and why should you wrangle over what is,
after all, a two-pence-halfpenny-matter-a
matter of £400 or £500 at the outside? When
you consider the magnitude of the work that
these men are doing to-dav and the fact

Mr. ROBB: I would like to suggest to the
Government the consideration of one matter,
and that is the institution of a Public
Trustee in our Northern area. The Public
Trustee was initiated and established in
England by the Public Trustee Act, 1906, and
it has been decided in the Courts in Ireland
that that Act does not apply to Ireland, and
that the Public Trustee in England cannot
he appointed trustee of Irish funds. The
Public Trustee in England has been found
to be an unmitigated benefit, and I may say
that personally I myself am aware of the
necessity for such an officer in this area.
From inquiries among various members of
the legal profession I have their entire
assent for suggesting to the Government the
desirability of creating such an office in
this area. It is not a matter that should
cause the Government very much hesitation
because as a matter of fact the Public
Trustee in England pays for himself. A
small percentage is charged upon the turnover of the income of each trust estate, and
that more than covers the total cost of the
institution of the Public Trustee. It has
been found there to be a benefit, and I think
we here should find it to be a great benefit,
and it certainly is a necessity, for the members of the legal profession are crying out at
present.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr. Andrews): I would like to say at the outset of
the remarks which I feel I ought to make
to-day that I appreciate very much the way
in which my hon. Friend the Member for
East Belfast (Mr. Donald) has raised the
question of unemployment, and I think it will
interest the House to know something of
what the Government are doing for our unemployed people, with whom we have the very
greatest possible sympathy, I am right, I
believe, in saying that no Government in the
world is doing so much in this direction
as our Northern Government, and we know
that in doing so we have behind us the
support of every Member of this House. In
the first place, we are paying unemployment
benefit to about 50,000 of our unemployed
persons. I am sorry, as everyone is sorry,
that the number is still so large, but hon.
Members will remember that when we took
over the reins of office here unemployment
was at its peak and approximately 100,000
of our people were either totally unemployed
or were on what is known as systematic short
time, so that roughly speaking the numbers
have been reduced by about one-half. Of
course, the payment of these weekly sums
has been a tremendous drain upon the funds
of our Exchequer. I think it will interest
hon. Members to know how this money is
raised. I have here the figures for the

My hon. Friend the Member for East Belfast

with that very Ministry are paid at a much
higher rate.

passed, at any rate two, and I think three,
schemes with which they are at liberty to
proceed at once, and for which, acting on
behalf of the Government, I have guaranteed
sixty per cent. of the labour cost. Of course
if the Local Authorities will not start to pull
their weight in this matter, and if they leave
the bricklayers unemployed and employment
can be found for them in Belfast, it is necessary, I think, that they should be brought to
Belfast. But I think Ballymena must be the
exception to the rule, because, speaking for the
Local Authorities generally throughout the
Six Counties, I have pleasure in stating that
they have shown great anxiety to co-operate
with the Government in this matter and take
their share in finding employment for our
people.

Mr. CRAWFORD: Do I understand the
right hon. Gentleman (Mr. Andrews) to say

of the sort. The delay is due entirely to what

which is ready for them if they would come

Mr. POLLOCK: I very much regret that I
must join issue with my hon. Friends who
have raised the question of the salaries of
certain officers in the employment of the Home
Department, and as my right hon. Friend, the
Minister of Home Affairs, is engaged elsewhere
I take it upon myself to reply on his behalf.
I join issue with my hon. Friends on two
grounds. The first is general, and the second
is particular. On the ground of general
economy I object to an increase of the salaries
of any officials at the present time, except
those who are inadequately provided for by
increments. If a question similar to that
which has been addressed to me were put to
the Finance Minister in the Imperial Parliament, the reply would be, "We cannot afford
it. The country is too poor." We, being a
part of the United Kingdom, and labouring
under exactly the same conditions as those
existing in Great Britain, must necessarily
act in a manner that at least bears some relation to the position in Great Britain, because
in respect to the contribution which we make
to the Imperial Services we are responsible
for our expenditure here to the Imperial
Treasury. That is the general ground upon
which I object to any considerable increase
in the cost of establishment. The particular
ground upon which I object is this: that my
hon. Friends failed to inform the House that
although the salary starts at £500 a year the
increments go on by £50 yearly, and at the
present time the officers in question have
salaries of £600 a year and bonus, which I
cannot accurately estimate, but which must
be between £200 and £300 a year. I do not
decry their services in the slightest, because
I do not know who they are. I am quite sure,
however, from what my hon. Friend, the
Member for the University, has said, that
they are fully efficient officers, but I cannot
admit that a salary of between £800 and
£900, which will rise automatically to about
£1,000 a year, is not sufficient for a permanent
Civil Service position which qualifies for pension at no very distant period in the case of
the two gentlemen concerned. That is the reply
I have very regretfully to make to my hon.
Friends. At the present time, under the unfortunate conditions in which we in the North
of Ireland find ourselves-conditions of unemployment, and conditions which are apparent
to the whole community and which I need not
Adjournment.
Adjournment.
28 FEBRUARY 1923.
emphasise-economy is so essential that it is
part of my business and my very unpleasant
duty to have to consider applications of a
similar nature day by day, and if I acceded
to them it would place us in a position of
financial embarrassment I cannot afford to
contemplate with equanimity.
In regard to the matter mentioned by the
hon. and learned Member for the University
(Mr. Robb), with regard to the appointment
of a Public Trustee, I must say that I sympathise very much with his ambition, and curiously enough I have had it in my mind for a
considerable time to investigate the necessity
of the establishment of such an official. There
can be no question of the accuracy of my hon.
and learned Friend's statement that the position has been an unqualified success in Great
Britain. I think the funds entrusted to the
Public Trustee amount to something between
£150,000,000 and £200,000,000, which gives one
an idea of the importance of the Public
Trustee. Our area is small, but at the same
time I think it would be an advantage to
persons who have difficulty in discovering
executors or trustees that they should have a
public official who would be responsible for
the conduct of trusts where it was impossible
for persons to secure the services of personal
friends who would undertake that work. I
cannot, of course, give any undertaking of any
immediate establishment of such a Department, but I can say at any rate that so far as
I am concerned I approach the matter very
sympathetically, and will have the whole subject investigated.

£1,200 rising to £1,500; that these men have no
