EX-SERVICEMEN'S COTTAGES.
Mr. DONALD asked the Minister of Home
Affairs, (a) if he can state the conditions
under the Irish Free State (Consequential
Provisions) Act, 1922, for the building of
ex-Servicemen's cottages; (b) what sum of
money is provided for this purpose; and (c)
what steps are being taken to further this
scheme in order to give employment?
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): Section 3 of the Act
referred to by the hon. Member provides for
the establishment of a Trust for the provision of cottages, etc., for ex-Servicemen in
Ireland.
(a) This Trust is to consist of 5 members, 3
appointed by the Imperial Government, one
by the President of the Executive Council of
the Free State, and one by the Prime
Minister of Northern Ireland.
In that Trust is to be vested all the
powers conferred on the Local Government
Board for Ireland under the Irish Land
(Provision for Sailors and Soldiers) Act, 1919,
regarding the provision of cottages for ex-
Servicemen. All the property, assets, rights
and liabilities of that Board are to be trans-
Written Answers.
Canals Bill.
13 MARCH 1923.
ferred to the Trust, and the Trust is to carry
out their powers and duties in accordance
with Regulations to be made by the Imperial
Treasury.
In order to enable the Trust to acquire
the necessary lands in Northern and Southern Ireland it is provided by sub-Section 7
of the section referred to above that the
establishment of the Trust shall not be
effective until the Legislatures of the two
areas have passed the necessary legislation
enabling the Trust to acquire and hold land
in the respective areas.
(b) In order to enable the Trust to carry
out its undertakings the Section provides that
the Imperial Parliament shall vote a sum
not exceeding £1,500,000 to be applied by
the Trust for the purpose for which it is
created.
(e) As the hon. Member is aware, a Bil

for the first time in another place on 28th

are now
Mr. DONALD asked the Minister of Home
Affairs how many of the 1,046 ex-Servicemen's
cottages, under the Irish Land (Provision for
Sailors and Soldiers) Act, 1919,
erected and occupied in Northern Ireland,
and whether sites have yet been acquired for
the 96 cottages allotted for Belfast, and, if so,
where they are.
Sir DAWSON BATES: Of the 1,046 cottages
allotted to Northern Ireland 225 have been
completed. Of these, 207 are occupied, and
the Ministry are taking steps to secure ex-
Servicemen as tenants for the remaining 18.
It is hoped that a further number of 19
cottages will be available for occupation at
Randalstown shortly; also that it will be
possible to install at a very early date, tenants
in the remaining 45 cottages which will be
available at Glengormley and Whiteabbey.
As stated by the hon. Member, 96 cottages
had been provisionally allocated to the City
of Belfast by the Local Government Board,
Dublin, and sites had been selected at various
places, including sites at Springfield Road,
Whiterock Road, Skegoniel Avenue, Serpentine Road, and Cregagh, but it would appear
that difficulties in regard to development,
water supply, etc., prevented the Local
Government Board from proceeding with
these schemes.
new
On the transfer of the service in July last
the functions of the Government of Northern
Ireland were restricted to proceeding with
existing building operations, and power was
not given to enter into
contracts.
Accordingly, it has not been possible, in the
meantime, to proceed with schemes on these
sites, and the Ministry of Home Affairs have
had to confine their attention to endeavouring
to clear up the difficulties that had arisen
in order that, when the administration is
placed on a definite basis, it would be possible
to proceed at once with the building.
In the meantime, however, the Ministry of
Home Affairs and the Ministry of Finance
are proceeding as actively as possible with
the Glengormley and Whiteabbey schemes and
are accommodating a considerable proportion
of Belfast applicants in these houses.

Canals (Continuance of Charging
Powers) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed, “That
the Bill be now read a Second time."
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY TO
THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE (Mr.
M'KEOWN): In moving the Second Reading
of this Bill, I should perhaps explain that
under the provisions of the Ministry of Transport Act, 1919, the Minister of Transport was
empowered to take over possession of canals,
and to order an increase of their tolls, dues,
and charges. He exercised his powers with
respect to the Newry Canal, and also the
Lagan Canal, with which the Ulster Canal
and the Coalisland Canal are associated, and
ordered in each case an increase of 150 per
cent. of their tolls, dues, and charges.
statutory authority for these increased charges
requires to be renewed for a further period,
and that is why this Bill is now before you.
A similar Bill, I may say, was submitted to
and passed by the Imperial Parliament last
autumn, but that Act does not apply to Northern Ireland.
The
With regard to the necessity for the Bill,
the Ministry of Commerce has been in communication with the canal authorities in
Northern Ireland, who state that they will
be unable to carry on their undertakings unless the increased charges sanctioned by the
Minister of Transport are continued, and their
statements are supported by their accounts.
The Bill is designed to continue the increased
charges up to the 15th February, 1925, subject.
however, to the power provided in the Bill
for the Ministry of Commerce to order a reduction of such charges if and when they are
proved to be excessive, and the Bill limits
any revision of charges upwards to the maximum represented by the charges in operation
on 15th February, 1923.
That is the reason that we have brought
this Bill before the House to-day. It is to
give us the same powers as have been obtained
by the Imperial Parliament, and also, I believe, by the Free State Government. I am
sure that the House will be quite satisfied
E

object to the hon. and learned Member (Mr.

I never made any such suggestion. I never

Mr. ROBB: I regret if I have misrepresented anything the hon. Member (Mr. Lynn)
has said, but the impression left on my mind
by the speeches made heretofore was that it
was the opinion of hon. Members of this
House that the Bill continued control in the
Ministry of Commerce over waterways in
Northern Ieland which was existing at the
present moment. What the Bill says is that
in the case of paticular undertakings, by
way of inland navigation, certain charging
powers-which are the charging powers of the
companies running these undertakings-shall
be continued until 1925, and shall not cease
at the date on which under the earlier Act
they would have ceased.
Mr. McGUFFIN: Is not that control?
Mr. ROBB: The only power of control in
the hands of the Ministry of Commerce is
to permit a revision of rates in a downward
direction after representations convincing the
Ministry that such reduction is justified have
been made to them. Sub-Section (2) of
Section 1 is the one that deals with the
power of the Ministry of Commerce in
Northern Ireland, and what it says is that,
while these companies have these extended
powers of charging higher rates,
"If at any time during the continuance
under this Act of the powers of making
charges so directed as aforesaid it appears
to the Ministry of Commerce for Northern
Ireland (in this Act referred to as "the
Ministry") that owing to changes in the
cost of labour and materials or other
circumstances affecting a canal or inland
navigation undertaking, of which possession was so retained or taken as aforesaid,
the powers of charging are excessive or
insufficient, the Ministry may make an
order revising the powers of charging, so
however that the revised maximum charges
shall not, in the case of any undertaking,
be less than the maximum charges authorised by any statutory provision in force
immediately before the directions of the
Minister of Transport relating to the
charges of that undertaking were originally
issued, or more than the charges which the
undertakers were entitled to make on the
fifteenth day of February, nineteen hundred and twenty-three."
So that what the Ministry of Commerce is
to do is to listen to representations that may
be made to them that the charges are either
too great or are too small. If the charges
are too great the Ministry of Commerce may
order them to be lowered. If the charges
are too small they may permit an increase
but they are not to permit an increase
above the maximum which is legal at the
present time. It seems to me that the power
vested in the Ministry of Commerce is not
an unreasonable power to be given to them,
and I am prepared to support the Second
reading of the Bill.

actually or really understood the position.
It was implied undoubtedly that it was the
intention of the Ministry of Commerce to
do something which would enable them to increase to a very considerable extent these
charges. That, as has been pointed out by
my hon. and learned Friend (Mr. Robb), is
not at all the case. These companies in connection with the canals have been going on,
and under the Ministry of Transport Act
they were enabled to increase the charges at
a time when it was absolutely necessary.
They can co
come to the Ministry of Commerce
and can put up a case, and after we have
examined that case--and we have examined
the case we have power to reduce or to
increase, within a certain limit, which is
legally defined, as has been pointed out by
my hon. and learned Friend (Mr. Robb).
That is actually the position the Ministry
of Commerce occupies. With regard to the
canals generally, I quite agree with the
observations that have been made by some
of my hon. Friends. I quite agree that in
all probability sufficient use has not been
made of our canal systems, but hon. Members must remember that very little opportunity has yet occurred for the Government
of Northern Ireland to make these changes.
We have proposed now to set up a Royal
Commission which will inquire into the industrial position in Northern Ireland with a
view to making the best use of everything
that would tend to the prosperity of the
Province. Canals, undoubtedly, will come
under the observation of that Commission.
Mr. McGUFFIN: Why not wait for their
report:
Mr. M'KEOWN: I can honestly say with
regard to the attitude of the Ministry of
Commerce towards this matter that, as far
as it is possible, it will use all its power not
only towards the development of the canals
but towards the development of everything
that would tend to the prosperity of the
Northern Province. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.)

THE MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(SIR DAWSON BATES): This Bill is
identical with the Criminal Law Amendment
Act which was passed last year in the
Imperial House of Commons, with
important difference which I propose to refer to afterwards. This Bill is brought
forward to meet the wishes and desires of
all those who take an interest in the welfare
and the morals of the young. It marks a further stage in the progress that has been
made for some years past in providing more
effective means of protecting young girls and
punishing the guilty. The Bill which is
analogous to this one, and which received
the Royal Assent last year in the Imperial
House, met with a good deal of what I may
call unreasonable opposition, and it was only
after a third Bill of the character was introduced that it ultimately became law. The
only reason I can imagine why it did receive
this opposition was perhaps not so much the
hostility which every new Bill which is brought
forward to alter the criminal law evokes, but
I think it was rather the opposition of
a certain section of the public which seemed
to be more anxious to protect the criminal
than to protect the innocent. After
all, this Bill only extends the principle laid
down by the various Acts which have been
passed dealing with this particular matter.
I feel assured that the public of Northern
Ireland are just as jealous of the morals of
the young as our fellow citizens in Great
Britain. (Hon Members: Hear, hear).
Clause 1 provides that where a young
person under the age of 16 is indecently
assaulted the consent of that child who was
so assaulted shall be no defence on the part
of the person accused. Under the Act of
1880 a similar provision exists, but in that
case it is limited to the age of 13. Experience
has shown, I think hon. Members will agree
with me, that it is essential that the age
should be increased from 13 to 16. I think it
is perfectly ludicrous that a criminal could
plead that a child of 13 and under had given
her consent to a criminal assault.
With regard to Clause 2 of the Bill, under
the Criminal Law Amendment Act of 1885,
which is more familiarly known as Stead's
Act, it is provided that it should be a
eriminal offence for any male person to have
carnal knowledge of a girl under 16, but a
proviso was inserted in which the accused
person could plead as a defence that he had
reasonable grounds for believing the girl was
over that age. Clause 2 of this Bill proposes
to do away with that defence. It also proposes to allow a charge of this sort to be
brought forward within a period of nine
months from the date on which the offence
was committed. Previous to that such a
charge had to be brought forward within a
period of six months. Many arguments could
be adduced to justify the proposed alteration
of the law, but I think hon. Members will
agree there can be very few arguments
against it. It has been found in practice
that this defence of a reasonable belief that
the girl was over the age of 16 led to many
It
glaring cases of miscarriage of justice.
may be said that a girl very often looks over
16 and that the result of making this alteration in the law might lead to innocent men
being convicted, and that it might also lead
to cases of blackmail arising. My answer is
this, that if innocent people choose to take
this method of sowing their wild oats they
may take the risk. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear). Far better they should get into
trouble and be convicted than that young
girls of the age of 16 and under who leave
their mothers' homes and perhaps enter into
a business career should be debauched and
ruined by these young fellows sowing their
wild oats. If young fellows knew the risk
they run of becoming criminals I think they
would act more cautiously towards the other
sex, particularly the young.
There is one point more to which I wish to
draw the attention of the House, and that is
in the recent English Act there is one exception. It allowed a man of 23 and under
who had never committed an offence of this
character before to plead that he believed
the girl was over the age of 16. I cannot
see any merits in this defence. I see a
great many difficulties. The insertion of
this particular Clause in the English Act was
the result of a compromise, and like very
many compromises it often leads people into
difficulties. I am advised that this particular Clause will give rise to many difficulties in the future in the administration
of the Act in England. I will tell you why.
If a young fellow of under 23 is tried for
an offence of this character and does not
plead that he had reasonable ground for
believing the girl was 16 it must be perfectly
obvious to the jury that he had committed
such an offence before. Therefore it violates
the law under which the jury are not allowed
to know whether a man has ever committed
an offence before. We are not hide-bound to
overy alteration of the law in England, and
I do suggest that this is a case in which this
House would be thoroughly justified in not
following this particular example so far as
England is concerned. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.)

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Clause 3 speaks for itself. We propose in
that Clause to increase the penalties for
keeping brothels up to three months' imprisonment or a fine of £100 for a first
offence, and for a second or subsequent
offence to a fine not exceeding £250 or imprisonment for six months.
With regard to Clause 4, charges of incest
are always tried in camera. We propose to
do away with that. I do not see why cases
of this sort should not be heard in public.
The object of trying cases in public is to
let the public see that such cases do exist
and to let the public know what penalty
must follow. It is suggested that the young
should not know anything about this sort
of case. I do not agree with that. I have
sufficient belief in the Press, at all events
in the Press of the North of Ireland, to
know it will not insert anything that might
lead to any damage being done to the minds
of the young. Another very strong argument
I have for putting forward this particular
proposal is that the judges are very strongly
in its favour. I beg to move.

three months in jail for one of these detestable pests-one of the worst pests that society
could have is to my mind an absolute

it, I at least will propose that whipping be
added to the fine or to the imprisonment.
Sir DAWSON BATES: What about women?

for a man. If we use the "cat" on those

"cat" on those who try to destroy what is

very

dark picture, but if you
below the surface you will also find a compensatory picture that helps to relieve it.
I think that in the Malone Home, which is

you will find a redeeming feature. It is

which places the limit of time after the

Mr. HANNA: With the object of the Bill

Mr. McGUFFIN: The present Bill marks

With regard to Clause 2, where it is proposed to deal with the excuse that is
frequently raised by an accused person-tha'

The only argument raised against the measure in the British House of Commons which
ever appealed to me was that of blackmail,
but my mind in respect of that matter was
absolutely set at rest by the testimony of Sir
Donald Maclean, who said that out of 200
cases he had privately conducted he had
never found one where blackmail was alleged.
That is a most important statement on the
part of a man who has had such a wide
experience. He testified that blackmail
played a very small part in the cases that
came before the Courts. To put forward the
case against this Bill that it was a pure
matter of education, and cannot be cured by
threats or penalties, and that if we did away
with all law with regard to sex we should
breed the very same class of persons as we do
to-day, I regard as absolutely ridiculous. The
answer to that is this. If we cannot
exterminate crime, it is no reason why we
should not try to restrain it, and moreover,
to adopt that attitude with regard to that
matter would justify us in taking a similar
attitude with regard to all crime.
They say that as a man becomes more
educated he will be less criminal. I have
only to refer the Minister of Home Affairs to
some great men in English literature to convince him that that is not true. We have men
of culture who have been sadly immoral, and
we have only to refer to our Divorce Courts
to find that it is not the common people who
provide the class that go before these Courts.
I am of opinion that we should do all we can
to prevent the expansion of this evil, and I
feel that the Bill now introduced is calculated
to do so.

brought in by a private Member, and he put
up such a good case at that time that he
divided the Committee and there was an equal
vote. He persisted in his case and it was
further brought before the House and received the Government support, with the
result that it was brought in as a Government
Bill. I congratulate my right hon. Friend on
bringing it up here. We all welcome it. The
matter of the protection of children goes back
a long way. For a great many years this
question has been under the consideration of
different Governments, and amendments have
been introduced time and again as regards
the matter of ages and punishments The
age was increased from ten years to twelve,
then to fourteen, and I am glad to say we are
living in a time when we will extend the age
to sixteen years. Like the hon. Member for
Derry (Mrs. Chichester) I think we should be
satisfied to let this Bill go through with the
age at sixteen years. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) Personally, I will support that clause
so far as the age is concerned. The effect of
bringing in this Bill for young girls is to ask
girls to support the legislation of this House.
As regards Clause 3, my hon. Friend for
West Belfast (Mr. Lynn) said something about
the penalties. I think the penalty is a very
severe one. Some advancement has been
made in that direction too. My right hon.
Friend will correct me if I am wrong, but I
think under section 13 of the original Act the
penalty for brothel keepers was £20 and three
months imprisonment for the first offence, and
£10 and four months imprisonment for the
second offence, but when you raise that to
£100 and three months for the first offence,
and £250 and six months for the second
offence. I think there is a wide difference. I
am also in agreement that the Bill should be
passed in its present form with regard to the
penalty. This Bill is only assimilating the
enactment passed in another place. At the
same time my right hon. Friend has made
some alteration, and I am in agreement with
previous speakers that cases of this description should certainly be held in camera.
Although I am not a lawyer, I have taken a
special interest in courts. I have attended
the courts and listened to the cases heard, and
I think it would be a crime to put a young
girl in the witness box in the open court and
have matters of this description discussed.
With these few remarks I wish to support the
Bill. I hope that the Bill will go through
with that modification in Clause 4. I hope
my right hon. Friend will make that alteration in Clause 4 and let the Bill go through.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY TO
THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS (Mr.
Megaw) Rising on behalf of the Government to deal with some of the criticisms that
have been made with regard to this Bill let
me say in the first place how the Government
welcome the criticisms that have been offered
from all sides in the House, because the Government feel that the House appreciate the
motive that has brought about their introduction of this measure. (Hon. Members :
Hear, hear). As my right hon. Friend the
Minister of Home Affairs (Sir Dawson Bates)
said in introducing the Bill the idea of the
Bill was to assimilate the law in this
country with the law in England. We feel
that so far as the criminal law is concerned
and so far as a good many other legislative
enactments are concerned it is a good thing
to keep pace with England. There is one
particular factor that has got to be regarded
in this, that is with respect to the administration of law-the great difficulty that we
have as a small community of having our legislative enactments different from what they
are on the other side. It means that different
law books must be prepared, and considering
the very small area we have got to deal with
that is not an easy matter in itself. Of
course, it is merely an administrative difficulty, and it is one that can oe got over.
One of the first criticisms offered on the
Bill was by the hon. Member for West Belfast (Mr. Lynn) who objected to some extent
to the penalties that were introduced in the
Bill. I think I am right in my recollection
that the hon. Gentleman recommended that
for the shocking crime of keeping brothels the
punishment of flogging should be applicable.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear). It is a very
easy thing for this House to pass measures
Criminal Law Bill-
Second Reading.
13 MARCH 1923.
indicating that certain punishments sho
be given, but it is a very difficult thing to get
judges to put those punishments in operation.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear). I would just
call the hon. Member's attention to what was
done in the Children's Act. With a view to
keeping boys out of temptation the
English Legislature in Westminster passed
the Children's Act, which imposed a penalty
on the vendors of tobacco for selling
cigarettes to children. These enactments
have become practically a dead letter. You
have got by your legislation to see how far you
keep in touch with the feeling of the community. I agree with my hon. Friend that
no punishment is too great for the horrid
business of keeping brothels. One must
recognise the damage that it does to the community, but one has got to deal with the
ordinary feeling of the community, and I do
not think that that feeling would permit of
the flogging of a woman, even for such a degraded occupation as keeping a brothel.
What I have said in regard to punishments
applies, I think, to punishments generally.
The punishments that have been suggested
by this Bill are the punishments that have
been enacted in the Act in England, and I
doubt very much whether there could be anything gained by putting in anything more
severe than what has been already enacted in
the Act on the other side. If those penalties
were inflicted by the judges in many cases it
certainly would, I think, have a very strong
effect in putting down the evils that have
been aimed at in the Bill,
I listened with considerable interest to the
criticism of my hon. Friend the Member for
the University (Dr. Morrison) with regard to
the time at which proceedings might be
taken. We shall consider the matter before
the Committee stage and see what can be
done about that matter. Of course, hon.
Members must recollect that this has been
very carefully considered on every side. We
are not bound, as the right hon. Gentleman
said in introducing this Bill, to slavishly
follow the example set in England. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) We shall certainly
have regard to the expressions of opinion
that have been given by Members of this
House.
There was one provision in the Bill that
seems to be unanimously approved, that is
Clause 4. dealing with the crime of incest.
It is not altogether so clear a matter as it
might seem to be from the unanimity of
opinion. I am not at all sure myself as to
whether it is not a proper thing that society
generally should know what incest actually
means. Within the last week, I am sorry to
say, I have had an unpleasant experience on
this very point. At the last Armagh Assizes
there was a shocking case of this kind. The
details of it were revolting almost in every
particular. It concerned two young girls, one
of whom was absolutely ruined by her own
father. The case, when it came on for trial,
happily did not last long, because the
poor wretch who was in the dock pleaded
guilty, and it was not necessary to swear a
jury. The Court was absolutely cleared,
except the policemen in charge and the man
in the dock. No word of any kind appeared in
the newspapers regarding the case. So far as
I could see there was no suggestion that such
a thing as incest has been possible or has
existed in the North of Ireland. I am not at
all sure that if it had been known, or if there
was a little more publicity with regard to it,
the poor girls who were involved might have
known a little more and had a little more
knowledge of what might have been useful to
them when the temptation came to them in
the way it did come.
I am told by my right hon. Friend (Sir
Dawson Bates) that there have been five cases
of this kind in Belfast during the last year.
I was not aware up to this that there had been
anything like that number. Certainly the
one experience I have had, which is so fresh
to me at present, has been one that is a very
saddening thing indeed. With regard to the
age limit the suggestions that have been
made on the other side will be carefully considered, but I doubt very much whether we
could stand over increasing the age from 16
to 18 years or anything like that. A very
considerable advance has been made in bringing the age to 16, and I think it would be
well, for the present, to see what the result
of that may be and whether any good is
likely to be obtained by increasing the age.
When the Committee stage comes we shall
consider and see what can be done in all these
matters.
I am glad to see that the efforts of the
Government in this respect have been appreciated, and that we shall be backed up in doing
what we are doing-to introduce a much
needed reform in our community.

one bit too much by raising the age to 18.

Government is that it is going to create a
State second to none, and surely to patience
the best thing to do is to go as far as we

and innocent women of our country. I commend heartily the Government for bringing

MINISTRY OF FINANCE.
Motion made, and Question proposed.
"That a supplementary sum, not exceeding

to defray the expenses of the Ministry of

The PARLIAMENTARY AND FINAN-
CIAL SECRETARY TO THE MINISTRY
OF FINANCE (Mr. Barbour): Possibly before dealing in detail with the different
classes of the Estimates now submitted, it
might be of interest to hon. Members if I
made a few remarks applying generally to
the Estimates which are now being brought
forward. In the first place I should not like
hon. Members to assume that the mere fact
that Supplementary Estimates are now being
brought forward is any indication that our
anticipated expenditure when the original
Estimates were introduced in this House has
in any way been exceeded. I am glad to be
able to give them the assurance that very
considerable economies, savings as they are
usually termed, have been effected. Some of
these are due to real economy, some are due
to expenditure which was contemplated
earlier in the year, but which from one cause
or another may have been deferred, and other
savings are due, may be, to purely fortuitous
circumstances. But in any case the
total of these savings would be sufficient
to meet many times over the total
amount of the Estimate which is now presented to you. Hon. Members will, of course.
understand that it is quite within the province and discretion of the Ministry of
Finance to utilise savings on any sub-head
within a Vote to meet a shortage on another
sub-head, so long as that other sub-head is of
such a character as has already been duly
authorised and sanctioned by Parliament, but
when the expenditure assumes a different
character, or takes place in another Vote, and
where the character of it has not received
such sanction, we are bound to call that expenditure to the attention of Parliament and
to ask for its authority and the necessary
Vote.
Another assurance which I am sure hon.
Members will be glad to receive is that
although the total of these Supplementary
Estimates amounts to over £44,000, the read
new expenditure involved in these is a very
much smaller figure. The amount is built up
partly by statutory obligations. I will
illustrate the matter by taking one case,
Grants to Local Authorities. Of the amount
named, £11,440 consists of subsidy to private
builders. This is an expenditure to which we
were committed, and expected to have to
meet, during the financial year of 1921-22, but,
as a matter of fact, the persons to whom this
subsidy was payable had not qualified for this
payment during that year, so that it had to
be amended accordingly and pushed forward
into the current year. Once again, under the
head of Grants to Local Authorities in respect
of labourers cottages, there is an expenditure
of some £7,000, which arises entirely from the
difference in the method of keeping accounts.

There is a small increase in stationery.

The remaining part of the estimate of the
Ministry of Finance, which I will go into more
particularly later on, is due to an increase in

with interest the reductions which are being
made almost daily in the Estimates submitted to the Imperial House at Westminster.
I hope hon. Members of this House will not
think that the conditions here are such as
would permit of any parallel being drawn
between the action being taken in Westminster and what necessarily has to be followed here. They will remember that, at the
time the Government of this Province was
entrusted to us, the Imperial House and the
organisations of the Imperial services were
just at the termination of a world-shaking
war during which nearly every Department
of the public service had to be extended and
inceased to the very utmost capacity of the
nation. The need for their existence had just
then begun to fall away. We were fully conscious of that, and were anxious to set up
our establishments over here on the most
modest and economical scale, SO that
there would be no unnecessary expenditure or no unnecessary inflation of staff to
cut down as the necessity for economy became
more pressing. Consequently it would
appear that the staff as we had originally
designed it in all the different Departments
had been rather closely estimated. It might
have been sufficient to carry on the services
had those services remained exactly as they
were in our minds when this original establishment was contemplated; but since then
various arrangements have been made with
the Imperial Government whereby we have
taken over various services for the Imperial
Government. We look after the upkeep of
the buildings and the property of the
Imperial Government, also the reserved
services, and we have to carry on our own
staff, the technical officers necessary to do
that work. Of course such services as we
cairy on for the Imperial Government are
paid for by them to us. In my own opinion,
so far from our having any excessive staff
at the present moment, I consider that our
services are being carried on with very great
economy, and I do hope in whatever criticism
may be made by hon. Members they will be
very careful not to show in any way any
lack of appreciation of the very earnest hard
work being given at the present time by the
members of the Civil Service of Northern
Ireland They do not spare themselves, and
it is a great pleasure to hear on more than
one occasion appreciation expressed of the
support and good service they are rendering
to the community in their various capacities.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)

in the Cabinet and to the very few whose

There are many

Written Answer to Question.
COST OF PARLIAMENTARY AND
STATIONERY OFFICE PUBLICATIONS.
Mr. DONALD asked the Minister of
Finance if he could state the reasons for the
high cost of Parliamentary and Stationery
Office publications; how are the costs arrived
at, and whether costs have not fallen
sufficiently to justify a roduction in the price
of this class of publication?
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): The printing of Parliamentary and
Stationery Office publications is carried out
under contracts whose terms compare favourably with the current costs of printing. In
arriving at the price of Parliamentary and
Stationery Office publications, the normal procedure is to take the total cost of printing
each publication, after making adjustments in
respect of departmental and sales agents'
harges, and then divide this sum by the
rumber of copies printed. With a few exceptions, where the balance loss on production is
borne on the Stationery and Printing Votes,
e.g., Report of Parliamentary Debates, the
resulting price is charged for each copy of
the particular publication. The price, therefore, normally depends directly upon the cost
of production, and the number of copies produced, so that if production costs fall, the
price also falls. It is possible that prices
seem unduly high as compared with commercial and literary publications, on account
of the comparatively small number of copies
of Government publications necessary, while
the initial cost is not correspondingly
diminished by this factor.

the health and welfare of school children and

employment of school teachers and for

The MINISTER OF EDUCATION (The
Marquess of Londonderry) who was received
the
with general cheers: I must ask

I am mainly responsible. May I be allowed

been accorded to me, a stranger in the Parliamentary sense, but I am glad to think not a

Hear, hear). I ask your indulgence not, I
regret to say, on account of youth or lack

but by reason of the fact that I am not a
member of this House of our young but important Parliament, and that I am undertaking a task in which many of my predecessors have failed to achieve an unqualified
success. I suppose more Ministers of Education have brooded over their failures than
gloried in their successes, and none, so far
as I am aware, have received universal congratulations on the product of their industry.
Be that as it may, I venture to present to
you our long promised Education Bill, with
personal diffidence it is true because I cannot claim either supernatural gifts, or even

that the offer of this measure of self-government has been made and accepted, it is inconceivable that we should fall below that

right to expect. It is well within your recollection here that the Ministry of Education
was set up simultaneously with the other

inherited from the National Commissioners,

the Six Counties--I should like hon. Members to appreciate that that is a very long
step from what we have been accustomed to--
the problem naturally arose as to the nature
of that local authority; as to which, if any,
of our existing local authorities could
Education Bill-

HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Marquess of Londonderry].
exercise the requisite powers; and if no such
local authority existed, what bodies could we
set up effectively to discharge the necessary
duties.
The Local Education Authority must
obviously be a very important body. Should
that body be elected or should it be
nominated? After the fullest consideration,
we have decided to make the County
Borough Councils and the County Councils
the Education Authorities, and to give the
County Councils the duty to set up within
their areas what we have called for want
of a better name Regional Committees.
These Committees follow generally the ideas
of the Lynn Committee, and the only real
differences-I use the word differences for
want of a better one, because they are not
real differences-between us and that Committee-and this is a matter for discussion
and argument, and there will be ample time
for both-are, first that we have made the
County Council by statute occupy a position
which, as the rating authority and final
arbitrator in that matter, the County
Council does actually occupy, and will always
occupy in local administration; and secondly,
that we have in view a smaller number of
local bodies, although the larger number recommended by the Committee can be set
up, if this is still thought to be necessary.
This may be fairly said to be a departure
from the recommendations of the Lynn
Committee, but it is a departure in detail
rather than in principle. Our main difference is that we have at once adopted that
body to be the local education authority,
which the Committee are clearly of opinion
must ultimately be the authority, even under
the system which they recommend. I will
not quote the words of the Committee, but
it is very clearly put in the Report that
this is a variation which they envisage, and
which they think will very likely come
about. I think that anyone reading the
paragraphs of the Interim Report dealing
with this question of the form of the local
authority, will see the difficulties the Lynn
Committee found in coming to their decision,
and that the only certain view they expressed
was that the County Council, even if it were
not to be the local authority now, must inevitably succeed to that position by process
of evolution.
our
I have said that we feel bound to
adopt the County Conneil as
Local Education Authority because it is the
recognised rating authority. The question of
rates is a very difficult one. An Education
rate is almost an unknown thing in Northern
Ireland. I say "almost," because the rate
for Technical Education has been in existence
since 1899, but a general Education rate is
a complete innovation. I think, however,
from the results of Technical Education, we
can draw the most happy auguries for the
future. The great step from the centralised
system to one which is to be the embodiment
of democratic control postulates a rate, and I
have endeavoured in the Bill to take that
step-and it is a long step-in such a manner
as to command the assent of all who realise
and are prepared to shoulder the burden of
our responsibilities in this connection.
Other systems may form a guide, and it is
well to consider them. The English and
Scottish systems are based upon at least a
50 per cent. Education rate-I mean £1 of
local money for every 1 of money from the
State. That means that the whole of the
cost of Education in England and Scotland
is divided, under those systems, between the
State and the rates, the trend at present
being in the direction of increasing the contribution from the rates beyond the 50 per
cent. minimum. I may say at once-and I
think it will be a relief to those who are
doing me the honour of listening to methat that is not our policy nor anything
approaching it.
We have been educated, perhaps badly
educated, but still educated by successive
British Governments to expect that practically the whole of the expenditure upon
the services of Education should be defrayed
by the State, which means by the tax-payer.
This involved, as I have said, centralisation
and the negation of local democratic control.
In our new position under the Government
of Ireland Act it is incumbent upon us to
range ourselves in line, in principle at all
events, with British democratic ideas. This
attitude entails local control and consequently
local responsibility. The Bill, therefore,
makes provision for the striking of a local
rate for general educational purposes. The
salaries of the Primary Teachers-hon. Members are aware that is by far the largest
item we have to meet--remain as they have
been, a charge on the State, but the provision of new schools, the maintenance of
existing and future schools, and the lighting,
heating and cleaning charges, hitherto a
burden on the State, we propose to transfer
to the rates. I shall have something to say
in that connection later on. The benefits
of expenditure in these directions are local.
and the cost should fall upon the locality.
The Lynn Committee have made recommendations involving no less a sum than
425,000, so far as we can estimate it, of
new expenditure. It is impossible to find
fault in principle with any single one of
these recommendations, but I want the
country to realise that the system of education which we require and expect carries
with it very heavy expenditure. A considerable portion of this new expenditure will be
an additional charge upon the State, in particular I mean the additional charge which
strict enforcement of compulsory attendance
will entail, in meeting the increased number
of pupils with a corresponding increase in

The new expenditure that we contemplate

But a grant in aid of rates from the Exchequer to the extent I have just indicated
would relieve the ratepayer from two-thirds

Rate would not, therefore, exceed fourpence

Hear, hear.) But I am not empowered to

Evans, and Sir Josiah Stamp-which is

and until we know exactly where we stand,

It is our desire that the House and the

be in possession of our policy regarding
education. What I have said must,
therefore, be taken simply as an earnest
of the Government intention. The fulfilment of which depends upon the final
settlement of our financial position.

Lynn Committee anticipated a rate of fourpence for Primary Education alone, making
with the rate of twopence for Technical
The PRIME MINISTER (Sir James Craig):
Hear, hear.
The MARQUESS OF LONDONDERRY:
A centralised system may have many
advantages. In my judgment, it is out of
date. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) It is
inconsistent with the march of democratic
evolution and even more than that, it clogs
and hampers and I believe destroys local
interest and local activity, both of which are
so vitally necessary in this connection. I am
convinced that the actual change from centralisation to local administration will do
more to stimulate that universal and active
interest in education which has made our
Technical Schools what they are than the
most elaborate and perfect system of education centrally controlled in the world. It is
not so much the system, but the manner
in which that system is put into force and
the backing behind it.
I must now deal with the schools themselves, and I will first touch upon the
relationship between the Local Authority
and the Elementary Schools. We have
accepted the principle laid down by the Lynn
Committee that
"the amount of assistance to be given out
of the funds at the disposal of the Local
Committees should vary in proportion to
the extent to which the school comes under
the authority."
We have, therefore divided the schools into
three categories, each receiving a different
measure of assistance from public funds
according to the degree in which they admit
local control. We are dealing at present
almost entirely with privately owned schools
under managers, and I want our position
as a Government to be a very definite one.
We say to the school managers we go ninetenths of the way with you. We see in your
institution the framework of what we want,
and what, if you are not there, we are
bound in duty to provide-and I mean by
that, the machinery for educating the child
in secular subjects. We, therefore, undertake to pay your teachers. If, in addition,
you who have formerly been responsible for
providing this education are willing to come
under the control of the Local Authority,
the question of the additional expenditure
required is for arrangement on a basis laid
down in the Bill. I hope I have made that
clear to hon. Members. The schools at the
present moment are voluntary schools, and,
Education Bill-

HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Marquess of Londonderry]
in so far as they desire to come under the
control of the Education Authority, so far
will the Education Authority be able to assist
them out of public funds.
We are, of course, anxious to encourage
a consent to a measure of local control on
the part of the existing schools, and in order
to further the attainment of our ideal
of co-ordination, provision is made for
the acceptance of the transfer of
existing schools by the Local Authority,
and power is given to it for negotiation in the absence of free transfer, where
this seems advisable in the interests of
economy. We have agreed that it is necessary to give them the power to purchase.
This power to purchase was absent from
the proposals of the Committee, and I think
the addition of this power makes for the
improvement of the scheme, because it supplies a bridge in case of difficulty and makes
possible transfers which would otherwise
never have taken place, while not in any
way prejudicing free transfers.
The obligation of the State to grant free
education virtually comes to an end, when
the child reaches the age of 14, and after that
age further education is available generally
only to those children whose parents are in a
position to pay fees. By the means of scholarships and free places for the more promising
of the pupils at the elementary schools, we
propose to afford from public sources to children less fortunately placed the opportunity of
ascending the educational ladder. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) This we deemed to
be the duty of the State, not only as a measure
of simple justice, but also of public policy.
I have often thought that the curse of the
poor man's lot has not been so much his
poverty, his lack of means, as his ignorance,
his lack of knowledge. His need of education
through the want of opportunity has often
rendered him the easy dupe of demagogues and
schemers of every kind. The seed of discontent and social unrest is sown in the ignorance of the poor and uneducated. Carlyle's
appeal for the spread of knowledge still rings
true:-
"It is not because of his toils that I
lament for the poor; we must all toil. The
poor is hungry and athirst; but for him
also there is food and drink; he is heavy
laden and weary; but for him also the
Heavens send Sleep, and of the deepest.
But what I do mourn over is, that the lamp
of his soul should go out; that no ray of
heavenly or even of earthly knowledge
should visit him. Alas! while the body
stands so broad and brawny, must the soul
lie blinded, dwarfed, stupefied, almost
annihilated? Alas! was this too a breath
of God, bestowed in Heaven, but on earth
never to be unfolded? That there should
one Man die ignorant who had capacity for
knowledge, this I call a tragedy."
But whether we supply such education free
or no, it is the duty of the State to satisfy
itself that adequate opportunities of acquiring secondary education exist in the province.
It is an indispensable part of the machine,
and it is on this basis that the claim of
secondary education to State assistance rests.
Secondary education has lately come prominently into the public eye by reason of the
inadequate salaries paid to some of the
teachers. I know it is quite easy to say that
these material matters should not be allowed
to assume such dimensions of importance as
to obscure the real object we have in view,
which after all is Education. But, justice to
the teacher, the contentment of the teacher,
the removal from his or her mind of removable worries and distractions, such as his
actual existence and his anxieties as to the
future, are after all the lubricating oil of the
machine, without which that machine can
neither operate smoothly and efficiently nor
turn out the products we all desire. We have
decided, therefore, to accept in principle the
recommendations of the Lynn Committee.
But the scales laid down in the Report require further consideration in the light of
recent movements in the cost of living and
the trend towards the reduction of the
Burnham rates, on which those salaries
are based. My hon. friend, the Parliamentary Secretary (Mr. M'Keown) is giving the
closest attention to this difficult question in
consultation with the officials of the Ministry
and he tells me he hopes to arrive at a
satisfactory solution without undue delay.
We have decided that the salary scales
adopted shall be applied retrospectively from
the opening of the current School Year-that
is back to August or September last, and J
have the consent of my right hon. Friend.
the Minister of Finance, to make payments
on account, while the exact figures are still
in process of examination. In future, schools
will be called upon to pay the minimum of
the scales to be laid down, and, where the
financial circumstances of any school, which
is contributing efficiently to Higher Education, are such as to make assistance necessary for the payment of the appropriate increments, the State will bear its share of the
burden. This means that all the schools of
this description which are carried on for
profit will not be entitled to assistance from
the State. This is a recommendation which
was laid down very fully and very eloquently
in the Report of the Lynn Committee
This arrangement will no doubt be an acceptable change for all those concerned, managers and teachers alike, and we claim that
it is a measure of justice from which Education itself and the Province generally will
reap undoubted benefits.
Passing to Technical Education, I may say
at once that we have accepted the recom-

While, therefore, the new local authorities

I have now reached that part of the Bill
which deals with the question of Religious
Education, and I refuse to look upon this as
either difficult or dangerous.
same
The State is non-sectarian, but not secular
in the sense that it takes no interest in the
moral upbringing of the children. The
State, as does the individual, looks to the
Churches to give the lead in Christian
idealism, and I feel we need not look in vain.
Do not let it be said that these
churches, all possessing a proud history of
good deeds, responsible as they have been for
all the education in past years, are now, with
all the opportunities that the community can
possibly give, the stumbling block in the way
of an ideal system owing to a determination
to segregate their flocks and create from birth
a division, when union is so essential to the
well-being of this province. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) There are schools in
existence where children of different de
nominations work together and play together,
and who will assert that this association is
anything but beneficial for all concerned?
The State itself can do but little in this
direction, if it can do anything at all. It can
afford, and under the Bill it does afford,
opportunities, and I look with confidence to
the future, believing that in the new spirit
of the new era now dawning before our eyes,
tolerance and mutual respect will replace
prejudice and jealous mistrust. But beyond
giving opportunities for denominational instruction the State cannot go. The suggestion, if it ever has been made, that the State
is antagonistic to religion generally, or to
any particular denomination is entirely
erroneous-in fact, an utter travesty and
fabrication of the basest description.
I will not attempt to go further into detail
upon the particular provisions of the Bill. I
am not suggesting that some of the other provisions are not of the highest importance,
but I think that they will be best dealt with
on the other stages of the Bill-on the Second
Reading and the Committee Stage. I have
already trespassed upon the patience and indulgence of the House. (Hon. Members:
"No, no.") I will, therefore, simply inform
hon. Members that they will find there, in
addition to the matters I have already mentioned, provision for the universal and compulsory attendance at school of children between the ages of 6 and 14, for the regulation
and restriction of the employment of children,
and for their medical inspection and treatment at school. We deal, moreover, with the
feeding of necessitous children in our schools
and the case of those who are neglected. The
feeding of school children is a matter of vital
importance, because the endeavour to teach a
starving or even a hungry child is a waste of
effort on the part of the teacher, and consequently an uneconomic expenditure of public
money. Further, we have made provision for
the education of afflicted children generally
and the assistance of voluntary organisations
dealing with Nursery schools, and for the
establishment of such schools, where this is
found necessary. Nor have we neglected the
teacher, upon whose efforts after all the
whole success of our measure in its working
ultimately depends. Let me quote the words
of another Minister of Education:-
"I wish to draw attention to the fact
that all does not depend upon equipment.
There are many village schools in England,
which do not possess the latest system of
desk, which do not possess the best lighting
and heating, which do not possess large
cloakrooms and hat-pegs, or accommodation
like some of the large board schools
in London; and yet I feel sure
that no one will contradict
when I Say that these village schools,
incomplete as they are compared with
others with respect to equipment, are giving the very best education to those children
who receive education within their walls,
and fitting them for their future career in
life. It is. to my mind, because the teacher
is in absolute sympathy with the interests
of the children in his or her charge."

We have tried to see our problem as a
whole. There are many provisions, therefore,
which doubtless we shall not be in a position
to bring into operation for some time, because
of the expenditure involved. But we have
sought to lay down a policy which gives room
for development, and to set before our rising
local authorities a goal the attainment of
which is well worth their highest endeavours.
Such then are the proposals of the Government in regard to the training of the young
during the years of childhood and adolescence.
The Report of the Lynn Committee embodies
in its recommendations many hopes and
aspirations. This is an advantage that the
report of a Committee has over a Bill, which
has to be framed in colder and more dispassionate language. Nevertheless these are,
as far as possible, translated into clauses of
the Bill, couched in legal phraseology, laying
down rules and giving administrative
powers. I could tax your patience and
endurance to the fullest capacity were I to
embark to the full on the expression of my
own hopes and aspirations which I know well
are shared by the great majority. Of course
I have a personal pride in the fact that to
me is given this great opportunity of inaugurating a great and far-reaching scheme.
Perhaps no better occasion could be chosen
than the present when so much throughout
the world is still oscillating and vibrating by
reason of the great war, during which
naturally material institutions, and even
spiritual beliefs were shaken to their foundations, when doubts were born which assailed
and are still assailing so much that we
believed to be immutable and consecrated for
all time by the wealth of old tradition.
Surely this is the moment to take stock of
everything, to realise what it is that has
hampered progress in the past, what has
enabled us to survive and regain our
equilibrum, and with this acquired knowledge
to lay our plans for the future. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)

I like some others had my forebodings. Prob
ably I was one of those who sat up at night

I am glad to be able to come here to congratulate him whole-heartedly on the broad
principles of the Bill he has laid down. (Hon.
Members: Hear hear.) I would like to take
this the first opportunity I have had of congratulating the Minister of Education and his
whole staff on the excellent way in which

It is not easy for the general public to realise
what it means transferring a whole system
from one city to another, without suitable
buildings, with what you may call a short
staff, and yet carry on all the work as if

under a debt of obligation to the Minister of
Education, and to those who have been associated with him, for the excellent way in which
they have done their work since they took it

We in this House, and more especially those
outside it, are apt to be critical of the Civil
Service, but I think we ought in fairness to
acknowledge the debt of gratitude we owe to

Chairman of the Committee, to which the
Noble Marquess has referred, I had opportunities of studying the work of at least four

Service of the United Kingdom you would
find men better equipped, better qualified,

Ministry of Education of Northern Ireland.
I think I ought to say that because it is important in running a system to know that the
men behind it are not mere mechanical
machines, but people who take a live and real
interest in the work and want to do the very
best they can to make it a success. I, on my
own behalf, and more especially on behalf of
the Committee, feel grateful for the thanks
the Minister of Education has given to that
Committee.
The only desire of every Member of that
Committee has been to produce, or to help
in producing, the best possible educational
system for Northern Ireland. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) We had no personal prejudices
to serve, no fads to air. We simply wanted
to get the very best system of education that
we could get, and I am glad that it has met
so fully with the approval of the Minister of
Education and with the approval of his colleagues in the Cabinet, that practically the
Bill we are to have in a few days has been
modelled on it. Nobody is foolish enough to
expect that in all the details they were bound
to follow the Report of our Committee as if
they were dealing with the Ten Commandments. We do not say it is the last word in
educational wisdom. We do not say it has
not a wide margin to play with, but I think
on the whole we have laid down broad principles on which any successful scheme of
education can work in this Province of ours.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)

I was also glad to hear him say that he is
making provision in the Bill for the universal
compulsory attendance of children. I would
ask the House to remember that in England
they began by allowing each district to make
its own by-laws with regard to compulsory

system which calls for more thorough reform
than this part dealing with compulsory attendance. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) Compulsory attendance for all practical purposes
is a dead letter not only in Ulster but
throughout the whole country. I am not
going to go through all the other points the
Noble Marquess has dealt with so ably and so
eloquently, but I must not sit down without
saying how much I appreciate the sympathy
he has shown for the teaching profession.
A great educationist 400 years ago wrote that
the first grounding should be imparted by the
best. I think that principle is as sound today as it was 400 years ago. I am glad that
the Minister of Education realises that and
that he is anxious that the teacher should be
made not only comfortable but feel that he
is a living part of a living machine, that it is
his business to turn out the best finished
article. No person in the State, be he high
or low, has got such an influence in moulding
the opinion of the public as the teacher who
starts with the children. Therefore, I say
I am glad to find that the Minister is in
sympathy with the teachers, and that he
realises their difficulties. I know I have
come across people who say "Is it worth
while paying such salaries to people for teaching the three R's?" I am afraid there is an
opinion abroad that teachers are millionaires.
I know in the past that even in France, which
is ahead of us educationally, the teacher had
to earn his living generally by digging graves,
and the rest of his time was spent in trying
to educate the young and tender. Even up to
two years ago the teaching profession in Northern Ireland, indeed in all Ireland, was
simply starved, and because teachers are being
paid what, to my mind, is a reasonable salary
to-day you find people coming along and saying that they are really overburdened with
wealth. The evidence that was before our
Committee showed that the average salary of
a male teacher is £350 a year, or, in the case
of a woman, £266 a year. Does any hon.
Member or right hon. Member in this House
suggest to me that that is too large a salary
for the duty a teacher has got to perform?
Then I turn to the question with which the
Minister of Education has dealt very ably and
very sympathetically-the question of secondary education. The average salary paid to the
secondary teacher in Northern Ireland to-day
is £240 a year against £400 paid in England.
The greatest danger with which the Committee was confronted, and with which the
Minister of Education is confronted, is that if
something is not done, and done speedily, for
secondary education you will have no secondary education in Ireland, because your best
teachers, your best blood, will be drained out
of the country, and when the time comes when
you want to establish a good system of
secondary education you will not have native
teachers with which to establish it. I am
glad therefore, that the Minister of Education has accepted in principle the suggestions.
contained in our Report. I do not for a

he has paid to the Technical Committees. I

Mr. M'GUFFIN: I would not have intervened in the debate this afternoon were it
not for the desire I have to congratulate the
noble Marquess upon the very eloquent disquisition he has delivered in respect of education. A more admirable summary and survey of the question I have perhaps never
heard. It is only due to the noble Marquess
that the hon. Members who are here will
recognise the importance of this his first
appearance here to pay a tribute to the
extraordinary talent which he has exhibited
in the discharge of his duty to-day. I want
to say, however, that I demur to the method
of the introduction of this Bill. I intimated
to my right hon. Friend, the Prime Minister,
that I did not concur with the idea.
always thought that according to Standing
Orders when a Bill was presented it was regarded as being read the First time, and I
thought that the mere presentation of the
Bill at the Table was quite sufficient for that
purpose. The reason I objected to the introduction of the First Reading with a speech
was that it practically disarms criticism. We
all, of course, accept the exposition of the
Bill made by the Noble Marquess, but at the
same time it is quite a different thing to
listen to a speech outlining the provisions of
a Bill than to have the Bill in your hand
and thus be in a position to criticise everything that is set forth in the course of the
speech.
Mr. SPEAKER: I ought to point out to the
hon. Member that in the Imperial Parliament Bills of first-class importance are invariably introduced by this method, as, for
instance, all the Home Rule Bills-a First
Reading speech followed by a debate.
Mr. M'GUFFIN: I am much obliged for
your reminder in respect of that matter. As
my memory serves me at the moment, and
as you say, it only refers to first-class Bills.
The Bills you refer to in the Imperial
House involved great constitutional changes,
whereas the Bill introduced in this House
this afternoon is one of merely local interest
and local importance. In that respect 1
would prefer that the Standing Orders
should be adhered to in the introduction of
Bills in the future, and particularly with regard to one very important Measure we have
in anticipation which may be very soon introduced into this House. I would like to
say with respect to this matter of the composition of the Lynn Committee that I felt
considerably aggrieved that in the personnel
of that Committee Labour had only one representative, although an admirable one in
the person of my hon. Friend the Member
for North Belfast (Mr. Grant). I imagine
the working class, whose children I suppose
would be 90 per cent. of those attending the
primary schools, should have had better representation. There is only one Labour
member in such a large Committee. Of
course, I know that the gentlemen who compose the Lynn Committee are experts in
their way in respect of education, but it required representation from the working class
or the industrial class in order to give it
the necessary leaven to have made its Report
all the more acceptable to the democracy of
Belfast. I am sorry that the working class,
for whom the primary schools are intended to
provide, lacked that representation. Then I
do not know if my Friend the Member for
West Belfast (Mr. Lynn) when considering
the position of the Advisory Committee, did
not make a similar mistake, because in that
case, too, he has suggested there should be
only one representative. I understand it is
the fashion now, in the South of England at
least, to invite parents to a school to offer
advice and suggestion and in some instances
to give instruction, thus associating the
parents with the children as one would
desire. At least it is a method of enlisting
their sympathy. The noble Marquess has
emphasised the point, and rightly too, that
we cannot well dispense with the loyalty,
devotion, and fidelity of the teacher. I quite
agree with that. Neither can you do so with

saying I greatly regret the noble Marquess

Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: I have
desire to enter into the general discussion
upon the many important questions raised
by the noble Marquess in his very able, very
brilliant, and, if I may say so, very statesmanlike speech in this House this afternoon.
The First Reading of the Bill is not the
occasion for entering into details which will
arise later on, but I would like to say in a
sentence or two that with the general principles laid down by the noble Marquess in his
extremely interesting speech I find myself
in complete agreement. There are some
things that probably will require to be very
closely examined, such as the question of
the purchase of schools, the question of
whether the teachers are to give religious
instruction or not, and the question of the
County Council or Authority outlined in the
Lynn Report. Personally, I have always been
of the opinion that the people who strike
the rate and find the money ought to be the
people in charge and in control. I think
we have to congratulate ourselves as a
House to-day on the splendid statement that
has been made by the Minister of Education.
I do not think that any hon. Member could
find fault with the occasion of the First
Reading to have such a lucid and clear statement. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) We
were in an expectant state in this House and
the people outside were also in a state of
expectation to know what exactly the main
provisions of this Bill would be, and I think,
if I may say so, the wise course has been
taken when the first opportunity was given of
making the main provisions of this Bill
known. I believe that the foundations of this
Bill are being well and truly laid, and I sincerely hope that when the Bill itself is pub
lished the main provisions will be such as will
commend themselves to the House and to
the people as a whole. I know very well
the danger of expressing general approval of
everything. I know full well that it takes a
Bill to be read in detail to understand all
its implications, and I have often known the
main provisions of a Bill to receive almost
universal approval, and then the dangers and
difficulties arise when the details come to be
discussed. Sometimes details are just as
important as first principles. With this
proviso I desire to say that the speech which
has been given to-day to this House and the
main outlines of the educational proposals
of the noble Marquess are such that I believe
we will be able to have an education for the
young life of this Province that will do them
incalculable good, and an educational system
which I hope other countries will be happy
to copy in the days that are to come.

A PUBLIC AUDITOR'S APPOINTMENT.
1. Dr. MORRISON asked the Minister of
Commerce if he is satisfied that all the
Public Auditors appointed by his Department
are fit for this responsible position and
worthy of the confidence of the Commercial
and Agricultural community?
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY TO
THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE (Mr.
M'Keown): I have been asked to reply for
my right hon. Friend (Mr. Archdale), and to
say that the answer is in the affirmative.
Dr. MORRISON: Arising out of that
answer, I should like to ask the Minister if
he is aware that full information as to the
record of Mr. John Reilly as a public
auditor was put before Mr Litchfield
previous to his re-appointment, and that in
commercial and co-operative circles the
appointment of this man is looked upon as
a deplorable mistake?
Mr. M'KEOWN: The attention of my right
hon. Friend, the Minister of Commerce, was
drawn to the matter raised by my hon.
Friend, and, after full investigation, he could
not see any reason for withholding the
appointment at the present time.
Mr. LYNN Arising out of that answer,
would my hon. Friend consider the advis
ability of concentrating these auditors in a
central body-I do not mind whether it is
Finance or any other-in Northern Ireland,
and of having them under the direct control
of the Government?
Mr. DONALD: May I ask my hon. Friend
if, before these appointments are made.
inquiries are made into the previous record
and character of the applicants?
Mr. M'GUFFIN: I would also like to refer
to this question, and to inquire further if
the Department really knew that this
auditor had been guilty of gross and flagrant
negligence in the discharge of his duty, and
whether that fact was actually brought before
the attention of the Minister before he
sanctioned the appointment of this man?
Mr. M'KEOWN: The Minister fully considered the case in question. There is act
any doubt that some irregularities were discovered in connection with a company of
which he was auditor. The irregularities
were in the nature of an inflated increase
of the turnover. This is a matter which, when
certain figures are put before any auditor,
might be overlooked. The Ministry on this
occasion did not think there was anything
in the case to prevent them making the reappointment.
Mr. LYNN: May I have an answer to my
question? Will the Minister consider the
advisability of these public auditors being
placed under the direct control of his Ministry or some Ministry?
Mr. M'KEOWN: The Minister will consider that.
Dr. MORRISON: May I ask was the fact
that this auditor was found guilty of serious
dereliction of duty as a liquidator in Dublin
not brought before Mr. Litchfield before this
appointment was made.
Mr. M'KEOWN: I am not aware of anything of that nature having been done.
Dr. MORRISON: I think this matter is so
serious that I wish to give the Minister
notice that on Wednesday next I will bring
the whole matter before the House on the
Motion for the Adjournment.

he can suggest a remedy?

Petty Sessions Bill.

to
Mr. M'KEOWN: I have been asked
reply for my right hon. Friend in this case

that serious damage is done to
crops by
crows, which, as the honourable Member
suggests, have become numerous in recent

licence in regard to dogs.
Clause 1 is to give the Governor power to
alter those fees. I think it well to point
out to hon. Members that the salaries and
the expenses of administering the Petty
Sessions Acts, including the salaries of Petty
Sessions clerks, at the present time are paid
entirely out of the fines and the fees received.
For some twenty years after the passing of
the Act of 1858 the receipts were more than
sufficient to meet the expenditure, but for a
considerable time past the Petty Sessions
Fund has been a bankrupt concern.
1920 the total expenditure all over Ireland in
respect of the costs of administering the Petty
Sessions Department amounted to the sum of
£84,000, but the sum received in respect of
fines and fees amounted only to the sum of
£27,000, showing a deficiency of £57,000.
Under the Act of 1865, which first imposed
a dog licence duty in Ireland, the balance of
the receipts, after paying all the small administrative costs, was handed over to the
Local Authorities in relief of the rates, and
in 1881, under the Petty Sessions Act of that
year, it was provided that if the receipts
of the Petty Sessions Fund were insufficient
to meet the expenditure, the Lord Lieutenant
had power to make an Order under which the
In
155 Petty Sessions Bill-
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Second Reading.
[Sir Dawson Bates]
deficiency in the Petty Sessions Fund was to
be made good out of the Dog Fund. I say
here I did not think it was ever in the mind
of the legislature at the time that Act was
passed that any very large sum should be
taken out of the Dog Fund for the purpose
of making good such deficiency. Owing to
the bankrupt state the Petty Sessions Fund
had got into, very large sums had been diverted for some years past out of the Dog
Fund which really should have gone to the
Local Authorities. I find that in 1916 the
sum of £33,000-I am speaking, of course, of
the whole of Ireland-was diverted from the
Dog Fund to the Petty Sessions Fund. That
sum really should have gone to the relief of
the rates. In 1917 the sum of £35,000 was
diverted, and so on until we come down to
the year 1920, when we find the sum of
£57,000 diverted really from the Local Authorities. There is real justification for
bringing forward this particular Bill so that
the Local Authorities should again be put in
the position of receiving these fees which
the legislature had originally intended they
should receive. I do not suppose the fees
should be increased to such an extent as to
make the Petty Sessions Fund an entirely
self-supporting institution, but if the fees of
6d were doubled I think it would go a long
way to make the Petty Sessions Fund a
self-supporting institution.
With regard to the second part of the Bill,
that is the question of the election of Petty
Session Clerks, I might point out that the
law at the present time is that the Justices
are entitled to elect a Petty Sessions Clerk
in their own particular district, and we do
not propose to do away with that. Where
it was deemed advisable by the Lord Lieutenant that two or more districts should be
served by one clerk, the election of the Petty
Sessions clerk so appointed took place at
the Quarter Sessions by the Justices of the
districts concerned. We have been advised
that where one of the districts which the
Government suggests should be amalgamated
is in a different county to the other district
proposed to be amalgamated, we have not
power to amalgamate, and we propose to
remedy that defect so that if the Governor
deems it advisable that two or more districts, whether they are in the same county
or not, should be amalgamated, power should
be given to him to bring that about. Under
these circumstances it is proposed that the
first clerk appointed to serve in these amalgamated districts should be appointed by
the Governor from one of the existing clerks,
but at subsequent elections the appointment
will take place by the magistrates themselves. We feel it would not be fair to ask
an existing clerk who has already gone
through an ordinary election for his original
appointment to stand another election. The
Government feel, and I am sure hon. Members will agree, that every facility should be
given to the grouping of these different districts together because by doing so we are
able to provide better pay, and as a result get
a more efficient man as Clerk of Petty Sessions. I think this is more essential at the
present time than heretofore having regard
to the increasingly technical character of the
various Acts of Parliament which have to
be administered by Petty Sessions. It is not
proposed to do away with any one district.
we only propose that these districts might be
grouped together and served by one Petty
Sessions Clerk. No inconvenience will be
caused to the public as such clerk would have
to attend on regular days in the different districts. With regard to Clause 2, Sub-section
2 (a), it has been found that a great many
disputes have arisen from time to time in
regard to the validity of magistrates voting
at the election of Petty Sessions Clerks, and
as a result litigation has occurred and the
Petty Sessions service has suffered generally

cannot make up their minds as to who would

entitled to intervene in the case of a tie.
These are the main provisions of the Bill.
I beg to move.

because we in this House know very well that
