The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY TO
THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS (Mr.
Megaw): To the observations that have been
made by hon. Members who have spoken
on the Bill I should like to reply seriatim.
With regard to the criticisms of the hon.
Member for West Belfast (Mr. Lynn) it is
recognised, as he says, that the duties of the
Petty Sessions clerks are increasing. They
are increasing from year to year, and it is
intended by any increase of fees that are
rendered possible by the Bill to give something in the way of increased remuneration
to Petty Sessions Clerks. With regard to his
point about bringing the Governor into disputes, I think at this time it is clearly recognised that the Governor, as he says, acts
on the advice of his Ministers. His administration is based on that and I do not think
anything is really to be gained by putting a
Minister in the position of the Governor in a
case of the kind. However, we will consider
the matter, but I think according to the prinas
ciples of law the Governor should be the
person who shall approve or disapprove, as
the case may be, and decide these disputes.
The hon. and learned Member for the University (Mr. Robb) mentions the point of the
disputes also and says they ought to be determined in the way they have been determined heretofore, by the courts. The history
of the past has been that for some little
miserable appointment Petty Sessions
Clerk there have been a couple of men who
by dint of canvassing have got an equality
of votes. All the magistrates turn up. There
is an equality at one election. It is postponed, and there is an equality at another
election. Then when that equality has
occurred it is found that one of the magis
trates has some disqualifying feature attached to himself-that he has not been properly appointed-and one of the men brings
proceedings in the Courts to declare that
he has been elected. And So,
for this

but before two. Another election may be

an equality of votes once and for all which

Sir DAWSON BATES: This measure is
introduced to meet a temporary difficulty
which has arisen by the disbandment of the
old Royal Irish Constabulary. Under the
Weights and Measures Act of 1878 the duty
of inspecting weights and measures was imposed upon and confined solely to members
of the Royal Irish Constabulary who held the
necessary Board of Trade Certificate. When
the Constabulary Act forming the Royal
Ulster Constabulary came before this House
last year we believed that a sufficient
number of the old Royal Irish Constabulary
who had these qualifications would be prepared to enlist in our new force. We provided for that by giving the same powers to
the Royal Ulster Constabulary as had been
formerly held by the Royal Irish Constabulary. Unfortunately it transpired that the
necessary number of the old Royal Irish
Constabulary who held these qualifications
did not join our new Force, and at the
present time the number of men holding
these qualifications in the Royal Ulster Constabulary is entirely inadequate to carry out
the duties. The inspection of weights and
measures has for some time rather fallen
into arrears owing to the disturbed condition
of the country and the heavy demands on the
Police Force, and it has become a matter of
vital necessity to commence actively to carry
out the work of inspection. We cannot postpone this until the members of the Royal
Ulster Constabulary are trained in this new
work. The training is rather a long process.
The examinations are of a technical
character. Hon. Members may be interested
to know that the examination for the position
of Inspector under the Weights and Measures
Act involves a knowledge of mechanics,
physics, the practical verification of weights
and measures, and so on. I am sure it is unnecessary to lay stress upon the vital
importance of efficiency in such a matter.
Apart altogether from the question of protecting the public from fraud, they have to
carry out periodic inspections of weights and
measures and correct the various inaccuracies
that occur owing to scales being in use
for some time. As the men of the Royal
Ulster Constabulary become trained in
sufficient numbers they will take the places
of the temporary Inspectors whom we are
appointing at the present time. The men we
are appointing are the old members of the
Royal Irish Constabulary who hold the
necessary qualifications. I beg to move.

Mr. CRAWFORD: I would just like to add
a word or two to what has been said in semiopposition to this Bill. I would like to point
out the way in which Inspectors of Weights
and Measures were appointed in times past.
The head constable, or some other officer of
the Royal Irish Constabulary, submitted one
or two names to the local Justices in the
petty Sessions districts. They generally
approved of the names, but if not they asked
for other suggestions. These men were
appointed with the approval of the local
Justices. I would like to ask why the
Government should depart from that
practice? You will have to remember also
that these appointments were ex-officio. No
salaries were paid for them at all, and the
various County Councils bore the expense of
carrying the standards from one place to
another, and of paying the rent of a little
room in which the weights were tested. So
that the right hon. gentleman (Sir Dawson
Bates) was not fortunate in saying that it
would put no additional expense on to the
rates of the counties. Another point which
I would like to make is that for many years
there was no certificate at all issued from
the Board of Trade in connection with these
appointments, but the change was made
afterwards. Surely it is a reflection on the
men who are serving in the Royal Ulster
Constabulary to insinuate that they are not
able to pass an examination, which, I am told
by a head constable who has held one of these
positions, could be passed by a schoolboy in
the fifth class.
There is no hurry, surely for speeding this
thing. We can wait until men have been
trained. I understand that there have been
already a few appointments made in County
Antrim. (An hon. Member: Surely not.)
One is a retired R.I.C. man, who was
appointed at an age when he could have
joined the Royal Ulster Constabulary, and
did not agree to do it. I understand he is
also engaged in a trade in which he uses
weights and measures, and I would like to
ask who is going to examine his weights and
measures? If these things are done, they ought
surely to be done in such a way that we can
stand thoroughly over them. I do not think
it would take a man long to do this work.
It would not take up his whole time. It is
certainly not a whole-time job, and there is
no necessity for appointing men. I have
heard a rumour that these inspectors get £3
a week, and 10s a day expenses. That would
be a considerable charge on the ratepayers of
the county. All these things could be
managed in olden times with practically no
expense to the county, and I see no reason
why we should rush a Bill through that
would involve considerable expense. I saw
recently where there was a dispute between
a grocer and a farmer's wife. The latter
complained that a pound of soap was not the
correct weight, and the grocer retorted by
saying that he had weighed it against a
pound of butter which he had got from her.
It shows that there is some reason for these
things being done, but I think the work can
be done well by the splendid men who are
serving in the R.U.C.

another these small things are being put on
it worth
the people, and nobody thinks
while to object to them, but these small

Criminal Evidence Bill (Northern
Ireland).
Order for Second reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed,
That the Bill be now read a Second time.;"
Sir DAWSON BATES: This Bill is for the
purpose of assimilating the law in Northern
Ireland to the law in England in regard to
the competency of an accused person and
wife or husband of such person to give evidence on his or her trial, and is identical
with the Criminal Evidence Act, 1898, whicn
only applied to England and Scotland. Prior
to the passing of that Act the law in England
and Scotland was, and is at present in
Northern Ireland, that no accused person
could give evidence, nor could the wife or
husband give evidence. There were certain
exceptions to this rule, and under certain
Statutes creating offences the accused person,
his or her wife or husband, could, if they
desired, give evidence, and even in certain
cases the husband or wife could be compelled
to give evidence either for the prosecution or
defence; therefore, the Act of 1898, which applied the general principle to all cases, was
not by any means an innovation.
The English Act was brought forward at
the instance of some of the most famous
Judges in England, and received the approval of practically everyone in the British
Parliament, except the Nationalist Members,
who offered the strongest opposition to the
Measure. The result was that Ireland was
excluded from its provisions. The working
of the Act in both England and Scotland
has been of the utmost success.
In many
cases it has resulted in innocent persons
being acquitted, and the guilty convicted in
cases where, if such a law had not existed,
a grave miscarriage of justice might have
resulted.
This Bill leaves it entirely optional for an
accused person to give evidence, and if the
accused person declines to do so it is not to
be a matter for comment by the prosecution.
As I have said, the husband or wife cannot
be compelled to give evidence, except in a
few rare cases, and in connection with
offences specified in the Schedule to the Bill.
I believe this Bill will provide a much needed
reform in our Criminal Law in Northern
Ireland. I beg to move.
Mr. McGUFFIN: This is a purely legal
Measure, and I suppose ordinary laymen are
not expected to express an opinion in regard
to it.
Sir DAWSON BATES: Oh, no.
Mr. McGUFFIN: At any rate it is a
Measure on which a layman would be very
timorous about offering an opinion. It occurs
to me, however, that while a person can
volunteer to give evidence on his own behalf

Local Government (Roads) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed, "That
the Bill be now read a Second time."
Sir DAWSON BATES: This Bill will, I
think, meet with general approval when I
say it has for its object the general improvement of the roads in Northern Ireland. The
Government has had recently a strong
representation from the Roads Advisory
Committee pointing out the serious state of
disrepair into which many of the trunk
roads in Northern Ireland had fallen, and
urging that every possible facility should be
extended to County Councils in Northern
Ireland to institute a wholesale scheme of
reconstruction. They pointed out very properly, in my opinion, that much of the
ratepayers' and motorists' money is being
wasted by the system that prevails in certain
areas of merely patching roads which really
require wholesale reconstruction from the
bottom up. In fact many of these roads do
not seem to have any bottom, judging from
the amount of material that is put into
them. I believe if the work is properly done
now it will be more economical in the long
run. Before these works can be carried
out on anything like a systematic basis it
will be necessary for us to modify and
simplify procedure in regard to the maintenance and construction of roads.
Before I refer to the effect of the provisions on the Bill I would like to briefly
explain to those who are not familiar with
County Council management what the
present system is, so that they may understand to what extent we propose to alter
this. Roads are divided under the Local
Government Acts into 2 classes-main roads
and district roads. The cost of the first of
these is borne as to one moiety by a countyat-large charge," and as to the other moiety
by the district in which the road is situate,
subject to the assistance which I will refer
to hereafter from the Road Fund., The cost
of the district roads were entirely borne by
the district. As regards the administration,
this is largely in the hands of the Rural
District Councils, the procedure being that
the Rural District Councils put up proposals
to the County Councils as to the amount
that should be spent on the roads for the
forthcoming year, and, while the County
Councils have the right to say that the proposal involves too great a sum of money,
they cannot urge upon the Rural District
Councils the fact that in many cases the

of this system is that a County Council
which desires to have good trunk roads is
entirely at the mercy of the Rural District
Councils through which these main roads
run. Experience has shown that while in
many cases the Rural District Councils concerned deal with their roads in an enlightened
manner, their efforts are neutralised by the

neighbouring Councils. The result has been
want of uniformity in construction and

no fewer than 32 Rural District Councils
controlling the expenditure on the main
trunk roads in the Six Counties
The passing of the Ministry of Transport
Act, 1919, added to the difficulties of road
This Act introduced a new
management.
system of classification under which roads
have been classified under three heads-
Class I. being main trunk roads connecting large towns and cities:
Class II. being secondary roads, connecting
smaller towns or with Class I. roads; and
Class III. minor roads.
Following on this classification grants are
payable to the Road Authorities out of the
Road Fund, which represents the proceeds
of the motor taxation on a basis up to the
present of 50 per cent. Class I. roads, and
25 per cent. Class II., of the expenditure by
the Authorities on these roads.
The result is we have in Northern Ireland
two systems of classification super-imposed
on each other. Some of the main roads are
Class I. roads, and others are Class II. roads.
All this involves difficulties in accountancy,
and it has become, as a result, very difficult
for the Government to check over the actual
expenditure on the various classification
roads, and to keep proper statistics which are
necessary in the administration of the Road
Fund. Under the present law Urban Councils, although Road Authorities, are
Highway Authorities under the Roads Act,
and all grants made to them out of the Road
Fund must be made first to the County
Council who pass the money on to the Urban
Council; a most unsatisfactory arrangement
and one which does not give them the
position they should have in the management
of their roads.
a
not
I suggest that is most unsatisfactory
arrangement, and one which does not give
the Urban District Councils the position they
-hould have. The result throughout the
counties has been that the roads have
suffered. The object of the Road Fund,
which is contributed by motorists, is to try
to improve the roads and make them more
suitable for motor traffic, and at the same
time to reimburse Local Authorities for the
extra expenses put on them by the large increase in traffic in respect of motor vehicles.
I do not think hon. Members will differ
from me when I say that the roads in
Northern Ireland are for the most part a
disgrace to any community. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) I believe that is very largely
due to the want of co-ordination in the
management of the roads, which is caused
mainly through the large number of controlling bodies. Under this Bill we propose to do
away with the old classification under the
Local Government Acts, and we propose to
have three classes-Class 1, Class 2, and Class
3 roads. As regards Class 1 roads which, as
I have said before, are the main trunk roads
running right through the Six Counties, we
propose that they should be put entirely
under the control of the County Councils
and made a county-at-large charge. So far
as these main trunk roads are concerned, this
will ensure that instead of having 32 controlling bodies they will be confined to six
bodies, the County Councils. I believe that
will effect economy, and bring about far
greater efficiency in the management of these
roads, while the fact that the expenses of
the Class 1 roads are made a county-at-large
charge will relieve the districts to a considerable extent. We propose to allow Class 2
roads and Class 3 roads to remain under the
control of the Rural District Councils.
As regards the cost of Class 2 roads, we
propose to make them half a district charge
and half a county-at-large charge. The Class
3 roads we propose to make entirely a district
charge. We propose also to allow Urban
District Councils to have complete control
over the roads in their particular areas, and
they will only be responsible for the roads
within those areas. Any of these Urban
District Councils, if they so wish, can, under
the Bill, make any arrangements they like
for the County Councils to maintain their
roads for them as their agents. We also propose to abolish the limit of expenditure
which is at present imposed on Rural District
Councils in regard to roads by the Act of
1898, when it was felt that the Councils might
perhaps be too extravagant with the ratepayers' money, but the Government feel they
are perfectly safe in believing that the Rural
District Councils will not spend any excessive
sum of money on the roads. I may say here
that we can hardly look forward to having
as good roads in Northern Ireland as they
have in England or Scotland without placing
a greater burden on the people; but at the
same time I do think that without imposing
an additional halfpenny upon the ratepayers
of the Six Counties the roads under this new
management will be brought up to a very
much greater state of efficiency. I would
hope that when these additional powers are
conferred on the County Councils they will
see their way to incur what I may refer to

in Northern Ireland will not be, as they are
at the present time, a disgrace to the community.

Exchequer and Financial Provisions
Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That the Bill be now read a Second time."
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY TO
THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (Mr. Barbour): I think that hon. Members looking
over the clauses of this particular Bill will
not find anything of an unusual nature in
it. The main objects of the Bill are merely
to define and lay down the exact procedure
with which the Ministry of Finance will have
to comply in dealing with and reporting on
its accounts both in respect of the past period
and of times to come until any alteration
may be found necessary. A good many of
the clauses merely provide that in respect
of national income or State income and expenditure, and also of capital sums and
income accruing from those capital sums,
due accounts should be kept and regularly audited and thereafter submitted to
this House. In fact, it is the ordinary
course which I am sure hon. Members have
expected to be followed and for which we
have a precedent in the accounts of the
Imperial House at Westminster.
There are, however, two clauses which have
been rendered necessary owing to the special
conditions of North of Ireland finance. No.
3 Clause is specially designed in order to
protect for all time what might be regarded
as the perpetual income value of certain
funds transferred to us. The Minister of
Finance has repeatedly referred to what the
Imperial Government describe as the "free
gift" to the North of Ireland Parliament of
Land Purchase Annuities. Hon. Members
will of course be aware that these Land
Purchase Annuities are of a terminable
character. The period of termination depends entirely upon the terms of the Acts
under which loans were granted to enable
Land Purchase to be carried out and the proportion of that period which has already
expired. Similar to this is the income from
the Church Temporalities Fund which has
also been transferred to us. These are also
terminable, but a larger portion of their
period of existence has already expired than
in the case of Land Purchase Annuities.
The total of the Land Purchase Annuities
has been spoken of in various ways. It is
variable in amount from year to year, but
we may take about £613,000 a year as being
the amount we receive under this head. It
has been calculated that of that about
£589,000 represents what we might regard as
the terminable income from that source, and
this Bill which is now presented to Parliament for the First time is a suggestion that
we should be willing to forego a certain
amount of this payment in order that a
Sinking Fund might be formed which during
the period of these annuities would be sufficient to provide a fund so as to secure for
all time to the Northern Ireland Parliament
an income equal to this £589,000 which is
calculated as being the perpetual income
value of the annuities we are now receiving.
It is the same in the case of the Church
Temporalities Fund. The annual income
there is somewhere about £17,000 a year, but
owing to the longer period which has already
expired it will take an annual sum of about
£6,000 to provide a similar Sinking Fund.
Then it will be necessary that we should lay
down some lines on which the various Endowment Funds transferred to us should be
treated. Hon. Members will be aware that
in the old state of Irish finance there were
many Bills passed, and in order to endow
them with sufficient income to enable them
to be carried on there were special capital
sums set aside to provide income.
different sums have now been transferred to
us in great part and some of them are still
under consideration by an Arbitration Commission in order to determine the exact proportion due to Northern Ireland and to
Southern Ireland, but we wish to provide in
the case of all these capital sums that may
be transferred to us. It is proposed that
instead of these being ear-marked, as they
have been in the past, as Endowments, all
these capital sums should be merged, and
the income arising therefrom should be paid
into our Exchequer, and the annual sums
required for the different services voted out
annually in the regular way as provided in
the estimates.
These
Clause 5, "Extension of powers of Ministry
of Finance to make loans, etc.," does not
contemplate any new feature in our Parlia
ment. It is merely designed to transfer to
the Ministry of Finance powers to borrow
which existed under the different services
that have now been transferred to this Ministry. The objects are duly set forth. You
will see that we have now taken over the
power to lend money in connection with
the Department of Agriculture and Technical
Instruction for Ireland, the Forestry Com-
Exchequer Bill-

Second Reading.
[Mr. Barbour]
missioners, and the Intermediate Education
Board for Northern Ireland. Sub-Section B
is of course a necessity to loan which arises
with the creation of our own Parliament and
the transfer to the North of Ireland of Civil
Servants who have been hitherto located in
Dublin. This item has already appeared in
our estimates, and the loans to be made to
our Civil Servants in order to enable them
to secure housing accommodation or build
houses for themselves has already been approved in principle by this House.
Section C. I think, has been put in in order
to meet one particular instance, and this is
to enable assistance to be given to the Bridge
Commissioners in Derry. Another very important section deals with the disposal of
surplus. Under the United Kingdom National Debt Sinking Fund Act, 1875, any surplus
that may arise on annual accounts is automatically applied to the extinction of debt.
It is well that in the first part of our existence we are in the happy position of not
having any actual debt of our own creation,
although I would not go so far as to say
we did not have any liability, as of course
we pay the very heavy annual contribution
to the United Kingdom of £6,000,000 for the
services of the Navy, Army and Air Force,
and other services of the Imperial Government. Part of it is devoted to interest on
the National Debt of the United Kingdom
in which we are partners, I hope to the same
undiminished extent we always were. No
part of that National Debt has been allocated
to us, but still we are to bear in mind the
somewhat indirect liability that rests on our
shoulders in that connection. The first
actual debt of our own creation was of course
when the first of our Ulster Savings Certificates was issued, and although that debt
was incurred not for carrying on the
ordinary services of the Government it was
ineurred partly, we might say, to assist us
to help the Unemployment Fund and also
to put us in a position of making the necessary local loans. So in the future it is
proposed to take powers to utilise the surplus
in any financial year to the reduction of any
debt that may be in existence and in the
reduction of capital liabilities. Secondlyand this is also a provision for the futuretowards making good any principal or
arrears of interest extinguished, written
off or remitted under the authority of
an Act of Parliament in respect of any
loan out of public moneys.
To clear away any apprehension that may
arise I will say that there is no such Act in
existence at present, but it may be possible
that in course of time Parliament may think
they are justified in waiving the interest or
even to write off the principal of some loans
seeing that many loans are not met. So it
is right they should have funds in hand to
put them in the position of being able to
exercise discretion in that direction. Thirdly,
power is taken to create a capital fund. We
are a very young Government and there may
be many institutions which we may think it
wise to create as time goes on, the expenditure on which would be of a capital nature
and might be too heavy to be borne out of
the revenue of any one particular year. I do
not believe the Government have any institution of this character in mind at the moment, but it seems a reasonable provision to
make and a tendency that is not unlikely to
arise as time goes by.
Clause 3 is merely a safeguard that surplus
should not be used for the purpose of paying
off what are strictly current liabilities and
properly chargeable against income rather
than capital. There are two special clauses
which have reference only to the financial
year of 1922. When the accounts for that
year were closed there was no procedure as
to how the reports on those accounts should
be laid before Parliament, so the second paragraph on Page 4 merely states what should be
done in respect of those accounts which now
have reference to a past period. The same
applies to Section 4 of the third paragraph
at the head of Page 5. Clause 7 merely
authorises the Ministry of Finance to submit
the account of the charitable donations and
bequests to the examination of our Comptroller and Auditor-General. Otherwise I think
the different provisions of the Bill will be
quite clear to hon. Members, and I beg to
move.
Mr. LYNN: I am really ashamed to speak
so often. I have adopted a critical tone towards some rather loosely drafted Bills presented to the House to-day, and I can only
express regret that there is not a larger House
to discuss this Bill, because in my judgment

do not take finance as seriously as they ought
ta do, and yet it is the very foundation on
which any Parliament must rest, and on
which any community must rest. There
fore, I am glad that the Finance Minister has
had the courage to bring in this Bill, and to
bring it forward in the way he has done,
because in reading it through-and I have
read it very carefully; I want to emphasise

I saw several clauses where it would have

he has tied up not only himself but future
Finance Ministers and tied them up very
hard and fast. For that we have every right

has grasped this whole situation in

There is only one other point to which I
wish to refer, and that is in Clause 5, section
2, which provides that the Ministry of
Finance may, in such cases as it thinks fit,
waive the payment of interest imposed by
section 5 of the Public Works Loans Act,
1897, in respect of loans made by that
Ministry. I presume-I am sure I am right
in presuming-that the Ministry of Finance
means that if in any case in his judgment he
exercises this privilege, it will be brought
under the notice of Parliament. That would
only be in keeping with the whole policy outlined in this Bill.
business-like way not for the Budget
of next year, but for 40 years hence, when
probably not a Member who is in this House
now will be present. I ask hon. Members to
remember this. Take the case of the finance
of the Land Purchase Act. Even the earliest
annuities are only 20 years old, and they have
to run for 69 years, so that we may take
it that even the earlier cases of land purchase
in Northern Ireland have still three-fourths
of the 70 years to run, and yet we find the
Finance Minister providing for the time when
those annuities will cease. He might have
gone on-it would have done him for his time,
and for mine, too-without making any provision for the future, spending up to his last
shilling, but instead of doing that he is making provision so that at the end of the 69
years whoever are our heirs and assigns in
this House will find themselves in no worse
position than we are in to-day. I think that
is sound finance; I think it is common sense
as well. I want, therefore, as one who has
been occasionally a critic, to say how
thoroughly I agree with it.
Then there is another very important point,
to which I think the attention of the public
should be drawn, and that is in regard to
Local Loans. Those of us who have studied
National Finance will remember-I think it
was in 1887; the Finance Minister will correct
me if I am wrong that the Imperial
Government discovered in going into the
question of Local Loans that they were losing something like £12,000,000 a year in Local
Loans of £100,000,000. Things had been
managed so badly that they did not know
exactly how they stood. They may have
been borrowing money at 2 per cent., and
giving it out at 13 per cent., but the Finance
Minister here, if I read this Bill aright, is
making provision so that in the case of Local
Loans or anything of that sort, if there is
a deficit in any one year the deficit will be
put down in the Parliamentary papers and
be brought under the notice of Parliament.
Again I say that is very sound finance, and
I congratulate the Minister of Finance upon
the fact.
I say again that I am exceedingly sorry
there is not a larger House, and that there
are not more people who take an interest in
this Bill, which in my judgment is one of the
strongest foundation-stones in the new edifice
that we are trying to build up in Northern
Ireland. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)

1. Mr. DONALD asked the Minister of
Commerce whether parcels from America for
Northern Ireland are forwarded first to Dublin and examined, then forwarded to London
and examined, and then despatched back to
Belfast, thus incurring a delay of several
days in delivery.
Mr. M'KEOWN (Parliamentary Secretary
to the Ministry of Commerce): I have been
asked by my right hon. Friend (Mr. Archdale) to reply. There is no reason to suppose
that any arrangement such as is suggested in
the hon. Member's question has been brought
into operation. If, however, the hon. Member has any specific case in which parcels
have been dealt with in this manner to bring
to my notice I will have the requisite inquiries made.
Mr. DONALD: May I ask my hon. Friend
if he has made inquiries with regard to this
matter?
Mr. M'KEOWN: We have made inquiries,
and up to the moment have not had any
reply.
DISPATCH AND DELIVERY OF LETTERS

why the last dispatch of letters from the
Head Office, Belfast, for Knock, Bloomfield,
and Strandtown Districts takes place at 2-30
p.m., and that for Cregagh, Malone, Purdysburn, Ligoniel and Whitehouse at 4-15 p.m.,
and whether Bloomfield, Knock and Strandtown Districts could not be brought into line,
regarding postage and delivery, with all the
other districts.
Mr. M'KEOWN; I have been asked by my
As the hon.
right hon. Friend to reply.
Member is aware, the Ministry of Commerce

of the Post Office service, but inquiries are

RENT RESTRICTION ACT.
3. Mr. DONALD asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether the Government propose setting up a Committee to consider the
Rent Restriction Act; if so, whether such
Committee will be composed of Members of
both Houses?
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): The answer to the first part
of the hon. Member's question is in the
affirmative. While it is intended that the
Committee will comprise Members of both
Houses, it cannot be exclusively confined to
Members of Parliament, as it is necessary to
include on it representatives of the various
interests affected.
Mr. DONALD: Could my right hon. Friend
say when this Committee will be set up?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I hope to be able to
make an answer in the course of the next
few days.
R.I.C. PRE-WAR PENSIONERS.
4. Mr. GRANT (for Mr. M'Guffin) asked
the Minister of Home Affairs whether it is
a fact that by a circular, dated February
1st, 1922, it was announced that all pre-war
Pensioners of the Royal Irish Constabulary
serving with the Special Constabulary would
receive the same pay as the members of the
Royal Irish Constabulary then serving
according to each rank; whether it is a fact
that in the case of ex-members who retired
before the war the matter was never complied with although they were promised, by
the circular quoted, that their pay would be
brought up to existing rates; and whether
it is not a fact that a member of the Special
Constabulary concerned made application on
March 11th, 1922, to have his pay, etc.,
brought up to existing rates, and, if so, what
is the decision of the Government on the
matter, and when is the claim likely to he
paid?
Sir DAWSON BATES: Might I ask the
hon. Member to postpone this question?
Mr. GRANT assented.

Mr. M'KEOWN: With regard to the amendment proposed by the hon. Member (Mr.
Crawford) to restrict the operation of the present Bill to the 31st December, 1923, it may
be pointed out that the English Act extends
the application of the charges to the 15th
February, 1925. Furthermore, hon. Members
should bear in mind that the maximum
charges which these canals were authorised
to make were fixed a great many years ago
when labour and material cost a great deal
less than they do today. It is scarcely to
be anticipated that the wages and materials
required for the maintenance of the canals
will be reduced down to pre-war level by
the 31st December, 1923, and, accordingly,
it will be much more satisfactory to allow
the Bill to go through as drafted. This does
not mean that the charges at the present
time in operation will be necessarily continued to the 15th February, 1925. I would
like to draw specially the hon. Member's
attention to this, that it does not follow that
these charges will be maintained to the 15th
February, 1925, because under sub-Section 2
the Ministry of Commerce is enabled to
make any revision of charges that appears
to be necessary owing to changes in the cost
of labour and materials or other circumstances affecting the canals. I can assure
hon, Members that the Ministry of Commerce
does not wish to maintain charges of this
kind beyond what are absolutely necessary.
Hon. Members have stated in the House
that it is their desire that everything
should be done to encourage those in
control of the canals So as to make a
better and more effective use of these
systems. Now if this amendment was
accepted those in control of canals in
Northern Ireland would on the 31st December be in a less favourable position than
those in control of the canals in England
and also those in control of the canals in the
Free State. I am sure when hon. Members
consider that that would be the position of
those in control of the canals in Northern
Ireland, with the consequence that our
services might be restricted, they would not
desire to place those in control of these canals
in a worse position. Therefore, I think
that hon. Members will agree with me that
the amendment should be rejected.

Criminal Law Amendment Bill.
Considered in Committee.
Mr. ROBB in the Chair.
Clause 1 (Consent of young person to be
no defence). It shall be no defence to a
charge or indictment for an indecent assault
on a child or young person under the age
of sixteen to prove that he or she consented
to the act of indecency.
Committee.
Criminal Law Bill-
20 MARCH 1923.
Mr. CRAWFORD: On behalf of Mr. Lynn
I beg to nove in Clause 1, page 3, line 7,
leave out "sixteen" and insert 'eighteen."
Sir DAWSON BATES. With regard to the
Amendment moved by my hon. Friend (Mr.
Crawford), I think that the hon Members
who raised this question at the time of the
Second Reading brought it up rather from
the moral than from the criminal standpoint.
Might I suggest that you cannot improve the
condition of people's morals by the Acts of
Parliament? I do suggest that you can
lessen crime by Acts of Parliament, and it
is for that purpose that this particular Bil
is being brought in. What we want to do
is to prevent a wrong being perpetrated on
a girl who has not reached the age when
she ought in the ordinary course of events
to understand the difference between right
and wrong, and we suggest that that age
should be sixteen. It was suggested by some
hon. Members at the Second Reading that
some girls at eighteen are more innocent
than girls of sixteen. I suggest there are
some girls of twenty-one who have been
brought up in the country or in certain
surroundings who may know less than girls
of sixteen. The law at the present time allows
girls of seventeen to marry, and presumably they must know the difference between
right and wrong. I do not think if this
Amendment is accepted by the House it
will prevent any girl under eighteen from
marrying and I want to suggest, furthermore,
that if the age was extended to eighteen the
law ought to apply to both sexes. Let me
take an extreme case-perhaps hon. Members
will differ from me-to show what may result
if we pass an Amendment of this sort. Take
a girl of, say, seventeen who is married and
whose matrimonial life is not so pleasant
as it might be. She meets a young fellow
of about sixteen or seventeen, and that young
fellow proceeds to take an interest in her and
to try to protect her from her husband's
ill-usage, or something of that sort, and
illicit intercourse takes place between the
two of them. What happens? That boy of
sixteen or seventeen can be convicted of a
criminal offence while the woman gets off.
Surely it is absurd to think that that girl
knows less than that boy, and does a case
of this sort not leave the door open very
much to blackmail on the part of the
husband? Might I go further and say that
if this Amendment was accepted under
which the age should be extended to eighteen
it would become a dead letter because in
many cases the juries would not convict?
They look upon offences of this sort as more
or less technical, and know the injustice that
might easily be done to an accused person.
Mr. McGUFFIN: May I ask if the right
hon. Gentleman has in his mind the probability of blackmail? It was proved at the
Second Reading that in the experience of
lawyers it does not arise once in 200 cases,
so why mention it here?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I think hon, Members who have studied this question know
that blackmail exists in these cases more
than in any other class of offence.
Mr. M'GUFFIN: I agree.
Sir DAWSON BATES: This is a new House
and we ought to be very careful as to the
legislation we pass. This subject was brought
up in the British House of Commons first of
all in 1885. A few years ago the Act was
amended by taking away the defence of
reasonable and probable cause, but no one
suggested in the Imperial House that the age
should be raised above 16. I have discussed
this matter with a very eminent authority in
criminal law, and he suggested that from
many points of view it would be a great mistake for us at the present time to make such
a grave difference in the law in Northern Ireland from that which prevails in England.
Take another absurdity that might arise.
Take the case of a young fellow who takes
a girl to the Isle of Man, and something happens there. That young man would not have
committed an offence. On the other hand,
a young fellow who took a girl to a seaside
resort in Northern Ireland would have committed an offence. I do suggest that the more
we try to make the people moral by force of
law the greater our difficulties will be. There
is another difficulty. In Northern Ireland we
have no Court of Criminal Appeal, and therefore in connection with the various points
that arise from time to time it is of enormous
advantage to us to have the decisions of the
English Courts. We would not have that advantage if we proceed to make a great difference in the law in Northern Ireland as compared with that in England.
Mrs. CHICHESTER: 1 feel that, unfortunately, I cannot agree with the Amendment
proposed by the hon. Member for Antrim
(Mr. Crawford). It is a matter, I think, of
common knowledge that girls of from 16 to 18,
except in very rare instances, cannot possibly
be considered as children, and I feel that in
taking up the position which I am adopting
I will in no way act other than hon. Members
would wish that their womankind should act.
On the contrary, I should like to point out
that our women's associations-at any rate
the ones which we have locally-are not at
all anxious that this point should be pressed
with regard to the raising of the age from
16 to 18. I think we cannot forget that we
are here to preserve the interests of all
classes of the community, to see that justice
is done to all, that fair play is dealt out
to all, and that we are not here merely to
legislate for the protection of our girls and

cannot possibly support the Amendment, and
I feel very strongly that hon, Members should
reflect gravely before they press it

Mr. MEGAW: So that the judge will have
no discretion to give less than the fixed
penalty. There may be isolated cases-very
possibly there are isolated cases-in which
the judges perhaps do not inflict the penalty
that some people think the offence should
really bear, but a very great change would
be introduced in jurisprudence generally if
the right of a judge to exercise his discretion
were taken away. There are very few
offences in the criminal law in which a judge
is compelled to give a sentence, but there
are undoubtedly such cases. It is well to
remember here that magistrates have no
jurisdiction over these offences, and that
they can only be dealt with by a judge and
jury, and generally it is by a High Court
judge. I think that when a man has reached
the position of a High Court judge he is
in a position to weigh the pros and cons of
a case and to give a proper sentence. Some
cases may arise in which there may be circumstances such as the question of the capacity of
the man who is guilty. The guilty man may
not be responsible for his acts at all.
may be on the verge of madness or something
of that sort, and it is always of the greatest
importance that the judge should be able
to size up-if I may use that expressionall the aspects of the case before he inflicts
punishment. The suggestion of my hon.
Friend (Mr. McGuffin) opens up a very much
wider scope, and I do not think it can be
dealt with properly under this section. If

the criminal law generally that a judge shall
have no discretion with regard to sentences,
well and good, it is a matter that will

The reason for this is that this Bill when

the difficulty was got over and the accused

Mr. McGUFFIN: Was that not under the
Courts-Martial?
Mr. MEGAW: No; under the ordinary
regulations. Where offences were charged
under the regulations of our own Act there
was a proviso that the accused person could
give evidence on his own behalf. These
Sections are absolutely unnecessary now,
seeing that there is a general law affecting
them all. On the other hand this will introduce an addition to Schedule 1, namely, that
the Summary Jurisdiction Act, as it was
passed should be enforced. This Bill of ours
only enables evidence to be given by the
accused on his own behalf or by his wife
in case the accused shall so determine, but
there are some Acts of an earlier time which
enable the wife or the husband of the accused
to give evidence whether the accused is
anxious for them to do so or not. For
instance where the wife suffers from bad
treatment by her husband, it is absolutely
necessary in that case that the wife should
be enabled to give evidence, and the Summary Jurisdiction Act, 1908, provides for that.
If that were not preserved by being put into
this Schedule it would make the law such
that the wife could only give evidence against
her husband if the husband himself consented to it. Consequently the provisions
that were already enforced in that Act require to be preserved. That is what is being
done by this amended sub-Section.
Amendment agreed to.
Clause as amended ordered to stand part
of the Bill

Mr. POLLOCK: I beg to move in Clause 5,
page 7, line 25, at end add "And any payment so waived shall be shown in the
accounts of capital receipts and capital expenditure kept under this Act." Perhaps I
should explain the purport of this addition
in view of the possible obscurity and doubt
as to the waiving of interest upon money.
Probably I could explain it better by means
of an illustration. In the case of land purchase annuities there are very many small
payments, and under the Act it is impossible
for the Department to waive the interest if
by any chance the payment is not made
upon the exact date upon which it is due.
But it often happens that the payers of these
small amounts postpone these payments for
two or three days, and the amounts of interest accrued are only possibly a penny or
three halfpence; therefore, it can be understood that it is not an economical process to
undertake the recovery of any such small
amount. The object of this Clause is to provide
that these amounts may be waived to a particular time, and that any amount so waived shall
be shown in the accounts of capital receipts
and capital expenditure kept under this Act.
I beg to move.
Amendment agreed to.

Major SHILLINGTON: I have not put
down any Amendment in reference to this
matter, but I would like to ask the Government to give an assurance that temporary
officials will not be appointed in districts
where there are men of the R.U.C. at present stationed who have the Board of Trade
certificate qualifying them to do this work.
When the Minister of Home Affairs moved
the Second Reading of this Measure, I criticised it, and from information I treated it
with a certain amount of suspicion. From
further information that has come to my
215 Weights and Measures Bill- HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Committee.
[Major Shillington]
knowledge since then that suspicion has been
more or less confirmed. The Minister of
Home Affairs told the House that there were
only some five men transferred from the
R.I.C. to the R.U.C. who had the necessary
certificate to enable them to do this work,
and, although it was not actually stated, he
rather led the House to believe that this
Measure was absolutely necessary, as those
five officials were being more or less snowed
under with the tremendous number of
weights and measures that were simply crying out to be stamped. Instead of that being
the case, I find that two men in a certain
county-in Armagh-have the certificate, and
are not at present doing this work. It would
appear as if their jobs had been taken from
them by some temporarily appointed officials.
In my opinion-and I am sure hon. Members
will agree with me-in a case like that there
was no necessity in that particular county
for these extra officials to be appointed at all.
I would also like to have some information as
to how these officials were appointed, and if
an opportunity was given to all ex-members
of the R.I.C. who had the necessary qualification to apply for these positions, or if
simply a few were selected and appointed?
The CHAIRMAN: I would point out to
the hon. Member that it would have been
better to have raised this matter on the
Second reading than on the motion now before the House. The Third reading will be
taken presently, and I think his observations
would be more appropriate then.
Major SHILLINGTON: I would like a
guarantee from the Government that they
will not appoint these officials in areas in
which there are men of the R.U.C. with the
necessary certificates and able to carry out
these duties.
Sir DAWSON BATES: With reference to
the point raised by my hon. Friend (Major
Shillington), I would like to clear up any
misunderstanding that has arisen. At the
present time there are fourteen members of
the Royal Ulster Constabulary who hold
Board of Trade Certificates. Of these eleven
are head-constables, and I think hon. Members will agree with me that it would be
neither economic nor suitable to utilise the
services of head-constables for this class of
work. Head-constables act in the place of
district-inspectors in the absence of those
officers. In addition there are three sergeants
who have Board of Trade certificates, and
for similar reasons it is inexpedient that
those three sergeants should be utilised for
that particular work. Apart altogether
from the question of efficiency of the
services of the whole I would like
to
remind the House that a sergeant
receives, I think, something over £5 a week,
and these temporary inspectors receive a
sum of about £3 a week. From an economical point of view it would be very undesirable to utilise those sergeants, but we propose to limit this Act to one year, and at
the end of that time it will be impossible
for the Government to employ anybody but
members of the Royal Ulster Constabulary,
I hope by that time we will have a sufficient
number of men of the Royal Ulster Constabulary, constables or whoever they are,
who will be in a position to act.

As hon. Members can see, the Bill is of

bring our local Acts up-to-date. But there
are several important matters which I hope
this House will agree to and allow to go
into Committee, because they are of the
greatest importance to the Corporation. The
most important matter, perhaps, is in connection with our City Tramways, and it is
included in Clauses 5 to 18. Here I should
explain that the Belfast Corporation own
the City tramways, which is an undertaking
of which the City is justly proud.
financial undertaking it is all that could be
desired, but hon. Members will no doubt
know that when constructing a tramway, and
in particular when constructing this new
electric tramway, the Corporation could not
lay down lines to meet the requirements for
ten or twenty years hence. The cost of
construction, independent of the cost of upkeep, is a very serious matter. What will
inevitably take place on any tramway is
that where you have a tramway going out
into the country a new colony will spring
up, and in a few years there is a call for
transport to this place. This has occurred
in several parts of Belfast, and the Corporation feel that the time has now arrived
when it will pay them to proceed with the
construction of lines, to the greatest possible
advantage of the people living in those
localities. Naturally here again we have
opposition from the railway companies to
those lines which will run parallel to the
railways. They rightly claim that the tramways will interfere with their revenue.
The greatest opposition, however, comes
from the County Councils, who are pressing
for demands which, if we agreed to, would
render it impossible for the Belfast Corporation to construct the lines. They are asking
the Corporation to agree to street widening,
the making of street footpaths, etc., and they
ask to be relieved entirely of the expense. I
am not in a position to-day to enter into
details. An opportunity will be afforded in
Committee to try to settle these matters in
dispute, because in my opinion these are questions that must be settled between the parties
concerned, otherwise the Corporation could
not proceed with that part of the Bill. This
applies to the Dundonald route, where the
Corporation are seeking powers to extend
the tramways as far as Dundonald Cemetery.
There is great traffic on that route every
day, and the extension of the tramways to
that point would be a great convenience.
The same remark also applies to other
routes. There is one proposed extension of
the line that this House will have to
sanction, and that is from Belmont Road
to Stormont, to give facilities to the workmen who are engaged in the building of
the Parliament House and afterwards to the
vast army of officials located in the Parliament House. The Corporation are also
asking for powers to construct lines within
the City and I do not anticipate there will
be any objection to that in this House.
Another question of a controversial character is contained in Clauses 19 to 25, with
reference to the running of omnibuses within
and without the City of Belfast. I am free
to admit that those Clauses if passed as
they stand in the Bill would give very extensive powers to the Corporation. They
could, if they so desired, run omnibuses to
Holywood, Bangor, Lisburn, Carrickfergus,
or wherever they desired, but I wish to
explain that that is not the intention of
the Corporation. Instead of putting down
tramway lines at present at great cost, their
intention is to use these omnibuses until
such time as it will pay to lay down lines.
There are also some connecting links in the
tramway system where omnibuses would be
very useful, but I recognise that Clause 19
as it stands requires amendment, and if the
House will allow these lauses to go into
Committee they can be amended there. To
give the Corporation powers to run omnibuses where they liked within a radius of
twenty miles might be very dangerous.
Another very important matter in connection with the tramways is the Corporation's
desire to acquire property known as
"Hazelwood," which adjoins Bellevue Gardens, and includes certain water rights and
221 Belfast Corporation Bill-

21 MARCH 1923.
Second Reading.
a mansion house that would be of the
greatest service to the Corporation.
Now I come to another very important
matter in connection with our Gas undertaking. The Corporation own the Gas works
and we are proud of them as a commercial
concern. I am sure this House will be
pleased to know that although the Corporation have to bring coal from across the
water, gas is supplied to the inhabitants
cheaper than in any other place in the
United Kingdom. At great expense the
Corporation have constructed huge works
which when completed will be capable of
turning out more gas than is required by
the citizens of Belfast. Therefore in this
Bill the Corporation are seeking power to
sell gas in the neighbouring districts, which
will confer a great boon on those districts.
The Corporation is also asking for power
to purchase the North of Ireland Chemical
Works to manufacture residuals, and we
believe that will be a paying proposition so
far as the Corporation is concerned. I hope
that in considering these two branches of
the Corporation's services hon. Members will
realise that it will be for the benefit of the
City if they allow these matters to go to
the Committee and any little amendments
that may be necessary can be made there.
Another question that has been the subject
of a great deal of controversy is that of
chemists' shops. In Clause 46 the Corporation are seeking power to open chemists'
shops. That again is a very dangerous
practice, and I am happy to state for the
benefit of this House that the Corporation
have already made an arrangement with the
chemists of the City whereby medicine can
be procured at all times of the night. The
reason the Corporation put in this Cause
was that so many chemists' shops were lockup shops, and in cases of urgency there
was great difficulty in obtaining medicine.
However, I am glad to say that the chemists
of the city have come to an amicable arrangement with the Corporation in regard
to that matter, and thus there will be no
opposition to that Clause.
Combined opposition from all over the
Six Counties has been offered to Clauses
50, 51 and 52. I must take them together
because they deal with milk and meat. Some
of the country districts seem to think that
the Corporation have no right to interfere
with work that they think they are perfectly
entitled to do, but I would like to point out
that the Corporation have no desire whatever to interfere with the County Council,
but they consider they have a right-and I
believe they have-to see that the milk and
meat that come into Belfast for consumption
by the inhabitants are pure and wholesome.
All they ask for in this Bill is that they
should have power to go out and inspect
at the source of supply. That only applies
to dairies which supply milk to Belfast. The
Corporation have no desire to interfere with
milk supplied ontside the City. If the
Water Commissioners go to Woodburn,
Stonyford, and the Mourne Mountains and
buy up villages and houses and land, what
is it for? Is it not to go to the very source
of supply so that the public of Belfast are
assured of having pure water? If it is
important to have a pure water supply
surely it is as important to have a pure milk
supply. Then take meat. The Corporation
of Belfast have gone to great expense in
erecting an Abattoir up-to-date in every way.
At considerable cost they employ professional men to see that no meat leaves the
Abattoir that is not perfectly sound. I am
sure it will surprise this House when I tell
them that of the cows slaughtered in that
Abattoir 20 per cent. are suffering from
tuberculosis. I do not mean to suggest that
the owners are aware of that fact, but professional men can detect the disease and they
remove the parts which are not fit for consumption and allow the rest to pass out.
What happens? Take a man-and unfortunately there are some-who has no regard for the class of food he sells. He knows
before an animal is slaughtered whether it
will pass or not. He slaughters the animal
outside the city boundary, removes the
traces of the disease,-which is very easily
done, and brings it back into the city.
There is then no means of detecting the
disease and the meat is sold for consumption.
It has been suggested that a compromise
might be arrived at by the Corporation
adopting a limit of five or six miles outside
Belfast and there is a precedent for that in
England. But I do not think that would
meet the case because if a man will go six
miles out of the city to slaughter an animal
he will go seven or eight miles. I am in a
position to say on behalf of the Corporation
that they recognise that if they do not come
to some arrangement with those who oppose
these Clauses the Bill might never reach the
Committee stage, and having regard to the
fact that the members of County Councils
have expressed themselves in the
way they have, the Corporation
are prepared to drop these Clauses
altogether. At the same time I feel very
strongly on this question, and I hope that
although the Corporation will drop these
Clauses the Government will bring in a Bill
dealing with this very important matter.
After all, the people in Coleraine, Ballymena,
and Armagh have just as much right to get
sound meat and pure milk as the people of
Belfast.
I think this is a matter that should
be taken up for the Province as a whole,

Milk comes into Belfast in very, very large

depots and properly handled, so that it will

Another very contentious Clause is Clause
69. This Clause is just as strongly opposed
by the ratepayers of the city of Belfast as
the other Clauses, to which I have just referred, are opposed by the representatives
of the country districts and by the County
Councils. It has reference to coal. There

Belfast by a long way. They use it for their
gas and electricity departments; they sell
coke in large or small quantities, and at
certain times during recent years when there
was a shortage of coal they passed it to the
poorer people. The idea at the time this
Bill was drafted was to supply the poorer
people with quantities of coal at practically
cost price. But if the Clause is passed as it
stands in the Bill there is no doubt it would
give the Corporation very extensive powers
to open depots all over the city. In addition success would be very doubtful, and the
loss, if any, would certainly fall upon the
ratepayers of Belfast. To this Clause great
objection has been taken. I do not
an
know what view this House would
take, whether they would like
assurance that this Clause would be dropped,
or whether they would like to allow it to go

If it is the view of the House that it should

deals with the sale of our markets, and 1
do not see that there will be any objection

an opportunity might occur to dispose of

desires to have the power to do so. There

which I take it, will not really concern this

Mr. JOHNSTONE: I beg to second the
motion for the Second reading of this Bill.
I do not think I need add very much to the
very extensive and exhaustive summary of
its provisions which has been given to the
House by the hon. Member for South Belfast
(Sir Crawford M'Cullagh). I should like
to emphasise very much the hope that was
expressed by him that the Government will
take up this question of the inspection of
meat. My name appears on the back of this
Bill as one of its promoters, and it never
would have appeared there if these
Clauses with regard to the inspection
of meat and milk had not been in the Bill.
This matter was considered by a meeting of
the Ulster Medical Society, which is composed
of members from all over the Province, and
they unanimously approved, and those of us
who had the honour to be at that meeting
and to be Members of Parliament were asked
to press this Clause in this House. I realise
that perhaps the Belfast Corporation have
taken the best way they could out of the
matter by withdrawing these Clauses altogether. It was a very expensive way of
remedying a very serious fault, and was more
or less certain to lead to friction. There is
a very much better way and that is by the
County Councils doing their duties and inspecting dairies and meat in the same way
as those articles are inspected in Belfast at
present. That is really the only way in
which it will ever be effectively done, and it
will never be effectively done until the whole
public health administration of Northern
Ireland is put on a proper basis.

The PRIME MINISTER (Sir James Craig):
I would like only to intervene in the debate
for a few moments, because some hon. Members of the House may not be thoroughly
familiar with the custom that has grown up
in connection with Private Bill legislation,
and I think everyone in this House would be
more than sorry if anything happened to the
first venture of the Belfast Corporation in
coming to this new Parliament for power to
control matters connected with the great city
of Belfast. Therefore, I would like to point
out to hon. Members that it is very seldom
there is any debate upon the Second Reading
of a Private Bill. The procedure after the
Second Reading is that the Committee-a
special Committee, consisting of three Members of the Senate and three hon. Members
of our own House-go into all the Clauses
most exhaustively. having before them
learned counsel who are able to bring out all
the pros and cons of the questions at issue,
and it is after that, if something of a very
serious character still remains in the Bill
that causes opposition, that this House has
the right-and a perfect right-to review it.
I would ask hon. Members, therefore, to
allow the Second Reading to take place, in no
way pledging them to accept the Third Reading, but to give the Committee of this House,
vigilantly acting upon tradition, and acting
for the individual Members of this House,
an opportunity, first of all, of studying the
Measure with that meticulous care which
is more easily attained when assisted by
learned counsel, and then afterwards to pass
our judgment upon the Bill. I think so far
the hon. Member-and if I may I would compliment him upon his lucid speech-and the
representatives of the Corporation have
treated this House with the utmost courtesy
and have met the individual Members in the
most friendly way for the purpose of endeavouring to smooth over those difficulties to
which serious objection might have been
taken. May I just say, with regard to the
hints which have been thrown out, that
possibly the Government might take over
Clauses 50, 51, and 52 with a view to legislating at some future time, I am very
hopeful that the hon. Member for Derry
(Mrs. Chichester) who has just spoken is
voicing the sentiments of this House and of
Ulster as a whole when she expressed the
hope that this short debate will really penetrate to those who have to carry on the
anxious duty of inspection of all sorts in
the Six Counties, because, undoubtedly, the
health of the community is to a large extent
dependent upon the vigilance with which our
Inspectors carry on their work. It may be
that this debate will have the desired effect
without the Government having to legislate
in the matter. I can only say that personally I am proud to be here to-day to listen
to the first request of the great City of Belfast
to be allowed to introduce a Bill of far-reaching effect, and which, I feel perfectly certain,

Dr. MORRISON: On Thursday last I asked
a question with regard to the appointment
of Auditors in this House, and I gave notice
that to-day I would raise the matter. In
connection with the co-operative movement
and as a wise provision on the part of the
Government special auditors had to be
appointed under the Industrial Acts. In
the past those auditors, I gather, were
appointed from London and we had very
little control over them. Sometimes they
were reliable and sometimes they were not
reliable. When we got authority in this
House to carry on our Bills and our legislation this control was transferred. A certain
gentleman was appointed to represent this
House, and he had for his duty the selection
of the auditors who were to carry out this
most important work. In carrying out these
duties of auditing I maintain it is essential
that men of the most upright character
should be chosen. These men are appointed
to deal with friendly societies and they are
appointed to deal with co-operative societies.
Every man who knows anything about the
co-operative movement knows that it is run
by societies organised by voluntary effort,
that is, certain individuals in, say, an agricultural community join together and a
Society is formed. They elect a President,
and they elect a Managing Committee, and
these people are responsible for the carrying
on of the work of that Society, but it is
obvious that these people who are not paid
must in due time get tired of the duty.
Sometimes they get indifferent to examinations, and occasionally, indeed very often,
serious abuses arise. Take, for instance,
the Society in connection with whose liquidation this question has arisen.
established 23 years ago. I was elected as
president, and I remained as president until
now simply because no other member could
be got to take my place. We had a big
turnover in connection with that Society,
and there was a great deal of business done.
Obviously it is impossible for a man like
me to look into the affairs of the business
as closely as a business man devoting his
It was
whole time could do. The result was that,
perhaps, ten years ago I had a deputy appointed. That man died and a further
deputy was appointed, and in the end that
deputy was more or less responsible for the
whole of the administration, except that we
had a manager who was responsible and was
paid, and we had the safeguards that were
conferred upon us by this wise provision of
the Government in the shape of an auditor
who would go into the accounts and detect
any irregularity that existed.
We started our creamery 23 years ago. I
may tell this House there are 190 co-operative
societies in the Six Counties area, and if
these societies are loosely managed, as they
inevitably must be owing to the fact that
there is no personal incentive in the shape
of money for the men who are administering
them, there is all the more necessity for
having auditors who will examine into and
detect any irregularities that exist.
As a
matter of fact, I have been looking up the
minutes of this particular Society, and I find
that for the last four years I have been at
only three meetings of the Committee. I
had devised various checks by which I
thought business could be kept safe, and
I will tell the House how these checks failed
and the result. There is one thing I should
like to say.
After the discussion in this
House the Minister who replied to me asked
me if this matter was going to be raised,
and I said "Certainly." Then he said, "I
want to tell you that if you raise this
question it will not be the auditor whose
conduct will be inquired into, but in conjunction with him it will be that of the
president and the Committee." I maintain
that this was an attempt to close my mouth.
Mr. M'KEOWN: No.
Dr. MORRISON: I maintain it could have
no other meaning than an attempt to close
my mouth in denouncing what I told the
Minister was, in my opinion, a job. I
naturally want to defend the Committee as
far as I can, and to place the whole facts
before the House. The Society got £500 from
friends who were interested in promoting
these co-operative societies. It was a community of farmers co-operating for produce
and for sale, men who had no business
training. There was not a man on the
Committee who had any business training
-I had none-and we were dependent wholly
on the auditor. These friends contributed
£500 to help the farmers in starting this
Society. That history is typical of all cooperative societies. As soon as the Society
got a little better and stronger it paid back
this money it had got from the friends,
because the farmers recognised that if they
were able to pay there was no need for them
to be paupers and be asking for help when

they were able to provide for themselves.
They paid back the loan from the bank,
got a bond they had signed, brought it down
to the Creamery, framed it and set it on
the wall. It is there to this day.
As a
necessary precaution in order to protect ourselves when we got the bond back I arranged
with the bank that the overdraft should not
exceed £1,000, and that there would be no
personal liability on the part of any member
of the Committee, the bank manager in
Coleraine would keep me advised as to the
position of the Society. You will learn before
I have done how he discharged that duty.
For those 23 years the audit was always
very satisfactory, including the last audit,
namely that of 1921.
We had this audit presented in 1922. I was
not at the annual meeting, but I take it I got
the auditor's report. That was probably in
February, and it was of a very satisfactory
nature, but trouble arose in June, 1922. As
a result of that trouble our secretary was
induced to part with £700 as a temporary
loan, and he was asked to keep the transaction quiet, that is, I was not to hear
anything about it, and the Committee was
not to hear anything about it. You will
understand what was the object in that.
Notwithstanding the fact that was done
in June I did not know about it till the
end of October, although I had had several
interviews with the bank manager and bank
directors. Nothing was said to me when I
was negotiating with them, nothing was said
about this £700 that they had got from our
secretary. In addition to that, the creamery
manager carried round to the farmers, and
induced them to sign, a bond for £1,000.
The bank had inside knowledge of the state
of the Society and got £2,000 security in
the way mentioned. I think if they imagine
a working man being bled to that extent the
Labour Members of this House will surely
have some sympathy for the working man
who never got more than 30/- a week in his
life, and whose life savings were taken from
him by that little dodge of signing away
£500 in the back parlour in the Belfast Bank
at Coleraine.
The only man in connection with a Society
like this who is paid is the manager, and the
secretary is frequently also the manager, but
in the case of this Society the secretary was
paid £20 a year, and he gave half of that
salary back to the Society. During the 23
years this Society has been in business I
challenge the fullest investigation into its
workings. I challenge the fullest investigation into anything that I have done in connection with it, and I challenge the fullest investigation into anything that was done by
the Committee or by any member of the Com..
mitte. We may have been lacking in
business talent; we may have been, perhaps,
careless, and may have allowed things to
drift, but we were honest, and we did our
work with the object of promoting agricultural prosperity, and we had a right to expect that an auditor, appointed by the
Government, would have kept us informed
as to the condition of the Society. You
understand how a bank manager, having got
into a hole, endeavours to get out of it, and
he is perhaps not too scrupulous about the
way he gets out of it. You can understand
bank directors who think they have been
imposed on, and who, perhaps, have listened
to a great deal of censure from me, insisting
their pound of flesh. I challenge the
fullest investigation into the working of this
Society, which has sustained in every respect
the high traditions of the co-operative
movement, and nothing dishonourable
dishonest was ever suspected by any member
of the Committee or by me.

I went again to Mr. Litchfield. I had fol
lowed his advice. I had gone to the Home
Office as he suggested. I went back again
to him for counsel, and I told him the position which had developed and which was
worse than I anticipated. I asked him if he
had seen a report that appeared in the Dublin papers with regard to the action of this
man who was appointed a liquidator to an
estate in Dublin. Mr. Litchfield rang a bell
and brought in one of his clerks. He asked
the clerk if he knew about it. "Yes, sir,"
the clerk replied, "I saw the report." An
application had been made in the Courts in
Dublin for leave to serve a writ out of the
jurisdiction of the Court; that is, the solicitor in Dublin wanted leave to serve
the writ in Belfast, which was outside
the jurisdiction of the Court. It was a
very bad affidavit. The affidavit said the
man Reilly had been appointed auditor for
an estate, that he had been dismissed from
being liquidator, that he held money, and
that the action was to make him return the
£60 he held. Now this
was what Mr.
Stewart told Mr. Litchfield in my presence.
We talked about the thing. I said "There
is the type of man you have as public auditor
dealing with Friendly Societies and with
people who are depending fully on him."
Mr Litchfield admitted that it was a bad
state of affairs, and yet he has deliberately,
in spite of all that, re-appointed him. I
sent him the liquidator's report of these
things in Aghadowey. I told him where
the books and fullest information could we
obtained, and yet this worthless auditor has
been appointed with the sanction of the
Ministry of Commerce in Belfast. That has
had a far reaching effect.
If the Committee in Aghadowey had had
any information that they were in danger
they could have reconstructed their society.
There was no need for the farmers to lose
their Creamery. There was no need for the
traders to be robbed of £3,000. If we had
got timely warning and known a couple of
yeais sooner what was going on we could
have reconstructed our Society and put it
on a basis that would have prevented this
disaster following. I have placed the whole
facts before you. It is for you to determine
what course should be taken. I think it is
a monstrous thing that we here in the Six
Counties who are desirous of promoting
honesty, decency and exemplary conduct in

who is paid a salary of something like £1,200

what the Minister of Commerce
may have
against me or against this committee of

Mr. MARK: As one who has heard a great
deal before to-day with regard to the
Aghadowey Creamery, and as one who
knows a little in regard to the consternation that exists in County Derry owing
to this failure amongst the agricultural
community, I would like to say a
few words. I do not intend to wade through
the whole voluminous business in regard to
the winding up of this Society, but I should
like to say a word or two as to how it appears to farmers generally. This Society has
been in existence for over 23 years. Until
quite recently it was a thriving concern. Undoubtedly, the manager has been guilty of
embezzlement, or something of that nature.
These embezzlements, or defalcations, have
been spread over a period of four years. Each
year the accounts have been audited, and so
far as the Committee was concerned the report was a rosy one, and they had a right to
feel every confidence in the concern they
were managing. So far as the Committee
was concerned, I cannot see they were in any
way to blame.
I had the honour to be a
member of a similar committee
for many
years in a co-operative society, and I know
the business there was carried on in a similar
way to the Aghadowey Society, but we had
the good fortune to have a straightforward,
honest official on whom we could depend. We
had also the good fortune to have our accounts audited by a gentleman who I am
not prepared to say did his work in a proper
way or not. At any rate, the manager was
an honest man and kept the accounts right.
In this case, the auditor was either guilty of
gross negligence in not discovering that embezzlement was taking place, or he knew it
was taking place and tried to screen the
gentleman who was committing the sin. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) In either case, I
think he was equally guilty. There are only
two explanations. He either knew of it and
tried to help the manager out of the difficulty, or he did not take the trouble and
pains as an auditor to do his duty.
The upshot was that the Committee were
let down and that several farmers lost a
great deal of money. That has undoubtedly
shaken their confidence in the co-operative
movement, at a time, too, when COthe
operation should be
order of the
day, and when it was never more
needed than now amongst the ranks of the
agricultural community. The hon. Member
for the University (Dr. Morrison) said that
these facts were brought before the Ministry
of Commerce, and that it was pointed out to
the Ministry that this auditor failed to find
different matters in which there was difficulty. The liquidator, on examining the
books in a short space of time, ascertained
and reported fully on every point on which
embezzlement had taken place. I think if
this auditor had gone into the books in the
thorough fashion in which the liquidator did
he was bound to find out what was wrong,
not in the fourth year but in the very first
year when the matter was starting, and have
it nipped in the bud. Had that been done, I
say the concern would to-day be a thriving
concern. It was by the negligence of this
auditor that the Committee have been let
down, and that this valuable property of the
farmers in the locality has gone to ruin. If
the Minister made the appointment knowing
these facts, I would like to hear the explanation that can be given, or how he can stand
over the appointment of a man who has been
guilty of such gross negligence as this gentleman.
