The audit of this Society's accounts in
1921 showed a surplus of £678 whereas there
was an actual deficiency. Could the result
of such an audit be due to a careful inspection of the books? I do not think so.
The auditor was either guilty of indifference
or he was the tool of some other person. I
do not think it is the prerogative of this
House to pronounce an opinion. This matter
concerns an institution in which working
men are largely interested, and there are
some 170 of these Societies throughout the
Province of Ulster. It concerns an institution in which working men have a great
interest and therefore it behoves the Ministry to be very careful in the appointment
of auditors in order to see that the interests
of these men and their investments are safeguarded beyond their own power to do so.
There is nothing more important than this
that should weigh with the Ministry in appointing an auditor. The Ministry could
not deny that they had the record of this
auditor before them when they re-appointed
him. This is a case that is almost without
parallel. I do not know how the Minister
will account for it, but one thing is sure,
and that is that it will shake the confidence
of people in co-operative societies if those
who are appointed by the Ministry to act as
public auditors cannot be trusted. This may
be only one case, but if the Ministry, in view
of all the circumstances, re-appoints this auditor year after year it will very much shake
the confidence of the community in public
auditors. I am particularly sorry the Ministry took the corrse it did in this matter,
because the evidence seems to be conclusive,
and in view of all the facts I think the hon.
Member for the University has put an unanswerable case before the Ministry, and it
will be very interesting to the House to see
how the Minister will attempt to answer it.
The Ministry of Commerce generally do
things with scrupulous care, but I hope that
in the appointment of public auditors it will
be more careful in future.

When
a Company goes into liquidation it is a very
different state of affairs to having books
audited. Take, for instance, one point alone.
An auditor has got to accept the valuation
of stocks as given by responsible officials of
the Company. An auditor cannot be expected
to value stocks, because he knows nothing
about them. When a company is being
wound up, the first thing a liquidator does
is to bring in competent people and pay them
to value the stocks at what they consider is
a fair market price at the time. It seems to
me that all this discussion about the matter
being discovered by the liquidator is due to

auditor to carry out the duties of a liquidator. I think that if some means could be
devised whereby these societies could get expert advice in the management of their affairs
it would be a good thing, but there being no
such machinery at present they have to do
the best they can.

This matter is not only serious from the
point of view of the auditor concerned, but
raises, to my mind, a very important question of principle, and I world venture,
therefore, to lay before the House the facts of
the case as we knew them. Prior to 1922
all appointments of public auditors under the
Friendly Societies and the Industrial and Provident Societies Acts for the United Kingdom
were made by the Treasury, but as from 1st
January, 1922, the powers of the Treasury
with respect to such appointments in Northern Ireland were transferred to and vested
in the Ministry of Commerce. It should be
noted that the society in question-I refer to
the Aghadowey Creamery-was an Industrial
and Provident Society-these societies are
usually known as Co-operative Societies-and
that the auditor of such a society must be a
public auditor. When the list of public auditors for 1923 was under consideration, obviously the majority of the gentlemen seeking re-appointments as public auditors in
Northern Ireland were those passed on to us
from the Imperial Government, and the
gentleman to whose appointment the hon.
Member (Dr. Morrison) has taken exception
was one of that majority. It would appear
that he was first appointed a public auditor
for the United Kingdom in the year 1897,
and that his appointment was renewed every
year up to the year 1922, when he was appointed for Northern Ireland. It is, therefore, well to remember that this gentleman
in question had been a public auditor for
twenty-five years without a stain upon his
character.

to state whether he would accept re-appointment for the year 1923, and his reply was in
the affirmative.
I desire that hon. Members should understand that this was our position-the
position of the Ministry of Commerce-at the

On the eve of the publication of the appointments of Public Auditors, representations of
semi-confidential nature were made
a

It is well to remember that the Registrar
of Friendly Societies had no power to step

negligence the liquidator could bring an

misconduct, the matter could be brought be
fore the Society of which he is a member.
Proper attention was given to the matter
by the Ministry of Commerce, and both the
liquidator and the auditor were invited to
attend at the Ministry. After a discussion
of the case with these gentlemen separately
it was decided-and this was the decision
come to after serious consideration-that
upon the balance of all the considerations
there was not sufficient evidence on which to
withhold the re-appointment of the auditor
in question.
Hon. Members will agree that it would be
a very grave matter, and scarcely in accordance with the principles of elementary justice
and fair play, if the professional career of
any gentleman, and especially a gentleman
with twenty-five years of honourable service
behind him, could be prejudiced, and in fact
brought to an abrupt termination as regards
an important section of his activities as the
result of confidential or unofficial representations made by a Member of Parliament or
by other persons (hon. Members: Hear,
hear) and as there was no power on the

or to hold an inquiry into the manner in
which the audits had been conducted and at
which the gentleman might have been
present, it was decided as a pure matter of
justice that he should be re-appointed, and
that, if and when definite charges against him
were made and proved, his appointment could
be cancelled.
Mr. M'GUFFIN: Why not suspend his
appointment? Would not that have been

Mr. M'KEOWN: It would have been
agreeing to a charge made against an
honourable gentleman that had not been
proven. I would like after the discussion
that has taken place in this House, shortly
to state what are the actual duties of an
auditor? It is important that gentlemen who
are in touch or associated with societies of
this kind throughout the country should
know exactly what the duties of an auditor
are. The duties were defined by Lord Justice
Lopes in the following terms:
"It is the duty of an Auditor to bring to
bear on the work he has to perform that
skill, care, and caution which a reasonably
competent, careful, and cautious auditor
would use. What is reasonable skill, care
and caution must depend on the particular
circumstances of each case. An auditor is
not bound to be a detective, or, as was said,

to approach his work with suspicion, or
with a foregone conclusion that there is
something wrong."
That, as has been pointed out by my hon.
Friend (Mr. Lloyd Campbell), is more the
work of a liquidator.
He is a watchdog, not a bloodhound. He
is justified in believing tried servants of
the company in whom confidence is placed
by the company. He is entitled to assume
that they are honest, and to rely upon
their representations, provided he takes
reasonable care. If there is anything calculated to excite suspicion, he should probe
it to the bottom; but in the absence of
anything of that kind he is only bound to
be reasonably cautious and careful.
It is not the duty of an auditor to take
stock; he is not a stock expert; there are
many matters in which he must rely on the
honesty and accuracy of others. He does
not guarantee the discovery of all fraud.
The appointment of an auditor of any society
or company cannot be regarded-and it is
well for those who take responsibility to remember this-as an absolute insurance
against embezzlement or fraud. The fees are
moderate, and there is no obligation on the
part of the auditor to attend at the offices
of the society So far as the Industrial and
Provident Societies are concerned, one of the
best safeguards they have or should have is
a careful supervision throughout the year by
the Committee of Management-I think that
will appeal to all fair-minded men--and this
Committee of Management should meet at

over the books that are kept. My hon. Friend

The question confronting the Ministry at the

unblemished reputation, and who was himself unaware of the complaint against him by
withholding his re-appointment as a public

largely dependent. It is an axiom of British

If the hon. Member (Dr. Morrison) and

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Thursday, 22nd March, 1923.
The House met at Three of the Clock, Mr.
SPEAKER in the Chair.
ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS.
Movement of Potatoes.
AN APPLICATION REFUSED.
1. Mr. BURN (for Mr. Lynn) asked the
Minister of Agriculture whether an application made by Robert Maxwell, Ballygraffin,
Kircubbin, for leave to sell 80 tons of
potatoes in the City of Belfast to a dairyman
for the purpose of feeding cattle, at 8d. per
cwt., was refused, notwithstanding that the
potatoes were of immune variety, grown on
a farm where black scab was never found,
and where a permit had been granted to
dispose of seed outside of the area; and
whether any compensation will be made to
Mr. Maxwell?
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY TO
THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE (Mr.
M'Keown): I have been asked by my right
hon. Friend to reply. An application as
stated for movement of 80 tons of potatoes
was received from Mr. Robert Maxwell, and
was refused after careful consideration.
While black scab was not actually found
on Mr. Maxwell's farm, the townland of
Ballygraffin is in close proximity to several
townlands in which serious outbreaks of
disease occurred. The hon. Member is misinformed when he suggests that a permit
had been granted to dispose of seed potatoes
outside the scheduled area. The case of
Mr. Maxwell is similar to many others, and
no question of paying compensation arises.
PERMITS IN KIRCUBBIN-PORTAFERRY
AREA.
2. Mr. BURN (for Mr. Lynn) asked the
Minister of Agriculture how many permits
were applied for by farmers in the Black
Scab area of Kircubbin to Portaferry; how
many have been granted, and why, if immune
varieties are grown, are permits granted to
sell seed of these potatoes outside the Black
Scab area while permission is refused to sell
the main crop outside the area?
Mr. McKEOWN: Six applications for
permits were received in the Ministry from
persons in the area mentioned. No permits
have been granted. In no case is a permit
granted to sell seed potatoes grown in the
scheduled area to parts of Ireland outside
that area.
QUANTITIES IN BLACK SCAB AREAS.
3. Mr. BURN (for Mr. Lynn) asked the
Minister of Agriculture if he has any knowledge of the quantities of potatoes in the
several Black Scab areas in the Six Counties;
what, if any, assistance is given to the
farmers to dispose of their potatoes; how
many permits have been asked by farmers
in Black Scab areas to dispose of their
immune varieties of potatoes outside of the
Black Scab area, and how many of these
permits have been granted
Mr. McKEOWN: The Minister is aware
that there is a considerable surplus of
potatoes in the Black Scab areas. The Ministry has taken all practicable steps to assist
farmers in the scheduled areas to dispose of
their potatoes so far as is consistent with
the Ministry's duty of protecting clean areas
against the introduction of disease. Twentyone applications for permits have been received from farmers within the Black Scab
area to dispose of their immune varieties of
potatoes outside of these areas. Fourteen of
these applications have been granted in an
area between Ballyhalbert and Ballywalter
which was scheduled a few years ago on
account of one case of disease on one particular farm. Since then no case of disease
in this area has been discovered.
LARGE STOCKS IN ARDS PENINSULA.
4. Captain MULHOLLAND asked the Minister of Agriculture whether he is aware that
farmers in the Ards peninsula have very
large stocks of potatoes on their hands; that
the wholesale price of these potatoes is sixpence per hundred-weight; that the farmers
will be involved in ruin unless they can
dispose of these enormous stocks at a fair
price; and whether he will state what steps
he has taken to assist them in their
difficulties.
Mr. McKEOWN: The Minister is aware
that in the Ards peninsula as throughout
the potato-growing districts in the Northern
area, large stocks of potatoes remain unsold.
The latest returns show that in the Ards
peninsula the price paid locally is about 15s
per ton. The Ministry realises that the whole
potato position is very serious but it is a
question of supply and demand. The situation in non-scheduled districts is just as
serious as in scheduled districts.
The Ministry have taken every step to try
to procure markets in Great Britain and
abroad.
Captain MULHOLLAND: Arising out of
that answer, may I ask my hon. Friend what
steps have been taken to get rid of these

potatoes in the Ards peninsula. He has not

INTERMEDIATE CERTIFICATES.
5. Dr. MORRISON asked the Parliamentary
Secretary to the Ministry of Education
whether he can state why the Intermediate
Certificates awarded for the Examinations of
last June are not yet available, as on previous occasions such Certificates were dispatched before Christmas?
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY TO
THE MINISTRY OF EDUCATION (Mr.
McKeown): It is the case that the Intermediate Certificates have not yet been issued.
The delay is explained by two facts, namely,
that fresh designs for the Certificates had to
be prepared, and that the provincial firm
which secured the printing contract has taken
considerably longer than was anticipated to
finish the work. The Ministry greatly regret
that the delay has occurred, but they are
assured by the Stationery Office that the
printing will be completed at an early date.
As soon as the prints are available, the issue
of the Certificates by the Ministry will be
proceeded with at once.
RULES OF COMMISSIONERS OF NATIO-
NAL EDUCATION.
6. Mr. McBRIDE asked the Parliamentary
Secretary to the Ministry of Education
whether the rules of the Commissioners of
National Education in operation on 1st February, 1922, were still in force in Northern
Ireland; whether Rule (96) of the Code is
applicable to all cases of dismissals, and
whether under the proposed legislation it is
intended to give the same safeguards to all
teachers?
Mr. McKEOWN: The answer to the first
part of the question is in the affirmative.
The Ministry exercises the right of reviewing
all cases of dismissal, if it is considered that
the circumstances of the case render intervention desirable.
The answer to the last part of the question
is in the affirmative, and the proposals of
the Government are now before the House.

The PRIME MINISTER (Sir James Craig):
Perhaps my hon. Friend would put the question down for Tuesday next.
Exchequer and Financial Provisions
Bill.
POINT OF PROCEDURE.
Mr. McGUFFIN: On a point of procedure,
Mr. Speaker, may I ask for your ruling? In
connection with the Exchequer and Financial
Provisions Bill that has received its Third
Reading in this House, may I ask if it is
in conformity with the rules governing the
procedure in respect of Money Bills that this
Bill should be introduced in the Senate of
this Parliament and receive its First Reading?
Mr. SPEAKER: No, I do not think that
would be in accordance with the Statute
creating this Parliament, but the Bill was
introduced in this House. I do not think
it could have been introduced in the Senate.
Mr. McGUFFIN: My point is, have they
any control over the procedure with respect to
Money Bills? Have they the power of revision
or amendment?
Mr. SPEAKER: No. Under Section 16 of
the Government of Ireland Act the Senate
cannot amend any Money Bill. That is
roughly the position.
Mr. McGUFFIN: The difficulty arising is
that we have already had intimation that
there is an intended Amendment in respect
of that Bill before the Senate.
Mr. SPEAKER: As a matter of fact that
point is receiving my consideration together
with that of my legal advisers. I have not
yet got their opinion. The hon. Member may
rest assured that the matter has not been
lost sight of.

The MINISTER OF FINANCE: Mr.
Pollock): The Committee considered yesterday
the Vote on Account for the Estimates of
Expenditure for the coming year. It is
customary at that stage of the Measure for
the Minister to make his statement in regard
to the general finances of the State, and for
Members to have an opportunity of discussing
the Estimates generally. But the state of
business in the House yesterday rendered it
necessary that we should defer this statement
and discussion until the Report stage of the
Vote to-day, and the Committee unanimously
approved of this decision and passed the Vote.
Before I enter upon a short general outline
of the Estimates of the coming year's expenditure, it may, perhaps, be convenient to
bring into relief some of the prominent
features of the experience of the present year,
so far, at least, as this can be done before
its close.
On the 24th of May last I submitted my
Budget statement of the prospective revenue
and expenditure of the Province for the
current year. Whatever judgment the House
may pass upon the figures when comparison
comes to be made between the forecast and
the results, due allowance must be made for
the peculiar and novel conditions under which
the experiment of framing a first pro forma
Balance Sheet of the Province was undertaken. We had no previous records to guide
us. If I may describe our position by a
metaphor which I have used on another
occasion-we had just been started on
Columbus-like voyage, on an unknown and
uncharted sea, and could only hope that we
would find our bearings by definite experience. I estimated that after meeting all
our normal obligations, and accepting the
forecasts of the Imperial Treasury as
gards revenue, we should have a surplus of
£69,000. I was careful to add, however, that
all Budgets are estimates, and that any
Finance Minister taking on himself the role
of a prophet, moved in a region of conjecture.
There are still ten days of the year to run,
and it is, therefore, impossible to make any
guess
a
reas to how closely the forecast will
approximate to the outcome. In order to
provide a surplus of £69,000. I had to assume
a contribution to the National services of
almost six millions, which was nearly two
millions less than our original obligation.
This necessity was imposed upon me by
reason of the fall in our revenue of a corres
ponding sum. There was also an increase in
expenditure of almost a similar amount, due
to the action of the Imperial Government,
and if I had calculated on the original surplus which we understood was assured to us,
our contribution would automatically have
been reduced to four millions. But in such
a period of National stress as we were experiencing it was impossible to disregard our
On arriving at my Budget figures and the
expectant surplus of £69,000, I had the
advantage of the assistance of some of the
most experienced and brilliant minds in the
Civil Service, and I shall be surprised if our
collaboration and calculations are not justified by the results. If there should, perchance be any considerable variation, it can
only arise from some miscalculation on the
part of the Imperial Treasury authorities in
respect of our revenue. I do not mean by
this to cast any reflection upon them, as it
is a work of extraordinary difficulty to estimate and adjust revenue arising from Income Tax which is collected in so many
parts of the Kingdom, and must be adjusted
and apportioned to suit the particular circumstances of the case. All those services which
we directly control present no difficulty, but
we cannot admit responsibility for matters on
which we can exercise no oversight. Bear in
mind that the estimates which we submit today relate to expenditure only-expenditure
which comes within the ambit of our own
Parliamentary authority, the amount of which
depends on the exercise of our own sense of
economy or the reverse. That is to say, they
are entirely in our own hands. Members will
find in the foreword, under the signature of
my hon. Friend, the Parliamentary and Financial Secretary (Mr. Barbour), to the estimates
very full explanations of their incidence, and
also comparisons with the previous year to
enable them to form their judgment of the
work of the departments concerned. In the
administrative expenditure there will be found
comparatively little variation in the cost as
compared with last year. Under ordinary cir
cumstances a reduction might have been expected, due to the cut in the bonus which will
have effect next month. But during the year

the hon. Member for Tyrone and Fermanagh
(Mr. Coote), a short summary of the number
and variety of the activities of the Ministry
of Finance a department with which naturally I have the most intimate relations and
also the most direct knowledge. This example, however, may be accepted as a fair
illustration of the departments as a whole.
There are portions of no fewer than 20
United Kingdom departments now brought
together and worked as a whole in the
Ministry of Finance. Obviously, to cover the
whole ground in detail would be impossible,
within reasonable limits, but it must be
apparent that considering the small number
of officers employed, a much greater range of
knowledge is required in each one than was
previously necessary in one department only.
That is to say, their versatility must be of
a very marked character.
A short resume of the work is as follows:-
In the capacity of Treasury the Ministry
submits the ordered financial proposals and
estimates for the Province to the House, and
assumes complete control of the Government's
finances. once the necessary services are
anctioned. This control comprises supervision of all financial transactions, varying
from negotiations with the Imperial Treasury
regarding the Reserved Taxes, down to the
details of accounts in all the departments in
Northern Ireland.
In addition to this supervisory capacity,
there are the administrative duties in connection with all the departmental services
which have been embodied in the Ministry,
the executive action in which is carried on
mostly through the Accounts Branch.
Some of these services are:-
(1) Collection of Land Purchase Annuities
and Church Temporalities Income.
(2) Administration of Charity Law in
Northern Ireland.
(3) Calculation and payment of Teachers'
Pensions.
(4) Organisation and issue of Ulster Savings
Certificates.
(5) Investigation and issue of Public Works
Loans and collection of the annuities.
(6) Assessment of Schedule E Income Tax on
all Government Officials.
The whole personnel of the Northern Irish
Civil Service is kept under review in the
Ministry, which assumes the functions of the
Civil Service Commission and the Treasury
Controller of Establishments,
At present one type of revenue, Excise,
comprising mainly Entertainments Tax and
Licence Duties, is collected by the Imperial
Customs and Excise Department on an agency
basis.
All Stamp Duties are impressed in the
Ministry and the revenue collected there. It
requires little imagination to visualise the
volume of work in this branch, taking into
consideration all the deeds, cheques, bills, &c.,
which must be stamped day by day throughout the Province. All the operations from
adjudication of the amount to the actual
stamping are carried out.
The Estate Duties accounts are examined,
and all the processes in regard to the assessment of the duty and its ultimate payment
take place within the Ministry.
The administration of Old Age Pensions is
still carried on by Customs and Excise Officers
as an agency, but will soon be taken under
control by the Ministry.
Coming now to the technical or specific service side of the Ministry, there are certain
services which must retain their individuality
on account of the nature of the work.
chief of these are:-
The
(1) Public Works in which a technical staff
look after the buildings and equipment of the
various departments, and all Government
offices and premises throughout the Province.
Then the report goes on to describe all the
activities of this immense work.
(2) The Valuation and Boundary Survey
Branch carry on the duties formerly performed
by the Dublin Department of that name in
Northern Ireland.
(3) Registrar General's Department carries
on all the work of supervision of the registration of Births, Marriages and Deaths in Northern Ireland, and, in addition, comprises the
cognate services of the collection of statistics
for the Province, and the office of advertising
actuary in all actuarial problems.
(4) The Stationery Office, supervised by the
Ministry, looks after the supply of stationery
and printing facilities for the Houses of Parliament and for all the Government Departments.
It will be readily recognised that the conduct of all the services outlined above brings
in its train innumerable legal points. These
are dealt with by the legal officers of the
Ministry, who, in addition, have been able
to assist the Inland Revenue in the collection-

of arrears of Income Tax. In connection with

intimately connected with the work of the

These are the activities of the Ministry of
Finance, and I hope it will satisfy my hon.
Friends. I am sorry my hon. Friend from
Tyrone and Fermanagh (Mr. Coote) is not here
to-day to hear about them.
Mr. M'GUFFIN: He will read about them.
Mr. POLLOCK: I hope he will. I will
come now to a very short survey of some
of the items which appeared in the Estimates
for last year and which may be dealt with,
I hope, with not too great prolixity. Might I
touch upon the Ulster Savings Certificates? I
recall to hon. Members, and I do so with
some sense of satisfaction, the issue of our
ten years' Saving Certificate at the price of
12s 6d. Hon. Members will perhaps recall
that the Imperial Government decided to discontinue the issue of National Savings Certificates in Ulster on the 1st April of last year.
These certificates had been sold at the price
of 15s 6d-increased to 16s on 1st April-to
be redeemed for £1 at the end of five years.
Following the decision of the British Treasury
to discontinue the issue in Ulster, we decided
that it would be opposed to the public interest to permit such a valuable incentive to
thrift to be closed. I made up my mind,
therefore, that we should try the experiment
of offering a certificate redeemable for £1 at
the end of ten years at the price of 12s 6d.
In response to our application the Imperial
Government agreed to join our Government in
guaranteeing an issue on these terms to the
value of £500,000. I estimated that such an
issue would possibly produce cash applications
during the year to a maximum of £350,000.
The year has still ten days to run, but if I
may judge by the rate of recent sales, approximately the full issue of £500,000 will be
disposed of by the 31st of this month. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) We have been so
greatly heartened by the outcome of our experiment, we have applied, and have already
secured, the guarantee of the British Treasury
to a further issue of £500,000 on similar
terms. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) The
security is of such an unimpeachable character
and the rate of interest and other conditions
so attractive, these certificates offer the small
capitalist an opportunity of piling up his
little accumulations of savings that no other
security provides.
The House will doubtless expect to learn
something of the operations of the short but
important Act known as the Loans Guarantee
Act, passed in the last Session of Parliament.
The principal object of this Measure was the
mitigation of the evil of unemployment, by
offering under certain defined conditions the
guarantee of the Government for the repay.
ment of loans made by bankers and others to
public bodies, corporations, etc., who desired
to expend money on capital objects. Some of
the largest ship-owning corporations have already taken advantage of the Measure, with
results which give promise of the speedy return of moderately normal conditions in our
great shipbuilding industry and the consequent
provision of work for large numbers of skilled
workmen in the varied crafts associated with
ship construction. The House will learn with
satisfaction that the operation of the Trades
Facilities Act in Great Britain has materially
assisted us here. The construction of a ship
in Ulster involves the provision of considerable labour in Great Britain in connection
with the manufacture of steel plates and many
other articles entering into the make-up of a
vessel.
The Committee charged with the administration of the Trades Facilities Act in Great
Britain has agreed to guarantee the cost of
all the materials produced in Great Britain
for use in our shipbuilding yards here. The
result of that is that our own guarantee is
limited to expenditure incurred in Northern
Ireland. This is very substantial, and may
amount in many cases to a full half of the
cost of the vessel. The relief which is thus
given enables us to extend the scope of the
operation of this Measure to the great benefit
of the neighbourhood. Already 1,200 men
have been taken on by Messrs. Workman
Clark and Co. in connection with the completion of a ship partially built for the
Lamport and Holt Line. Messrs. Harland
and Wolff report that they have taken over
3,000 additional men during recent months,
and when the negotiations, which are now
well advanced, for the early prosecution of
work on five additional ships to be built on
the slips of the Queen's Island for
various leading shipowners in Great
Britain, are fully completed, we may rely on
the further employment of all classes of
labour to the extent of 6,000 or 7,000 men.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Our Local Committee is dealing with
applications from other parts of the Province, and it is almost certain that our
Government will shortly find it necessary to
come to the House and ask for an
extension of the powers contained in the
recent Act from the £2,000,000 already provided to £3,000,000. It is a great source of
satisfaction to my right hon. Friend, the
Minister of Labour (Mr. Andrews) as well as
to myself personally that the operation of
this small Act has already led to such great
Vote on Account. 262

and beneficial results. It is difficult to overestimate the value of the personal interest
taken in this matter by our great Ulster
citizen, Lord Pirrie, in the furthering of these
schemes to ameliorate the deplorable conditions of labour. Lord Pirrie has laid the
Government and the Province under obligations which it will be difficult to repay. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) I should also like to
make public recognition of the self-sacrificing
work of the members of the Advisory Committee, who, at my invitation, placed their
wide commercial and financial experience at
the disposal of the Ministry of Finance, and
have undertaken a large part of the work of
administering the Act.
I come now to matters which are contained
in the Estimates in the hands of hon. Members, that is leaving the past year to some extent behind except in so far as it is necessary
to make comparison. The first item I touch
upon is that of housing. During the coming
year the liability of the Government to the
public authorities under the head of Housing
is estimated to amount to £27,500, an increase of £12,500 on the previous, that is the
current year. This increase arises from the
maturing of the Government obligations to
the Public Authorities under the Housing
(Ireland) Act of 1919 and the regulations
made thereunder, whereby the Imperial
Government undertook to subsidise these
bodies under certain conditions to the extent of 25s for every £1 of rent collected from houses built or contracted for up
to July 15th, 1921. This is a continuing obligation, but the regulations governing the
subsidy provide for a review or revision of
the grant in the year 1925. The houses built
by the Belfast Corporation under this scheme
form the largest part of the liability, and business prudence and foresight suggest that the
Corporation would now be well advised to
realise this property before a greater loss supervenes consequent on natural depreciation
and the return of more normal conditions of
value. Most of the houses in question were
erected during a period of very high cost,
and the inevitable loss on realisation must
be heavy, but in view of the fact that the
Imperial Government exercised pressure on
the Corporation to provide this property, my
sense of justice compels me to admit that
our Government should bear some of this
loss. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear). This I
am prepared, on behalf of the Government,
to undertake, but if the Corporation continue
to procrastinate in regard to this matter, and
the loss is thereby increased, the Government
will have to be guided by the technical
conditions attached to the grant.
I think the House will realise that this is
necessary in view of the fact that our share
of the responsibility in regard to these houses
is very considerable, and, therefore, we are
entitled to offer an opinion upon the policy to
be pursued in regard to them. The housing
shortage, as the House well knows, is in some
respects the most pressing problem of the day,
both here and elsewhere. Its present position
is fraught with great possibilities of danger to
the community. The solution, in my opinion,
can only be accomplished by the promise of
inducement to private enterprise to enter the
field. While it cannot be contended that costs
have yet reached an economic basis, foresight
and enterprise on the part of the local authorities should be able to bridge the gulf, and
enable those who have ground suitable for
building to proceed with the work of covering
it with the much-needed dwellings for the
people.
I come next to a very important subject, as
the House will realise, and that is education.
Reference to the Estimates will show that the
greatest burden which our small State is called
upon to bear is Education. With the exception of a negligible contribution from the rates
for technical schools, the entire cost of the
educational system of the Province for the
current year has been provided out of State
funds. It may, perhaps, provide some food
for thought if I submit the figures of our
recent progression in the cost of this important branch of national welfare. Three years
ago, before we assumed responsibility for the
public services of the Province, the Estimate
for education was £1,099,000. Two years later
when I submitted my Budget Estimate for the
financial year now closing I had to provide
from State funds the very considerable sum of
£1,798,000. I am advised that the recommendation of the Departmental Committee,
over which my hon. Friend, the Member for
West Belfast (Mr. Lynn) presided with such
conspicuous ability, when fully matured would
call for an additional expenditure of some
£400,000. This huge increase of over
million pounds in the cost of our educational
system is largely due to the enhanced remuner.
ation of the teaching staffs.
one
Now finance has a very unfortunate habit of
interposing itself into the best devised schemes
of men, and in the present instance it is my
bad luck to be obliged to remind my colleagues
that even in such a laudable enterprise as the
provision of a comprehensive and correlated
scheme of national education there are limits
to the depth of the State purse. When discussing our own schemes we cannot overlook
our responsibilities to the Imperial services. If
we enjoy all the advantages of British citizenship-and they are many, as we shall discover
more and more as time goes on-we must
equally bear our share of its burdens. I have
no doubt that the Imperial Government will
admit this year's figures for education, namely,
Supply-

HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Mr. Pollock]
£1,798,000, as provided in my last Budget, as
a basis of calculation for our contribution to
the National Services, seeing that this amount
was a legacy of their own creation. But if we
ask for a reduction of our contribution based
on the increased cost of our own educational
ideals, we shall probably be reminded that the
people of England and Scotland provide half
the cost of their education from local rates,
and that we are not warranted in imposing
practically the entire expense upon the State,
thereby robbing the National Exchequer of
money which should be devoted to the relief
of the country's burdens.
There are a number of outstanding financial
differences between the Imperial Authority and
our own Government. The Chancellor, in a
spirit of fairness which I am bound to acknowledge, has agreed to remit the claims to an
independent Arbitration Board composed of
three of the most distinguished men of the
Kingdom, mutually chosen, in whose impartiality and righteous judgment we have the
fullest confidence. If we succeed in establishing our claims before that tribunal, we may be
able to provide such an additional subsidy for
education as will relieve our Edreation Ministry of the present financial embarrassment in
which it finds itself in respect of this important question. But, on the other hand, if the
Arbitration Board cannot accept our view,
then we must be prepared to shoulder some of
-in fact all-our own fresh responsibilities,
as the result of the Board's decision will regularise our financial relations to Great Britain
for some years to come.
Critics have hinted to me from time to
time that I lack imagination and spiritual
insight in this and other important matters of
State policy; that if I had only greater faith
money would fall into the Treasury like
manna in the wilderness, I suppose. But what
would be the ultimate fate of a man whose
income was strictly limited, say to a thousand
pounds, but who deliberately spent eleven or
twelve hundred year after year? I do not
think I need enlarge upon the moral. But I
do not wish to be misunderstood. I entertain
no gloomy views in regard to our financial
position if we only pay due regard to the
governing economic factors which must be
present to the mind of every responsible member of the community in this cycle of unusual commercial and industrial depression.
Under the head of Labour the estimate of
the Government's contribution to Health Insurance is about £150,000, whilst the unemployment insurance scheme costs £265,000
It will be remembered that this House
passed a grant of £50,000 to enable my right hon. Friend, the Minister
of Labour, to cope with unemployment in the districts outside of Belfast.
This Vote has been practically used up during
the year.
The unemployment problem still
continues to give the Government great concern, not only because of the financial liability
involved, but the hardships entailed on such
large numbers of our people, and the acute
commercial and industrial depression which,
of course, is really the root cause of the
trouble. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
I included in my last Budget an estimate
for loans to the Unemployment Insurance
Fund of £860,000, which included a sum of
£160,000 in respect of the Northern Irish
share of the deficit on the Imperial Fund.
The actual amount advanced under this head,
including the £160,000, promises to reach
£1,000,000 at the end of this month, and I
expect that the coming year will require further advances to the extent of approximately
£700,000. Should trade revive and employ.
ment become normal, the fund will be required
to repay the loans. In the meantime we are
under the necessity of borrowing to meet
these advances, and it will, I think, be necessary shortly for me to introduce legislation
so as to enable the Fund to increase its present borrowing powers of 1 million pounds
to a maximum of 2 millions.
As will be realised, the administration of
these large sums of money necessitates a considerable staff both at Headquarters and at
Labour Exchanges, and although under Section
7 of the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1922,
these administrative expenses, amounting in
the coming year to £119,500, are chargeable to
the Fund, it will be realised that so long as
the fund has to exist on borrowings the money
for these charges must be found by the
Northern Exchequer. We are bringing all
the pressure possible on the Imperial Govern.
ment to expedite the building schemes on the
Parliament House, Administrative Offices, and
Law Courts. If these great works were well
under way it would relieve my right hon.
Friend of some of the weighty burdens he is
carrying in his Ministry.
The peaceable conditions prevailing in the
Province are reflected in the greatly reduced
Vote for the Special Constabulary. When I
submitted the Vote a year ago for this service,
the Government was engaged in a struggle
with the forces of disorder and anarchy which
threatened at one time to overturn and
destroy the whole fabric of society. It is
largely due to the unswerving loyalty and
untiring vigilance of this splendid organisation, that we owe the blessed tranquillity we
now enjoy. I feel, therefore, that last year's
estimate of £2,875,000, colossal as it may
seem, cannot be regarded as a price too great
for the happy results which followed its employment. (Hon. Members: Hea", hear) The

22 MARCH 1923.
Imperial authority bore the burden of the
cost of this efficient force, and we must
frankly make our acknowledgment for the
protection which was provided.
I am advised that the present estimate for
the coming year at £1,580,000 is cut down
to the lowest point consistent with the necessary provision for security. There is an old
Roman aphorism, "Salus populi lex suprema "
(the safety of the people is the highest law),
and every consideration, financial and otherwise, must give way to this factor in our
national life. The Imperial Government has
contributed £1,500,000 to our estimate, leaving a prospective balance of £80,000 to be
borne on our own votes. This may seem a
considerable sum to fall on our little State,
but the Imperial authority has recognised its
responsibility for our security so generously
in the past, I think the House will agree we
would seem ungrateful if we appeared to cavil
at the comparatively small contribution we
are called upon to make for our own peace
and security. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
The Imperial Chancellor proposes to submit
the Budget of the Kingdom on 16th April.
Our local Finance Statement cannot appear
until we learn the effect of the changes, if
any, which may be made on the rates of either
direct or indirect taxation. I need hardly
remind the House that if any changes are
made they will be reflected in our own revenue
in the coming year. I hope, therefore, to be
in a position towards the end of next month
to bring before Parliament a complete estimate of the likely revenue and expenditure
of the Province for the financial year on which
we are about to enter. When that period
arrives, the House will have a much better
opportunity of realising the nature and results not only of the revenue collections but
also of the expenditure of the Province for the
year on which we are about to enter. I beg
to move. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)

27 MARCH 1923.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Tuesday, 27th March, 1923.
The House met at Three of the Clock, Mr.
SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
PETROL IMPORTED TO NORTHERN
IRELAND.
1. Mr. DONALD asked the Minister for
Commerce if he will state the amount of
petrol imported to Northern Ireland during
the years 1919, 1920, 1921, and 1922; whether
petrol imported to Northern Ireland is all
consumed in Northern Ireland, and what
amount is consumed in Belfast?
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY TO
THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE (Mr.
M'Keown): I have been asked by my right
hon. Friend to reply. I regret to inform my
hon. Friend that no official statistics of the
importation of petrol into Northern Ireland
are at present available. Petrol reaches Northern Ireland mainly by trans-shipment from
ports in Great Britain, and my hon. Friend
will realise that such movements have been
regarded in the past, and are still regarded
so far as Northern Ireland is concerned,
merely as trade movements within the
United Kingdom, and, therefore, outside the
purview of the normal statistical data compiled by the Commissioners of Customs and
Excise. I may add, however, that such unofficial data as are available indicate that
the importation of petrol into Northern Ireland is in the neighbourhood of 4,000,000 gallons, but it is impossible to give the exact
figure for the reasons which I have stated.
The petrol imported into Northern Ireland
is not all consumed in Northern Ireland, as
certain of the Petrol Companies established
here operate outside the Six County area.
I regret that it is not possible to give the
hon. Member any indication as to the amount
of petrol consumed in Belfast, as no data
whatever are available on this point.
Mr. DONALD: May I ask my hon. Friend
if the Government have made any representations, or intend to make any representations, with regard to the high cost of petrol
in this country as compared with Great
Britain?
Mr. M'KEOWN: Such representations have v
already been made..
Ex-Service Men.
COTTAGES AT WHITEABBEY.
2. Mr. DONALD asked the Minister for
Home Affairs whether ex-Servicemen's cottages have been in course of erection at
Whiteabbey since November, 1921; whether
work on these cottages has ceased since November, 1922; whether no provision has been
made for either water, gas, or sewage, and
whether the schemes for ex-Servicemen's cottages are now at a stand-still, and, if so, for
what reason?
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): The answer to the first part
of the hon. Member's question is in the
affirmative.
The Board of Works, Dublin, entered into
a contract on the 29th November, 1921, for
the erection of 30 houses under the above.
scheme, but made no provision for sewerage
or water facilities. The work was commenced
immediately, and good progress was maintained, with the result that the actual building was reported to be complete on the 12th
February last, although the time limit for
the completion did not expire until the 31st
instant.
The provision of sewers and water is a
matter primarily for the Belfast Rural District Council, and the delay in the provision
of these services has apparently been due to
the difficulties that arose in regard to the
negotiations between the local authority and
the Government.
However, a satisfactory agreement has been
reached between the Rural District Council
and the Technical Officers of the Ministry of
Finance in regard to these services, and there
should be no delay in providing these essential services now and enabling this Ministry
to install tenants.
Mr. DONALD: May I ask my right hon
Friend for an answer to the last part of my
question?
Sir DAWSON BATES: The answer is--No,
the scheme is going on as rapidly as possible.
Mr. DONALD: Arising out of that answer,
is my right hon. Friend aware that the
question of the erection of these cottages is
giving very great concern to the ex-Servicemen, and that they are under the impression
that a dead stop has occurred in the building?
I would like further information on this
point.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I would like to
remove any misapprehension on the part of
the hon. Member. There is no stop in conrection with the schemes already arranged
for. As to the future, the hon. Member is

aware that under the Free State Act provision is made for £1,500,000 to be devoted to
this object, that a Trust is to be formed, and

the matter.

GAELIC FOOTBALL MATCH NEAR
LURGAN.
4. Major SHILLINGTON asked the Minister of Home Affairs whether the Police
Authorities in Lurgan have brought to his
notice the fact that posters have been
displayed in that district, announcing that
an Exhibition Football Match, under the
auspices of the Gaelic Athletic Association,
between teams from Drogheda and Dundalk,
is to be played near Lurgan, on Easter
Sunday, April 1st, 1923, and if it is proposed
to take any action in the matter.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The reply to the
first part of the question is in the affirmative.
The Police Authorities have made very
careful inquiries, and I am satisfied from
their report that there is no seditious object
connected with the holding of the match.
The Police also report that there is no reason
to anticipate that any disturbance will arise
involving any undue demands upon them.
In the circumstances I would not be war.
ranted in exercising the powers which are
conferred upon me by the Civil Authorities
Act for prohibiting the holding of this match.
Major SHILLINGTON: Arising out of that
reply, does the right hon. Gentleman not
think that the Government are asking for
trouble in allowing this match to take place
when it is not wanted by the big majority
of the inhabitants of this place?
Oral Answers.
Supply.
27 MARCH 1923.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The hon. Member
will understand that my responsibility begins
with the question of the maintenance of the
peace, and from the reports I have received
from the Police there is no anticipation that
there will be any breach of the peace in
connection with this match.
Major SHILLINGTON: Arising out of that
reply, is the right hon. Gentleman satisfied
that the Police in this particular district
are aware of the public opinion that has been
expressed openly in reference to this match,
which is proposed to take place on Easter
Sunday?
Sir DAWSON BATES: Personally, I think,
and I am sure hon. Members agree with me,
that it is a very objectionable thing to have
football matches played on Sunday, but that
is not the point that arises here. The
question is whether there will be a breach
of the peace, and I am advised that there
will not. I must rely on the Police officers
in the neighbourhood, who are most efficient.
FRIESIAN PEDIGREE CATTLE.
5. Mr. COOPER asked the Minister of
Agriculture if he is aware that Mr. T. J.
Mavitty, J.P.. Cultragh House, Lisbellaw,
Co. Fermanagh, purchased in Yorkshire over
five months ago, three Friesian pedigree
cattle, one of which he sold to Sir Basil
Brooke, and that both Mr. Mavitty and Sir
Basil Brooke have applied to the Ministry
for permits to get these cattle to Northern
Ireland, but have failed to get them, and
if he will state why these permits are not
forthcoming, and who is to pay for the five
months' keep of the cattle in England?
Mr. M'KEOWN: I have been asked by my
right hon. Friend to reply. Owing to the
existence of foot and mouth disease in England, the importation of cattle from that
country to Northern Ireland, which is under
the control of the Imperial Secretary, has
not been permitted for some time past. To
meet this recurring difficulty an Animals
Quarantine Station is being established in
Northern Ireland, and will, it is expected,
be ready for the reception of Animals about
the end of April. The applications from Mr.
Mavitty and Sir Basil Brooke have been
noted, and will be considered with others of
a similar nature, subject to compliance with
the Regulations.
Mr. COOPER: May I ask in regard to the
last part of the answer, was the same reply
not given to the gentlemen concerned about
four months ago?
Mr. M'KEOWN: I understand that the
Ministry of Agriculture accepts no responsibility.

CABINET OFFICES.
Motion made, and question proposed:
"That a sum not exceeding £9,901 be
granted to His Majesty to complete the sum
necessary to defray the charge which will
come in course of payment during the year
ending 31st March, 1924. for the salaries of
the Department of the Prime Minister, the
salaries of the Cabinet and of the Cabinet
Secretariat, and other expenses in connection
therewith."
The PRIME MINISTER: I think it is
proper that in all questions of Estimates
the Minister chiefly concerned should make
an introductory statement in order that he
may acquaint the Committee with the duties
which have been performed by his Department during the past year, and to explain
the Estimates for the coming year. It will
be observed by those who have the Votes
in their hands that there is practically no
change in the amount that is being asked
for by my Department for the coming year.
My hon. Friend, the Member for West Belfast
(Mr. Lynn), I think, raised the question not
only last year but the year before, as to
whether it would be possible for me to
institute some further economy in regard to
the Department of the Cabinet, and I have
been most anxiously searching through every
item to see whether it would be possible
to save money in the Estimates applicable
to my own particular Department.
It will be observed that I have cut down
the Estimate for the coming year to some
extent, but taking the whole machinery I
fear that it will be impossible to do away
with any of the personnel. May I just
explain that I have to assist me at the
Cabinet offices two responsible persons,
Colonel Spender, who, as everybody is aware,
is the permanent secretary, and Mr. Blackmore, my trusty friend, I may almost
call him, who has followed me from the
Ministry of Pensions through the Admiralty
to his present position. When one takes into
consideration, not altogether the amount of
work that has to be performed, but
the responsibility of it and the care that
has to be exercised in its performance, I think
the Committee will consider it very reasonable
that I should have beside me two trusted
friends as well as paid officials to help me in
the heavy task that lies on my shoulders.
During the past year the work has been
exceptionally heavy and onerous. Very few
understand how difficult it is-if I myself
happen to be presiding over a Cabinet meeting
and the whole time of the Secretary of the
Cabinet is occupied thereby-to carry on
unless I have someone to meet deputations
and to attend to the ordinary running of
the office. On the other hand, there are
times when it is necessary for me to be
across the water. Last year I am talking
about this financial year, which means last
year as far as these Estimates are concerned
-I crossed the Channel I cannot say how
often with one or other of my two right
hand men for the purpose of negotiating with
the British Government, and whilst I am
away, and one of the other two is away.
it is absolutely essential that there should
be someone of responsibility left behind to
see that the machinery is not interrupted
in any way during my absence. The question
of the necessary help for them and for myself
naturally arises as well, and if one is away
someone is required to remain behind to watch
over the interests concerned with the functions of the Prime Minister as well as the
functions of the Cabinet.
With regard to the work itself, we divide
it as well as we can into two departments.
Colonel Spender, who sacrificed so much to
come to Ulster at a critical period of its
history, is so well acquainted with all the
Special Constabulary-with all the protective
branch, if I may say so, on the Ulster side
-that I feel it would be detrimental to the
interests of Ulster to part with him at any
stage of our proceedings, and also it would
be impossible for me to carry on without
his help. As to the duties he has performed
as Secretary of the Cabinet, I think we
may say that there has been a minimum
of errors during the past two years. I know
of none.
At all events there has been a
minimum of errors in regard to the transactions carried on at our Cabinet meetings.
Some persons have it in their minds that
it would be possible to revert to the old
system of having no Secretary to the Cabinet
at all. That would be impossible quite impossible. The old-fashioned slipshod way of
the Cabinet meeting and discussing matters,
and parting without recording in writing the
decisions come to, only led to great confusion,
Supply-
Committee.
27 MARCH 1923.
to great difficulty, and very frequently to
errors which it was difficult to make right
at a later time.
The system we have adopted is that whatever decision is arrived at it is recorded in
writing, and each Member of the Cabinet
can be supplied with that record if he so
desires, so that there can be no misunderstanding, and no overlapping between Departments. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) All
that work and the co-ordinating of the various
duties that come to hand have been admirably
performed by the two gentlemen I have
named, and to them I tender my most grateful
thanks for the way they have supported me
in very trying times.
Another point of great importance, over
and above the work to which I have just
referred, is that the Cabinet Secretariat and
myself are the only means and only channel
of communication between the Government
of Northern Ireland and the British Government. I do not refer to small matters, such
as inter-departmental communications, but
all questions of real importance must pass
through the hands of myself and the Secretariat. For instance, in connection with
army matters we are the only persons who
have the right of entry to the General Officer
Commanding in Northern Ireland. The
other Ministers take their orders from the
Cabinet as a whole, and they do so after we
have consulted with the General Officer
Commanding in this district. Then there is
the question always cropping up of the
financial relationship between Great Britain
and ourselves. Although, of course, on such
occasions we invariably consult or take with
us to London our Chancellor of the Ex.
chequer our Minister of Finance or whoever
he may designate for the work, I have to be
in constant consultation not only with the
British Prime Minister, the Chancellor of the
Exchequer, the Home Secretary and others,
but there is not a single Department that we,
as head of the Government, have not to be
in closest touch with in order to have things
running as smoothly as possible.
We enter upon a year in which, I trust,
very great strides will be made in regard to
the erection of our various Parliamentary
and Ministerial offices. That work will throw
an additional amount upon our shoulders.
The plans for our Parliamentary building
and for our offices are, I believe, now perfect
and the work is proceeding. There again
the First Commissioner in London has his
correspondence and personal interviews with
us and not from any other Department.
Lastly, of course we have the general
carrying on of the Government of Northern
Ireland itself, and the co-ordinating of all
the Departments, so that everything will run
sweetly and efficiently. I may say that
we have had no difficulty whatever in
that matter. I never knew a team of
Cabinet Ministers and Parliamentary Secretaries that pulled together so well as
the team which represents this House.
We have never had one word since we first
took on this onerous duty. Taking it all
round, I feel there is no waste of money
either in my own Department or in that of
the Cabinet. The country is well served by
those who are working for us here. I can
say from my own knowledge of departmental
work across the Channel that there are not
two of the staff there who ever worked half
so hard as the two gentlemen who assist
me to carry the burdens that rest upon my
shoulders. Therefore, I hope the Committee
as a whole will recognise the splendid work
they are both doing, and that they will
allow me to continue to have their help for
the twelve months covered by these Estimates.
Mr. McGUFFIN: I do not intend to oppose
the Estimates in respect of the Cabinet and
Cabinet Secretariat which we are considering
at the moment. The only comment I
wish to make is that I thought that on the
last occasion when this question was discussed
in this House the Prime Minister gave an
assurance that it was only a temporary
arrangement owing to the difficult exigencies
that then existed. I do not know if it is
his intention to make the arrangement permanent.
The PRIME MINISTER: T do not think
the hon. Member (Mr. McGuffin) quotes me
correctly.
Mr. McGUFFIN: I would be very sorry to
do otherwise.
The PRIME MINISTER: If the hon.
Member looks at the Debates he will find
that I asked the House to allow me to try
how this arrangement would work, and see
if at a future date I could make economies
with regard to the staff. After two years'
experience I cannot see any possibility of
any Prime Minister, let alone myself-and
I work very hard--carrying on with less than
two. I think it would be a danger to the
Department not to have them, and things
would not run smoothly.
Mr. McGUFFIN: Of course, a statement
like that, to the effect that their services

House. Under those conditions I would be

After all, I cannot help but think it is

introduces into Cabinet matters, Cabinet

THE CURFEW ORDERS.
Motion Made, and Question proposed,
"That this House do now adjourn."—(Mr.
Burn.)
Major SHILLINGTON: I rise to ask the
Minister of Home Affairs a question in reference to the Curfew Orders. Perhaps the
Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry will
be able to answer. I think I am right in
saying that some months ago in Belfast and
within a radius of 15 miles from the city, the
Curfew time was extended to 11-30, and I was
wondering if the Ministry could see their
way to extend the limit to that time for
places outside the radius referred to. Our
people have borne the difficulties of the Curfew Order with a great deal of patience, and
I think things are now in such a state that
it might receive favourable consideration
from the Ministry. As far as my part of the
Northern area is concerned, I understand
that if Curfew was put back another half
hour or so the Great Northern Railway would
be prepared to run a train every night from
Belfast at 10 o'clock. They cannot do that
at present, as the passengers and officials
would not have time to get home before the
Curfew Order comes into operation at
11 o'clock. I hope that this matter will receive early and favourable consideration.
Mr. MEGAW: I have to say that I, as the
representative of a county, have in one sense
the same feeling as my hon. Friend. The
matter has been occupying the attention of
the Ministry of Home Affairs, and the
Police, who are the body responsible for
law and order, have been asked to report on
the question. The question of the Curfew
Orders is being very carefully considered at
the present time, but until there is a
definite report from the Police it is impossible to state exactly what we shall be able
to do. Of course, we feel that is more or
less of an anomaly that the City of Belfast
has half-an-hour more than the country
districts. We have been acting on our
Police reports up to the present, and we
hope that with the advent of Summer Time
there will be some relaxation of the Curfew.
Question put, and agreed.

Wednesday, 28th March, 1923.
The House met at Three of the Clock, Mr.
SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answer to Question.
R.I.C. PENSIONERS IN SPECIAL
CONSTABULARY.
1. Mr. M'GUFFIN asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether it is a fact that by a
circular, dated February 1st, 1922, it was announced that all pre-war pensioners of the
Royal Irish Constabulary serving with the
Special Constabulary would receive the same
pay as the members of the Royal Irish Constabulary then serving, according to each
rank; whether it is a fact that in the case of
ex-members who retired before the war the
matter was never complied with, although
they were promised, by the circular quoted,
that their pay would be brought up to existing rates; and whether it is not a fact that
a member of the Special Constabulary concerned made application on March 11th, 1922,
to have his pay, etc., brought up to existing
rates, and, if so, what is the decision of the
Government on the matter, and when is the
claim likely to be paid?
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): I am obliged to the hon.
Gentleman for drawing my attention to this
matter.
The circular in question was issued inasmuch as certain R.I.C. pensioners, when employed as Special Constables, received both
their pay and their pension, the total being
in excess of the emoluments enjoyed by the
corresponding rank in the R.I.C.
It was not anticipated that the circular
would have the effect of increasing the
amount to be received by any member of the
Special Constabulary Force in the shape of
pay and pension, but inasmuch as the announcement was publicly made, I am obtaining the concurrence of the Ministry of
Finance to fulfil the strict letter of the circular.
I may mention, however, that payment can
only be made up to 1st November last, when
an amended instruction was issued to the
police.

CLASS II. VOTE 4.
REFORMATORY AND INDUSTRIAL
SCHOOLS.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That a sum not exceeding £9,280 be
granted to His Majesty to complete the
sum necessary to defray the charge which
will come in course of payment during
the year ending on the 31st March, 1924,
for the expenses of Reformatory and
Industrial Schools and Places of Detention."
Sir DAWSON BATES: In bringing forward
this Vote may I at the outset say there
has been no change of any importance in the
present system of administration of Reformatory and Industrial Schools? I am not
satisfied with the present system, far from it
Mr. McGUFFIN: Hear, hear.
Sir DAWSON BATES: With the object of
devising a better system the Ministry ap
pointed a most representative Committee,
which was presided over by the Chairman
of Ways and Means (Mr. Moles) whom I am
glad to see restored to health. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) I hope to receive their Report at
an early date. I would like to make one
or two observations on what I regard as
some of the defects in the present system.
Whatever may be the cause, I find a growing
disinclination on the part of local magistrates
to commit children to reformatories or industrial schools. In the year 1913 there were
228 persons admitted to industrial schools in
Northern Ireland, and in 1922 there were
only 48. The admissions to reformatories in
1913 were 39; last year there were only 15.
I do not think this reluctance has had a
good effect upon the community at large.
Cases have been reported to me where a boy
has been before a Court on repeated occasions,
and, notwithstanding the adverse reports the
magistrates had in regard to this boy, they
refused to commit.
and
I believe the system of confinement to these
classes of institutions may have certain drawbacks, but at the same time I think the advantages outweigh the disadvantages,
certainly the system as worked in England,
where the magistrates do not show the same
disinclination in regard to committals, has
been a marked success. I submit that it is
a great mistake to allow a number of boys to
imagine that because they are young they
Supply-
Committee.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Sir Dawson Bates]
somecan defy the law. Our own experience during
the last trying year we have gone through
has shown that most of the worst offences
committed during that year have been committed by boys just out of their 'teens-some,
indeed, in their 'teens. One of the most painful duties I have to perform is
times to have to interview the parents
of these boys. Some are most respectable
men-men who abhor crime, and yet
they find their boys have become criminals. That has arisen from one or two
causes. We find that owing to the absence
of the fathers during the war, or through
some other cause, the boys have been neglected, and had any preventive measures
been available and made use of I believe
many of those boys would have been saved
from becoming ordinary criminals.
The object of these schools is to try to
prevent youths becoming common criminals.
Money spent in that direction is saved ten
times over. I would like to quote from a
letter which was written by one of the best
experts on this subject, Sir Edward Troup,
late Under-Secretary to the Home Office in
London. Speaking in regard to the question
of magistrates committing boys to these
schools he says:-

Magistrates are also, I fear, sometimes
misled by their own experience. There
must always, in the best institutions, be
some failures, and it is only the failures
that the magistrates see, because they alone
find their way again to the police courts.
The far more numerous successes of the
schools join the ranks of law-abiding
citizens, and those who administer justice,
rarely or never see them or hear of them
again. If magistrates would visit the schools
and learn the history of the boys who have
left them they would form a very different
impression of the work that is being done."
I observed not long ago in a paper that one
of the officials of the Belfast Corporation
stated that the damage done by the breaking
of street lamps alone cost the ratepayers
£1,000 last year. I was astounded to find, on
making inquiries into the ages of the criminals who are in our three prisons in Northern Ireland, that there were on the 26th
January, a date taken at random, 225 prisoners under the age of 25, of whom 115 were
between the ages of 16 and 21. That does not
include Northern Ireland prisoners detained
at the present time in England and Scotland.
I only mention these few points so that the
House may realise that this is one of the
most important subjects which the Government has to deal with in the near future. I
hope, when I receive the Report from the
Committee that has been set up, to bring
before the House some Measure and ask it to
pass it with the object of trying to remedy
what I have described as one of the greatest
defects in our present system. I beg to
move.
Mr. McGUFFIN: Being a member of the
Committee referred to by the right hon.
Gentleman so ably presided over by yourself,
I am precluded from making the remarks
that I might otherwise have made on this
question, but I am absolutely in sympathy
with the right hon. Gentleman in his interpretation of the case. I think these
institutions are not being used in the way
they were originally intended to be used.
They were effectively used in the past. When
you consider that these institutions have
provision for perhaps more than 200 per cent.
of the number that occupy them at the
moment and that the overhead charges are
the same, I think that is a reason for a
proper use of these institutions or for their
abolition entirely. The Report that will be
presented to the right hon. Gentleman will
perhaps provide him with some information
on the matter. In view of the fact that
the Report will be forthcoming at a near
date I do not propose to enlarge further on
the subject. I accept and fully endorse the
interpretation put on the situation by the
right hon. Gentleman.
Mr. GRANT: I do not intend to criticise
what has been said, but I am one of the
individuals to whom the right hon. Gentleman referred when he said that the
magistrates in Belfast are not very willing

or homes. It must be remembered that we
have got to go by the opinion of the officials

is really very awkward for magistrates, when
appeals are made by the mothers or guardians
of children not to send them to the reformatory, just to turn round and send them away,
especially when you have got the opinion of
the officials in Court that the reformatory is
not the proper place to send boys to.
Suggestions
We have been told on many occasions in
the other Courts that the younger criminals
who are brought up so often are mostly boys
who have come out of the reformatory, and
that it did not do them any good to send
them to such an institution.
have been made by magistrates at different
times that if there were some sort of scheme
whereby boys could be sent to homes in the

Like my hon. Friend (Mr. McGuffin) I would

to offer any opinions on the subject.

Class II. No. 5.
GRANTS TO LOCAL AUTHORITIES.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That a
sum not exceeding £310,568 be
granted to His Majesty to complete the sum
necessary to defray the charge which will
come in course of payment during the year
ending the 31st March, 1924, to provide for
grants to local authorities in respect of
health, housing, etc., and in relief of local
rates."
as
Sir DAWSON BATES: The Estimates which
I have to submit to this Committee under
the head of Grants to Local Authorities
present no unusual features, as the basis
on which the grants for the coming financial
year have been calculated are the same
those which were accepted by this Committee
last year. There is one satisfactory feature,
however, and that is that the Estimates
this year show a saving of £155,555. The
amount estimated last year was £526,123.
This saving is due primarily to the fact
that in the Estimates presented to the Committee last year we found it necessary, in
the case of several sub-heads, to make provision for payment of grants to the local
authorities not only for the year ending
March, 1923, but also for the half-year ended
March, 1922. For example, the normal grant
payable under heads K and M for the year
1922-23 should have been approximately
£80,000; the balance, £40,000 was provided
to make up grants payable during the preceding half-year. The same remark applies
to the grants payable under heads M, N,
O and P, where instead of £90,000 it should
have been £60,000, but for the fact that we
had to provide for the extra six months. I
may say this, however, that we have had
negotiations with the Imperial Government,
and the Imperial Government have recognised
their responsibility for two of those six
months-that is, for two months of the year
for which we had no liability.
Another feature in the present Estimates
is the fact that we have now segregated the
various types of grants. Under the old
regime these grants were all grouped together.
The two main sources of grants were Estate
Duty Grants and the old Local Licence
Duties Grants. The Estate Duty Grants
comprised payments to Boards of Guardians
in aid of expenditure on salaries, and also
payments to road authorities in aid of expenditure on roads and bridges. The Licence
Duties Grants comprised a series of four
grants, and they come under the heads of
M, N, O and P, that is to say, grants to
Boards of Guardians in aid of medical and
educational expenditure, grants to sanitary
authorities in aid of sanitary officers' salaries,
grants to asylums, and grants in aid of
railway and harbour guarantees. I am sure
that hon. Members will agree with me that
it is far more satisfactory instead of grouping
all together we should set out the items so
as to let Parliament and the local authorities
see the exact amount of grant coming under
each head and the type of local authority
to whom that grant was made.
I do not propose to make any observations
in regard to any of the items where they
appear the same as last year. I will only
refer to some of the items which show either
an increase or a decrease over the amount
last year. The first of these is item C. That
is a grant in aid of the treatment of venereal
diseases, and in respect of that we are able
to show a decrease of £2,500 this year. As
hon. Members are aware, this grant takes
the form of a subsidy of 75 per cent. towards
approved expenditure of county councils and
borough councils under their schemes for
the treatment of venereal diseases. We think
that the amount shown in the Estimates will
be sufficient to meet the claim for the coming
year. Now, with regard to the grants
towards the medical treatment of school
children which comes under F-
Mr. DONALD: Will D be eliminated
altogether?
Sir DAWSON BATES: There is no change.
I am only dealing with items where there
is an increase or decrease in the expenditure
of last year. With regard to F, the medical
treatment of school children, we show in
this an increase of £1,000. Up to the present
time these grants have been only made to
voluntary institutions. I am glad to say the
Belfast Corporation have now prepared a
scheme, which has been approved of, for the
medical and dental treatment of school
children in the city, and it is owing to
that scheme having been put forward and
approved that it is necessary to provide this
amount. Hon. Members who have studied
the Education Bill will see that it is proposed under that Measure to transfer this
service to the Education Authority, and
probably this will be the last time I will
have to put forward this particular sub-head.
In regard to item H, the grant for treatment of tuberculosis shows a slight decrease
of £2,800, and this, no doubt, is due to
general fall in prices.
