HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Sir Dawson Bates]
Regarding item I, the grants to local
authorities under the Housing Act of 1919
show an increase of £12,500. This increase
is a normal one, and may be explained by
the fact that the schemes of the local authorities concerned have now practically been
completed, and, under the Regulations, we
are now called upon to pay subsidies to the
local authorities on a maximum basis of 25/-
per
of rent collected, whereas, up to this,
we have been merely paying to the local
authorities the actual loan charges for which
they were liable on foot of the capital sums
borrowed by them in connection with their
housing schemes.
It has repeatedly been explained to this
House that the arrangement to pay 25/- per
£ of rent applies, in accordance with the
arrangement made by the Imperial Government in 1921, only to Housing Schemes in
respect of which contractual commitments
had been entered into prior to 31st July, 1921,
and accordingly our commitments under this
particular head apply only to the case of
459 houses in Belfast, 25 houses in Portadown,
8 houses in Bangor, 8 houses in Tanderagee,
and 2 houses in Omagh, a total of 502 houses.
In connection with this matter I would
also draw hon. Members' attention to the
fact that our liability in connection with
subsidy to private builders expired last year,
as, under the approved Regulations, grants
were payable only in respect of houses completed prior to the 23rd October, 1922.
Consequently, so far as existing arrangements are concerned, the Government's
liability under the Housing Act of 1919 is
determined, but, in view of recent developments, it appears questionable whether it
would not be desirable for the Government
to make a further effort to assist and encourage building, whether by local autho
rities or private builders, and my right hon.
Friend, the Minister of Finance, and I are
in consultation on this matter with a view
to ascertaining whether it would be possible,
and, if so, to what extent, to assist by means
of State subsidy the provision of further
houses in urban centres in Northern Ireland.
The decrease in sub-head J, Agricultural
Grant, is due to the fact that, in respect
of the year 1922-23, we had to make provision
for three half-years' grants instead of two
half-years' grants. The Grant is a stereotyped
one under the Local Government Act, and
the figure £128,644 is the fixed amount of
the Northern Ireland share of this grant.
Sub-heads K and L represent the normal
grants payable in respect of the salaries of
workhouse officers and expenditure on roads
and bridges, and are based on the principle
which was approved by this House last year,
i.e., on the basis of the average of the
payments in respect of the three financial
years, March, 1918, 1919 and 1920.
Sub-heads M, N, O and P, have been calculated on a similar basis, and accordingly
call for no comment from me at present.
.Item R. As regards the grants to local
authorities under the Labourers Acts, hon.
Members will see that they are based on
the same basis as for 1922-23 and, under
existing arrangements, we are liable for an
annual subsidy of approximately £11,520.
However, as there has been considerable
delay in clearing up the financial adjustments
under this head, we find that it will not be
possible to spend the whole of the amount
voted for the year 1922-23 during the course
of the year, and it has been found necessary
to include an additional sum of £4,950 in
the present year's estimates, representing the
saving on last year's estimates.
I may mention that we have now secured
an undertaking from the Imperial Government that rural district councils in Northern
Ireland will still be entitled to obtain loans
out of the Land Purchase Fund for the
purpose of formulating further schemes for
the provision of labourer's cottages, and my
right hon. Friend, the Minister of Finance,
and I have under earnest consideration at
present the question of continuing the relief
to local authorities in respect of the local
charges payable by them on foot of the loans
advanced to them from the Land Purchase
Fund.

Some very
important matters are dealt with, and they

Dr. MORRISON: There are some items in

I merely want to point out that this question

How much of that is spent in the country?
If you take two or three centres in Ulster

whether they get a grant from it or not. The

shall give notice of motion to discuss the

ment, or their successors, should be responsible for any loss that might be incurred.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Thursday, 29th March, 1923.
The House met at three of the clock, Mr.
SPEAKER in the Chair.
Written Answer to Question.
POSTAL ARRANGEMENTS IN FER-
MANAGH.
Mr. COOPER asked the Minister of Commerce if he is aware that a large number of
the inhabitants of Fermanagh are still receiving their letters and parcels from Post
Offices in the Free State, such as Clones and
Belturbet, and if he will make arrangements
to have all such letters and parcels delivered
from offices within the County, as at present
there are many complaints that such correspondence and parcels are tampered with.
THE ASSISTANT PARLIAMENTARY
SECRETARY TO THE MINISTRY OF
FINANCE (Mr. Burn)--I have been asked by
my right honourable Friend to reply.
The answer to the first part of the question
is in the affirmative. With regard to the
second part, the Honourable Member is of
course aware that the control of postal
matters in Northern Ireland is still vested
in the Postmaster-General in London. I may
inform the Honourable Member, however,
that the possibility of effecting such a rearrangement as he suggests has been engaging
the attention of the Ministry of Commerce
for some time past. The Honourable Member
will realise that the matter affects not oniv
County Fermanagh, but also the other
Counties along the Border, and that, in
negotiating with the Postmaster-General for
any re-arrangement of the kind which he
suggests for County Fermanagh, the Ministry
must have regard to all the areas affected. In
some of those areas the matter is complicated
by the effect of any such re-arrangement
upon the frequency and the hours of collection and delivery, and also by considerations
of the additional expense which would be
involved.

Payment of Members.
Motion made and Question Proposed :
That, in the opinion of this House, as and
from the beginning of next financial year,
provision should be made for the payment
of a salary at the rate of Two Hundred
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
Payment of Members.
Payment of Members. 316
now of subordinate Parliaments; that is,
Parliaments of the same character as our
Pounds a year to every Member of this House
who has subscribed to the necessary Oath and
taken his seat, excluding any Member who is
for the time being in receipt of a salary as
an Officer of the House or a Member of the
Government.
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock); Representations have been made to
the Government from time to time recently
that the question of the payment of Members
might now be suitably considered by this
House. I think the majority of hon. Members will agree that it would hardly have been
seemly to have raised the matter in the
initial stages of our existence as an autonomous State. I feel that such a course would
have been regarded with, or at least have
given ground for, the suspicion that candidates for the representation of the various
constituencies had been inspired rather by
mercenary motives than laudable ambition to
give their best in the service of the State, but
while it can scarcely be argued that we have
fully emerged from the probationary stage of
our career we may regard our position as
sufficiently stable to warrant the discussion
of a question which sooner or later is certain
to arise. In approaching the consideration of
this subject I prefer to regard any claims of
hon. Members rather as a matter of reimbursement of expenditure made than as a
payment for actual services rendered. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) The Government,
therefore, was anxious that assuming the
principle was conceded the amount should
not be so large as to suggest the idea that
we were simply voting the taxpayers' money
without regard to our financial obligations
and necessities while at the same time doing
fairly and justly by hon. Members in reimbursing them for any outlay which necessarily does attach to the position of Members
of Parliament. I am not aware of any
Parliament in the world where the principle
of payment of Members does not obtain,
whether the Parliaments are sovereign Parliaments or subordinate Parliaments. In the
limited time at my disposal to-day, I took
the opportunity of looking up the arrangements which exist in other Assemblies of a
type similar to ours, and, having examined
these with some care, I am satisfied that the
suggestion contained in the Resolution of
£200 a year is a fair basis and consistent
with the amount of our work, and also with
the importance of our duty and with our
numbers. The number of our Members who
would qualify under the Resolution is about
thirty-five. This would involve an increase
in our Estimates of, approximately, £7,000,
and, when compared with the total expenditure in other similar bodies, I do not think
this charge upon our Votes can be regarded
as other than moderate. It may interest non.
Members to know that in all the subordinate
Parliaments of the Empire-I am speaking
own, and not the central authority-an
average rate of about £300 obtains, and in
almost all cases travelling expenses .re
provided. For example, beginning near at
home with the Free State, which, of course,
regards itself as a sovereign and independent Parliament, the Members receive £30 per
month-that is £360 a year-and about
for travelling expenses. In New Zealand,
which has a population approximately similar
to our own, the remuneration is £500, with
travelling expenses, but deductions are inade
for non-attendance.
Mr. M'GUFFIN: That is perfectly right.
Mr. POLLOCK: In Australia, the Members
of the House of Representatives receive
£1,000 per annum and travelling expenses,
while in Canada the Members of a number
of the subordinate Parliaments of the
Dominion receive no remuneration, but in
the central Parliament they receive 1,000
dollars, which would be about £800 a year.
These are the particulars and parallels upon
which I think we can justify our action today, and if Members agree that we have
waited sufficiently long with the necessary
dignity before embarking upon this change
I hope they will regard the Resolution favour
ably. I beg to move.
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: I must congratulate my right hon. Friend (Mr. Pollock)
upon the very brief but very forceful and
effective speech he has made in introducing
this proposal this afternoon. I am sorry that
I find myself in a position of complete disagreement with my right hon. Friend, and 1
have to oppose the Motion that he has submitted to the House, and will have to go into
the Division Lobby against it. Let me state
briefly why I am opposed to the present proposal of the Government.
First of all I oppose it on the ground that
we as Members received no mandate when we
were elected to vote ourselves a salary-none
whatever. When we were selected by the
Selection Committee and went before the
electors seeking their suffrages there was no
understanding of any sort that those of us
who would be elected to this Parliament
would desire to be paid for our services. I
consider it would be quite open to any of the
electors to-day to say to us if this proposal is
carried into law: "When you were selected,
and when you were elected to represent this
constituency we thought we were electing a
Member who considered that a great distinction and a great honour had been conferred
upon him in sending him as one of the first
Members to represent us in the Ulster Parliament, and we thought that we were getting
a Member who was going to serve us without
any thought of fee or reward."

Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: That is my
first point, that our constituents have given us
no mandate whatever to come here and vote
ourselves salaries for our services. Now, the
second point I wish to make is this: Seeing
that this Parliament has been in Session for
close on two years-I think we will have
been in Session two years in the month of
May coming-and seeing that the life of this
Parliament at the best can only be for five
years, we might have continued to the end
of our existence as a Parliament unless by
any chance--and I do not think there is any
such chance the Government is defeated on
any important question; or unless they take
the notion themselves to appeal to the
country at a date earlier than the five years.
That is a possibility that all Governments
think about occasionally. Therefore, it
would have been much better that we should
have continued, as we have continued up to
the present moment, to serve our constituencies to the end of the five years, and then
if we desired to offer our services again to
the electors they would know clearly and definitely what our position was in regard to a
question of this character, and that no matter
who might be elected as members to the
next Parliament, the electors would understand fully and beyond the shadow of a doubt
that they would be called upon as taxpayers
to pay for the services of their representatives in Parliament. My right hon. Friend
(Mr. Pollock) has spoken, and from his standpoint very effectively spoken, of what has
been done in other subordinate Parliaments
throughout the world in regard to the salaries
of Members. I do not dispute his statement
at all, but I hope that we have reached a
stage in this Parliament and in Ulster when
we will strike out upon lines of our own-
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear) and not always
slavishly copy the Imperial Parliament or
copy the Parliaments of other countries.
Mr. HANNA: Or America.
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: Surely there
are 52 people throughout the entire
Six Counties to be found who will consider

Province of ours, especially in the initial

passed. I say that Ulster can produce 52

One of the things that weigh with me, and
I am sure it will weigh with a good many
hon. Members to-day, is this. Let us look
at the economic and social condition of the
Six Counties to-day. My right hon. Friend,
the Minister of Labour (Mr. Andrews), told
us here in this House that in order to meet

mortgage the future. I think those were
the words that he had to mortgage
the future very heavily, and nobody complains

wants to help those who cannot help
themselves. What I want to ask is-Is this
the time, when we have thousands of
people in our industrial centres walking about
the streets with no employment, when a great
many of them and their families are living
on a miserable dole, when they are not living,
but only existing-is this the time for us as
Members of Parliament to vote ourselves £200
a year as an allowance or salary, whatever
you like to call it? Just think to-day of the
unemployed that we have. Thousands of
men who served their country in the Great
War are struggling for an existence. They
have sore hearts, and some of them-I do not
blame them-have stormy feelings in their
breasts because of what they consider is the
unfair treatment that has been meted out
to them. They cannot find work, and they
want to find it. What will they say of us
here in this House if, while they are in that
condition, we vote ourselves £200 a year of
an allowance?
Then think again of the conditions in the
agricultural districts. Agriculture in Eng-

allowances, and it comes before the Minister
of Home Affairs (Sir Dawson Bates), I can
imagine my right hon. Friend sending down
a peremptory letter to say that such a thing
could not be thought of, that the purity of
public life was a sacred thing, and that the
honour of serving the people in a public
capacity was such that he hoped the Members
would not for a single moment entertain a
proposal of that kind, that it would be a
lowering of their dignity, and would certainly
not to be conducive to the effective or efficient
carrying on of the public work that they had
to discharge. They could put in their claims.
and on the same grounds that this claim
is put forward to-day it ought to be met.
Then I think I see another class in the
community who might put forward a similar
claim and I sympathise with them-namely
the men who have to serve on juries in the
administration of public justice throughout
the Six Counties. These men have
to leave their homes in the interests
of justice, and while everybody else
in connection with a Court of Justice is
paid they have to render these public services
for nothing.
Taking all these things into consideration
I think this question should not be pressed.
but if it is pressed I shall have to vote against
it, and in voting against it I am not only
satisfying my own conscience on the whole
question, but I believe I am respresenting the
views and the feelings of the majority of
my constituents. I believe, further, that in
opposing it I am doing something which at
the moment is the wise thing to do, considering the conditions that exist throughout
this Province of ours. I believe that
we as a Parliament here would strengthen
our position throughout the country, and
would gain the confidence and esteem of the
community as a whole, if we were willing
to practise this bit of self-denial and selfsacrifice until this first Parliament of ours
has run its course. Then the constituents
can ask the men and women who are going
to enter the next Parliament whatever questions they like, and they, on their part, can
tell them on what conditions they want to
be elected. In the meantime I take leave to
say that this proposal is one which should
not receive the sympathy and support of the
majority of this House.
Dr. CAMPBELL: I think it would not be

-when you consider the feelings of all these

can you help realising that they will be

the people will be taken by surprise by it.

Payment of Members.
When we were elected to represent the

has been said about what has been done in
other places, but what has been done in other

been many wrong things, many things which

places, and we, setting out anew in a young
Parliament, should endeavour to set an
example and to adopt a high standard of
conduct in regard to our constituents. I much
regret that this has been brought before us
at the present time. At the very least we
should have waited until an opportunity had
been given to hon. Members to consider the
matter and to veto it or stamp it with their
approval.
Dr. MORRISON: I should like to say, a
word with regard to this question which
has been brought before the House, and I

representative of the party asking my views

Dr. MORRISON: Asking my views on this

man who comes here, perhaps not very largely

The common man has come into his own,

so. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
The qualifications that we require are very
numerous. To be a Member of this House a

He must have a certain amount of money.
He must have ideas, and he must be able to

is a combination that is very hard to getmy hon. Friend (Sir Robert Anderson) laughs
-because my experience is that plenty of
men have ideas and cannot express them,
and some have the gift of expression without
ideas. My memory goes back for a very long

politician in this House. I have been actively

in the cock-pit of Ulster politics and I was
actively engaged in fighting the Unionist
cause. We had at that time a wealthy
English manufacturer, who was on his way

South Londonderry by the way. He did not

electors. He simply thought that if he walked
in the House of Commons in obedience to the
Whip and gave subscriptions with an open

the constituency he had actively discharged
his duties. He was succeeded by two very
brilliant lawyers, one of whom at the present

judicial system in the Six Counties, and who
is an honour to the constituency and an
honour to the Bench. Those men also called
in South Londonderry on their way to these
high appointments, and they spent their

their objectives. There is nothing offensive
in that, and the men themselves would admit
that politics constituted a necessary evil,
and they had to go in for them in order to
get where they wanted to go.
But I wish the House to remember that
times are changed. We no longer open our

taking the larger fish to the good feeding
grounds, and they called them "Pilot Fish."
But scientific research has discovered that
the small fish, instead of guiding the larger
ones, have in their head a small cavity, and
in that cavity a strongly-developed muscle,
by which they attach themselves to the
larger fish and are able to arrive at their
destination without moving a fin. I do not

you are all aware, times are exceedingly bad

There is the whole question the Government has to solve. It is all very well for
my hon. Friend, the Member for Derry City

quite a number of persons throughout Ulster
prepared to serve the country, without payment. The persons we want in this House are
not those who are able to serve Ulster without being paid on every occasion. It would
be a sad day if the best of our working men
could not come into this House simply because people said, "There is no use for you
there. You have not got the means and you
cannot be allowed into that very select House
of Commons of Ulster, because there is no
payment there to carry you on." Therefore,
it really affects the Government where Members get paid if they are not paid fairly and
openly by the people of Ulster themselves.
That is the whole crux of the question, and I
do hope that on the ground that we wish this
House to be open to all classes my hon.
Friend (Sir Robert Anderson) will not press
this main Question to a division. It is all
very well for hon. Members to say that they
themselves are poor men. They are not so
poor that they cannot come here and do their
duty, but there are certain Members who
might be so poor that they could not come
to this House, and they would be debarred
through not having the money from representing their constituency, although the constituency might want them Then you have
in that case payment from outside and a very
bad system growing up in our midst, whereas under the Motion before the House each
man would be fairly paid and would be able
to say, "I have quite as much right to my
salary as any other Member."

Therefore, just as the Government kept clear

me personally--
satisfaction as well as encouragement. The
subject is one of so complex a character,
urrounded as it is by so many seemingly

Since this Bill was read a First time, I
have, I hope, usefully employed the intervening weeks in studying and appraising at their
correct value the different criticisms which
these proposals have evoked. These criticisms show very clearly the deep interest in
Education which exists throughout
province, an interest of which I was already
well aware, and I feel convinced that the
the

knowledge that Great Britain is giving to
our efforts an obviously friendly approval
will act as an incentive to us in our further

problem.
Most of these criticisms have been directed
to what have appeared as omissions from the
Bill rather than to the actual provisions
specifically contained in the Bill. My Parliamentary experience led me to expect this,
but I hope that when the Second Reading is
passed, as I trust it will be in a short time
from now, there will be no doubts as to the
policy which, as a Government, we desire to
pursue.
Meanwhile, I cannot help feeling that there
is a certain amount of misapprehension as
to the proper form of a Parliamentary Bill.
It is quite impossible to include in the provisions of a Bill a great part of the phraseology which can quite properly appear
in the reports of Committees or in
speeches, phraseology which conveys
to
the public mind a certain idea as
to policy. But this policy must not be supposed to be abandonded or lost sight of, if
the same phraseology does not appear in the
Bill itself, which is designed to carry out
that policy. A Bill is a document framed
for the purpose of giving effect to a certain
policy to certain ideas which we hold, and
the terms of a Bill are couched in such
phraseology that when an interpretation in
a Court of Law is required there can be no
possible mistake as to its provisions. That
is the reason why every Government contains
a Draughtsman specially trained for work of
this nature, and I am glad to be able to
take this opportunity of saying how singularly fortunate our Government is in being
able to command the services of so efficient
a Parliamentary Draughtsman as the present
holder of that post. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear). I would venture to suggest to our
friends and critics, therefore, that, because
the specific words which they are expecting
to see in the Bill do not actually appear in
it it does not follow that those matters to
which they attach great importance are excluded from the Bill.

The second of these general principles is

cational reform during recent years that the

But compulsory education entails free
education and these things which I have

this House that parental responsibility is
fully recognised at every stage of this Bill.
The duty of causing the child to attend

can be compelled to discharge that duty. In

The third general principle to which the

Finally, in explanation of the length of the

I should like to say that, while there is a

Passing to the Measure itself, the first

Advisory Council. The Committee over

As I said in my speech upon the First
Reading, I agree in principle with these recommendations, but I must make very clear
the opinion which I hold, namely, that the

I now come to the Local Education Authorities. The establishment of a Local Education Authority marks the great change
through which the system of the control of
Education will pass under this Bill. I mean
by that the change from the centralised to
the decentralised system. A Local Education
Authority, apart from Technical Instruction
Committees, is a body hitherto unknown in
Ireland. and I think the time is fully due
when the voice of the locality should be
heard in matters of education here in the Six
Counties, as it has been for many years on
the other side of the water.
The functions of our proposed Education
Authority, which is the County Council, or
County Borough Council, may be stated
briefly. The Authority must retain in its
own hands the power to raise money by rate
or loan, and to acquire, to hold, and to dispose of land, while it may retain the whole
of the general control of expenditure, or just
The question has arisen now, the same
question which arose so acutely in the discussions of the Lynn Committee, as to
whether the County Council is the body best
suited to become the new Education Authority. The Lynn Committee maintains what
I may call an open view, and the members
of that Committee deliberately agree that in
the future the County Council will, in ail
probability, be the Educational Authority. In
the framing of the Bill we have decided-and
we decided only after very careful consideration-that the County Councils and County
Borough Councils should be established as the
Educational Authority, for the simple and
obvious reason that the County Council is the
general rating authority now, and cannot properly be excluded from being the authority
responsible for the raising of an education
rate. I think it is obvious that any other
system sets up two rating authorities, and 1
cannot believe that such a system could be
conceived in the best interests of that
economy in administration which we desire
rigidly to maintain.
The powers of the County Council as an
Education Authority, other than those I have
just indicated, are delegated to Regional Committees, and in setting up these latter bodies,
the consideration which has influenced us is
the desire to associate local interest and
local responsibility with the requirements of
education. These Regional Committees will
bring the people belonging to the locality
itself into closer contact with local responsibilities in regard to education.
The area of a Regional Committee may be
that of a single county district or a combination of such districts. If a suitable educational area cannot be otherwise obtained.
county districts situated in more than one
county may be combined. The urban districts are included in the county districts for
all purposes except for Technical Instruction.
While we go somewhat further than the
recommendations of the Lynn Committee, we
do not, I submit, substantially differ from
them. Our scheme has the additional advautage that the areas contemplated are sufficiently large to enable the Committees to
work towards the real co-ordination of educational effort, while not too large to hinder
the development of local interest in education.
Naturally I have in my mind an actual
plan by which we believe we shall be able to
divide up the Counties into appropriate Regional areas. The areas have purposely not
been scheduled to the Bill, because it appears
to me to be a matter entirely connected with
local administration, and so, capable of ad-

In so far as the expenses of the Education
Authority have to be met from rates, the
amount required in each Regional area will
be raised within that area, and the local representatives on the Authority will be in a
position to place an effective check upon local

such a form of local administration will be
expensive, but there is no reason why this
should be so. We are making special provision whereby inspectors or other officers of
the Ministry will act as education advisers
or assessors to the Committees, and it will
accordingly not be necessary for these Committees to employ special technical officers at
high salaries. In the case of most of the
Committees the clerks and treasurers will not
necessarily be whole-time officers, and it will
surely be possible for them to find such office

the offices of Urban or District Councils, or
in Model Schools, or other schools under the
Committees.

The terms 'elementary education" and
"public elementary school" occur very frequently in the text of the Bill.
A "public elementary school "-and I am
quoting the definition in the Bill-is a
"school, or department of a school, in respect of which grants are paid out of
moneys provided by Parliament and in
which elementary education is the principal
part of the education provided."
All the existing national schools are, therefore, "public elementary schools," and will
remain, so long as they are necessary,
whether they are transferred to the Education Authority or continue on a voluntary
basis.
The Lynn Committee place in one class
schools provided by or transferred to Education Authorities, and in another class schools
not so transferred, but accepting a measure
of local control in the shape of a Committee
of Management on which the Education
Authority is represented. And in a third
class, again, appear those schools under managers which elect to remain entirely independent of the Education Authority.
In the Bill we have practically adopted the
same classification; but we have avoided the
somewhat invidious distinction which the
term Class I., Class II., or Class III. may be
said to involve; and, accordingly, we have
divided the schools as being either "schools
provided by or transferred to Education
Authorities," or "voluntary schools," of
which there may be two varieties corresponding to Classes II, and III. of the classification of the Lynn Report. It is only a small
distinction, but I am sure that it is one with
which the House will agree.
I now come to the next point upon which
a certain amount of criticism has centred-
I mean the transfer of existing schools from
their present owners to the local authority
The Lynn Committee express the view that
"it would not be desirable or possible
for the State to purchase the buildings
outright."
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: Hear, hear.
The MARQUESS OF LONDONDERRY.
It is quite clear that in an Act of Parliament the Education Authority must be
either empowered to purchase the buildings
or prohibited from doing so. In framing
this Bill we have desired not to rule out
the possibility of purchase, which, in certain
cases, might easily be the best and most
economical arrangement.
For instance, the case might, and certainly
will, arise of a school built in connection
with a church, a school which has provided
for years past the education required by the
Ministry, while at the same time it has
been utilised essentially for purposes connected with that church. In such cases the
transfer to the Local Education Authority
might be so hampered by restrictions, so
encumbered by rights of user, that the
transfer would be of so unreal a character
as completely to destroy its own object.
With schools like these it would, in some
circumstances, probably be far better for
the school to remain a voluntary school.
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: Hear, hear.
The MARQUESS OF LONDONDERRY:
In other cases it might be advantageous, both
to the Education Authority and to the
church, to transfer for some monetary consideration which would enable the church,
which, after all, was solely responsible for
the building of this school, to transfer its
denominational activities to some other
building.
There is the additional safeguard provided
in the Bill that the terms and conditions of
transfer have in all cases to be approved by
the Ministry. The Ministry would probably

I do not propose to delay the House long
over the provision for Higher Education, not
because I do not consider that Higher Education is as important in itself as Elementary
Education, but because I think that that part
of the Bill which deals with this form of
education requires but little in the nature of
an explanation.
It is our intention to provide, as far as
possible, that no child, simply through lack
of means, shall be prevented from obtaining
an education suitable both to his future requirements and his present capabilities.
Public money in profusion has been wasted
in England and Scotland in the vain endeavour to give a course of Higher Education to
children who are incapable for various reasons
of profiting from it. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) It would be a great misfortune if we
did not profit by the experience on the other
side of the water; but it would be a still
greater misfortune were boys and girls of real
capacity, through no fault of their own,
deprived of the advantages offered by a
further course of instruction. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) The loss of this educational
opportunity is not borne by the children
alone. It is shared through them by the
community. Good material is not so plentiful that it can be neglected, and we cannot
afford to disregard the importance of a wellconducted scheme of assistance on settled
principles for children who can usefully
assimilate such knowledge.
Power is given to the Ministry to prescribe
by regulations laid before Parliament the
conditions to be fulfilled in respect of any
school for the purpose of Parliamentary
grants or of aid from local rates. These
regulations are not set forth in detail in the
Bill, but I can assure the House that when
they are laid before Parliament they will be
found to contain generally the application of
the recommendations of the Lynn Committee.
I now pass from the Intermediate and Secondary system to the Continuation Schools
and Classes for Technical Instruction.
Our Education Authorities are the Local
Authorities in their respective areas for all
forms of education, and we are laying upon
them the duty of making provision for Technical Instruction by means of day or evening
Continuation Schools or Classes.
In order to carry out the recommendation
of the Lynn Committee in regard to urban
committees of Technical Instruction, established under the Technical Instruction Act
of 1899, we have made provision for allowing
these committees to continue their functions
in regard to Technical Instruction for the
urban areas and to give them exactly the
same powers and position in this department
of educational administration as the Regional
committees enjoy elsewhere.
In this connection it will be remembered
that I foreshadowed in my Speech on the
First Reading of this Bill a Government
grant in aid of taxation raised locally for the
purposes of education, and I now wish it to
be clearly understood that whatever grant is
enjoyed by other parts of the country in
relief of local expenditure on Technical Instruction will be equally shared by those
urban committees which elect to retain their
present functions. I am not sure that that is
quite clear in the Bill, but I should like it
to be perfectly clear to all who are interested.
I should like to add that while we have made
provision for the continuance of these committees in the urban areas it is our hope that
with the consent of all parties the Education
Authorities established by this Bill may
ultimately be the Authorities for Technical
Instruction in the urban areas and so become
responsible for all forms of education in their
respective areas without any exception whatsoever.
It is my opinion that when our regional
committees have shown themselves, as I feel
confident they will, capable of intelligent and
impartial administration, the urban committees, in their own interest, and in the interest

I now come to the question of Religious
Instruction. The question of religious
teaching in the schools has naturally aroused
a certain amount of controversy, and I hope
I shall not incur any censure from Members
of this House if I do not make the position
perfectly clear. In framing the Bill, I was
particularly anxious to give full opportunity
to the churches for denominational instruc
tion, and I think I may fairly claim to have
been successful. The question arose as to
how this instruction could be given in accordance with the tenets of all the various
denominations, and yet inflict no hardship
upon those children whose parents belong to
a particular denomination. I, therefore,
decided to grant the use of the school
buildings to the representatives of all denominations, outside those hours during
which children are required to attend compulsorily.
Each denomination, naturally, would prefer a fuller measure of spiritual education
for the children, and I am thoroughly in
agreement with this sentiment. How, then,
is this spiritual training to be imparted to
the young and to be interwoven with the
daily curriculum? I never had any doubt
in my mind but that each regional committee would prescribe in the curriculum a
certain length of time every day, or its
equivalent in the week, during which teachers could impart to the children the
lessons of Christian teaching and those moral
principles to which we all subscribe.
therefore, I did not think it necessary, at

Bill. However, from the various representations which have been made to me, since
the introduction of the Bill, and from the

agree that we should include in the Bill such

this description will be imparted to the
children.
Mr. LYNN: Hear, hear.
And,
The MARQUESS OF LONDONDERRY: I
intend, therefore, on the Committee stage,
to introduce words calculated to give effect

The controversies, which have arisen over
religious instruction in connection with the
various Education Bills which have been
brought forward from time to time, have
caused me to proceed very warily, and I feel,
that in endeavouring to tread the least controversial path I have, perhaps, incurred the
suspicion, if I may use the expression, that
the State, as represented by the Government,
does not to the full realise the vital importance of the formation of character--
Mr. LYNN: No, no.
The MARQUESS OF LONDONDERRY:
But attaches too much weight to the secular
training of the young. I can assure the
House that this is a complete fallacy, and,
speaking for myself, and, indeed, for all my
colleagues, I am of opinion that no instruction is of any real value unless combined
with that instruction are those influences
which are indispensable to the making of the
upright and God-fearing citizen. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
I regret to have to say it, but we must
realise that a great number of children in
the Six Counties enter the schools without
any spiritual upbringing whatever, and I
have come to the conclusion that, unless we
lay down, as a Government, our adherence to
Christian principles and the belief we hold
in the necessity for associating Christian
ethics with secular teaching, we shall not
be discharging the duty which we owe to the
rising generation. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.)
Having dealt with the various forms of
State provision of, or assistance to, education, I now come to deal with the children
themselves, for whose benefit these burdens
must be undertaken. Our first step is, naturally, to secure their attendance at school.
The broad, general principle of the Bill
is that school attendance shall be compulsory
between the ages of six and fourteen. I do
not think that we can go further than this,
at present, in the matter of compulsion. In
England and Scotland, in the Education Acts
of 1918, power was taken to enforce school
attendance up to eighteen years of age; but
it has not been found possible to bring those
provisions into effective operation. The time
is probably not far distant when a measure
of compulsion can be applied to "continued
education" during the critical period following the age of fourteen, when the child leaves
the prima y school. But, if for the present
we have secured the attendance of all children between six and fourteen, we shall have
mado a very considerable advance.
I have said that school attendance may be
enforced at six years, but the lower limit of
five years may be fixed at the option of the
local education authority, because I feel that,
where the facilities exist, or the will to provide them, is present in a particular locality,
no attempt should be made by the Ministry
to discourage local effort or to exclude these
children from the benefits of an earlier education. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)

The upper limit we have fixed at fourteen,
and normally every child under this age will
be in regular attendance at school, unless he
has a reasonable excuse for non-attendance.
But there is a possibility, under the Bill, of
children between twelve and fourteen being
exempted from school attendance by the
local authority for the purpose of enployment at specified times, in specified
occupations, and upon specified conditions.
Let me remark at once that such exemptions
are not intended to be, and will not be, of
general application. They will meet the
case of those children alone, who, without
any serious detriment to their general
education, may be usefully employed from
time to time in what we call seasonal occupations. We do not mean to allow the
provisions for compulsory attendance to
become farcical in their application or to
allow any relapse into those conditions
which have, for so long, made the attendance
at Irish public elementary schools a byword and disgrace among modern systems of
education.

There can be no question of the necessity
for the consolidation and amendment of
existing enactments which deal with the
health and well-being of the children. Apart
from the waste of educational effort, it is
nothing short of cruelty to attempt to educate, along with normal children, neglected
children or children who through lack of
medical treatment, or lack of sufficient food
and clothing are not in a position to take full
advantage of the education provided.
There is nothing here that will undermine
parental responsibility. Full provision is
made for the recovery of any expenditure involved in all cases where the parent can
pay. Neglected children and children also
who are sick or starving will be attended
to, and it is essential, not only for their
own benefit but for the benefit of other
children at the same school that this should
be done before any attempt is made to educate them.
The Lynn Committee deal with the
question of schools for afflicted children in
their Report. They say-
"We see no reason why the education of
children who are deaf, dumb, blind, or
otherwise afflicted, should be less a matter
of concern than the education of normal
children

Mr. McGUFFIN: Hear, hear.
The MARQUESS OF LONDONDERRY:
And they add-this occurs in paragraph
242-
"The Ministry should, we think, have
ample powers and resources for dealing
with the education of all types of afflicted
children."
The soundness of these conclusions can
hardly be disputed. But, in Ireland, the
education of afflicted children has hitherto
been mainly dependent upon private philanthropy or private enterprise. Consequently,
nearly the whole of Part IX. of the Bill
embodies proposals for new legislation, a
fact which might, otherwise, create the
impression that undue prominence is given
to this aspect of education in the Measure.
Such legislation is urgently required,
almost as much in the interests of the normal
child, as in the interests of the afflicted
child. The presence of afflicted children in
the ordinary school classes affects prejudically the course of instruction, the discipline,
and the general arrangements of the school.
The fact is being more fully recognised
every day, that many children pass through
a course of elementary instruction without
deriving any substantial benefit therefrom,
and leave school lacking almost entirely the
very rudiments of education. This is
admitted to be due to no fault, no avoidable
fault, I mean, on the part of these unfortunate children, or of those who have done
their best to teach them. It is due to the
system under which the afflicted have
been herded together with the normal children, and the inability of the children in
question, through some degree of mental deficiency, to assimilate the instruction provided. This is a state of affairs which I hope
will be to a great extent remedied under the
provisions of the present Bill.
The question of the teachers comes second
only in importance to that of the children,
because we recognise that our teachers must
be of the best description and capable in the
highest degree of effectively imparting information to the children. For this purpose

Returning to the subject of the Bill, I note

without thought of any other reward than
the educational well-being of the community.
But, in these days, we are constantly being
told that the teachers have abandoned the
old ideals, that the well-being of the children
has become to them no more than a secondary
consideration. I have seen attacks made on
the teachers from various directions, and the
substance of them all is the apparent disregard which they show for anything and
everything but their own material advantages.
I need hardly say that personally I do not
feel that these charges are justly laid against
them-(Hon. Members: Hear, hear)-but they
must do nothing themselves to encourage
suspicion. Of course, their whole position
can be said to have been changed by the
assumption by the State of the responsibility
of educating the children, and the teachers,
instead of occupying their old unique position,
now hold a similar position to that of many

that is involved in building schools, for I
helped to build one. I know the difficulty
that is involved in attendance at school, in
inspecting schools, and even in writing out
certificates and forms for salaries. The clergy
have done this since the Middle Ages. They
have done it in Ulster for three hundred
years. They have built and managed schools,
and while we might occasionally see little
things that perhaps we thought we could have
avoided, I think the clergy have done their
duty in a way that commends itself to the
favourable consideration of this House and of
all right-thinking men. I would say this from
my experience, chiefly of primary teachers,
that they constitute one of the finest bodies
we have in rural Ulster. If you have any

more education than the average man possesses, you will find the primary teachers assisting and co-operating, and I think that
both teachers and clergy should have their
wishes granted where it is at all possible. If
you do that you will certainly be smoothing
your path.

would be provided by the State. The great
difficulty we labour under here in Ireland in respect of education is the legacy
which has fallen to us from the Imperial
Authority. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
That legacy for long years familiarised the
people of Ireland with the State system of
education without any contribution from local
sources, and without any local responsibility;

must continue ad infinitum. The second difficulty under which we labour is this: that we
have taken over governmental responsibility
in the North of Ireland at a time, a very unfortunate time, of great commercial and industrial depression, and the burden of taxation is so heavy that obviously our people
in the North of Ireland look with very grave
concern on the possibility of any additional
burden incurred through local taxation.
Therefore, with the question of a local contribution to education, a new system altogether, I say it is not unnatural that they
That is the one side of the question, but
let me take the other. We find ourselves

Well, I agree that the Bill is an important
Bill.
But I am not inclined to attach to it
the importance that is frequently conveyed by
speeches from the platform and letters to the
Press. I am afraid that this Bill has been
boomed. For months past we have heard of
nothing but the Education Bill. People have
been reading of it in every day's issue. My
hon. Friend, the Member for West Belfast
(Mr. Lynn) is largely responsible for that.
His paper, which I take in every morning-
(bon. Members: Hear, hear)-and read most
diligently, has indeed contributed very much
to the enlightenment of the public with respect to this most important question. But I
am not disposed to believe that the importance that has been attached to it, in the
opinion of some people, would justify us in
anticipating from it the results that have
been predicted. If we are to have the great
results that are anticipated with respect to
this Measure we will require to re-define the
meaning of the term education. The word
education, as we all know, is derived from a
word which means to lead out-that is, to
lead out the mental faculties of the child, but
our modern interpretation of education seems
to be to dump in or to cram in, and we are
asked to believe that it is educating a child
to cram into its mind so many facts and so
many data with respect to things the purpose
and principle of which it does not understand. Is that called education? We must
revise our conception of education if we are
going to realise the great results that are
anticipated from this Bill. Education, I take
it, is not an act of limited duration or calculable results. Education, to my mind, is a
process, continuous and progressive-(hon
Members: Hear, hear)-and in the words of
the late Professor Huxley, "However early
begun and long continued must always be
reflected upon with dissatisfaction and regret."
We will never accomplish our education.
We may tend that way. But it would be
a good thing in so far as we are mistaken
in respect of what true education means,
that we should remodel our system and
bring it more into touch with the
modern ideal. It is not the manipulation
of the mind of the child with a view to
equipping it for some specific profession in
life. That is not the idea. It may be a
necessary part, but it is a very bad ideal to
place before the child. The child is given
to understand that when it reaches the Sixth
Standard it will be educated, that it will
have all that is necessary for it to make its
way in the world. I do not say that it is
put in those specific terms to the child, but
it is the impression that most children have
-that when they quit school they have done
with their education. The thing to do is to
change the incentive to the child from merely
thinking that he is preparing for his future,
so as to enable him to see not only here but
so far as hereafter is concerned he will be
called upon in future to improve.

sure that
if we anticipate results they are likely to be

I could wish that our schools had been
established upon a secular basis, and when I
say a secular basis let no hon. Member come
to the conclusion that I am advocating anything in the nature of a Godless school.
Nothing of the sort. I hold that knowledge is
sacred, and I take up the position that we are
not entitled to differentiate with respect to
the theological views of any section of the
community, and say that this is sacred and
the other is profane. I say all knowledge is
sacred. If a geologist delves in the crust of
the earth and brings up proof, written on
tablets of stone, with reference to the age
of the earth, by which we are enabled to
apprehend the greatness of creation, and in
that way to approach to the greater ideal of
God, has he done a disservice? If an
astronomer casts his telescope through the
heavens and discloses that beyond our solar
system there is illimitable space and
innumerable worlds, does he not improve our
ideas of God's majesty in so doing? So I
might multiply instances if I wished, but I
am not going to. Because certain knowledge
is called profane by a certain section, there
is no necessity why it should be regarded as
such. I am of opinion that the best thing
we could do under the circumstances would
be to exclude religious education from the
school entirely.
An Hon. MEMBER: No, no.

That is the deliberate opinion, not
expressed in the Committee, but written in

afraid it will multiply trouble for us in the

was introduced in connection with our school
life it had a different significance to what it
has to-day. It meant then piety, but what
do we find now? It has been very wisely
put by a celebrated authority who flourished
Et the latter end of last century and was
looked upon as the most philosophic mind of
his age-Dr. Martineau. He said:-
There is no surer mark of decline in the
spirit of a people than the corruption of
its language and the loss of meaning from
its highest and most sacred words.
He continues:-
In the affairs of Government, of
Morality, and of Divinity we retain the
phrases used by our forefathers in
Shakespeare's time, but it is impossible to
notice the dwindled meaning which they
frequently contain without coming to the
conclusion that the currency struck for the
commerce of giants' souls has been clipped
to serve the traffic of dwarfs.
How does he illustrate his meaning in this
matter? He takes the word "religion" and
he says:-
If you ask a man nowadays what his
religion is he will reply by telling you
something about where he goes on Sunday
or the preacher he objects to least; his
likes or dislikes; his habits and opinions:
his conventional profession; but who from
all this could infer anything as to his
character? It might enable you to find him
in the street, or give you some impression
as to how he looks and the manner of man
he is, but it will give you no insight of
what he is.
Did not Matthew Arnold say that morality
plus emotion represented his ideal of religion?
which simply means enthusiasm in goodness,

Mr. JOHNSTONE. I should not like this
debate to close without taking the opportunity to make one or two points which I think
have not yet been touched upon. I should
like, first of all, to congratulate the noble
Marquess, the Minister of Education, upon
his very lucid outline of this scheme of education. It seemed to me as I listened to
him that I was being shown an outline
drawn by the hand of a master, but unfortunately a great many details remained to be
filled in by the hand of the master in his
studio, and would only be shown to us later
on. I should like to say a word or two about
one or two points that came forward in that
outline; and, first, I shall refer to the Cominittees which are being set up under the
Bill. My hon. Friend the Member for West
Belfast (Mr. Lynn) has already spoken about
the modification of the number of Committees. You have got a regular hierarchy of
Committees. You start first of all with the
Ministry. Then you have the Advisory Committee and the County Committee. The
County Committee appoints the Regional
Committee, and the Regional Committee ap
points the School Committee. There is no
special object in piling authority on the top
of authority. The great advantage of that
is seen in the Army, where a man can always
evade responsibility by sending on the business to somebody higher up. That is not the
sort of thing you want to encourage in connection with education. You want to encourage local interest. That is only obtained
when you come down to the very last of the
series, the Local Committee. That was the
Committee which the Lynn Committee in its
consideration of this problem was specially
anxious to see established. It was explained
in what way these Local Committees should
be co-ordinated. The Lynn Committee had
before it the question of the County Committees as they are carried on in England and
Scotland, and they also considered the question of the Regional Committees. The Lynn
Committee after deliberation rejected the
County Committee and suggested the Regional
Committee. The Minister of Education, after
considering the matter, decided to have them
both in, and I think one of them is unnecessary. I cannot see what object it really
serves except to multiply officials, and consequently to multiply expense. I hope this
matter will be re-considered in Committee,
and that some way will be found of reducing
the number of committees through which the
business of education is to be carried on.
The second point I should like to speak
about is in regard to the Technical Committees which are being allowed to contract out
of the scheme of education, for that is really
what the Bill permits them to do. That is
one of the recommendations of the Lynn
Committee which I should be very glad indeed to see the noble Marquess rejecting,
and for two reasons. You are going to establish a number of committees to look after
education. At the present time there is liter-

no
ally not one single person in the whole of
the North of Ireland who has any experience
of the local administrative work in connection with education except the members af
the Technical Committees already in existence, and now you are going to allow these
people to stand clean out of your scheme of
education. That will not be good for
them, because it is very important that Technical Education should be linked up with all
other forms of education. There is
essential distinction between Technical,
Irimary, and Secondary Education. They
are all part of a great whole. I am quite
prepared to safeguard these Technical Committees in any way that may be considered necessary, to establish them as committes as they stand at the present time
under the Local Education Authority, but I
would not be prepared-and I hope the House
would not-to permit these Technical Committees to stand clean outside of the whole
scheme of education. That is one
reason.
The other reason is if you retain these Technical Committees under the Local Education
Authority you will have a basis on which you
can build a very excellent working Education
Authority. Everyone knows the advantage
of experience in regard to administrative
matters I need not go further than this
House for an illustration. Most of the
Members of this House are comparatively
new to Parliamentary ways, and I do not
know what we should have done if it had not
been for the old Parliamentarians amongst

I should also like to emphasise what has

it will be
dealt with over as wide
an area as possible, so that a man who
distinguished himself, will have an opportunity of rising from a lower school to a
higher school, from a school in a small district to a school in a bigger district. and so
on.
That can only be done if the appointments are made by large bodies, and, if possible, after consultation with the Ministry
itself.
Then there is one other point I should like
to mention, and that in in regard to Secondary Education. I notice that the noble
Marquess drew our attention to the great
number of Acts which have been repealed,
and I see that a very large number of those
Acts had to do with Secondary Education.
The provision for Secondary Education in
this Bill is most sketchy. No one could
possibly understand what is going to happen
to Secondary Education under this Bill. I
should like to have some assurance from the
Minister of Education in regard to one
matter at any rate, and that is in regard to
the provision for the salaries of teachers,
because under this Bill you are doing away
with the present grants which are available
to enhance the salaries of Secondary
teachers, and unless some provision is made
in the Bill for providing proper salaries for
Secondary teachers they will not be in any
better position than they are at the present
time.

Written Answer to Question.
RENT RESTRICTIONS COMMITTEE.
Mr. M'BRIDE asked the Minister of Home
Affairs whether he has yet established a Departmental Committee to consider the question of Rent Restrictions, and what is the
cause of the delay in setting up the Commitee, having regard to the fact that the present Act expires next June?
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): The Committee has now been
established, and is constituted as follows:-
Serator Greer, D.L., M.P., Chairman.
Mr. James Cooper, M.P.
Mr. Thompson Donald, M.P.
Mr. William Grant, M.P.
Mr. Robert M'Bride, M.P.
Mr. H. H. Graham, Chairman of the Belfast
Auctioneers' and Estate Agents'
Institute.
Mr. Wm. Dowling, President of the Belfast
Property Owners' Association.
Mr. Harry Midgley, Secretary Irish Textile
Trades Federation.
Major Geo. A. Harris, D.S.O., Assistant
Secretary, Ministry of Home
Affairs.
Major H. Connacher, Assistant Secretary,
Ministry of Labour.
Mr. G. H. E. Parr, M.B.E., Assistant Secretary, Ministry of Commerce.
The delay in establishing the Committee is
due to difficulties which have arisen in connection with the appointment of members on
the Committee representing the interests of
Tenants.
The Belfast Tenants' Association were
asked to nominate four members representing
their Association, out of which two might be
selected to act on the Committee, but the Association decided not to recognise the Committee or to nominate representatives.
I greatly regret this decision on their part,
as I should have welcomed their advice and
assistance, and I am keeping two places open
on the Committee in the event of the Association deciding to reconsider their attitude
in this respect.

CLASS V. No. 2.
AGRICULTURAL SERVICES.
Motion made and Question proposed:
"That a sum not exceeding £36,656 be
granted to His Majesty to complete the
sum necessary to defray the charge that
will come in course of payment during the
year ending on the 31st March, 1924, in
respect of Agricultural Institutions, Improvement of Live Stock, Agricultural
Research Development, including Sundry
Grants-in-aid."
Mr. ARCHDALE: In Vote 2 we have our
Agricultural Services. Agricultural Research-Sub-head A-is one of the ways that
we most depend on to help the farmers
through the bad times they are having. In
England and Scotland the Grants for
agricultural research are a great deal more
in proportion than we can hope to be able to
have in this country, but perhaps in a short
time we may be able to get nearer their
proportion. The Seed-testing and Plant
Diseases Division, through the courtesy of
the Queen's University, has been housed in
the University, and the head of our Department is there. He is Mr. Mercer, who came
over from the Botany Institute at Cambridge.
One of his assistants is a lady and the other
is a gentleman, one being English and the
other Scotch. Both have got very high
scientific degrees, and the man served in the
war, and is a graduate of London University.
We shall now be very glad to show any
Member over the Seed-Testing Institute at
Queen's University. The Plant-Breeding
Division is situated at Stormont. The head
of it is Captain Hunter, who was for many
years in the Department of Agriculture at
Cork. He served in the war, and was afterwards in the Agricultural Department at
Committee.

Supply-
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Mr. Archdale]
Leamington, where he did a great deal of
valuable work in connection with the crossbreeding of plants and producing new
varieties of barley and wheat, which nearly
doubled the yield of the old varieties. We
hope he will be equally successful here. We
have just had a cage put up for plantbreeding, and a great many people passing
the entrance to Stormont thought it was
cage for canaries or something of that sort,
but it is really a plant-breeding cage put
up for cross-fertilization and to exclude
weeds and other plants we do not want to
introduce.
a
The Animal Diseases Division will be at
Queen's University. It will be for scientific
research, but we have not yet appointed a
Head. There is considerable capital expenditure required, because the loss from
animal diseases in this country is a good deal
over £1,000,000 every year. We hope to go
in for research in connection with nonscheduled diseases. The scheduled diseases
are Foot-and-mouth and Anthrax, which are
reserved by the Imperial authorities; but
we have such things as Abortion, Braxy, &c.,
which are responsible for a loss of over
$1,000,000 a year. We hope to make a serum
to inoculate against some of these diseases.
Ordinary veterinary practitioners will be
entrusted with the work of inoculation, and
we hope to produce a serum for inoculation
that will prove a cure for some of the
diseases that afflict agriculture in this
country. The Poultry Division is also at
Stormont, and this year we had 52 pens-
25 for research and 27 for the egg-laying
competition. We found that the number of
people applying for pens was much in excess
of what we had arranged for last year, and
this year we are putting up more pens, so
that we will be able to go in for
more experimental work. It is a curious
thing that since the egg laying
competitions were started at Cork about ten
years ago more than 60 per cent. of the
competitors came from the Six Counties.
That shows that farmers and others realise
that egg-laying is one of the most important
of our industries. In 1913, when the competition was first established, the average
number of eggs laid per bird was 120. Last
year the average number of eggs laid per
bird was 185.7, so if that result could be
attained all over the Six Counties the cost
of the egg-laying competitions would be fully
justified.
-
In the Chemical and Animal Nutrition
Division we have a very excellent man in Dr.
Robertson. He belongs to Queen's University
and we consider him one of the best officials
we could possibly get. He is now carrying
out a great many tests both in connection
with the fattening of animals and phosphates. In connection with Agricultural
Education we are obliged to put down a little
more this year for the Ulster Dairy School
at Cookstown. Last year, owing to various
causes, there were only 11 students, but in
January this year there were 41. We have
had to put up a good deal of fencing, which,
as everybody who is connected with the land
knows, is an expensive job. The number of
students at the North West School at Strabane last year was 11, and the number in
January this year was 17. We hear of a
good many more who wish to attend this
Institute owing to the propaganda work of
the Farmers' Union and other agricultural
organisations which encourage boys and girls
to go to the Institute. The North-west
School is for short courses for girls only in
housewifery work, dairying, washing, etc.
The Greenmount School belongs to the Ministry and is managed by the Antrim County
Council under a deed of arrangement with
us. There are 21 students in residence, and
we are building a separate house for the
principal, erecting additional laboratory
accommodation, and making provision
for giving instruction in gardening.
We hope the College will take the place of the
Agricultural School in Dublin, and we hope
that the cost of the buildings we are erecting
at Greenmount will be paid by the
Imperial Government. The Farmers'
Union and
various County
Committees encourage boys to come to this
school, and we expect that in future we shall
have 44 pupils instead of 24, which is the
most the school will accommodate at present.

With regard to the sum allocated for the
improvement of live stock, it is devoted to
the purchase
of stallions and bulls
and grants to Cow Testing and other Live
Stock associations. In my opinion, cow
testing is the most important thing we can
do for Ulster agriculture. When you realise
that by cow testing Denmark has raised milk
production from 400 gallons to 800 gallons
per cow it is impossible to tell how much
money we will be putting into our pockets
by the use of these cow testing associations.
I am glad to say that farmers are begiuning to appreciate them. In 1921 there
were 6 cow-testing associations with 1,244
cows, and in 1922 there were 13 associations
with 3,560 cows. This year we estimate
there will be 17 associations with 5,000 cows.
At every show we have attended we have
urged with all the power we could the formation of these cow-testing associations, so that
a man will know that he need not feed a bad
cow when he could feed a good cow that
would give double the quantity for the same

is the estimated cost of inspection for licences

These will be self-supporting, as the amount

As regards Grants to County Committees,
there is, I am afraid, a large increase. I
would like to explain that during the last
two years our Six Counties schemes have cost
more than the amounts that were allotted to
them, but they have been paying those
amounts out of the savings from the Six
Counties which had been in the hands of the
Department in Dublin. If it had not been
for that they would not have been able to
carry on their work. We believe, indeed we
are almost certain, that that money will be
transferred to us very soon, and will go towards re-paying the extra money now given
to the County Committees. They did not get
it during the last year, and, therefore, we had
to make this addition to the Estimate. The
old Department used to allocate also to the
counties £50,000 a year, this sum being equal
to 1d in the £ on the rates in the rural
districts. They not only allocated that
£50,000 for county schemes, but they paid for
the cost of one agricultural instructor in each
county. Two counties had two such instructors. They also paid the living bonus
of all instructors and county officials, and
they further paid grants from the Development Fund. We propose following the old
Department's precedent. The sum of £16,010
would be the amount of the grant-in-aid to
the Six Counties, and this would equal 11d
in the £ on the rural rates, and not 1ad in
the £, which the old Dublin Board used to
pay. In addition we would pay the salary
of one instructor in each county, about £2,000,
as well as the bonus of all agricultural officers. This amount, however, would be given
on one condition. We would like the County
Councils to have a penny rate struck for
agricultural instruction. The County Councils have as a rule been paying a penny in
the for agricultural and technical instruction. Some of them have been paying
1d, and some more, but very few gave more
than 75 per cent. of what they allocated to
agriculture. We want them to give annually
a penny in the £ towards agricultural instruction. If they do not give the penny
towards agricultural instruction we will make a
corresponding diminution in the amount we
want to give them to make up for what they
used to get from the Department in Dublin.
They will not get the maximum unless they
provide the penny in the £.

Now, as regards flax and potato industries,
I find the area under flax was 3,315 acres
less last year than it was in 1921. There were
32,432 acres in 1921, and 29,117 acres in 1922.
Of course, everyone expected that owing to
the bad price offered for flax last year. We
hope that there will be a much larger growth
of flax this year, and that there will be a
very considerably higher price for it.
Members: Hear, hear.) In the potato industry there was, I am afraid, a slump every-

where. I do not think there was ever a year

them to the market for the price they get.
Whether it is any consolation or not, I may
say that both England and America are in
the same boat. I was told the other day by
a gentleman who has just come back from
California that a 6,900lb. railway truck full of
potatoes was sent from California to Chicago
by a friend of his, who received 2s back as
the profit on that consignment of potatoes. I
think, therefore, we cannot say that they are
any better off there than we are. I believe the
farmers in the country are feeding their
cattle on the potatoes as much as they can.
Unfortunately, there is a small lot of pigs
in the country. If we had more pigs we
could make more use of the potatoes.
hope before next year there will be an increased number of brood sows and young

Black scab is, of course, prevalent, and we
are taking great pains to schedule only those
parts where it is. What we have got to 100k
out for is to prevent England and the Continent stopping our potatoes going to those
countries. They are very fond of putting
a stop to produce going from this country.
I think lately they have made it a sort
of method that instead of minimising an
outbreak of black scab they make a great
deal more out of it than it really is. We
have not nearly as much black scab as there
is in England, and still they threaten to stop
the export of our potatoes if not accompanied
by a licence. I know cargoes of potatoes
sent to the Canary Islands and elsewhere
were returned to the produce merchants here
in Ireland because they said they were bad.
One of the best men in our Department who
inspected the potatoes before they went
clearly told the produce men that they were
the best lot of potatoes he had ever seen.
Mr. DONALD: To what extent does black
scab exist in the Six Counties, and where
does it exist?
Mr. ARCHDALE: It exists in the County
of Down principally, and also in Armagha little about Newry.
Mr. LAVERY: Southern Down?
Mr. ARCHDALE: Yes. It generally starts
in a garden, and is very hard to eradicate.
It is very infectious. People discover black
scab, and do not report it to our inspectors.
A man will empty potatoes affected with
black scab on to a manure heap, and
that is only a means of spreading
the disease all over the land. It
we could persuade the people of the country
to sow new potatoes there would be no diffi-

The animal quarantine station is a thing
we have been trying to get for a long time.
People have had cattle bought in England
for nearly a year some of them for six
months--and there has been so much bother
about getting the cattle into the country that
we have decided, with the assistance of the
Ministry of Finance, to put up this quarantine station. It was very much wanted for
bulls and new breeds that were coming into
the country, and we have found an excellent
place at the Twin Island at the mouth of
the River Lagan.
Mr. M'GUFFIN: Is that where the old
Fever Hospital used to be?
Mr. ARCHDALE: It is next the Electric
Station. We keep away from the Fever
Hospital.

the same site probably.

cargo coming. We are having rather a lot

about rules and regulations, but I hope it

as we used to, we have now a part time

on whatever we want. Therefore his
us
cost is only £150. The receipts in aid

themselves, and the fees for the inspection

There are two other items here on which
I want to make a few observations. One is
the grant of £1,200 to the Ulster Agricultural
Organisation Society for the organisation of
Co-operative Societies. I approve very highly
of that. I am very glad that the Minister
has made an arrangement, which I think
will be eminently satisfactory, whereby his
Department looks after the technical work,
such as machinery, the cleanliness of the
preduce, and other details of butter making,
and all those things alone. The Agricultural
Society confines itself wholly to organisation,
and the inspection of books, and giving
advice with regard to such matters. As the
right hon. Gentleman (Mr. Archdale) has
already told the House, there used to be a
grant for all Ireland. That grant has been
continued by the Free State to its own people
on the condition that no amount of that
money is to be spent in the Six County area.
I think if the Department here, now that
they have come to the assistance of those
living in the Six County area and have made
this grant, would see that the Agricultural
Organisation Society looks after the books
and accounts of the different Co-operative
Societies they would be doing a good turn
not only to those societies but a good turn
to agriculture.
With regard to the grant to the Farmers'
Union, that is a new thing, and I think a
very wise thing. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) In my opinion the farmer suffers
from many disabilities, and many heavy loads
were placed upon him that should not have
been placed upon him. I see that a distinct
attempt is about to be made by the English
farmers to introduce some measure of redress for the many grievances from which
agriculture is suffering at the present time.
I hope that if any efficient means is devised
for relieving those burdens, some such policy
will be adopted in Ulster. One of the most
important things-I think perhaps some other
hon. Member could explain it more fully than
I can--that militates against agriculture is
the enormous increase in the cost of transport. How that could be prevented I
cannot tell. The transport rates from Belfast
to Liverpool, or from Belfast to Glasgow, are
exactly four times what they were a few years
ago, and this has damaged very seriously the
trade in cattle. That opens up a very wide
question with which I need not deal, but I
am sure the Minister of Agriculture has been
thinking about it.
The quarantine station is another new idea,
and I think it is an excellent thing that
cattle can be brought over here and the
country protected from disease. An outbreak
of infectious disease is a very serious thing,
and I think this is a very wise expenditure.
With regard to forestry, we are spending
£1,270 on it, and I do not think any money
could be better spent.
Mr. DONALD: It is not nearly enough.
Dr. MORRISON: It is not nearly enough.
I think there is a vast field in Ulster for
expenditure of this kind, and a very remunerative return could be secured, perhaps
not at an early date, but coming generations
would benefit by it.
Mr. M'GUFFIN: A hundred years hence.
Dr. MORRISON: Much less. In thirty
years, or even in twenty years. Certain
kinds of timber will mature in thirty years,
or even in twenty years, and become very
valuable. There is no question that, as the
Minister knows, there are large tracts of
land, that are practically valueless at
present, that could be planted with timber
that would grow quickly, and become very
valuable, and would increase the resources of
the country. I think on the whole we may
congratulate ourselves that the Ministry of
Agriculture is doing good work, and under the
wise guidance of the present Minister it will
have in the coming year even a more successful period than has already been attained
