Companies (Reconstitution of
Records) Bill (S.).
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed, "That
the Bill be now read a Second time."
Mr. ARCHDALE: This is a small Bill, but
a very necessary one. The House will recollect that in May, 1921, the Custom House
in Dublin was burned. All the files of
companies were destroyed, except three
which happened to be with the Board of
Trade in London at the time. This Bill is to
provide for the reconstitution of the companies' records so that the businesses can be
carried on properly in the Six Counties.
There was a list kept in London of all companies, and fortunately English, Scotch and
Irish companies were shown separately. The
Assistant Registrar of Companies in Dublin
and the Registrar in the Ministry of Commerce in Belfast went through that list and
other papers, and after a great deal of work
they identified the names of 1,300 Northern
Ireland companies. What we wish to do now
is to reconstitute the records of those companies. The Bill requires every company in
Northern Ireland to furnish a summary of
its past history, and a statement of its position on 25th May, 1921, in the form given in
the Schedule. They must also furnish copies of
the Memorandum and Articles of Association.
Every effort has been made by the Registrar here and by the Draughtsman of the
Bill to reduce the trouble occasioned to the
companies and to make the burden placed
upon them as light as possible, but the necessity is very great and the Government inherited it owing to the burning of the Custom
House in Dublin. The Bill requires companies
to furnish the particulars before 31st March,
1924, under penalty, and in case any company
through any unforeseen cause is not able to
do so, a Court of Justice may restore it to
its position as if it had furnished the records
in the prescribed time. The Bill has been
before the Senate and there are one or two
drafting amendments which will come before
the House in Committee. I beg to move.
Mr. McGUFFIN: I only want to ask a
question. Seeing that the original records
have been destroyed, and that there is no
trace of them except in London, has the
right hon. Gentleman any means of checking
the returns made by these companies? Is
he in a position to check the information or
to say whether it is genuine or not? I do
not understand the position.
Mr. ARCHDALE: There is no means of
proving whether the companies are furnishing
the correct records.
Mr. McGUFFIN: You cannot check them?
Mr. ARCHDALE: No, but this is the only
thing to be done. You have got to trust the
companies to give a true return of shareholders, etc. There is no other way of
doing it.
Question put, and agreed to.
Bill read the Second time, and committed
to a Committee of the whole House for tomorrow.
Promissory Oaths Bill (S.).
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed, "That
the Bill be now read a Second time."
The PARLIAMENTARY AND FINAN-
CIAL SECRETARY TO THE MINISTRY
OF FINANCE (Mr. Barbour): The Promissory Oaths Bill of 1868 is the general
authority governing the taking of the oath
known as the Oath of Allegiance. This Act
is in force in Northern Ireland by virtue of
Amendment 61 of the Government of Ireland
Act, which specifies certain office-holders
from whom the Oath of Allegiance is required, the same being given to the King,
but this does not include Civil Servants.
During the war, however, Civil Servants
serving in an established capacity in His
Majesty's Civil Service were required by a
Defence of the Realm Regulation to take the
Oath of Allegiance. Shortly after the termination of the war this Regulation expired
so far as the Civil Service in England was
concerned, but by a Regulation under the
Restoration of Order in Ireland Act it was
extended to Imperial Civil Servants still
executing duties in Ireland. Under the
Local Government Act and the Constabulary
Act, which will be fresh in the minds of hon.
Members, Oaths of Allegiance were required
to be taken not only to the King but also to
the Government of Northern Ireland by anyone serving in either a Local Government
capacity or under the Royal Ulster Constabulary. So it is felt now that the
introduction of this Bill is only a very logical
sequence to our having imposed an Oath of
Allegiance on two such important branches
of our Northern Ireland Civil Service. There
has been a general expression of opinion that
those who are responsible for the teaching
of the children in the schools of this Province and are in receipt of Government
grants should also take the Oath of Allegiance, and I should like to say that in Committee we propose the introduction of an
amendment to this Bill to extend this provision to this class of persons, who, although
not in the employment of the Government,
are really paid by the Government to do
work of immense importance.

Mr. McGUFFIN: I must express
regret that Bills slip so lightly through the
House. I do not under-estimate the importance of this Bill in the slightest degree. I
think it is highly necessary, but it seems to
me to suggest an indifference on the part of
the House, or rather lack of interest in the
legislation that is brought forward, when so
few participate in the discussion. If it were
not for our respect for the dignified position
you hold, Mr. Speaker, one would be almost
tempted to play the part of obstructionist,
in order, if possible, to delay the passage of
these Bills. I do not propose to play that
role. I am not opposed to the Measure, but
I do question its utility, and on this ground.
You cannot make people loyal by Act of
Parliament. That policy has been tried for
a century and more in the history of this
country, and what have you done? You have
forced crime below the ground. You have
made it disappear to re-appear again, and it
is almost an innate characteristic, a sort of
kink, to be disloyal, and it is often expressed
in the aphorism, "to be loyal to Ireland is to
he agin the Government." What is going
to be your standard of loyalty: Loyalty is
a comparative term. It does not exist in two
individuals in this House to the same degree
I suppose that a Conservative in politics
represents what is called the very acme of
loyalty. A Liberal represents loyalty in a
less degree, a Nationalist in a lesser degree
again, and a Sinn Feiner in no degree at all.
Then a very important question arises. The
hon. Gentleman (Mr. Barbour), who so very
eloquently and suitably introduced the Second
reading of this Bill, must have seen that
it somewhat interferes with the freedom of
speech, If there is one thing more than
another that is valued by the citizens of this
country it is freedom of speech, and I do
not suppose that the right hon. Gentleman,
the Prime Minister, who may be responsible
for this matter, and is head of the Government, proposes for one moment to interfere
with the freedom of speech. Let us take a
case. The hon. Gentleman has put it before
the House that this will apply to school
teachers. Did I understand him to say so?
(Hon. Members: Yes.) The school teachers
as a rule are a loyal body of men. (Hon:
Members: Hear, hear.) But they are not
exclusively that. What I look at is this:
We have a section of teachers in the North
of Ireland who are affiliated with an association called the Irish National Teachers'
Organisation, which comprises men of very
opposite views politically, and very extreme
views too. Supposing that one of our teachers
--and there are quite a number belonging
to that organisation-journeys to Dublin, and
in the course of the deliberations of that
body gets up and expresses certain opinions,
will that be looked upon by this Government
as an act of disloyalty. I suppose you will say
it depends upon the nature of the speech.
Quite so. But have you anything to say with
regard to the Association of which he is a
member, what it purports to do, and what
its policy is?
I do not want to throw any aspersion on the
character of that organisation for one
moment. I know this-and it must be within
the knowledge of nearly every Member of
this House--that they are certainly not in
favour of the present partition of this
country. Would it be an act of disloyalty
if representative teachers from the North of
Ireland expressed an opinion favourable to
the unification of government in this country?
Would it be an act of disloyalty if they
co-operated with that organisation in order
to bring that about? These are matters that
occur to my mind. They are some of the
reasons why I think the House should hesitate
to pass the Bill without carefully looking
into this Measure. If we had the assurance
that by the passing of this Bill you would
inevitably make men who would otherwise be
disloyal loyal I would accept it without the
slightest reservation. If on the other hand
it appears from any reason provocative and
may drive men who otherwise might be loyal
to become disloyal, that is a reason why you
should hesitate to pass the Bill. I am not
going to quibble with respect to the desirability of having all the officials in connection
with the Government loyal. I wish we could
assure ourselves of it. The right hon.
gentleman, the Prime Minister, in his
splendid effort to govern the North of Ireland,
which he has done so successfully, has had
the co-operation of the Civil Servants. I am
sure it would be only his wish that we could
dispense with this arrangement. If he thinks

The PRIME MINISTER (Sir James Craig):
My hon. Friend started off his speech by
complaining that some Bills got through the
House too rapidly. That is a compliment to
the Government, especially to the draughtsman. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) Our Government draughtsman, I think, is perhaps deserving of more praise than any individual
inside the Government that I am aware of. If
there was any fault in the Bill, if there was
anything that my hon. Friend could fasten on
to, I am sure we could rely on him not to
miss the opportunity. His charge against
this Bill is that it is unnecessary. Well,
I hold, and my colleagues in the Government
hold, that it is most necessary. In the first
instance, it seemed to us to be an anomaly
that we should ask for and obtain from
members of the various local bodies throughout Ulster an oath of allegiance to His
Majesty the King and to the Government
of Northern Ireland, and not to exact from
those civil servants at headquarters a similar
oath, so that the whole machinery should be
on the same level, and that there should
be no chance of having one Department
possibly escaping taking that oath of allegiance whilst others did.
Mr. M'GUFFIN: Would the right hon.
Gentleman permit me for one moment to correct W..at may have conveyed a false
impression? I did not say it was unnecessary. The words I used were that I questioned its utility, which is a different matter.
The PRIME MINISTER: I will not split
hairs with my hon. Friend on the subject
of whether it is a question of utility or
whether the Bill is necessary, but I would only
like to point out to him this, that there is no
reflection whatever cast on the civil servants
in our employment. We do, however, think
it is only a common precaution on our part
to provide not only for the present but for
the future, and to leave no loophole for
people to creep into departments such as we
are well aware occurred in past times-not
under our regime but in past times-those
who were not in favour of British rule, for
instance, who used their positions in the
Civil Service in certain directions to undermine the loyalty of those departments towards
the Crown and the Government. (Hear,
hear.) This is a very serious matter, and one
which we have carefully considered as a
Government. We are determined that every
man, whether he be actually a civil servant
or whether he be a teacher charged with
bringing up the youth of Ulster, and in many
instances under the direct engagement of the
Government, not in the employment of the
Government but in the pay of the Government-we are determined on each and all of
them taking the oath of allegiance to His
Majesty and to the Northern Government.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
There is just one point that my hon.
Friend (Mr. M'Guffin) touches on that I
would like to make a remark about. He said
that this would not or might not prevent
those who took the oath from making speeches
which might be taken by us to be against the
spirit of the oath, and that, therefore, it
might be useless imposing this upon them.
I doubt it. I think there are very few who
have come into our Civil Service, or who
would be appointed as teachers under our
new educational scheme who would take the
oath of allegiance and then proceed to break
it.
Mr. M'GUFFIN: Not deliberately.
The PRIME MINISTER: Deliberately?
Mr. M'GUFFIN: Not deliberately; I did
not suggest deliberately.
The PRIME MINISTER: Well, not intentionally.
Mr. M'GUFFIN: Yes.
The PRIME MINISTER: At the same time
my hon. Friend has to bear in mind that
civil servants are not permitted to take part
in politics in any event. They make no
political speeches, and take part in no political
demonstrations. Therefore, this oath does
not impose on them any limitation that is
not already in existence. I do not think,
however, my hon. Friend was really very
sincere in his criticism, even to the extent he
did criticise, and I do not think he will force
a division on the House.
Mr. M'GUFFIN: Certainly not.
The PRIME MINISTER: I think the whole
country-the whole of Ulster-will be only
too delighted to see this safeguard in our

[Mr. Campbell]
And later, by Sub-section 5, it says:-
"The said Ministry of Finance shall have

I cannot see why a person who is employed
on full time should take the oath, and that
in the case of another person who is only
employed part time it should be left to the
Ministry of Finance to say whether he shall
take the oath or not. It seems to me if a

the oath. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Mr. DONALD: The hon. Member who has
spoken last has really forestalled me. I was
going to raise that exact point. I take it that
in the setting up of our Government we had
a large number of temporary officials. I say
that it is very necessary indeed that they
should take the oath. I may say at once
that I am in agreement with the Bil, and I
am also in agreement with my hon. Friend
(Mr. Lloyd Campbell) that it does not go far
enough. What I am anxious about is as to
how it is to be administered, and will
it be administered? Those of us who
move about some of the departments
know perfectly well the way in which this will
be looked upon.
I hope there will be no
alteration even in this oath. There were two
oaths, I understand, in the previous Bill.
However, I am quite satisfied with the form
of this Bill. We had an example quite recently in the case of the school teachers.
The noble Lord (the Marquess of Londonderry) told me himself that quite a large
number of the school teachers refused to take
their salaries from this Government. What
happened? When their salaries ceased to
come from Southern Ireland they were very
glad to come here and receive them.
Mr. M'GUFFIN: Did that convert them to
loyalty?
Mr. DONALD: I do not say this would
convert any man or woman to loyalty, nor
yet do I agree that the question of taking
oaths will interfere with any man who makes
firebrand speeches. We have the example of
the Imperial House of Commons, where men
take the oath one day and the very next day
they go outside and make speeches which
would be sufficient to create a charge of high
treason. I have heard them myself in Hyde
Park. That will not make any man loyal.
It is necessary, however, in a loyal Province
like ours for every man in receipt of a salary
to take the oath. I have heard a great many
Roman Catholics say that they are quite prepared to come in now and serve under our
Government and become loyal subjects of the
King. Why should they not? We make too
little about our loyalty. We do not make
enough of our loyalty. Any man who wishes
to hold a position under our Government, I
do not care who he is, and does not take that
oath is not entitled to hold the position. I
am quite in sympathy with the Bill, but it
will not make anyone loyal.

from the North Division of Belfast (Mr.

and as to the power which the Measure provides for giving the Ministry of Finance
authority to deal with such officers. In
Clause I it will be found that the power
given is within the discretion of the Ministry
of Finance, but it was decided not to include
in the scope of this Clause that all part-time
officers should take the oath, as in many
cases the oath would be only ludicrous, and
in other
cases it would be absolutely
ultra vires. It might enlighten the hon.
Member and the House if I instanced one
or two cases which will give an idea of what
is meant by the employment of part-time
servants. These include charwomen; Imperial Civil Servants doing occasional work
for the Northern Government, such as Permanent Secretary in the Law Courts, Chief
Examiner of Title, etc.; this would raise an
awkward question of jurisdiction; occasional
consultants, such as bacteriologists and cloth
tester; scavengers employed on odd jobs;
Clerks to local Pensions Committees, who are
really responsible to the Customs and Excise
Department, although their allowances are
paid by this Ministry; and a few other cases
somewhat analagous. As I have said, the
administration of this oath to these people
would be ludicrous in some cases, and in
others it would be absolutely opposed to the
law, and, therefore, my hon. Friend (Mr.
Lloyd Campbell) will see that it was necessary that the Bill should only refer to wholetime employees.

THE HOUSING SUBSIDY.
1 Sir CRAWFORD M'CULLAGH asked the
Minister of Finance if, when the negotiations
for the transfer of services were in progress
between the British Treasury and Northern
Ireland, he was aware that the British
Treasury had agreed to the increase of the
Housing Subsidy for the whole of Ireland
from twenty-five shillings to thirty-five
shillings, and from twenty-seven shillings and
sixpence to forty shillings?
The following question also stood on the
Paper in the name of Sir CRAWFORD
MCULLAGH:
2. To ask the Minister of Home Affairs if,
during the negotiations relating to the
transfer of services and the financial adjustments between the British Treasury and
Northern Ireland, consequent upon the passing of the Government of Ireland Act, 1920,
provision was made for the payment by the
Imperial Treasury to the Government of
Northern Ireland of an amount sufficient to
meet the increased Housing Subsidy of thirtyive shillings and forty shillings, as approved
by H.M. Treasury in January, 1921.
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
POLLOCK): I have arranged with the
Minister of Home Affairs to reply to the
questions regarding the Housing Subsidy
addressed to him and to myself, and, in view
of the public interest which has been aroused
r this matter, I hope I may be pardoned
by the House for replying in some detail.
The negotiations to which the honourable
Member refers are apparently those in
November, 1921, immediately preceding the
taking over of the various services. These
negotiations were not carried out with the
British Treasury, but with His Majesty's
Government as a whole, and did not involve
discussions on points of financial detail, but
were governed by political necessity and the
wishes of the people of this Province. The
general financial relations between this Province and the Imperial Government were
fixed by the Government of Ireland Act, and
the Act provided for the adjustment of details
Departmentally, with the Joint Exchequer
Board as final arbiter. The amount of the
Heusing Subsidy was not relevant to any
suck preliminary arrangements.
In November, 1921, when it was known that
the Imperial Treasury had definitely decided
to increase the Housing Subsidy in
Southern Ireland to 35s, representations
were made to that Department by the
Minister of Home Affairs that an allowanco should be granted by the Joint
Exchequer Board from Imperial funds for
the increased cost which would arise by the
extension of this arrangement to Northern
Ireland. These representations were unsuccessful. As Minister of Finance I was then
faced with the problem whether I could
impose on the revenues of this Province a
charge which was not in existence on the
date of the transfer of the service, more particularly as I was not myself satisfied that
the scheme was itself a sound one in view of
the altering conditions of the building trade.
On 6th March, 1922, a deputation from the
Belfast Corporation, the body most intimately
Concerned, waited on the Government to discuss this amongst other matters, and Was
dennitely informed by a representative of my
Ministry that the Northern Government
could not undertake in respect of existing
schemes payment of a higher subsidy
than 25s.

CENSUS OF NORTHERN IRELAND.
3. Mr. LYNN asked the Minister of Home
Affairs, when he intended to take a Census of
the people of Northern Ireland?
Mr. POLLOCK: I also take this question
from my right hon. Friend, the Minister of
Home Affairs.
The question of the taking of a Census has
been engaging the attention of the Government for some time. As the hon. Member
is doubtless aware, an enactment of the
Imperial Parliament, the Census (Ireland)
Act, 1920, provided that a Census should be
taken in Ireland on the 24th April, 1921, but
in consequence of the disturbed conditions
prevailing in the country at that time the
taking of the Census was indefinitely postponed.
a
The Government are fully alive to the
necessity of having up-to-date population
statistics, and as they understand that
Census may be taken in Great Britain in
1926, are now considering the advisability of
arranging for a Census to be taken in
Northern Ireland on the same date.
Mr. LYNN: Can my right hon. Friend say
why we should wait until 1926 before taking
the Census? Is he aware that a good deal of
trouble is caused by the fact that the figures
in regard to the population are not really
known? We are already, as he knows, two
years late.
I
Mr. POLLOCK: I am fully aware of the
difficulties which my hon. Friend has touched
upon, but I would remind him of the great
advantage of having our Census concurrently
with that of Great Britain, for purposes of
comparison as well as for other matters.
would also remind my hon. Friend that it
requires at least a year, and possibly eighteen
months, to make the necessary preparations
for carrying out the work of taking the
Census. Therefore, I suggest that there cannot be any great delay if it is necessary
wait till 1926 when our Census would
taken concurrently with that of Great Britain.
REFORM OF POOR-LAW SYSTEM.
to
be
4. Mr. LYNN asked the Minister of Home
Affairs whether he is aware that the reform
of the Poor-law system is long overdue; and
whether he can state what action the Government intends to take in order to bring the
system into conformity with modern needs.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I am aware that the
reform of the Poor-law system is a matter
that demands early attention, and I have had
under consideration for some time the question of establishing a Committee of Inquiry
with a view to making recommendations to
the Government on the subject.
However, as it is a very important and comprehensive matter, involving not only Poor
Relief but the Medical Services, I felt that
the Ministry could not undertake it until the
process of transfer of Services had been fully
completed, and until the extraordinary
pressure of work consequent on such transfer
had somewhat abated. For this reason, and
in view of the number of other Government
Committees which have had to be appointed
to deal with matrers of urgent necessity, I
felt it was not expedient or possible to take
up the question of Poor-law reform for the
present. However, I hope, at an early date,
to be in a position to appoint a Committee
for this purpose
In the meantime everything possible is
being done to effect reforms by administrative
action, and, in this connection, I may say that
it has been possible to secure the closing of
eleven Workhouses in Northern Ireland,
namely, Antrim, Ballycastle, Ballymoney,
Cookstown, Clogher, Irvinestown, Kilkeel,
Larne, Lisburn, Newtownards, and Strabane.
Mr. LYNN: I beg to give notice that I will
raise this question at an early date.

Motion made, and Question proposed:
"6
Nothern Ireland; and as the Registrar of

I should add that prior to the transfer of
similar duties to the Law Societies of
England and Ireland, it was necessary,
should occasion arise requiring investigation
into the conduct of a solicitor, that there
should be a direct application to a Court of
Law, and it will be readily understood that a
great many persons who thought they had

following which a committee consisting of
experienced solicitors investigate the complaint, and, if they find a prima facie case
exists, report accordingly, and a full investigation is then carried out by the Lord Chief
Justice. The Incorporated Law Society of
Northern Ireland is, therefore, as respects
certain aspects of its activities, part of the
administration of justice.

In asking the House to agree to this
Motion, it will perhaps not be out of place
if I remind hon. Members of the Statutory
duties imposed on the Incorporated Law
Society by the Solicitors (Ireland) Act, 1898.
as amended by our own Solicitors Act
(Northern Ireland), 1922. Some learned Members present will be very familiar with the
history of the Society of the Attorneys and
Solicitors of Ireland, and in latter years of
the Incorporated Law Society of Ireland, and
also of the Northern Law Club, which ultimately became known as the Northern Law
Society. On the establishment of the
Supreme Court of Northern Ireland it followed as a logical conclusion that a separate
governing and disciplinary organisation over
the Solicitors in Northern Ireland should be
established, and with this end in view the
Northern Law Society applied for and were
granted a Royal Charter of Incorporation
under the name of the Incorporated Law
Society of Nothern Ireland, under which

examination authority over all apprentices to
Solicitors in Northern Ireland; as the disciplinary authority over all Solicitors in
Representations have been made by the
Society to the Ministry of Finance for a grant
to cover the expenses of discharging the
above functions, which are in the nature of
public duties, and the Government have
decided to recommend the House to approve
the payment of an annual grant of £200.
This sum, while not as substantial as the
sum asked for by the society, is considered
to be an adequate grant in aid of the expenses
attendant on carrying out those duties which
can properly be regarded as of a quasiadministrative character. I do not think
that any society regulating a profession or
trade for the advantage of its members and
also for the advantage of the public is necessarily entitled to claim a grant from this
House. The Ministry of Finance have, however, been influenced by the fact that the
Incorporated Law Society is in a peculiar
position, because the profession of a solicitor
is one in which it is necessary for laymen to
have implicit confidence, and if that confidence was misplaced and fraud committed it
often happens that the client is too poor to
obtain any remedy himself or to take action
to protect the public against similar frauds
in the future. Therefore, to a limited extent
the Incorporated Law Society and the
solicitors' profession stand in a different
position to that of most other professions or
trades. There is another point which might
be said to differentiate this case from almost
any other that can arise, and that is that
there is a special tax on the profession of
solicitors. Solicitors, on being articled, pay
Stamp Duty, they pay duty on admission,
duty for the purpose of being at liberty to
practice their professions, and the funds thus

camp at Larne and the steamship"Argenta"
and also the cost of the maintenance of convicts in England and Scotland and the
Borstal prisoners. Hon. Members will observe that the Estimate which I ask the
Committee to pass appears to be abort

But I might point out that the decrease is
really more than that because in several of
the Sub-heads which I will refer to afterwards certain moneys had to be re-voted now
which were voted last year amounting to

compared with last year will amount to
something over £16,000. I must say I think

this is satisfactory having regard to the

Now, in last year's Estimate-in the
original Estimate-hon. Members will
recollect that there was a supplementary
Estimate passed in October-in the original
Estimate it was calculated the daily number
of prisoners would be 470, but owing to
the disturbed conditions which arose
during last year we found it necessary to
make further provision for 860 additional
prisoners, making a total of 1330 prisoners.
I do not feel justified in estimating for a
lesser number than 1,280. This, however,
does not include the convicts in Scotland
and England, for which we are making provision for 186; and Borstal prisoners, for
which we are making provision for 76.
Before I deal with the various Sub-heads,
I would like to refer to two matters. One is
the question of prison discipline. I am glad
to say that discipline in our jails has been
completely restored, and the prisoners perform the work allotted to them; and for
this state of affairs I would like to bear
testimony to the efficiency and zeal shown
by the Governors, the officers and the subordinate staff, which have brought about such
a satisfactory result. I cannot speak too
highly in regard to the loyalty which they
have shown to the Government during ar
extremely trying period.
With regard to the internees, the provision
which is being made is for a total of 500
prisoners. Certain charges have been made
against the Government of Northern Ireland
in regard to the treatment meted out to
internees, and that as a result the health of
the prisoners had suffered. I have before
ine
no
certain figures which show that the
health of the prisoners-and we have passed
through our hands something like 600-has
been extremely good. We have had
deaths. Where prisoners require operative
treatment they are at once removed to the
Victoria Barracks where, through the courtesy of the General Officer Commanding,
facilities have been placed at the disposal
of my Department, where the best possible
surgical treatment is available.
Mr. McGUFFIN: How many are on the
ship "Argenta"? The number is 502. Is
that Larne and the ship both? How many
are on the "Argenta"?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I think over 300
on the ship at the present time. I must
say that the health of the prisoners is the
best answer to the charges which have been
levelled against the Government.
I came across the other day a letter which
was sent by one of the internees. I would
like to read a portion of it to the House.
I think it bears greater testimony than anything I can say in regard to the condition
of affairs on that ship. The letter, after
referring to some matters of a personal
character, goes on-
"For propaganda purposes (this is a
prisoner who is writing) we have to describe ourselves as being badly treated, so
I don't expect any of you to feel sorry
for me when you read the ordinary letters.
It is part of the game. You can tell this
to my people, and then tell everyone else
that the 'Argenta' is a floating hell."
There is another point to which I would like
to refer. Charges have been levelled at the
Government that the prisoners are retained
in the ship without their cases being investigated. I would like to clear this matter
up. Hon. Members are aware that at the
time the internment principle was established
an Advisory Committee was set up. This
Committee consists of the Deputy-Recorder
of Belfast, a Roman Catholic barrister of
very high standing, and a retired officer of
His Majesty's Army. On internment each
prisoner is served with a notice which informs him that if he so desires he can
have his case investigated by this tribunal.
It has been alleged that, notwithstanding
the fact that the internees have gone before
this Advisory Committee, none of them have
been released. On going through the figures
I find that out of 606 internees who passed
through our hands 401 have declined to go
before the Advisory Committee on the ground
that this would involve recognition of the
Northern Government. Of the 205 who
appeared before the Advisory Committee,
one-third have been dealt with and released
on varying conditions laid down by the
Advisory Committee. Therefore, there is no
excuse for anyone to say that an individual is
interned without his case being investigated
by an impartial tribunal. I hope after this
statement is made that those individuals who
indulge in these mendacious criticisms will
cease their activities.

Sir DAWSON BATES: In regard to the
various points which have been raised by hon.
Members, there is one thing of which I would
like to remind the House, and that is that
you cannot make omelets without using eggs,

whatever you like so long as you get peace.''
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) But while that
is so, the Government have taken every possible care to economise, having dre regard to

referred to the item of 1s 5d for food, and

I would remind hon. Members that these internees are not convicted prisoners, and it
would be a most improper thing for any
Government that had to take that extreme
step of interning them, which, I think, none
of us like but which we had to do, to feed

occupying that rank of life are accustomed
to enjoy. The hon. Member for Antrim (Mr.
Crawford) has raised a question in regard to

overstaffing there. The numbers of inmates
of the jail vary from time to time, but we
must have a permanent staff there ready for
the full complement of prisoners or the average number of prisoners that we are accustomed to receive. The numbers may vary
from day to day. We cannot, if a large
number of prisoners come in, go out on the
streets and employ a woman, saying,

As to the general question with regard to
the running expenses of the internment ship,
we established the ship there because the experience of the Imperial Government was
that internment camps had proved a failure
in many ways, and at the time we arrested
those prisoners we did not know what was
going to happen next. We came to the conclusion that if we had a large number of
these men located in any place it might prove
a source of danger to the community, and for
that reason we put them on this ship. The
more one goes into the question the more one
realises what a success this ship has been.
Having regard to the fact that after all we
are new Parliament, that
a
we have to
govern people who differ from us politically,
I think we should be scrupulously careful to

over here, many of whom I have had the

the ship-they were opponents of this Government all came to the conclusion that the
ship is carried on in a fit and proper way.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) With regard
to the chaplains, I am glad to inform the
hon. Member for Down (Mr. Lavery), who
raised the question, that the salaries of the
chaplains were not in proportion to the religious proportions in the Six Counties, that
the religious proportions of the inmates of
the jails are not necessarily the same as the
religious proportions of the Six Counties.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) As to the
question of journeys, the amount, of course,
varies. The amount for escort and the cost
of travelling vary in accordance with the
number of times a prisoner is remanded from
time to time. It may be that he may be
remanded three or four times, and on the
other hand, he may be sent for trial straight
away. After all, these are ordinary railway
charges over which we have no control. There
is another point which my hon. Friend (Mr.
Megaw) has reminded me about. Some of
the prisoners we have to send over to England and Scotland are of the most dangerous
kind, and the greatest possible care is taken
to ensure that they will arrive at their destinations safely.
Mr. DONALD: Could you not deport them
altogether?
Sir DAWSON BATES: The hon. Member
knows perfectly well we have no power to
deport prisoners. I come now to the Borstal
cases in the South of Ireland. Those cases
were there at the time we took over adminis
tration, but their time is running out, and
I hope within ten or twelve months there
will be no further prisoners in the South of
Ireland. As regards the general principle of
Borstal treatment, we hope to make regulations under which we will have our own
Borstal Institution and also our own convict
prison, but that is a matter which is occupying the very careful attention of the Government. The hon. Member for Antrim (Mr.
Crawford) raised a question in reference to
the lunatic asylum. He will understand that
we pay capitation to the different asylums.
That varies as a rule. It runs to about £60
a head in the case of prisoners becoming insane after conviction. As regards the Central
Criminal Lunatic Asylum, that runs to about
£160 a head. Here again, as I have already
pointed ort, £2,000 of the £7,500 is re-voted
money this year. I have already said that
we have succeeded in getting the Scottish
Office to reduce their charge for convicts, and
I may say that we are negotiating with the
English authorities with a view to getting
them to reduce theirs also. With regard to
the work on the "Argenta" we have no power
to force internees to do work. If this House
chooses to pass an Act empowering me to
force these men to do work, well and good,
but I have no power at present to force them.
I have power to make them cook their own
food and clean their own quarters, which
they do. With regard to the question of the
release of prisoners, I cannot give any undertaking as to what action the Government will
take in the future with reference to internees. The whole question depends upon the
future situation in Northern Ireland, and we
may be compelled to take further steps if
there is any fresh trouble in our midst. I
cannot at the present time hold out any hope
at all of any general release of these
prisoners.

THE HOUSING SUBSIDY.
Position of Belfast Corporation.
MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
That this House do now adjourn." (Captain

Sir CRAWFORD M'CULLAGH: My reason for bringing this matter before the Horse
at this stage is really to get some information, information to which I think this House
is entitled, and certainly to which the public
and the citizens of Belfast are entitled. I
feel that in this great question there is something of which we have not yet got to the
bottom. Indeed, I would venture to suggest
that there are even some points of which the
Government are not aware. The questions
which I put down to-day raised two very important matters, important to the city of Belfast, important to the Province, and also important to the men who are occupying the
houses built under the Government subsidy
scheme. One of the matters is finance, and
in the other there is a principle involved-a
principle that goes to the very root of good
government or of confidence in any Government. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Pollock)
on the 28th of March, 1923, in Committee,
said:
"as I pointed out in my statement on the
Vote on Account, a revision of the whole
conditions can ensue in the year 1925-and
we are not so far from that period, only a
matter of two years-when the Government
The Housing Subsidy—
Position of Corporation.
19 APRIL 1923
may, by taking advantage of the technical
provisions, relieve itself in whole or in part
of a very large share of the financial responsibility."-[Official Report, 28th March,
1923, col. 309, Vol. 3.]
With that I will deal later on.
This Housing
Act has given great anxiety to the Government, and I think to everyone who has had
anything to do with it, and I think I would
be right in saying that a great deal of the
blame can be traced to the Government of
the day-the Imperial Government, I meanand the Imperial Parliament who insisted on
building houses far and away in excess of
what was required in the country, and at
rents that the people could not afford to pay.
I would like to deal with the situation as it
was on the passing of that Act and as it is
to-day, and, of course, it will be necessary
for me, as briefly as possible, to review the
entire position.
There are two Acts-and I want to make
that perfectly clear-there are two Acts. One
is the English Act, which has thrown the responsibility on the municipalities to pay a
penny rate towards the cost, the Government
reserving to themselves the right to fix the
rents and to pay the difference, that is, the
loss-the difference between what is fixed and
what the houses cost. And there is a Clause
in the regulations which sets clearly out that
in 1927 the whole position can be reviewed.
The difference between that Act and our own
-the Irish Act-is this: the Irish Act was
to cost nothing. That is clearly set out in
the negotiations which have taken place and
when the matter was going through the House
of Commons. Now Mr. Macpherson, the then
Chief Secretary, devised a plan, a most ingenious plan, I admit. His plan was that the
Government should pay pound for pound of
the rent collected, which many people understood to mean 50 per cent. of the cost, which
was based, I think, on the report of the Irish
Convention. But that went very much further, because it also paid 50 per cent. of the
cost of the land, cost of the streets, upkeep,
and general rates. On that particular occasion the Belfast Corporation gave some consideration to it, and they arrived at the conclusion that the terms offered in that Bill
were of a very exceptional character.
The Bill got a Second Reading, and then
went into Committee, and the Belfast Corporation sent a deputation over to London to
watch that Bill going through Committee and
endeavour to get the best terms possible. Let
me say in passing that I would like to express my gratitude to the Ulster Members of
the Imperial House who are Members of this
House for their assistance on that occasion.
I am glad to see so many of them here, because they at least will have sufficient knowledge of the position of affairs and of what
took place on that occasion. In the Committee stage we arrived at a point where it
simply meant that we came to a standstill,
because prices had begun to advance at such
a rate that we found that pound for pound
was not enough. Certainly it did not satisfy
some of the authorities in Ireland. The Belfast representatives, that is, the Members of
the Imperial Parliament, as representing the
Corporation of Belfast, put forward a claim
to make the Bill a permanent Bill that could
not be gone back upon by either this or any
other Parliament. At that point we reached
an impasse. We had a conference which was
held in the Chief Secretary's room, and
over which I had the honour to preside. A
compromise was reached. It was arranged
that the Government should pay 25s in the
pound, and a draft Clause was arranged,
which Mr. Macpherson, then Chief Secretary,
intimated they could not put into a Bill of
a financial character, but it would be embodied in the regulations.
But before dealing with the regulations I
would like to refer to what Mr. Macpherson
said on that occasion. On the day the Committee adjourned he said:
Now what have I done? I may be wrong
in my scheme, but I take entire responsibility. I know that hon. Members of all
parties have received my scheme with great
misgivings. They have had the advantage
of consulting with their experts. Their
experts may have received my scheme with
great misgivings, too, but in any case my
scheme is definite. There is no talk about
raising rents to economic levels-no talk
about four-fifths of penny rates, or anything else. It is a clear and definite
scheme enunciated upon my responsibility,
and I take the full responsibility for believing it is far and away the better scheme
of the two. It is a scheme which says, if
the local authority can produce a thousand
pounds in rent, then without a doubt, or
without any debt of any sort or kind, the
State comes forward and says, "We give
you a thousand pounds, plus a quarter-
£1,250." And if the locality is one where
there are exceptional cases, we go a step
further and say, "for these exceptional
cases you have the equivalent of an extra
half-crown in the pound." Now I ask you,
have I not endeavoured to meet you fairly?
I have done my level best. I have put the
case for both sides. I have put what I regard would be my great difficulty with the
Treasury. Can I make out a case? Is it
not for you to tell me you have tried and
you have failed? It is a dangerous thing
Position of Corporation. 464
The Housing Subsidy-
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Sir Crawford M'Cullagh]
for the representatives of the people to
bring this Bill at the present time through
this small thing to an impasse."
That was with reference to the security
Clause we wanted in the Bill.
"The whole case for the Bill has been
the urgency of the housing question. The
whole case for the Bill has been the immediate need of these houses. I have
struggled, and I think rightly, to procure
the very best possible terms.
I have procured certain definite terms. My terms are
not indeterminate. They are not indefinite.
They are absolutely certain; and yesterday
the Financial Resolution in the House practically agreed to all these terms."

After that speech of the Chief Secretary we
adjourned, as I have explained, and held a
conference, and this is the Clause which we
agreed to and which was afterwards
bodied, as arranged, in the draft regulations,
and submitted to the Belfast Corporation by
the local authority, the Local Government
Board in Dublin:
"The Exchequer subsidy, as determined
under this Article, shall be payable, in respect of each financial year subsequent in
whole or part to the period mentioned above
in Sub-division (1) (a) of this Article, during
the currency of the loans raised by the Local
Authority for the purposes of the assisted
scheme. Provided that in respect of any
financial year subsequent to the 31st day of
March, 1927, the ratio of the Exchequer subsidy to the amount of collected rents shall, in
respect of any assisted scheme, be liable to
reduction if the Board consider that there is
sufficient evidence to show that the Local
Authority concerned has not exercised due
economy in management and has not secured
the best rents obtainable."
There were threats also that if the Corporation of Belfast did not proceed with the
scheme they (the Local Government Board)
would take advantage of the clause in the
Act of Parliament and proceed themselves to
erect the houses and charge the Corporation
with the expense. I am told by my right
hon. Friend (Mr. Pollock) that there is a
technicality involved in the matter, and the
Government may take advantage of it. I do
not think they will. If ever there was a binding contract entered into between two parties
it was that entered into by the Local Government Board and the Belfast Corporation.
It was on the strength of those regulations
and on the strength of the instructions received that the Belfast Corporation proceeded.
My right hon. Friend (Mr. Pollock) says it
may be necessary for the Government to reconsider their position, and perhaps pay
nothing. I do not think that can be done.
What is the technicality? I will explain
that later. Time went on, and it was found
that the prices of these houses were rising
rapidly. It was found that even 25s in the
£, which seemed an exceptionally good offer,
would not produce houses that some of the
citizens would like. Negotiations went on,
and finally it was intimated to the Belfast
Corporation that the Imperial Treasury-I am
making no charge against our Government, I
want that to be clear-had agreed to raise the
subsidy to 35s. I wish to say that a member
of the Local Government Board informed
me that the matter had been arranged. I
have here a copy of a letter which I think
the House should at least know something
about. It is dated the 1st January, 1921, and
it is signed by Sir John Anderson. It says:
Sir.
The Lords Commissioners of His Majesty's
Treasury have given careful consideration
to Mr. Duggan's minute of the 1st December last, in which His Excellency the Lord
Lieutenant proposes that the rate of Exchequer subsidy to be granted in respect of
Housing Schemes under the Housing (Ireland) Act, 1919, should be increased.
My Lords recognise that there has been a
appreciable increase in the cost of building
since the rates of subsidy at present embodied in the regulations were fixed, and
they are prepared to admit that some increase of subsidy is now necessary. On the
other hand, the steady and appreciable
rises of wages which have taken place in
most employments since July, 1919, justify
the expectation of rents higher than those
contemplated at that time. Further, the
operation of the Increase of Rent and Mortgage Interest (Restriction) Act is to bring
about an increase in the rents of houses
which will have a natural reflection in the
rents which will be obtainable in respect of
subsidised houses. In these circumstances,
my Lords consider that in estimating the
amount to which the subsidy should be increased, allowance must be made for an appreciable increase in the rents which will
actually be paid in all cases. On this basis
they are willing to agree that the amount
of the subsidy should be increased to 35s
for each pound of rent collected in normal
cases, together with a subsidy of 40s per
pound in those cases of exceptional necessity for which a rate of 27s 6d was originally proposed.
His Excellency will observe that this arrangement differs slightly from that proposed in the minute under reply, as My
Lords consider that some increase of rent
The Housing Subsidy-
Position of Corporation.
19 APRIL 1923
must be expected in all cases, and that the
basis on which the higher rate was to be
allowed should remain unaltered.
Under the existing regulations, the ratio
of the Exchequer subsidy to the amount
of collected rents is subject to reduction
after 31st March, 1927, if the Local Government Board consider that there is sufficient
evidence to show that the Local Authority
has not exercised due economy in management and has not secured the best rents
obtainable. In view of the considerable
increase of subsidy now agreed to, and of
the more definite prospect of a rise of rents
in the future, My Lords consider that review of the subsidy should now be mandatory at the expiration of four years in the
light of the rents then exigible, and that,
therefore, there should be inserted in the
regulations a provision that the amount of
the subsidy in respect of the financial years
after that ending on the 31st March, 1925,
shall be such as the Board with the consent of the Treasury may determine.
Subject to these modifications My Lords
will be prepared to give their consent to
new Regulations embodying the higher
rates of subsidy proposed.
I am, Sir,
Your obedient Servant,
JOHN ANDERSON.

In reply to your inquiry as to the subsidy, I am happy to inform you that the

It has been arranged that subsidies to

same arrangement as that which exists for
England.

Question for Oral Answer.
EMPIRE SETTLEMENT ACT.
1. Mr. CRAWFORD asked the Minister of
Labour whether, under the Empire Settlement Act, special facilities are granted to
people residing in England, Scotland, and
Wales who wish to settle in the Colonies;
whether the same privileges are granted to
residents of Northern Ireland; and, if not,
whether he will take steps to have similar
facilities given to our people.
Co-
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): The Empire Settlement Act empowers the Imperial Government to
operate with the Governments of any of his
Majesty's Dominions in carrying out agreed
schemes for assisting suitable persons residing
in the United Kingdom who wish to settle
in any of his Majesty's Dominions, and
Northern Ireland, as a part of the United
Kingdom, shares in the advantages of the
Act.
Schemes have so far been agreed between
the Imperial Government and the Governments of Australia. Canada, and New
Zealand The Dominion concerned is
naturally entitled to select the classes and
persons to be assisted. For instance, the
New Zealand Scheme applies only to domestic
servants, and the Canadian Scheme, which
was concluded last week, to children, domestic
servants, and persons nominated by British
subjects resident in Canada, and guaranteed
to be proceeding to work on the land. The
Australian Scheme is similarly limited to
domestic servants and those prepared to take
up farm work. The Australian Government
has hitherto been dealing with applications
only from Great Britain, but, as a result of
negotiations between my Department and the
Australian Authorities, it is hoped that
applications from Northern Ireland will be
dealt with at an early date.
Mr. CRAWFORD: Arising out of that
reply, may I ask the right hon. Gentleman
if he will see that Northern Ireland obtains
its proper share of the grant made for this
purpose by the Imperial Government?
Mr. ANDREWS: Yes. The cost is being
borne between the Government of the
Dominion and the Imperial Government,
and as Northern Ireland is still, I am glad
to think. considered part of the United
Kingdom (hon. Members: Hear, hear)—it
will share to the full the advantages of the
£3,000,000 to which my hon. Friend refers.
Mr. DONALD: As this is a most important question, may I ask my right hon.
Friend if he can tell us the financial
arrangements with regard to the Empire
Settlement Act of last year, under which
£3,000,000 was granted for this purpose?
Mr. ANDREWS: The financial arrangements are a good deal involved. Those who
are going out to the Dominion are expected
to bear a share of the cost, provided they
are in a position to do so. But if they are
unable to bear a portion of the cost arrangements have been made by which the
Dominion advances certain sums which are
repayable. In other words, those proceeding from here will get so much as a free gift
towards their passages, and, in addition to
that, if it is necessary, they will get so much
as a loan, on the understanding that the
net cost will ultimately be borne in the proportion of half and half between the two
Governments. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear).

As I explained last year when submitting
the Supplemental Estimates,
have
adopted the policy of building up the staff

upon

With regard to the particular sub-heads, I

and Allowances-shows a gross increase of

Additional work was also thrown on the
Audit staff in connection with the grants for

I can assure the House that every effort is
being made to keep the expenditure on the
staff down to the lowest possible figure, and
that even while the present volume of work
would justify a larger staff we have not increased it, in the hope that the existing

has been given. In some cases it has been

In regard to some of the sub-heads, we have

Unemployment Insurance Bill,
SECOND READING.
Order for Second Reading read.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): This House, I am aware, is
always kind and sympathetic towards any of
its Members who have a responsible duty to
perform, and as I rise to move the Second
Reading of a Bill amending our Unemployment Insurance legislation I cannot help but
feel that it is a very important and farreaching Measure, which affects the interests
not only of more than a quarter of a million
insured persons in Northern Ireland, but also
of their employers, and of the taxpayers
throughout our area. My task is very much
lightened, however, by the knowledge that
every member
as
of this House is just
anxious as I am to do all that is possible for
our unemployed persons, with whom we have
the greatest sympathy in the trying times
through which they are passing. I need not
be told that what our people want is work.
I know it-we all know it. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) Unfortunately, however, the
479 Unemployment Insurance Bill HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Second Reading.
[Mr. Andrews.]
efforts of the nations engaged in the late
European War inevitably resulted in an
upheaval of the world's economic and industrial system. For more than four years
millions of pounds a day were spent by all
the leading countries of the world on the
tragic struggle which brought so much misery
to millions of homes-and carried Europe to
the verge of economic ruin. The necessaries
of life soared up in price to an extent previously unknown, and when a glorious victory
in war at last came for us it left many peace
problems to be dealt with. Amongst them
all it soon became apparent that the most
important, the most far-reaching, the most
difficult, and the most urgent would be the
problem of unemployment. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.)
Judged from many standpoints, matters
were at their worst when our Parliament was
opened by his Majesty. The industrial
pulse of Northern Ireland, in common
with the rest of the world, was slow,
weak, and intermittent. Almost 100,000
of our people were either totally unemployed or on systematic short time, and
how best to deal with the problem along
practicable lines has given much anxious and
wearing thought to my colleagues in the
Government and myself, as well as to the staff
of my Department, to all of whom I feel
deeply indebted. Firstly, we asked the members of this House to continue unemployment
insurance in Northern Ireland along parallel
lines with Great Britain, and they agreed;
and the Shillington Committee--composed of
all classes of the community--have endorsed
our action, after the fullest and most careful
inquiry. Secondly, we obtained, through the
influence of our Prime Minister, £500,000 from
the Imperial Government for relief works in
Belfast and neighbourhood. Thirdly, we
asked this House to vote £50,000 for relief
works throughout the rest of Northern Ireland. Fourthly, under our Loans Guarantee
Act, in which our Minister of Finance has
taken such special and praiseworthy interest,
many enterprises have been launched, giving
much employment which would not otherwise
have been afforded. And, lastly, our Ministry
of Commerce and the Ministry of Labour are
working together in close co-operation, with
a view to encouraging trade and preventing
the disturbance of industrial peace. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) The Government is
also looking ahead, and, as the House knows,
we are appointing a Commission to inquire
into the development of the natural and industrial resources of Northern Ireland, with a
view to increasing employment generally, and
the prosperity of our area as well.
By means of our new Local Employment
Committees, which are composed of representatives of employers and work people, as well
as of the general public, and which are now
closely associated with almost all our Employment Exchanges, we are not only more
thoroughly administering our Unemployment
Insurance Acts, but we are keeping in the
closest possible touch with the whole industrial situation, so that matters may never
again be allowed to drift into the terrible
state in which we found them. There is an
old saying-and a true one-that "prevention
is better than cure," and our Government, in
steadily pursuing its course, is bearing that
consideration always in mind in this as in all
other matters.
With regard to the relief schemes in
Belfast and Northern Ireland, I am glad
to be able to tell the House to-day that
2,950 men are directly employed on these
works of public utility, which will be of lasting benefit to Northern Ireland-(Hon. Meni
bers Hear, hear)-and now that the schemes
are fully under way I expect that this number
will be doubled within a few weeks. With
the invaluable assistance and support of the
Belfast Corporation and certain other public
authorities throughout the Six Counties, an
carnest attempt is being made, not only to
help our unemployed, but, at the same time,
to lessen the housing shortage, the importance
of which, I am sure, will not be under-estimated. In addition to those receiving
employment directly on these schemes, I estimate that approximately an equal number,
who would not otherwise be employed, are
working in producing the materials which are
required for the work. For instance, brickkilns which otherwise would undoubtedly still
have been closed are now working at full
speed. The £500,000 for Belfast and neighbourhood, supplemented by large amounts
from our public bodies and certain charitable
organisations undertaking relief schemes, will
last, at any rate, till the 31st March, 1924.
As, however, the £50,000 for the rest of
Northern Ireland will all be expended in a
very few months' time, I am glad to be able
to announce to-day that the Government has
decided to take an early opportunity of asking
this House to vote £25,000 from the last financial year's Budget surplus to enable relief
works to be continued by our local authorities
outside Belfast. This the House will be asked
to do, for two reasons. First, because the
Government feel that these assisted relief
works should be continued during the present
abnormal times; and, secondly, in order to
comply with the Prime Minister's pledge that
our Budget surplus would be devoted towards
furthering labour interests. I am sure that
all classes and creeds will agree that this
undertaking cannot better be fulfilled under
existing conditions than by the absorption
of our unemployed into industry.
I have felt it necessary to make this, for
me, unusually long preliminary statement
prior to dealing with the Bill itself, because
so many of our people feel that we are pursuing a mistaken policy in paying unemploy-

Clause 1, Section 2, of this Bill we ask for

ment benefit at all, or, as it is wrongly called,

not demoralising to give to our people something to keep them from starvation while
they are deprived of the means, through no
fault of their own, of earning their daily
bread. It is the want of work for them to do
that is demoralising; and work can only be
permanently provided for them, now that law
and order have been restored, through the
increased enterprise of our capitalists, and
the sustained industry of our working classes
themselves. I am aware that many hold the
view that we should use the money collected
in the form of contributions to our Unemployment Fund for relief work purposes.
am afraid that there is a good deal of loose
thinking in this connection. In the first
place, it is especially difficult if not impossible, to arrange relief works for women on
anything but a very small scale indeed. We
have still 15,211 women totally unemployed
in Northern Ireland besides a considerable
number on short time. When our Parliament was opened by his Majesty we had
actually 24,880 women totally unemployed.
Again, we have juveniles to consider, for
whom also-for obvious reasons-unemployment insurance benefit would have to be con
tinued. But there is a further great difficulty, which applies also to men, namely,
one cannot expect employers to pay contributions to a fund if it is to be used to subsidise other employers to induce them to
employ labour, especially as some of the
undertakings so subsidised might in practice
be competitive. It is my considered opinion,
for what it is worth, therefore, that while
unemployment insurance and relief works
are both necessary to tide over abnormal industrial depression, relief works can only be
successful when carried out by public
authorities supported by Parliamentary
grants. This is the course which we have
been pursuing in Northern Ireland, and I
believe I am right in saying that we have
provided work for a larger proportion of
unemployed by means of relief schemes than
has ever been the case elsewhere. I was very
delighted to hear Sir Philip Lloyd-Greame,
the President of the Imperial Board of Trade,
state on Friday last that he looked forward
to the industrial future of the Empire with
hope and confidence. This is a most encouraging statement coming from a distinguished statesman who has the means of
keeping in touch with the pulse of the
world's industrial life. I am glad to be able
to say to-day that I am absolutely satisfied
that in this general trade revival Northern
Ireland is sure to benefit to its full share.
Our shipbuilding trade is improving; our
staple industry-linen-is undoubtedly on a
more satisfactory basis; practically all our
other allied trades report progress; and I
think there is reason to expect that in this

I am aware-too well aware--that two
forms of criticism can be levelled, by those
whom we represent, against this Bill, and
against the policy which we are pursuing in
connection with unemployment. There will
be those who, following the lead given by the
uninformed criticism of the "Daily Mail
as regards Unemployment Insurance, will say
that we have gone too far, that we are
destroying the morale of our people and
training them to enjoy leisure rather than
honest work. I hope that I have been successful to-day in showing that this is not
so. What we are doing is by a contributory
insurance scheme fulfilling our obligations to
unemployed insured persons, and dealing with
a very difficult problem in many ways, but
always along reasonable, humanitarian and
Christian lines. On the other hand, there
will be those who will accuse us of not going
far enough. To them I say that, in governing a country be it great or small, one must
respond not only to those impulses which
naturally flow from the heart, but also to
those reasonings which come from the head,
and which, if ignored, would inevitably speli
disaster. I now beg to move "That the Bill
be now read a Second time."

realise that that would not be possible,

ur employed too hard. He has pointed out

To on his claim.
With reference to Clause 9, Insurance by

I received a letter this morning-I have it

There is nothing more important, I would

and we decided that we would double the

The old method was that a man must be consecutively employed for a period of six days.
A man might have been unemployed for a

continuity rule there laid down that a period

are not being attended as they should be.
For the purpose of giving a greater incentive
to the committees, and impressing upon
them the necessity of assisting the Ministry of Labour, my right hon. Friend
(Mr. Andrews) some time ago invited
all the chairmen and vice-chairmen of
the various Local Employment Committees to meet him in conference at
Belfast. We had an excellent meeting and
various proposals were put forward for the
better working of the Labour Exchanges and
of the Committee, and we hope at an early
date to have a further meeting with the
chairmen and vice-chairmen, and in that
respect the suggestion thrown out by the hon.
Member for East Belfast (Mr. Donald) will
enable us to impress upon them the vital
necessity of giving better attention to the
work of the Committee, and thereby assis
ting the Ministry of Labour to carry on their
good work.
of
I should like just in one word to reply to
my hon. Friend the Member for Armagh
(Major Shillington). His difficulty was
similar to that which faced the hon. Member
for East Belfast (Mr. Donald), namely, when
the Imperial Government were in a position
to change their Act with regard to the contributions towards the Fund, how would the
Government of Northern Ireland act? The
Prime Minister was able to secure
for us £530,000 for the purpose
keeping us on parallel lines with the Imperial Government-(hon. Members: Hear,
hear) and it is our intention that when the
time comes, if there is necessity to go off
the track, we may call upon him for the
purpose of using that £530,000 for the
purpose of making us keep exactly
--or probably not exactly, but as far as
possible-in line with Great Britain, so that
the Ministry of Labour of the Imperial
Government and the Ministry of Labour in
Northern Ireland may march hand in hand,
endeavouring to do good to all those who in
times of hardship and unemployment require
a helping hand. I desire in conclusion to
Congratulate my right hon. Friend (Mr.
Andrews) on the manner in which he introduced this Bill. It made my task exceedingly
simple, and the criticisms were of such a
cordial and courteous character that I was
enabled to answer them with very little
difficulty. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)

the House I wish to submit it for your

Mr. SPEAKER: The rule is that a question of privilege can be raised at any
moment, and as soon as possible after it has
arisen, so the hon. Gentleman, I think, had
better raise it at once.
Mr. McGUFFIN: At your instance and on
your authority a Writ has been issued for
the election of a Member of this House to
fill the place of the late Mr. Twaddell. In
prosecution of the election, which is going on
at the moment, a meeting was held last
night in a place called the King's Hall of
Ye Olde Castle Restaurant in the City here,
and certain speches were delivered, to which
I do not want to advert except in one instance. The instance to which I refer is in
the case of Mr. R. J. Woods, who was supporting one of the candidates, and who has
referred to this House in terms of a most
contemptuous character. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear. May I submit the substance of
his speech in order to hear your ruling with
respect to it?
"Mr. R. J. Woods said he was not an
Orangeman, but he belonged to another
Order, of which he was equally proud."
He does not say what that Order is.
"He had not up to the present ever taken
an active part in politics, nor in supporting
a candidate for Parliament; but now it
became absolutely necessary for him to do
so if he were to be saved from the tyrannical clique which ran that pocket edition
of a so-called Parliament, so that they
could defy all opposition. Opposition in
the Northern Parliament to-day did not
exist. The whole thing could only be
likened to a Gilbertian absurdity, a great
rehearsal of a farce."
Though I am jealous of the honour of the
House in its entirety the portion in which
I am especially interested comes further on.
"It was good for only one thing, and that
was getting jobs for Englishmen. Certain
persons had gone in calling themselves
Labour men, but they only laboured until
they got a job and then they came out as
paid touts."
Mr. DONALD: Is that fellow a Free
Stater?
Mr. McGUFFIN: The speech goes on:
"After accepting the Judas bag they were
now adding insult to injury by ridiculing
and insulting and hounding out of society
the men who went out to France to save
them, while they stayed at home living on
the misfortune and poverty of the soldiers'
wives, families and dependants."
I think that is a very serious reflection on
the honour of this House, and that the
language that has been used in this connection is of the most contemptuous character.
What we resent chiefly are the suggestions of
dishonesty and dishonour that are associated
with this statement. To allege, for instance,
that one section of this House, the Labour
Members, came here to get jobs and to retire
from Parliament as soon as they obtained
them, is to suggest what in fact is an absolute
untruth. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) It is
not true in connection with any individual
who is a Member of the Labour Party in this
House. I speak for myself-and perhaps I
may be regarded in some degree as speaking
on behalf of my Labour colleagues-when I
say that I never entered this House for the
purpose of securing a job. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) Our idea was the same as that
of the other hon. Members to serve as representatives. If we had ever contemplated
emolument we should never have entered the
House at all. Our idea was to discharge the
duty of representatives of those who had
committed the trust to us. We have fulfilled
the trust to that extent, and I am sure there
is no possibility of producing evidence to
show that we have done otherwise. The question concerns the honour of this Horse in the
highest degree. Moreover, this is the first
instance in which the question of Privilege
has been raised, and in submitting it to you
I would ask for an expression of your opinion
with regard to the matter, and as to how
under the circumstances the House should
proceed.
Mr. SPEAKER: From what I have
gathered of the nature of the speech which
the hon. Member has quoted, it does very distinctly amount to a breach of the Privileges
of this House.
Mr. McGUFFIN: May I hand you a copy
of the newspaper?
Mr. SPEAKER: Thank you. The Privilege
of Parliament is established upon long years
of struggle, and the Privileges of the Imperial
Parliament have been by Statute accorded to
this House. Any breach of that Privilege is
always dealt with by Parliament in some manner depending upon the individual case, the
desire of Members, and the seriousness of the
offence. It would be difficult, I think, to find
more extreme breaches of Privilege than the
description of this House as
"that pocket edition of a so-called Parliament,"
and
"the whole thing could only be likened to a
Gilbertian absurdity.”
503 Privileges of the House-

HOUSE OF COMMONS.
West Belfast Election.
[Mr. Speaker]
That is clearly a breach of Privilege of Parliament in the sense that it traduces the institution of Parliament. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) Then again, the reference to
the conduct of individual Members, charging
them with corruption—that is practically what
it amounts to-has been held over and over
again to be a breach of Parliamentary Privilege, provided that the charge is in respect
of their conduct as Members of Parliament.
I, therefore, think that there is no question,
but that this does amount to a breach of the
Privilege of Parliament.
Now the question arises as to what action
the House should take. I think the ordinary
action is for a Member to move formally that
the passages complained of do amount to a
breach of the Privilege of this House, and,
when that is passed, if it is passed, the question arises as to what Parliament can do. We
have the power to summon those who infringe our Privileges to the Bar of this House
and to demand an explanation, and if that
explanation is unsatisfactory, and if the House
so decides, we have power to commit them to
custody. That is a power inherent in Parliament, a power just as great as the right which
Courts of Law have of committing people into
custody. So that I think it should be realised
that the Privilege of Parliament, if infringed,
may involve very serious consequences for
those who infringe it. As to the action that
should be taken in this case, it is entirely for
the House to decide. I suggest that perhaps
an hon. Member will move, and another hon.
Member will second, a Motion that this does
constitute a breach of the Privileges of this
House.
Captain MULHOLLAND: I. as the
youngest Member of this House, perhaps am
not unduly qualified to defend its honour, of
which I and other hon. Members are exceedingly jealous, and perhaps I may be allowed
formally to move:
"That the passages complained of in the
speech delivered by Mr. R. J. Woods on
April 23rd, and reported in the "Belfast
News-Letter" of this day's date, constitute
a gross breach of the Privileges of this
House."
It is unnecessary for me to go into any detailed argument with reference to this passage, but, as an instance of unexampled ignorance and spiteful and false allegations of

(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) As an exsoldier, I am particularly anxious that the
country should realise that the accusations

that ex-soldiers in the Six Counties are adequately represented in this House-(hon. Members: Hear, hear)-and that their future is
being very carefully watched. Such wild
language will reap its own reward. I beg to
move that this Motion be put before the
House. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Mr. McGUFFIN: Having introduced this
matter to your attention, and seeing that I
quite acquiesce in the Motion that has been
submitted to this House by the hon. and
gallant Gentleman (Captain Mulholland), I
beg to second the Resolution.

The PRIME MINISTER (Sir James Craig):
We are a very young Parliament, and therefore it is only proper at the outset that we
should make it known to all the community
how jealous we are of any aspersions that are
cast upon our character or upon the character
of any of the individuals who comprise either
House. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) What
has taken place is far worse than anything I
can recollect in my own time-(hon. Members:
Hear, hear and I can go back to the time
when as a boy I sat in the Galle y and Mr.
Speaker Peel had to reprimand someone for
a breach of the Privileges at Westminster.
From that time till now nothing so gross, so
base, so unforgivable, has taken place, and,
therefore, I think it is only proper that this
has been formally brought before the consideration of the House, and that you should
have laid down in such clear and dignified
language exactly how we stand with regard to
dealing with this offender who made aspersions on our character. It is a very serious
matter, and if it had been allowed to go by
it might possibly have led to most serious
consequences, because, as my hon. Friend (Mr.
Grant) behind me has just said, there are persons who might take advantage, if this were
to pass on this occasion, to make worse references to those Members who represent this
House. It does not matter what quarter is
attacked. That is not the point. That the
Labour Members in our midst have been attacked is particularly offensive-(hon. Members: Hear, hear)-because everybody knows
that since they were returned to this House
they have shown a single-minded courage;
they have never hesitated for a moment to
offer what they considered as criticism of the
Government, and I do not think any section
of the House has shown, if I may say so,
more eager anxiety to serve their constituents
in every possible way. That being so, I think
there is no section of this House that less
deserves this bitter and unforgivable attack
than the Labour Party in our midst.
You have divided the question into two
parts. The first part records what is a breach
of the Privileges of this House, and I have
no doubt it will be carried unanimously. You
then went on to point out the consequences
of that, and that if any Member rose in his
place and moved that a certain action be
taken it would be very hard for the Members
of this House, and certainly for the Government, to refuse it. I would suggest, however,
that the second course be not pursued, and
that we allow the matter to drop. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) We cannot allow it
to go without expressing our contempt of the
man making the charge. At the same time,
I believe as it is the first occasion on which
an attempt has been made to infringe upon
the Privileges of this House it would be wise
of us if we did not proceed further except to
carry the Motion which is at the moment before the House. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)

Mr. POLLOCK: I ask the Committee to recall that in the month of December a short
Measure was passed empowering the Government to guarantee certain loans for the purposes of providing work for the unemployed
through the machinery of the investment of
money in capital undertakings. When
making my statement on the Vote on Account
I suggested that if the Measure were taken

tal en advantage of, I am happy to say, to

hon. Friend for East Belfast (Mr. Donald)
mentioned, that one of the shipbuilding yards
is unfortunately short of work at the present
time. Under this scheme there had been

The Government ask the Committee to pass

a

Education Bill.

CLAUSE 1 (Advisory Council on Educational matters).
(1) For the purpose of advising the
Ministry of Education for Northern Ireland
(in this Act referred to as the Ministry ")
on
"
educational matters, there shall be
