the Advisory Council shall always consist,
as to not less than two-thirds of its members, of persons qualified to represent the
views of bodies interested in education.

CLAUSE 2 (Local Education Authorities
and Committees):-
(1) For the purposes of this Act the
council of each county and county borough
shall be a local authority for education (in
this Act referred to as an "Education
Authority') and the county or county
borough shall, for those purposes, form the
education area of the Education Authority.
(2) The powers and duties under this Act
of an Education Authority, being the
council of a county borough, shall, except
as respects the raising of money by rate or
loan, the general control of expenditure to
such extent as that control may be retained
by the Education Authority themselves,
and the acquisition, holding or disposal of
land, be exercised and performed through
an Education Committee of the council,
consisting of twenty-one members, sixteen
of whom shall be appointed by the council
either from the members of their own body
or partly from those members and partly
from other persons. as the council think
fit, and five of whom shall be appointed by
the Minister.
The powers and duties of the council of
a county borough as an Education Authority, other than those required to be

As regards other schools which come into

the flat education rate has led England and

suggested, instead of sanctioning the raising
and striking of a rate which will be drawn

The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr. Aadrews): I think it would meet with the approval of the Committee, and shorten the
time necessary to discuss the various Votes
of my Department if I make a short general
statement in the first instance and then deal
with these Votes separately in detail later.
The work of the Ministry is divided into four
Departments. First of all, there is the Industrial Department, which endeavours to help
employers and their workers to prevent industrial disputes. The work or the Department
in that connection is fairly well known, and
I do not think it is at all necessary that I
should enlarge upon it. This Branch
also deals with the Trade Boards, a very
delicate matter which requires a great deal
of care in order to deal with it effectively.
The next Department of the Ministry deals
with insurance-both Unemployment and
Health Insurance-and, in connection with
Unemployment Insurance, the Labour Exchanges. I dealt so fully on Tuesday with
matters connected with unemployment in
introducing the new legislation that I fel
it is unnecessary that I should take up
the time of the Committee by going over
the same ground again. As regards the
Labour Exchanges, we found them in a
shocking condition in many respects, but I
am glad to be able to state that I think they
are giving more general satisfaction to those
who are affected by them than was heretofore
the case. I am perfectly satisfied that there
is still room for improvement in several ways,
and shortly we will be able to bring about a
better state of affairs still. One trouble which
was very plain to the Department right at the
beginning was that the buildings were SO
cramped, so insanitary, and so unsuitable for
the work they were designed to do that the
staffs did not get a reasonable opportunity of
fulfilling their duties.
Mr. McGUFFIN: Hear, hear.

Mr. ANDREWS: In the second place there
was no sufficient waiting accommodation to
prevent the queues being formed-
Mr. McGUFFIN: Hear, hear.
re-
Mr. ANDREWS: To which the hon. Member for North Belfast (Mr. McGuffin)
ferred on Tuesday last. With the approval
of my right hon. Friend the Minister of
Finance (Mr. Pollock) we have almost completed negotiations in reference to taking over a
new building, which will provide a central
Exchange in a very central part of the
city, and which will give our staff a much
better opportunity than they have had in
the past to discharge their duties under
more favourable conditions.
Mr. McGUFFIN: Could the right hon.
Gentleman (Mr. Andrews) state something
in particular with respect to that matter?
We have heard a great deal, but I think the
present is an opportunity when he might
ventilate the subject and tell us something

Mr. DONALD: Will not that arise on the

The CHAIRMAN: Yes, it would arise on
one of the Votes, but as the right hon.
Gentleman (Mr. Andrews) is making a
general statement; he can deal with it here
and now if he so desires.
Mr. ANDREWS: I can do it in either case.
I had intended to do it on the Vote.
Mr. McGUFFIN: That will do.
Mr. ANDREWS: But if it meets with the
approval of the Committee I will do it now.
These premises are situated close to the
Royal Academical Institution. They were
approved of by the Local Employment
Committee, of which my hon. Friend the
Member for East Belfast (Mr. Donald) is a
member. I have been through the place
myself and it appears to me, as it appeared
to the Local Employment Committee and to
the technical officers of the Ministry of
Finance, extremely suitable for the purpose. It is situated in a satisfactory
position, as I have said already. It
has a good many storeys and quite a
number of entrances, and in every way
I think we will be fortunate if we get
it. The only matter that is holding it up
now is the question of title, which necessarily must be inquired into before the
transaction can be completed. However, my
hon. Friend (Mr. McGuffin) may rest assured
that no time will be lost, and no one could
be more anxious than I am to see our staff
housed in these comfortable quarters.
As regards the next Department of the
Ministry, I think I should refer briefly
to the Finance Department. The importance
of the work which this Department does will
be recognised when I say that it is dealing
with a sum not less than two and a half
million pounds.
The fourth Department is called the
Inspectorate, and is in my opinion the
most important Department. There is
no use in passing laws unless you see
that they are enforced, and non-compliance in many directions, as hon.
Members know, has been far too common in Northern Ireland in the past.
Our inspectors now are very carefully seeing
that our Factory Acts are carried out as it
was intended that they should be, and that
when our Trade Boards fix rates of wages
that they are adhered to by all employers,
and not by some to the disadvantage of
others, as well as to the disadvantage of
the workers affected. In the next place,
the Department has to see that there
is compliance as regards contributions, both
in reference to Health Insurance and Unemployment Insurance. The income of the
Fund was, in my opinion, very much less
in the past than it ought to have been,
because in a great many instances those who
ought to have complied with the Act did not
do so.
In proceeding to deal with the individual
Votes of the Ministry, I think I should
refer, in connection with each Vote, to a
few of the most important sub-heads.
In Vote 1, Sub-head A deals with salaries,
wages, and allowances. It will be observed
that there is practically no difference between last year's estimate and that of this
year, but at the same time I think it
should be remembered that in this year's
estimate is an item in Sub-head S-sundry
services in connection with unemployment
insurance. What that means is that last
year we provided for the cost of our claims
and record work as an agency; but during
the year we have brought all our records to
Northern Ireland,, and they are now stored
and looked after and referred to at the place
known as Arnott's Buildings. This change
increased the estimate under Sub-head A to
about the same extent that it wiped out.
practically altogether, Sub-head S. It is satisfactory therefore to see that, notwithstanding
this addition to Sub-head A, the total amount
asked for has not been increased. In Subhead B, which deals with travelling, removal,
and subsistence expenses, you will see there
has been a reduction of £250. I may say
there has been a substantial reduction as
regards non-recurrent items, such as removal
expenses from Dublin, &c.; but there were a
good many vacancies in the inspectorate in
the year 1922-23, and substantial increases
in the travelling expenses of the inspectors will now be involved. I think
this is a desirable increase of expenditure
for the reasons which I have already given.
There is no object in keeping inspectors in
Committee.

is due, as I have already pointed out, to the

Umpire, Courts of Referees, and Local Employment Committees-you will see there is

bers: Hear, hear)-and we are getting the

ought to say here that I feel very deeply
grateful to all the members of these Committees who are giving me such invaluable
assistance in connection with the administration of this Fund.
are
Mr. McGUFFIN: Is the Court of Referees
in existence new?
Mr. ANDREWS: There are certain statutory duties which have got to be performed
still by the Courts of Referees, but we are
gradually lessening those duties, and later
on it may be possible to arrange that they
will disappear altogether. My hon. Friend
will understand that a change of this kind
requires to be done gently, otherwise you
may run the risk of a breakdown, and a
breakdown in this connection would be particularly unfortunate since it would mean that,
instead of the claims being dealt with more
expeditiously than heretofore, as undoubtedly has been the case, they would take longer
time. As regards Sub-head O, payments to
associations in respect of cost of administration of unemployment insurance, there is a
reduction due to the fall in unemployment
and also to some extent to the fact that there
was a reduction from 1s. to 6d. per week in
the amount allowed for administration which
took effect from 1st June, 1922, and which
will be felt for the whole of the present
financial year. I need not again refer to Subhead S. Shortly, it means simply that this
sum of £17,000 was incurred last year as an
agency item when the Imperial Government
were looking after our claims and record
department for us at a charge, while now we
are able to do it for ourselves very much
cheaper. It is a great advantage in settling
claims to have the records on the spot,
because a good deal of the delay which took
place in the past was entirely due to the
fact that Belfast had to refer to Dublin,
Dublin to London, London back to Dublin,
and Dublin back to Belfast. Now headquarters have only to go a few yards in order to
visit the claims section where the records
are all kept, and a matter can be settled in
a few minutes which took a very considerable
number of days hitherto. You will see there
is a very great increase as regards the sale
of stamps. That is a matter over which we
in the Ministry of Labour have very little
control. The Post Office do show us certain
figures to prove that this is a fair and reasonable charge for them to make. The work is
all-important, and it is done very thoroughly,
and if we are paying so much on the one hand
I understand we are getting it back on the
other, as the cost of the Post Office service in
Northern Ireland has to be borne by Northern Ireland, although it is a reserved service.
Sub-head U is for the audit of accounts of
approved societies and insurance committees.
This is a matter which is not of very great
importance as a scale rate is fixed, and
although it is a very substantial sum, we
have really got no control over it. As regards
Sub-head V, receipts appropriated in aid,
you will see that this year we have got very
much more in appropriation in aid than we
obtained during the previous year, as shown
in the Estimates. An adjustment is necessary
owing to the fact that there was £43,940 rot
shown as appropriation in aid last year,
which would have brought the £74,660 up to
£118,600. That is due to the fact that in the
first Unemployment Insurance Act of 1922,
as hon. Members will remember, the proportion of the Fund's receipts applicable as
an appropriation in aid was increased from
one-tenth to one-eighth, while by the absorption of the Dependants' Fund in the Unemployment Fund the amount to which the
fraction applies was also augmented, and the
original estimate was accordingly increased

The Minister has said that he has resolutions from various bodies throughout the
country calling for the winding up of the
National Insurance Act. I think that would
be a disastrous policy. In one of the debates
here the hon. Member for County Derry (Sir
Robert Anderson) said he thought that agriculturists, farmers particularly, had practically
no disease amongst their workers, and should
not be called upon to have anything to do
with insurance societies. That is a very
short-sighted policy. I am old enough to
remember the conditions of the working men
in olden times. I have in my mind at the
present moment the case of one working man
who died of consumption, leaving a large
family. He had absolutely nothing, as far
as I remember, but half-a-crown a week from
the Poor-Law Board. He was left there. He
died in his misery and his poverty without
having the disablement benefits that are now
got from these societies. I think it would be
a criminal thing, it would be an unthinkable
thing, that we would ever contemplate going
back on the Insurance Act and demolishing
it. The working men in the rural areas are
unfit to make any provision for sickness
except under such a scheme as this. If properly administered it is of immense value to
the agricultural, and indeed to the industrial
population. It is one of the many Acts of
legislation passed in recent years that have
done so much for the working classes.
There has been an agitation with regard to
medical benefits. I have had experience of
the administration of the Act in England,

the
Dr. MORRISON: I wrote to them in reply
that I thought as far as my judgment went
it would be a wise thing to extend medical
benefits to a big industrial city like Belfast,
but that in rural Ireland it would be unwise
and inadvisable to do so. I am entirely in

Minister with regard to this matter. We
ought not to rush rashly into this thing. It
is a wise policy to wait for the decision of
this Commission which is sitting in England
before we take any action. I know this, that
the whole agricultural community,
workers as well as the farmers, would resent
any attempt at the present time to extend
medical benefits to them. There is just one
other point I want to bring before the Minister. I have read many reports of these
insurance societies. They are all glowing reports, but the striking thing about them all
is that they count up the money paid in
medical benefits. but they say absolutely
nothing about their income. Before we are
able to judge whether they are paying a
decent contribution for the relief of sickness
we should know what their income is. They
have doubled their income, as the contribution is double. Would it not be the
natural thing, if they do not want to throw
dust systematically in the eyes of the public,
to publish the income? That is a system.
which I think the Minister should prevent.
We have a right to know where we are going
in regard to this matter, and whether we are
getting value for the money we are expending. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
They have no right to publish this amount
of money that they have given for meeting
disability, temporary or permanent, without
showing what their income is. If they have
doubled their income I think we have a right
to know if they have doubled the benefits to
those who are depending on them. I am glad
we have the chairman of a big insurance
society here, and I submit that to his clear
vision. What is the use of advising the
public that we spend £70,000 or £100,000 in
disablement benefits if we do not know what
the income of the society is, or if they have
doubled their income why have they not
doubled the disability benefit? They have
accumulated profits of a huge amount.
How are they spending those profits? I think
the Minister should give the committee some
information as to what has been done with
these accumulated profits. I always thought
they were to go to the insured. So far as I
know they give increased benefit, but we
should really know how much of an increase
they have given. They have adopted dental
schemes and convalescent homes that are in
my opinion white elephants to the society
and of no practical advantage to the insured.
Except in regard to those things we know
absolutely nothing, and I think the Minister
should consider the advisability of insisting
that these societies will publish a clear
definite statement that the average man, not
the cute business man, will know whether he
is getting benefit for these large sums that
are being extracted from the working man
and from the employer, and that are consequently oppressive and a hindrance to
industry.

is this, because I would hesitate to
ask insured persons
for higher contributions. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
I am looking forward to the time when unemployment becomes much less, when the
deficiency period will be past, when it will
be possible to reduce the contributions to the
unemployment fund; and when this is being
done, possibly to a substantial extent, a small
increase in the contributions to Health Insurance might not be objected to.
But in the administration of this fund I
think that one cannot altogether separate
unemployment from health. After all, I
think it is fortunate that the same Department administers both funds. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) After all, one fund is for
helping unemployed persons because they
cannot get any work and the other fund is
for helping persons who cannot get work
because they are not in a physical or mental
state to perform the work. Many people
think that the two funds should be amalgamated. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) I am
not satisfied that those "hear, hears" are
right. At the present time it would be impossible to do it. While you have a very
large deficit against one fund and a surplus
to the credit of the other fund would not, in
my opinion, be a favourable time for amalgamation. I know for instance, dealing with
the matter as a practical business man, it is
not a favourable time to amalgamate one
firm that is bankrupt with another firm that
is very flush. Certainly it would be to the
disadvantage of one or other. And besides,
the interests are not always the same. You
have got in Health Insurance certain
persons included who are not included
in unemployment insurance at all. You
would have to bring a great many persons
into insurance in connection with one or other
of the funds who are not in it at the present
time. Therefore I think it would be best for
me to put a little brake upon the wheels of
progress just to allow a period to elapse sufficient to make us feel that, when we do propose
to make radical changes, beyond all doubt we
shall be making them in the right direction.

CLASS III. No. 4.
UNEMPLOYMENT GRANTS.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
That a sum not exceeding £187,000 be
granted to His Majesty to complete the sum
necessary to defray the charge which will
come in course of payment during the year
ending on the 31st March, 1924, for grants
to local authorities, etc., in Northern Ireland for assistance in carrying out approved
schemes to relieve unemployment.
Mr. ANDREWS: I do not think that I
need say anything in moving that this be
agreed to-
Mr. McGUFFIN: Neither need we.
Mr. ANDREWS: For the reason that I
have already dealt with it under the heading
of unemployment. If there is any question
which any hon. Member desires to direct to
me I shall be very glad to answer it.
Mr. LYNN I rather congratulate myself
on the fact that I initiated what I think was
one of the most interesting discussions that
we have had in this House for a long time
and which has drawn a statement from the
Minister which really appertains to this Vote
probably more than to the Vote before it.
He said to the Committee that in future the
Government had no intention of allowing unemployment to drift into the condition in
which he unfortunately found it when he took
office. I think that is one of the most important statements that have been made in
this House. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
We realise that we have a Minister of Labour
who is a man of vision as well as a man of
business capacity-(Hon. Members: Hear,
hear) and that he knows from experience
how this unemployment thing like a snowball
goes rolling on, and that the farther it rolls
the more harm it does. I agree with the hon.
Member for East Belfast (Mr. Donald) that
undoubtedly when a man is out of employment for two years he cannot possibly be as
efficient when he starts work again as if he
had been in employment all the time. Think
of the terrible suffering that these people with
the threat of unemployment hanging over
them have to endure. I can think of nothing
more terrible, not even disease, for a man,
the father of a family, to be confronted with
always than this threat of unemployment,
and I would like to join with the hon. Member for North Belfast (Mr. McGuffin) in the
tribute he has paid to the shipyards, because
they have suffered terribly, suffered in companionship with others, of course, in other
parts of the world. They have suffered terribly, and they have borne their suffering
with great courage. Therefore, anything
that we as a House and anything that the
Government can do to reduce this unemployment to as small proportions as possible to
make it difficult for unemployment to occur
in future ought to be done. I have risen now
to congratulate the right hon. Gentleman (Mr.
Andrews) on the statement he has made. I
am sure he can rely on the whole-hearted
support not only of his colleagues in the
Government but also of his colleagues in this
House and of every man of goodwill in the
community to help him in establishing any
scheme that will reduce unemployment-I do
not suppose it is possible to overthrow it altogether-but to reduce it to the smallest
possible proportions. That is what the Members of this House want to do, and they will
help the right hon. Gentleman in every way
they possibly can. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.)

that the money has been well spent. The
portion which the Government is providing

Promissory Oaths Bill [S].
Considered in Committee.
(Mr. MOLES in the Chair.)
Clause 1 (Taking of Oath by persons in
Government Employment), and Clause 2
(Short Title), ordered to stand part of the
Bill.
(1) This Act shall apply to every person
who, on or after such date as may be determined by the said Ministry of Finance,
after consultation with the Ministry of
Education for Northern Ireland, is employed or taken into employment as a
school teacher, in like manner as it applies
to a person employed in a department of
the Government of Northern Ireland, except
that the time within which the requirements
of this Act are to be complied with by a
school teacher shall be such time as may
be determined as aforesaid.
(2) For the purposes of this section, the
expression "school teacher" means a
teacher in any national, public elementary,
or other school in Northern Ireland to or
in respect of which any grant is payable
out of moneys provided by Parliament or
any aid is given from funds raised by means
of local rates, whether by way of salary to
such teacher or otherwise.
Brought up and read a First time.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That the Clause be now read a Second time."

The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): I beg to move that the Clause as
it appears on the Order Paper be introduced
into the draft of the Bill following the First
Clause as it appears in the Measure. I need
not explain at length the object of it because
this matter was fully discussed when my
hon. Friend, the Parliamentary and
Financial
Secretary moved the Second
reading of the Bill. It was then clearly
opinion of the House that all
teachers who were in receipt of moneys from
the State should be placed in the same position in regard to the taking of the oath as
other Civil Servants. Toward that end,
therefore, these two sentences have been introduced by way of an amendment to the
Bill. Apart altogether from the desirability
of only such teachers being employed in
educating the young persons of our Province
as are loyal to our Constitution, an anomaly
would certainly arise if this amendment did
not appear in the Measure, because, under
the Local Government Act of 1868 I believe,
the teachers in those schools that will be
transferred to the education authority will
automatically be required to take the oath
when they come under the jurisdiction of
the local bodies. Therefore the amendment
provides not only for the taking of the oath
by teachers in primary schools, I would
remind the committee, but also the teachers
in schools of every other category in Northern Ireland; in fact, in all schools that
receive grants out of moneys provided by

Parliament or by means of local rates.
need not argue the merits of the case because

Mr. McGUFFIN: At the Second Reading
of this Bill I took occasion to make certain
observations that were replied to by the
right hon. Gentleman the Prime Minister.
This new clause is a Government proposal,
and I do not know under what circumstances
or for what reason they have introduced it.
Does the Government or the right hon.
Gentleman (Mr. Pollock) say he will accept
the oath subscribed by a teacher of professed
Republican opinions? If a man proclaims
himself a Republican and at your instance
subscribes the oath, are you satisfied you
have done any real work in so far as making
him a law-abiding citizen is concerned, or
have you added any greater security to the
Government? What I want the right hon.
Gentleman to remember is this. that the
teachers are not what they used to be. They
used to exist almost as individuals, to-day
they exist as an organisation very much on
the same basis as trade unions do. What 1
would ask the right hon. Gentleman to consider is if under these circumstances teachers
went into their unions and discussed certain questions of a political nature and
made strong statements and adopted strong
opinions with regard to these mattersdoes the right hon. Gentleman propose that
under those circumstances he should send a
representative to the union to furnish the
Government with information? My opinion
is this, the best assurance of loyalty is to
be found in a free and tolerant government,
and I believe that our Government is both
free and tolerant. I am not sure that we
are improving our position in the slightest
degree by insisting upon a course of this sort,
because if it conveys an impression that
there is any restriction upon freedom of
speech that would not be good for our
Government, and would not be suggestive of
the tolerance that we all believe exists in
the Government.
When I was speaking on the Second
Reading of this Bill, I happened to give an
illustration, and was quite unaware at the
time that an incident had actually occurred
on the lines I indicated. I referred suppositionally to a teacher going to a congress in
Dublin and making a speech of a certain
class. As a matter of fact, in the very next
day's paper something amounting to what
I had said was reported, and it was quoted
in a letter that was contributed by some
person who signed himself "Verbum sap."
The writer of the letter quoted a statement
by a school teacher from the North going up
to Dublin and declaring publicly that he was
there because he did not believe in partition,
and expressing a sort of glorification in the
fact that as a teacher he had perfect freedom
to teach what political opinions he liked.
I do not know whether the right hon.
Gentleman saw that or not, or whether he
has taken that aspect of the matter into
consideration. But there is one thing sure,
and that is, it would be a very ill-advised
course upon the part of the Government
to make this Bill an Act if they are not
prepared to enforce it. If they are going to
allow their authority in this matter to be
challenged then a very serious situation will
arise, and I hope the Government have contemplated the matter before they introduced
this Bill. I do not want to discourage the
Government, but I think the committee is
entitled to advise the Government-they do
not want to dictate to them. The Government know their own business best, but
when they introduce a Measure of this description it is the duty of the committee to
consider what is the best course to pursue.
I was speaking to a very high educational
authority, who is a Member of this House.
This matter came round incidentally, and
he simply said that he thought it was a
great mistake. It is a test that we think
might be dispensed with unless the Government have good reason to believe that it
is absolutely necessary. If there was any
disloyalty shown by a particular section I
think the Government could intervene and
introduce a Bill to deal with the circumstances when they arise. But simply to forestall it, and make these people qualify for
the position of Civil Servants or people in
the pay of the Crown by subscribing to a
test, is an expedient that I would not advise
the Government to adopt.
Mr. LYNN: I must say that the hon.
Member for North Belfast (Mr. McGuffin)
somewhat surprised me when he started to
speak, and as I listened to his very able
speech-for he always makes a very able
speech-I began to wonder whether I had
been thrown back to 1907, when that distinguished statesman, Mr. Birrell, started to
govern Ireland. Mr. Birrell argued just on
the same lines as the hon. Member for North
Belfast, and contended that he should give
the most absclute freedom to all these people
to do exactly what they pleased. I am not
going to labour the point, but you have only
got to look at Ireland to-day to see what the
result is. I say to my right hon. Friend,
the Minister of Finance, that it is the duty
of a Government to govern-(hon. Members:
Hear, hear)-and a Government that is unable
to govern should get out. We have had enough
examples of the folly of weakness in this
country of ours, and we want no more of it,

My hon. Friend (Mr. McGuffin) asked the
Government what they would do with a
gentleman who took the oath, and afterwards
declared that he was a Republican. The only
answer I would make to that question is, that
such a person was a perjurer, and therefore
was an unfit and an improper person to teach
anybody or anything. A person of that
character has no right whatever to be in
charge of children and to mould the minds
of the rising generation. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.)
There is another point with regard to
school teachers being allowed to make political
speeches and all that sort of thing. I for
one am old-fashioned enough-I am a strong
party man, and I have been in politics all my
life-to resent the idea of civil servants entering into party politics.
Mr.. McGUFFIN: I agree with that.
Mr. LYNN: I think it is wrong. My hon
Friend (Mr. McGuffin) quoted a speech which
I missed seeing.
Mr. McGUFFIN: I read it in your own
paper.
Mr. LYNN: I must say that, so far as I
am concerned, if I were Minister of Education, and a teacher made a speech of the
character referred to by my hon. Friend, I
should dispense with his services very quickly.
School teachers are paid by the State for
teaching children educational things, and for
bringing them up to be good citizens, not for
developing this or that shade of politics.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) I do hope the
Government will stick to this. The only thing
to which I would like to draw the attention of
the right hon. Gentleman (Mr. Pollock) is the
question of what arrangements the Government are making in the Bill for enforcing the
penalties. There is no use coming to this
House and making speeches; there is no use
in introducing a Bill if you do not see that
the Bill is made effective. I see no hardship
whatever in asking any loyal person, who is
accepting the pay of the State, to take the
Oath of Allegiance to the State. If a man is
disloyal there is no reason why he need be
in the service of the State. Let him go out of
it. We in this House have to take an oath
of loyalty to the State before we are allowed
to transact any business whatever. Why
should every other one, down to the humblest
servant of the State, not take the same oath
of loyalty? If a man wants freedom, if a man
wants to be a Republican, he can be a Republican, and he can go to the South and air
his Republican views, but he has no right to
air his Republican views at the expense of the
Northern Government, and I hope he will not
be allowed to do so.
Mrs. CHICHESTER: I would like to say
that I am extremely glad that this new clause
has been moved by the Minister of Finance.
I should have thought that if the Government had not put forward this clause there
would have been competition amongst hon.
Members as to who should be the first to put

Mr. McBRIDE: Dolly's Brae.
Mrs. CHICHESTER: It would appear to
me that no one could possibly take exception

I was more than surprised by the attitude

As the hon. Member for West Belfast (Mr.

There is just one point before I sit down,
and it arises out of an observation made by

Lynn). You have the Oath of Allegiance to
which we are called upon to subscribe. When
we subscribe to that oath we do so with the

is another place the hon. Member for West

601 Unemployment Insurance.

26 APRIL 1923
Adjournment.
Unemployment Insurance (Money).
Mr. POLLOCK: I beg to move the following
two resoutions:
1. That, for the purpose of any Act of the
present Session to amend the law relating
to insurance against unemployment, it is
expedient to authorise the payment out of
moneys provided by Parliament in respect of
the period between the end of the deficiency
period and a date to be prescribed under the
Act, of a contribution towards benefit and
other payments to be made out of the
Northern Irish Unemployment Fund equal to
the present contribution, and from and after
the date so prescribed of such a contribution
at a rate not exceeding one-fourth of the
aggregate amount of the contributions received from employers and employed persons
in any year, being contributions at rates not
exceeding in the case of men one shilling,
in the case of women ninepence, in the case
of boys sixpence, and in the case of girls
fourpence-halfpenny.
2. That it is expedient to authorise a charge
upon the Consolidated Fund in respect of
any further sums required to be advanced
by the Ministry of Finance, not exceeding
in the whole Five Hundred Thousand Pounds,
under powers to be conferred by an Act of
this Session, for the purpose of discharging
the liabilities of the Northern Irish Unemployment Fund.
The first of these resolutions refers to
Section 4, sub-section 2 of the Bill, and the
second refers to Section 5. Briefly the former
provides that the existing rates and contributions by the employer, the employee, and
by the Government shall remain as at present until such time as the Ministry has a
surplus until the unemployment fund is
solvent.
Mr. DONALD: How long will that be?
Mr. POLLOCK: I am afraid that is
prophetic. The maximum rate of contributions given in the First Schedule is to become
operative. Referring to the point raised by
my hon. Friend (Mr. Donald) just now, it is
hardly necessary for me to state when the
schedule maximum rates can come into force.
It is quite apparent to the Members, who are
aware from their own knowledge and also from
the state of unemployment, and from the information received by my right hon. Friend
who will submit the Bill of which this resolution is the forerunner, that it is necessary
that further power for the advance of the
half million of money which will be seen in
the second part of this resolution, should be
given to the Ministry of Finance. I think
that with this explanation I may move the
resolution.
Mr. McGUFFIN: Is this arrangement a
sort of assurance that the liability of the
Ministry will be fully discharged as far as
you are concerned?
Mr. POLLOCK : The liability of the
Ministry is simply to lend to the Insurance
Fund sufficient money to carry it on until it
becomes solvent. When that solvency will
come is something beyond my calculation. So
far as the Ministry is concerned it is not a
question of a grant. Members must clearly
get that out of their minds.
Mr. McGUFFIN: I quite agree.
Mr. POLLOCK: The loan is an accumulating liability of the Unemployment Insurance
Fund to the Government.
Mr. DONALD: The only point I have in
mind is that I am just afraid we will have to
come back to this Parliament to ask for
further power.
The CHAIRMAN: Sufficient unto the day
is the evil thereof.

Secretary to the Ministry of Education if he
will state-
(a) The number of schools where boys
are taking educational courses in handicraft, technical training and physical
recreation.
(b) The number of boys by ages at present being taught the above subjects.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY TO
THE MINISTRY OF EDUCATION (Mr.
McKeown): With the permission of the hon.
Member I would like to circulate the answer
to this question instead of reading it, as it is
lengthy.
The following is the answer :

National Schools-
(a) Instruction in physical exercises is
given in all National Schools.
schools 1,922 are attended by boys.
Of these
Handicraft and technical training are not included in the programmes of National
Schools, as they are 1 ot elementary school
subjects. Sanction has recently been
obtained for payment of grants to Technical School Committees for instruction of
National School pupils in Woodwork, but
we have no information of the formation
of such classes.
(b) About 99,000 boys at present receive
instruction in physical exercises, but statistics showing classification by ages have not
been compiled.
2. Secondary Schools-
(a) Educational courses in Handicraft are
provided at 7 schools and 218 boys are
under instruction. These boys are between
the ages 12 and 18 years
(b) One school provides a special educational course in Technical Training
attended by about 100 boys whose ages
range from 14 to 19 years.
(c) It is known that in a large number
of these schools instruction in Physical
Recreation is provided. The Ministry has,
however, no information as to the number
or the ages of the boys who participate.
3. Day Trades Preparatory Schools-There
are 6 Day Trades Preparatory Schools. In 5
of these all the boys in attendance are required to follow a composite course of instruction including Handicraft, Technical
Training, and Physical Recreation. The total

18 years. The sixth school provides a composite course including Handicraft and Technical Training, which is attended by 123 boys
between the ages of 12 and 18 years.

2.-Mr. DONALD asked the Parliamentary
Secretary to the Ministry of Education if he
will state-
(a) The total number of Primary Schools
in Northern Ireland.
(b) The number where girls are taught
cookery, laundry, and domestic economy.
(c) The number of girls by ages at present being taught the above subjects.
(d) The number of Primary Schools
having no accommodation for teaching any
or all of the above subjects.
(e) And whether the Government propose
to have specially constructed buildings for
instruction in the above, or make special
provision in the new Primary Schools.
(a) The total number of Primary Schools
in Northern Ireland on 31st December, 1922,
was 2,066.
(b) The number of Primary Schools where
girls are taught Domestic Economy subjects, Cookery, Laundry, etc., is 1,060, but
it is to be observed that in addition to these
1,060 schools the pupils of 90 other schools
are taught these subjects in neighbouring
Technical Schools.
(c) Girls are taught Domestic subjects if
they are at least 11 years of age, or in the
fifth or higher standards. The number so
under instruction on 31st December, 1922,
was 19,315. There are no figures available
from which the number of girls under instruction could be given by ages.
(d) The number of Primary Schools
having no accommodation for instruction
in Domestic Economy subjects is about
1,000. This includes 200 schools for boys
only, 100 for infants only, and 90 schools
where pupils are taught these subjects in
Technical Schools. It
may be well to
point out also that the Ministry does not
require accommodation to be provided for
these subjects where the circumstances do
not permit of their being effectively taught,
e.g., where the teachers are not qualified,
and where the number of senior girls is
small. It is estimated that there are not
more than 100 Primary Schools in which
these subjects are omitted owing solely to
the lack of suitable accommodation.
(e) The Ministry has deferred consideration of the question of what further provision, if any, should be made for instruction in these subjects, pending the receipt
of the Final Report of the Lynn Committee,
which, it is understood, will make recommendations in the matter.

The PARLIAMENTARY AND FINAN-
CIAL SECRETARY TO THE MINISTRY
OF FINANCE (Mr. Barbour): I am sure that
at the passing of the Government of Ireland
Act many of those who now constitute the
members of this Committee had not been devoting much of their time to the administration of public affairs. They felt, however, a
certain call coming to them at this very important stage, when the whole complicated
machinery of Government was about to be
started here, that they should come forward,
if selected by their constituencies, to lend a
hand in order that the machinery should be
constructed on the most substantial, efficient
and enduring lines, so that it might well
carry on for all time to come the important
duties entrusted to this Parliament under
the Government of Ireland Act. As an ordinary business-man, if this had happened in a
commercial concern I would have felt that
after a certain time it would have been my
duty to come to my colleagues and tell them
what progress had been made in carrying out
this most important part of the setting up of
our Government; in other words, to report
progress, to explain the different functions
which had been confided to this Ministry in
particular, to enumerate the varied services
which have been combined within this one
Ministry, and to give you some idea of the
volume of work passing through those different sections, so that this Committee might be
in a position to form some opinion as to
whether the work was efficiently and economically carried on and whether the size of the
staff which is reported in our Estimates is
excessive, when due regard is had to the
volume and the varied and complicated character of the work which it has to discharge.
I think I may say the time has almost come
when we may consider all our different Ministries as finally constituted and fully launched
upon their career of service. It is true that
in the Ministry of Finance there is still a
great deal of work. complicated and difficult,
of a non-recurrent character to be carried on,
but it will still be the case that while the
greater part of the work is of a constant
character there will always be a certain
amount of a variable character. And so I
suppose that what is a transient thing to-day
will in due course be replaced by other duties,
possibly of a permanent, or maybe also of a
transient, character. With these preliminary
remarks I should like to warn the Members
of this Committee that I am proposing to-day
to go at some considerable length into the
different duties of this very extensive
Ministry.
Hon. Members will observe that, so far as
expenditure on this occasion compares vith
that of the previous year, there is only a
slight decrease of £106, the main changes
leading up to this result having been fully
set out in that part of the foreword dealing
with this Estimate. It will there be seen
that the decrease in the estimated expenditure
on travelling, removal, and subsistence
experses, and the disappearance of the item
relating to Housing Loans, together with an
increase in receipts resulting from the fees
chargeable under the Loans Guarantee
(Northern Ireland) Act, has more than
counterbalanced the increased provision
which has now to be made for a full instead
of a part year's salaries of certain branches
of the staff. It will further be noted that
the expenses in connection with the issue of
Ulster Savings Certificates is now borne on
this Estimate. Before turning to sub-heads,
it might not be out of place if I explain briefly
the principles underlying the existing grades
of Civil Servants, to which reference is made
throughout the Estimates. This grading
necessarily applies to a service composed in
great part of men who, on transfer, already
held the various ranks, and is common to the
Imperial and Northern Ireland Civil Service,
and took its final shape as a result of the
adoption of the recommendations of a Committee whose report was made in the year
1919.
Effective division of labour is the basis of
sound organisation, and, without a clear
general idea of the work to be done and of
the different degrees of capacity and effort that
the work demands, no effective solution could
be found of the problems of recruitment,
grading, and remuneration. Accordingly, the
Civil Service has been divided into three main
categories (a) administrative, (b) executive,
(c) clerical. In the first category may be
placed all such work as is concerned with the
formation of policy, the revision of existing
regulations and decisions, and the organisation and direction of the business of government. In the third category the work is
either of a routine kind or consists in the
application of well-defined regulations and
decisions to particular cases. The second
category deals with work demanding more
sense of responsibility and initiation, and the
control of sections of lower grade work.
Experience has shown that the higher
administrative work of the public service
requires for its discharge a proportion of men
of the standard recruited at the Universityleaving age, and, accordingly, the method
followed for some considerable time by the

Clerks, whose salaries range from £80 to

are also required to deal with particular

To the executive class is assigned the

is probable that this grade will in future be

rather than by any special examination.
Executive Officers, whose salaries range from
£100 to £400, are entrusted with the examination of particular cases of lesser importance
not clearly within the scope of approved
regulations, further investigations into matters of higher importance and the immediate
direction of small blocks of business. Higher
Executive Officers, whose salaries range from
£400 to £500, deal with matters of internal
organisation and control and with the responsible conduct of important operations under
the general supervision of a principal officer.
I will refer later on to the question of
recruitment, and will now turn to sub-head
(A) of the Estimate, from which it will be
observed that the total staff of the Ministry
numbers 276, and that the total expenditure
on salaries amounts to no less than £93,000.
The staff included therein is approximately
the same as that included in last year's
original Estimate as supplemented by the
Supplementary Estimate which was only
as
I propose to take each Sub-department
separately, and to place before the Committee some facts and information which I hope
will prove interesting to them relative to the
actual duties undertaken, and I am confident
that in the light of these facts, Members will
be as confident as I am that the staff has been
confined to the lowest possible number consistent with the proper discharge of the
various functions. The main branches with
which I propose to deal are:-
I. The Treasury Branch, which is
divided into three parts-
II.
III.
(a) Finance Branch.
(b) Accounts Branch.
(c) Establishment Branch.
Valuation Department.
Registrar-General's Department.
IV. Stamps Department.
V. Estate Duty Branch.
VI. Revenue Department.
VII. Office of Works.
VIII. Law Department.
IX. Registry and other Branches con.-
mon to all Departments.
The principal functions of the Finance
Branch fall under the following heads :-
(a) The control of public expenditure and
public loans in various degrees and various
ways chiefly through the preparation or
supervision of the estimates for Parliament,
and in a secondary degree by the day to day
scrutiny of proposals from other Ministries
for new expenditure not specifically covered
by the Estimates whether of a major character
or of a minor degree. In passing, I may say
that it is very often the control of minor expenditure which makes all the difference
between a deficit and a surplus.
(b) The arrangements for the provision of
the funds required to meet the necessities of
the public service, for which purpose it has
been entrusted with extensive borrowing
powers.
(c) Function of carrying out measures
affecting the public debt and banking.
(d) The prescribing of the manner in which
the public accounts should be kept.
(e) All matters relating to superannuation.

[Mr. Barbour]
(f) Certain matters which cannot be conveniently dealt with in other branches, most
of which required a separate Government
Department in Dublin, viz., the administration of the Statutes and Regulations governing the Teachers' Pension Fund, the administration of Charities and certain work
formerly carried out by the Land Commission.
Arising out of the above functions this
Branch also co-operates with officers of the
House and Whip's Department regarding
Parliamentary business, carries out work
in connection with private Bill legislation so
far as it affects finance, and the Loans
Guarantee (Northern Ireland) Act.
In this Branch is collected the information
required by the Minister of Finance for the
preparation of his annual Budget, and the
accounts of public income and expenditure.
As regards the provision of the funds required from day to day, I would remind
Members of the complexity of the existing
arrangements, whereby the Imperial Government is responsible for the collection of,
approximately, 88 per cent. of Northern Ireland revenue, and for, approximately, 60 per
cent. of its expenditure. The complicated
questions which must necessarily arise from
this arrangement, and which require the
close and consistent attention of this Branch,
will be obvious to all. In addition, the main
financial questions which were bound to arise
on the setting up of a new Government within the British Isles, have not yet been finally
settled, and, at the present time, the more
important of these questions are the subject
of consideration by an Arbitration Committee
in London, who are weighing up Northern
Ireland claims as against those of the Imperial Treasury, and whose meetings in
London require the attendance of certain
officers at frequent intervals.
an
These varied duties require, in the main,
administrative staff, involving as they
do, very little work of a routine character.
The actual staff employed on these duties is
as follows:-2 Principal Officers, 3 Assistant
Principals, 3 Clerks, making a total of 8,
who are under the direct supervision of an
Assistant Secretary. Personally I have, perhaps, more intimate knowledge of the work
of this Branch than of any other Branch
of the Ministry, and can vouch for
the great pressure of work which
has
obtained for a very considerable
time. In any case, I think that Members will
agree that the grouping of so many functions
demands, on the part of the staff concerned,
expert knowledge of a wider range of subjects
than is the case in its counterpart in the
Imperial Civil Service.
The control of public expenditure may be
regarded as the most important of its functions, and this duty naturally falls upon the
Treasury, seeing that if the Minister of
Finance is to establish sound finance, no
expenditure of a novel character must be
incurred without his knowledge. In other
words, if the Minister of Finance is to be
held responsible for providing supplies and
maintaining the necessary Government balanhe must also be in a position to regulate
the commitments. Thus the broad principle
is that no Department may adopt any measure increasing or tending to increase the
public expenditure, beyond that sanctioned
in detail in the Annual Estimates, without
the previous assent of the Treasury Branch.
ces,
No Department can undertake and execute
a new work unsanctioned in principle, without previous assent, a new clerical post
cannot be added to an establishment without
previous assent, a gratuity or ex-gratia payment cannot be made without previous assent,
and this rule applies in all its minuteness to
the various Departments which are charged
with the expenditure of public money. This
Lainute control ensures the most careful
scrutiny by Accounting Officers of all Ministries before they pass payments, and is the
most effective of all checks in securing economy in public administration. If a Department fails to observe these rules, the Auditor-
General, a Parliamentary Officer, would detect
the irregularity and direct the offending Department to obtain covering Treasury autho
rity. If such were not forthcoming, he
would report such expenditure to Parliament for disallowance. It is probably
unnecessary for me to add, however, that in
practice discretion is allowed to Departments
within certain limits, which is usually accompanied by an obligation to report the manner
in which such discretion is exercised.
Throughout the year the proposals of the
various Departments are receiving consideration, and when the time arrives for the submission of draft Estimates for the coming
year, agreement has in most cases already
been reached between the Ministry of Finance
and the Department concerned.
As
regards the miscellaneous functions
already referred to, one of the most important is the administration of charities in
Northern Ireland. It is the duty of the
Branch to ensure that Charitable Bequests
are properly disbursed, that the sales of premises owned by Charitable organisations are
carried out in the best interests of the Charity, and in certain circumstances, it has
powers to amend the terms of bequests so as
to make them harmonise better with existing
facts. It has to assist it in these functions
the services of an Advisory Committee, representing legal, religious, and charitable
interests.

exercise of powers transferred to the Northern Government in connection with holdings
which have been purchased under the various

or sub-let, to register their holding in the

in excess of ten times the Land Purchase

In all such cases it is necessary to consider

or involve the owner in financial embarrassment.
This Section further exercises the functions,
other than the actual hearing in Court formerly exercised by the Irish Land Commissioners, under the Land Law Acts in respect
of unpurchased land. These powers include
the fixing of fair rents on agricultural holdings, the making of orders enabling landlords
to resell land in the occupation of tenants for
sufficient reason, and the facts of the true
value of holdings, with a view to pre-emption
by the landlord. Any cases which come to
actual hearing are dealt with in Court by
two Assistant Commissioners who are engaged on the part-time basis, with legal and
professional qualifications, and their decisions are promulgated by the Branch.
A considerable amount of Parliamentary
work is performed-
(a) in connection with the examination of
all private Bills, as affecting the Ministry
of Finance, and in consequence a considerable amount of correspondence takes place
with other Departments and with the promoters of Bills. Reports are sent to Parliament, and the Bills are watched throughout
their course, with a view to securing that
the financial interests are not imperilled;
(b) as financial business forms the greater
part of the whole, the responsibility for
arranging the course of Parliamentary
business in conjunction with the officers of
the House and the Chief Whip's Office, and
subject to Cabinet approval, has been
placed upon this Branch. The work in
itself requires considerable care and attention.
The administration of the Loans Guarantee
(Northern Ireland) Act is undertaken by the
Treasury Branch. I might add that the administration of the Trade Facilities Act in
Great Britain is carried out by a separate
Department, which costs the Imperial Treasury approximately £14,000 annually.

The work of the Accounts branch employs
54 of the staff of the Ministry, namely, one
accountant, ranking as a principal officer,
one assistant accountant, one assistant principal, three higher executive officers, and 48
officers of executive and clerical rank. These
are all under the control of one of the two

into which are paid all the revenues of

necessary, temporary borrowings by way of

Accounts for Land Purchase Annuities.
Church Temporalities Revenues, and Ulster

The dispersal of the annual income amongst

Additional duties result from the responsibility of this Branch in connection with the

I have enumerated in great detail the functions of this Branch as otherwise it would

Turning now to the other side of the Ministry of Finance, that which is known departimentally as the Revenue and Works side, the

In the Stamping Department it is necessary

I think that so far as the bulk of the large
ratepayers are concerned-I mean ratepayers
as apart from taxpayers-they have a serious
grievance against the Finance Department,
and I take this, the earliest, opportunity of
raising the matter for the consideration of
the Minister of Finance.
Mr. MARK: I should like to add a word
or two with reference to the question of valuations. I think the hon. Member for West
Belfast (Mr. Lynn) has dealt adequately with
the valuation of property, and I would like
to touch on the question of valuation in the
case of Death Duties on property, and particularly farm property. I have known
instances where the valuation insisted upon
was more than the property would have
brought if put up in the open market. Ι
know a case where a farm sold at £200 an
acre for the simple reason that the adjoining
owner wanted to buy it and did not like the
class of neighbour he would get. He bought
it, but that the valuation put upon it should
rule the valuations of the whole district or
county I think is preposterous. Of course
I know that farmers have a right to
appeal and that an arbitrator or referee
can be appointed to hear the whole case, but
imagine the expense a farmer is put to if he
has to travel from Derry to Belfast and take
back two valuers, who will charge him five or
ten guineas a day, and a solicitor, all in order
that he may get justice. The farmer would
probably be better off if he paid the duty at
once. I think the question of valuation in
Northern Ireland, whether for the purpose of
death duties or for the purpose of ascertaining
the value of improvements, is being overdone,
and I feel convinced that the people are
beginning to feel it, if they do not already
know it.

un the risk of the valuation. My point is

too far you are retarding the advancement
of the community, just as under the old land

land he had to pay an increased rent, with

land. Now they are afraid to build houses.

The ATTORNEY-GENERAL (Mr. Best):
If I would take a hint from the course of
the debate on the previous Vote, it
might be advisable for me to say nothing at
all, but simply to go rapidly through the
items, because if I happened to make a
speech, or what you might call a speech.
some hon. Member might say that there is
very good reason for it, namely, to cloak up

(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) Extra costs
are not about to be incurred in this case. I
am glad to say that in the Vote for this
particular item there is a decrease of £623
compared with the amount voted last year.
Before I go through the items it might be
perhaps advisable, notwithstanding the
danger I have foreshadowed, to say a few
words about the condition of affairs now
compared with the condition of affairs when
I was moving the Vote this time last year.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) I had the
curiosity to look up Hansard the other day,
and I find that in moving the Vote last year
I contented myself with saying nothing.
because at that time there was something
else to be done than to talk. Work was what
was before us, and work is what we have
carried out during the year.
Hon. Members will recollect that about this
time last year, or perhaps early in April, two
Acts of Parliament enabling us to deal with
the terrible situation that had then arisen,
were passed by this House. One of those was
the Criminal Procedure Act. I had the honour to introduce the Bill, and I think hon.
Members gathered from me, at least some
said so, that I did not regard that Bill as

good.
being very likely to do much
Well, the Bill as we all anticipated when
it became an Act was a dead letter. In
no case did any prisoner ask to be tried
by the special tribunals set up by that Act,
and in no case did I find it necessary to direct
a prisoner to be tried by those tribunals instead of the ordinary courts established in the
ordinary way, but there was another Act
which was also passed about the same time,
that is the Civil Authorities (Special
Powers) Act. That Act has been of enormous help to those of us who were fighting the
forces of disorder and crime. It really has
been of the greatest assistance to us, and of
all the work that was done by various
people, police, specials, and all those who are
employed in running down crime, I think
nothing has been so instrumental, nothing
has been so helpful as the powers granted to
us by this Civil Authorities (Special Powers)
Act.
Hon. Members will recollect that in that
Act we took power to increase the severity
of punishments, to inflict corporal punishment in many cases where it was not open to
us before to inflict corporal punishment, and
we took also powers of various kinds not only
in the body of the Act itself, but also by
means of regulations made from time to time
by the Minister. That Act has been, as I
say, of the greatest service to us. Really, if
it had not been for it, or something of that
particular nature, it would have been
almost impossible for us to carry on.
This time last year, hon. Members
will also recollect, we were about to
meet a horrible orgy of crime A wave of
murder and of arson and of destruction of
property in
various ways swept over the
country, and hon. Members will recollect, at
least those who have seen our charts, that
in one week as many as 32 murders were com-
Imitted in Northern Ireland, while hundreds
of thousands of pounds, aye, almost a million
pounds of property were destroyed in one
week. I am glad to say that at the moment--
I gladly say it, and God grant it will long
continue that we have reached normal
again. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear). I am
not saying that in any spirit of boast, but I
am saying it in the hope that that state of
affairs will continue, that the madness which
seemed to have overtaken the people will not
return to us again, and that we shall be
allowed to live in peace and quietness; to live
our own lives, to carry on and develop our
own business, free from those dreadful
crimes which were a disgrace to this part of
the country, but which were not in many
instances caused by people belonging to this
part of the country. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear). There is no doubt that about this time
last year, and from that time on, a deliberate
attempt was made to wreck our Government
and to make government impossible. We have
defeated that attempt, and I believe if such
an attempt should unfortunately be made
again we shall be in a better position to defeat it than we were this time last year. This
time last year the old Royal Irish Constabulary had just been disbanded. We were
building up a new Force, made no doubt of
the very best stuff possible, but, at the same
time composed of men who had not had the
necessary training and the necessary experience to cope with the wave of crime then
sweeping over our country. In addition to
having our men better trained and prepared
in that way I may say also that we are getting assistance now from quarters which some
time ago were, if not actually hostile to us,
at least indifferent to our success. So that I
think I may look forward with a great deal
of hope to the question of the amount of
crime that may be committed during the next
twelve months.

The Vote we ask for is a total sum of
£17,353. Before I go into details it may be
of interest if I give the Committee some
figures as to the number of cases that have
been dealt with during the past year. They
are not set out here. I tried to get them,
but, unfortunately, I have not got all the returns. Under the Explosive Substances Act
of 1883 and the Firearms Act of 1920 we
have dealt during the year with about 650
cases. Every one of those cases, of course,
had to come before the Attorney-General, and
directions had to be given as to what was
to be done. The vast majority of them were
dealt with by the Magistrates, but many of
them
my directions were sent forward for trial by a judge and jury;
in other words, indictments were brought
forward in those cases. Hon. Members will
also remember that under the Civil
Authorities (Special Powers) Act we took
power to order whipping as a punishment
for certain firearms offences. We already
had power under the ordinary law to whip
for armed robbery and robbery with violence,
but we extended that power to certain
offences under the Firearms Act. It may
possibly interest hon. Members to know in
how many cases under our various powers
whipping, or birching as the case may be,
was ordered, and in how many cases they
have been carried out. Whipping was
ordered in twenty-seven cases, and birching
in nineteen cases. Now, very often a Judge
will find that, although a person has made
himself amenable to one or other of these
forms of punishment, and although that
person might deserve such punishment, a report comes through from the Medical Officer
that the particular subject of the case is not

got returns, figures as to the number of indictable cases that were dealt with by a judge
and jury at the Assizes, at the Commission,
or by the Recorders and County Court Judges.
It may interest hon. Members to know that,
under the heading of indictable offences, in
Belfast and Antrim we have 985-practically
1,000 cases, in Fermanagh 52, Tyrone 132,
and Down 206. I regret to say I have not got
the returns either for Londonderry or for my
own county-County Armagh. We sent out
requests some time ago, but there has been
some hitch about it, and I think possibly I
understand the reason. No, it is not what
hon. Members think. I happen to know that
one at least of the responsible officials is in
very bad health and away for the moment,
and that is probably the cause of the delay;
but hon. Members will see that a tremendous
amount of work has been done in the way of
bringing offenders to justice.
Mr. LYNN: Roughly, about how many
cases would there be in all?
Mr. BEST: I think for the Six Counties
there would be probably about 1,500 or 1,600
cases. That is a rough estimate. Of course,
that does not mean that all those people were
convicted. As I have always maintained, the
juries in Northern Ireland have been accustomed to do their duty and do it well, and
if juries do their duty, then they are bound
to acquit in a great many cases, because hon.
Members will recollect that when a case is
sent to the Attorney-General
to decide
whether or not a prosecution should be instituted he has only got the Crown side of the
case before him. He has only got sufficient
material to enable him to say whether a prima
facie case has been made out, and once he has
got that information before him it is his duty
to direct a prosecution. Very often a different tale is told when the actual trial comes
on, and the witnesses for the defence are put
up.
With these preliminary observations, which
I hope are not too long, I will now proceed
to deal with the various headings of the
Vote. The first item with which I want to
deal is the Legal Adviser. We ask for £600
to pay a part-time Legal Adviser. This appointment was made last year, I think a little
earlier than this, but the salary, if any, re
quired that year was paid out of savings.
The salary, as hon. Members will see, is at
the rate of £600 per year, and the appointment is a part-time one. The appointment
is held by a practising Barrister, and was
necessitated by the large number of points
requiring the advice and opinion of Counsel.
In the absence of a Legal Adviser it would be
necessary to send out the different cases to
Counsel in each particular instance, and those
of us who know the fees Counsel would be
expected to earn in such cases, know that it'
would cost a great deal more to send out
these individual cases than the £600 a year
for which we are asking. I know very intimately the kind of work the Legal Adviser
is doing. In some weeks he has as many as
twenty or twenty-five points on which to
advise the various Ministries. He advises
the Ministry of Home Affairs in so far as
their Local Government work is concerned,
and, in passing, I may say that in Dublin
for that work alone there was a Legal Adviser and an Assistant Legal Adviser.
present Legal Adviser does all that work.
He advises the Ministry of Labour on points
on which they want the advice of Counsel, and
also the Ministry of Education, and the Ministry of Commerce-in fact every Ministry except the Ministry of Finance so that really
I think £600 a year for a part-time adviser is
not at all extravagant pay, in fact it is anything but extravagant.

In the next Sub-head-Under Sheriff'sthere is no change, because their salaries are
fixed by Statute. The next item-Prosecutors' and Witnesses' Expenses-is rather
a large item, and I am sure hon. Members
will ask me why there is an increase. Last
year under the heading of Prosecutors' and
Witnesses' Expenses at Assizes, Quarter
Sessions and Petty Sessions
asked for
£3,150. At that time we had not the experience necessary to say what would be an appropriate figure. We have now had the experience of last year, and for the coming
year we ask for £4,000. This amount is
really in aid of local rates. Under various
Statutes, the last of which was 18 and 19
Vic. cap. 126, the expenses under this heading
were charged on local rates, but so far back
as 1860 it was decided, with the approval of
Parliament as expressed by their Vote year
after year, to relieve local rates of this burden
by recouping their expenditure under this
head out of Government money. What
happens is really that these expenses of witnesses and various other people coming to
Assizes, to the Commission, and to the
Quarter Sessions and Petty Sessions, are paid
in the first instance by the Clerk of the
Peace and we have to repay them. If they
were not paid in that way they would fall as
a burden upon local expenses.
The next item is Fees to Counsel for conducting Crown prosecutions at the Commission, and at the Assizes throughout the
Province. Here there is a decrease from
£4,000 to £3,075. This again is due to our
better experience during the past year, and
we are hoping that if things remain normal,
as I believe they will, even this figure will
not be required. These fees are paid to the
Counsel who go round with the Judges to
the Assizes and Commissions and conduct
the prosecutions on behalf of the Crown.
The next item is that of "General Law
Expenses." There is an increase of £115
under this head, and that is due to various
powers that had to be exercised under the
Civil Authorities (Special Powers) Act. The
Minister was empowered by that Act to
order inquiries in lieu of inquests, and in
that case, of course, the Ministry had to bear
the expense.
The next sub-head is "Rewards for Evidence and Information." We asked for £500
last year; we ask for only £200 this year.
Of course, it is obvious that I cannot be expected to give any particulars under this
sub-head.
The next item is "Defence of Public
Officials." Last year we asked for £200; this
year we ask for £100. This sub-head is
designed for the purpose of enabling public
officials who may have to defend actions in
relation to the discharge of their public
duties, to defend the proceedings. The
amount that might or might not be required is
obviously very problematical. There may be
a year in which public officials would
entirely escape; on the other hand there
might be two or three big actions brought
against them, and a substantial sum might
be involved under this head, but we have put
down tentatively the sum of £100. Printing,
Stationery and Office Supplies, Postages,
Telegrams and Telephones, and Receipts
Appropriated in Aid are the same as last
year. The amounts are trifling, and do not
call for any comment. I have no further
observations to make, but I shall be very
pleased to answer any questions that hon.
Members may wish to put in reference to
these Estimates. I beg to move.

have always preached economy I have held

Morrison), has raised the question of doctors'
fees. No one is more anxious than I am that

There is a scale of fees fixed by the Treasury
in the old days and adopted by the Minister
of Finance, and we cannot go outside
that scale. I have absolutely no power to
alter it and therefore any representations
that might be made ought to be made to the
Minister of Finance, and if he will give way

adopted no one would be more pleased than
I. I quite recognise that in the case of
professional men who leave their work and
lose the opportunity of earning fees by at.
tending to their patients it is utterly ridiculous to say that a fee of two or three guineas

Sir DAWSON BATES: This Vote has one

the expenses incurred by local authorities in

to 14th January, 1922. The first instalment

among the local authorities on the basis of
60 per cent. of payments made by them on

injuries which were committed between the

1920, and 14th January, 1922. According to
the returns which We have received, the

strong representations to the Imperia! Government because we feel a further grant
