CLASS VI. No. 1.
MINISTRY OF COMMERCE.
Motion made, and question proposed:
"That a sum not exceeding £16,273 be
granted to His Majesty to complete the sum
necessary to defray the charge which will
come in course of payment during the year
ending on the 31st March, 1924, for the
salaries and expenses of the Ministry of
Commerce."
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE (Mr.
Archdale): As the Ministry of Commerce is a
new Ministry, I think it would be well if I
said something about the work that has been
done by the Ministry of Commerce in the
past year and something of its intentions for
the future. The Department is divided into
two parts, one part dealing with the administration of certain statutory matters, such as
companies, friendly societies, business names,
electricity, water power, gas, mines and quarries, canals, harbours, docks and piers,
weights and measures, and other matters. 1
am glad to say that all this work is proceeding smoothly, and during the ensuing year
it is hoped that the Department will be able
to examine how far existing legislation which
we took over as it stood may be changed to
make it more suitable to the conditions in
Northern Ireland. Already there are several
matters which the Department hopes it may
be possible to simplify considerably. The
functions of the other side of the Ministry,
the Commerce and Economic Department,
may be broadly classified as follows:-
(1) Assistance to traders, e.g., dissemination of commercial information and dealing
with special inquiries.
(2) Investigation of current problems and
difficulties affecting Ulster traders, and advising traders and trade associations on
these matters.
(3) Examination of all economic matters.
(4) Keeping in constant touch with the
condition of trade and with the factors
affecting it.
(5) Examination of matters of potential
Jevelopment.
Committee.
Supply--
1 MAY 1923
(6) Dealing with certain special matters
entrusted to the Ministry.
It may interest the Committee if I give
some indication of the progress that has been
made on these lines. We have now in the
Department confidential information regarding practically all manufacturers, merchants
and agents in Northern Ireland. On the
other hand, we are gradually perfecting arrangements whereby we collect day by day
reliable, accurate and most varied information of all markets that are, or might be, of
use to us.
Following upon this the Ministry set up a
Trade Development Committee, composed of
various business men who have voluntarily
and most willingly given their assistance to
the Department. That Committee, which is
under the chairmanship of the permanent
Secretary, among other things set up panels
of each trade. These panels meet at the
Ministry of Commerce from time to time,
and by this means the particular needs and
possibilities of each trade are presented to
the Department which is able, accordingly,
to see how far these possibilities can be realised. It is hoped by this means very considerably to extend the export trade of
Ulster. The Trade Development Committee
is also considering the question of the stimulation of home demand for Ulster goods, and
while the strength of such a demand must
depend on the nature of the article and the
enterprise of the manufacturer, merchant
and retailer, yet there is no doubt that there
is room for considerable stimulation, and the
Committee is at the present time engaged in
considering what action could usefully be
taken by those concerned.
The Ministry has since its inception, in
conjunction with other bodies, been actively
engaged on removing the misapprehensions
that have existed in England and abroad
regarding the condition of affairs in Ulster,
and I am glad to say that those misconceptions are, as the House will appreciate,
almost entirely removed. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear). The House will have some idea
of the economic problems that arise for consideration and the branch of the Ministry
dealing with these is well equipped for doing
so, and serves as an advisor in this respect
for the rest of the office.
If I may summarise what I have said I
would say that the policy of the Ministry is
as follows:-
(1) Not to interfere with or control trade.
(2) To strengthen the link between
Ulster and the rest of the United Kingdom,
and to preserve the identity of Ulster with
Great Britain.
(3) To develop export trade.
(4) To stimulate the development of industry on the lines of individual enterprise, but on lines that may enable the
present day fierce competition to be met.
In short, to do all that is consistent with
this policy that may lead to increased commercial prosperity and go to reduce the
volume of unemployment in our midst. In
that aim, I may say, the Ministry of Labour
and the Ministry of Commerce are at one,
and between us we will leave no stone unturned in our endeavours to bring about real
and enduring employment for our people.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
I have not, of course, attempted to inform
the House of all the matters that have been
dealt with by the Department in the past year.
There are many confidential matters with regard to which the Ministry has been consulted.
but the Ministry has in many other respects
done a good deal to assist industries in the
peculiar difficulties with which they have been
faced.
I could not finish what I have to say without referring first of all to the very cordial
relations that have existed between the
Ministry and the Board of Trade and the
Department of Overseas Trade. We are in
the closest touch with those Departments
and with the trade policy of the Imperial
Government, and we make it one of our most
important functions to preserve that link
unimpaired. A few days ago Sir Philip
Lloyd-Greame, the President of the Board of
Trade, attended a meeting of our Advisory
Council and gave that body the benefit of his
views on trade matters generally, and
assured us of the cordial co-operation of his
Departments; that Advisory Council is composed of public spirited men who have never
hesitated to give all the assistance in their
power. Moreover, we have had great assistance from the various Chambers of Commerce and Trade Associations who have
worked most cordially and most loyally with
the Department.
I will now turn to Vote 1, which is before
the House. I should explain that on Sub-
Head "A" £1,250 of the increase in this
Sub-Head is caused by the transfer to this
Vote of half the salaries of the Minister and
Parliamentary Secretary, which were
previously borne on the Votes of the
Ministry of Agriculture and Ministry of
Education respectively. We are two unfortunate people who belong to two different
bodies. A substantial part of the remainder
of the increase is due to salaries of additional staff already engaged during the year
1922-1923 with the concurrence of the
Ministry of Finance, and includes the salary
of the
Assistant Secretary, who was
appointed in May, 1922. This latter is down
in the Vote for the first time. The employment of this additional staff was rendered
necessary by the increase in the volume of
651 Unemployment Insurance Bill- HOUSE OF COMMONS.

work undertaken by the Ministry since the
preparation of the Estimates of 1922-1923.
The actual increase in staff proposed for 1923-
1924 over and above the existing establishment is not so large, and is due to the increasing demand on the services of the
Ministry made by the commercial community.
Sub-Head "J" (Special Enquiries) is a
new Sub-Head, and provides £500 to meet
the expenses of the new Government Coinmission on Development. I do not think
there is any other Sub-Head which calls for
any remarks. I beg to move.

Oral Answer to Question
SALARY OF MEDICAL INSPECTORS.
Dr. MORRISON asked the Minister of
Home Affairs if the medical profession of
Ulster have informed him that in their
opinion the medical inspectors of the Local
Government Board should be paid a salary
of £800 per annum, rising to £1,000, and
what steps have been taken to meet this
request?
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): In fixing salaries of individual Civil Servants, regard must be had to
the principles affecting the Civil Service as
a whole under which salaries are determined,
with reference to the responsibilities devolving on and the duties performed by the
officers affected.
The question of the salaries of the officers
referred to in the hon. Member's question
had been under consideration for some time
prior to the receipt of the representations
made by the Ulster Medical Society, and it
had been decided, having regard to all the
circumstances of the case, to improve their
position by fixing a scale of £500 to £800
instead of a scale of £500 to £700, which was
the scale allowed for the medical inspectors
of the Local Governinent Board, Dublin.
Mrs. CHICHESTER: Arising out of that
answer, may I ask if it is correct that the
scale of salaries which is now being paid to
these officers was fixed 45 years ago, and has
never since been altered?
Sir DAWSON BATES: It is for that reason
that the alteration is being made.
Dr. MORRISON: I should like to ask a
further question-Is it a fact that it is impossible for these officers ever to attain full
pension, owing to the fact that they cannot
accept office until they have been six years
practising in other work?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I cannot agree with
the hon. Member.
Dr. MORRISON: I give notice that I shall
raise this question on the Motion for the
Adjournment

Mr. McKEOWN: I come now to sub-Head

Estimate compared
last year's
Estimate are those arising from re-organisation of staff. During the past year it
became necessary to augment the administrative staff by an additional assistant
principal, possessing special legal qualifications, an additional executive officer, six
clerks and a telephonist typist. This increase
was made only after actual experience had
shown that the existing staff was inadequate.
On the other hand, however, it was found
possible to leave two of the higher posts (a
principalship and an examinership) unfilled.
The total increase in staff is therefore seven
individuals.
It will be observed that the number of
clerks on the scale of £80 to £250 has been
increased from 17 to 38, whilst the number
of temporary clerks has been reduced from
16 to 1. The increase of 6 in the number of
individuals in the two grades combined is
explained above; the decrease in the number
of temporary clerks is due to the fact that
in the course of the past year nearly all of
them were appointed as permanent clerks
(£80-£250). I desire to point out that these
clerks are all ex-Servicemen, and were only
recognised in the position of permanent
Civil Servants after they had proved themselves to be competent to undertake the
duties of the grade to which they have been
admitted.
I come now to the inspection and organising
staff. The staff transferred to the Ministry
from Dublin consisted of inspectors and
organisers who had been serving under three
distinct educational departments, each of
which had its own system of grading and
payment. During the past year this staff
was re-organised and the scales of payment
co-ordinated. Prior to 1st April, 1922, the
salary scale for junior inspectors of schools
commenced at £200 per annum and increased
by annual increments of £15 to a maximum
of £400 per annum together with cost-ofliving bonus, whilst the salary scale for the
organisers commenced at £120 and increased
by annual increments of £5 to a maximum
of £140 per annum with cost-of-living bonus.
I recollect that this matter of the remuneration of these servants was raised in this
House, and I think rightly raised. It was
our opinion also that these scales were quite
inadequate, having regard to the importance
of the positions filled by the officers in question, and particularly in view of the liberal
salary scales provided for the national school
teachers.
This unsatisfactory state of affairs has now
been redressed, as the Ministry, with the
sanction of the Ministry of Finance, has introduced the following greatly improved salary
scales with effect from 1st April, 1922:
Inspectors.-Commencing salary £300 per
annum increasing by annual increments of
£15 for each of the first five years and
afterwards by annual increments of £20
each up to a maximum of £550 per annum,
together with cost-of-living bonus.
Organisers. Commencing salary £150 per
annum increasing by annual increments of
£10 to a maximum of £250 per annum with
cost-of-living bonus.
I am sure that hon. Members will agree that
the Ministry have done the right thing in
making this necessary alteration. (Hon.
Members: Hear hear.)

in Belfast from other centres. Under Subhead C, rent, rates, maintenance, &c., there
is a decrease of £300. Under Sub-head D,
lighting, heating, etc., there is a decrease of £115. I may say that these

is an increase of £300. I may say with regard
to that the requirements last year
underestimated by this amount. It was very
difficult when starting the administration to
know exactly in the early stages what would
be required for Estimates of this kind, and

CLASS IV. No. 2.
EDUCATIONAL SERVICES.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That a sum not exceeding £1,316,795 be
granted to His Majesty to complete the sum
necessary to defray the charge which will
come in course of payment during the year
ending on the 31st March, 1924, to provide
for educational services, including grants
in aid of Teachers' Pension Fund."
Mr. McKEOWN: For these educational services the Estimate for this year is £1,816,795.
For the corresponding year it was £1,727,622,
and there is an increase of £89,173. It is my
intention to refer to the various points regarding this Estimate.
The first is "A" and refers to training colleges, and there there is a decrease of £3,900.
The Estimate provides for capitation grants in
respect of the students at this college, and
also in respect of a limited number of Northern Ireland students who are completing
their course of training at the Church of
Ireland Training College in Dublin under
conditions approved by this Ministry. The
Ministry does not propose to sanction the
admission of any fresh students to this latter
college. As a matter of fact, it will not to any
college, but we have now made provision for,
and will look after the training of, our own
teachers. Provision is also made for the payment to Training Colleges, whether in the
Free State or in Northern Ireland, of the
authorised bonus in respect of any national
school teachers now serving in Northern Ireland whose qualifications are in the opinion
of this Ministry, such as would prior to the
Committee.

Supply-

transfer of educational services have entitled
the particular Training College in which
such teachers were trained to the appropriate bonus. Provision is also made under
this head for the cost of summer courses of
instruction in horticulture for teachers of
national schools. The new Training College
for the teachers of primary schools in Northern Ireland commenced operation in October,
1922. For the opening session 47 men students
and 151 women students were enrolled. A
suitable hostel providing residential accommodation for about 30 of the men students
was made available from the commencement
of the session, but it was not found practicable to provide residential accommodation for any of the women students for
the session 1922-23. Arrangements have been
made by which all the women students, and
the men students for whom hostel accommodation was not available, receive suitable
weekly allowances in respect of their lodging
and maintenance expenses. Stranmillis
House and the grounds attached to it have
been acquired by the Ministry for the purposes of the new Training College, and works
are now in progress for effecting the necessary alteration in Stranmillis House so as to
fit it for use as a hostel for the
students; additional temporary hostels are
also in course of erection on the grounds.
and it is confidently expected that at the commencement of the second session of the college
in September next hostel accommodation
will be ready for about 150 women students.
I am quite satisfied that hon. Members will
agree that this is a very considerable achievement on the part of the Ministry in view of
the fact that this question of the training of
teachers was taken over by the Ministry in
a very hurried manner indeed.
Mr. ROBB: Hear, hear.

Mr. McKEOWN: A Training College Committee under the chairmanship of my right
hon. Friend the Minister of Finance, consisting of representatives of educational bodies
in Northern Ireland and of certain members
of the senior administrative staff of the
Ministry has been set up for the transaction,
under the control of the Ministry, of all
matters relating to the training and certification of teachers. An arrangement is in
operation on trial for a period of two years
under which the instruction of the students
in training is given in part in the Queen's
University, in part in the Belfast Municipal
College of Technology, and, in respect of work
which could not be provided for in either of
these institutions, by a staff of teachers
appointed by the Ministry. The eagerness of
candidates to secure admission to the new
College is shown by the fact that the candidates for admission to the entrance examination he'd in April, 1923, were more than twice
as many as the candidates who applied for
admission to the corresponding examination
last year.
Mr. McGUFFIN: Might I ask if the
Ministry will be able to absorb so many as
that? Are you not making too great provision for the supply of teachers in view of the
fact that you have increased the number so
much?
Mr. McKEOWN: We cannot refuse the
candidates who come forward for examination. It is not that we expect we shall be
overstaffed in that respect, but it must be
understood that when teachers come forward
and pass the necessary examinations we cannot make appointments for them. They have
to take the risk the same as in any other

arise.
Mr. McGUFFIN: Are they made aware of
the fact that they must take the risk?
Mr. MCKEOWN: I am quite sure they are
aware of it from the very start. Regarding

eleven months' payments at the full rate and
one month's payment at the lower rate.
£16,000 of the increase is due to this cause.
£6,000 is due to the award of increments to
the teachers, and the remainder is principally due to increased average attendance of

that the payments as provided for the national school teachers under the Estimate
are those accruing under the scales of
salary and other grants sanctioned by

Ireland was under the control of the

Perhaps it would be interesting for hon.
Members to know that the average salary

and assistants, is at the present ime £370
a year; for women teachers the average
salary is £270 a year, and for junior assistants the average salary is £132 10s. I mention
these figures because it is of interest to hon.
Members that they should know the averages.
Mr. DONALD: Do I take it that in these
Estimates provision is being made for this
financial year?
Mr. McKEOWN: Quite so. We come now
to the question of equipment grants, and
there there is no variation. In new works,
alterations and additions, there is an increase

services for which provision is made in these

Hear, hear.) I think that hon. Members will

part of the duty of the Ministry of Education
to see that these long-standing grievances are

any Committee with greater pleasure than
the Committee that is considering the question of the salaries of secondary teachers.
Perhaps I may be allowed here to express
my gratitude to those Departmental members
of the Committee who have given me their
assistance in such a whole-hearted way. As
I said, we are not doing piece-work; we are
doing our work in a very thorough way, and
it is our intention to bring our proposals
before the House, and we expect to get the
approval of the House which will put this
question on a basis such as has never existed
before, and which will give satisfaction to
the community generally.
We come now to the question of technical
instruction and grants to local Committees,
and to school managers, and there there is an
increase of £7,363. This is a very welcome
increase-I am sure hon. Members will agree
it is a welcome increase and is entirely
owing to the fact that we have a very largely
increased number of students. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) A larger number of
classes and a better attendance of students
It is exceptionally satisfactory to know that
such interest is being taken, and that interest
is being reflected in the number of students
coming forward for these higher grades of
education. Under the sub-head Technical
Instruction-scholarships, examinations, etc.,
there is an increase of £1,420. Provision has
been made in the current year's Estimates
for an increased number of Science and Commerce Scholarships, which are made available
in educational establishments which provide
the highest type of instruction in these
branches. The holders of the scholarships
are intended to become teachers of the subjects in question in Intermediate or Technical
Schools in Northern Ireland, and have
entered into an agreement to that effect. Provision has also been made for a substantial
increase in the number of Trade Scholarships provided by the Ministry. These
scholarships are awarded to youths who
have completed two or more years of an ap
prenticeship to a trade, and secure for each
holder such a weekly maintenance allowance
as enables him to attend an intensive course
of instruction in the theory and practice of
that trade, imparted in a suitable institution
such as the Belfast Municipal College of
Technology. The scholarships are eagerly
sought after, and have proved most beneficial,
This is another very important part of the
work of the administration, and I am sure
it will meet with your general commendation.
It enables students through these grants to
come forward and take courses in such an
important institution as the Belfast Municipal College of Technology, and helps to
promote that higher class of training which
perhaps could not otherwise be obtained.
Provision for allowances to teachers attending summer courses has been transferred
from this sub-head-sub-head "B," intermediate education-
-as it is intended that in
future joint courses shall be held at which
both intermediate and technical teachers can
attend. I think this is a wise provision.
With regard to Queen's University, there is
no variation, and with regard to Receipts
Appropriated in Aid there is an increase of
£500. It has simply been found possible to
form a more accurate Estimate of the probable amount of these receipts.
In presenting these Estimates there are,
I think, two outstanding points. One is
that during the year we took over the
training of our own teachers, and I think that
that has been done with very marked success.
The Committee, under the chairmanship of
the Minister of Finance has been doing very
excellent work, and we have reason to expect
that under our own system of training

Captain MULHOLLAND: Allow me to add

who gave us such a very interesting and instructive discourse

of such tender years as 9. 10 and 11, they

life they are far more apt to become good
and healthy citizens of the British Empire
than they would have been had they not been
taught these subjects. If there is no course
of training on these lines I would ask the
hon. Gentleman to take such steps as will
enable students in the training colleges to
teach these subjects.

The other question I would like to raise is
an unpopular one, but I feel I should be
wanting in my duty if I did not mention it.
It is the question of the salaries which are
now paid to teachers in elementary schools.
Of course, we all agree that it is necessary
to pay a good teacher a good salary, but the
point which arises in my mind is whether
an average of £370 for a male teacher is not
more than we in the Six Counties can afford.
I think I am right in saying that the Minister
of Education (the Marquess of Londonderry),
in one of his speeches, made an appeal to
teachers in the elementary schools to voluntarily come forward like the English teachers
and say they were prepared to accept some
reduction in their salaries in order to show
their patriotism towards the Six Counties.
I would like the Parliamentary Secretary to
inform me whether any reply was received
to that appeal, and whether he thinks the
Six Counties is able to bear the burden of
paying such large salaries to teachers in
elementary schools.
Mrs. McMORDIE: I should like to ask the

Dr. MORRISON: Some uncharitable critic

I think we should have a flag pole and put up

I want to say a word with regard to Secondary Teachers. I am glad to hear the strong
language the Parliamentary Secretary used
with regard to them, as to the deplorable
condition in which they were until this matter was taken up, and the anxiety shown by
all the Members of this House and by the

a
That is the question I want to submit to him,
and, of course, if there is any laxity in respect of this matter, or there is not that complete control over the management of schools
that he hopes to have in the future, it would
be largely due to the fact that we are in a
period of transition at the moment. This is
a very important matter, and it appears that
there are quite a number of children served
in that way. It arises, I suppose, from the
fact that the school roll is not marked until
after religious instruction. Whether
child is to be regarded as late after that
hour or not is a question with which the
hon. Gentleman (Mr. McKeown) hes to deal,
but the important part, so far as the parent
is concerned, is that a mother sends her child
to school in the expectation that the child
gets there. Under such circumstances as I
have outlined the child may become truant
or may take an unlicensed holiday at the
instigation of the teacher. We all know the
danger that such a thing implies in a great
city like Belfast, and that he or she in
all probability may go to a park and run very
great risks there. I do not think such
arbitrary action on the part of the teacher is
to be tolerated and I do not know whether the
Ministry condones such conduct or not.
In regard to the salaries paid to the
teachers I do not want at this stage to offer
any comment, because I think the proper
time to do that would be when the subject is
discussed on the Bill now before the House.
But on this point as to whether there is to be
an economy effected by amalgamation, I would
suggest that there is great danger of an increase in expenditure in respect of the reduced number of children whom a teacher
will have under control if all that we hear is
likely to be carried into effect. Forty was
an ordinary class-and fifty in some instances
-for a teacher to have under control. If it
is proposed now that that number should be
reduced by twenty--

and gallant Member for Down (Captain Mulholland), I may say that it is the intention
of the Ministry to so arrange education that
we will produce good citizens-(hon. Members: Hear, hear)-because, after all, no system of education that fails to produce good
citizens can be considered a good system of
education. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) The
hon. and gallant Member asked did we intend
to encourage the teaching of civics in national schools. I may tell him at once that
it is our intention to arrange the curriculum
so that that subject will be taught. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) He also raised the
point regarding the salaries of national school
teachers. It is true that in England the
teachers
suggested
came forward and voluntarily

With regard to the matter raised by the
hon. Member for South Belfast (Mrs.
McMordie) about the training of afflicted
children, this is to my mind an important
and a humane point. Only a few days ago

in the Protestant community perhaps two or

in Kirkcubbin.

our intention to act as fairly as we possibly
can. In regard to the point raised by my
hon. Friend, the Member for the University-

the intention of the Government-

The PARLIAMENTARY AND FINAN-
CIAL SECRETARY TO THE MINISTRY
OF FINANCE (Mr. Barbour): The function
of this Bill has already been alluded to on
many occasions by my right hon. Friend, the
Minister of Finance, and I am sure it is unnecessary for me to go into the principle of
it at all. Hon. Members will at once recognise that it is their own Bill which was promoted in this House in order to endeavour to
combat the tragedy of unemployment that is
going on in our midst. By guaranteeing loans
which borrowers may be able to raise on
satisfactory terms, the Bill has undoubtedly
proved a success to such an extent that the
amount already authorised by this Parliament
has been completely absorbed. I can assure
hon. Members of this House that no loan is
guaranteed unless very satisfactory security
is forthcoming to the Ministry of Finance,
and I do not consider that any risk is being
incurred by the guarantee which is being
given under this Act. The purpose of this

SALARIES OF MEDICAL INSPECTORS.
Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That this House do now adjourn."-(Mr.
Burn).
Dr. MORRISON: It will be within the
memory of the House that on a very recent
occasion I brought before the House the
question of the inadequate salaries of th
two Local Government Board inspectors. I
did not go into detail with regard to that,
and I left myself practically at the mercy
of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Pollock). He
had no difficulty in flattening me out, and 1
do not like to be flattened out. I regret, too,
that after the process you allowed me to ask
a question, and I endeavoured to compare
the salaries of some of the officers employed
in the Department with those of the inspectors of the Local Government Board. I
made use then of this expression,
"squandering money in this fashion." I did
not intend to make use of that expression. It
came out of me in the heat of the moment.
I should not have used it with regard to these
officials. I regret that I made it, and I
apologise now to the House and to the officials for having done so. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.)
I regret exceedingly to have to bring this
matter again before the House, because we of
the medical profession, as the House in its
generous moments will admit, do not make
the securing of money our primary object in
life. That is, I think, admitted by everybody.

AGRICULTURE IN THE SIX COUNTIES.
Captain MULHOLLAND: I rise this afternoon to draw attention to the condition of
agriculture in the Six Counties. I think
there is no question whatever that agriculture in the Six Counties is in a very
deplorable state, and my right hon. Friend
the Minister of Agriculture in a very good
speech which he made at Banbridge on April
25 used words which conclusively prove that
agriculture in the Six Counties is in a very
serious condition. He said;

"No country could be prosperous unless
the farming community was also prosperous. Agriculture was the greatest industry
in the Six Counties but it had not been
sufficiently supported in the past, and unfortunately in the last few years farmers
had suffered shocking bad times."
I consider that this is sufficient evidence for
us when the right hon. Gentleman with all
the knowledge which must be at his disposal
speaks these serious words. The House well
knows that during the war prices were very
high, and farmers could obtain enormous
But,
prices for the produce they raised.
suddenly, towards the end of the war, there
came a great slump in prices and the farmers
lost very heavily, and I may say that taking
it generally they lost even more than they
made during the years of the war. Such
money as the farmers did make during the
war was-and I think this is very humandissipated in new buildings, in pedigree stock
and so forth. Of course, it is human nature
to think that because splendid conditions
are prevalent at the moment they are likely
to continue. I am sorry to say the farmers
in the Six Counties for the greater part did
not conserve the money they made during the
war, but spent it in improvements and in
other ways. I may mention just to show the
House the fall in prices that hay, for instance, could be sold during the war at £15
a ton, and now its value is £3 to £4; a cow
was worth £60, and now you can get a cow
for £18; a good horse fetched from £100 to
£120, and now you can get a first-class horse
for £30. It is the same all through, and last
of all come potatoes which you could get £10
a ton for and now it is hard enough to get
10s a ton in certain areas in the Northern
Counties. On top of this farmers have enormous burdens to bear. For instance, they
have heavy rates and heavy taxes, they have
rent, repairs and wages to meet, and are
burdened in many other directions. To give
one instance, in the paper this morning I see
the case of a scutcher who was prosecuted
because his insurance card had not been
taken out. The general practice of scutchers
is to work for a farmer on a one-year's contract, to work in agricultural labour for nine
months and in the scutching mill for three
months. The House can see that little irritations like those bear very hard upon the
aimer; in fact, it is not too much to sav
that the majority of farmers throughout the
Six Counties at the present time are faced
with insolvency. If this case is good, and if
my right hon. Friend told the truth at
Banbridge, which I have no doubt he did,
when he said that agriculture was in a deplorable condition, how much more so are the
scheduled areas in County Down?
They
have been labouring under the most drastic
estrictions, and rightly so. I may say that
potatoes in the black scab area are most
carefully inspected in every possible way and
most strict Regulations are laid down to see
that this disease does not spread out of the
small area in which it is prevalent at the
present time. Some time after this disease
broke out the Ministry of Agriculture discovered immune varieties, and these immune
varieties, you may say, saved the industry in
County Down. It was very hard to get seed,
and the seed of the immune varieties was
very expensive and also it was very limited
in quantity. The reduction of the area in
County Down to a quarter of the average
acreage before the war is, for those who know,
a very serious state of affairs, because the
farming community in my part of the world,
in the Ards peninsula, is entirely dependent
on the potato crop. There is, practically
speaking, no other source of revenue to the
farmer there than potatoes. Last year the
farmer was at last able to procure enough
seed potatoes to sow his normal acreage,-
and this class of seed was called Lochar.
Unfortunately he was faced this year with a
large crop of Lochars and no market in
which to get rid of them. I should like to
read to the House a short letter from a big
potato importer at Cardiff. He writes:
"I regret to report trade here growing
worse daily. English dealers are running
round this district selling truck loads at
any price they are offered for them. I
cannot see that there can be any improvement. We have enough potatoes in the
various stores here to carry us on for a
month. We are only moving about 50 per
cent. of our normal output. We should
have moved more County Down potatoes
had they been good; shopkeepers will not
buy them at any price, they turn colour
when boiled, and 'chippers' will not buy
them because they are round shaped. Personally, I think it would be a good thing
for farmers and the trade if they decide to
grow only half the acreage next season.
Scotland are begging us to take cargoes
on commission. There is an Irish cargo
on passage now not sold, and no merchant here will take it-stores full up
and very slow demand. To get back your
trade farmers must grow kidney-shaped
potatoes of good quality and scrap
Lochars."
That is what a big importer tells us from
Cardiff-" scrap Lochars." That is the position in the scheduled areas in County Down.
They have got a large quantity of Lochar
seed, but according to this man-and I think
it is correct-farmers in the scheduled areas
should clear out of Lochars altogether and
should plant some other variety which will
obtain a better market. But they cannot buy
another variety because they have not got the
money to do it. They did not make money
during the war, and they have not got any-

The farmers in County Down, like the
farmers in the rest of the Six Counties, do
not want a dole unless it is absolutely

water. But farmers in the scheduled areas
are in such a desperate condition that they
ask the Minister of Finance to give them a

Mr. ARCHDALE: I am very glad to hear

scheduling the area, but I have been nearly

Mr. POLLOCK: I am very sorry, indeed,
that this matter is under discussion at this
late hour, with such a poor attendance of
hon. Members, because I do not think there is
anything of greater importance to the Province of Ulster at the moment than the condition of agriculture. For some time past it
has been brought under my notice in my
position as Minister of Finance, and I have
been, in conjunction with some of my advisers
and the Government generally, discussing how
relief could be afforded to an industry, which,
after all, is the premier and greatest industry
in the country. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
It is not a question as to whether County.
Down or County Tyrone is suffering more or
lesss at the present moment. The trouble is
universal. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) The
question that concerns us is how we can relieve it. It means money. To carry out in
Northern Ireland the intention of the British
Government in Great Britain in respect of
the relief of agriculture would require, approximately, by way of relief to local rates, I
estimate, possibly £150,000, and the conditions in Northern Ireland are so dissimilar to
those in Great Britain that I have grave
doubts as to whether that relief would be of
sufficient importance to individual farmers as
to warrant the outlay. It must be remembered
that we have in our Province in round figures
120,000 farmers, and of those 80,000 farm
under fifty acres, and a large number under
twenty acres. If you take the rating under
twenty acres and contribute by way of relief
one-half of the rates, as is contemplated by
the British Government, you will realise that
the small individual farmer would only get a
few shillings, and, after all, that would be no
sufficient relief for him under the deplorable
conditions in which he finds himself. Therefore, it would have to be a matter for serious
consideration as to whether relief of that
kind should be adopted, or whether we should
adopt some system of discrimination, that
is to say to endeavour to discover those who
are in real need of assistance and relief as
distinguished from the better class farmers,
the larger farmers, who are not in such
straits.
The difficulty, as I apprehend it, with most
small farmers at the present time, as has
been indicated by my hon, and gallant Friend
(Captain Mulholland), is that they are unable
to purchase the materials for their farms.
The seed time, unfortunately, is gone, or
practically gone, and, therefore, it is too late
now to afford any relief in the way of providing seeds for their crops. But they have
liabilities to the merchants who have supplied
them in the past, and the merchants who
supplied them in the past have objections
to continuing their accounts, because they
have accumulated, and the farmers are not
able to reduce them. As to how relief is
to be accomplished, as I say, I cannot tell
standing here at this moment, but my right
hon. Friend (Mr. Archdale), who has this
thing very near to his heart and very much
on his mind at the present time, is engaged
in an endeavour to discover how relief can
be given.
There is another matter, namely the
position of farmers, and there are many of
them, who could borrow from their banks
the small amounts necessary for the purpose
of securing supplies, but who have to pay
the ordinary large overdraft rates, and my
right hon. Friend (Mr. Archdale) has it in
contemplation, I think, to recommend that
the Government may guarantee the banks
such interest as would be in accordance with
their ordinary scale, and at the same time
reduce their rate of interest to the farmers.
Some schemes of this kind are under consideration, and I do not think my right hon.
Friend (Mr. Archdale) will object if I have
entered into some details in order that the
House may realise that the Government are
not unappreciative of the condition of affairs
at the present time.
One other point and I have finished.
The British Government have adopted
certain measures in regard to the relief of
agriculture. We in the North of Ireland
contend that, existing under similar condi
tions, as we do here, we are entitled to adopt
analogous measures in Northern Ireland, and
to claim that whatever the cost may be it
shall be a proper deduction from our contribution. That is to say in other words that
the Imperial Government should contribute
to the relief of Northern Ireland agriculture
on exactly the same scale as to the relief
which is being granted to British agriculture.
We are endeavouring now, before the very
important Committee, which, as is well known,
is sitting, to assert the principle that we in
Northern Ireland, being British subjects and
part of the United Kingdom, are not entitled
to exist under lower social conditions than
It is on
those existing in Great Britain.
that principle, therefore, that we are arguing
for this particular matter which I am discussing now, that it should be a question of
Imperial liability, and, therefore, deductable
from our Imperial contribution. That is as
far as I can explain, speaking extemporaneously, the position the Government has
taken up in this important matter.

UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT.
1. Mr. MARK asked the Minister of
Labour whether persons in the whole-time
employment of bona-fide farmers, but who
may be engaged for a portion of their time
daily in the work of distributing milk direct
from the farm, are exempted from the provisions of the Unemployment Insurance Act?
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): Persons in the whole-time
employment of bona-fide farmers and engaged
on farm work are not insurable under the
Unemployment Insurance Acts, notwithstanding that they may be engaged for a portion
of their time daily in the work of distributing milk direct from the farm.
2. Mr. MARK asked the Minister of
Labour whether agricultural labourers who
may be engaged part time during the season
in the work of attending threshing mills or
baling machinery are exempted from the provisions of the Unemployment Insurance Act?
Mr. ANDREWS: Agricultural labourers
engaged whether whole or part time during
the season in the work of attending threshing machines or baling machinery carried
out on and for the purposes of a farm are not
insurable under the Unemployment Insurance
Acts.
3. Mr. MARK asked the Minister of Labour
whether agricultural labourers who may be
engaged as flax scutchers for only a few
months each season are exempted from the
provisions of the Unemployment Insurance
Act?
Mr. ANDREWS: I have received certain
representations that employment in flax
scutching should not be regarded as insurable under the Unemployment Insurance
Acts, and inquiries on the subject are proceeding. If I am satisfied that there is a
general desire on the part of both employers
and employees for the exclusion of this industry from insurance under the Unemployment Insurance Acts I shall be prepared to
consider the issue of a special Order excluding flax scutching on the ground of its being
an occupation ordinarily adopted as subsidiary employment and not as a principal
means of livelihood.
Mr. MARK: Arising out of that last answer
might I ask the Minister of Labour if he
will consider the question of granting a re.
fund to those men who have paid insurance
in the event of issuing the Order he suggests
in his answer?

Mr. MARK; Is it the practice that when
a man is scutching flax for three months of
the year and is a farm labourer for nine
months he is liable to unemployment insurance for the nine months?
Mr. ANDREWS: No. The position is
really this, that a man who is in an insured
occupation pays contribution when in that
occupation. As regards these flax scutchers,
the position is, that on the average they are
employed at flax scutching for about three
months of the year, and then they are entitled when they become unemployed to draw
benefit to the extent of the contributions
which they have paid on the 1s 6d rule, but
they are not entitled to draw uncovenanted
benefit in the way that the whole-time insured person would do.

Mr. McGUFFIN: I feel some timidity in
rising to speak upon this matter, in view of

at the moment, with whom I may be found to

in this age, as in Shakespeare's age, that boys
creep unwillingly to school, and I suppose the
pace of the snail would be as the speed of an
aeroplane compared with the rate the modern
child would be inclined to go to school. My
difficulty is limiting the age in this matter.
I see that by a by-law of the education
authority the age may be reduced from six
to five. I would like to ask if that makes for
the physical development of a child. A
healthy generation is even more important
than an educated one, and what you would
require to do in this case would be to see if
you are not doing serious injury to
health of infant children by compelling them
to attend school not only regularly but at
such an early stage. Infant children have
frequently little ailments which they must
endure but often cannot explain. Many
medical men are not brought into contact
with them, and it is a point that may be
taken into consideration. But there is a
more important point still, and it is this.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Mr. McGuffin]
Perhaps the members of this Committee, and
even the medical profession, have not taken
into consideration the limitation which these
children suffer in respect to sleep. It is
quite a common thing to see these little infant children romping about the streets, or
being compelled to wander about the streets
up to eleven and twelve o'clock at night.
They go to bed and are wakened again
carly in the morning, because the parents
are going to work. They snatch a hasty
breakfast, and then go off to school, and I
wonder if under the circumstances it is good
for the health of the child. I am inclined
to believe it is not, and if there is one thing
more than another that is essential for the
progress of a child at school, it is that its
nervous system should be normal, and that
it should not in any sense be afflicted with
enervation. But I am afraid the children
will suffer in this respect. We know what it
is in the case of adults. We know that
adults, boys at school, and young men at the
University do not always feel equal to the
task before them, and the progress they make
very much depends on the degree of their
health. Therefore, I suggest that it might be
in the interests of the children if at least this
clause could limit the age to six years, and
not give discretionary power to the Education Authority to reduce it to five years.
I remember that the Labour Party in the
Imperial Parliament very strongly favoured
reducing the age to five, but we all know
what was undelying that. It was that the
children should be school-fed, and there was
a great deal to be said in favour of that. But
I do not think that is the object the Ministry
here have in mind. It is rather that the education of the child might be begun at the early
age of five years. Dr. Garrett, Chief Inspector, a very distinguished authority, was speaking upon this question, and he said that progress in education very largely depended upon
the interest that could be taken in it. I would
go further and say that the interest taken
very largely depends upon health. I would
urge that something should be done in this
matter to see that these children get all the
opportunities that are necessary for their educational development. Nothing is more important to the child at school than the cultivation of its memory, and I defy any medical
gentleman to say that the child's memory is
in any sense in a normal condition when the
child is enervated or when it is suffering from
nervous prostration. It has been asserted,
and not yet disproved, that the delay of a
year or two is in the end compensated for
in the improved facility in a child's power
of acquisition, and I believe that that is so.
There was a very large volume of opinion
in the Imperial House in favour of extending
the age, and I am one of those who think
that that is the proper thing to do under
the circumstances. I do not know whether
I may appeal to the noble Marquess on this
point, but I would seriously commend the suggestion to his consideration, and urge him to
at least limit the age to six years, and not
under any circumstances to make it possible
for a local authority to reduce it to five
years. A compulsory measure is necessary,
and I believe is admirable in its way, but
in respect to infant children it must be very
judiciously exercised. That is practically all
I have got to say in the matter. It is a
question that I have frequently turned over
in my mind. It has not occurred to me for
the first time on this Bill. I have been frequently reflecting upon it, and I could not
have allowed this Clause to go through
without offering these observations upon it.
I hope my suggestion will commend itself
to the noble Marquess.

Mr. JOHNSTONE: That is an extremely
difficult question to answer, but as a matter

ciple. The Minister of Education
speech on the Second Reading, invited any of

tion Office to see the map which

I said it would be very hard to elect a committee when you had two rural districts, an

district. That was a calculation made by me

the regional committees in my part of the
country seem to cover districts in which the

that there is no hard and fast rule. The one
that I have in my mind is for a population
of about 35,000. From the principal town,

opinion, it would be ridiculous to ask that

were not at school.
The idea I have had from the first, and the
idea that is in the amendment, is that our
school attendance committees should be continued as they are, and that they should form
committees under the regional committees.
It was pointed out to me by the noble
Marquess, on the Second Reading, that this
was provided for in the Fourth Schedale to
the Bill, in paragraph 12, which states:
Subject to the provisions of this Act, a
regional education committee may draw up

may from time to time appoint sub-committees consisting in whole or in part of
members of the committee for the exercise
of any of their powers, but no ub-con-

When I read that paragraph over carefully it struck me it was rather for the
appointment of Committees for a special
purpose, not for a Committee like a School
Attendance Committee, which must have a
certain amount of permanence in order that
it may carry on its work, because you want
to know what has been going on, and what
is the history of each of the children. You
want a permanent Committee and not a
Committee set up for a few weeks or months
to take charge of a special subject. Besides
that, I think School Attendance Committees
ought to keep to the work they are doing.
As far as I know, in those places in which
they do work they are about the right size,
and the areas are about as large as one man
can reasonably cover. In the district which
I have most experience of we have 27 schools,
and we find from month to month they are
quite as many as one man can look after.
The difference between what the Goverment suggest and my amendment is simply
that they ask the Regional Committee to do
this work of school attendance. I do not
see how they could possibly do it. They
would have to sit regularly, as we sometimes
had a dozen children to come before us.
The School Attendance Committees have not
done all they might have done, because the
Act of Parliament gave them no opportunity
of enforcing it, but if you have a large area
I think it would be impossible to do any
school attendance work at all. The whole
thing would merely be a greater farce than
ever it was. I would, therefore, ask the
Government, even if they do not accept this
amendment to consider the matter and put
something in in their own words that would
ensure that School Attendance Committees
would be carried on under this Bill in the
same way as before, or in the same way
as they have not been carried on, as
I believe there are some places where the
work was not done as it should have been.

CLAUSE 33 (Summary proceedings on disobedience to school attendance order).
A court of summary jurisdiction, if satisfied on complaint made by the education
authority that a school attendance order has
not been complied with in the case of a
child required by or under this Act to
attend school, shall have the following
powers:-
(a) In the first case of non-compliance,
if the parent of the child does not appear,
or appears and fails to satisfy the court
that he has used all reasonable efforts
to enforce compliance with the order, the
court may impose a fine not exceding (including costs) forty shillings; but if the
parent satisfies the court that he has
used all reasonable efforts as aforesaid,
the court may, without inflicting a fine,
order the child to be sent to a certified day
industrial school, or, if it apears to the
court that there is no such school suitable
for the child, then to a certified industrial
school.

CLAUSE 35 (Duty of Head Teachers to
furnish Certificates of School Attendance).
When a child who is required by or under
this Act to attend school is removed from
any school recognised by the Ministry as
providing efficient education, it shall be
the duty of the head teacher of the school
to issue to the parent of the child a certificate showing the period during which the
child was in attendance at the school, the
number of attendances made during that
period, and the class in the school in which
the child was placed for the purposes of
instruction at the time of the removal.
The certificate shall be exhibited by the
parent upon any application for the admission of the child to any other school
recognised as aforesaid, and shall also be
taken into consideration by an education
authority upon any application for the exemption of the child from the obligation
to attend school.
