Intoxicating Liquor Bill-
First Reading.
11 MAY 1923
INTOXICATING LIQUOR BILL.
Prime Minister's Statement.
Motion made and Question proposed,
"That leave be given to introduce a Bill to
make provision for the closing on Sunday
and Christmas Day of premises licensed for
the sale of intoxicating liquor by retail, the
abolition of certain off licences, and the settlement of claims for compensation arising
thereout; to impose restrictions on the sale
of methylated spirits; to extend the law with
respect to illicit distillation of spirits; and to
amend the law relating to the sale and
supply of intoxicating liquor by retail; and
for purposes connected therewith."
The PRIME MINISTER: Mr. Speaker,
when I had occasion to issue as leader, my
first manifesto to the electors of Northern
Ireland, I drafted that document with exceptional care, having particular regard to the
general conditions then prevailing and to
optimistic hopes for the future. The fourth
paragraph reads:-
"The first Parliament"-
that is, our first Parliament-
"will be faced with problems gravely affecting the future. The best way to extend
our resources, expand trade, stabilise agriculture and other industries, re-model
education, amend the licensing laws, and
to ensure a brighter future for the great
masses of workers in our midst."
When Parliament assembled on the 23rd
June, 1921, the King's Speech, for which this
Government was responsible, included the
following paragraph :-
:-
"The people, whom you represent, understand the impossibility of introducing
legislation until these Departments"-
referring to Government Departments-
"are in full working order. They understand equally well that, when this has been
accomplished, an earnest endeavour will be
made to develop still further the resources
of Northern Ireland, expand trade, improve agriculture and other industries, remodel education, amend the licensing
laws, etc."
Can it be said then that this Government
is breaking or travelling beyond any of its
pledges in endeavouring either to improve
our educational system or to amend the law
relating to intoxicating liquor, or that
before making any pronouncement on the
subject I awaited the result of that critical
general election? Emphatically no! I wish
to get that out of the way in order that hon.
Members in all parts of the House may understand that this question was referred to
by me before and immediately after the
general election.
I recollect very vividly in my early political career introducing a measure in the
Imperial House of Commons, to improve the
system of our Poor Law; like this occasion
it was on a Friday afternoon, and although
it was impossible to get it through as a
private Bill, I am hopeful that it may yet
prove the foundation of a Government measure to deal with a phase of our domestic
system urgently requiring reorganisation.
However, at the moment we are engaged on
two other ameliorative Bills of primary importance; time alone will reveal whether our
wisdom in these as in other matters is of as
high an order as our genuine aspirations.
Before I touch on the contents of the Bill
immediately before the House, may I say
that if it is given a First reading to-day,
which carries with it the necessary authority for printing and circulation, I will
arrange that a copy be dispatched to hon.
Members to-morrow and supplied to the
Press in time for it to appear in Monday
morning's papers, and will aim at taking
the Second Reading on the 18th of this
month, as I have just announced in answer
to a question by my hon. Friend (Mr.
Crawford).
In tackling the problem of the amendment
of the licensing laws, I have been especially
struck with the dimensions of the task. In
England the law relating to licensing was
codified in a Consolidation Act in 1910, but
here in Northern Ireland we have been
under the necessity of going back over a long
series of Statutes dating from as far back
as the reign of George II.
In the forefront of the reforms to which
I think the great majority of the people
of Ulster look forward must be placed Sunday
Closing. We in Ulster have been brought
up to regard the Sunday as a day of rest,
and I am sure the House will agree with
the clause which we place first in our temperance measure to provide for the total
closing of public-houses on Sunday.
In this connection we consider it would b
unfair to penalise residents of hotels in the
sweeping alteration we are making, by for.
bidding them to have, in what are for the
time being, their homes, intoxicating liquor
if they so desire. In dealing with this particular question we have naturally had to
consider very carefully the practicability of
allowing such bora-fide residents to have in.
toxicating liquors, and at the same
time to enable the police and excise
authorities to exercise control over the
supply of intoxicating liquor on such
premises. Accordingly the present measure
provides that intoxicating liquor may be supplied to anyone having a substantial meal on
Intoxicating Liquor Bill-
First Reading.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[The Prime Minister]
Sundays in the dining room of an hotel, no
distinction made between genuine residents
on the premises and visitors. All drinking
bars in hotels, however, will be kept closedthe same as public-houses-throughout
Sunday.
We propose to abolish entirely the special
concessions now enjoyed by bona fide travellers. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear). As
hon. Members are aware the loophole left
in the existing Acts in regard to the supply
of liquor to bona fide travellers has given
rise to very great abuse, and I think it will
be generally agreed that the case for a revision of the law in this respect is strong.
Then we come to the question of the spirit
grocers. This class of trader has come in for
a large measure of criticism; and undoubtedly
abuses, mainly in relation to secret drinking,
have crept in in the conduct of these mixed
businesses. This, of course, does not mean
that all spirit groceries are badly conducted,
but unfortunately the abuses which have
grown up around this class of trader have
become so flagrant as to lead to a widespread
movement for the total abolition of spirit
grocers' licenses. This we propose to effect
in the present measure by abolishing at the
end of the current licensing year, which expires on the 30th September next, all off
licenses in respect of premises on which any
other class of business is carried on. The
effect will be that the mixed business we are
wont to associate with the grocer and the
chemist will entirely disappear,-(hon. Members: Hear, hear)-though we shall still have
certain traders' licences for the sale of intoxicating liquor for consumption off the
premises. We have purposely provided that
this separation of off license businesses is to
come into effect not immediately on the passing of this Act, but by a date five months
ahead. The intervening months will enable
off-license holders to get rid of stock, or so
to re-arrange their premises as to comply
with the provisions of the Bill.
In withdrawing from spirit grocers a lucrative class of business we have been faced
with the much-debated question as to whether
any compensation is legally payable. I do
not propose to detain hon. Members at this
stage by discussing the pros and cons of the
legal case for and against compensation.
Without prejudice to this question the
Cabinet are unanimously of the opinion
that no citizen of Ulster should be seriously
penalised through the legislation we are now
introducing withdrawing the right to carry
on the sale of intoxicating liquor as an adjunct to a grocery business. We have, therefore, in the Bill provided that spirit grocers
who come within the scope of the abolition
clause shall receive compensation up to the
aggregate amount of their profits from the
trade in intoxicating liquor for the past
three years as well as compensation for
fittings and utensils which may be rendered
obsolete by the withdrawal of the licence.
Similarly, we have provided that persons
interested in the premises shall be compensated in respect of the reduction in the
annual value of the premises due to the
withdrawal of the licence.
For the purpose of dealing with claims for
compensation we propose to set up a tribunal
to consist of the Recorder or County Court
Judge, a person nominated by the Minister
of Finance, two persons nominated by the
Minister of Home Affairs, one of whom is
to be a Resident Magistrate and a Justice
chosen by the Justices for the petty sessions
district where the premises in respect of
which the claim is made are situate. The
actual compensation fund we propose shall
be raised by a general levy upon the remaining licensed houses-(hon. Members: Hear,
hear) which levy we propose to spread over
a period of approximately 20 years, thereby
making the annual payment due by any
license-holder a comparatively small amount.
I may mention that at practically no stage
in the scale does the licence duty and proposed
compensation charge in Northern Ireland
amount to as much as the licence duty and
compensation charge payable in respect of
premises of a corresponding value in England.
In
The next feature of the measure to which
I would like to refer is the provision of more
stringent regulations for the sale and supply
of methylated spirits. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) I do not think it is necessary
for me to dwell upon the evils of this traffic,
for it is well known and only too true that
the drinking of methylated spirits has become a veritable curse among certain sections
of the poorer classes in our province.
endeavouring to cope with this evil I am
glad to say the Cabinet has had the hearty
co-operation and support of representatives
of the trade as well as of temperance bodies.
Both have given my colleagues and myself the utmost assistance in this regard.
The main alteration in the existing law we
propose to make here is to treat all retail
sales of methylated spirits in the same
as sales of poisons are regulated,
namely, no retailer can sell to any person
unless he knows the purchaser or the purchaser is introduced by some person known
to the seller. In addition, it will be
necessary for the purchaser to sign a book
wherein he will state the purpose for which
he requires the methylated spirits. The
Bill also provides for licences for the sale of
methylated spirits being brought under
magisterial control.
manner
The next question we have tackled is that
of the traffic in illicitly distilled spirits.
841 Intoxicating Liquor Bill-
11 MAY 1923

First Reading.
commonly know as "poteen." Here again
representatives of the licensed trade as well
as temperance bodies have come forward with
valuable suggestions. The extent to which
this evil has grown in our province may be
gauged by the fact that responsible members
of the licensed trade allege that it is no
exaggeration to say that 50 per cent. of the
spirits consumed in Northern Ireland to-day
are illicitly distilled—a very large proportion.
The existing penalties are totally inadequate--(hon. Members: Hear, hear) and we
accordingly, while increasing heavily the
pecuniary penalties, at the same time propose to give magistrates power to
inflict a term of imprisonment as
well. (Hon. Members. Hear, hear). Where
the person convicted is the holder of a license
for the sale of intoxicating liquor his penalty
may be increased by immediate forfeiture of
the license. We also propose to
grant
further powers to the police authorities in
regard to searching for illictly-distilled
spirits or materials and utensils used for the
making of such spirits.
We now come to a most vital alteration
in the existing law, which, from my conferences and discussions. I have grounds for
believing will be regarded with favour by
all sections of the community. I refer to the
composition of the Court which deals with
licensing applications or licensing offences.
(Hon. Members. Hear, hear). Allegations
of abuses-and I may say that these allegations of abuse reached us equally from
both sides in connection with the "packing"
of Licensing Courts have been freely made
and the problem of how to provide an
Independent Court which could be regarded
with confidence by all sections and classes has
given me and those associated with me in the
preparation of this measure cause for much
grave thought. But here again our labours
have been considerably lightened by the deputations representing trade interests and
those representing temperance societies, who
each have favoured the hearing of all licensing cases before a resident magistrate.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) This is in
complete accord with our own view, consequently we have so
determined and have
also made the power of appeal to the Recorder or County Court Judge. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.)
In the case of applications for the granting or renewal of licenses, we have given to
the police the same powers of appeal as are
now enjoyed by the applicants. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Hon. Members who watched the progress
of Lady Astor's Bill relating to the sale of
intoxicating liquor to young persons, will remember how that measure passed its Second
reading with a very large majority in the
Imperial House of Commons. For a private
Member's measure, the result was certainly
worthy of special note, and upon us, on
whom rests the responsibility of guarding
the training years of the young men and
women of to-morrow, falls the duty of carefully considering in what way we can best
amend the laws relating to the sale of intoxicating liquor to young people, and we
think that it can be best done by adjusting
enumerated
principles
in what is
popularly known Lady Astor's Bill.
Already we have on the Statute Book an
enactment-the Intoxicating Liquors (Sale
to Children) Act of 1901, which imposes
penalties upon any licensee who knowingly
sells or delivers intoxicating liquor to anyone under the age of fourteen, and after
careful deliberation We
have decided to
amend this Statute by substituting eighteen
years for fourteen. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) This means that no liquor can be
sold on licensed premises to anyone under
the age of 18. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
the
as
Another provision of the Bill deals with
the structural arrangements of fully licensed
premises. The same arguments which
apply in the case of the spirit
grocer have been adduced even more strongly
in the case of composite business carried on
in fully licensed premises. In the measure
which we will shortly consider, we have provided that where any business other than the
sale of intoxicating liquor is carried on in
the premises, the part of the premises devoted
to the sale of intoxicating liquor shall be
structurally separated from, and have no
internal communication with, the remainder
of the building. (Hon. Members. Hear,
hear). A special exception has been made of
course in the case of hotels and restaurants.
To forestall criticism on this particular
portion of the Bill, I may point out that
under the existing law, the presence of other
business on the licensed premises could
reasonably be regarded as a good ground
on which to object to the grant or renewal
of a license. Our proposal, therefore, simply
has the effect of strengthening the existing
law by making it a regulation that there
should be no other business carried on on
the premises where intoxicating liquor is
sold. As, however, it would be unfair to
introduce such a change without adequate
notice we propose that this provision shall
not come into effect until 1st October, 1924,
and propose that a public notification of the
alteration in the law shall be made.
In addition to those main provisions of the
Bill, we have included a number of what I
may describe as minor amendments of exist-
Intoxicating Liquor Bill—
First Reading.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[The Prime Minister]
ing legislation relating to licensing. Licensing Courts will have power to require plans
of licensed premises to be deposited with
them, and in particular upon objection being
made may require a licensed holder to remove
or replace by glass certain portion of screens
and partitions in drinking bars which make
proper supervision of the premises impossible.
Numerous complaints have been made in
regard to the existence of these enclosures
commonly known as "snugs" in public-houses.
It is not proposed that the section dealing
with this particular point shall become
operative until 1st October, 1924, so that
everybody may have proper notice to make
the structural alterations that may be insisted
upon by the Licensing Court. More stringent
provisions have been provided for the endorsement, and in some cases the forfeiture
of licenses (Hon. Members. Hear, hear)
while the laws relating to the conduct of
registered clubs have been considerably
strengthened.
Those are roughly the principal headings
of the Bill, which, as I have promised hon.
Members before, may be distributed to them
to-morrow. I hope also that the Bill will be
in print and in the Press on Monday morning. In asking the House to give the Bill
a First reading, I wish to explain that an
earnest attempt is being made, not alone to
fulfil the promise I gave regarding specific
proposals, but to deal with several other
outstanding matters of a less controversial
character with a view to closing the acrimonious controversy that has been raging
for some time past both on the platform and
in the Press.
I gratefully acknowledge the courtesy and
assistance extended to my colleagues and
myself by the influential representatives of
the trade and of temperance organisations
whom we met in conference. Both sides
were so helpful and so moderate in dealing
with the thorny question, that I am amazed
that they do not call regular meetings
amongst themselves, and not only call
regular meetings, but arrange half-yearly or
yearly meetings as a regular scheme amongst
themselves to thresh out and discuss their
differences and difficulties with a view to
attempting to reach conclusions which
would enable whatever Government was in
power to legislate without arousing acrimony
and controversy for the best interests of the
community as a whole.
I hope, however, that unless by some such
general agreement, no further legislation on
a scale of any importance will be necessary
in my time, and that temperance reformers
will bear in mind when preaching total prohibition or local option, that alternative
taxation to that now wholly borne by the
trade, or else a very heavy increase of local
rates, is the hard fact to be faced if their
hopes are to be realised. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.)
Moreover, and perhaps this brings it home
to one more realistically, as we in Northern
Ireland under the 1920 Act, if I may call the
Act of 1920 our charter, cannot increase the
Income Tax, the combined burden of loss of
revenue and of compensation on the people
as a whole (and compensation is made
obligatory by the British Government under
section 5 of the Act of 1920) would be
greatly felt through the necessary increase
of duty on tea, sugar, mineral waters, or
other necessaries of life, or alternatively by
an
enormous increase, as I have said, on
local rates. I put this immediately and
seriously before all Members of the House
that in future when they make great demand
and preach earnestly in favour of either of
these systems of total prohibition or local
option, they should at the same time inform
their audiences exactly what these schemes
mean financially and not allow the people
to be carried away and then disappointed
because they have been found to be outside
the realm of possibility. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear).
Mr. McGUFFIN: Might I ask the right hon
Gentleman would he take into consideration
the fact that there are certain assets to be
set against the prospective losses from revenue he talks about in that case?
The PRIME MINISTER: If my hon.
Friend will be ingenious enough to lay before
this House and the country what assets would
amount to anything like what the trade pays
at the present time towards the revenue of
Northern Ireland and of Great Britain, I am
sure we will all be very delighted to consider
the matter. (Hon. Members Hear, hear).
This Bill goes as far as we think fair and
proper without exacting any direct contribution from either the taxpayer or the ratepayer, but modest measure as it is viewed
from some standpoints, even it brings up the
cost of publicans' licenses approximately to
the English level, and we calculate will take
contributions for some 20 years to compensate the spirit grocers, besides imposing a
permanent loss to the Treasury of Northern
Ireland which may amount to some £8,000
a year. I instance that to show that even a
measure of this sort entails that amount at
all events of indirect burden upon our taxpayers.
I hope the trade throughout Northern
Ireland will organise for itself some effective
system of self-supervision with a view to
assisting the Government in future in carrying out the law, and will not countenance as
Intoxicating Liquor Bill-
First Reading.
11 MAY 1923
a body of traders or any of its members
attempting to circumvent or to evade the
law, which conduct inevitably leads to a
further strong demand by the people for
further penalising and restricting legislation.
On this occasion my colleagues and I
desire to reiterate the words of the Governor
when addressing us through the King's
Speech at the opening of Parliament: "I
earnestly trust that the discussion on these
two primary measures will be conducted
with a spirit of helpfulness, toleration and
goodwill, to the end that there may be
placed upon the Statute Book Acts conferring
lasting benefits upon the people as a whole."
I beg to move. (Hon. Members: Hear
hear.)
Mr. CRAWFORD: If ever there was an
occasion since the opening of this Parliament
when words of a congratulatory nature could
be extended, I think this is the occasion.
(Hon. Members. Hear, hear.) But I see that
some people have a great objection to anything in the nature of compliments either to
the Prime Minister or to Members of the
Cabinet, and I refrain from offending people
of that description at the present time. But I
would respectfully try to extend my congratulations to the people of Northern Ireland as
a whole upon this marvellous fact that this
little infant of self-Government that was given
to us two years ago, brought into existence
in very stormy times when even its friends
-and they were many-were sometimes afraid
to prophesy great success, and its enemies,
and they were numerous, prophesied sudden
failure-nevertheless before it has reached its
second birthday it has not only laid the manyheaded fiend of violence flat and established
law and order within its borders, but made
these two magnificent attempts to uplift the
people by introducing the Education Bill and
the reform of the licensing laws. (Hon.
Members. Hear, hear).
There is no question in the wide world but
that the Government have correctly and
wisely diagnosed the feelings of the people
of Northern Ireland. Behind them there
stands both for the Education Bill and for
the reform of the licensing laws an immense host of the very best people in the
country. Even the most degraded, if there
are any such in Northern Ireland, and those
who are addicted to habits of strong drink-
I believe there are strivings, yearnings and
longings in their hearts and a reaching out
for better things-eagerly appreciate the
efforts of the Government in this respect and
in respect of the Education Bill.
An eminent American has recently written
the following:-
All movements for human welfare can
be interpreted in terms of desired release
from pinching handicaps into a fulfilment of
a state of better things. To lift the economic burdens that depress life and spoil
opportunity, to liberate the people from the
slavery of their diseases and habits and to
set men free by education from stupidityall these endeavours to give persons a chance
to be their best selves are crusades for
human emancipation and happiness."
I say that no sane person at this time of
day would doubt the fact that education and
temperance reform are among the foremost
of Life's Liberators, as far as this portion of
the country is concerned. It has been said,
and I think wrongly said-that temperance
reformers are a set of bigoted and ignorant
people. I, as one who has taken a great
interest in temperance reform for over thirty
years, can give absolute denial to any such
allegation. We are amongst the most
moderate people in the Province.
We are
determined to uphold law and order. We are
asking that a chance may be given to people
to lead better lives and that temptation may
be taken out of their way. We recognise
that there are two sides to every question.
We are prepared to consider the case of
those that differ from us. We are prepared
to consider their case reasonably.
There has been a great deal of talk quite
recently against temperance reformers. It
is said we have been out for prohibition.
That is not the issue. I do not hide the
fact that I do hope before I am called from
this sphere to see the time when local option
will be placed before the people. The people
should have an opportunity of saying whether
they want public-houses or not. But I am
prepared to keep the bargain made with the
Prime Minister. We treat these matters
fairly and squarely. We will at least give him
for this Parliament leisure from our attacks.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) The Prime
Minister ventured to express the hope that it
would not be in his time that we would have to
touch this matter again. I would not agree
with that, because I hope the Prime
Minister will be in the same place again-
(hon. Members: hear, hear)-and that he will
deal with this matter. I promise that at all
events some attempt will be made in time to
come to extend the benefits of the measure. I
Intoxicating Liquor Bill- HOUSE OF COMMONS.
First Reading.
[Mr. Crawford.]
think he has struck three big blows undoubtedly at the liquor traffic. Doing away
with the spirit grocer and the bona-fide
traveller, and introducing Sunday closing
are three blows at the liquor traffic.
There is an incident relative to one
of the Kings of Israel that occurs to me,
and I think the Prime Minister is very
much in the same position with regard to
this traffic. The King was pressed by his
enemies, and he went to see the dying Prophet. The Prophet told him to shoot an
arrow. And he shot. Then he told him to
strike an arrow on the ground, and the
King smote three times and stopped. Then
the Prophet said: "Thou shouldst have
smitten five or six or seven times, then
shouldst thou have destroyed thine enemy,
but now thou shalt smite them only three
times" (Hon. Members: Hear, hear). I am
inclined to think that advice of that description would be exceedingly useful to the
Prime Minister.
I do not know that I have very much to
say in the way of finding fault with this Bill.
This question of compensation has given me
great searchings of heart. I think 20 years
is a long time. If compensation is given it
should be levied on the publicans remaining
and they should pay it not in 20 years, but in
three years. (Hon. Members. Hear, hear).
If compensation is levied I trust it will be
three years, and that it will be based on the
income tax returns? (Hon. Members. Hear,
hear). They should take this into consideration in this Act, that any of those people
brought before the magistrates and convicted
should receive less consideration than the
people who have kept the law in times past.
It would not be good that those people should
get great profit from this Act at the expense
of the State.
I was sorry to hear the Prime Minister
stress this revenue question so much. I know
pounds, shillings and pence are serious things.
(Hon. Members. Hear, hear). But while I
think that, I think there are some higher
things than money in this world. I think
the statement is often made if anyone refers
to anything in the nature of God's word or
the teaching of Jesus Christ that they are
canting hypocrites. But I think we might ask
the ancient question asked by One who spake
as never man spake. That question is:
"What shall it profit a man if he gain the
whole world and lose his own soul?" I
think I could paraphrase that and say: What
shall it profit Northern Ireland if it gain
great revenue and lose its soul?
I was reading recently Mr. Punch's History
of the Great War. One of the pictures in
it struck me very forcibly and very irresistibly. That picture was a representation
of the German Emperor with a great black
cloak around him. He stood before the magnificent-looking King Albert, and said to
him: "You have lost everything." "No," said
the Belgian King, "I have kept my soul."
That was a magnificent statement for him to
make. He had lost nearly everything, but he
had kept the best and highest thing. It
would be well for us in Northern Ireland to
remember that there are better things than
money. If we can only be established in
Northern Ireland by a revenue that is causing
harm it is a bad day and a black day for us.
I sincerely hove that the prosperity of this
Province will be such that it will not be
necessary to us.
Some
There were one or two things I was greatly
pleased to hear the Prime Minister saying.
One was where he proved that those who
said that there is no pledge on the Government are totally wrong. He has proved
himself to be what I thought he was a man
of his word. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
He has proved it successfully. He has
brought in Sunday closing, excluding hotels.
He says that any man going into a hotel and
getting a substantial meal on Sunday will
have the right to get intoxicating drink. I
am afraid there is a loophole there.
people will be content with a biscuit. I
think if they are going to exclude hotels it
must only be for those who sleep on the premises. It is a pity that when the poor man
cannot get a glass of porter, the rich man,
who is able to pay 2s 6d or 5s for his dinner
in a hotel, can get as much as he likes. I
think the Government should treat the rich
and poor alike. He has abolished the bonafide traveller, but he leaves it open to any
person to go a few miles out of town or even
in the town itself, and go to a hotel, order
a meal, and he will be able to get drink. I
believe the Government will raise the ire of
a great many mothers and bring sorrow on
a great many children if they continue that
in the Bill.
I will not say anything very definite with
regard to the compensation question. I will
consider the thing very carefully. Before I
can approve of compensation based on these
lines I will require to see the Bill and see
exactly what its terms are. At all events, I
do not think I will ever consent, so far as
my
vote is concerned, to it being spread
over twenty years. There is such a thing as
saving money at the expense of freedom.
I am thoroughly in sympathy with with-

I think can be said by the Prime Minister
too strong about the sale of methylated spirit.
I know of my own knowledge several people
who have been ruined body and soul by
drinking methylated spirit. It seems to be a
great deal worse in its effects than the ordinary whisky. It lowers their moral sense. I
wish to see the sale of methylated spirit
abolished. It should be labelled poison, and
bone oil or croton oil or some other thing
of that sort be put into it. If they do that
they will have the support not only of the
temperance people but of the trade also.
Nothing too strong can be said against
poteen. Nothing strong enough has been said
against it. I think any publican found with
it on his premises should have his license
cancelled at once and he should be liable to a
fine of at least £500 and six months' imprisonment. The very strongest measures we
can possibly take should be adopted in order
to abolish the making or selling of poteen. I.
quite agree with the suggestion that there
should be structural alterations in the houses.
There should be no connection between the
place where intoxicating liquors are sold and
the place where other things are sold. It
is not fair competition with the people
who have not got a license. I know a case
where people have a grocery business and
have a license attached to it, and it is very
unfair to people who have only a grocery
business, because the people with the license
are able to attract customers from the other
place. It is only right that no other trade
should be carried on in the place where intoxicating liquor is sold, and the houses in
which it is sold should have a valuation of
at least £25 in the city, £20 in
provincial town, and £14 in country
districts. It is not right that
with small houses should have opportunities of bringing people into the premises.

I do not know that I can say anything regarding the suggestion that the temperance
party and the publicans should meet together.
It might be a case of the Kilkenny cats
and there might not be much left of either

for is that the rising generation shall have
a better chance of doing right and to make
it more difficult for them to do wrong, and
in saying that I speak not only for myself,

will encourage the people who are interested

his most beautiful flights of imagination, has
told us how that famous Knight of his creation, Sir Launcelot, after undergoing many
trials and tribulations, and encountering
many set-backs finally came across a castle
which he had great difficulty in entering.
He thought he would never be able to
achieve success on his journey, when he
heard far above him,
lark in the

by that, he climbed what seemed to be endless
stairs to a room in the topmost tower of the

he saw the red rose-like rays of the Holy light.
Temperance reformers will take this Bill as
a great encouragement, and although they
may have to work for years and years to
get better things, they are encouraged by
what the Prime Minister and the Cabinet
has done, and I congratulate them very
heartily on doing it.

On the question of the sale to children, I
do not believe there is a man or a woman,
either directly or indirectly connected with
the trade, who will not at least welcome the
step that has been taken to make the sale to
those under eighteen years of age absolutely
illegal. I am delighted to see that, and I
am also delighted to see that steps are being.
taken to prevent the sale of methylated
spirits. I quite agree with what has been
said if I may respectfully say so, by both
the speakers before me, that the publican who
is found with poteen must lose his licence
without any question. There should be no
other penalty except imprisonment. And any
man who makes poteen, or sells it, or has
anything to do with it, should be dealt with
in the same way.
There is another question.
I hope my right hon. Friend the Prime
Minister will see that provision is made in
the Bill in reference to adulteration. A man
or a woman who has a license who, when I
or anybody else go into his or her place for
a drop of whisky-a big drop if possiblegives something that might have been whisky
before it met with an accident, should also be
dealt with, and when you are making orders
regarding glass windows in order to see from
one "snug" into another you should provide

Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: I do not rise
to make anything in the nature of a Second
reading speech. This Bill has been introduced
here to-day, and I understand that the usual
course followed on the First reading of a
Bill is merely in a cursory manner to deal
with the various matters that should be
raised in connection with it. Before carrying
out that intention, let me say with what
pleasure and with what unqualified delight
I listened to the very able, the very effective,
and the very sympathetic speech made by
the right hon. Gentleman (the Prime
Minister). He gave us a rough outline of
the main provisions of the Bill, and I think
most of us can to a large extent fill in what
will eventually be the details. I desire to
say, having on former occasions criticised the
Prime Minister and his Government for not
having dealt with this question, that he and
his Government have carried out to the fullest
possible extent the pledges they gave in connection with licensing reform. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) They have not only

If a
man who has a license to carry on a trade
cannot conduct the trade within the terms
and conditions of that license, he should not
have it. As far as the right hon. Gentleman
goes in the direction of increasing the
penalties for breaches of the licensing laws,
I am absolutely with him. But is it to be
suggested that just in the same way as a
doctor, in making up a prescription, puts in .
something to colour the medicine or to give
it a sweeter taste, the temperance advocates
should be allowed to adopt a similar course
in formulating their demands? In their first
manifesto, drawn up with exceptional care,
they said, "amend the licensing law," and
then they come here and want to take valuable property away from a certain class of
people that is not amendment; it is confiscation. The people have never been asked
to say a word in regard to that. But the
spirit grocers are to be compensated on the
rate of their earnings for three years, and if
my hon. Friend gets his way the compensation is to be based on their income-tax returns. Would he accept that basis in his own
case? The levy for compensation is to be
spread over twenty years, and the Member
for Antrim also objects to that.
I am reminded of the time when I used to
try to learn something about the land lawalthough I do not know that I was very successful. There used to be great talk at that

the man who cannot be a spirit grocer unless

You can start in nearly any other business,

character. I have got a letter from the Ulster

this morning. I am not going to read it all,
but I would like to quote a little extract from
it.
On the eve of the introduction of the
Licensing Bill this Association appeal to you
that in discussing and voting upon its
clauses you should keep ever before you the
consideration: "what is this going to mean
to the women and children?"
Then listen to this:
The thousands of silent and suffering
women.
Are there a
thousand silent women?
(Laughter.) The ladies who sign this, Hilda
S. Richardson and Emily Moffatt Clow, ask

Are they to be forgotten? Do they mean

we are being complimented on restoring law
and order to secure the maintenance of the
law? I am glad to recognise, and this I do
welcome, that the law is to be so changed that
breaches of the Licensing Acts generally are
to be brought before resident magistrates.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) It will be a
delight to everybody who is concerned in the
case except the man who is charged. You
will have confidence in going into court, and
the man who is charged will have confidence
that he will get a fair "do." They say the
Benches are packed. My hon. Friend (Mr.
Crawford) admitted that he was asked to go
to court, but did not. It must almost have
broken his heart to stay at home. I am glad,
and I congratulate the right hon. Gentleman
on this, that we will have clean courts and
that justice will be done. The magistrates
were not bigoted or ignorant, out they knew
whom to vote against, no matter what the
evidence was. It was terrible in the old
days. I am glad there is going to be an end
of that.
On the question of the sale to children, I
do not believe there is a man or a woman,
either directly or indirectly connected with
the trade, who will not at least welcome the
step that has been taken to make the sale to
those under eighteen years of age absolutely
illegal. I am delighted to see that, and I
am also delighted to see that steps are being
taken to prevent the sale of methylated
spirits. I quite agree with what has been
said, if I may respectfully say so, by both
the speakers before me, that the publican who
is found with poteen must lose his licence
without any question. There should be no
other penalty except imprisonment. And any
man who makes poteen, or sells it, or has
anything to do with it, should be dealt with
in the same way. There is another question.
I hope my right hon. Friend the Prime
Minister will see that provision is made in
the Bill in reference to adulteration. A man
or a woman who has a license who, when I
or anybody else go into his or her place for
a drop of whisky-a big drop if possiblegives something that might have been whisky
before it met with an accident, should also be
dealt with, and when you are making orders
regarding glass windows in order to see from
one "snug "into another you should provide
1 for somebody to go round and examine the
contents of the bottles that are there. I think
you will find that reputable traders as well as
my hon. Friends on the other side, and particularly that minority of the population who,
like myself, take a drink if they want it, will
be sincerely obliged to this Northern Parliament if they see that the stuff we order is the
stuff we get. My hon. Friend (Mr. Crawford)
has said it is not right to compliment any
body, but while, as I have said, there was no
intimation at any time that there would be no
confiscation of any licenses, I do say that
I welcome the Bill. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) I say that in spite of the fact that at
a meeting under the presidency of my hon.
Friend, who is neither bigoted nor ignorant,
I have been represented in my own constituency as being a fit subject for the nethermost
regions, the bottomless pit. To one of my
temperament and inclinations that country is
too dry. But, seriously, I claim to be
as sincere a temperance reformer as any
reasonable man. I have no madnesses that I
know of. I only want to be fair, and if the
House thinks it will be for the general good
that those who have had spirit licences should
have them withdrawn I agree. I only want
this, that the spirit grocers are fairly dealt
with. With reference to the trader having a
seven-days license, if you are going to take
one day from his trading-I am not dealing
with the moral aspect, I am dealing with it
as a business proposition--I only want him to
get some compensation for that. It is only
fair that he should. Then I could join wholeheartedly and, as I hope, helpfully with the
right hon. Gentleman the Prime Minister
in seeing that this Bill will not only get a
First reading but a final and satisfactory
reading.
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: I do not rise
to make anything in the nature of a Second
reading speech. This Bill has been introduced
here to-day, and I understand that the usual
course followed on the First reading of a
Bill is merely in a cursory manner to deal
with the various matters that should be
raised in connection with it. Before carrying
out that intention, let me say with what
pleasure and with what unqualified delight
I listened to the very able, the very effective,
and the very sympathetic speech made by
the right hon. Gentleman (the Prime
Minister). He gave us a rough outline of
the main provisions of the Bill, and I think
most of us can to a large extent fill in what
will eventually be the details. I desire to
say, having on former occasions criticised the
Prime Minister and his Government for not
having dealt with this question, that he and
his Government have carried out to the fullest
possible extent the pledges they gave in connection with licensing reform. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) They have not only

Mr. LYNN: I find myself somewhat handicapped because I came here to-day to speak
as the man in the street and not as one who
spoke either for the temperance interests or
for the liquor trade. But I find those who
spoke for the temperance interests and those
who spoke for the liquor trade embracing
one another, and as they seem to have no
objections whatever to this Bill it is very
difficult for the man in the street to find
any point that he can have a shot at. I
agree thoroughly with the Prime Minister
that in introducing this Bill he is in no way
exceeding the pledges that he gave prior to
the General Election. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) As I listened to his speech and to the
subsequent debate, I asked myself what all
the pother has been about for the last two
or three months? Surely no one- and certainly no one in the trade-will argue for a
moment that there has not been need for the
reform of the licensing laws. It is a longstanding need, and the Prime Minister has
not introduced this reform a day too soon.
I know the view of the temperance people
for many years. I have been trying to find
out the view of the trade in regard to this
matter, and, if I have been able to diagnose
their opinion correctly, I think the one complaint they will have to make against the
Prime Minister is that he has not gone far
enough.
After all, what is the object we have in
view? Surely it is to abolish drunkenness.
Is there anyone either in the trade or
calling himself a temperance reformer who
is in favour of drunkenness? I have never
met one in the trade yet who has શ
word to say in favour of drunkenness,
and I am sure the trade are just as
anxious as my friend the Member for Antrim
that drunkenness should be wiped out. What
we have got to ask ourselves is what is the
best possible way to promote sobriety? I do
not say that it is always possible to make
people sober by Acts of Parliament, but they
are helpful and they can do something. I was
glad to hear my friend who speaks for the
advanced wing of the Temperance party
saying that he was not out for prohibition.
He may believe, as many other good people
believe, that prohibition would be good for
the country, but there are a great many
others who do not share his views, and,
therefore, he has shown his wisdom in not
forcing that view on the House or on the
public at the present time.
As I listened to the Prime Minister's speech
I thought-if I may say so without indulging
in flattery for which I may be criticised elsewhere it was a wise and statesmanlike
speech. Take the spirit grocers. Is there
any great necessity for those spirit grocers.
After all, they are a modern development.
I think it was Mr. Gladstone who in the
'seventies introduced the spirit grocers.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY TO
THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS (Mr.
Megaw): They were introduced in 1791.
Mr. LYNN: Oh, they date back further
than I thought. At any rate as far as this
country is concerned, spirit grocers are
rather a modern innovation. I do not know

whether I gathered it correctly or notmeans that all off-licences are to be abolished.

Mr. LYNN: I only wanted the right hon.
Gentleman to clear up the point. I have
no doubt the Cabinet in carefully considering
this question were afraid, in view of all the
noise that had been created outside by the
two opposing armies, that they ought not to
go beyond the distance they have gone. I
think everyone who is in favour of temperance reform-and there are people engaged
in the trade who are in favour of it just
as well as those who are in the temperance
ranks--would have welcomed provisions in
this Bill for getting rid of redundant publichouses. I was glad that my hon. Friend the
Member for Antrim raised the point, because
I think there are a whole lot of public-houses,
especially in cities like Belfast, that are
absolutely unnecessary, that are badly conducted, that are conducted under conditions
that do not make for temperance, but on the
other hand make for intemperance, and I
think it would have been an advantage if
the Government had made provision in this
Bill for dealing with such houses. There are
houses that are badly conducted, houses that
are in no way suited for the work, and I
think they ought to be got rid of. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) I am strongly in
favour, as my two hon. Friends are, of
Sunday closing, but there is just one point
-I want to be practical in this thing-I
want to bring to the notice of the Government, and that is, can they make their
Sunday closing effective? While I object to
seeing any houses, whether licensed houses
or others, open on Sunday, I do not want
to see our young people driven to shebeens
and to other illicit places to get drink under
the most deplorable conditions.
I hope in connection with this Sunday closing that the Government will take such
stringent measures to deal with those who
break the law that they will make it absolutely impossible, or nearly impossible, for them
to do so. The Prime Minister said nothing
with regard to the hours at which licensed
houses are to be opened. I know how difficult
it is to deal with a big question like this in
the course of one speech. Might I suggest to
him that, now that the temperance people and
the trade seem to be really inclined to woo
each other, the conference which he proposed
some months ago, but which did not come
off, might come off with advantage, and that
they might consider such questions as the
hours at which the houses are to be open?
The hours are unduly long at the present time
---(hon. Members: Hear, hear) and I believe
that at a round table conference, with reasonable people like the hon. Member for Antrim
(Mr. Crawford) and the hon. Member for
Derry (Sir Robert Anderson) meeting the
trade, you would get such a scheme as would
be a help to the whole community.
I think a most valuable provision in the
Bill is that of having the licensed premises
absolutely separate from the dwelling-houses.
That is a proposal that will meet with universal approval, not only from the temperance
people but from every decent publican, and
I am glad that point has been met.
I am
glad also to hear of the provision with regard
to the licensing laws being administered by
resident magistrates. The existing method of
administration of these laws has become one
of the most horrible scandals, and it is time
it was abolished. I do not think any man on
any side will have the slightest objection to
that.
Another point to which I would direct the
attention of the Prime Minister is that of the
penalties. I think he should make the penalties so severe that it would be impossible for
a man to break the law, or at any rate that
he would find it unprofitable. At the present
time the fines are so light that it pays a man
to break the law, and he breaks it with impunity. If the Government in this Bill
would make a provision so that a publican
who breaks the law would find himself de:
prived of his licence, either permanently or
for a time. I think it would have a salutary
effect.
There are other reforms to which the Prime
Minister might usefully direct his attention,
such as dealing with public houses where they
give more than is ordered, or where they give
credit. That ought to be made absolutely
illegal, for I think it conduces more to
drunkenness than anything else. With regard
to poteen, of course, we shall have to wait
until we see the Bill itself, but I think the
Prime Minister cannot make the penalties for
making, selling, and distributing poteen too
severe. He will have the whole-hearted support of the country in regard to that.
With regard to methylated spirits, again I
will have to wait until I see the Bill, but this
is an increasing and a very dangerous evil that
will have to be put down with a firm hand,
and the sooner the Government take it on the

Mr. DONALD: My object in rising this
afternoon is not to criticise what has been
said by the Prime Minister in introducing
this temperance legislation. Like other hon.
Members I prefer to wait until I get a copy
of the Bill. My object is to congratulate
the Prime Minister on his opening remarks.
Before coming to the House to-day I thought
I would look up some old papers containing
criticisms of the Government and what has
taken place throughout the country for several months past. The Prime Minister read
a clause from his election address, which I
hold in my hand. It is headed:
"To the Loyalist electors of Northern
Ireland,"
and for the benefit of the House I will
repeat what the Prime Minister read out.
"The first Parliament will be faced with
problems gravely affecting the future. The
best way to establish our credit, resuscitate trade, stabilise agriculture and other
industries, re-model education, amend the
licensing laws . . ."
Our Government are steadily but surely
carrying out that programme. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) I say that the criticism
outside to the effect that no pledge was given
is absolutely untrue There it is in writing,
issued to every elector in Northern Ireland
previous to any of us coming to this House.
As I said, my object in rising this afternoon
is to congratulate the Prime Minister. Why?
Because I have some little experience of
Ministers in the Imperial House, and I say
here and now that one thing above all others
that will give confidence to the people of
Northern Ireland is the knowledge that they
have a Cabinet and a Prime Minister composed of men of backbone and determination.
We who had the privilege of being in another
House know that much of the trouble of this
country was due to the fact that the men who
took the reins of office in another place were
not men of the firmness and stability of the
men whom we are now thankful to have at
the head of our country.
Having said that there is another aspect of
this question to which I want to refer, and
which I have often thought should at least

Now that our Parliament has been in existence for two years, I am going to quote a
few words from a speech which the Prime

This Bill is only carrying out what the Prime
Minister had in his mind. I say "Carry on,
Sir." I welcome this Bill.
I have never been an extreme man either on
this question or any question, but it struck me
when the Prime Minister referred to the hotels
that I am one of those who will not support
any measure whereby the working man will
be deprived of any privilege that is given to
another because he belongs to a particular
class. I have been talking to several people
who understand this question, and very
strong representations have been made to me
by working men, and I am going to speak
now on their behalf, and not from my own
point of view at all. The public houses are
closed in Glasgow on Sundays, and I am informed by the heads of the police there that
on a Saturday night all the closes and entries
are practically full up with broken bottles.
What is the object? The object is that what
they cannot drink right up till the last minute
on the Saturday night they carry home.
This is a matter which should engage
the attention of the Government in
drafting this Bill, because I feel that
that is what is going to happen here,
at least until our people get accustomed
to this thing. The case that has been put up
to me by men who can take a drink and let
it alone is that the working man should not
be deprived of a drink on a Sunday if he
wants one. What they are afraid of is that
they will carry it home in large quantities on
a Saturday night, and will drink it on Sundays in the presence of their wives and
families, which would be far worse than
going out on a Sunday to have a drink if
they could get one. That is the view that has
been put to me. I leave the responsibility to
the Government. I am only expressing the
views of a very large number of working men,
who would not allow you to call them drunkards or anything of that description.
I was just reading the other day a speech by
one of the greatest statesmen of our country-
I refer to the late William Ewart Gladstone.
In 1880 he made a speech, in the course of
which he referred to the liquor laws. In his
opinion, he said:
there were
three principles involved
which ought to guide the consideration of
this difficult question. The first was that
a serious effort ought to be made, and some
steps taken to abate this terrible mischief.
The second was that these efforts should
be made just as the remarkable efforts that
were successfully made to close the publichouses of Ireland on Sunday
I could not find the time to look up when

what the public thought on both sides on
this question, and I quietly attended but
took no part in meetings held by both the
temperance people and the liquor people. I
found that for every one person against this
Bill there were twenty who wanted the Bill.
Therefore, this is a question that this Government has got to consider-the question of
public opinion. It must be considered if this
Government is going to represent the people.
With these few remarks I take this oppor-

tunity of thanking the Prime Minister for

Mr. LAVERY: At this late hour of the
evening I do not intend to keep the House
very long, indeed only a few minutes.
should like to say at the outset how very
pleased I am with the Bill brought forward
by the Prime Minister. We of the temperance party have waited long and patiently
for a Bill of this kind. Sir Wilfrid Lawson
tried to bring forward Bills of this kind,
but he was not able. It remained for the
Prime Minister (Sir James Craig) to do so.
He is certainly to be congratulated on having
brought forward a Bill which, to my mind,
should please not only the Temperance party
but the anti-temperance party. I am very
glad he has raised the age of young children,
or proposes to do so, from sixteen to eighteen
years. That is very commendable. There is
one other matter I would like to point out.
With regard to those little huts, or, as they
are commonly called, snugs, I have been
spoken to by people who have the interest
of the youth of our country at heart, and
they say there is no greater means of spreading intemperance than having these snugs
in public-houses. I do sincerely trust, from
what I have heard about them both as to
drinking and other vile business that takes
place therein, that something will be done
to eradicate them entirely out of licensed
houses. There is a matter I am not at one
with my temperance friends on either. There
is a difference of opinion on it. I am one
of those who believe-and I have a strong
feeling on the matter-there should be no
attempt to take the licence from these grocers
without compensation, but the compensation
should be moderate and fair. We should not
spread it over too long a period. Instead of
twenty years I would like to see the whole
thing cleared up inside five years. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.)
I am very glad indeed also that licences
for the future will, in accordance with this
Bill, be in the hands of the resident magistrate. I have been present myself in court
when, I must admit, we could not find seats
for the magistrates attending. I am very
glad to know that we are not going to have
that perpetuated in connection with this Bill.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) I am also
pleased that when policemen bring forward
cases and they happen to be dismissed they
will have the right to appeal. I have often
thought that was a serious blunder in legislation in the past with regard to the temperance movement. I would like to impress upon
the Prime Minister the necessity of at least
considering, if it is at all possible, the question of bringing the clubs within the four
corners of the Bill. I do not see why they
should not be brought in the same as other
licensed premises. It is not fair by any means
that the poorer classes should be prevented
from getting their porter or their beer while
those who are better off can go into their
clubs and obtain it. I am afraid that that
will not give any satisfaction. On the whole,
however, the Bill to my mind is such that we
have every right to congratulate ourselves,
and I am very glad indeed, if we may judge
from the speech delivered by the hon. Member for Antrim (Mr. Crawford), that the antitemperance party are at one with him. I
must say with regard to the suggestion of the
Prime Minister for a round table conference,
that I have not much faith in it. The Bill,
as a matter of fact, is more than the Temperance party expected, and I certainly do congratulate the Prime Minister.
Mr. COOPER: I do not wish to occupy the
time of the House, but coming, as I do, from
the County of Fermanagh, I could not let
this opportunity pass without congratulating
the Prime Minister on bringing in this Bill.
We in Fermanagh and Tyrone resented very
much the appearance a short time ago of the
leader of the liquor traffic who came into our
constituency with a deliberate purpose-to
split the vote in that constituency. (Hon.
Members. Hear, hear). I may tell him that
he never did anything in his life which did
his own cause so much harm. (Hon. Members.
Hear, hear). Most of the people who were
moderate on this question deeply resented his
intrusion, and I would like to tell him in
this House that he gained a host of enemies
towards his trade. I would only just like
to say one or two things about the Bill. One
thing is about "guests." In my part of the
country when a publican is summoned for
having people in his house on Sunday he
always comes into court and says these people
were his guests. They may be schoolmasters,
policemen, and all sorts of people from all
parts of the country, but no matter who they
are or where they came from they were people
the publican knew well, he invited them in
just for a drink and no money passed. On
every possible occasion he will come and swear
it, and everyone of the witnesses that
he produces will swear it. I would ask the
Prime Minister to see inserted in this Bill
something that will prevent the publican
from having guests in his house at all on
Sunday.
There is just one other point, and that is
the question of new licences. Under the Act
as it exists wherever a house was licensed
in the year 1901 the publican can get a new
licence for that house to-day. I know in my
own town several houses which had licences
in the year 1901, and which have ceased to

INTOXICATING LIQUOR BILL.
"To make provision for the closing on Sunday and Christmas Day of premises licensed
for the sale of intoxicating liquor by retail,
the abolition of certain off licences, and the
settlement of claims for compensation arising
thereout; to impose restrictions on the sale
of methylated spirits; to extend the law
with respect to illicit distillation of spirits;
and to amend the law relating to the sale
and supply of intoxicating liquor by retail;
and for purposes connected therewith."
Presented accordingly, and read the First
time; to be read the Second time upon Friday
next, and to be printed.
ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Local Government (Franchise) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed, "That
the Bill be now read a Second time."
Mr. MEGAW: The Bill of which I move
the Second Reading is one that was brought
in with the object of remedying grievances
and abuses connected with Local Government
Franchise. There has arisen through certain
phraseology of Acts of Parliament a scientific
system of creating votes which has proved
most expensive and troublesome to those who
are connected with registration matters. The
result is that a very large number of irresponsible people who pay no rates still have
an effective voice in the disposal of the rates.
I wish, in the first place, to disclaim a desire
in any way to affect the vote of any man who
has any substantial interest in the country.
Every householder and his wife will still, if
this Bill passes into law, be entitled to the
Local Government Vote; that is, they will be
so entitled absolutely regardless of the valuation of the house they hold.
The Local Government Franchise itself is
rather a confused system of law. The qualification of a Local Government elector is intertwined very closely with the Parliamentary, inasmuch as, apart from the universal
franchise, the women's franchise is entirely
based on it. In Local Government there are
two main qualifications for a man. First of
all, the ownership and occupancy of a dwell.
ing-house. This Bill does not propose in any
way to interfere with that. The second is
ownership and occupancy of land and premises
that are not a dwelling-house. So far as
women's Local Government franchise is concerned, a woman is entitled to the Local
Government franchise if she is 30 years of age
and the wife of a man who is so entitled. It
is with the second qualification that this Bill
deals.
Under the law as it stands at present the
Owner or occupier of land or premises,
whether rated or not, and no matter how
infinitesimal his interest may be, is entitled to the Local Government vote, and that
whether he has a vote in another Local
Government district or not. This has led
to some very curious anomalies and abuses,
and has given great scope to the ingenuity
of election agents. In fact, votes have been
manufactured wholesale.
In one county in our Six County area more
than half the men, women and children, are
entitled to votes through the care and energy
of those interested in electioneering. There
are 50 votes in one place out of a bog plot
that is not valued at all. These 50 voters all
have votes in their own districts in which
they have houses, but they get additional
votes with respect to these bog plots which
have no value whatsoever. In another case
there is a stable in which there are thirty
stalls. These thirty stalls also give rise to
thirty votes to men who have votes in their
own districts, and I think they also give the
qualification to their wives to vote in respect
of this same stable. Last year there was an
attempt made to have votes created out of
graveyard plots, but I may tell the House
that with the registration officer the question
of occupancy arose, and as these persons
had not yet occupied the graveyard plots, he
could not see his way to give them votes in
respect of them.
This Bill proposes to put an end to that.
While the vote, as I have said, in regard to
the dwelling-house remains, it is proposed in
the case of land premises other than a
dwelling-house that £5 valuation should be
required. This has the incidental advantage
of assimilating Local Government Franchise
with the present Parliamentary Franchise
for women. In the case of women who have
the Parliamentary Franchise, it is necessary
that they should have either a dwellinghouse or land or premises other than a
dwelling-house of £5 valuation. We are well
Franchise Bill-
Adjournment.
11 MAY, 1923.
aware that there is another kind of bogus
vote, the creation also of skilled electioneering agents, arising through an artificial
interpretation of the word dwelling-house itself. We sometimes find that one building
that is valued at £2 or £3 only expands itself into five or six dwelling-houses for the
purpose of the franchise. I regret to say that
we do not feel ourselves able, through the
trammels of the Act under which we carry
on our Government, to deal with that aspect
of the abuse I am referring to at present.
The attempt to do so would infringe on the
Parliamentary Franchise and the Bill carefully avoids coming into contact with that
Parliamentary Franchise in any way. It
simply adopts the value that is necessary to
give women a Parliamentary vote. I do not
think there can be any opposition to the Bill,
which is really in the interests of all parties,
and is very much in the interests of the ratepayers in so far as it secures that the voters
have some tangible stake in the country. I
beg to move.
Mr. COOPER: I wish to give my wholehearted support to this measure. I think
this abuse of the Act probably affects County
Fermanagh, which I represent, more than any
county in Northern Ireland. I would like to
tell you some of the means by which votes
have been obtained.. There was a certain
gentleman who came to me on one occasion
and told me that the only property he had
in the world was beehives, in which he had a
certain number of bees. These hives were on
another man's farm, and I suggested
to him that he should go and take the land
on which the bee-hives stood and then he
would have premises and be qualified according to the Act. This gentleman duly signed
an agreement taking as tenant one square
yard of land on which stood the bee-hives.
He came to me and produced his agreement
showing he was the owner of premises within
the meaning of the Act and he duly got his
Local Government vote. There was another
case where a lot of people attended a chapel
and at the back of this particular chapel
were twenty-five stalls in which the people
put their horses on Sunday. They suddenly
cenceived the brilliant idea of becoming
tenants of these stalls, so they went to the
clergyman and took over the stalls as tenants
from year to year and they all duly got votes
in this electoral division. In a certain fair
where cattle are sold every month the people
took stalls on yearly tenancies and got votes.
Then the people sub-let all the hen-houses
in the country. A farmer had two daughters,
and he sub-let the hen-houses to his daughters
and got two votes for them. Finally, people
tried to get votes for the graves in the
cemeteries.
This Bill is not brought in for the purpose
of doing away with the vote of any person
who is legally entitled to vote. Its only
object is to abolish what are absolute frauds
on the Franchise. I would suggest to the
Minister of Home Affairs that he should reduce the valuation from £5 to £2, because I
do not think any of these places would be
rated at even £2. If he reduced the valuation to £2 he would still leave alone persons
entitled to vote.
Mr. MILLER: I welcome this Bill very
much. It was long overdue, and I was afraid
it was going to be strangled at its birth under
the phrase, "to-morrow." But "to-morrow"
has at last come, and I rejoice exceedingly.
I am sorry the Minister of Home Affairs could
not deal with the case of dwelling-houses in
the Bill, because the dwelling-house franchise
is very nearly as bad as the grave-yard franchise. It reminds me of some evidence
given before a Commission in Glasgow in
which it was stated that in a room about
fourteen feet square there was a family residing in each corner and a family in the
centre. When the witness was asked how
they got on under these circumstances, he said
they got on very smoothly and very nicely
until the people in the centre of the room
began to get uppish and keep lodgers. That
is an illustration of the way things are done
under the present Act. The smallest houses
are divided into compartments and the persons who are supposed to reside in these compartments swear before the Registration
Agent that he or she is the owner of their
own little compartment and they are always
careful to produce the key to the official. I
have had a good many talks with the Minister
on this subject and I cannot lay the
blame for its omission from the Bill
on him. I am afraid the charter he talked
about some time ago prevents him from
carrying out a reform in this direction, but I
hope that later on he will take courage and
produce a Bill that will give everybody what
the Legislature intended they should get, and
that will contain none of these frills. I am
not quite in accord with everything in the
Bill, but I will deal with that in Committee,
where I presume I will be beaten as usual.
Question put and agreed to.

Oral Answers to Questions.
MULLAGHFAD PROTESTANT NATIONAL
SCHOOL.
1. Dr. MORRISON (for Mr. Cooper) asked
the Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry
of Education whether he proposes to close
Mullaghfad (Co. Fermanagh) Protestant
National School, and if he is aware that this
is the only Protestant school in that district,
and that the Protestants of all denominations
are strongly opposed either to closing or
amalgamation?
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY TO
THE MINISTRY OF EDUCATION (Mr.
McKeown): No decision has been reached by
the Ministry in regard to the closing of
Mullaghfad (No. 2) National School, County
Fermanagh, which is a small school under
Protestant management with only fifteen
pupils on the roll. Inquiries are being made
through the inspector as to the practicability
of conveying the pupils by van to one of the
adjoining schools under similar management,
the nearest such school being 43 miles distant
by road.
Before any decision adverse to the continuation of the school is arrived at full
consideration will be given to the representations of all interested local parties.

CLAUSE 50 (Recovery of the Cost of
Meals).
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That Clause 50 stand part of the Bill."
Mr. McGUFFIN: I have not very much
to say with respect to this particular Clause.
It is an important one, but in my opinion
it requires to be very carefully and delicately
administered.
Mr. LYNN: Hear, hear.
Mr. McGUFFIN: I have particular views
with regard to this question, for I think in
many instances the dignity of respectable
families may be seriously infringed. I do
not deny that there are certain children
in the schools who require to be fed,
children who are neglected at home, and
so far as it relates to them the provision
is quite admirable. There are some who
think that, even under any circumstances,
the Clause would not be necessary. We have
instances of where some very weak children
have been very scholarly children too, and
it really is a matter for experts to determine
whether or not under any circumstances it
is necessary to make a provision of this
sort. I heard a very distinguished authority
during a debate in the Imperial House say
that the best scholars who came to the
University were those who in many instances
were the scns of crofters, and had no special
food or dietary to enable them to prosecute
their course.
The dignity of parents must be considered
in this matter. All working-class houses are
not badly administered. There are plenty of
houses where the finances are very careful
looked after, and where the administration of
the houses is carefully conducted, but even
in those cases the Bill will enable the Education Authority to take charge of the child
and to feed him at school and to charge the
expense thereof upon the parents. Now, that
may mean more than their family budget
will afford. It may mean that that child
will get preferential treatment as compared
with any other member of the family. We
know that there is a tendency amongst-I
will not call them degraded, but rather poor
families to take advantage of free meals, and
when public occasion offers we have seen
thousands of children take advantage of those
offers and go in for the free meal. That is
all very good if it is done from a humanitarian standpoint, but the purpose of this
Clause is to feed them in order that they may
I do not think on the whole that the results
that are anticipated from this Clause with
regard to improved education are likely to be
realised. Children may be underfed, but that
seldom interferes with their faculties. If a
child has a certain degree of endowment my
opinion is that it will assert itself even
though he is underfed and we should be
very careful indeed in interfering with the
private administration of a family household
in order to bring about that result. There
are people who would resent that sort of
thing, and I for one, if I were doing my best
to feed the child, would not like outside authority to come and dictate to me what I
should do with respect to my child, or take
it from my custody and do as they think
right and best under the circumstances and
then charge the expense to me. Where it is
necessary the children should be fed. I suppose there is no objection to that, but where
it is necessary that a child should be fed and
when it is done for educational purposes I
do not think that a claim should be made as
far as parents are concerned.
I take up that attitude with respect to this
matter, and I hope that the Minister will
give it consideration. I can hardly hope he
will accede to it, but I trust that in the
enforcement of this Clause he will at least
see that it is done in a merciful way and in
the most delicate way possible so as not to
offend the susceptibilities of the parents
concerned. When we look over the history
of our great men we find that in many instances they were delicate from youth, and
yet it never interfered with their educational
attainments. I could quote many such instances, but will only just refer to one at the
moment-the celebrated poet, Pope. He was
an invalid not from youth but from infancy.
Throughout his life, indeed, he was no other
than an invalid, and yet he accomplished
more than any scholar of his time in the
translation of the immortal Homer. Many
other instances of a similar class, both in the
domain of science and literature, could be
given to show that the success of a child is
not very largely dependent upon how it is
fed but rather upon its endowments.
Mr. LYNN: From my reading of this
Clause I do not think the Ministry in undertaking the feeding of children in Northern
Ireland, want, nor does this House want, to
pauperise any parent, but on the other hand

Mr. McGUFFIN: Quite so.
The MARQUESS OF LONDONDERRY:
But who, in times of unemployment, or times

nor have we thought it right to say what we

obvious to hon. Members that children may

If the hon.
Member (Mr. McGuffin) will take Clauses 49,
50 and 51 together, it seems to me that the
Bill is really contemplating some procedure

Firstly, I will put it, the authority has

Secondly, I would say food is not to be

Hon. Members will understand me when I

cases will be in the best interests of what we

Mr. McGUFFIN: I would like to make

those I am perfectly satisfied. But my

Mr. DONALD: My object in rising is to
say that I welcome these Clauses in the Bill.
If anyone will take the trouble to investigate
this matter in England and Scotland, he
will see for himself how this thing is done,
and I am pleased to see that provision is
made in this Bill for the feeding of the
children. A very large sum of money is
spent in England in this way. I think it
went to £600,000 at one time, but they were
forced to reduce the amount. A child gets
a substantial meal, but it gets more than
