CLAUSE 53 (Duty of Education Authority
in regard to Neglected Children).
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That the Clause stand part of the Bill."
Mr. McGUFFIN: I was looking into that
part of the Clause dealing with the conddition of children described as being filthy
and verminous. I would suggest that under
those circumstances those children should be
segregated from the remainder of the pupils.
We know how easily children are contaminated in that respect, and where that condition is found to prevail I would urge that
those children should be segregated. In
doing so you would make an example of
the parents concerned. I think it is unfair
to the other children that they should be
asked to mingle with children of that class,
because that condition does not arise from
destitution. It arises from sheer criminal
negligence. I think there are one or two
London schools where that course is taken,
and my suggestion is that some similar provision should be made here. I have known
of several occasions when parents complained
about the contamination of their children
through being associated with this particular
class of children. Under the circumstances
I think the noble Marquess should see if
he could not amend the Clause in such a
way as to make provision for dealing with
the condition under discussion.
Dr. MORRISON: From my knowledge of
conditions in rural Ulster. I do not think
that such an extreme course as that suggested by the hon. Member for North Belfast
(Mr. McGuffin) is necessary. How is he to
segregate them? Is he going to put the child
in a corner by itself?
Mr. McGUFFIN: Yes, I would put all
those children in a room by themselves.
Dr MORRISON: I submit that that is impracticable. I do not think that there are
any extensive filthy conditions such as would
necessitate the adoption of that course. I
was brought up in a national school, and
my recollection does not remind me of any
gross offence against taste or cleanliness.
While occasionally, as a medical officer of
health, I have heard complaints from the
National Society for the Prevention of
Cruelty to Children that children have been
neglected, I think the activities of the inspectors of that organisation are quite sufficient
in this matter. I know that if the like
does occur and it is a rare occurrence-the
teacher points out the fact to the child or
to the parent, and does it perhaps reluctantly
lest offence should be caused. I would call
attention to the wording of the Clause,
"When as the result of medical inspection
or otherwise "-" or otherwise." That is,
any person may make a complaint to the
Education Authority if the like of this takes
place, and when the people know that there
is provision for bringing these children
before an authority such as is outlined here,
they will attend to their children, and extreme measures such as segregation will not
be necessary. I do not think that there is
any necessity for making special provision
such as has been suggested.
Mr. MILLER: Shortly after I had the
honour to be asked to take part in the
deliberations of the Lynn Committee I was
talking to a friend of mine in Belfast, and
knowing that I was interested in the matter
he asked me if I would like to attend a
meeting of the Medical Association of Belfast
who were going to consider the question. I
said I would, and I took the trouble to come
all the way from home to attend the lecture.
When I got in, to my surprise I found it
was a paper written by my hon. Friend, the
Member for the University (Dr. Morrison).
We had a very interesting discussion on the
question, but, as some of those who were
sitting near me admitted, it left us with a
very creepy feeling. This question, among
others, came before the members of the
Association, and they gave evidence of
what had happened in England, of the
difficulties that there were in the way
of the teachers reporting the children, and
of the odium that they incurred because they
did so. What I rose to say was this, I came
away from that meeting with this in my
mind, that it was not medical inspection
was wanted so much as a good, strong-minded
nurse.

Mr. LYNN: I should like to raise a discussion generally with regard to the
Ministry's control over Homes for mentally
defective children. Take the Institution for
the Deaf and Dumb in Belfast, probably the
only institution of its kind we have got in
Northern Ireland. That institution derives
most of its income from the philanthropy of
the public, but once an education rate is
struck people will cease contributing to an
institution of that kind, and it may find
itself in a very difficult position. Then there
is the other aspect of the question-that you
may find different Education Authorities not
agreeing to have one school, say, for Northern
Ireland, but each of them wanting to run
their own school. That would be a costly
thing, and I am wondering if the Ministry
would give us some indication as to
whether they will to a large extent take
over control of these institutions.
Take the Institution for the Deaf and
Dumb. I believe that at the present time
it costs something like £60 to £70 a year for
each inmate, and yet the amount being påid
by Boards of Guardians and other people who
send afflicted children there ranges from £20
to £45. An institution like that has a great
deal of trouble in dealing with these local
Boards, and I would like to ask the Ministry
whether they do not consider they shou
take this matter in hand and deal with the
afflicted children in the whole of Northern
Ireland. Probably on this amendment my
hon. Friend (Mr. McKeown) will tell us
whether or not the Ministry will do so.
After all, you are under an obligation to do
something in the way of training these
afflicted children, and surely if there is any
section of the community that appeals to our
sentiment and our best natures it is the unfortunate people who are blind, deaf or dumb.
You are setting apart a sum of money for
educating normal children. Quite right, but
ought you not also to set apart something
for the education of these afflicted children
who are largely in a very helpless state? I do
urge the Ministry to take this whole question
into their very sympathetic consideration, and
see if they cannot do something to have this
one central place where you have had the
work carried on for nearly a century by
people who understand it. I do think the
Ministry ought to look into the question
very sympathetically between now and the
Report stage.
Mr. LLOYD CAMPBELL: I desire to
support what the hon. Member for West

leave them as at present under the Bill.
There may be two or three of these children
in each education area, and they will get no
proper accommodation, whereas if they were
sent to a central institution they might derive some benefit from their training.
the cost was collected by the Ministry from

Dr. MORRISON: The average case of a defective child that you come across is due to
sickness or some visible defect. There is the
case where a child may be absolutely insane.
I remember seeing a child of three years of
age, seemingly a bright, intelligent child,
that was absolutely incapable of doing anything for itself, that would have gone to a
burning fire and taken out a coal. No person could tell by looking at it, that it was
in any way defective, it was bright seemingly
in every respect. There was no provision
made for such a case, the Poor Law provided
no substitute, and we had to bring the child
before the magistrates and swear an information that it was a dangerous lunatic and
have it committed to an asylum. There is in
Dublin an institute for the treatment of these
children. Occasionally cases like this
happen, and provision should be made for
them. I am in entire sympathy with the
remarks made regarding the Deaf and Dumb
Institution and the Blind Institution. There
is a fine opportunity to co-ordinate all these
things, and also to make provision, which
I think is necessary for the Catholic portion
of the population. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear). I think it meets with the approval of
all hon. Members, that we should all do what
we can for the helpless under the Ministry
of Education.
Mr. McGUFFIN: I would like to add one
word in support of the matter raised by the

The institution concerned is a very old one
founded on a strictly voluntary basis and
carried on for a great number of years very
successfully. Its administration has never

and I think it affords an excellent opportunity to the Ministry to concentrate its

Mr. McKEOWN: In the recommendations

It is within the recollection of hon. Members that apprehensions have been expressed
as to what steps could be taken under the
Bill if an education authority were to act in
a manner prejudicial to the interests of persons or schools. Clause 96 of the Bill enables

it is still possible that no remedy has been

ance of its duties, and performing ther

vening the underlying principles of the

Clause 1.-(Amendment of Law as to Local
Government Franchises, 7 & 8 Geo. 5, c. 64).
The Representation of the People Act,
1918, shall have effect, for the purposes of
the local government franchises, as though
"(a) is on the last day of the qualifying
period occupying in that area, as owner
or tenant, any land or premises (not being
a dwelling-house) of a yearly value of not
less than five pounds, or a dwellinghouse; and
(b) has during the whole of the qualifying period so occupied, either in that area
or, if that area is not an administrative
county or a county borough, in any administrative county or county borough in
which the area is wholly or partly situate, any land or premises (not being a
dwelling-house) of such yearly value as
aforesaid, or a dwelling-house."
Mr. MILLER: I beg to move, in Clause 1,
page 1, to leave out paragraphs (a) and (b)
and to insert instead thereof:
"(a) is in that area, on the last day of
the qualifying period, owner or tenant, and
in occupation of a dwelling-house, or of
land or premises (not being a dwellinghouse), of a yearly value of not less than
£5; and
(b) has, during the whole of the qualifying period (unless he derives by descent, devise, bequest, succession or promotion to an
office) so occupied any such land, premises
or dwelling-house in that area, or if that
area is not an administrative County or
a County Borough, in any administrative
County or County Borough in which the
area is wholly or partially situate."
This amendment is taken word for word
from the amendment that I brought forward,
on what I call competent authority, to the
Act passed in June of last year. As to paragraph A there is not very much difference
between my amendment and the paragraph
that appears in the Bill. In one respect,
however, there is a great difference. The
Clause as it appears in the Bill repeats an
old phrase that has been used, I suppose, for
over fifty years, or perhaps more, that a
That
man should occupy as tenant or owner.
gave us great bother in County Tyrone, where
perhaps legislation is carried to an nicety,
and at last we had to take it to the Court of
Appeal. The ordinary layman reading that
would say that if a man occupies land or
premises he is tenant or owner, but the
Court of Appeal held that the words "as tenant or owner" meant not being tenant or
owner, but as if he were tenant or owner.
A trespasser who went into the house when
the owner was away would be treated as
tenant or owner and get a vote. It was for
that reason, and owing to the great bother we

had in working these things, that we decided
it would be much better to say that a man
"is in that area, on the last day of the qualifying period, owner or tenant, and in
occupation of a dwelling-house.' The Act
puts first the qualification of land or premises. What we want is that every man who
has a dwelling-house, whether it be a cottage
or a castle, should have a vote, and also his
wife should have a vote. Then there
what I call the frills-little bits of outside
property-being done away with under the
words " any land or premises."
are
I picked up the first register I met the
other day, and I find there are 371 voters on
it. With the exception of eleven, these come
under the category of dwelling-house, which
in the Bill before us comes in as a sort of
afterthought. You see at the end "land or
premises, or a dwelling-house." There were
thus 360 registered for dwelling-houses and
only 11 for land or premises. The principal
thing I want to draw attention to is the
words as tenant or owner." Paragraph (b)
is to me very important. The only difference
I have made practically in that is the words
in brackets:

"unless he derives by descent, devise, bequest, succession, or promotion to an
office."
It will be within the recollection of this
Committee that prior to the Act of 1898 the
Local Government register was a very small
thing. No man under £4 valuation had then
a vote, and no man under £4 valuation paid
rates. The Act of 1898, as I understand it,
provided that the onus of paying the rates
should be upon the occupier, and not on the
owner. That is, that every householder, no
matter how small, should be entitled to pay
rates, and, in addition to that, they gave
every householder a vote. The Act of 1918
extended that, and gave every man's wife a
vote as well. But that does not touch the
point. The point is that the franchise was
put on, as it were, the household. What happens at present is this: The 15th January
begins the qualifying period. Α man
dies on the 16th January.
Naturally
he loses his vote, and his wife also
loses hers when it
comes up at the
next revision. The son and his wife come
up at that revision, and they are put off the
register because, instead of having the six
months' qualification required under the Act,
they are one day short. Therefore, they go
off the register. That means that that householder is disfranchised from the 15th January
up to the revision sessions. Nothing more
happens until you come to the next revision
sessions. The son and his wife then get on,
but they do not get their votes until the new
Act comes into operation on the 1st January,
or it may be the 15th December. Simply because the nominee died the household is practically disfranchised for a period within a
fortnight of two years. When the franchise
was put on the household, as it were, I do
not see any reason why there should be such
a hiatus of two years.
These words I have used in the brackets in
the amendment are taken from one of the old
Acts, I think the Act of 1857, when the rated
occupier franchise was in existence. The rated
occupier in those days had to be in occupation for
he
twelve months, unless
got
by descent or bequest. The qualifying period
was the 15th July, and if a man's father
died, his son immediately got in. If he was
one day in occupation, before the 15th July,
before the succeeding revision sessions, he
got the vote. The amendment is simply
following out that old procedure where land
got the vote and not the person. The last
part is also taken from that old Act, but
leaves out one item-"or in succession to an
office or benefice." Benefice is done away
with in Ireland since the Disestablishment.
Take the case of a Methodist minister who
is changed every three years. He is changed
about the 1st July. He is in residence up to
the 1st July. When it comes to the 15th
July, he is not in residence, and when the
revision sessions come he loses his vote, because he has gone away, and his successor
cannot get on for a year after, so that a
Methodist minister can only get a vote once
in every three years. Is there any reason
why the office should not get that vote? The
same would apply to bank managers, or
station masters, or persons like that. Why
should these men be disfranchised simply be
cause they are changed from time to time?
That is the reason I put forward this amendment. I hope it will receive the consideration of the Front Bench with all its legal
talent that I referred to the other day. I
think it is a fair and reasonable demand
that I put forward. I cannot see any reason
against it. Why should these people be disfranchised, simply because the owner had
gone out to listen to the music of the harps
above, or the jingling of the tongs below?
Although these men have no vote for two
years, they still have to pay rates, and I do
not see why they should not have the vote.

The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY TO
THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS (Mr.
Megaw) I listened with very great interest
to the points made by the hon. Member for
Tyrone (Mr. Miller) and the hon. Member for
the University (Dr. Morrison), and I regret
that it is not possible for the Government to
accede to the amendment proposed. It is all
very well to refer to the anomalies of the registration law, but we have not the full power
here just yet to legislate in such a way as to
remove these anomalies. I mentioned in moving the Second Reading of this Bill that we
were hampered because the Parliamentary
franchise was so interdependent on the Local
Government franchise; in fact, it is tied up
in such a knot that it would require a great
amount of acumen on the part of those concerned to see a way in which the grievances
made could be removed. If my hon. Friends
would look at the Representation of the
People Act, 1918, they will see that the Parliamentary franchise of women is entirely dependent on what the Local Government franchise is. The Local Government franchise,
therefore, as it is settled here, must determine the Parliamentary vote. The Local
Government franchise is determined by this
Act of Parliament of 1918, and if we change
it in any way except with regard to putting
on the £5 qualification we will straightway be
affecting the Parliamentary franchise, and any
action that we took would be held to be ultra
vires. The greatest pains have been taken in
drafting the Bill before the Committee. The
matters referred to by the two hon. Members
who have just sat down would affect the Parliamentary franchise, and, however great the
grievance may be, I think my hon. Friends
will have to wait until twelve months hence,
or a little more, when they can deal fully with
all these questions of the franchise and put
the matter on something like a scientific basis.
For the present, as I have said, we cannot
admit of any amendment to this Bill that is
now before the Committee, and there is nothing for it but to insist on the Clause as it
stands.

Order for Second Reading read.

STRY OF FINANCE (Mr. Barbour): I beg

That the Bill be now read a
Second time."
It will be within the knowledge of Members
of this House that on the passing of the
Government of Ireland Act, and the Irish
Free State Act, there were certain revenues
transferred from the Imperial Parliament
to the respective Parliaments of the Free
State and Northern Ireland. The principal
ones were the Stamp and Estate Duties,
and consequent upon each of those three
separate Parliaments being entitled to raise
those taxes within their respective areas, it
became necessary to safeguard against what
is known as Double Taxation. That is to
say, if anyone died having property in, say,
Northern Ireland, England or Scotland, it
would not be right that death duties should
be paid twice over on the same property. In
the same way with Stamp Duties, there are
certain documents which are stamped within
the one area which may be required to be
produced in courts of law, or for other purposes, in either of the other two areas, and so,
unless some such arrangement as is provided for in this Bill were made, taxation
might be levied in the other area in
which that document might be produced.
The explanation of the working arrangement
made under this Bill is really shown in the
two Schedules, Part II referring to Estate
Duty, and Part III to Stamp Duties. Briefly
it provides that should the same rate of duty
apply in the two areas in which the document is required any payment in the one
area shall be regarded as payment made in
the other area, and deducted from the sum
leviable in the second area, but should in
one area the rate of taxation be higher than
in the first area, the additional rate of duty
payable would be levied even though the tax
had already been paid in respect of that
portion of the property in the first area
where the rate of taxation was lower. This
Bill is designed to give relief to the taxpayer.
It has already been agreed to by what is
termed a Declaration in Council between the
Imperial Parliament and the Free State and
the Government of Northern Ireland, and we
come here now in order to seek statutory
recognition of the arrangement which has
been entered into. I think it will recommend
itself at once to the acceptance of this House.
Question put, and agreed to.
Bill read a Second time, and Committed to
a Committee of the Whole House for Tomorrow.
The remaining Orders were read and post
poned.

HOUSES COMMANDEERED FOR USE AS
BARRACKS.
1. Mr. MILLER asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether it is a fact that when a
house has been forcibly taken over by the
Military or Constabulary for use as a barracks,
no rent will be paid by the Authorities unless
the owner signs an agreement to be responsible
for all loss from fire or dilapidation or any
acts of the King's enemies; and whether,
since all such buildings-especially near the
border are both a target, an arsenal, and a
no
risk which
insurance
petrol store--a
company would undertake-he does not consider that the evicted owner and occupier is
not very hardly treated, and will he secure
that a more equitable arrangement is made?
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): The ordinary form of agreement when premises are taken for a police
barracks provides that this Ministry is to keep
the interior of the premises in good condition
-reasonable wear and tear and destruction or
damage by the King's enemies, or by fire,
storm or tempest excepted. This is the form
which was always used by the R.I.C., and
there is no obligation on the landlord to accept
it if he does not wish to do so. If he declines
to enter into an agreement he can, when the
premises are commandeered under the Civil
Authorities (Special Powers) Act, bring his
claim for compensation before the County
Court, under Section 11 of that Act.
I may add, however, that the question of
amending the form of agreement as regards
liability for loss from fire is at present under
consideration.

The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY TO
THE MINISTRY OF EDUCATION (Mr.
McKeown): There was a question raised
yesterday by the hon. Member for West
Belfast (Mr. Lynn) regarding the building
by-laws and their application to the building
of schools. I desire to say that these by-laws
are not necessarily applicable to such buildings as schools. The by-laws deal with the
usual class of buidings, namely, houses and
shops. There might, accordingly, be a provision in the building by-laws which would
prevent the erection of a school according
to a plan, which, while very suitable for a
school, would not be suitable for a house or
a shop, to which class of buildings alone the
by-laws were originally directed. Further,
I venture to call hon. Members' attention to
the fact that all buildings, if they are to
rank for grant, must be approved by the
Ministry. I think it may be taken for granted
that the Ministry will certainly not take such
action as would nullify the effect of the bylaws of the Local Authorities in a case where
these by-laws are applicable and should be
complied with.
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: I had not the
good fortune to be present at the discussion
on this particular question yesterday, but I
quite appreciate the present position of the
Ministry of Education in regard to the question of conformity to the by-laws. My hon.
Friend (Mr. McKeown) has given a very
plausible reason why the officers of the
Ministry of Education should not be called
upon to carry out the regulations of the
Local Authority. Now I think they are the
people who ought to set an example to the
other folk in the community.
Mr. JOHNSTONE: Hear, hear.
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: I think that if
the schools are erected throughout the country, or in municipalities, the Ministry of
Education ought to conform to the by-laws
set up by the Local Authorities. The ordinary individual has to observe these by-laws.
The house builder has to observe them, and
they are made for good and sufficient reasons
in the interests of the community as a whole.
Surely the Ministry of Education ought to be
willing to make no exception whatever in the
case of buildings that are to be erected for
school purposes, and ought to conform to the
rules and regulations and bring themselves
up-to-date instead of being rather retrograde
in their building ideas. I cannot for the life
of me see what is behind the opposition of
the Ministry to conforming to the by-laws
as laid down by the local authorities.
Mr. McKEOWN: I have listened with interest to what the hon. Member for Derry
(Sir Robert Anderson) has said regarding
this question. It has been found in England
and in other countries that it is necessary
in the case of schools to have this exemption.
It does not follow at all that those who
build the schools are going to go contrary to
these building by-laws, but they want to
have certain liberties. The same thing, I
believe, refers to churches.
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: Why?
Mr. McKEOWN: It was found necessary
that there should be that exemption, because
the case of a church or a school may be
different from that of a house or shop.
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: Why?
Mr. McKEOWN: Because of the special
ideas and special grounds. It has been found
necessary, as I say, in England to have the
same exemption. I think hon. Members are
satisfied that it is not the intention of the
Ministry to break these by-laws, but we
want to have the liberty if at any time we
find it necessary to use it.
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: To break them.

CLAUSE 107 (Definitions)
In this Act, unless the context otherwise
requires-
(1) The expression "higher education"
means any form of education other than
elementary education, but does not include
agricultural education:
(2) The expression "intermediate school"
means a school or department of a school
providing at least a three years' course of
instruction in languages, mathematics,
science and such other subjects as may
from time to time be deemed suitable for
pupils who before entrance have reached
such stage (hereinafter in this section referred to as the "qualifying stage") of
attainment in elementary education as may
be prescribed by the Ministry:
(3) The expression "secondary school"
means a school or department of a school
providing at least a five years' course of
instruction in the subjects aforesaid beyond the qualifying stage:
(4) The expression "practical instruction"
means instruction in cookery, laundry
work, housewifery, dairywork, handicrafts
and gardening, and such other subjects as
the Ministry may by regulations declare to
be subjects of practical instruction:
(8) The expression "managers" includes
persons who have the management of the
school, whether the school is or is not
vested in them as owners:

or districts assigned to that committee,
and in relation to other powers or duties
of an education authority, the county or
county borough of that authority.

My experience of the working of the
National Board goes back for more years
than I would care to mention, and I think
in this matter of the appointment of teachers
it has worked uncommonly well. There never
was very serious friction, and there was no
trouble so far as I recollect. There were
objections made occasionally that managers
sometimes sought qualifications from teachers
for doing church work that had no connection
with educational work, and that the educational work was in some cases made
subservient to this other work. I
admit that there may be justification
for charge like that,
a
but it does
not apply generally. I think on the
whole the plan of the National Board of
leaving the Local Authorities the right of
appointing the teachers has worked well, and
I confess that I view more or less with alarm
this revolutionary measure of taking the
appointment of teachers wholly out of the
hands of the people, who really up to now
have been responsible for the work of the
educational machine in rural Ireland at
least.
I think you should go very carefully before
you make this revolutionary change. You get
rid by the amendment proposed to-day of
the defects of the old system. You get rid
of what you sometimes may find, an autocratic manager. I do not think there were
many such, but there were some. In the
matter of selecting a teacher you pick out
a large number of qualified men, and you
send them up to the Ministry. The Ministry
picks out four of these men and sends them
to the local Committee so that you secure
in that way the appointment of a good man,
and you eliminate the evil effects of the old
system while still retaining the advantages
of that system which commended itself to
all sections of the people of Ulster. I would
ask seriously the Minister of Education and
his deputy, and the Government, why do they
needlessly, as in my opinion they will, rush
into a revolutionary plan like this that rubs
every section of the community against the
grain?
Hon. MEMBERS: No, no.
Dr. MORRISON: That may be, but I am

a
draw the attention of hon. Members to Clause
98, as amended. That clause, as amended,
states that if any committee of this kind

That gives the authority very wide and very

Ministry and as a Government that with

Educational Authority or
Regional Committee to act in any way unjustly towards any particular school.
Reference has been made to the fact that
this Clause will be conducive to denominationalism or sectarianisn. In our opinion
it will just have the opposite effect. It seems
to me that the adoption of the amendment
of my hon. Friend would mean an attempt to

hon. Members, and one is that the Committee
is, de facto, the owner of the school. That
is a very important point. Another is that
this provision will enable a regular system
of promotion for teachers to be established
under each authority. That has been a very
great drawback in the system as it exists
at the present time. Another point is, that
it will enormously ease the difficulties which
always occur under the present system whenever it is proposed to amalgamate existing
schools under private managership. These
are all very important points, and have been
considered seriously by the Administration
in adopting this particular clause. We are
aiming at that hearty co-operation of all
classes, of all creeds, and of all sections
which I believe the Government has every
reason to expect, and we believe that this
clause will tend towards that.

Dr. MORRISON: I should like to say a
word or two in reply to the criticisms which
have been uttered against my amendment. I
think the house is not conscious of the
serious dangers that are involved to the prosperity and happiness of Ulster and the peace
and harmony of Ulster by this Bill. I
thought at first that opinion would become
smooth and people would be satisfied, but
I regret to say that opinion is hardening,
and hardening at a very serious rate against
some of the provisions in this Bill, and may
induce opposition to the Bill itself in regions
that I greatly deplore. This amendment has
been produced by me after consultation with
the education authority at the head of the
Presbyterian Church in Ulster. You may
call it reactionary, you may say it is not
modern, that it is not up-to-date, but it is
a cautious reform that should appeal to the
moderate man. Instead of going slowly, and
gently, and cautiously, as we recommend
should be done, you take the plunge.
The plunge may be successful and
may come off safely, but I say there is
great danger. You have to learn to creep before you try to walk, and to walk before you
try to run. Anyone who reads the history of
this Empire to which we belong recognises
that our greatness is owing to the fact that
we give the people authority; we recognise
the prejudices, even the follies, of the people,
and conform to their wishes. In this matter
it seems to me you are rushing against them.
I have listened to the appeal of the noble
Marquess, and I desire, as an Ulsterman, to
thank him for the interest he has taken in
this matter of education. I think he deserves
the thanks of Ulster, and I am perfectly certain that he is animated by a sincere desire
to promote its prosperity. (Hon. Members :
Hear, hear.) But I also have that object before me.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
I was working in connection with educational matters for a long time, and I think
my hand can make a more correct diagnosis
of the pulse of Ulster than the hand of the
noble Marquess. I have no object but to promote the interests of education. This matter
has never been discussed between the teachers
and myself, but I do say this, that while I
claim to look after the interests of the
teachers and would be willing to do what they
want, so long as it is right and proper, there
are other interests-there is the claim of the
people, there is the claim of the managers
and the claim of the owners of schools.
should like to take the middle course, a moderate course that should have due regard to all

CLAUSE 67 (Procedure on dismissal of
teacher).
If at any time within six weeks after the
adoption by the employers of a decision for
the dismissal of a teacher in a public elementary school a petition is presented to
the Ministry by the teacher praying for
an inquiry into the reasons for his dismissal, the Ministry shall cause to be made
such inquiry as it thinks fit, and if, as the
result of such inquiry, the Ministry is of
opinion that the dismissal is not reasonably
justifiable the Ministry shall communicate
such opinion to the education authority,
or in the case of a voluntary school to the
managers or school committee of such
school, with a view to reconsideration of
the decision, and in the event of the education authority, managers, or school committee not departing from their decision,
the Ministry may withhold or reduce any
grant payable to or in respect of the school
out of moneys provided by Parliament.
Provided that nothing in this section
shall affect the power of the education
authority, managers, or school committee
as the case may be, summarily to suspend
a teacher from the performance of duty.

The Ministry may withhold or reduce
any grant payable to or in respect of the
school out of moneys provided by Parliament.
The Ministry will withhold payment of
salary to any successor appointed to take
the dismissed teacher's place, and thereby
in fact make any further appointment impossible. That, I may point out, is the
present practice. I do not think the Government can accept an amendment of this kind
that would bind them under those circumstances to continue the salary.
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: I think most
teachers will say that the present system
has been defective on this particular point.
How does it stand in this Clause? The
question of the dismissal of a teacher is
being dealt with by the Ministry, and they
find that the local authority has not acted
fairly or justly. Who is going to be punished
as a result of that? The Ministry suggest
that the grant should be withheld from the
local authority, and the teacher is left out
in the cold-the teacher that the Ministry
has found to have been wrongly dismissed. Is
not that really what it amounts to? (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) The Ministry has
no remedy except to punish the local authority by not granting any money in
case a successor is appointed. But, where
does the teacher come in? The teacher is
going to be penalised all the time. He or
she may look out for another place. In the
meantime that may not be an easy thing to
find; the teacher may have to wait for months
and months before a suitable opening arises,
and this through no fault of his own, because
under this Clause the Ministry find that the
teacher was not to blame. What does the
amendment suggest? That the Ministry
have power to make an allowance by way
of salary to the teacher placed in these
peculiar circumstances to an amount not
exceeding twelve months' salary. They can
give a month's salary, they can give two

Mr. POLLOCK: This raises a question
that has been brought before me on several
occasions by hon. Members, namely the
hardships under which those who are known
as old pensioners labour by reason of the
smallness of their pensions based upon their
original salaries. As this affords an opportunity of remedying the grievance I would
like to call the attention of the Committee
to the exact import of the amendment. The
proposed changes are intended to effect two
purposes, firstly, the relief of pensioners
whose original pensions were so small that
the maximum increase permissible under the
Pensions (Increase) Act was, comparatively
speaking, trifling, and with the approach of
old age was not sufficient to keep the pensioner in anything like decent circumstances,
and, secondly, for extending to teachers
pensioned between the outbreak of the warand I wish hon. Members to observe the
significance of that--and the coming into full
operation of the present salary scale initiated in 1920 the full benefit of the Pensions
(Increase) Act.
At present the Pensions (Increase) Act
divides pensioners into two categories:
firstly, those who were pensioned before the
4th August, 1914, that is before the war, and
upon the old scale, and, secondly, those who
were pensioned after that date. The first
class now
receives the full benefit of the
increase permissible under the Pensions
(Increase) Act of 1920-that is those who
were pensioned before the 4th August, 1914
by an addition of approximately 30, 40 or
even 50 per cent. on their original pension
as the case may be. The second class, namely,
those who were pensioned after the 4th
August, 1914, are, by Part II. of the Schedule
to the Pensions (Increase) Act, to which I
have referred, debarred, in all cases where
pension scales have been improved or pay
increased since the 4th August, 1914, from
participating in the full benefit under the
Pensions (Increase) Act, and they can only
receive an increase sufficient to make the
increased pension equal to the amount to
which their pensions might have been increased if they had retired before the
outbreak of the war. The significance of
that is that teachers who were pensioned
before the 4th August, 1914, had their pensions dealt with under the Act, but those
who were pensioned after that period were
not so dealt with, and had to accept the existing conditions. But the date of the
settlement of the latter class was the 9th
October, 1914, and was really based upon
corditions that had been approved by the
Treasury six months earlier, so that while
they were in the same category as pre-war
pensioners exactly the same category-yet
from the technical position they occupied,
through their pensions having been settled
on the 9th October-that is four months
after the war broke out-they were debarred
from the increases provided in the Act of
1920 It is to remedy that grievance, therefore, and to give these pensioners to whom I
have referred equal benefit to those who were
pensioned in pre-war days, that these provisions are made. As I say, it was purely
accidental that their pensions were settled
on the 9th October, because it might just as
readily have been settled before.
Again in the case of any pensioner whose
pension, even when increased, is found to be
very small, it is proposed, as the Committee
will see by Sub-section (b), to grant a further increase, according to the circumstances
in which the pensioner may find himself, up
to the amount of £50. The last part of the
amendment reads
"Any increased pension accruing under
this sub-section shall come into force on
such date as may be prescribed by the
Ministry of Finance, being a date not
earlier than the date of the passing of this
Act."

SPIRIT GROCERS' LICENCES.
1. Mr. MILLER asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he will state how many
spirit grocers' licences there are in Northern
Ireland; how many are in the City of Belfast, the City of Londonderry, and in each
of the Six Counties.
2. Mr. DONALD had the following question
on the Order Paper :-
"To ask the Minister for Home Affairs
if he will state the number of off-licensed
premises for the sale of intoxicating liquor
which there are in each county in Northern
Ireland, and the number in Belfast and
Londonderry respectively."
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr. Pollock): I have arranged with my right
hon. Friend to reply to this question as well as to the question standing on
the Notice Paper in the name of the hon.
Member for East Belfast (Mr. Donald).
Since the passing of the Finance (1909-10)
Act, 1910, there has been no special spirit
grocers' licence for the sale of intoxicating
liquors. Under Schedule 1 of that Enactment
the class of trader commonly described as a
"spirit grocer" has carried on his business,
in so far as intoxicating liquors are concerned,
by means of a spirit retailer's off-licence, beer
retailer's off-licence, and a wine retailer's offlicence.
According to the latest returns available,
the number of traders in Northern Ireland to
whom the description of "spirit grocer "
would apply is 410, made up as follows:-
County Borough of Belfast
County Borough of Londonderry
...
County Antrim (excluding the County
Borough of Belfast)


County Armagh
County Down

County Fermanagh

County Londonderry (excluding the
County Borough of Londonderry 15
County Tyrone


In addition to these, licences have been
issued to 18 traders whose business is confined
to the sale of intoxicating liquor for consump
tion off the premises.
There are also 287 cases where licences for
the sale of wine for consumption off the premises have been issued to chemists, etc.
Mr. DONALD; Arising out of that answer
may I ask my right .hon. Friend (Mr
Pollock) if he can tell us how many of these
410 will be abolished under the Bill?
Mr. POLLOCK: I do not know that I can

which I have referred will, at any rate.
come under the purview of the House in the
discussion of the Bill.
Mr. SPEAKER: The hon. Gentleman can

THE RENT RESTRICTIONS ACT.
3. Mr. DONALD asked the Prime Minister
if he will state whether it is the intention
of the Government to introduce a Bill extending the Rents Restrictions Act, 1920,
which expires on the 24th June; if so, to
what date, and whether provision will be
made in the Law as to what would happen
in the cases where notices to quit have been
given by the landlord to re-enter upon his
house at a date which will expire when the
Rents Act expires?
MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): I have received the Interim
Report of the Departmental Committee
appointed by me to report on this matter.
The Committee make it clear to me that
they cannot under any circumstances present
a considered report for several weeks, and
they recommend a temporary continuance of
the Act to enable them to complete their
inquiries and to afford the Government time
to consider their recommendations and
decide as to the form of the Amending Bill.
I hope to lay before this House
immediately a short Bill extending the
present Act for six months.
I also propose to publish the Committee's
Interim Report at once.
Mr. DONALD: Arising out of that answer,
is my right hon. Friend aware of the importance of this question? As a member of the
Committee of Inquiry, I feel disappointed at
this matter being put back for a further period
of six months. The truth of the matter is-
Mr. SPEAKER: Order, order. The hon.
Member cannot make a statement. As he
knows well, he can raise the question on the
adjournment.

Supply.
17 MAY 1923
QUESTION OF PROCEDURE.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY TO
THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (Mr. Barbour): I should be glad if you will kindly
give us some guidance as to our procedure.
Under the laws governing our procedure ten
days are allotted to supply. We are proposing to take a few Estimates this afternoon
which will be the ninth day of the ten allotted days for Supply. There are one or two
Estimates for which we should like further
time for discussion, and I would like to know
what the procedure would be under our Standing Orders (Rule 14, Sub-sections 7 and 8).
Will it be necessary to report on all the remaining Estimates this afternoon?
Mr. SPEAKER: As this is the ninth allotted day of Supply it will be necessary,
under Standing Order 15, paragraph 7, that
all the outstanding votes must be put to-day
in Committee. That, however, leaves still one
of the allotted days upon which discussion can
take place on any of the Votes which have
not yet been reached. The last of the Votes
must be taken in Committee of Supply. I
understand there is a Police Estimate on
which there is likely to be some discussion.
That can be taken on the last day,
but the discussion will have to
be on
Report; that is to say, provided of course
that the House will not agree to discuss it
to-day. It is not until six o'clock that the
Question has to be put, and consequently
I suggest to the House, as I understand the
Ministry of Finance are not prepared to
deal with the Police Estimate to-day, that
that estimate should be allowed to go through
Committee to-day without discussion, on the
understanding that discussion will take place
on the Report.
QUESTION OF PRIVILEGE.
Dr. MORRISON: There is a matter that I
would like to bring before the House, because it appears to me that it involves a
question of privilege. I moved an amendment to a clause in the Education Bill here
yesterday, practically proposing to abolish
the Regional Committees. I pressed for a
division, and the chairman asked the members in support of it to stand up, but denied
me the right which belongs to every member
of this House to have my protest against any
measure entered on the books of the House.
Three Members stood up during the clearing
of the lobbies in support of my amendment.
Two others assured me they would go into
the division lobby with me. The reason that
I ask for information and guidance in
this matter is, that a division was taken on
another occasion in this House, in which
only two members went into the "No" lobby,
I
and if two members can go into the "No"
lobby, I do not know why I should not be
allowed to go into the lobby when I had five
members, and possibly ten, supporting me.
would like some decision on this matter, because we should not have contradictory rulings. I am willing to submit to the Rules
of Procedure of the House, but one ruling one
day and another ruling another day is very
unfair to the Members.
Mr. SPEAKER: As I was not present when
this incident occurred, I cannot say exactly
what happened, but I take it that the hon.
Member is correct. I am supposed to know
nothing of what takes place in Committee of
this House. Of course, I am supposed to
interpret the Standing Orders. The Chairman of Committees was, I think, perfectly
right under Standing Order No. 29 to call
upon the Members to stand up if he thought,
as apparently he did, that a division was
unnecessarily challenged. Of course, that is
a matter of opinion. In this House one must
give a much more generous interpretation to
what is an unnecessary challenge, than one
would in a House of larger numbers, and
even a very small number of Members may
be justified in going to a division. At the
same time it was entirely a matter for the
Chairman to act within the Standing Orders,
and I do not think the hon. Member has
really been seriously prejudiced, at least I
hope not, by what has occurred..

in Council, transfer to the Ministry such
powers and duties of the Ministry of Home
Affairs in relation to reformatory and industrial schools as appear to the said Gover-

Mr. McKEOWN: I beg to move, "That the
Clause be read a Second time."
Sir DAWSON BATES: This is purely an
enabling clause. At the present time the responsibility of administering Industrial and
Reformatory schools devolves entirely upon
the Ministry of Home Affairs, but the
Ministry of Education is good enough to
assist the Ministry of Home Affairs in the
education, both literary and technical, of the
inmates of these institutions. At the same
time the Government feel that in many ways,
if the inmates of these institutions are to
take full advantage of what I may call the
blessings of this Bill, it is necessary that
greater facilities should be afforded to the
Ministry of Education in carrying out the
education of these inmates. The clause,

Mr. MILLER: I beg to move
Clause be read a second time."
"That the
This is a rather important matter which has
not been dealt with either in the Bill or in the
report of the Lynn Committee. At present
the insurance of teachers and children is done
in a very haphazard manner. In some schools
the teacher has to pay it out of his Own
pocket. In other instances-for instance, in
the Diocese of Derry and Raphoe, from which
I come the provision for the insurance of
teachers and children is made out of the
diocesan funds in a bulk sum. Of course, if
the schools are transferred, that will be done
away with, and the question is who is to look
after the insurance of teachers and children
in future. This new clause suggests that it
should be done by the Education Authority.
I would put forward an alternative, and that
is, that the Ministry should take the responsibility themselves and not make the insurance
at all, in the same way as public buildings
are dealt with. I do not think the risk would
be very much; it would probably be much
less than the cost of the insurance. However,
this is a matter for the Ministry to settle. I
have not the slightest hope that they will take
any advice of mine, but I would ask them to
consider this matter, and put the proposal in
their own words, because I am afraid they
will not take mine. That is all I have to say
on the matter.

Mr. McKEOWN: I regret that though this

I desire to say that, owing to the peculiar
circumstances of the case, it is very inadvisable to make transfer obligatory upon the
education authority, while it is outside the
scope of this Parliament to make such transfer equally binding upon the officers whose
duties are transferred by the Act. Every
Member of this House who has interested himself in this important Schedule will be aware
that by Section 8 of the Local Government
(Ireland) Act, "If any officer of a local
authority who holds, on the passing of this
Act, a pensionable office, is removed from his
office for any cause other than misconduct or
incapacity. ... he shall be entitled to receive
from the local authority an allowance not
exceeding two-thirds of the salary, fees, and
emoluments which he was in receipt of at the
time of the removal."
Education Bill.
Committee.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Mr. McKeown]
By Sub-section 2 of Section 68 of the
Government of Ireland Act, 1920, the Civil
Service Committee has been empowered to act
as referee in substitution of the Local Government Board, which disappeared upon the
coming into force of the Act of 1920, to which
I have referred.
It will be understood, therefore, that it is
possible that the provisions of the Bill under
discussion, which transfer certain powers and
duties from existing local bodies to a new
body, called the Local Education Authority,
may be held thereby to cause the dismissal of
the officers engaged by the existing bodies for
the execution of those powers and duties now
transferred,. Such constructive dismissal
would, of course, be a removal from office for
a cause other than misconduct or incapacity,
under the Local Government (Ireland) Act or
1919.
To make the transfer of these officers mandatory would, therefore, be liable to create a
Gilbertian set of circumstances, under which
one local authority would be compelled to
accept the transfer of an existing officer from
another local authority, which at the same
time would be compensating him, on a possible ruling of the Civil Service Committee,
by the payment of a pension for his discontinuance in an office which had disappeared
to give place for the creation of the new office,
the enjoyment of the salary and emoluments
of which was guaranteed to him by the same
Act as enabled him to secure compensation.
If, on the other hand, we make, as the
Schedule at present does make, the transfer
of existing officers permissive, and so an affair
for arrangement between the officers concerned and the various local authorities, we
remove this possibility, since it will leave a
particular authority free to refuse to re-engage
an officer who has claimed his pension, ur
enable them to re-engage him only on the
understanding that his pension shall stand as
part of his salary.
I may well point out here that the sole
object of the Government is to secure equitable
conditions for all parties affected by the
transfer of powers and duties from existing
local bodies to new local bodies under the
present Bill. The administrative difficulties
which I have endeavoured to point out are
not of our own creation. They proceed from
legislation which is part of the law of our
Constitution, and which consequently we are
powerless to amend.
For the general information of the House,
I may add that all the Superannuation Acts
dealing with the officers of local authorities
contemplate the cases of whole-time officers
alone, as a general principle. It is not the
intention of the Government to extend the
purview of these Superannuation Acts to cover
part-time officers of local authorities, and, by
so doing, to saddle the already heavily burdened ratepayer with additional local expenditure.
This is a long reply to the hon. Member,
but the object is to make it quite clear that
any transferred officer might be considered
dismissed, although he has not been guilty of
misconduct or incapacity. Under the existing Act he could claim a pension and at the
same time make application and be employed
in his former position. So it would be
possible to have an officer drawing a pension
and at the same time being employed. This
is the point I have tried to convey in the
reply.

Education Committees of County Boroughs.

SPEAKER in the Chair.

-(Mr. Burn.)
ORDERS OF THE DAY,
Intoxicating Liquor Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
OF
The PARLIAMENTARY AND FINANCIAL
SECRETARY TO THE MINISTRY
FINANCE (Mr. Barbour): On the occasion
of the First Reading of this Bill, the Prime
Minister dealt very fully with its general
features, pointing out the earnest intention
on the part of its promoters to meet the desires, on the one hand, of the Temperance
party, as expressed by many resolutions
passed at public meetings, and, on the other
hand, to correct those breaches of the law
and abuse of license privileges which all lawrespecting members of the community, no
matter what their attitude to the liquor
question may be, must condemn. The Bill
is far from being revolutionary-(hon. Members Hear, hear and its hope of success
lies in its moderation. How often we have
seen laudable desire for reform, even of acknowledged evils, delayed or frustrated by the
advocacy of, or insistence on, too extreme or
drastic demands. In every community there
are large sections entertaining very conflicting
views, and it is only by mutual forbearance
and reasonable submission to restriction that
the highest attainment of their respective
ideals becomes possible. We are a young
Parliament. Very wide powers have been
entrusted to us, and in their exercise we
must remember the responsibility that
attaches to their use, and endeavour, in
whatever action we may take, to leave no
just cause for rankling or resentment in the
minds of those upon whom it may be necessary to enforce closer control or restriction,
or disappointment in the minds of those who
may not find in this Bill such complete
fulfilment of their aims as they may have
anticipated.
It is one thing to pass legislation, and it
is another to ensure compliance with its
enactments, whether such compliance originates from a sense of their reasonableness
or whether it be brought about by effective
supervision and enforcement, and in
considering this Bill the relation of those
Sections setting forth the objects aimed at
to the other Sections providing the means
for their attainment must be borne in mind.
Undoubtedly, of those who indulge in stimulants the great majority do so without
apparent injury to themselves or offence
against either the law or other members
of the community, but, unfortunately, there
is a minority for whom the use of alcohol
in its various forms has an irresistible allurement, to yield to which brings misery and
sufferings not only to themselves but to
others dependent on or connected with them.
Mr. McGUFFIN: Hear, hear.
Mr. BARBOUR: Similarly in the trade
in intoxicating liquors; while the greater
part may be conducted in conformity with
the law, evasion and defiance of regulations
on the part of others render necessary
considerable strengthening of supervision
and more effective means of deterring
offenders. How to do this without unduly
restricting or penalising those who, either
in the consumption or sale of intoxicants,
have afforded no moral or statutory ground
of offence has been so difficult a problem that
no solution has yet been found. This difficulty is fully realised by the promoters
of this Bill; they do not claim it will unfailingly terminate all those evils which it
seeks to combat, but they do claim with
confidence that if passed into law it should
mark very substantial progress and bring
about materially improved conditions as
compared with what the administration
of existing legislation has been able to
accomplish.
Apart from the expressed provisions of
the Bill we hope to effect a great deal by
the institution of the new tribunal, before
which all licensing cases will be tried, by
giving the police the right of appeal, by
structural alterations in the internal fittings
of public houses whereby police supervision
should be facilitated, and by the endorsement
of convictions upon licences and the permanent disqualification of premises; and
these general provisions and their anticipated
987 Intoxicating Liquor Bill-

HOUSE OF COMMONS.
Second Reading.
[Mr. Barbour]
effect must be remembered when discussing
the particular clauses which are framed to
achieve the main objects of the Bill. The
reception accorded the Bill on its First
Reading was, on the whole, favourable
Mr. McGUFFIN: Certainly.
Mr. BARBOUR: But since the circulation
of the Bill, when hon. Members and the
public have had the opportunity of studying
its text, certain criticisms have been made
with which I shall endeavour to deal. As
regards Clause I, which deals with Sunday
closing, the only criticism of substance
which has thus far reached me centres
round the term "substantial meal.”
Mr. GRANT: Hear, hear.
Mr. BARBOUR: My colleagues and I have
very carefully considered the use of this
phrase, and as will be readily appreciated
have found it a matter of extreme difficulty
to define a general phrase of this nature.
Our proposal is, briefly, that we should
leave the construction and interpretation of
the words "substantial meal" to the Court,
which, as hon. Members will remember, is
now to be composed of one or more resident
magistrates. I am
sure hon. Members
themselves in suggesting a loophole of
evasion, which is apparently contained in
these words, would never entertain a doubt
in their own minds as to whether they would
discriminate between an untasted ham sandwich placed on the table by the man in
charge with repeated calls for intoxicants,
and a really substantial meal necessary to
keep one going for the remainder of the day.
Surely similar confidence may be reposed in
those who will form the Court to try cases
as to whether a substantial meal was really
being taken at the same time that liquor
was being served. I shall ask hon. Members
in considering this phrase not to focus their
attention exclusively upon these two words.
I hope they will bear in mind that in order
to obtain liquor on Sunday there are other
stipulations which must be complied with.
They can only get it in a hotel-in that part
of the hotel as is regularly set apart for the
serving of meals. That hotel if found supplying liquor not in accordance with this
provision runs a risk of being brought before
a Court, and if convicted that conviction is
recorded on the licence. A certain number
of convictions recorded on the licence will
entail permanent cancellation of the licence.
It will be seen that to serve liquor in an
unauthorised way on Sunday involves a great
risk for any respectable house to run. Taking
these different provisions together, it leads
us to hope that what we aim at will be
achieved by the wording of this phrase.
Clause 2, which deals with the abolition of
what are popularly referred to as spirit
grocers' licences, has come in for the main
criticism.
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: Hear, hear.
Mr. BARBOUR: The main argument is
that this clause as it stands does not gc
far enough, in that it allows the larger
traders to divide their premises and the
smaller traders to clear out their grocery
business and to carry on simply as off-licence
retailers of wines and spirits.
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: Hear, hear.
Mr. BARBOUR: It is far from being an
easy task to ascertain what proportion the
trade in intoxicating liquor bears to the
total trade carried on by the spirit grocer.
Mr. McGUFFIN: 90 per cent.
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: It is not
abolition at all.
Mr. BARBOUR: The intention was, and
is, however, that the sale of intoxicating
liquors should be merely ancillary to the
main business of grocer, and the main objec
tion to the spirit grocer arose from the fact
that he carried on a mixed business and
In
therefore faciliated secret drinking.
this Bill we have not only abolished the
spirit grocer as such, but we have also gone
a step further and provided that no fullylicensed publican shall carry on in the same
premises as he carries on his publican's
business any other class of trade. It has
also to be borne in mind that the general
administrative machinery for dealing with
applicants for the grant or renewal of
licences has been very materially strengthened. To those who fear that the spirit
grocer in every case will clear out his
grocery business and continue his business
as a retailer of intoxicating liquor, I would
draw attention especially to the provisions
of Clause 7, from which it will be observed
that wide powers are conferred upon resident
magistrates in considering any application for
a certificate which will enable a retailer to
sell intoxicating liquor. I am informed that
a very large proportion of spirit grocers
carry on businesses in comparatively small
premises, and any attempt by these traders
to divide such premises structurally would
doubtless come up for consideration when the
question of the suitability of the premises is
before the licensing court.
We have also had criticism on the ground
that more direct action is not proposed to
secure the elimination of a large number
of licences, but we anticipate that the effect
of the legislation now proposed will be that
many spirit grocers, chemists, and others who
have carried on the sale of intoxicating liquor
along with other businesses, will abandon
such sale; and in addition to the reduction

Second Reading.
of licences that would be thus brought about,
much might be done to the advantage of
both parties if both the Temperance advocates and those interested in the liquor traffic
would, as opportunity might offer, buy out

The main ground upon which the Bill has
been sought for the abolition of these spirit
grocers' licences was that the spirit grocer
part of the name was merely a cloak under
which illicit or secret drinking could be
carried on with greater impunity. It was
held that not only were women who had to
go to spirit grocers for the purchase of
necessary supplies brought unnecessarily into
contact with the sale of liquor, but that
spirit grocers by connivance with them would
supply them with liquor and charge the
same on any invoice or bill that might be
rendered as other legitimate goods. Further.
that drinking was actually permitted on the
premises. In fact, the whole trade was of
a clandestine surreptitious character, and it
was only due to those breaches of the law
that the use of the spirit grocer's licence
became as popular as it has done. We are
now entirely altering the environment under
which such sales shall be carried on.
Mr. GRANT: No.
Mr. BARBOUR: We feel that we have not
only discharged to the full the expectation
that has been formed in divorcing entirely
the sale of intoxicating liquors from that of

wall.
Mr. BARBOUR: It has been said and I
know it seems to me that some Members

Mr. McGUFFIN: Your own Bill suggested
it.
informed that the
Mr. BARBOUR: As a matter of fact I do
not know whether those hon. Members who
have promulgated such a proposition have
taken the trouble to look into the class of
premises in which this trade has been carried
on up till now. I am
bulk of these are very small indeed, and do
not as a matter of fact lend themselves to
sub-division. I have also learned, from what
I have heard in this House, that structural
alterations in the city of Belfast at the

to take into consideration all the factors
bearing upon a case, and we find when we
take all these into consideration that the

we have in view in one way, whether directly
or otherwise, and to fulfil the wish that is

of business. On the other hand, if by carrying out what this Bill promises, namely, the
divorcing of the grocery business from the

should henceforward become off-licence
dealers pure and simple, hon. Members suggest that there would still be such a large
demand for the supply of liquor by that
method that it would be possible for so many
spirit grocers to carry on a paying business
and make it worth their while to do so, I
think they are rather undermining their

many matters there is machinery for distribution which is a legitimate convenience to
the public, and it is not everyone who obtains
his supply of intoxicants at a spirit grocer's
premises that is necessarily offending against
either the law or due observance of that
temperance which we must take as the right
of every man so long as he keeps within those

I notice that in certain quarters the question has been raised as to the practicability
of introducing into methylated spirits some
substance which would render the spirits so
nauseous as to prevent their use for human
consumption. This point we considered very
carefully when the present measure was
being prepared, and as we have no methylators in Northern Ireland we found it necessary to consult the Imperial Customs and
Excise Department as to the feasibility of
the suggestion I have mentioned. The Imperial Government analysts have advised
that they do not know of any non-poisonous
substance that would render the spirit wholly
undrinkable without at the same time interfering with its legitimate use.
Mr. McGUFFIN: What about glauber
salts?
Mr. BARBOUR: I am not a chemist, and
so I naturally have to accept the decision of
those who I believe are more qualified than
myself. Of course there would be a method
of introducing some absolute poison that
would put an effectual stopper, at any rate,
on the use of methylated spirits, which alone
would seem to satisfy the demands of some
reformers. Under these circumstances we
have had recourse to the provisions of Clause
4 of the Bill, by means of which we hope to
secure the effective control over the trade in
methylated spirits. In plain words, that
means that we put the sale of methylated
spirits practically on the same basis as the
sale of poisons.
991 Intoxicating Liquor Bill-

HOUSE OF COMMONS.
Second Reading.
[Mr. Barbour]
So far as I have seen no serious attempts
have been made to criticise the provisions of
Clause 5, which deals with offences in connection with illicit distillation, and on this
point I think we are agreed as to the urgent
necessity of taking steps to stamp out this
traffic. The other provisions of the Bill have
not thus far called forth any serious criticisms with which it is necessary that I should
deal at this stage. Doubtless some degree of
hardship will be occasioned to certain individuals by remedial legislation such as is
embodied in the present measure, but I
would mention that in framing the Bill we
have endeavoured as far as practicable to
meet all possible cases of hardships. In
framing a Bill there is the difficulty that
always presents itself to the promoters of
which the ordinary critic or reformer does
not have to bear the responsibility.
It is so to word the clauses of a Bill that it
carries out the main objects aimed at.
Critics generally have in their minds some
particular instance, and in framing laws and
regulations to deal with that particular instance words when they become embodied in
an Act and are used in general application
may very easily be found to bring within
their scope a very much wider class of trade
or of individuals than it was ever intended
to interfere with when starting to frame the
Act.
As regards the consideration of the Bill
generally I hope that hon. Members will bear
in mind a quotation which I have taken
from the local daily Press which says:-

In any measure of social reform it is
almost impossible to clear away a mass of
admitted wrongs without at the same time
inflicting hardship in individual cases here
and there. It is the greatest good for the
greatest number,' and the mitigation as far
as practicable of hardship for others is
the golden rule."
In preparing this measure the Government has been guided by the principle enunciated in the quotation I have mentioned.
If I might intrude a personal note, apart
from any official inclinations I may have in
supporting the measure, I do not know what
attitude the public or Members of this House
may believe I take up personally towards
this measure. It has been a disappointment
to me on more than one occasion-although I
am glad to say the occasions are rare-when
I have had to consult someone of the medical
profession-I have had it said to me, after
they had heard my complaints, that I would
do better to avoid the heavy wines and
rather take the lighter wines. As a matter
of fact, although not pledged in any way,
I have been practically a teetotaller, I think,
for 25 or 26 years at any rate. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) I am so, not from lack
of any confidence in my own ability to resist
these temptations, which, I think, are undoubtedly associated with intoxicants. In
backing this Bill, I have not the slightest
care-I do not care to inquire even-what
measure of political influence or support I
may gain or lose. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) I do so as a member of the community.
I would be glad if any action or influence of
mine might confer that slight degree of
moral support which I feel, in many cases,
in different classes of society, and in
different circles, is of very great assistance
to the waverer-(hon. Members: Hear, hear)
--who maybe does not wish to join in the
round of drinks which are being proffered.
If he sees me refusing, it gives him greater
confidence if his conscience prompts him to
follow my lead. I am very anxious indeed
that a Bill shall receive the sanction of this
House, but I hope that whatever Bill receives
that sanction it may be of such a character
that it will command for itself the ready
acceptance of the members of the community,
and that they will feel imbued with such a
sense of its justice that they will always be
ready to act as its champion, and show that
those ideals which we have in view-the real
moral good and welfare of each individual
member of the community-may be helped
along by what we have endeavoured here to
provide. I beg to move. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.)
Mr. CRAWFORD: May I just in a word or
two congratulate my colleague in the representation of Antrim (Mr. Barbour) upon the
admirable statement he has put before the
House this afternoon? It is a great pleasure
to me indeed to have heard him try to explain what I could not understand. He says
he has been a teetotaller for 25 years; I can

be a Bill passed on this matter. I sincerely
hope that whatever feelings may exist in the
different sections of this House good sense
will prevail, and that there will be give and
take on both sides, and that a Bill really
useful will be passed by this House
I agree thoroughly with his remark when
he said this was not a revolutionary Bill. I
think the calmest critic would quite agree
with him in that. It is not revolutionary in

Temperance Party are not satisfied with this
Bill. When I had the honour on this day
week of hearing the Prime Minister's speech.
I put an interpretation on the Bill which I
find, when I have read the Bill in cold, calm
print, is not one that I would be disposed to
put upon it to-day. Yet I am bound to admit
993 Intoxicating Liquor Bill—

18 MAY 1923
Second Reading.
that the Prime Minister and the Government
in bringing in this Bill are desirous of carrying into effect the same purpose as the
Temperance Party are desirous of carrying
into effect. It is simply a matter of finding
out the wisest way of bringing about these
reforms. The Temperance Party want the
things the Government have endeavoured to
put into this Bill.
The first thing promised was the abolition
of the spirit grocers' licences. I think that
even a friendly critic of the Bill would say
that this Bill does not abolish the spirit
grocers' licences. We must look at the thing
fairly and frankly. We are bound to admit
that if they conform to what the regulation
requires them to do they can still continue
in another name to carry on the business.
The Bill will undoubtedly help. I feel certain that a great many of these people will
not be able so to alter their places as to conform with these laws. The fact still remains
that those who are able to alter their premises to such an extent as to satisfy this
particular tribunal will be able to remain in
the business. Whether that is the wisest way
-to go about it in that roundabout fashion--
of getting rid of the spirit grocers in the
way the Bill suggests, or whether we should
have the clean-cut is a thing we may differ
about. It may be that the clean cut would be
the best way; it may be that the way suggested by the Government would be the best;
but I sincerely hope that when the Bill
comes to be committed that those responsible for it will be prepared to consider
amendments along that line.
Coming next to the abolition of the bonafide traveller: in olden times the bona-fide
traveller had to go three miles; now he will
only have got to travel next door. No one
can say that the bona-fide traveller has been
abolished. If he has got enough money to
get a substantial meal he will be able to get
drink, but the poor man will not be able to
get drink because the public-house will be
closed. Here also there is room for compromise. In all seriousness I would press on
those responsible for the Bill that they
ought to consider the other side, and not
leave the thing in that peculiar way.
Then the matter of Sunday closing. We
have not got that in the Bill, because by this
arrangement the hotels will be opened, and
those who take a meal will be able to get
drink. The bars of course will be closed.
Surely it would be a fair and reasonable thing
that people who want this should at least
sleep in the hotel, and that there should be
some decision as to size, so that the ordinary
public-house would not be counted a hotel.
No licences should be given to hotels that
have not ten rooms, and any person to get
drink must be sleeping in the hotel. It must
be his home for the time being. In that way
something could be done that would be
helpful.
I do not know that I quite caught what he
suggested about methylated spirits. I understand that the Germans-we do not like the
Germans, but we must admit that they are
a very clever people-the Germans have discovered something called "perodine" that
is of such a nature that it does not do the
methylated spirit any harm from the point
of view of its legitimate uses if it were mixed/
with it, but would make it absolutely of
such a nature that it could not be used for
human consumption.
He
Then the matter of compensation. The hon.
Member (Mr. Barbour) went over it just in
the way one would expect a person to go over
a place where there was very thin ice.
said precious little about this compensation.
So far as I can see if this compensation is
carried into effect it seems to be entirely
forgotten that spirit grocers who evaded the

law most times and made the most moneywill get the most compensation; and that the
poor unfortunate people who tried to keep

raade less money-are now going to get less

along the lines that those who did not keep
the law and were convicted by the magistrates should get less compensation than
those who kept the law. I have not a large
experience of spirit grocers. In the town
that I live in there is only one, and there
has been no complaint against him. I think
it would be a great injustice for a person who
kept the law to be treated on the same lines
as those who evaded the law and broke it. I
think the Government should take that into
consideration.
I should like to draw attention to this
matter of railway stations at the same time.
If the bars are to be separate in another
place, I do not see any reason why they
should continue together in the railway
stations. I hope they also will be included

there should be some arrangement under

way in which they can be got. It would be
open for people to give the wrong name. Any

I do not think the hon. Member (Mr. Barbour) made a very good case when he spoke of
divorcing the grocery from the liquor traffic.
