This Bill might as well be called a Bill for
abolishing a certain class of grocer as for
abolishing the spirit grocer. A man can give
up the grocery business and keep the spirit
trade. The result will be the establishment
of the spirit grocery and the abolition of the
other business.
The new tribunal is one with which I expressed my agreement. I think it is an
immense advantage that these cases should be
tried before the resident magistrates. Our
judgment has been somewhat confused by the
ingenuity of the legal luminaries who came
to the court for the express purpose of trying
so to arrange things that the person charged
appeared to be an angel who had just dropped
an unimportant feather out of his wing. They
made it appear that the magistrates were
hound to give a dismissal. My experience was
not so much that of trying to find out the
right or wrong of the case as trying to find
out the truth from the irresponsible statements of these legal men.
I am quite in agreement with its being taken
out of the hands of the ordinary magistrates
and being put into the hands of the Resident
Magistrates, and I am more, if I may say so,
in agreement with the fact that the police
and those others complaining will have the
right of appeal in the future which they have
not had in the past. I think it would be a
great shame if one side had the right of appeal, and the other had not. I congratulate
the Government, if on nothing else, on introducing that because I believe it is exceedingly
useful. As President of the Temperance Alliance, as a Member of this House, and as
one who can honestly say he has tried his best
to help humanity as far as he possibly could,
I make an appeal to the Government here
this afternoon that they will in a kindly
and sympathetic manner consider such
amendments to this Bill as would give us the
three things we ask for and the three things
we expect, and that along with them they will
give us those other things they have been kind
enough to promise. If they do then I believe
they are doing a good thing for themselves, a
good thing for the Northern area, and a good
thing for the cause of the people in which
we are interested.
Mr. LLOYD CAMPBELL: I would first of
all like to make one personal remark, if I
may, and that is there has been a very considerable amount of controversy going on
both or platforms and in the newspapers as
to whether this Parliament has received any
mandate from the voters to deal with this
temperance question. I can only speak for
myself, and I think it is due to my constituents and to this House to know that on
almost every platform I spoke during my
election campaign I made one promise, and
only one, and that was that I would maintain the Union between Great Britain and
Northern Ireland. But in addition to that
I hoped for two things. The first was educational reform and the second was temperance reform. I think that the same thing
took place on a great many platforms, and
that we are not going behind the backs of
the electors in proposing to deal with the
question of intemperance.
Mr. ROBB: Hear, hear.

Mr. LLOYD CAMPBELL: I would like
also to say that I am a strong advocate of
temperance, and, as I will show later on,

years, but I also want to make it perfectly
clear that I am not in favour of Prohibition
I would like to congratulate the Government
oa bringing in this Bill as they have done

getting very much forrarder " towards

It is quite true that they have made

Imise in that matter-but beer only, no

I want to see temperance brought into this
area in which we are living, and what I do
feel about this Bill rather reminds me of a

something of the meaning of the word "eternity." He said it was a word the true meaning of which the human mind was incapable
of realising, and he gave a little parable
He said that if there was a block of granite,
and every person in passing by it rubbed his

of granite would be rubbed away. He said

The PRIME MINISTER (Sir James Craig) :
I am quite prepared to admit the ignorance,

Mr. LLOYD CAMPBELL, I accept that.
know perfectly well they threshed every letter

The real issue is, in my opinion-I know I do
not hold the same opinion as many hon.
Members of this House, let alone the public--
not the consumption of alcohol, but the over
consumption and the undue consumption of
alcohol, and that is what this House and this
Government and this community as a whole
are trying to prevent. I trod on the toes of
the Government just now in a remark I made,
but I will thank the Prime Minister for
having said that he pleaded guilty to the
ignorance but not to the haste. I, perhaps.
stand in an almost unique position in this
House to-day. There is no Member of the
House who can say that I am not
ardent advocate of temperance, but
probably hardly a single hon. Member
is aware of the fact that I also stand here
as a member of that wonderful organisation
that is spelt with a big "T," called "the
Trade." I am part-owner of a public-house.
and have been for a great number of years.
How many Members of this House have ever
heard of the Public-house Trust Co., Ltd.?
Of those who have heard of it, how many
have ever studied the subject, and still, to
go one further, how many know that for the
last twenty years the Public-house Trust
Company have been working in Northern
Ireland? I am glad to say that after twenty
an
years of hard digging and hard work we have
now got to the stage that we are not ashamed
to show our balance-sheet and to appeal to
the public to come and support us in a cause
which I consider is doing more good with 1egard to temperance than perhaps many of the
clauses of this Bill could do. One clause.
which I happened to notice in the Bill is
one of our foundation principles in the
Public-house Trust Company, and that 18
there should be no screening off of any portion of the premises, that all the shop should
be in full view the whole time. That is one
of our rules. Another of the great benefits
it has is that the question of private gain is
to a large extent done away with. The dividends which we might happen to earn are
limited to a very small figure payable to the
shareholders, the balance goes to the benefit
of the community, as, for instance, to workmen's clubs or district nurses, whichever the
local people seem to think should get it.
There is another point which I do not
think has probably been sufficiently
considered. Again, I ask, how many hon.
Members here know anything about the
Quebec liquor laws? The province of
Quebec has been through three phases. It
has been through the phase that we are in
here at present, it has been through prohibition, and it is now working under its own
liquor laws. When I was in Canada last
year I took a good deal of trouble to find out
how those laws were working and what the
effect of them was. I got into touch with
Sir William Stavert the head of the liquor
control in Montreal. I talked to police, I
talked to clergymen, I went up to absolute
strangers in the street, people I had never
seen before, and probably shall never see
again, and got their views on the working of
the laws. They were every one, even those
who had been prohibitionists, in favour of
the new laws of Quebec. They are interfering
very little with the freedom of the subject.
When the laws were first put in force a large
army of police and such like had to be employed, because everybody said it would be
impossible to carry them out. When I left
last November I believe the whole army in
the Province of Quebec had reduced itself
to six detectives, and the law was
being well carried out and well observed.
I think those are opinions that ought to be
considered. If I may perpetrate an Irish bull
the brightest star in this Bill is not in the
Bill. It is in the words the Prime Minister

force, and he appealed to the community to

two sides would come together and so arrange matters between themselves they could
practically put up a Bill to any Government
-no matter what it was-in power that would
unanimously go through the House.

Colonel WOODS: I beg the indulgence
of the House on this very momentous occasion. The hon. Member (Mr. Lloyd Campbell) who has just sat down referred to his
unique position in this House. I do not think
it is any more unique than the one I occupy
as the only Opposition. I am not connected
with, nor do I own part of, either a public
house or a coffee stand. I am a very temperate person-temperate in all things except in
loyalty to my friends. That I am temperate I
think the clergy have demonstrated in the
Press by publishing my application for employment with the Irish Temperance League.
There are other applications that could be
published, and, may be as occasions arise,
which I have put in for the same honourable
object-employment. The Prime Minister on
Friday introduced the Intoxicating Liquor
Bill amid a chorus of congratulation from all
sections of the party. I quite agree that the
congratulations were deserved, with one exception to which I will refer later. The
Prime Minister also read a manifesto which
he said he had drafted with extreme care. In
that he said:-
"The best way to extend our resources,
expand trade, stabilise agriculture and
other industries, re-model education, amend
the licensing laws, and to ensure a brighter
future for the great masses of workers in
our midst."
He has kept his promise regarding two of
those things. In fact he has always kept his
promise. That is one of the things for which
I admire him most. About the time that
manifesto was written a deputation of ex-
Service men waited upon the Prime Minister,
and he then promised them that they would
have direct representation upon every public
body once the Governmental departments
were all fully functioning. In fulfilment of
that promise I am here. With regard to the
other promise about this Intoxicating Liquor
Bill, some considerable light has been thrown
upon that by the hon. Member for Antrim
(Mr. Crawford) who speaking on Friday last
said:
"We will at least give him for this Parliament leisure from our attacks."
That speaks for itself. The Intoxicating
Liquor Bill has materialised, and in its present form, which includes Clause 1, is one of
the most perfect documents if the policy of
the Government is meant to create Bolshevism in Ulster. If it is meant to stir up strite
and create that which has never been in
Ulster-class hatred-it is a perfect document, and an eminently suitable weapon. The
Prime Minister said in effect that the trade
and the Temperance Party regarded this Bill
favourably, but he made no reference to the
ordinary sane electors. They do not matter
in the ordinary times when there is no election; but there will be another election perhaps some day.
Regarding the Bill itself, with the clauses
dealing with methylated spirits, illicit
stills, and some of the clauses dealing with
spirit grocers there is no fault to be found,
and they do not tend for anything but the
good of Ulster. But there are some clauses
of the Bill which I think should be put in
the form of a public competition and a prize
awarded for the best solution of the meaning
intended. I am not a lawyer myself, and I
possess no reference library, so I must depend upon the hon. and learned Members of
this House to elucidate the meaning of some
of the clauses. The compensation clause appears to me to be a base upon which to build
an argument. There are so many exceptions
for which no provision has been made that
there is nothing definite or final on which to
form an opinion.
I would respectfully beg the Government to
reconsider Clause 1 from another point of
view than that expressed, and to take into
consideration the working man. Sunday is
his only holiday. It is the only day upon
which he can get out, go where he likes, and
enjoy the freedom which is open to most
hon. Members of this House on any day. He
is not able in many instances to afford to pay
for a substantial meal with his drink.
will tell the House what I know of the operation of the substantial meal regulation in
another country. In South Africa, somewhere about eighteen to twenty years ago a
law was brought in on the Rand whereby no
one on Sunday could be served with drink in
Johannesburg unless he had passed over the
frontier. As the nearest point of the border
was 362 miles away he would have to start
early to get a drink at lunch time. So this
substantial meal regulation was introduced.
At first they used the ordinary sandwich. I
may tell you that the sandwich was a pretty
healthy affair, but when it had stayed there
for weeks it got dusty, so they got in wooden
ones; but after a while when the customers
got enthusiastic in the evenings the windows
got broken, and so they imported rubber
ones from Germany. In order to carry out
the promise to brighten the future for th
werkers in this country the Government
might bring in a few balloons or something
like that instead of ordinary sandwiches or
these rubber ones.

I ask you seriously do you think our working men are going to do without a drink
when they really want one? They will not
do it. Do you think that any Act passed by
this House will change the nature of the
rank and file Ulsterman? He will only
break the law, and you will turn him into
that most despicable creature, a sniffling
hypocrite. No one wants to see that happen
to the men of Ulster. There must be some
way out of that. They will only be filled
with envy of those who can pay for their
meals. Do you honestly consider that these
men are not intelligent enough to be out of
leading strings, that they are incapable of
thinking or incapable of judging for
themselves? Surely nothing will make
these men sober-or not exactly scher,
but you are not going to make these people
become righteous or absolutely teetotal abstainers by an Act of Parliament.
It was
not for this kind of legislation that the men
fought and died, that the men at home
worked and sweated, and that the women
took up the workmen's tasks. It was not for
this. If the Germans had won we might
have expected restrictions of this kind. I am
not connected with the Irish Temperance
Alliance, or with the trade. I only belong to
the class of ordinary and reasonably sane
citizen who has no "isms" to think about or
to worry or drive him out of his course.
I would like most respectfully to draw the
attention of the Government to that clause
in the interests of the men who are outside,
and who have not been taken into consideration in this Bill. Their opinion has not been
sought. I appeal to the Government, and
especially to the Prime Minister, to add to
the services and sacrifices he has already
made for Ulster, to endure a little further
discomfort at the hands and tongues of the
extremists, of whatever variety they may be,
for the sake of his less fortunate countrymen
who are SO feebly represented in this
House. He will be well repaid by the
understanding and the respect of the most
intelligent and most loyal democracy in the
world.
Mr. GRANT: I am sorry I cannot congratulate the hon. Gentleman (Mr. Barbour)
who moved the Second Reading on what he
said, but I can at least congratulate him on
how he said it. After the experience we had
in this House on this day week I think we
should not be rushing in to congratulate. If
we had the Prime Minister's speech as it was
given on Friday last as the Bill, I am quite
sure every hon. Member of this House would
have been perfectly satisfied. But when we
received the Bill we also received a rude
awakening. Clause 1, about which there has
been so much discussion. deals with the
question of the "substantial meal." That is
a subject on which there will be a great deal
of discussion all over the country. The hon.
Gentleman (Mr. Barbour) has stated that
the Government are prepared to leave this
matter to the Court. I think that is rather
a risky proceeding, for the gentlemen who
preside over that Court might have an
opinion about a substantial meal for themselves which might mean starvation for the
person who appeared before them. It also
leads to another grave evil, and that is that
the hotel proprietors may commence profiteering on these substantial meals. They
may charge a man 3s 6d for a biscuit, and
there would not be any provision against
that.
There is also the question, about which I
am sure the Minister of Finance will worry--
that to establish these convictions it will be
necessary to place a policeman in every hotel
in the Six Counties. I do not know whether
it is the intention of the Government to have
a Court set up in these hotels to determine
whether a meal is substantial or not before
a person gets a drink. I would suggest that
in Clause 1, page 2, the Gevernment should
leave out lines 1 to 5. That would be a
compromise in the right direction. It would
also satisfy those who at the present day are
getting up and claiming to champion the
cause of the working man. It is very
amusing that it is only on the temperance
question that these people are taking up such
an attitude, and that on all other occasions
they never give any consideration to the
working man. I think this would be a fair
compromise. If you look round the City of
Belfast to-day you will see a placard issued
by the anti-Prohibition party which seems to
my mind to furnish a strong argument for
the Temperance party in favour of the
losing of these places on Sunday. The
placard shows a wealthy man driving up to
an hotel in his motor car. He steps out and
goes into the hotel to have a "substantial
meal." On the other side of the picture is a
group of poor working men-and I may say
I cannot congratulate the Anti-Prohibition
Party on their portrayal of the working
man, because he is much more respectable
than he is shown to be in this picture. A
naval man coming home on leave, with his
bundle on his shoulder, is shown standing at
the door of the public house trying to get in,
while a policeman tells him that the public
house is closed on Sunday. I think we would
get rid of that grievance if the Government
closed all these places on Sunday, and
abolished the "substantial meal."
There is also the question of spirit groceries. I do not wish to say anything that
will be misunderstood, but in the Prime
Minister's speech on Friday last he told us
that all spirit groceries would be abolished.

. pensate people for selling illegally-manufaetured spirits and the Government will place

Sir DAWSON BATES: Hear, hear.
Mr. GRANT: I quite agree with that
Clause in the Bill, which provides that the

I would like to ask the Prime Minister,

8. Does it mean that spirit grocers who are
deprived of their licences are to be given

determine the law as it is sent to them and

spirit grocers to stick up a sort of partition

Might I point out in conclusion that the

A good deal has been said with regard to
the value of appeal. I think that is right,
but will the Crown in these cases of appeal
in which they are defeated stand in exactly
the same position as an ordinary civilian who,
when he appeals and loses his case, has got
to pay the costs, because it could be very
easy for frivolous appeals to be made even on
the part of the Crown? With regard to
Section 5, probably I am very old-fashioned
in raising the point, but you give to a constable the right to enter any place whatever
in connection with illicit alcohol. I am as
strongly in favour as any Member of this
House, or any member of the community in
Northern Ireland, in stamping this thing out,
but I am desperately jealous for the liberty
of the subject. Has one constable a right to
enter any place whatever and make investigation or inquiries? I would suggest in cases
of this sort that probably you could make
some arrangement whereby a districtinspector, or a head-constable or some other
senior officer should be present. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) We have a fine police force.
It is a young police force, and we are all
proud of it, but still in every force there must
be black sheep, and it strikes me in reading
this clause that you are putting an enormous
power in the hands of one man.
There are other points left out in this Bill
that ought to have found a place, such as
giving credit-the long pull. I do not know
whether the Prime Minister knows what the
long pull is. It is quite different from the
long pull politically. Nothing whatever is
said with regard to the strength of whisky.
Could not that be reduced? I know there
are some people who think it is much too
weak at present. I think in the interests of
the community generally it could be reduced.
I am told that the standard is much higher-
I am not sure of the exact figures-in Northern Ireland than it is in Great Britain.
There is a very important point which I am
sorry the Government have treated in a very
cavalier manner, if I may say so without
offence, and that is in reference to clubs.
The only thing that this Bill does with regard to clubs is to point out that clubs have
got to put up a notice on the wall giving
the hours during which drink can be sold.
What advantage is that going to be? I
suggest, and I think it is a reasonable suggestion, that the hours in clubs should be
the same as in other licensed houses-(Hon.
Members: Hear, hear)-and that the strictest
care should be taken that the clubs are not
established as drinking and gambling dens.
There is as much necessity for the supervision
of these clubs as there is even for getting rid
of spirit grocers or curtailing the hours for
selling drink. I do hope before the Bill
leaves Committee that the Prime Minister
will alter the measure so that clubs will be
put in exactly the same position as licensed
houses.
There is another point. I do not know
whether it will appeal to the hon. Member
for Antrim (Mr. Crawford), but I think the

liquor is sold in off licensed houses except in

in spirit groceries is due to the fact that il-

few observations. So many hon. Members

At the same time I would like to say this,

Perhaps it was my natural caution, perhaps
it was the caution developed in me in the profession I pursue, which led me to hesitate
complimenting the Prime Minister on what
he said until I had seen the terms of the Bill
he was introducing. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear). From what the Prime Minister then
said the impression certainly left upon this
House was that the Bill which the Government was introducing intended to abolish
spirit grocers. The words used by the Prime
Minister were these:-
"The abuses which have grown up around
this class of trade-(that is, the spirit
grocer) have become so flagrant as to lead
to a widespread movement for the total
abolition of spirit grocers' licences. This
we propose to effect in the present Measure
by abolishing at the end of the current
licensing year, which expires on the 30th
September next, all off-licenses in respect
of premises on which any other class of
business is carried on."
I took that, and I venture to say that 99 per
cent. of the Members of this House took that
to mean that the Government intended to
abolish spirit grocers' licenses.
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: Hear, hear.
Mr. ROBB: I took abolition to mean that
those which exist to-day should exist no
longer and that there should be no more in
the future. What was our amazement when
we got the Bill and found that that was not
what the Government intended to do at all,
but that they intended that those spirit
grocers, who before the end of the present
licensing year put up a division between one
part of the shop and another, could go on as
before, and that those who would not be in
time for the 30th September this year were
to get another year to do the same thing. The
net result was going to be this, that people
who had been accustomed to see a spirit
grocery at the corner of their street, and who
had come from knowledge of the spirit
grocery trade and the way it was carried
on to regard that house as a festering sore
in the district, would still pass that house
day and daily, seeing the same man in the
same house, selling the same thing despite
this great Government Bill.
I hope I have not been too indignant. 1
am only expressing the impression left
on my mind when I came to read
the Bill after listening to the Prime
Minister's speech. I certainly understood,
and certainly hoped, that the Bill meant
what the Prime Minister had said, or what

abolish spirit grocers, and abolish them in

Finding the provisions to be what they are
it would be with great hesitation that I

principle of our criminal law, as old as the
jury system, that no man is to be twice
vexed for the same affair. Now just let me
picture a scene. A policeman steps into a
hotel on a Sunday and comes in just at the
time that the maid has removed from
in front of me the last dish that
had contained anything to eat. Beside
me still-because I am a great person-I have
a brandy liqueur. The policeman comes in
finds me sitting there. The meal has been
removed-by me. (Laughter). The dishes
have been removed by the waitress. He gives
me a summons. He must have evidence that
I have had a substantial meal. Have I that
evidence? I can assure him I had a meal.
What otherwise can I do? He is not satisfied. I have to go down to court; the owner
of the hotel and the maid, and all the temperance reformers who came in to see what
was happening go down. I have to prove I
had a meal. Then the policeman, who is
hard to convince, says," he has only had soup,
fish, a bit of joint, some pudding, and a cup
of coffee. That is not a substantial meal."
"Oh, it is," says the magistrate. "It is
not," says the policeman, "I will take it
further." You are going to give him the
right to put me to the expense, and to put
the owner of the hotel to the expense of
going there to prove that I have had a substantial meal.
Mr. GRANT: More money for the lawyers.
Mr. HANNA: If I were to be brought to the
Bar of the House for it I would say the whole
thing is Gilbertian. A person can only once
be tried for an offence, and if you have got
a proper court, that is a court that is not influenced by any other consideration than the
discharge of its duty, that has sufficient intelligence to understand what is said to it,
that has sufficient knowledge of the law to
be able to follow the arguments even of an
irresponsible lawyer, that can do justice between the parties without any need for appeal-if the man has not been convicted. It
is a different matter to have the right of
appeal if a man has been convicted, because
there is nothing we exercise the same care
over as the liberty of an aggrieved subject
to carry his case on to a court of appeal. But
an informer-that is what a policeman is on
the occasion, though I do not say he is determined to suspect me how can he be
aggrieved? Or is it only my hon. Friend
and members of these associations, or can
any man cause the owner of a hotel to run
the risk, to satisfy the whims of my hon.
Friend, of having two trials and double expense. I do not think, whatever may happen
here, that if the public understand that and
appreciate it they will support it.
I have taken up too much time already,
but there is another matter I want to ask

during the last number of years. I refer to

most part they meet in a room rented on

well known. Will a policeman under
this Bill have the right
to go
up
on the evening that the lodge meets and

offence been committed. It should be made
perfectly clear what the intention is
in that regard. However much has

Mr. MARK: As one who did not speak on
the First Reading of this Bill, I am glad to
say I can stand here to-day and congratulate
the Prime Minister and those associated with
him on having brought in what I term a
real attempt to do away with the anomalies
which have existed in the licensing code. I
feel certain the Government are approaching this question in the way in which they
approached all other questions, and are perfectly open to be persuaded and to receive
amendments if they appeal to them as worthy
of being received. I may say, like the hon.
Member for North Belfast (Mr. Grant), that
I am not associated with any temperance
organisation, nor have I any interest whatever in the trade. I am here as the representative of a section of the community in
Northern Ireland, and I know that they have
hopes and expectations in regard to what
this Government is going to do for them in
the way of temperance reform. I feel that
when I stood to seek admission into this
House, I did give pledges which compel me
to-day to support this temperance Measure.
I do not want to criticise, but I would like
to throw out some suggestions, and if they
do verge on criticism, I am sure the Prime
Minister and those associated with him will
give them credit as being friendly criticisms.
In regard to the first Section of the Bill, a
great deal has been said, particularly as to
the substantial meal and the difficulties that
may arise concerning it, and I feel quite
satisfied that after the speech by the hon.
Member for Antrim (Mr. Hanna) the
question of the substantial meal will disappear from the Bill altogether. He has
made an unanswerable case, and whether it
is on behalf of the liquor people or on behalf of temperance reformers, I believe it
is such a case that only a person will receive
drink in the hotel in which he is a guest,
either having slept there the night before,
or having bona-fide taken a room in order to
stay there next night. I do not say any
more in regard to the first Section.
In regard to the second Section, and this
is the section that exception has been taken
to touching the Prime Minister's speech
when introducing the Bill, I cannot say that
I misunderstood a single word of what the
Prime Minister said. When he approached
this question some difficulty might have
appeared in regard to the first part of the

by the remaining words the right hon.
Gentleman used, and if any difficulty arose
in the minds of hon. Members, I am sure the
question asked by the hon. Member for West

air so far as the spirit grocers' licences were
concerned. I am one of those who believe the
spirit grocer must go absolutely. I am inclined to think as I read this Bill that part
two of the second Clause is an afterthought
pure and simple, and I came to that conclusion when I read the third Clause, which
says that compensation shall be paid in any
case where a licence becomes incapable of
being renewed. No licence under this Bill
so far as I can see, observing the regulations
will ever become incapable of being renewed.
That being so, in the Bill as it stands to-day
no compensation whatever will ever become
payable. Undoubtedly Clause 3 has been
drafted in the firm belief that the spirit
grocer was a thing of the past and
that his licence would become incapable
of being renewed. I ask the Government to stick to their first love
in this respect and to strike out the Second
Clause from line 30 starting with the words
"in respect of any premises" to the foot of
the page, and to allow Section 3 to remain
as it is, because if they retain the second
part of Section 2 they will of necessity have
to alter Section 3. I should also like, and in

the hon. Member of West Belfast (Mr. Lynn)
as well as the hon. Member for Antrim, who
has just sat down (Mr. Hanna), to add a
word in regard to the case of a person electing to give up a license, rather than make
structural alterations. He also would be entitled to receive compensation similar to that
to be given to a spirit grocer. I heard my
hon. Friend from Antrim (Mr. Hanna) saying
something about an Order which met on
licensed premises, and asking if a policeman
should have the right to enter there. I think
that if they meet on licensed premises, a
policeman should have the right to enter.
They should meet off licensed premises. Besides, I think all licensed premises should
be lock-up shops. That, I feel certain will
meet with the approval of the trade, because
it will put the honest traders, many of whom
I know, on exactly the same basis as the
dishonest man who wants to sell drink in his

with a trader for whom I have very high respect, and in discussing another individual,
he said to me: "Oh, but he made his fortune
in his kitchen." I know he made his fortune
in the kitchen, but if we could get it inserted in this Bill that a liquor shop must
be a lock-up shop then we will be placing the

As to Clause 4, 1 believe that it has the

In regard to Clause 5, where the punishment is referred to a fine of £500 or imprisonment-I do not read that to mean an

the form of an alternative so that the Resident Magistrate could award a fine of two,

It is entirely a matter of construction, and I
think the alternative should be given to the

difficulty in getting the money out of him,
whereas if you had power to say £100
or six months," it is probable that the money

Upon any application
•
I take that to mean, not any application

plication whatever for a spirit licence.
When you come down to what the Licensing
Court may require I would add there that
"The Licensing Court shall be satisfied
that no internal communication exists between the licensed premises and the remainder of the building, and that entrance
to the said licensed premises must be from
a street, county road, or other public
thoroughfare, and not from a private
yard, roadway, mews, lane, alley, or other

In many of our market towns there is no
accommodation for stabling of farmers'
horses except in the yards of public houses.
When these men come in there to prepare to
go home, or possibly when they arrive in the
morning, the first thing is a run through
the back door to get a liquor. I believe there
is much more whisky, or spirits, sold in
this country through the back doors than
there is sold through the front doors, and
it a licence holder can put a structure across
his house leaving the back door for the
trade in spirits and the front door for the
grocery trade the last state of affairs will be
worse than the first. I would ask that this
door must open on to a public thoroughfare,
or county road.
There are other minor matters which will
undoubtedly be raised
on the Committee stage. I do not wish to delay

lated spirits and poteen, upon which both the

Another matter, which I have heard put

State drink. We will find the good people

perhaps of Ballymoney and Ballymena, adjourning down to "The Point," and after
a substantial meal at the Magilligan Point
Hotel we will find them having recourse
to Greencastle on the Free State side, and

The average valuation of the farmers in that

fully fledged publican roll in wealth, with

In the speeches of some of the members on

Mrs. CHICHESTER: May I just say a few
words from the point of view of one who
does not belong to either section holding
very extreme views on this question? First
of all I join with my colleague in the representation of Derry (Mr. Mark) in his
congratulations to the Government on this
Bill. I cannot understand the observations
of the hon. Member for Antrim (Mr. Hanna)
when he said that this Bill was framed in a
hurry. It does not seem, to my mind anyway, to bear the smallest imprint of haste.
We know it is some months since the right
hon. Gentleman (The Prime Minister) who
brought in this Bill made his promise to the
House, and the Bill is the result of his own
considered deliberation and that of the
Cabinet. I want to congratulate him on the
fact that they have not been swayed in any
way, or carried away by the flood of
impassioned oratory which has been
poured forth in the last few months
or by the floods of literature which
have been poured out in the same way.
In bringing this Bill forward I considerand I am sure many other hon. Members of
the House, although they have put forward
certain criticisms, will also consider-that
the Prime Minister has shown himself to be
a veritable Ulysses in his ability to steer a
straight course, and the course he considered
to be the right and proper one. He has
passed between Scylla and Charybdis, and he
has passed all the Syrens who have been
singing sweetly to him from all sides.
But in doing this he has only carried out
what we expected of him. He has steered the
ship of this Bill into what I hope will be
calm waters when it goes into Committee, just
as he has steered the ship of our State so far
safely past so many rocks and shoals.
He
has given us not only a Temperance Bill but
a moderate and temperate Bill, although some
hon. Members may not agree with the definition. I am one of those who believe that
drink, taken moderately, can do no harm.
But I am afraid that unfortunately moderation is not always met with either in the
taking of drink or in the expression of views
on this particular subject by either side. I
do not believe that evil can be eliminated by
any Act of Parliament. That is merely a
truism. I have seen some of the results of
prohibition in the United States of America,
but I do believe you can make it difficult to
do wrong, and I also believe this Bill will
make it difficult for the publican and the
spirit grocers who may be left and the illicit
distillers to infringe the law.
I cannot agree with the statement that has
been made that this is a Measure which will
do comparatively little good. I look upon it
as the greatest blow that could possibly have
been struck for temperance reform. It has
been said that it is not a revolutionary
Measure, but to my mind it will in time send
the tree of intemperance crashing to the
ground, because it has struck at its very root,
and the branches of that tree will wither and
fall off for want of sap. I refer particularly
to the last half of the Bill, and if only the
last half had been brought in I think the
Prime Minister would have deserved our

rate, this is a terrible vice, and one which

The PRIME MINISTER: I think I am
wise to rise at this moment after, if I may
say so, a most eloquent and charming speech
from the hon. Member for Derry (Mrs. Chichester)-(hon. Members: Hear, hear)-to

I would like, first of all, to reply to the complaint made by the hon. and learned Member

scolded me somewhat severely for having put
a better aspect upon the Bill than the Bill
deserved, when he had his legal eye trained
upon it the day after it was issued. Well, I
wish to assure the House how difficult it isand I am sure the House will recognise the
difficulty-in a First Reading speech to cover
not only all the questions that appear to the
person himself, but all the questions which
may be anticipated from others who look
upon his Measure with a fresh eye, and of
the utter impossibility of anticipating exactly
where serious charges may be made such as
have been made by my hon. and learned
Friend (Mr. Robb). I had no intention whatever of misleading the House in any way.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) And may I
say to my hon. and learned Friend (Mr. Robb)
how foolish it would be for any Minister to
make a speech on one day in terms which he
thinks are rather glowing and to give instructions the very next day to send to hon. Members the Bill that they might see whether he
has properly interpreted its terms or not.
No, if there has been a misunderstanding in
the matter I am quite prepared to take the

arose, perhaps from negligence on my part,
but certainly not from any intention to misrepresent the Bill to a single Member of the
House or of the public. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.)
Mr. ROBB: Will the Prime Minister allow
me to say that I never intended to charge
him with deliberate misrepresentation.
The PRIME MINISTER: That is very
handsome, and I am quite satisfied. I shall
not pursue the topic any more, except to reiterate that if one is addressing one's own
child one may take, perhaps, a view which
is different from that which those may take
who are looking at it afterwards in the cold
light of day. The serious difference arises
bere over the question. not of total Sunday
closing, but of mixed businesses.
Mixed
(Hon.
businesses gave the trouble.
Members: Hear, hear.) On making a close
inquiry I and my colleagues discovered that
there were no complaints-no serious complaints-by the police authorities or the
public generally against the owners of offlicences who dealt with wines and spirits
alone. Very few, if any, complaints reached
us of the style of house that sells wines
and spirits for consumption off the premises.
The whole of the charges surrounded those
places where the mixed businesses of
groceries and spirits were carried on. I do
not believe any wording could be invented
more strict to carry out that purpose than
the wording implied here in the Bill. I
am going to elaborate this so that hon.
Members may see the great difficulties one
gets into.
Having first of all closed all mixed businesses, whether on-licences or off-licences,
the fact then remains that by the choice
which is allowed in the Bill a certain
number of off-licences still remain, but not
off-licences affected by the mixed businesses.
The question is how to deal with them
after we get them totally separated from the
other business, and have imposed upon them
a much more strict supervision by the police
and by the magistrates. Certainly it was
a democratic move on our part, and not a
move dictated by what we call the upper
classes, that led us to believe that a large
section of the Belfast public would really
resent and suffer from the complete extinction of the whole of these licences at
once. I will tell hon. Members why. It
appears and I heard this argued very
forcibly by representatives of the shipyards
-that there is a certain section who do not
send their wives or their children into the
public-houses to get a bottle of ale or a
bottle of stout, or whatever the men take
with their supper or any other meal. They
prefer to send their wives or their children
into one of those off-licence premises which
have hitherto been known as spirit groceries
in order to get hold of what they want to
drink after a hard day's work at the Island.
The question arises, if you wipe out with
a cut of the knife the whole of these licences
that are at present attached to the mixed
businesses there are only two courses for
those men to pursue. You either drive them
straight into the nearest public-house to get
their bottle of stout or their bottle of beer
for their meal, or else you create an absolute
monoply for one firm alone who deal with
this off-licence business-the wine and
spirit business. There seemed to us
to be a strong case there to meet, and
we decided to get rid of the mixed businesses
altogether. Well, we did that by a stroke
of the pen. They are got rid off as mixed
businesses. They are then converted, where
conversion can be done, into a self-contained

Members seemed to talk about running up
a partition and the trick is done! Not at all.
The utmost care is taken in the Bill to ensure
that these cases must come before the Licensing Authority. Plans have to be produced,
and it has to be proved that the premises
are suitable to be carried on as such. We
say, first of all, that you cannot tell how
many will fall by the wayside in the normal
course, owing, say, to their profits being so
small that it will be hardly worth their
while to carry on the mixed business any
longer. Second, you cannot tell how many
will be affected by breaches of the law,
because the machinery in the Bill is very
much tightened up to catch them if they
misuse the privilege. You cannot tell how
many will fall by the wayside there. Third,
you cannot tell the number of those who,
having a chance of picking up three years'
profit, putting it in their pocket, and
stopping the business altogether, will add
largely to the number of those who fall by
the wayside.
This is the first attempt with a Bill of this
kind in Ireland for I cannot say how many
years, and it is utterly preposterous for any
hon. Member to prophesy what the actual
results of this Bill will be in the future.
What I say to the House is this: Give the
Act a trial. We are a young Parliament.
One great advantage we have is that we can
discuss all these points that have been raised
in a very friendly way in Committee, and
see what it is possible for the Government to
do without upsetting the balance of the Bill,
because we must not upset the balance of the
Bill. I do not say we can go very far, but
where we can meet Members in the smaller
matters raised, or put in some word which
will make clear our intention with regard
to the spirit grocers, then I say that can be
done quite amicably among ourselves. I
may go this far-supposing, for the sake of
argument, my intentions-I cannot tell what
the intentions of anybody else in the House
are supposing my intentions with regard to
these spirit grocers' licences, to give them
their old name, are not fulfilled by this Bill,
then I am prepared to pursue the matter
further, and to see that the spirit that I
intend to be in the Bill is faithfully and
justly carried out. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) I do not suppose for a moment that
the Bill will be completely perfect. This is
the start-off, but I will say this, that the
Bill has been framed most cautiously in
order to hold the balance of what I consider
fair between those who are licensed by the
Bill and those who are desirous of helping
forward the temperance cause in our Six
Counties.
There have been several other matters
discussed, and I would like to speak rather
cautiously about them, because some are
legal points and I propose during the Committee stage to have beside me the Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of Home
Affairs (Mr. Megaw) along with my hon.
Friend whom I would like to congratulate on
his speech this afternoon (Mr. Barbour).
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) We have taken
great pains in the matter of methylated
spirits. We have made inquiry, and as my
hon. Friend (Mr. Barbour) said this afternoon, there seems to be no better remedy
than to class the sale of methylated spirits
as poison. You could not go much further
than that. All you could do would be to put
into the spirit something of such a noxious
nature that even the most thirsty individual
would hesitate to take it as a drink.
But I
am told that there are grave objections to
that course. However, we will make still further inquiry between now and the Committee
stage, and if our London advisers can make
any suggestion from the chemical standpoint
we will be only too happy to incorporate
something of the kind. We will also consider
the point raised by my hon. Friend the
Member for Derry (Mrs. Chichester) who
has just left the House-with regard to the
other intoxicant, ether.
I would like to deal with the speech of my
hon. Friend the Member for North Belfast
(Mr. Lloyd Campbell). The gravamen of his
charge was that the Bill did not go far
enough. That again is a matter of opinion.
Another thing he said was that the penalties
are not half severe enough. I say let us give
the Bill a chance. Let us get it made an
Act as quickly as we can. Let us put it into
operation. Hitherto there has been great
laxity in carrying out the Licensing Laws,
and this Government is determined to see
that the law is properly enforced in every
way it possibly can be under the new Statute.
He then said that the fines were not suffici
ently severe. Well, we can talk over that in
Committee. Do not let us go too far and
perhaps make the thing absurd, but let us
consider very cautiously whether it is possible
to amend here and there these penalties that
have been prescribed under the various
sections.
My next remarks are in regard to the whole
question of Sunday closing, and if I may I
will take the opportunity of congratulating
the hon. and gallant Member (Col. Woods)
who has taken his seat and has made his
maiden speech. I may congratulate him on
the way he made that speech. I think it is
a credit to the House that a new Member
has been able to stand at the Table, under
some possible embarrassment, and to give
his views, which views will receive the cour

tesy they are entitled to. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) His objection was to having
Sunday closing at all. But if we cut Sunday
closing out of the Bill, then I will have
nothing more to do with the Bill. The Bill
is for the Sunday closing of public houses,
which is the great claim made by the
Temperance Party in this House, to which I
gave my assent. Therefore, it must be
carried out or the whole Bill goes.
After all, Sunday closing exists in the Six
Counties. It is only in the City of Belfast
that there is the opening of public houses
at all. It is no great hardship. They have
it in Scotland, and quite recently they have
brought in a Bill in the Isle of Man. The
Isle of Man at one time was a place where
people went over to enjoy themselves and
there was any amount of drinking on Sunday.
The Isle of Man came to the conclusion that
the tourist traffic, I presume, will be increased
by the fact that the public houses will be
closed on Sunday. Therefore it does not
annoy me in the slightest degree when it is
pointed out that we are taking a step which
will cause great inconvenience to the public.
I can only say myself-and as Prime Minister I am just as much entitled to let myself
go in a personal way as the hon. Member
beside me (Mr. Barbour)-I can only say this,
and I say it from my heart, that when I
was a boy and as I steadily grew up I met
a great many good and dear friends who took
far too much drink. A very large number of
those friends of those days are dead and dead
for many years. They died undoubtedly as
the effect of having taken too much drink.
My hon. Friend struck the right note when
he said that half of the drinking was due to
the sporting instinct-standing drinks for five
because the other five stood him. I do think
that a vast amount of good would be done
if the younger generation in Ulster would
not look upon it so much as a point of honour
to see that those debts are paid very early
in the day and certainly not on Sunday.
That has been my personal experience. I am
quite sure hon. Members can testify to the
fact. But is it not to be hoped that there is
some pleasure to be got in some other form
than by spending the whole Sunday morning
in a club instead of going out and enjoying
one's self in the fresh air. Must one remain
inside a bar in a small room and sit there
drinking? It does no one any good. That is
my personal feeling about Sunday closing,
that temptation is taken away especially
from the young people.
Then we
come to the vexed question as
to how far we can carry it out. I do not
say we can carry it out absolutely
straight away.
I do not know that very
restrictive measures all over will tend to
help, if it is carried out in any vindictive
manner. I would like to carry the community
with us.
I would rather this Bill was not
necessary, and that we could effect the same
thing by persuasion. This will help those
who are anxious and desirous of preventing
the youth of Ulster being brought up with
the idea that drinking is a manly way of
spending time. Therefore, we do take the
responsibility in the Bill of taking a step
in that direction. I would point out that
there are now 2,162 public-houses holding
seven-day licences in Northern Ireland. There
are only 55 hotels, which pay a reduced
licence duty as hotels, and on these premises
entertain bona-fide travellers. I think in
future if there are only 55 instead of 2,162
surely that is going a long way, at all events,
without coming down upon those who are
stopping in hotels and counting the hotels
as their homes for the time being. Whatever
takes one into the hotel everyone looks upon
it as being his home for the time being.
If we can get so far the full sense of the
House will agree. Then we ome down to
the person who calls in one of these hotels
in order to meet a friend there and have
a meal and have a drink. I say let us consider
very carefully exactly what the sense of the
House is. Do let us see how far the House
can go. Do not take it from me that there
is any promise on my part. I do not want
it to be said afterwards that I said something
that I was not able to perform. Criticise the
actual words of the Bill. There is another
point. The hon. Member for North Belfast
(Mr. Lloyd Campbell) and the hon. Member
for Antrim (Mr. Hanna) have both said that
there was no compensation being given for
on-licences, that we were differentiating
between off-licences of a mixed nature and
on-licences of a mixed nature where they are
compelled to adapt their premises. I think
I recollect mentioning on this day week when
I introduced the Bill on First reading-I
think I pointed out that the very fact that
licences had been granted-on licences to
these particular premises, which really should
not have been done if the strict law had
been observed and the justices at the time
the licence was granted had done their duty,
gave no claim. I am apprised at all events
that a good case could have been made that
they should not have been allowed to have
the licences on those premises. What really
is the state of affairs? It means that for
some years many years-these grocers, originally grocers, have enjoyed licences, which,
if a strict application of the law had been
made, they could not keep. In other words
there was a good case for not granting the
licence. Therefore, I think in that case it
is really not a matter for compensation
because they have enjoyed a privilege which

The PRIME MINISTER: I really think

It seems to me he has met a case of great

Friend stated, that he knew the Trade would

Friend made that statement, because it confirms what I said last week that there is
not so much difference after all in some
things between the Trade and the hon. Member
for Derry (Sir Robert Anderson). I think my
hon. Friend from West Belfast (Mr. Lynn)
also made the same suggestion. There is not
such a great difference that they could not
come together and talk to one another like
reasonable beings, as all Ulstermen are. If

differences I am perfectly certain they can
produce on the Table here something we
could all accept as an agreed Measure. Of
that I am quite confident. What action did
my hon. Friends representing the Temperance
party in this House take? I came quite
sincerely and offered a Commission to inquire
into all these matters that have been threshed
to and fro, and my hon. Friends opposite all
objected. They said, "No, if you have a
Commission you have delay; if you have a
Commission it will go on for years, and we
want to get temperance reform." Then what
did they do? They threw it on me to do
the thing for them, and when I do it for
them they pick holes in every word of the
Bill. They have entrusted me with about as
difficult a job as anyone was ever asked to
do, to tackle this without arousing great
feeling through the whole of Ulster and
upsetting the equilibrium to such an extent
that to go further might be a danger to
all of us. Therefore, this Bill has been
brought up in no vindictive manner, but with
the desire to help all those causes which hon.
Members have so much at heart.
My hon. Friends have been working sincerely and earnestly for some months past
with one single desire to produce something
which will be fair between all parties, and
I do hope and trust that when this Bill is
on the Statute Book, as I confidently believe
it will be, that a truce will be called, and
all this acrimony will cease, and that the
thousands and thousands of pounds that are
thrown away in advertising and in pasting
up all sorts of things on our hoardings will
be saved. As my hon. Friend (Mr. Donald)
said very wisely last Friday this money could
be given to some of the charities in our
midst who are suffering every day, and who
must be nauseated by seeing the money
flowing about when they themselves are in
so much need and want. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) I know the difficulties; I know
perfectly well that between now and the
Committee stage of the Bill there will be
considerable talk. The hon. Member for
North Belfast (Mr. Grant) said, "No compensation," other hon. Members say "Vary your
compensation; give those good boys who never
had a conviction recorded against them more
than the bad boys." I think for the credit
of Ulster, if we look at it in a financial way,
it is much better for us to recognise that
compensation is due. It would be a terrible
thing for all classes of business if there was
any feeling that the principle was laid down
that you could take away those privileges
that were granted in law and not give the
owners some compensation for such a great
disturbance of their business.
Then there is another point. I was always
taught, and here again the lawyers will at
least keep me right, that when a man was
brought before a Bench and sentenced, that
the sentence, whatever it was, high or low,
good or bad, wiped out the offence. I do
not know what those persons have been

over - consumption. Immediately he

Here is the importance of this matter. A
question was asked in the Imperial House
as to the total number in Great Britain,

of these places for the sale of intoxicating
liquor-more than three times our quota.

We have got to go very cautiously.

1. Dr. MORRISON asked the Parliamentary
Secretary to the Minister of Education what
position Registered Secondary Teachers
engaged in educational work that is not done
in a grant-earning institution will occupy
under the new Education Act in regard to
salary and pensions?
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY TO
THE MINISTRY OF EDUCATION (Mr.
McKeown): The new Education Act will in
no way directly affect the salaries of
Registered Secondary Teachers engaged in
educational work that is not done in a grantearning institution.

THE BUDGET.
Statement by Minister of Finance.
Motion nade, and Question proposed,
"That this House approves the proposals of
the Government for meeting the financial requirements of the year."
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): I am sure the House will realise
that it is not always easy to make figures
either illuminative or interesting, but I
trust I shall not have to test the physical
endurance of hon. Members to too great an
extent to-day.
Introducing his Budget the Imperial
Chancellor appropriately remarked that a
Budget framed in a world of rapidly changing values must necessarily test to the
greatest extent the powers and wisdom of
the men engaged upon it. It may seem presumptuous to compare the presentation of the
modest statement of our Provincial accounts
with that of the balance sheet of the Kingdom. And yet it cannot be gainsaid that
our Budget-simple and unpretentious
though it appear-is, mutatis mutandis-exactly affected by the same varying conditions of uncertainty, both of revenue and
expenditure, which render the Imperial
Chancellor's task so difficult.
We are, perhaps fortunately, relieved of
any discussions in this House on the incidence and effect of various forms of taxation,
and of that much-debated question as to
whether a free trade or protective policy is
best suited to our general economic conditions. Our Southern neighbours have already begun to realise the complexity of the
problem, and no doubt before long we shall
hear a great deal of this subject from that
quarter.
Our main concern at present is not whether
our present fiscal system is good or bad, but
rather to reach some settled principle as to
how the revenue produced by the system
should be apportioned between the Central
Authority and our own State.
Hon. Members will, of course, have
observed the reduction in the rate of Income
Tax, etc., and the lowered duties on beer,
proposed in the Chancellor's Budget last
month. The effect of these reductions and
the cloud of depression still overshadowing
our industries, and the establishment of a
new Customs frontier between Northern and
Southern Ireland, all introduce elements of
speculation into our estimates of Revenue,
which can only be resolved a year hence,
when we make up our accounts.
Forecasts of expenditure are more definite
in their character than revenue, but even in
this department the elements of conjecture
necessarily enter.
The legislative proposals at present under
discussion in this House will have their effect
on the expenditure side of our account, whilst
the measures directed to the provision of a
housing subsidy, and the amelioration of

Australia at present the identical problem

is causing some concern, and threatens
to disturb the harmonious relations of the
different States of that great Commonwealth
--that is, the allocation from the federal

If, then, Australia with more than 20

a difficulty in apportioning its revenues to
the different units of the federation, we in
Ulster, with our limited experience of the
system, can hardly expect to adapt ourselves
to the changed and novel conditions, at the
very beginning of our autonomous career.
These generalisations, which I have ventured to submit, may seem scarcely germane

their relevancy.

GENERAL REVIEW.
Reviewing last year as a whole, the outstanding feature of the finances will be seen
to be the realisation of a surplus. While
the revenue, for the collection of which the
Northern Government has responsibility, has
shown an increase of about £140,000 over the
Budget Estimate, the revenue from the taxes
under the control of the Imperial Authorities
has failed to reach expectations by as much
as £500,000. As already mentioned, it will be
obvious to Members that only by the closest
possible examination of every detail of proposed expenditure and by the enforcement
of the strictest economy in every branch of
administration has the realisation of a
balance on the right side been rendered
possible. The realisation of a surplus on the
first full year of the Northern Government's
operations is specially significant in view of
the oft-repeated assertions of the state of
bankruptcy into which Northern Ireland
would soon fall once it had taken over its
own self-government.
There are still some questions in respect
of last year's accounts outstanding, which
will be decided by the Colwyn Committee, and
which we trust will accrue to the benefit of
our finances. On these matters, which are
sub judice, I can obviously make no comment.
This matter, however, cannot now affect
last year's accounts, and must be dealt with
as adjustments in the present year.
1923-24
I have now taken leave of the first complete
financial year of our existence as an autonomous State, and turn my attention to that
which still largely lies ahead of us.
Following the method I adopted in setting
out last year's estimates, which had the great
advantages of clearness and simplicity, I propose to divide my statement into the three
separate departments of-
First: our normal accounts of income and
expenditure;
Second: our special accounts;
Third: our capital accounts.
I will, therefore, proceed at once to submit
estimates of expenditure under the first head,
and afterwards show the revenue which may
be expected to meet it.

The increase in this estimate is accounted
for by a larger provision for borrowing for
Local Loans and Unemployment Insurance,
as well as the increased Sinking Fund, cost
of Ulster Savings Certificates and Land Annuities,

TRANSFERRED REVENUE.
Hon. Members will appreciate the difficulty
of framing an estimate of the yield even of
those taxes under our own control, having
regard to the lack of statistics and our
limited experience upon which to work.
With regard to Estate Duties, for instance,
it must be obvious that the revenue from
these duties is from its very nature subject
to wide fluctuations which engender caution
in framing an estimate, particularly as the
receipts in the past year included a windfall
of seventy thousand pounds from one single
estate.
Similarly, with regard to stamps, there was
a single receipt last year of approximately
£25,000, which must be regarded as
windfall.
a
With regard to Excise Duties, the main
item is the Entertainments Duty Tax.
It will probably be of interest to the House
to know that our Government propose to incorporate a provision in the Finance Bill
freeing Agricultural Shows from the impost
of the Entertainments Tax. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) This, however, will make little
or no difference to the total revenue from
that duty.
The full effects of the reduction in the
proceeds of licence duties, consequent on the
passing of the Intoxicating Liquor Bill, will
not be felt this year, but the total reduction
is estimated at £8,000 a year.
Having regard to the general conditions of
employment-which are not peculiar to our
own Province, but which are world-wide-1
have tried to avoid over-estimating the revenue from our own taxes, although I do
not think that the decrease which I estimate
is likely to arise in the current year need be
taken as a pessimistic outlook
finances.
on our
I venture to hope that my estimates will be
fully realised, and with a revival in trade
and a nearer approach to more prosperous
conditions of industry such as we hope will
obtain in the very near future, I think that
the year will show even better results than
I have anticipated.
RESERVED REVENUE.
The establishment of a Customs frontier
between North and South Ireland introduces
new conditions affecting our revenue, and in
a minor degree, perhaps, our expenditure.
which have not yet been fully felt.
That the change will involve both North
and South in additional cost is inevitable.
The expense of maintaining Customs' stations
on our side of the Border we regard as a
British charge, and therefore that part of
the arrangement need give us little concern.
But whilst we fully realise that the change
will result in considerable inconvenience to
commercial interests, both North and South,
it is impossible to state at this early stage of
the experiment the exact effect on our
Customs' revenue.
The Estimates which I have submitted on
this head have been framed by the Imperial
Treasury authorities-that is Customs and
Excise who admit their difficulty in making
accurate forecasts of the yield of Customs
and Excise duties in the changed conditions.

AGRICULTURE.
The conditions in Ulster in regard to
agriculture are by no means similar to those
obtaining across the water, and the steps
which should be taken to give some measure
of relief to the agricultural community in
these days of serious depression is at present
under the consideration of my right hon.
Friend, the Minister of Agriculture..
though it is not possible at present to indicate
with any degree of certainty what relief
measures will be adopted, the proposals will
be submitted to the House when the various
schemes, now under consideration, have been
fully explored.
HOUSING.
Al-
The present provision in the estimates for
housing grants to local authorities amounts
to a sum of £27,500, apart from the sum of
£16,470 provided by way of relief to rural
district councils under the Acts relating to
labourers' cottages, but this latter expenditure is in a category by itself and does not
need any particular comment.
As regards the £27,500, this sum is almost
entirely required to meet the subsidy payable
to the Belfast Corporation in respect of
housing schemes under the Housing (Ireland)
Act, 1919, the subsidy being based on a figure
not exceeding 25s for each pound of rent
actually collected.
Arising out of a question recently put, I
stated in this House that the Ministry of
Finance would be prepared to consider proposals to get rid of this liability by means
of a cash payment, the loss on the sale of
the houses being borne both by the Government and by the Corporation. On the
assumption that some such course will be
adopted before the close of the financial year
I have made suitable provision in my Capital
Budget for such a commutation scheme, my
intention being that Government shall raise
the money to pay to the Corporation the
Government's share of the loss by means of
borrowings on Capital Account to be repaid
by a terminable annuity chargeable annually
on the votes.
I anticipate, however, that this will not
be my only liability in respect of housing
subsidies for the current year. Although
our Government has not come to any final
decision in the matter, it seems evident that
some further measure of assistance, possibly
on the lines of the English Bill now before
the Imperial House of Commons, the outstanding feature of which is a subsidy not
exceeding £6 a year per house for a period
of 20 years, may have to be made in Northern
Ireland, and I have, accordingly, made some
provision under this head in my item for
supplementary estimates.
EDUCATION.
Hon Members may inquire whether I
have made provision in this year's Budget
for any special expenses which may arise in
the event of the Education Bill becoming
law at an early date.
To this I would reply that the machinery
set up by the Bill cannot in the main
become operative until a considerable period
has elapsed.
The transference of elementary schools to
local authorities, and the time occupied in
working out the numerous details will be
considerable. I anticipate, therefore, that
during the present financial year very little
more than the normal assistance hitherto
given to local authorities for education purposes will be required. For this I have made
provision in the Estimates.
Some increased expenditure, however, over
and above the provision now made in the
Votes of the Ministry of Education may be
incurred in implementing the undertaking
given by the noble Marquess, that in the
case of teachers in Secondary schools such
Government assistance as would be given in
supplementing their exigious salaries would
materialise in the present financial year.
Provision for an increase in the staff of
the Ministry may also have to be made, and
for these two purposes I propose to include
a sum in the Supplementary Estimates.
Hon. Members may desire to know what
the ultimate cost under the Bill will be, so
far as the Northern taxpayer and the
Northern ratepayer are concerned.
Mr. McGUFFIN: Hear, hear.
Mr. POLLOCK: I do not, however, care
at this stage to assume the role of a prophet.
more especially as my opinions must, to a
certain extent, be affected by my hopes and
fears as to the decision of the Colwyn Committee on the question of Ulster's contribution to the Imperial services. If the
arguments put forward by the Northern
Government are accepted, there need be no
fear that all the educational benefits for
which provision is made in the Bill will be
available for the Province.
The only other educational matter on which
I need comment is the provision of a College
and Hostel for the training of National
School Teachers. I have included a sum of
£32,000 in the Estimates for the preliminary
part of the work, the whole cost of which

The Budget.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Mr. Pollock].
will be very considerable, and will, I hope,
be recoverable from the Imperial authority.
The provision I have made for Supplementary Estimates in connection with these
services is a sum of £225,000. Deducting this
figure from the total of £4,681,000 it will be
seen that there is a sum of £4,456,000 available as our Imperial contribution.
Before making any statement on the
question of our contribution, I desire to draw
attention to the other two items of our
Balance Sheet-the Special Department and
Capital Department-about which I think no
very minute explanation will be required.
SPECIAL DEPARTMENT.
The principal item of expenditure in the
Special Department is that of the Special
Constabulary, the provision for which is not
such as might be expected in normal times,
but still continues a necessary part of the
defence forces of the State.
The estimated cost of the force for this
year is £1,580,000, of which the Imperial
Government has agreed to contribute
£1,500,000. Thus £80,000 must be borne on
our own Votes, and appears under its own
head in our "normal" Budget.
We have always contended that the responsibility for the protection of the State from
attack by hostile forces falls outside the
ordinary preservation of law and order by
the Civil power, and the Imperial Government
has generously admitted this claim. It will
be noted that the reduction in this Estimate
as compared with last year's expenditure
exceeds one million pounds.
The additional items in the Special Department are the provision of £750,000 as the
second instalment of the grant from the
Imperial Government for malicious injuries,
and a further Vote of £200,000 as part of the
Unemployment Relief Grant of £500,000 to
be administered by the Ministry of Labour.
CAPITAL COMMITMENTS.
The third department of my financial
statement deals with capital undertakings,
which are not expected to impose any liability on the State.
These undertakings are mainly concerned
with the borrowing of funds to be loaned to
Public Authorities, and Unemployment Insurance, which should naturally be repaid
in due course.
In furtherance of these aims I anticipate
that the Ulster Savings Certificates will produce £500,000, and in order to meet the heavy
calls by the Unemployment Insurance Fund,
temporary additional borrowings will have to
be undertaken to the extent of £531,000.
The outgoings on this account during the
year are estimated-for loans to local authorities at £300,000, and for the Unemployment Insurance Fund, £700,000.
For small repayments of Ulster Savings
Certificates I have provided £35,000.
CAPITAL BUDGET.
Loans to Local Authorities.
As I have just indicated, provision has
been made in the Budget for Capital Loans
to local authorities and for other analogous
purposes, amounting to a sum of £300,000.
Last year a sum of £50,000 was provided and
the actual expenditure only amounted to
£14,000. The present figure of £300,000 is
largely conjectural, and if I were merely to
make provision for loans to which the Exchequer is definitely committed at the present
date, a sum of £50,000 would suffice. But I
am aware that in carrying out schemes in
respect of which grants have been received
from the Unemployment Relief Committee,
a number of local authorities intend to avail
themselves of borrowings from the Government in order to raise the money required to
meet the considerable expenditure on such
works, for which they themselves remain
responsible. In addition, I anticipate that
before the year is closed, borough and urban
councils may have embarked upon extensive
schemes of house construction for the working
classes, and I therefore consider it right to
make a fairly liberal provision in this
respect. Of course, if such anticipated
borrowings do not mature, it will be unnecessary for the Government to raise, by
means of temporary borrowings, the whole
of the considerable sum, viz., £531,000, for
which provision has been made in the
Capital Budget for the year.
In this connection it may not be inopportune for me to dwell for a moment on the
policy to be adopted by the Northern Government in lending money to local authorities
for public utility purposes. As Members are
aware, this money was, under the Imperial
Parliament, advanced from the Local Loans
Fund-a fund which was created by the
floating of Local Loans Stock. So far as
Northern Ireland is concerned, the Local
Loans Fund has ceased to be available either
for the Government itself or for local authorities who seek to obtain loans, and so
far the only substitute which the Northern
Government has provided is the issue of
Ulster Savings Certificates.
It may be of interest to note that under
the Imperial system it was incumbent upon
the Treasury to invest in Local Loans Stock
Finance Minister's Statement. 1054
The Budget.
28 MAY 1923
half the proceeds of National Saving Certificates. The object of this was two-fold, viz.,
to give local authorities, so to speak, a larger
credit in the Fund from which they could
draw, and incidentally to encourage them to
take an active interest in the sales of
Savings Certificates in their localities.
point of fact, however, this requirement was
to a great extent unnecessary, as the borrowings from the fund fell far short of half
of the amounts realised by the sale of the
Certificates.
In
So far, no attempt has been made by the
Ministry of Finance to co-relate the sales of
Ulster Savings Certificates to the borrowing
needs of local authorities. It would be unsound finance to borrow, by means of Certificates repayable in 10 years, a sum of money,
and then lend the same amount to local
authorities for a term of years which, in most
cases, would vary from 40 to 60 years. So
long, however, as the demands of local authorities keep very much below the amounts
raised by the sale of Ulster Savings Certificates, as so far has happened, there can be
little danger in such a system of finance,
but if during the course of the coming year
borrowings by local authorities show a rapid
upward tendency, it may be necessary for the
Government to consider the flotation of a
Stock corresponding to the Local Loans Stock.
The financing of advances to the Unemployment Fund, which are in the nature of shorttime loans, could very properly be left to the
sale of such short-dated security as Savings
Certificates.
I do feel, however, that in deciding on
individual applications from local authorities
for loans for public utility services, due
weight must be given, at any rate in the case
of the larger centres, to the amounts raised
in the several localities by means of the
sale of Ulster Savings Certificates. Smaller
localities, who have not the same facilities
for borrowing either from banks or in the
open market, can hardly be hampered by any
such proviso: but the whole subject of securing closer co-operation between the various
localities and the Ministry of Finance in
regard to the sale of Certificates, more particularly to the small investor as a thrift
measure, is one which I am now carefully
considering.
I have endeavoured to explain in detail
the full financial requirements of the State
for the present year and the provision which
has been made to satisfy them. It only now
remains for me to summarise our position.
I have shown that after providing our
actual necessities for the year, there should
remain a sum of £4,456,000 to make good our
Imperial contribution and to furnish us with
such a surplus as will enable us to carry
out measures of education and social welfare,
which have suffered by neglect in the past.
I had hoped that the decision of the committee which will settle the amount of our
contribution would have been reached in
time to enable me to incorporate the result
in my Budget Statement, which I deliberately
held up with that object. I felt, however,
that I could not, without discourtesy to the
House, continue longer to withhold the statement of our financial outlook for the year.
But no one has a fuller appreciation of the
magnitude and complexity of the task of the
Colwyn Committee than I have, and I can
hardly pretend to feel surprise at the amount
of time and deliberation which are being
devoted to the solution of the many difficult
problems which necessarily surround the
whole question of the financial relations of
the subordinate State to the Central
Authority.
Although our financial future is still undetermined, I am sanguine enough to feel
confident that full justice will be done to
Ulster by the distinguished men who constitute the tribunal which determines the issue.
I beg to move.

There was one thing that struck me in

Here again, even at the risk of being guilty

hon. Friend (Mr. Pollock) to exercise the

My right hon. Friend has said, with regard

with
people
whom it would fructify,
