Before I sit down there is one point that
arises in regard to the Budget statement to
which I would like to direct the attention
of my right hon. Friend, namely, our whole
system of accounting in connection with our
new Parliamentary system. It strikes me
that we are sticking to old traditions, though
we are living under new conditions. In my
judgment we need a new system of accounting,
which will fit in with the peculiar conditions
which have arisen. There is another point
to which attention ought to be directed, and
that is that only something like 12 per cent.
of our revenue and 40 per cent. of our

millions really the amount for which we are

I am sure my right hon. Friend, with his

on the Joint Exchequer Board, but I am
sure he is doing his best to see that there

the things that reconciled me to the establishment of this Parliament was that it would
be possible for us to carry on our work

es-
I have been one of those who have claimed
for some years, since the 1920 Act came into
force, that we never could find ourselves in
a satisfactory financial position, as the
Minister of Finance finds himself this
afternoon, until some fixed principles
were established governing the contribution of Northern Ireland to the Imperial
Services. I do not say that the contribution should be a fixed one. It is
perfectly obvious that that would be impossible seeing that taxation changes from year
to year; income tax has been altered, beer
duties have been altered, and these things
will be altered again, and possibly there
will be lessened duties on tea and sugar and
other stores that the people of Northern
Ireland have to buy. That will consequently
mean that any fixed sum is absolutely impossible. But, then, I think it should not be
beyond the powers of the financial experts
who are trying to settle this question in this
Committee to fix upon some principles which
will give us here from year to year some real
basis to go upon. The Minister of Finance
when he gets up in this House annually will
be able to say within a reasonable margin,
I do not think he could be absolutely accurate, bearing in mind the principles upon
which the contribution is fixed, that during
the next twelve months he believed the contribution we have to make towards Imperial
Services will be so-and-so and the balance
remaining over will then be available for
us to spend in any way we desire. Until
that position is arrived at I do not think our
position from a financial standpoint can ever

Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: It is, and that

The tendency of things in the Imperial Parliament, from the financial standpoint and from

drastic reductions in all these things he

I do not think I shall labour any other

heartily congratulate the Finance Minister

like to refer to. It is the taxation upon

House when the minister made his last Budget speech; but I had the pleasure of reading
it. It appeared equally satisfactory with the
one made here this evening. But on a
previous occasion I do remember referring
to this tax as a most undemocratic one. To
my mind it is so. I think the Prime Minister
made mention of the fact, on a certain public
occasion, that all surpluses will be devoted
to the good of the industrial classes. I think
if the surplus that is anticipated in connection with this budget were applied
to the reduction of this tax it could
not be more suitably applied. We
find it refers more particularly to the industrial classes than to any other. I think
their interests are more bound up in it than
those of any other section.
I would say
seven-eighths of those who attend these
entertainments are the industrial classes. It
seems very hard that it should be so continuously applied. It was a war tax, and it
was imposed when the workers were earning
100 per cent. more than they are to-day. Yet
the tax is being continued in spite of the
fact that serious reductions have taken place
in wages.
These workers are immured in
the works, and the only opportunities that
are open to them are in the evenings, and
they are taxed before they can make use of
them. I think it is an undemocratic tax,
and I think it should be removed immediately
as one of the reforms of peace.
On the whole the Budget is an admirable
one. It is one of great complexity though
very clearly elucidated. It will require to be
very carefully studied in order to be perfectly understood. As far as I can see the
situation is very hopeful. We had a surplus
last Budget. We hope there will be one on

this occasion. But whether or not the

settle once and for all what is the proper

apply, not only to this first amendment, but
also to the other amendments to the clause.
The Bill, as it stands, provides for the establishment of education committees for the
two county boroughs and for regional education committees in the case of the counties.
The regional committees are to be established
by orders of the Ministry throughout each
county, and the constitution, powers, duties
and procedure of these regional committees
are regulated by the provisions of Part 1 of
the Fourth Schedule. By an amendment
approved by the House in Committee the
constitution, powers, duties, etc., of the
education committees of the two county
boroughs are to be in accordance with schemes
framed by the Councils of the County
Boroughs and approved by the Ministry.
After very careful consideration of the whole
matter and in the light of the discussion
which took place at the Committee stage
the Government believe that as regards the
setting up of the regional committees the
same principles should apply, as nearly as
may be, as in the case of the education committees of the county boroughs.
the
Mr. McKEOWN: That is to say
regional committees should be set up by the
county councils themselves subject to the
provisions of the Act under schemes to be
approved by the Ministry. In this respect
no fundamental change is proposed in the
Bill. Briefly, as the Bill stands, the regional
committees are to be set up by orders of the
Ministry. It is now proposed that the committees shall be set up by schemes framed
by the county councils, but in every case the
schemes have to be confirmed by order of
the Ministry, and the powers given to the
Ministry are in no way restricted by the
proposed amendments. There is, however,
one important modification proposed, namely
that the education committees-whether for
the county boroughs or the countiesshall not include members directly appointed
or nominated by the Ministry. It is thought
that the fullest administrative control is
secured for the Ministry in the approval of
schemes for setting up of the committees
and for all the other purposes of the Bill,
and that the local authorities should not be
hampered by what would be, in effect, a
further element of official control. No change
is proposed in the Bill as to the powers and
duties which may, or may not, be exercised
by the education authorities and education
committees respectively. Hon. Members will
at once recognise that this change adds to the
democratic nature of the Bill. The Government, I believe, is right in assuming that the
education authorities and Committees, realising their responsibilities, will aim at making
the best use of the provisions of the Bill. I
beg to move.
Mr. LYNN: On the Second reading and also

I think this amendment which my hon.
Friend (Mr. McKeown) has moved will do
away with that difficulty, and will make not
only for the more harmonious working of the
Act, but also for economy in administering it,
which, after all, is a matter of considerable
importance. I think the amendment should
commend itself to the House, and I, for one,
have much pleasure in supporting it.

Mr. MILLER: It was with great sorrow

ideas by this plan at all. The educationist
has nothing to do with either the County

He is probably a man who keeps to himself, and has
nothing to do with politics at all, and everyone knows that politics run through the Rural
District Councils from top to bottom. The
real educationist is going to be left out
altogether by this idea. It was a great safeguard I thought-and we discussed this at the
Lynn Committee very thoroughly-to get a
certain number of people nominated by the
Ministry-people who would take no heed of
either religion or politics, but who, from the
educational point of view, would run the
thing as best they could. I am very sorry to
see that this has been departed from, and
even now I would appeal to the Ministry to

very bad thing for the country that everything
should be left in the hands of people who go
in more for politics than for education.

presided at a School Attendance Committee

Dr. MORRISON: I beg to move, in page 29,

I look upon this question of compulsory
attendance as one of the vital things in the
Bill. The hon. Member for Fermanagh and
Tyrone (Mr. Miller) has just told you of
the difficulties experienced by the School
Attendance Committees. I am a member of
a School Attendance Committee and I know
these difficulties. I know that this Bill will
be totally defective in rural Ulster, as the
present system has been in the past, owing
to this matter of the power to deal with
non-attendance at school. The present
system is in my opinion a sham. It costs a
great deal of money. I venture to say that
in County Derry it is costing £500 a year,

and so far as I know it is not worth the
paper it is written on. There is a section
of the population in each dispensary district
in Ulster who never go to school, who neglect
the ordinary attentions that children require,
who neglect their children. I do not suppose
the noble Marquess knows very much about
the conditions that prevail among the lower
classes in Ulster-amongst some of the
farmers and amongst some of the labourers
--but a man who has experience and who
has worked amongst them could tell when
he looks at a house before he enters it at all
whether the children are at school, whether
they are at Sabbath school, or whether they
are properly fed. The first things you see
are two or three broken panes in the windows
stuffed with rags. When you go to the door
to step in you find a "dub" of water.
venture to say that perhaps there is no
man on the Front Bench here who ever heard
of a "dub" of dirty water. What is it due
to? It is due to the mother coming to the
door, and she is so careless and so lazy that
she will not take the trouble to step a few
yards to the drain, but simply throws her
suds and slops outside the door. When you
go in you find her sitting over the fire at
twelve o'clock in the day, and the breakfast
dishes and utensils unwashed. I admit that
very few of these people exist, but there are
from twelve up to twenty of them in every
dispensary district in Ulster, and those are
the people with whom I want to deal.

Mr. LYNN: On the last occasion that this

arguments that have been put forward by
Mr. DUFF: I cannot see my way to agree

those deplorable circumstances are the

good many of these cases the parents

I propose this for the second time, and I

Dr. MORRISON: There is one thing that
has impressed me on my journey through
life, and it is this, the universality of religion
in practically every man that I came across.
Doctors have a knack of getting through the

be suppressed. Religion comes from the

in human nature that are indestructible. It

felt in eastern and western worlds, and
springs from aspirations that breathe in men
and women of every class and every clime.
I say that the people who are responsible for
the religion of the people of Ulster cannot
afford to take any chances on this vital
question, because without the sanction and
restraint of religion-and I say this advisedly
-you have no basis on which to build morals.
Force is the only remedy of primitive man.
When he emerges into the world, either as
a result of a creative act or as a development
from some lower form, he is governed by force
and force alone, and without the restraint of
religion there is no other element in his
nature, there is no other system, there is
nothing, to prevent him depending absolutely
and wholly on force.
You have, I think practically for the first
time unanimous, ministers of the different
Protestant sections of Ulster. You have the
ministers of all these denominations joining
harmoniously together in defence of what
they think, and what many of the laity think,

went last week to a Roman Catholic school

There was nothing in the teaching that

of a
Protestant teacher to the Roman

point a Protestant teacher? The priest

This Bill is far reaching in its influences,
and the dangers I see are very great.
remember being impressed after the battle of
Colenso with the opinion of an American
officer who was attached to General Buller's
Army. After looking at the damage done to
the British forces by three frontal attacks he
asked, "Was there no way round?" That
was a very natural suggestion for a wise and
cautious man to make. I suggest to the
Ministry that they should look and see if

of principle involved in this matter-I mean
the principle of contribution to the support
of Voluntary schools. You agree that Voluntary schools, whether transferred or not,
should get a grant from our Parliament. If
that is so then there is no difference of principle between you and me. The question is
a matter of degree. You say that provided
and transferred schools are to get the whole,

the third-class schools are to get a fifth.
There is absolutely no question of principle.
It is only a question of amount. In
this matter you cannot over-rule the sentiment of the people of Ulster without creating
serious friction. I could give you very serious
instances of how sentiment dominates logic
and reason. What I would be inclined to
recommend to the Ministry is this-it is a
principle that I have adopted as far as possible in my own weak and helpless fashion to
guide me in my public life and in religious
matters-in things essential, unity; in things
non-essential, liberty; and in all things,
charity. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) There
is no essential or no principle violated by the
clause which I propose. It is one that should
commend itself to all reasonable men who
want to see peace and quietness in this land.
It should commend itself to every man who
recognises the immense sacrifices that have
been made for practically 300 years by the
people of this country in providing education
for their children, and in doing it successfully. I think if you do that and approach
the question in a spirit of compromise and a
spirit of charity, you will be acting wisely
for your country and acting wisely for your
future education. I beg to move.

cation that is managed by private individuals?

Considered in Committee.
Mr. MOLES in the Chair.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That it is expedient to authorise a
charge upon the Consolidated Fund in
respect of any sums which may be advanced
by the Ministry of Finance under powers to
be conferred by an Act of the present
Session, amending the law relating to the
sale and supply of intoxicating liquor, for
the purpose of paying claims arising or expenses incurred by the Claims Tribunal
under such Act."
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr. Pollock): If I may say by way of explanation in
very plain and simple language the ob`e.
this Resolution, it is that the Ministry of
Finance may be empowered to release from
the Consolidated Fund the necessary money
to provide for compensation in the case of
the extinction of licences under the Bil!
which is now before the House, and which
presumably will receive the imprimatur of
this House. The amount required for compensating the licensees who are expected to
be extinguished is estimated roughly at
£150,000, but it is not contemplated that anything like that amount will be required
during the present year. I have made provision in my Budget through my Capital
Account for a sum of £50,000 to carry on the
work which is expected to be required for
the purposes of carrying out the object of the
measure, assuming it to be carried out in the
course of this year.
Mr. LYNN: There is just one point on
which I would like enlightment from the right
hon. Gentleman (Mr. Pollock). There is laid
down in one of the Schedules to the Bill a
scale of charges, which I presume are the increased charges to go towards the paying of
this money. Assuming that one hundred public
houses that are included in your calculations
now were closed is there any arrangement
made whereby you would make that loss good
in such a manner that it should fall upon the
publicans and not upon the taxpayers?
Mr. POLLOCK: It is intended, of course,
that the money required for the extinction
of these licences shall be provided by the
trade itself, and that the scale laid down in
Part III. of the First Schedule to the Bill
shall be adhered to in the provision of that
money. It is contemplated that the period
for the extinction of that money will be arranged at twenty years, or it may be less,
but in the initial stages the Ministry of
Finance, under the Resolution which I have
now moved will be empowered to provide
capital sums to be handed to the Claims
Tribunal for the purpose of paying those who
are to receive compensation under the award.
As I say, that money will be borrowed by
the Ministry of Finance, and a Sinking Fund
will be provided from year to year for the
purpose of extinguishing that perhaps in
twenty years, or possibly less, as the case
may be.
Mr. McGUFFIN: Say less.
Mr. LYNN: But ultimately no part of the
burden will fall upon the taxpayer.
Mr. POLLOCK: No part of the burden will
fall upon the taxpayer.

question I asked the Minister of Home Affairs, whether a wet canteen will be provided for the use of the men of the C.1 Special

30 MAY 1923
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Wednesday, 30th May, 1923.
The House met at Three of the Clock, Mr.
DEPUTY-SPEAKER in the Chair.
MESSAGE FROM THE SENATE.
The Senate agree to the Loans Guarantee
(Amendment) Bill without amendment.
Oral Answers to Questions.
COMPENSATION
FOR LICENCE HOLDERS.
1. Mr. MILLER asked the Minister of
Finance whether charges for compensation
will be levied on the licence holders in Fermanagh and Tyrone in respect of licences
which may become incapable of being renewed in the County Borough of Belfast, and
vice versa.
The PRIME MINISTER (Sir James Craig):
I am sorry my right hon. Friend (the Minister of Finance) is not here. I am not prepared to give a very reasoned answer to this
question, but I can say this, that none of the
licence holders in Fermanagh and Tyrone
will become chargeable with the cost of compensation in case of non-renewal of licences
in the County Borough of Belfast, and vice
versa. The country and town have been
divided in such a way that one is not dependent on the other.
2. Mr. MILLER asked the Minister of
Finance whether he will make it clear in the
Intoxicating Liquor Bill that the charges
for compensation will only be levied by the
Claims Tribunal on the district in which a
licence becomes incapable of being renewed.
The PRIME MINISTER: My answer has
practically covered that also. The schedule
at the end shows that the compensation in
town and country is different.
Mr. MILLER: Is it in the print of the
Bill?
The PRIME MINISTER: It is in the print
of the Bill.

Intoxicating Liquor Bill-
Committee.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
ORDERS OF THE DAY
Intoxicating Liquor BIll,
Considered in Committee.
(Mr. MOLES in the Chair.)
CLAUSE 1 (Closing of licensed premises
on Sunday and Christmas Day).
(1) It shall not be lawful for any person
at any time on Sunday or Christmas Day--
(a) to sell or expose for sale intoxicating
liquor; or
(b) to open or keep open any premises
for the sale of intoxicating liquor:-
Provided that nothing in this sub-section
shall apply to the sale of intoxicating liquor
in a hotel, where such liquor is sold for
consumption at the same time as a substantial meal, in a portion of the hotel
premises usually set apart for the service
of such meals.
(2) All drinking bars in hotels shall be
kept closed during the whole of Sunday and
Christmas Day.
(3) For the purposes of this section the
expression "hotel" means premises licensed
for the sale of intoxicating liquor by retail,
which are structurally adapted to be used
and bona-fide used for the purpose of the
reception of guests and travellers desirous
to sleep in the premises.
(4) The provisions of any Acts relating
to the sale of intoxicating liquor by retail,
which forbid the doing of any act, matter
or thing at any times during which such
sale is prohibited by those Acts, shall be
construed as if the times during which
such sale is so prohibited included the
whole of Sunday and Christmas Day; and
the penalties in force under the said Acts
shall be applicable to cases in which any
such act, matter or thing is done in contravention of the provisions of this section.
Colonel WOODS: I beg to move on page 1,
line 6, after "time" (time on Sunday) to
insert ["except between the hours of ten and
eleven in the morning and of four and six in
the afternoon."]
From as far back as Ulster history goes we
find that the predominant feature of the
Ulster character is independence, which has
intensified and become moulded into a great
force of thought as years have rolled on. It
has shown itself in a thousand different ways
in recent times, and we had earned the respect of nearly every country in the world
because of that independent spirit, and because we were solid in our loyalty to our
country and ourselves, and because we were
always against tyranny in no matter what
.
guise it was clothed, whether it appeared in
the person of an individual, a clique, or a
league. We have always held as our dearest
possession the liberty of the subject. At no
further date than twelve years ago we refused
to accept legislation which we considered was
a menace to our personal and civil liberty,
and even went to the extreme length of arming ourselves against constituted authority.
The Government at that time raged and
threatened, but we held to our ideals.
Clause 1 of the measure before the House
is an aggravated repetition of kindred
legislation. It is aggravated in so much as it
attacks the liberty of the working class of
Ulster only, the class which Ulster hahitherto held up as an example to the world
of industry, loyalty, and sobriety. The working man of twelve years ago is the same man
to-day. He loathes tyranny, he hates oppres
sion by the individual, the clique, or the
association, and is still jealous of his Godgiven freedom. If that independence of spirit
survives in the Government they will not
allow themselves to betray their countrymen
at the dictation of a small and, outside this
House, insignificant section of misguided
enthusiasts-extremists obsessed with one
idea and one aim, namely, to impose their
narrow-minded views upon the other 98 per
cent. of Ulstermen, and to sacrifice any person or principle in so doing.

when he wants it, as hon. Members can

then he will be as sober a citizen as any present. It is only human nature that what is

than an Englishman that he cannot judge

The Prime Minister suggested that to leave

That is an elementary law that is necessary

that section in West Belfast that believes in

Mr. LLOYD CAMPBELL: I beg to move:
"In Clause I, page 1, line 6, after "Day"
("Sunday or Christmas Day") insert "except as otherwise provided for in this Act."
In moving this amendment I hope you, Sir,
and the House will perhaps grant me a little
licence. This amendment is really what I may
call a fundamental or foundation amendment. There are several other amendments
standing in my name, and on their acceptance depends the fate of this amendment.
If this amendment is not accepted by the
Committee then my other amendments fall
to the ground. I hope I will be allowed. for
these reasons, to trespass a little beyond the
ordinary allowance of Parliamentary rules.
The first thing I would like hon. Members to
understand is the explanation of the term
"beer licence" which appears in my amendment on page 8 of the Paper.
The expression "beer licence" shall mean
an excise licence which entitles the holder
to sell or expose for sale, liquor which does
not contain more than twelve per cent. of
alcohol, but does not entitle the holder to
sell or expose for sale liquor which does
not contain more than sixteen and twothirds per cent. of alcohol.
That sixteen and two-thirds is not correct.
It should read "which does contain more
than twelve per cent. of alcohol." May 1
alter that?
The CHAIRMAN: The hon. Member is not
in fact moving that amendment at the
moment. He can make the change when he
comes to it.
Mr. LLOYD CAMPBELL: I would next
refer to the expression "hard liquor."
Perhaps that is not altogether a Parliamentary term, but I think most people know what
it means. It means liquor which contains
more than twelve per cent. of alcohol, whereas
"soft liquor" means liquor which does not
contain more than twelve per cent. of alcohol.
I put these amendments down for practically
one reason only; there are other reasons, but
they are subsidiary. The main reason why
I put this amendment down is the one that
I gave when I spoke on the Second Reading
of this Bill, and that is, that I want to use,
as far as I can, the best methods that can
be produced for making this community of
ours a more temperate community. I feel
that one of the best ways of doing that would
be to reduce the strength of the liquor consumed. In other words, I do not want to do
away with spirits as a whole, but I do think
that if the community could be accustomed
to drink beer and such like liquor a great
improvement would be made. I may say
that twelve per cent. of alcohol would take in
beer, stout, and a very mild claret. I think
if the community, or at any rate those who
cannot trust themselves with the harder
liquors, could be trained in some way to
consume these liquors, real good would be
done, and I would almost appeal to the extremists of the Temperance party to give
this idea a chance, because I think there are
considerable possibilities of success in it.
As regards the carrying out of such a
scheme, I would first of all, as I have said,
have this beer licence, which would only
entitle a person at any time--not merely on
Sunday but at any time, week-day or Sunday
--to sell anything not containing more than
twelve per cent. of alcohol. They would also
be allowed to sell meals, sandwiches and such
things. They would not be allowed on any
terms whatever to have spirits on the premises, even for their own consumption, in the
dining-room or anywhere else. It must be a
beer licence pure and simple. I would allow
a person who had that licence to be open
from one to three and from five-thirty to
eight-thirty on Sundays. I put down those
hours simply as a basis for discussion. That
law would apply to every person in the hole
area; there would be no exception made in
favour of anybody. Rich and poor would
have exactly the same terms on Sunday, and
I regard that as a very strong argument in
my favour. The only difference that I would
make in those rules would be that in the
case of a hotel the owner would have to be
trusted, and although spirits were on the
premises, he should not be allowed to serve
them or expose them for sale on Sunday, and
if he contravened that law the penalty would
be such that he would not have the opportunity of doing it again.
I have travelled a good deal over the world,
and some of my pleasantest evenings have
been spent in beer gardens. I do think that
in this community of ours there is a large
chance of doing good and of uplifting the
community as a whole if we could only bring
into being some such system as that which
prevails on the Continent. I know that in
using such an expression I will be met with
the statement "Oh, you want the Continental
Sunday." I do not. That is the very last
thing I do want to see I want Sunday to be
as carefully observed in this country as it is
now, but I do not want to deprive people of
all pleasure in life on that day.
There is another point which may be raised
against this, and that is, that in some places
they will have an influx of travellers or
tourists who will go into the beer gardens
and behave in a disorderly manner.
answer to that is, that this Bill is so
strengthening the powers of the authorities,
and putting the carrying out of those powers

Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: I am extremely

equality. I think that those
The PRIME MINISTER: Perhaps the hon.

Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: I quite recognise that, but it is not everybody who is a
member of a club, rich or poor. The vast
majority of people are outside the membership of a club, and the idea I have in my
mind is that those who are members of clubs
should not receive any preferential treatment.
I think the club should be put in the same

the man who is a member of a club and occupying a bedroom in the club, if it happens
to be his home for the time being, being put
in the same position as a resident in a hotel.
During the past two days I had what may be
considered a strange experience. I have had
conferences with members of the trade in my
own constituency, and this morning they put
to me the question "Will you try to induce
the Government to put clubs in exactly the
same position as you put us in the public
house?" I was amazed to find that the trade
was in complete agreement with me and that
I was in complete agreement with the representatives of the trade. They were absolutely
unanimous on this particular point. I
thought that under such conditions it would
be possible to get the Government to say, as
the Prime Minister indicated some time ago,
"You can get what you want."
If the Government are not willing to include
the amendment in their Bill I have no desire
to press them, but I can easily see that a very
strong case can be made out for putting clubs
in the same category as hotels. I know that
the representatives of the licensed trade who
have interviewed me are emphatically in
favour of this, and as a temperance man I
thought there might be some chance of the
Government accepting the proposal But it
is a strange fatality that has happened to me.
On the first occasion that I find myself in
agreement with the trade and its representatives the proposal is turned down. It is not
very encouraging to go forward in that direction. I was hopeful that the Government
might be induced to accept this amendment.
Possibly the Prime Minister might say,
"Under these conditions I suspect both parties, and I will have nothing to do with
either." That is the attitude of mind he
might take up on this particular question.
I leave it at that. I quite recognise that the

it is an enactment that appeals largely to the
democracy, because they feel they will be

Mr. CRAWFORD: The next amendment

Mr. MEGAW: I beg to move in Clause 1,

The Bill was originally prepared on the
assumption that a person coming to a hotel
and having a meal in the hotel would be for
the time being a resident or guest in the
hotel. Very considerable criticism, to which
the Prime Minister has referred, was directed
to this proposal, and it was felt that there
was a good deal to be said for that criticism.
Accordingly the Government set about trying
to obviate that criticism without affecting
the principle of the Bill, and what they
have done is this: They recognise that
persons who are resident in hotels should be
entitled to the same treatment as people
living in their own house, and so far as
the residents in hotels are concerned they
are entitled under this amendment to have
such liquor of an intoxicating character as
they may desire.
The question then arose as to what were
bona-fide hotels, and it was thought that
if the clause was left without a close definition of a hotel it might lead to the evasion
of the proposal. In regard to these hotels
a different standard has been taken to that
adopted in an amendment I intend to move
at a later date with regard to hotels in
respect of which new licences may be granted.
We have recognised that there should be
equality, and that the small hotel should
have the same right as the large hotel, and
accordingly we have taken a very small
qualification for the bona-fide hotel, which,
it has been decided, must have four sleeping
rooms devoted to the reception of guests.
With regard to new hotels the proposal of the
Government is that there should be ten
sleeping rooms. In our desire not to hit
the small hotel a very few rooms are required
to qualify it as a bona-fide hotel. The Prime
Minister points out that I have gone outside
this particular amendment in giving a
definition of the bona-fide hotel. However,
in this amendment we have taken the precaution to try to provide against an abuse
of the residence qualification in hotels, and
we have provided that it is only guests who
have occupied a room on the night before,
or who have taken a room on the succeeding
night, who will be entitled to intoxicating
liquor on Sunday.

CLAUSE 2.-(Abolition of Off-Licences.)
Notwithstanding the provisions of any
enactments with respect to the grant or
renewal of licences for the sale by retail
for consumption off the premises of spirits,
wine, liqueurs, beer or other intoxicating
liquor, no licence, nor any renewal of a
licence, for the sale of any such intoxicating liquor by retail for consumption as
aforesaid shall be granted, held, or remain
in force after the thirtieth day of September, nineteen hundred and twenty-three, in
respect of any premises in which or in any
part of which any trade other than the sale
of any such intoxicating liquor, or of table
waters, is carried on:
Provided that nothing in this section
shall prevent the renewal of a licence, so
as to remain in force until the thirtieth
day of September, nineteen hundred and
twenty-four, in any case where, upon application being made to the licensing court
in respect of any premises, that court
certifies that they are satisfied that within
such period as they may fix (terminating
not later than the last-mentioned date), the
part of the premises in which the sale of
intoxicating liquor is to be carried on will
be structurally separated from, and cease
to have internal communication with, the
remainder of the building.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

[Mr. Megaw]
This amendment that I have the honour to
move is rather far-reaching, but it is also one
that is carrying out the principles of this
Bill that have already been mentioned in the
Committee, namely, that the intoxicating
liquor shop shall be a self-contained shop
carried on by itself, and with no other business of any kind. As the section was drafted,
it might have been possible for one with an
off licence to divide his premises, and to have
one part of the premises licensed for the sale
of liquor, and to carry on business of another
kind in the other part. It was felt that that
would give rise to abuses, and that it might
tend very largely to evasion. At least that
was the criticism that was put before the
House. I may say that the Government,
when this section was originally drafted, made
provision in its financial arrangements on the
be
assumption that all off-licences would
wiped out, believing that the consequence of
the section as it stood would be to put an
end to all, or practically all, off-licences.
They looked at it in this way that the two
businesses could not practically be carried on
together, that one of them might be profitable or the other might be profitable, but that
the two could not be carried on together.
But a considerable amount of criticism
arose, and there seems to be some justification for it. It might be possible still by
evasion-and we have to deal with evasions
unfortunately in licensing matters-it would
be possible for a man, in fact, to carry on
two businesses more or less as he had done
before. Now, this amendment that I have
the honour to propose does away with any
possibility of that, and the scheme that
underlies the amendment is this that a person up to 1st September, 1923, who holds an
off-licence with which he has carried on any
other business, whether it is that of grocer
or a chemist's business, or whatever sort of
business it is, has the option of choosing
which business he will carry on.
He may
carry on one or the other, but he cannot
carry on both. If he does not carry on the
liquor business, then he is entitled to compensation in respect of the business destroyed.
That is the general scheme that is proposed
in the amendment that I have mentioned.
The question of his licence will come before
the licensing authority that is mentioned
later in the Bill on 30th September. It will rest
with the licensing authority to say whether
the premises are or are not in a proper state,
or are such as can be properly licensed. It
does not follow that because an off-licence
has been carried on in the past that it will
be granted in the future. What has got to
be looked to is this-that the premises are
suitable and comply with the police requirements for the carrying on of the business;
and when the licensing authority comes to
deal with the matter on 30th September, it
will be open to the police and residents in
the neighbourhood, or to any one of the
public interested, to come in and say that
it is not proper that an off-licence should
be continued in this particular place. Now,
that is the reason for the second sub-clause,
or rather second proviso, of the amendment.
The amendment says:
any-

thing in this section, a licence for such
sale which is in force on the thirtieth day

twenty-three, shall, if application is made

be deemed to continue in force until the

The meaning of that is this-There will
probably be some time required to see, in

on of the business, and to find whether a

is continued until 31st December for that
purpose, and for that purpose only. Now,
the second sub-section deals with the part
I have already referred to, that if the premises are suitable there may be an opportu
ity of showing it, and an opportunity for

case before the Licensing Court as to

Of course, this must be taken in connection with Section 7 of the Act. Hon. Memhers, by referring to it, will see that the
provisions of Section 7 refer to both offlicences and on-licences, and that in future

as
peaking for myself, I had no knowledge of

It is revolutionary. We had our mandate to

most serious part. Instead of having his
licence renewed for his premises as they
stand as a right-that is the law now-this is

clauses dealing with that have now been

now disappears, I hope for all time. Now we

had not the good fortune to catch the
Speaker's eye to take part in the interesting

clause affect the original demand that was
made for the abolition of spirit groceries?
One of the greatest, perhaps the greatest
and the main objection that most people had
to the spirit groceries was that the grocery
business was combined with the spirit
business, and that certain abuses were created
owing to the two businesses being together.
Most of us considered that the mere structural
alterations that were proposed to be affected
under the original clause would not carry out
that intention. I gather from these two clauses,
although perhaps it has not been as clearly
stated as it might have been, that the proposal of the Government now is that those
who are conducting these combined businesses
to-day have got to make their choice and will
either have to be grocers or spirit dealers.
That in substance, I think, is what the clause
means. Therefore the argument that I and
others have constantly used is done away
with. If a man selects to keep his spirit
trade the temptations that arose for those
who patronised his establishment will disappear, because there is no grocery trade, and
women visiting a grocery will not be subjected
to the temptations that existed before. Under
that clause the Government clearly do away
with the spirit grocery as it has existed up
to the present moment. I am quite satisfied
that they have carried out their pledge in
that respect.
I want to point out to them that there is
a great danger if something more is not done
in connection with these Clauses to ensure
that the old difficulty will not arise again
and that the old abuses will not crop up
again and that the old temptations will not
arise again. I would throw out this suggestion to the Government that they should see
if they cannot make some provision, and 1
am quite sure they are just as anxious as I
am to remedy the evil that exists, that will
do so.

THE PRIME MINISTER Perhaps I may
be able to throw some light on this subject
and my hon. and learned Friend (Mr. Megaw)
beside me will correct me if I go wrong. The
desire of the Government was to meet the very
strong criticisms made on the Second Reading.
As soon as we brought the Bill forward we
were able to observe how the House accepted
the various parts and one of the criticisms
was that we were perpetuating evil because we
did not separate the businesses altogether.
By the amendment put down now the mixed
business, or what is called the spirit grocer's
licence, is gone for ever. There is no one who
can say that such a thing as a spirit grocer's
licence remains. Then the point arose when
wo drafted this as to how it was possible to
decide which of these off-licences were redundant-for it refers, of course, as my hon, and
learned friend (Mr. Hanna) knows to offlicences. In taking into consideration the
question of redundant licences the magistrates
are here empowered to consider the number of
on-licences in the immediate neighbourhood,
but so far as compensation for the abolishing
of the on-licences is concerned, that does not
arise under this Clause at all. It deals entirely with off-licences, but it seems to my colleagues and myself that it would be quite
absurd for say five or six off-licences to be
retained in a part of the city of Belfast
where they were not wanted and where there
were, perhaps, seven or eight on-licences in
close proximity to them. We agreed to have
two magistrates instead of one, as will come
on later in the Bill, and that they would
have to review the whole state of that particular part of the locality where the renewal
was asked for, and they would then hear the
local people with regard to the necessity for
having, or on the other hand, the necessity
for abolishing them. Consequently, it seems
to me that we have met all the criticisms of
the House fairly with regard to the continuity of these "off" licences, which hitherto
have been mixed up with the groceries.

questioned as to Clause 5 of the Bill. We
are advised by the British Government that
Clause 5 appears to be ultra vires as in so
far as it interferes with the power of the
Imperial authorities to prosecute for Excise
offences, it affects the rights of the Crown
of the United Kingdom.
Mr. DUFF: My hon. Friend and colleague,
the Member for East Belfast (Mr. Donald)
knows from past experience how little I sit
on the fence. Though we are told that section 7 has another reason why licences can
be disallowed, yet this particular clause that
you are considering here now, sub-section 2,
is perfectly clear, and the principle that will
govern the diminution of the licences is the
question of the number of premises licensed
for off or on together. And for that reason
I consider that you are bringing in a perfectly
new principle into this Bill, entering it by a
side door, and in a way that is not, I should
say, fair-bringing in the principle of local
veto in one of its worst forms.
Clause 2 as amended ordered to stand part
of Bill.
Resolved: "That the Chairman jo
report progress and ask leave to sit again."
(The Prime Minister).
Committee report progress; to sit again
to-morrow.
The remaining orders were read and postponed.

ANNOUNCEMENT BY THE PRIME
MINISTER.
Motion made and Question proposed: "That
this House do now adjourn." (Captain
Dixon).
The PRIME MINISTER: I have an announcement to make to the House that I
could not make in Committee on account of
the time. During the course of the preparation of this Bill, as hon. Members are aware,
we are obliged to communicate copies from
time to time to the British Government
We have only one alternative in a case of
this sort, which I am sure the House will
agree to, and that is we must drop
Clause 5. In the meantime, two of my hon.
and learned Friends are crossing over to
consult the advisers on the other side with
a view to arriving at some form of words
which will be acceptable to us, and, at the
same time, will not be ultra vires.
I need hardly point out to the House that
if we proceeded with a Bill that contained
a clause held to be ultra vires, we could not
get the Royal Assent to that Bill. We hope,
between now and the Bill being dealt with
in the Senate, that it will be possible to
get a satisfactory conclusion from the other
side. I am quite sure that the Imperial authorities are just as anxious as we are to
put down poteen and also the use of methylated spirits. I thought it only fair to the
House, as this intimation came to us somewhat as a shock and quite recently-we have
only just heard of it-that I should intimate it to the House at once, so that they
should understand the position, and will
not be taken by surprise if we cannot proceed with the clause to-morrow.
Question ("That this House do now adjourn") put and agreed to.
Adjourned accordingly at Twentyfive Minutes before Seven of
the Clock.

BANN ELECTRICITY BILL.
1. Mrs. CHICHESTER asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether he is aware of the
widespread alarm occasioned amongst the
farmers on the shores of Lough Neagh and
the River Bann, by the provisions contained
in the proposed Bann Electricity Bill, and,
if so, will he state what steps he intends to
take in order to safeguard their interests
and the interests of the agricultural and
commercial community which are so seriously
threatened.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (Mr.
Archdale): I have already had many representations made to me regarding this Bill,
and I must take this opportunity to make it
clear that this is a private Bill and not a
Government Measure.
In these circumstances, as the hon. Member is aware, the ultimate decision regarding
the provisions of the Bill and the protection
of all interests concerned lies with Parliament, and all persons who consider themselves aggrieved or prejudiced have an opportunity through Counsel of representing
their case before the Select Committee to
whom the Bill will be committed, if and
when it comes before Parliament. Subject
to that, I may add for the information of
the hon. Member, that in due course a report
will be made to Parliament on the provisions
of the Bill by the Government Departments
concerned.
Mrs. CHICHESTER: Arising out of that
answer, may I ask the Minister of Agriculture whether any report has yet been received
by the Ministry of Agriculture from the
engineer on this qestion showing that the
scheme is of an entirely speculative nature
and only promoted in the interests of a
private London syndicate, and if the report
has not yet been received can the right hon.
Gentleman tell me, pending a report, how
many acres of the best grazing land are
likely to be submerged and lost to agriculture all around the shores of Lough Neath
and down the Bann from Toome to Carnroe
if this Bill is passed?
Mr. ARCHDALE: No engineer's report has
been made to the Ministry of Agriculture as
we have no engineer, but the Ministry of
Commerce as Electricity Commissioners have
been in touch with the promoters. We
believe that about 600 acres of land at the
Northern end of Lough Neagh will be submerged.
Mrs. CHICHESTER: From Portna to
Carnroe?
Mr. ARCHDALE: We do not know the
amount of other land until the Bill comes
before the House.
CONTRIBUTION TOWARDS NATIONAL
ᎠᎬᏴᎢ.
2. Mr. DONALD asked the Minister of
Finance whether the Colwyn Committee has
had under review the question of Ireland's
contribution towards our National Debt.
Whether the nearest figure for the whole of
Ireland has been fixed at £110,000,000, and
what is likely to be the approximate figure
for Northern Ireland.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): I beg to inform the honourable
Member that the contribution of Northern
Ireland towards the reduction of the National
Debt will be included in the annual sum
which Northern Ireland will be called on to
contribute towards the cost of Imperial
Services. There is no question of fixing a
capital sum as representing Northern Ire
land's share of the debt, and I am not aware
from what source the hon. Member's figure
for the whole of Ireland has been obtained.

Mr. POLLOCK. The question put by the

DELAY IN APPOINTMENT OF
MAGISTRATES.
6. Mrs. CHICHESTER asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he will state the
cause of the great delay in the appointment
of Magistrates throughout the Six Counties
whose names have been recommended to him,
and whether it would not be possible to
expedite matters in this respect
Sir DAWSON BATES: In consequence of
the passing of the Free State (Consequental
Provisions) Act, the Clerk of the Crown and
Hanaper in Dublin, who formerly prepared
and passed Commissions of the Peace under
the Great Seal, ceased to have any functions
in Northern Ireland. It was, therefore, necessary to appoint a corresponding official in
Northern Ireland. His appointment, by the
Imperial Government, was gazetted on 25th
March last. Owing to the cumbersome practice at present existing, whereby it is necessary to recite the name of every Justice in
the County or County Borough in the Commission, and no records being in possession
of the Clerk of the Crown for Northern Ireland, it is necessary to compile them anew.
I hope as soon as this is completed to be in
a position to proceed with the appointment
of Magistrates where necessary.

Dawson Bates).
(Sir
Sir DAWSON BATES: For some time past
the Government has felt that the salary of
the Attorney-General was entirely inadequate
having regard to the responsibilities of his
office and the amount of work involved. Expression was given to that feeling during the
debate on the Law Charges and Criminal
Prosecutions Vote, and on that occasion the
Government undertook to bring in a measure
to deal with the matter Hon. Members will

recollect that the salary was fixed by a com
mittee appointed by this House, whose report
was subsequently adopted in an Act of this
House. At that time we had no practical
experience of how much work was involved
in carrying on the duties of Attorney-Gene
ral, and it was felt by this House-and 1
think I am speaking also for the members
of the committee-that the amount of work
involved would allow the Attorney-General
ample time to carry on his own private
practice. However, in experience it has been
found that the work of the Attorney-General
takes up practically the Attorney-General's
entire time, and he has practically no time
for dealing with his private work. Now the
Attorney-General's present salary contrasts
very unfavourably with the salary formerly
given to the Attorney-General for Ireland.
That official received a salary of £5,000 per
year, and he was also assisted by the Solicitor-
General, who drew a salary of £2,000 per
year.
Both these officers were entitled to
carry on their own private practices.
We have got to look to the future in regard
to this matter. The man who occupies the
position of Attorney-General as a result loses
his private practice. He goes out with the
Government, and he has thereupon to resume
private practice, but having lost that private
practice in the meantime, he has to start to
build it up entirely anew. Under these
circumstances, and paying the salary we do
I have no hesitation in saying that in the
future it will be found impossible to get a
barrister holding the qualifications which the
Attorney-General should hold, and which, 1
may say, are so eminently displayed by the
present Attorney-General. We do not propose
to appoint a Solicitor-General, but we do
propose that, in the event of the Attorney-
General becoming ill or being laid aside and
unable to do his work, power shall be given
to the Governor to appoint a deputy in his
place. We do not propose, however, to pay
that deputy any salary. I would remind the
House that certain prosecutions cannot be
initiated without the consent of the Attorney-
General, and it is quite possible that the
whole of the administration of law and order
in Ireland might be held up if the Attorney-
General could not attend to his work.
Accordingly, we ask for power to appoint a
deputy to act under those circumstances in
respect of the services transferred to us. 1
may point out to hon. Members that the
Governor has already got power to appoint a
deputy to carry on the work of the Attorney-
General in respect of the reserved services.
I beg to move.
Question put and agreed to.
Bill read a Second time, and committed
to a Committee of the whole House for
to-morrow.

INTOXICATING LIQUOR BILL.
Considered in Committee. (Progress 30th
May).
SECOND DAY.
[Mr. MOLES in the Chair.]
CLAUSE 3.-(Provision as to claims in
respect of abolition of off-licences.)
(1) Compensation shall be payable in accordance with the provisions hereinafter in
this section contained and out of the fund
in this section mentioned, in any case
where, by virtue of this Act, a licence for
the sale by retail of intoxicating liquor for
consumption off the premises becomes incapable of being renewed.
(2) For the purpose of dealing with
claims for compensation as aforesaid, there
shall be established a tribunal (to be called
"the Claims Tribunal "), which shall be
constituted in accordance with the provisions of Part I. of the First Schedule to
this Act.
(3) The following provisions shall have
effect with respect to the powers and duties
of the Claims Tribunal under this section:
(a) The Claims Tribunal shall, in dealing with the claims for compensation, be
governed by the provisions of Part II. of
the First Schedule to this Act.
(b) The Claims Tribunal shall in each
year, unless they certify to the Ministry
of Finance that it is unnecessary to do
so in any year for the purposes of this
section, impose, in respect of all licences
for the sale of intoxicating liquor by
retail, charges at rates not exceeding,
and graduated in the same proportion as,
the rates shown in the scale of maximum
charges set out in Part III. of the First
Schedule to this Act.
(c) Charges payable under this section
in respect of any licence shall be levied
and paid together with, and as part of,
the duties on the corresponding excise
licence, but a separate account shall be
kept by the Ministry of Finance of the
amount produced by those charges, and
that amount shall in every year be paid
over to the Claims Tribunal in accordance with rules made by the Ministry of
Finance for that purpose.
(d) Any sums paid to the Claims
Tribunal under this section shall be
placed to the credit of a fund to be called
the Claims Fund."

(e) Any moneys expended by the
Claims Tribunal in the payment of claims
under this Act, or otherwise in the exercise of their powers or the performance
of their duties, shall be paid out of the
Claims Fund.
(f) The Ministry of Finance may out
of the Consolidated Fund of Northern
Ireland make advances to the Claims
Fund, to be repayable in accordance with
rules made by that Ministry, for the
purpose of paying any claims arising or
expenses incurred by the Claims Tribunal
under this section.
(4) The Claims Tribunal shall continue
in existence for a period of three years
from the thirtieth day of September,
nineteen hundred and twenty-three, or for
such longer period as the Minister of
Finance may determine; and after the
Claims Tribunal has ceased to exist this
section shall have effect with the substitution of the Ministry of Finance for the
Claims Tribunal.
(5) The Ministry of Finance may make
rules for carrying into effect the provisions
of this section and may, in particular, by
those rules prescribe the procedure in connection with applications for claims, the
time and manner of making payments in
respect of claims and the manner in which
the accounts of the Claims Fund are to be
kept and audited.

The object I have in moving this amendment,
now that I have read the words in the proposed section to the Committee, must be perfectly plain. It is with a view to securing
compensation for all classes of licence holders who are adversely affected by this Act.
The ordinary seven-day licence holder under
the Bill will lose one day of his trade. Of
course, we will be told that in country places
there was no right of selling; but there
was a right to sell to bona-fide travellers.
That right is done away with under the Bill.
There was a right in the city of Belfast to
sell within certain hours on Sunday, and that
is entirely gone, and no matter what the Bill
does to the ordinary seven-day holder, no
matter how adversely the Bill hits him, no
provision is made to pay him any compensation. I do seriously ask the Committee to
bear with me for a minute or two, and give
this matter, as I am sure they will, very full
and careful consideration.
You do not want to take away valuable
rights to the hurt of anybody. I take it
that this Committee would regret that at
the end of their deliberations they should
bring hurt even to a few. I recognise and 1
know that it is the intention of the Committee, and the intention of the right hon.
Gentleman (the Prime Minister), and all
associated with him, as well as my hon.
Friends on the other side, that great good
may come from this measure. (Hon. Members: "Hear, hear.") But let us just have
good care and see that it will leave no man
worse off. By taking away the privileges
that the ordinary seven-day licence holder
had under his old licence, you will, in many
cases, break the man entirely. Take the
licence-holder at seaside places where people
go on Sunday. His place is now closed. At
the time he bought it he may have paid,
and likely did, a big price for it, because
trade was at its best. I am not on the
question of whether it is right or whether
it is wrong that he should sell drink on
Sunday. I am only talking of the effect.
You are going to leave that man worthless
premises. Is that for the good of the
general public?
Only yesterday the hon Member for Derry
(Sir Robert Anderson), in speaking of the
amendment proposed by the hon. and gallant
Gentleman (Colonel Woods), said that his
heart was not in it. I cannot believe that
the heart of any Member of this Committee will be for doing something that
may result in the financial ruin of
even one man. His valuable property will
be impaired, his turnover will, in many instances, be almost completely gone, and he
will be left with no income. As I said before, I do not believe that the Committee
is anxious for that. Let us, in pursuit of
the great good we all hope for under this
Bill, be fair, and let us be honest. Why
should not the ordinary licence-holder
have compensation

any men you must give them just compensation. I am not going to argue the moral
question, but there is this fact that
should bear in mind, if we are going to carry
out a reform for the public good then we
should not make the individual suffer because
of that. No man, for example, argued in the
days of the slave traffic that it was a moral
traffic, and yet the British taxpayer-and I
think rightly so-paid a large sum of money
to get rid of the slave traffic. Surely if we
are going to do away with it we have got
the right to see that
none of these
people suffer, no matter how humble the
Some of these men
position they may be in.
have purchased licensed premises, and purchased them at a large price. It is not, I am
sure, the wish of this Committee, or the wish
of the people of Ulster, that any of these
people should be driven into bankruptcy by
the acts of this Committee. I think we ought
to be not only fair but absolutely just to these
people. I am at one with the Government
in wanting to remove every one of these
abuses, but when I want to remove an abuse
I am not refusing to pay my share towards

think that, in spite of all the oratory of my
The PRIME MINISTER: My two hon.
Friends have raised a point that is new in
some respects, and perhaps I may be allowed
to add to what my hon, and learned Friend
(Mr. Megaw) has said on this subject. My
hon. Friend is dealing now with on-licences.
The off-licences are provided for, and he is
dealing with the on-licences. The point that
my colleagues and I had to consider was
this, those on-licences that were granted to
mixed businesses as we find frequently in
country districts are in shops where all sorts
of articles are sold, with children buying.
their small articles on one side and men
drinking on the other side. We decided that
it was time that stopped-(Hon. Members:
Hear, hear ")-because it really was in some
cases analogous to the spirit groceries in
this city. Then the question arose, if we
were giving compensation in the case of offlicences, whether we should not also deal in
some way with compensation to those in the
country districts who had on-licences, and
who would be compelled by this Bill to erect
a substantial barrier between the two sides
of their trade. The conclusion we came to
was this and I wish all Members to bear
Intoxicating Liquor Bill-- HOUSE OF COMMONS.
Committee.
[The Prime Minister]
this particular point in mind--had the law
in the past been properly administered there
was a bar to those men having an on-licence
for the premises.
You had a man on one
side of the street carrying on a legitimate
mixed business; he may have been a hardware merchant and a dealer in various other
matters, but he had not an on-licence. Then
you had a man on the other side of the street
with exactly the same type of business, and
he was in our opinion improperly granted an
on-licence. Therefore he has had all those
years of advantage over the person on the
other side of the street who did not get an
on-licence.
I can assure my hon. Friend (Mr.
Lynn) that we are most desirous of seeing
fair play meted out to all parties. I
may say in passing that we actually did take
up the point that my hon. Friend has made,
that is to say, we visualised to ourselves a
vast section of the public who are not represented in this House whose interests must.
therefore, be most cautiously investigated
before we entrench in any way upon them.
In other words, we have more or less taken
the same line in preparing the Bill as we
would have done had those of an opposite
political opinion to ours been sitting in this
House defending the case themselves. I think
it was the duty of the Government to bear
in mind very carefully the large community
that they have to govern, and to cause as
little disturbance as possible, but I really
think that, after the explanation I have given,
the Committee will agree with us that in
the case at any rate of those who enjoy this
privilege as against their neighbours there
is no just cause why we should ask the
Committee to supply compensation.

The PRIME MINISTER: Perhaps I may

Dr. MORRISON: I have some knowledge,

as a law-abiding man and a peaceable man

Mr. DONALD: My object in rising is to
say that I think there is another side to this
question. I want to be fair and I consider
we have got a reasonable and a just Bill here.
The trade is being fairly treated under this
Bill. When I say there is another side to this
question I refer to the people whose trade was
taken away from them during the war. Were
they compensated? Not a penny.
The gunmakers were deprived of their trade for
several years during the war and never got a
farthing. There is another section and a very
important section. What about our boys who
went out and fought? Many of them came
back and found that their jobs were filled
by other people. Were they compensated?
Not a farthing. But they were allowed to
walk the streets for years. There is no trade
I know of that employs fewer people than the
licensed trade. If compensation is to be
given I want to see it fairly administered.
If a man who has been serving behind the
counter for a number of years is going to lose
his employment as a result of this legislation
-a man who may possibly have a wife and
family and who has probably served his employer for ten years, will any of this money
be allocated to him or will he be thrown on
the street? There is far too much being made
out of this question of compensation. I want
to be perfectly fair and reasonable and I say
that if we are going to compensate people let
us compensate the boys who fought while
these people stayed at home and who are now
running about the streets. The persons you
propose to compensate profiteered and made
fortunes during the war. One of them admitted to me that he made a fortune and
could retire independent of your compensation
out of the profits he made during the war.
Let us be fair and reasonable in this matter
of compensation.

has suffered.
He paid for that licence, and

Mr. MARK: I cannot understand the arguments of hon. Members who get up here and
ask for compensation for a man who has been
in the habit of selling liquor on a Sunday.
I think the attitude of the Government is
the right and proper one and it is a wonderful

I cannot see how compensation can be arrived
at. We are told that under this Bill compensation will be paid by the trade. Then the
man whose licence is changed from a seven
to a six-day licence will have to pay for

basis will compensation be awarded? I hold
that a man who has five shillings to drink
will drink it whether it is Saturday night.
Sunday or Monday, and I submit there will
be no difference in the receipts of the publican. If a man has the money to spend there
is no reason why he should not spend it on
Saturday night and if he has it until Monday
morning he will drink it then. I think the
Government is perfectly right in disregarding
the claim for compensation for publicans who
are closed on Sunday. With regard to the
man who surrenders his licence voluntarily,

inclined to support the hon. Member for
Antrim (Mr. Hanna) in respect to that man.

prepared to waive the question of the man
who chooses to surrender his licence, although
that man can still carry on the business he
carried on before if he structurally alters his
premises. A person going into a country shop

drink as well. That is the only point the
Prime Minister failed to deal with. If a man
voluntarily surrenders his licence I would be
inclined to give him some compensation, but
I am not prepared to press that matter and
I hope the committee will not delay further
on this subject.

seems to me the Government may very easily

Mr. HANNA: The object of this amendment is perfectly clear. It is to alter
entirely the basis of compensation. The basis
of compensation as laid down in the Bill is
something in relation to Income Tax. I
cannot but believe that that is only put in
to show compliance with a sense of obligation, knowing perfectly well that it is not
a fair basis of compensation. The provisions
of the English Act have been repeatedly
mentioned, and that is the Act from which
I have taken the basis of compensation as
set out in the amendment. Can there be
any objection to that basis which I suggest?
Has it the merit of being fair? Has it the
merit of being a basis of compensation that
has been adopted in England for over twenty
years? Has it not worked satisfactorily? Has
not every word of it been judicially interpreted? There will be no cause for any
trouble here. I cannot see that there can be
any opposition to it, unless it be that compensation is only to appear in the Bill as
a word, and is to mean absolutely nothing.
I am beginning to lose heart. I am beginning
to be fearfully worried now. I have nothing
to gain in this matter. I simply wish that
we should be fair to these people from whoni
we are taking something. My heart and my
head are in accord and in unison in regard
to this matter. I say the basis of compensation in the Bill is not right. I want to use
no hard words, because I really want this time
to make an earnest appeal to the Committee.
I put this down as being a basis for compensation that has every merit one could
conceive. I rather believe it will satisfy those
who will be compelled, or those who will
elect to surrender their licences. If we adopt
this amendment I believe in my heart that
you will encourage them to give up their
licences, but if you refuse the amendment,
and leave the Bill as it is, and grant the
compensation according to Income Tax for
three years I say you are doing an injustice.
The trade for those particular years in Belfast
and many parts of the Six Counties has been
terribly affected, as I said on the First and
Second Readings of the Bill. They have not
had a normal year since 1911, and as soon as
the restrictions came off we had the unfortunate riots in the City of Belfast, and many
of their places are down. There could not be
trade, and therefore no returns of Income
Tax. My hon. and learned Friend (Mr.
(Megaw) in pursuance of his duty, in reference
to some of the spirit grocers whose places
were burned down, actually gave in Court to
the right hon. the Lord Chief Justice an
undertaking, which I take it was on behalf
of the Government, that they would be fairly
dealt with.
Mr. MEGAW: Not at all.
Mr. HANNA: If not on behalf of the Government then on behalf of his clients. "Mr.

The putting out of spirit grocers is going
to make the value of the premises for the
licensed trader very much higher, and I
believe that the licensed trade who are remaining are willing to pay for the advantage
they are going to secure through the extinction of the spirit grocer. I do not think
that the off-licence holder is being properly
compensated in the proposal put before us
in this Bill. I had a deputation with me
this morning of a few respectable men who
are members of the spirit grocers' trade in
Belfast. One man told me that his premises
are valued at present at £5,000. As soon as
he loses his licence he could not sell the
premises for more than £2,000. He has got
to lose £3,000 through the action of this
House of Parliament. He has always run
his business straight. He has never been
before the magistrates. He has been carrying
on a legitimate business, and tried to carry
it on in a legitimate way.
Another man told me-and he also is a
most respectable man-that he paid £4,200
for his premises in the year 1920, and that
if he has to give up the licence of these
premises in September next his premises
I will not be worth £1.500. These men say,
and they say to my mind very rightly, that
the compensation offered here is useless-that
it is no use to them. Two other men told
me-and I believe what they say is quite
correct-that under the compensation clause
in this Bill they will be ruined. They have
no show, they say, at all. I have asked these
men what they want, and the statement they
have put before me is that they would agree
to get compensation up to ten years on the
basis of the Excise returns. That may be
unreasonable in the view of this House, but
I would say let there be a compromise; treat
these men as generously as we can, because
we are taking away a legitimate business
from them which they have carried on with
the sanction of the law. We want to put
away this business, but we want to treat
them as fair and honestly and honourably
as we can.

houses are well known not only in the City

We had no means of ascertaining the aggregate volume of their liquor trade (that

Clause 6 (Extension of provisions of I Edward 7, c. 27):-
"The Intoxicating Liquors (Sale to
Children) Act, 1901, shall have effect as if

"
Major SHILLINGTON: I beg to move.
"In Clause 6, page 6, line 46, after years
(age of fourteen years') insert Notwithstanding anything in the said Act, no person
under the age of eighteen years shall be
employed in the sale or delivery of intoxicating liquors." "
In this clause, the Government propose to
alter Section 2 by changing the age at which
intoxicating liquor is sold to young people
from fourteen to eighteen years. I would
like to draw the attention of the Committee
to Clause 3 of the Intoxicating Liquors Act,
1901, which says:-
"Nothing in this Act shall prevent the
employment by a licensed person of a member of his family or his servant or apprentice as a messenger to deliver intoxicating
liquor."
I am anxious that this Bill should abolish
what I think was a well-known objection in
that provision, and that it should go further
than that and prevent any person under the
age of eighteen years being employed in the
sale of intoxicating liquors at all. I hope
the Government will see their way to accept
this. Surely, if it is thought wrong for a person under eighteen years of age to be sent to
a place to buy liquor, then we would be
wrong to have persons under that age employed in the selling of it. As I say, I hope
the Government will see their way to accept
this amendment.
The PRIME MINISTER: This matter
occupied the attention of my colleagues and
myself for a considerable time, and, although
there was a certain amount of anomaly about
forbidding people to go into public-houses
who were under eighteen years of age, and yet
allowing persons under that age to actually
serve in public-houses, on the other hand
there is this consideration about it, which is
the part of the matter that convinced us, at all
events, that on the whole it would be better
to allow the matter to stand. The State has
provided in the Education Act fourteen years
as the limit for compulsory attendance in
school, and we feel that a man who owned
a public-house and who desired that his
family should succeed him in the management of the public-house would be rather at
a loss what to do with a boy between the age
of fourteen and eighteen years. It might
possibly be adding a great hardship to the
family to say that if he wanted his son to
succeed him in business he would have to
spend four years elsewhere before he could
take him into the business. It seemed an
interference with the parental authority to
say that a man could not state what is best
for the boy's future career after he is of age,
and at the same time it was going further
than the demnad made by the House in the
first instance for reform in connection with
the licensing law. We did discuss that very
point which has been raised, and we felt on
the whole, as we are affecting the trade very
largely in this Bill, it would be going a little
bit too far to ask them not to judge whether
their own children would succeed them in
their business.
Mrs. CHICHESTER: I feel very reluctant
to say anything on this matter after what the
Prime Minister has just told us. At the same
time, I cannot let the amendment pass without a few words from me on the subject. I do
hope that the Government will reconsider
their attitude on this question. The Prime
Minister has stated that he sees very clearly
the point raised by the hon. and gallant
Member (Major Shillington); at the same
time, he cannot see his way to accept the
amendment. If the atmosphere of a publichouse is bad-we are all of one mind, I think,
on that subject-for those under the age of
eighteen years, surely it is very wrong not
only to allow young persons to go into the
house to take out drink for somebody else,
but that they should be put into the house
perpetually to help there and sell drink to
others. I certainly admit that in some cases
there may be hardship for a man who wishes
in this way to get free labour and employ
his own children, but I do not, and I cannot,
agree that that hardship should in this
instance be considered. The Government
must bear in mind that where they may be
allowing one man's hardship to influence
them they are perhaps going to ruin the lives
and characters of that man's children, be
they young girls or boys, by keeping them in
an atmosphere which we all recognise is a
bad atmosphere at the most impressionable
age in their lives. I do hope the Government
will reconsider this.

CLAUSE 7 (Structural Arrangement of
Licensed Premises).
(1) Where any business, other than the
sale of intoxicating liquor for consumption
on the premises, is carried on in any
premises licensed for such sale as aforesaid
(not being premises structurally adapted
for use and bona-fide used exclusively as a
hotel as hereinbefore in this Act defined,
or as a refreshment house or restaurant),
the part of the premises in which the sale
of intoxicating liquor is carried on shal
be structurally separated from, and have no
internal communication with, the remainder of the building, and nothing shall
be sold or offered for sale in such part of
the premises as aforesaid except intoxicating liquor, tobacco, table waters, and
food for consumption on the premises.
(2) Upon any application to the licensing
court for the certificate required for the
grant or renewal of a licence for the sale
of intoxicating liquor by retail, the licensing court may require to be produced before
them, and to be deposited with their clerk,
a plan of the premises in respect of which
the application is made, and on granting
or confirming such certificate the licensing
court may by order direct that, within
a time fixed by the order, such alterations
shall be made in the premises as the court
thinks reasonably necessary for the following purposes, namely:-
(i) for securing compliance with the
requirements of sub-section (1) of this
section;
(ii) for securing that no part of any
room, which is used for consumption of
intoxicating liquor on the premises, is
concealed or screened from observation in
such a manner as to obstruct proper supervision; and
(iii) for securing the proper conduct of
the business in accordance with the law
relating to licensed premises.
(3) This section shall come into operation
on the first day of October, nineteen hundred and twenty-four, and before that date
public notice shall be given of the provisions of this section in such manner as
the Minister of Home Affairs may direct.

would like to add, if possible, the words,
