The
This amendment which is to be taken with
two other amendments a little later will perhaps require a word or two of explanation,
and I propose to give that to the Committee.
The licensing law at present enables the magistrates to endorse the conviction on the licence.
That law has been more honoured in the
breach than the observance, and it has come
to be regarded as almost obsolete. I think
last year there were only two cases in which
a conviction was endorsed on the licence. The
1245 Intoxicating Liquor Bill-

31 MAY 1923
Committee.
result is that the law in that respect has
become practically useless. By this amendment that is now before the Committee, and
indeed by the section as it was drafted, it is
proposed to change the law, in that it is to
be the usual penalty to have a conviction
endorsed on the licence, but that it need not
be done if there are extenuating circumstances or if it is merely a technical offence.
The original words as drafted were in a somewhat different form, but it was thought
that the words contained in the amendment
meet the circumstances and leave the matter
very much less capable of ambiguity.
The
idea, of course, is that when a person is convicted of a breach under the Act-when it
becomes an Act-the Court will as a matter
of course record that conviction on the licence
and that a number of convictions will result
in the abolition or the annulment of the
licence. That is to be taken in connection
with the amendments in regard to Sub-Section 2, and I think perhaps it will be convenient if I mention now that those amendments are really drafting amendments. The
Bill as it stood contained provisions by
reference to the existing law. Two sections
of the Licensing Act of 1872 are contained in
the Schedule. It was thought that it would
be better drafting, and that it would render
the law more easy of administration, if the
actual law were set out in the Bill, instead
of having to go and refer to previous Acts of
Parliament. The two subsequent amendments are really the statement of the law,
but, of course, it is changed to this effect,
that where convictions are recorded the result
in those cases will be the annulment of the
licence. Formerly, that hardly ever came
into use, because no licences were endorsed.
Now it is expected that licences will bo
endorsed when an offence has been committed
unless there are extenuating circumstances
and repeated offences will result under the
ordinary law in the abolition of the licence.

CLAUSE 9 (Forfeiture of licence and recording of convictions for certain offences).
(1) Any licence for the sale of intoxicating
liquor by retail held by any person who is
convicted of an offence to which this subsection applies shall, in addition to any
other penalty or forfeiture, be annulled,
unless the Court by whom the conviction
has been made are satisfied as to the
existence of extenuating circumstances in
connection with the offence. The Court
shall cause notice of any such annulment to
be served upon the person convicted and
upon the owner of the licensed premises,
and where no such annulment is ordered the
Court shall specify the extenuating circumstances in their order.
Any person whose licence is so annulled,
and who, after service upon him of notice
as aforesaid, sells any intoxicating liquor,
shall be liable to the same penalties as if he
had been convicted for selling intoxicating
liquor without first having obtained a
licence for that purpose.
The offences to which this sub-section
applies are-
(a) the selling of methylated spirits
without being duly licensed or authorised
in that behalf, and

Mr. MEGAW: They enter into recognisances that they will pay the costs, and 1

of appeal provided. The person who appeals

NEW CLAUSE (Restrictions as to the issue
of new licences).
The Licensing (Ireland) Act, 1902, is
hereby repealed, and the following provisions shall have effect, that is to say :-
(1) From and after the passing of this Act
no licence shall be granted for the sale of
intoxicating liquor, whether for consumption on or off the premises, except-
(a) for premises which are lawfully
licensed at the date of the passing of this
Act, or which were lawfully licensed at
any time since the first day of January,
nineteen hundred and twenty; or
(b) for an hotel, which expression
means a house containing at least ten
apartments set apart and used exclusively
for the sleeping accommodation of travellers, and having no public bar for the sale
of intoxicating liquor; or
(c) for a railway refreshment room.
(2) Where, by reason of the expiration of
a lease, a licence for the sale of intoxicating
liquor for consumption on the premises
comprised in the lease is extinguished or
surrendered, the licensing authority may,
notwithstanding anything in this Section,
grant a licence for suitable premises in the
immediate vicinity of the premises to which
the licence so extinguished or surrendered
was attached.
(3) Where, owing to an increase of not
less than 25 per cent. of the population according to the last census, there is a growth
or an extension of any city or town, and the
licensing authority is satisfied, after hearing
any evidence tendered to it by any resident
or owner of property in such city or town,
that the restrictions in this Section on the
granting of licences may be relaxed, the
licensing authority may grant a licence to
any applicant notwithstanding that the
same would be otherwise forbidden by this
Section;
Provided that such licence shall be
granted only for premises situate in the
ward or district electoral division in which
such increase in population has taken place,
and in substitution for at least two existing
licences held in respect of premises situate
within the city or town (as the case may
be) comprising such ward
or district
electoral division.
(4) In the case of applications under subdivision (b) of paragraph (1), and under
paragraphs (2) and (3) of this Section, the
premises shall be valued under the Irish
Valuation Acts at not less than-
Thirty pounds in the City of Belfast;
Twenty pounds in the City of Londonderry;
Twelve pounds in any town over ten
thousand inhabitants at the census ascertained next preceding the application; and
Ten pounds in all other places.
(5) Nothing in this Section shall operate
to prevent the granting of new licences
where the licensing authority thinks fit, to
premises attached to or adjoining premises
licensed for the sale of intoxicating liquor
at the date of the passing of this Act:
Provided always that such new licence
as last herein before mentioned shall only
be granted in order to render the said
licensed premises more suitable for the
business carried on therein.
(6) Nothing in this Section shall be taken
to affect the law as to the transfer or
assignment of licences from one person to
another or as to the renewal of licences.-
(Mr. Megaw.)
Brought up and read the First time.

I think I have already made quite clear

the year 1920. It has been recognised there

NEW CLAUSE (Strength of Spirits).
In determining whether an offence has
been committed under the enactments relating to the sale of food and drugs by
selling to the prejudice of the purchaser,
whisky, brandy, rum, or gin, not adulterated
otherwise than by any admixture of water,
it shall be a good defence to prove that such
admixture has not reduced the spirit more
than 35 degrees under proof, and Section 6
of the Sale of Food and Drugs Act, 1879,
is hereby repealed.
No person shall either by himself or by
any servant or agent sell or supply in any
licensed premises any whisky, brandy, rum,
or gin, which has been reduced in strength
more than 35 degrees under proof.

Part I.
Constitution of the Claims Tribunal.
The Claims Tribunal, when hearing or
determining a claim under this Act, shall
be constituted of at least three of the following persons-
(a) a recorder or county court judge;
(b) a person nominated by the Minister
of Finance;
(c) two persons nominated by the Minister of Home Affairs, one of whom is a
resident magistrate;
(d) a justice chosen by the justices for
a petty sessions district;
Provided that no person who is a member
of the Claims Trubunal in his capacity as
recorder, county court judge, magistrate or
justice, shall sit to hear or determine a
claim, unless in that capacity he has juris
diction, or has been appointed for, the
county or petty sessions district in which
the premises are situate in respect of which
the claim is made.

HOUSES OF PARLIAMENT.
Motion made and Question proposed:
"That a supplementary sum not exceeding
£7,600 be granted to His Majesty to complete the sum necessary to defray the
charge which will come in course of payment during the year ending on the 31st
March, 1924, for the salaries and expenses
of the Senate and of the House of Commons.
The PARLIAMENTARY AND FINANCIAL
SECRETARY TO THE MINISTRY OF FIN-
NANCE (Mr. Barbour): On the 29th March,
there was a Resolution passed by this House
that an allowance should be made to
hon. Members of this House in respect
of expenses incurred by them in the
discharge of their Parliamentary duties.
It is necessary now by means of this Supplementary Estimate to provide the necessary
funds to enable that payment to be made.
It will be understood, of course, that the
only Members qualified to receive this payment are those who take the Oath and their
seats in this House, and who, moreover, are
not in receipt of any salary in respect of
any office they may hold. Provision is, therefore, made for the full number of 52 members
less the fourteen members who are in receipt of such salaries by virtue of offices held
by them, making the total charge of £7,600.
I beg to move.
Question put and agreed to.

CLASS 1. No. 2.
CABINET OFFICES.
Motion made and Question proposed.
That a supplementary sum not exceeding £1,000 be granted to His Majesty to
complete the sum necessary to defray the
charge which will come in course of payment during the year ending on the 31st
March, 1924, to defray the salaries of the
Department of the Prime Minister, the
salaries of the Cabinet and of the Cabinet
Secretariat, and other expenses in connection therewith.
Mr. BARBOUR: The exact intent of this
Vote will be seen in the last two lines on
page 4 of the Supplementary Estimates. The
Prime Minister has on several occasions,
both in this House and elsewhere, alluded
to his hope that an active branch of the
Royal Naval Volunteer Reserve might be
established in Northern Ireland. This
opinion when expressed has invariably received the support of those to whom the project has been submitted. As no provision has
been made in the Estimates at Westminster
to meet any expense that might be incurred
in connection with this, it was felt that, in
view of the anxiety that there should be no
delay in starting the scheme, this Parliament might for the first year bear the
expense of the preliminary inquiries and the
preliminary organisation that would necessarily have to be done before the scheme could
be started. Hon. Members will bear in mind
that it is not intended to ask next year for
any repetition of this sum. It is merely to
meet the inaugural expenses for one yearto start the scheme-and after one year it
will be for the Imperial Government to take
the matter into their own hands. I beg to
move.
Question put and agreed to.

Mr. BARBOUR: In the brief period which
has elapsed since this Parliament was inaugurated we in this Province have been
honoured by the presence of some very
distinguished visitors. We are, of course,
hoping that a repetition of those visits may
occur, and the more frequently they do occur
I am sure the more hon, Members of this
Committee will be pleased. Hitherto the
burden-or the privilege of entertaining
such visitors has been borne entirely
by one or two of our leading men.
It is felt that, in view of the fact
that such visits are of very material benefit to our Province the greatest public interest is stirred by the presence amongst
us of these distinguished men from Westminster, and' we have had indeed His
Majesty and His most gracious Consort
-it will be the wish of hon. Members
of this House, and, indeed, of the
of
general public
the Province, that
fitting hospitality should be extended to those
who thus come amongst us. In order that
the expense of entertaining such visitors
should not fall upon one or two individuals
it is felt only right that a Fund should be
provided to be available for such a purpose.
It is, therefore, proposed in the present
instance to vote a sum of £3,000, which
would be available to meet such expenses. It
is proposed that, should any proportion of
this sum not have been expended by the
end of the financial year, such balance as
remains shall be carried forward, and not
be re-voted, but the Fund once established
will be supplemented from time to time
by Vote of this House as occasion may require. The Fund will be under the control
of the Comptroller and Auditor-General,
and will have to be accounted for in the same
manner as any other public expenditure. I
feel that the propriety of making its provision will appeal to hon. Members, and I
beg to move.

UNEMPLOYMENT GRANTS.
Motion made and Question proposed:
"That a supplementary sum not exceeding £25,000 be granted to His Majesty to
3 G

HOUSE OF COMMONS.
complete the sum necessary to defray the
charge which will come in course of payment during the year ending on the 31st
March, 1924, for grants to local authorities,
etc., in Northern Ireland for assistance in
carrying out approved schemes to relieve
unemployment."
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): After the very spirited debates
which we have had during the last few days I
am not altogether surprised that the House
appears a little bit relaxed to-day, and in
moving this Vote of £25,000 for relief works
in Northern Ireland, excluding Belfast, and
neighbourhood, I desire that my language
should be particularly temperate under the
circumstances. I do feel that it is desirable
that I should take up a few minutes of the
time of the House in order to explain the
financial position regarding these various
grants for the relief of unemployment which
have been placed at my disposal. In the first
place you will remember that owing to the
influence and exertions of the Prime Minister
we received £500,000 from the Imperial
Treasury. I am glad to be able to say that
to-day there are actually engaged on relief
works in Belfast 3,500 persons, and in
addition to that I estimate that at
least an equal number are engaged in
carying out useful work in providing
materials for these relief works who
would not otherwise have been employed. As
regards the relief works in the Six Counties,
excluding Belfast and neighbourhood, hon.
Members will probably remember that a sum
of £14,000 was handed over to me as a remnant from the Unemployment Grants Committee in London, and that in addition to
that sum, this House about a year ago, voted
£50,000. Of those two sums making a total
of £64,000, £17,000 has actually been spent
and the balance has been completely allotted.
In addition to that, applications have been
received from our local athoritites for further grants amounting to £12,000. If this
grant of £25,000 is agreed upon to-day, it
will allow me to meet those requests and
leave my Department a sum of £13,000 to
go on with. I think hon. Members will be
interested to know that all these works
which we have carried out are works of public
utility. Houses have been approved for grant
in Banbridge, Enniskillen, Coleraine, Armagh, and in connection with the City and
County Asylum of Londonderry. In all,
about 2,500 men have received work through
the medium of these grants throughout our
country districts and smaller provincial
towns, and I think that this policy of endeavouring to obtain as far as possible work
for our people rather than giving them something for nothing is in accordance with the
often expressed wishes of hon. Members of
this House. Therefore, I beg to move with
implicit confidence this Vote.
Question put, and agreed to.

Oral Answers to Questions.
LAND PURCHASE IN NORTHERN
IRELAND.
2. Mr. MILLER (on behalf of Mr. Cooper)
asked the Prime Minister what progress has
been made in the negotiations for a Land
Purchase Bill for Northern Ireland, and if he
can state whether such a Bill will be introduced in the Imperial or the Northern
Parliament, and when?'
The PARLIAMENTARY AND FINAN-
CIAL SECRETARY TO THE MINISTRY
OF FINANCE (Mr. Barbour): In the
absence of the Prime Minister, I have been
asked to reply to this question.
His Majesty's Government have intimated
that they propose to introduce a Bill in the
present Session dealing with the completion
of Land Purchase in Northern Ireland. A
Commitee, on which the Northern Government will be represented, has been set up by
the Imperial Government to consider the form
of the Bill and all the financial points involved, and will, I believe, hold its first meeting this week.
Mr. DONALD: Can my hon. Friend tell us
the name of the representative of Northern
Ireland on that Committee?
Mr. BARBOUR: I understand that the
Permanent Secretary to the Ministry of
Finance has been appointed as the representative of Northern Ireland.
PRIME MINISTER'S PLEDGE.
3. Colonel WOODS asked the Prime Minister when he proposes to introduce legislation
to redcem the pledge given in his manifesto
of May, 1921, to "ensure a brighter future for
the masses of workers in our midst "?
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): In the absence of the Prime Minister I have been asked to reply to this question.
I am sure the House will agree that the
pledge to which the hon. Member refers has
been amply redeemed. Within the short
period during which the Prime Minister's
Government has been responsible for the administration of Northern Ireland many valuable Measures have been introduced to improve the condition of our people. I would
refer the hon. Member to the two first-class
Measures of far-reaching reform with which
this House has been engaged this Session-the
Education and the Intoxicating Liquor Bills.
So far as the relief of unemployment is concerned, it can be fairly claimed that no Government has done more to meet the situation
which has resulted from the War. Unemployment Insurance Acts have been passed which
have secured for our working people provisions on all points as generous as those in
force in Great Britain, and the Loans Guarantee Acts of last Session and of this Session
have enable financial assistance to be given
to industrial schemes which have created employment for large numbers.
In addition, this House voted £50,000 last
year to assist the promotion of schemes to relieve unemployment, and this sum has been
supplemented by a further £25,000 voted
last week to fulfil the Prime Minister's promise that if last year's Budget
showed a surplus that was at all substantial the bulk of the surplus would
go to the benefit of the working classes. As
a result of these relief grants, important
public works have been put in hand which
have given employment to about 2,400 men
outside Belfast in addition to the 3,500 men
who are at present engaged on relief works
in Belfast and its neighbourhood. The public
works that have been started under these
relief schemes include the construction of
about 1,560 working-class houses.
These measures by no means exhaust the
steps which the Government are taking, for,
as was stated by my right hon. Friend, the
Minister of Finance, in his Budget statement
last week, consideration is now being given to
see what measure of relief can be afforded to

ROYAL COMMISSION ON INDUSTRIAL

4. Colonel WOODS asked the Prime
Minister if it is still the intention of the
Government to set up a Royal Commission on
Industrial Development in Northern Ireland,
as promised at the opening of Parliament,
and if so, will he state the names of the

Mr. ANDREWS: I have been asked by the
Prime Minister to reply. The Ministries of
Commerce and Labour are completing the
personnel of the Development Commission,
as it is believed that the inquiries and recommendations of the Commission will prove of
great value to the whole industrial future
of Northern Ireland. I am glad to say that
the Right Honourable Viscount Charlemont
has kindly consented to act as Chairman,
and it is hoped to publish a complete list of
all those who have agreed to serve as members at an early date. The Commission's
Terms of Reference were announced in the
King's Speech delivered by his Grace the
Governor at the opening of the present Session, and I will repeat them for the hon.
Members' convenience. They are as follows:
"To consider and report as to how the
natural and industrial resources of Northern Ireland can be best developed with a
view to increasing the general prosperity
and reducing the extent of unemployment,"
It is intended to hold the first meeting of
the Commission on the 19th instant.
Colonel WOODS: Thank you.

THE AMBUSH AT CLONES RAILWAY
STATION.
1. Mr. HANNA: I desire to ask your leave
to put Question No. 1 standing in the name
of the hon. Member for Derry (Sir Robert
Anderson): To ask the Minister of Home
Affairs if any compensation has been paid in
respect of the constables who were killed or
injured at Clones Railway Station, and if on
enlistment the Government guaranteed that
the constables and their dependants would
be entitled to compensation under the Criminal Injuries (Ireland) Acts, and if not, if the
Minister will give the exact wording of the
guarantee and his interpretation thereof,
and whether the Government accepts responsibility for sending these constables armed
through Southern Ireland?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am obliged to the
hon. Member for affording me the opportunity of stating the position with regard to
the Special Constables who were killed or
injured at Clones Railway Station when they
were treacherously ambushed on the railway
journey to Enniskillen.
Four constables were killed and fourteen
wounded on the occasion in question.
Of those who were wounded, seven recovered and are still serving in the force.
Six have been awarded pensions under the
Pensions Order, varying, according to their
degrees of disability, from £136 10s per
annum down to £42 9s 4d per annum. The
remaining wounded constable continued to
serve in the Special Constabulary until
January of this year, when he resigned.
There was
no evidence that on retirement
his health had been in any way affected by
his being wounded in the ambush, and no
pension was payable under the Pensions
Order.
A claim for the dependants of one of those
killed was received, but under the terms of
the existing Pensions Order, no gratuity
could be paid. However, the Pensions Order
is under revision, and in anticipation of the
issue of the amended Order payment of a
sum of £45 10s has been authorised, and the
decision has been notified.
A few days ago a communication was received from a solicitor acting on behalf of a
second of the constables killed asking that
compensation be granted to the dependants.
We are now proceeding to determine the
amount which can be awarded under the new
Persions Order which is to be made.
Νο
claims have been received in the case of the
other two constables killed.
I should like to make it clear that the
persions or gratuities awarded by us must
be in accordance with the regulations contained in the Pensions Order. I fully realise,
however, that some of these constables who
have been injured and the dependants of
those who have been killed are placed in a

That a sum not exceeding £1,597,628 be
granted to His Majesty to complete the sum
necessary to defray the charge which will
come in course of payment during the year
ending on the 31st March, 1924, for expenditure in respect of the services included
in Class II of the Estimates, namely:
Special Constabulary, £1,050,385; Royal
Ulster Constabulary, £547,243.
Mr. HANNA: I have this day handed in
questions addressed to the right hon. Gentleman, the Home Secretary, in reference to
matters affecting the police, and to prevent
anything in the nature of a misunderstanding
in regard to one of the questions, I am taking
this opportunity of raising it on the report
stage of the Estimates for the Police. I want
to know when the representative body that
by statute it is necessary to set up for the
purpose of giving members of the police
force opportunities for discussing matters
pertaining to themselves is intended to be
set up.
Another matter that I am concerned about
is this: the Government are under statutory
obligation when they come to make appointments to the rank of district inspector to
choose one half of those appointed from
suitable head-constables. I am given to
understand that since the transfer of the
R.I.C. to the R.U.C. altogether eleven appointments have been made to the rank of
district inspector. Two of them have been
made by promotion of head-constables and
rine have been appointed without any test
or without any special qualification, or indeed
any police service at all. And I am further
instructed that only two of them, or three at
the utmost, belong to Ulster at all; and the
obligation on the Government is statutory.
Of course if what I have stated-if my facts
are wrong then there is no justification for
this protest. But I can hardly think that
the information that has been given to me,
and I have now given to the House, can be
wrong. I think it would be an exceedingly
curious affair. If the head-constables are
entitled, as they are, to one half of the appointments they should get them, being experienced men and knowing something about
the position.
I have no objections, and make none, to
the distinguished gentlemen who have been
promoted to the position. I say, as a matter
of law, that head-constables should get half,
and as a matter of decency and fair play.
If men who have no police qualifications are
to be put into these positions, then surely
instead of searching foreign places for men to
take the position they should get them from
the ranks of those who fought in the Ulster
Division.
Mr. DONALD: I should just like to put
a question. I had intended to mention this
matter when the estimates came forward. I
want to know on the question of the special
constabulary if there has been any reduction
in the pay and allowance for married men
or has that matter been put right? And
further, I want to support what has been
said by my hon. and learned Friend from
Antrim (Mr. Hanna). A very large number
of those promoted to the position of district
inspector have had no previous experience
in
any police force. I do want to emphasise the point that where there have been
constables who have risen to be sergeants and
who have ability and rise to the rank of
head-constables, the claims and experience of
those men will not be overlooked; and if
these men can qualify for the position of
district inspector that outsiders will not be
brought in, whether it is from England or
the Free State, and that the claims of Ulstermen will be considered, and rightly considered, in this new force of ours. We shall
not have the opportunity for a very long
time of warning the Government with regard
to this matter. We have excellent menexcellent fellows in our new force; and we
want to see some inducements offered to these
splendid young men in the future. There
should be promotion from the ranks. That
is the way to put it, because the late Sir
Henry Wilson, who was a great soldier, emphasised that point. When he saw a man
of ability he kept his eye on that man, and
he saw to it that some inducement should be
offered to the right man, that promotion
should be offered irrespective-I do not know
whether the thing is laid down, I may be
ignorant of that fact, by statute. I hope it
is not laid down that a man cannot rise
from the ranks, and I hope that anyone who
serves on this splendid force of ours who
qualifies will not be debarred from rising to
the highest position.

Sir DAWSON BATES: When these estimates were before the committee an undertaking was given that on the Report stage
they would be fully gone into. Therefore, although many of the points have not been
raised by hon. Members here, I feel it right
that I should take the House over the various
points, and in doing so I hope I will be able
to cover some of the questions raised by the
hon. Members who have spoken. Some of
those questions have arisen purely from misunderstanding. On the 30th of May last year,
on the eve of the establishment of the Royal
Ulster Constabulary, I had the honour of
presenting the first estimate for the Royal
Ulster Constabulary. On that occasion I
asked the House for £735,000 for a period of
nine months. For this year the amount that
has been asked for a period of twelve months
-that is three months in addition-is a sum
of £822,000; only £90,000 more. I was not in
a position last year to make any comprehensive statement in regard to the working
of the Police Force for the obvious reason that
it had not at that time come into being. For
that reason I think it right that I should say
a few words with regard to the working of
the Police Force during the last twelve
months.
Before I refer to the internal organisation
of the Force I would like to make some observations with regard to the situation generally as it affects the Police Force-both the
regular force and the Specials. No one who
remembers the very trying times through
which we have passed last year can fail to
appreciate the wonderful improvement that
has taken place during that period. I do not
want to worry the House with too many statistics, but I cannot refrain from pointing out
that a very striking instance of that improvement is shown in the fact that during one week
in May last year there were no fewer than
32 political murders, but since October we
have not had a single political murder. But
the public, if I may say so, are somewhat
premature in accustoming themselves to the
idea that peace has come to us on a permanent
basis. Perhaps I should be the last to remove
the idea that we have got peace permanently
here, but I think it right, and, indeed, it is
my duty to sound a word of warning, and to
ask the people of Ulster to recollect that they
are not yet entirely out of the wood. It is
perfectly true that we can maintain, and fully
maintain, peace if we in Ulster are left alone.
I am certain in my own mind that the vast
majority of the people of Ulster, irrespective
of creed or class, are desirous that the present
peaceable conditions should continue.
fear, however, is more of danger from the
outside than of danger from within, and our
sources of information, which have been corroborated by the events of the last few days
along the Border, go to show that danger does
still exist, and that we must maintain an
adequate Police Force to deal with the possibility of renewed disturbances. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) I think that in itself
answers the question raised in regard to the
reduction of the Police Force.
Our
The hostile movement against Ulster-if I
may use the expression-has been "scotched,"
but I am sorry that I cannot yet say it has
been killed. We receive reports from time to
time indicating that underground movements
are going on outside to subvert our Government and to create unrest inside our own
territory. We believe that the people of Ulster
are with the Government in our efforts at all
costs to maintain internal peace, and above
all, to maintain the integrity of our boundaries. While this is our policy we are very
careful not to interfere in any way with the
domestic concerns of the Administration in
Southern Ireland. I do not want for one

HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Sir Dawson Bates]
moment to attribute to the Free State Government as a Government any desire on their part
to disturb the peace that at present exists in
Ulster. We believe that the vast majority of
the people throughout the whole of Ireland are
sick of this campaign of murder and arson and
want peace.
At the same time we cannot
shut our eyes to the fact that disturbances are
still going on in the South of Ireland, and that
there are hostile organisations there still completely uncontrolled, organisations which last
year did not hesitate to operate in our territory, and which would not hesitate to operate
again in Northern Ireland if they are permitted by us to do so. Only within the last
few days along the Border our police were
deliberately attacked without the slightest
provocation by machine gun and rifle fire.
As I said before, so far as the people in our
own territory are concerned, there is abundant
evidence that they on their part desire to
support the Government in the steps they are
taking to preserve the peace. The police at
the present time are receiving most useful
assistance from the inhabitants of our territory of all creeds and of all classes-(hon.
Members: Hear, hear)-and I think we may
fairly claim that we have convinced the
population of our territory that our attitude
as a Government is not a provocative attitude,
but entirely one of self-defence (hon.
Members: Hear, hear)--and our one desire is
to bring all classes, no matter what their
political views may be, and no matter what
form of worship they may go in for, together
so that we may all dwell in peace and harmony.
Now with regard to some of the precautions
we have taken, we watch the situation from
day to day, and I can assure the House that
when we find that we can safely relax our precautions, then, and only then, are we going
to do so. Perhaps our caution has brought
upon the Government a certain amount of
criticism, but I would ask hon. Members of
this House, and also the public generally, to
realise that we have sources of information
which are not available to the general public. We have already made certain concessions with regard to the hours of Curfew, but
the time has not yet arrived when we can
safely remove what has proved a most successful regulation.
Mr. McGUFFIN: Hear, hear.
Sir DAWSON BATES: In the same way we
are not in a position to forego the powers
which we obtained under the Civil Authorities Act. Already we find that several of the
. individuals who in the general round-up last
year found themselves with a guilty conscience, and so safely fled from cur territory,
are drifting back into Northern Ireland. On
more than one occasion-and 1 would like to
emphasise this point-I have been pressed to
give guarantees of safe conduct to certain
individuals who expressed a desire to return
to Northern Ireland. My answer to such
requests is that if any individual is a peaceloving and a law-abiding citizen, and has got
an easy conscience, he has nothing to fear in
returning to Northern Ireland. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) As a result of the returning confidence of the people we have succeeded from day to day in getting information about some of the past activities of
those people who fled from our territory, and
the House may rest assured that once the
Government is satisfied about the correctness
of any information it will not hesitate to
take whatever steps are recessary to ensure
the peace of the community.
I may, perhaps, be expected to say a word
in regard to the question of internment.
Let me say here at once that we adopted
the expedient of internment, not because we
liked it, but because no other course was
open to us if the campaign of arson and
murder, which at one time threatened to
overwhelm, Ulster, was to be successfully
grappled with. To those critics who find
fault with the policy of internment, my reply
is, "Look at the results." Again the question may be asked, how long are we going
to continue the principle of internment? The
answer to that is that it is entirely in the
hands of those who seek to undermine the
Government of Northern Ireland. Before we
abandon what has been a most successful
law, we must have clear evidence that the
security of our Province is on a very much
safer basis than that on which I feel it is at
the present time. From the remarks I have
made, I think the House will agree that the
time has not yet arrived when we could
safely make any substantial reduction in the
police force, and certainly without the forces
which at the present time are under their
control the Government of Northern Ireland
could not secure the peace of the community.
Having said that, I would like to say a
word or two with regard to the internal
organisation of the police force, and in doing
so perhaps I may be able to clear up one or
two matters on which there appears to be
some misunderstanding. The details of the
Estimate, which hon. Members have already
seen, will show that the organisation is largely
modelled on the old Royal Irish Constabulary Force. We provided for a full establishment of 3,000, which is the number authorised under our Police Act of last year.
have not yet recruited that number. The
total number of our Force at present
amounts to 2,677, leaving 323 still to be
recruited. Of that 2,677 I find that recruits
from the Royal Irish Constabulary number
1,400, and those from the Special Constabulary 1,215. Recruiting was thrown open to

An hon. Member has suggested that we are
too rigid in regard to our educational and
physical tests, but I think the Inspector-
General is perfectly right in the line he has
taken of insisting upon proper educational
and physical tests for our permanent force.
I have been pressed, on more than one occasion, to secure the admission of candidates
who happen to fall short of these tests, but
I think hon. Members will agree with me
that if we reduce the standards in one particular case we must go on reducing until
the whole force suffers.
It may be of interest to the House to have
some information of the length and nature
of the training given to a recruit in the
Royal Ulster Constabulary. While the
amount of training given to members of the
Special Constabulary varies from about a
fortnight to one month, according to the
urgency for recruits, the training for a reeruit in the Royal Ulster Constabulary
consists of a six months' course at the depot.
luring which time he receives instruction in
Irill, musketry, both rifle and revolver,
Jombing, physical training, traffic control,
first aid to the injured, and police duties.
The police duties comprise his general duties
as a constable, elementary criminal law,
law of evidence, the taking of statements,
investigation of crime, and the various Acts
of Parliament relating to police work. As
regards each Act of Parliament, the constable is required to know what constitutes
an offence under the Act, and what are his
powers in dealing with such offenders. On
the conclusion of his six months' course, the
recruit proceeds to the country where his
instruction is carried on by the district
inspector and sergeant in charge of the
station. He there receives further instruction in the various subjects already enumerated, and also gains a practical knowledge
of his duties. At the end of a period of about
two years the constable, if he has worked hard
and is above the average in intelligence, can
be termed a useful policeman. When hon.
Members realise that the Force has only been
in existence for a year or less I think they
will agree that the organisation we now have
is a credit to the instructors. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.)
The educational test given to recruits for
the Royal Ulster Constabulary comprises
reading, dictation, and a simple examination
No one who had the opportunity of being
present at the reviews by Lord Derby, the
Secretary of State for War, could fail to be
impressed with the physique, the training
and the discipline of all our police forces,
and I think that the people of Ulster are
under a debt of gratitude to Sir Charles
Wickham for the services he has rendered in
building up these Forces in Northern Ireland. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) Sir
Charles Wickham has been often accused of
being a strict disciplinarian. I think he is. I
would, however, ask the public to remember
that this is a new Force, and that we must
enforce discipline from the outset. He is
assisted in his work by a band of able officers, who have been well tried, and who, I
am glad to say, are securing the respect and
admiration of the public generally.
My hon. Friend, the Member for Antrim
(Mr. Hanna), has raised a question about the
officers of the Royal Ulster Constabulary. The
hon. Gentleman is usually very accurate in
the statements he makes in this House, but I
do not know where he has got his information on this occasion. I find that out of 58
officers in the Royal Ulster Constabulary 44
were drawn from the old R.I.C., in accordance with the recommendations of the Police
Committee, the Report of which was approved by this House. The remainder were
drawn from the Special Constabulary. Therefore it is incorrect to say that there is not a
single member of the police force to-day who
has had a great deal of experience before he
got his commission as a police officer. In
some cases the officers have served a year or
two in the Special Constabulary, and I think
that is one of the best forces in which they
could get their training. We wish to make
this a democratic Force. There is an old
saying that every soldier carries a Field-
Marshal's baton in his knapsack, and in our
Force we want to make every policeman
realise that he can rise to the highest position that of inspector-general. I hope that
in the course of time it will be found that at
least 50 per cent. of the officers of our police
force have been recruited from the ranks.
There is another point to which I would
like to refer, and that is the improved relations that exist at the present time between

HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Sir Dawson Bates]
our police force and the public at large.
There is nothing which is more essential to
the success of the police force than that
amicable relations with the public should be
established and maintained. In this respect
the Royal Ulster Constabulary has a great advantage over the old Royal Irish Constabulary. In the old Force a policeman from Tipperary might be sent to, say, Portadown,
utterly unacquainted with the habits and outlook of the population. In the new Force
we can be reasonably sure that no matter
from what county in Northern Ireland the
policeman may come he will readily be able
to accommodate himself to the community
in which he has to serve. The population
generally are gradually realising that the
police are their friends, and the old spirit of
detachment is disappearing. This change in
the attitude of the population has, of course,
been largely created by the fact that such a
large proportion of the male population in
Northern Ireland are members of our Special
Constabulary, and their service inside the
Special Constabulary has enabled them to appreciate the difficulties of a policeman's
duties, and at the same time has instilled into
them a desire to see the law enforced.
The conditions, the pay and allowances are
practically the same as the old R.I.C., and in
the new Pension Order which will shortly be
laid upon the Table of the House we create
some additional benefits. An hon. Member
has raised a question as to whether or not a
single policeman could claim certain benefit.
Under the new Order a parent will rank as
a dependant as soon as the dependency
exists.
We have not yet succeeded in obtaining the
full number of Roman Catholics for our new
Force which was recommended by the Police
Committee, but we are always ready to accept
candidates of that religion who satisfy us that
they are suitable for enrolment in the Force.
Mr. McGUFFIN: Would the right hon.
Gentleman say how many have been recruited from that section?
Sir DAWSON BATES: 524 is the number.
Mr. McGUFFIN: Just a little more than
50 per cent. of what they are entitled to.
Sir DAWSON BATES: That is so. The
point may occur to some hon. Members why
we are estimating for the full number of
3,000 inasmuch as we have not yet recruited
up to the full strength. I may, however, explain that as a condition of receiving the
promised grant of £1,500,000 towards the
cost of our Special Constabulary we had to
undertake that any savings under the Royal
Ulster Constabulary Vote, allowing for a
Force of 3,000, should be taken into calculation in ascertaining the amount which the
Imperial Government may have to make out
of this grant. I think that is only a fair
arrangement.
I mentioned at the outset that while last
year our Estimate for a period of 9 months
was £822,000, this year, for the full period of
12 months, we are asking for barely £90,000
more. Apart from certain economies, this
small increase is due to the fact that our
Estimate for the present year is based on
figures calculated as a result of our experience
of working the Force, whereas last year, the
amount was estimated on figures supplied to
us by the old Royal Irish Constabulary,
which proved to be in excess of actual requirements.
I will just take hon. Members through the
figures roughly. Sub-head "A" has, of
course, been increased in proportion. There
is one item to which I would like to refer
specially-separation allowances. That is
larger than it should be. Hon. Members are
aware that some time ago the question of the
insufficiency of the barrack accommodation
that exists in Northern Ireland was raised,
and the Prime Minister undertook to have the
matter made right. For many years the
Imperial Government apparently regarded
these barracks as places that could go on for
ever without receiving any repairs, and I will
only say this, that the accommodation which
the men had when we took over control was
in many cases a perfect disgrace. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) This is one of the
legacies left us by the Imperial Government
and we are prosecuting in the adjustment of
our financial relations a claim for a substantial allowance to be made to us in view of the
heavy expenditure which we will have to
incur owing to the neglect on the part of the
Imperial Authorities in maintaining these barracks in proper condition. Owing to the con
ditions we have had to give separation allow
ances to married men living outside the barracks. I would like to say one word more in
regard to administration generally.

Dr. MORRISON: Very well; I leave that
between the Minister of Home Affairs and
the Member for Antrim (Mr. Hanna). I

Gases to deal with, nor many

Members: Hear, hear.) I have noticed, for

of affairs has arisen testifying to the efficiency

Empire. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) There
is nothing further that I can say on this
matter except to express my satisfaction with
the administration of the Home Office and the
Constabulary. I have sometimes said perhaps
unkind things about other things, but the
Home Minister carries a very large burden,
and while I think that we might perhaps get
some advice from me that would be useful to
him with regard to medical matters I bow
to him at once in his administration of the
Home Office. As far as my experience goes he
and his deputy have met and dealt with a
crisis in Ulster's history in a way that brings
credit on them and credit on the area that we
represent. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Colonel WOODS: I am in the same position
as the hon. Member for the University (Dr.
Morrison). I have used the Department of the
Ministry of Home Affairs in a rather shameless way. I worry them quite a lot. I ask a
lot of questions but the officials always meet
me with the greatest civility, and I have got
quite a number of matters adjusted that otherwise would have had to be discussed in the
House and would have used up the time of hon.
Members. There are three points in regard
to the police force to which I wish to draw
the attention of the Government. One is
about married constables. I am told that
married constables who enlisted as married
constables are given an allowance.
A man,
for instance, who joined last week gets an
allowance, but the man who has been in the
force for a year and a half, or since the
formation of the force, and gets married,
never gets that allowance. He is not granted
the married allowance. I think that is a
matter that ought to be looked into.
Then
the pay of the Special Constabulary is 3s
less, I am informed, than the Royal Ulster
Constabulary, although they do the same class
of work. Neither do they get a pension. 1
know it is only a temporary job for them, but
I think there ought to be a little more consideration for the Special Constabulary if it
is at all possible. I am also informed that an
extra allowance of £100 each has been made
to four County Inspectors at headquarters,
and members of the Special Constabulary
would like to understand why that is given.
It is hardly carrying out the idea of economy
that we have heard about, and some explanation should be made with regard to it.
Sir DAWSON BATES: Perhaps the hon
and gallant Member would explain the point.
I do not quite follow him.
Colonel WOODS: I understand there are
four County Inspectors employed at the headquarters in Waring Street, and that they
have been recently given an extra allowance
of £100 a year each. That is what the Special
Constabulary understand, and they feel rather
annoyed about it. It would be a good thing
if some explanation could be made so that
they would understand the matter. As to
the employment of Ulstermen this has become
gradually worse and worse. and to-day I am
informed that at Omagh 54 of the "B"
Special Constabulary threw down their arms,
or at least resigned, and refused to serve
under a new instructor, who is an Englishman and had been brought there, although
there were Ulstermen-ex-Servicemen and
unemployed-on the spot who were recommended for the job. I hope the right hon.
Gentleman will take into account what I
have said. I am not doing it in any criticising mood, but with the idea to help, because I think the Constabulary is a good
force. It is very well handled under the
circumstances, and a considerable amount of
credit is due to everybody concerned, but
there are a great many of what appear to be

attention was given to them.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY TO
THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS (Mr.
Megaw): There are a few points that have
arisen in the debate upon which wish to
say a few words. This time last year I had
the honour and duty of introducing the Bill
under which the Royal Ulster Constabulary
was formed. At that time I stated the

One of those difficulties was with regard to
the apportionment of the Royal Irish Constabulary in the new force. When statements
were made, such as are made to-day, about
the employment of Ulstermen in the new
Royal Ulster Constabulary I at that time
explained that we were under an obligation
to take over a certain number of the Royal
Irish Constabulary or else to pay their
pensions. If we had confined the selection
Ulster, men
of our officers to men from
without any special training in the police
force, I think we would have made a great
mistake apart altogether from the tremendous

saddled on this Government, because we
should have had to pay the pensions of

those men compulsorily retired if we had

the Committee that was dealing with the

from the Special Constabulary. This was

A great deal has been said about Englishmen being appointed to this police force. It
would be a disastrous day for this country
if we were to exclude suitable men from
the other side. The Prime Minister a few
days ago told how through his influence an
Ulsterman had been appointed to the Chief
Constableship of Hull. If we were to adopt
the attitude that none but Ulstermen can
apply I can very well understand how the
same cry would be made on the other side,
"We will not have Ulstermen, they exclude
us we cannot take them." Of course, it
is right-and I am sure this Government
have always followed the principle-that
when there are suitable Ulstermen who are
acquainted with Ulster conditions, and when
there are vacancies-I emphasise the word
vacancies-those Ulstermen will get a good
run for the post. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) Statements have been made about
the great number of Englishmen employed
in the Royal Ulster Constabulary. I have
already said that the Government have no
objection to men from the other side being
there, but how many such are actually in
posts in the Royal Ulster Constabulary?
Seven out of fifty-eight. That is a very
small number to make such a cry about as
has been raised from time to time by those
who wish to detract from the fairness of the
Home Minister and make attacks on the
Ulster Government. My hon. Friend has
already referred to the criticisms made about
the delay in the setting up of the Representative Body. It was understood when the Act
was passed, I am not sure if it was not
statutory, that no Representative Body could
be set up during the first year. As a matter
of fact, the first year only expired on 31st
May last, and steps have already been taken
to fulfil the pledge of the Government to have
such a Representative Body established.
The hon. and gallant Gentleman (Colonel
Woods) who has just spoken made some criticism with regard to the position of married
constables. He stated that if a married constable was taken on he got separation allowance, while an unmarried constable who
married did not get a separation allowance.
So far as I understand the position, it is this,
that if a constable who was unmarried gets
married he gets barrack accommodation if it
is available. In such a case, of course, he will
have no separation allowance, but if no such
barrack accommodation is available he gets
separation allowance in the same way as a
married constable who has been taken into the
force. With regard to county inspectors who
are in headquarters, they are provided for
and have been provided for by the estimates
because it is felt that they are in a very
responsible position in which there is more
expenditure likely to be incurred than by
those who are situated in the counties. That
allowance is given to the county inspectors
who are at headquarters. There were some
criticisms made about the objections which
the "B" constables had in regard to their
officers. It is necessary, no doubt, and will
be from time to time, that in what is practically a voluntary force there will be some
instances of dissatisfaction, but they are very
rare. I think it was a sight for the people of
Ulster to see the magnificent turn-outs
and the magnificent discipline of the "B"
Constabulary during the recent visit of Lord
Derby. Certainly it was a revelation to
those who had not seen the like before, and
to make any suggestion that those men who
turned out as they did, having the discipline
they had, were dissatisfied with the conduct
of their officers would require a large draft
on one's credulity, because it was a sight
that was well worth while seeing, and having
been seen, was well worth while remembering. There seemed to be absolute
confidence between the Special Constabulary
and their officers.

Sir DAWSON BATES: The effect of this
Bill is to continue in Northern Ireland the
existing Increase of Rents and Mortgage
Interest Restrictions Act of 1920 for a period
of six months. It is purely a temporary
Hon. Members are aware
measure.
that
the existing Act expires on the 24th of this
month. This Government set up a Committee
to advise the Ministry as to what alterations,
if any, were necessary regarding the continuance and amendment of the existing
Acts. I have now received 2n Interim
Report from that Committee, in which they
express the opinion that while control of
rents should be removed at the earliest
possible date, at the same time they are
of opinion that it is inexpedient that such
control should be removed at the present
time. The Committee point out that it is
impossible for them for the present to let
me have a complete report setting out their
recommendations as to the amendments that
should be made in the 1920 Act, and they
express the view that owing to the difficulty
of the subject and the many problems that
have to be considered, they will not be
in a position to let me have a final report
for some time to come, and, accordingly,
they recommend that pending the receipt of
their final report the present Act should be
continued temporarily. I am sure hon.
Members will realise the importance of
this subject and that ample time should be
given to this Committee to fully consider
the various problems with which they are
confronted. Having regard to these matters
this Bill proposes to continue the Act as it
now stands for a period of six months, and
in the meantime I hope to receive the final
Report of the Committee, after which it is
proposed to introduce a Bill dealing with the
whole subject matter in the Autumn Session.
Hon. Members will understand that this,
therefore, is only a stop-gap until the new
Measure has been introduced and passed by
this House. But there is one important
matter which the Committee drew my
attention to, and that is, the urgent necessity
for encouraging building in Northern Ireland.
They recommend that the Government
should adopt all means at their disposal to
and facilitate the erection of
houses during the next couple of years.

Scutch Mills Bill.
Order for Second reading read.
owners
The
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (Mr.
Archdale): The main object of this Bill is
to prevent scutch mill owners from keeping
tow as part payment for scutching flax, and
to provide that all mill owners shall not
purchase or offer to purchase any tow until
the flax has been scutched, and that they
shall buy it by weight. For many years
this has been a source of discontent amongst
the farmers, and of trouble between the
farmers and the scutch mill owners. In 1917
the Ministry of Agriculture and Technical
Instruction in Dublin appointed a Committee
to inquire into this matter, and that Conimittee reported that it was a most pernicious
habit as it tended to prevent scutch mill
from improving their mills and
finding better ways of scutching flax.
Department in Dublin tried to get a Bill
passed in the Imperial Parliament but the
war prevented it being passed. Since it was
established this Ministry has been pressed
in connection with this question and after
very careful consideration we drafted this
Bill. All the parties concerned have approved of the Bill, including the Scutch Mill
Owners' Association, the Ulster Farmers'
Union, the Ulster Agricultural Organisation
Society, and the Flax Advisory Committee
which is composed of all those bodies as well
as the Flax Spinners and representatives of
the Ministry. We drafted the Bill so as to
have as little supervision as possible while
we carried out the objects of the Bill. I beg
tɔ move.
Adjournment.

Mr. HANNA: It is very seldom that I
preface any remarks I have to make by anything in the nature of a compliment to a
Minister, but the Attorney-General reminds
me that this is the second time to-day I have
done so. On this occasion I have great
pleasure in doing it because I am satisfied,
as I am sure the House is satisfied, that the
right hon. Gentleman in charge of this Bill
is one of the greatest helps we could possibly
have in connection with this all-important
subject of agriculture. It is perfectly obvious
from the statement he has just made that
he has taken into consideration the
opinions of all the representative bodies
capable of giving any advice in regard to this
Bill. In my opinion the Bill is absolutely
essential, but in regard to the second section
of the Bill, which deals with the enforcement
of the Act, it is possible that some little
friction may arise if a wise choice is not
made of the officer to whom the duty of enforcing the Act will be delegated. The section
gives power to that officer to visit the scutch
mills at reasonable times and we know that
that duty can be carried out in a way that
will tend to the smooth working of the Act,
but if it were attempted in an officious and
over-bearing way it would lead to a considerable amount of friction. Therefore, I hope
that when the Minister comes to make the
appointment he will take that fact into consideration and endeavour to find a man who
has a thorough knowledge of the subject and
is thoroughly acquainted with the peculiarities of the people of Northern Ireland, and
particularly the peculiarities of the agricultural population generally.
Mr. DUFF: I wish to make one or two
comments on this Bill from a business standpoint. I happen to have a little practical
knowledge of the matters dealt with. I will
put it to the House, without in the slightest
degree trying to condemn the Bill, that this
is an extraordinary measure, because it is
the first attempt on the part of this House
to improve the machinery dealing with a
particular subject and, apart from the
dealers in liquor, attacking the probity of
business men, particularly those who have
scutch mills. I do not wish in the slightest
degree to say that it is unnecessary, but I
wish to draw attention to the fact that you
are for the first time doing these two things
by an Act of the Legislature. Now that is
initiated in the Bill which may be
fruitful to the business of the community if
it is carried out in a wise and intelligent
manner; and this is a precedent that may
possibly be followed by other Ministers. But
there is no question I think-and I think the
right hon. the Minister of Agriculture will
not deny it-that by passing this Bill you
are taking into the hands of the legislature
a power which you have not used hitherto
except in dealing with matters under the
Licensing Acts; and we shall watch the
development of this Act of the Ministry with
great interest, because if one of the benefits
of the smallness of the area of the Six
Counties is that Ministers are going to have
a direct influence on the actual conduct of
the manufactures and commerce of the
country, as distinct from an advisory
influence, then we may look forward to a
tightening up or a speeding up of some of
the more backward industries within the Six
Counties.
Mr. MARK: I would like to congratulate
the right hon. Gentleman the Minister (Mr.
Archdale) on bringing in this Bill. I think
I can disagree directly with the Member for
East Belfast (Mr. Duff) when he talks about
public legislation which has powers-the
Liquor Bill I think he suggested-to take
away the rights of certain people. Now I
think that the Minister of Agriculture gave
us to understand that this is only an agreement between some of the farmers and some
of the scutchers or mill owners in certain
localities. Other mill owners in other
localities did not directly agree to hold tow
as part payment for the scutching of their
flax. Therefore, I think he is only bringing
them into conformity with a line of action
which both farmers and mill owners will be
thankful to see brought into force. I think
we have a right to congratulate the right
hon. Gentleman, and I think this House
should be ready to pass this Bill without
any comments at all.

POLICE OFFICERS.
1. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Finance whether he can state the numbers of
civil servants and police officers employed by
the Government for Northern Ireland at salaries exceeding £300 per annum and not exceeding £600 per annum; exceeding £600 per
annum and not exceeding £800 per annum;
exceeding £800 per annum; and also the numbers in each category who are native-born
Ulstermen?
(Mr.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE
Pollock): An examination of the estimates already presented to the House will enable the
hon. and gallant Member to calculate the
numbers of civil servants and police officers
employed by the Government of Northern Ireland whose salaries fall into the three categories quoted.
As regards the second part of the question,
I think that the hon. and gallant Member
will, on reflection, agree that the definition of
the expression "native-born Ulsterman" is
a matter of some difficulty, as questions of
domicile and birthplace, not only of the individual himself, but of his parents, are involved. Having arrived at a definition, I do
not consider that the value of the information
sought warrants the expenditure of time and
public money involved in securing it.
The Northern Ireland Government, in selecting its staff, were bound to have regard
to the rights of existing Irish officers under
the Government of Ireland Act, and in selecting new entrants for posts requiring specialised knowledge, it was found impossible to
limit the field of selection.
The same arguments apply to the Royal
Ulster Constabulary. Furthermore, the enlistment of members of the Royal Irish Constabulary has reduced the pension liability to
be apportioned against Northern Ireland
funds.

Mr. POLLOCK: The necessity for this short
Measure arises out of the establishment of
the Irish Free State. In 1919 the Imperial
Parliament passed an Act which was known
as "The Irish Land Provision for Sailors
and Soldiers Act," under Section 4 of which
the Local Government Board for Ireland was
granted powers to acquire land either compulsorily or by agreement for the purpose
of erecting houses for ex-Servicemen. The
Act in question defined the various powers
and duties of the Local Government Board,
and laid down a time limit of three years,
during which land could be compulsorily
acquired, or acquired by agreement for this
purpose. This time limit expired in the
month of December last. On the establishment of the Irish Free State it became
necessary to make other provisions for the
continuance of the work in connection with
ex-Servicemen's cottages, which was then and
is still far from completion as is well known.
During the past year the Ministries of Finance and Home Affairs have conjointly,
pending the nomination of a successor to the
Local Government Board in Ireland, been
carrying on the existing contracts for houses,
but they have not under the limited powers
which were conveyed to them been able to
enter into fresh commitments, either with
regard to the acquirement of land or to the
erection of the cottages themselves. Therefore, it was their duty only to carry out
such contracts as the Local Government
Board had entered into.
In order to complete the progress of
housing for ex-Servicemen in Ireland provision was made in Section 3 of the Irish
Free State (Consequential Provisions) Act
1922, which appears in the Schedule to the
Bill, and which hon. Members can consult,
for the establishment of a new Trust, to be
designated "The Irish Sailors' and Soldiers'
1325 Land Trust Powers Bill-

members, of whom three are to be appointed
by the Imperial Government, one by the
President of the Executive Council of the
Irish Free State, and one by the Prime
Minister of Northern Ireland. To this body
will be transferred all the powers which
were formerly vested in the Local Government Board under the earlier Act, while the
Imperial Government has arranged to place
a sum of £1,500,000 at the disposal of the
Trust for the purpose of carrying on the
As

for the establishment of a Trust, dependent

Government of a similar character to that
which We are now entering upon.

We are
quite capable of looking after our own business and what right has the Free State to
ally itself with us in this matter? If we are

Finance, but if our Government is going to
govern why do they not take the reins in

right hon. Friend, the Minister of Finance,

houses. We want houses for ex-Servicemen.

circumstances? This thing is going on and
on, and still there is no progress, and

houses for these men.

The PRIME MINISTER (Sir James Craig):
I think my hon. Friend (Mr. Donald) by his
speech may have conveyed a wrong impression to the public outside that this Government has in some way been lax in its efforts
in connection with the very important question of securing proper houses for the ex-Servicemen. My hon. Friend bases his whole
speech on the assumption that we here have
the money in our Exchequer to meet the
cost, whereas, as a matter of fact. the
supplying of the ex-Servicemen's houses is an
Imperial obligation with which the Imperial
Government will not part; and in exactly
the same way as they pledged themselves to
the ex-Servicemen that they would see they
received proper pensions and that they
should be trained in the labour end to fit
them for future occupation, so do the Imperial
Government take upon their shoulders
the responsibility for providing funds for
building houses for ex-Servicemen.
From
the very beginning of the movement to do
so this Government has been urging the
Imperial Government to look upon it from
our point of view. They have from the
start always been referring to the population as the proper basis on which to
calculate the number of houses to be allocated
to the North and the South. We have from
the very commencement been strongly urging
them to take the proper course, which
obviously is to take as the basis the number
of those who enlisted in the Crown forces
and fought in the Great War, in which
event it would be a case of more like 50 per
cent. than the proportion which my hon.
Friend referred to. But if he had made the
speech he made to-day in the Imperial
Parliament where the money comes from-
Mr. DONALD: I was not there, so I could

The PRIME MINISTER : I am not
blaming the hon. Member. It is only that

Mr. DONALD: I could not deliver it; J

for something over which we have no control

been going for. My right hon. Friend (Mr.

that decision. If we do, we ought to be able

ex-Servicemen's houses was bungled a long
time ago. We are only the successors to very
many grave mistakes, and what I wish to
make a point of is that this Government ever
since it had the opportunity has been endeavouring to get out of the mess that was
created and is doing all it can to get as

from the Imperial Government.

edly there were many grave injustices to the
landlord done by the Imperial Government
in this question of rent restriction. They
restricted landlords from receiving one penny
of increase in rent when everybody else was
profiteering. Practically everybody
earning good money, but the landlord was
not allowed to receive a solitary penny of
increase in rent. That is where the Government blundered, because had the landlord
been in receipt of increased rent it would
have been different. He was not allowed to
get any increase. Many of these small landlords had all their money invested. They
were not allowed to get any remuneration.
That is the argument that is now put to
us by the landlord. They are standing out
for an increase now when really we should
be reducing rents. That is the trouble.
Rents should be coming down. We will find

the 25 per cent. for repairs which are not

Mr. McGUFFIN: Though this is a short
Bill it is quite an admirable and important
one. It relates to an industry that, I take
it, is perhaps the most precarious in which
one could be engaged. From the moment
that the seed is put into the ground until
the fibre leaves the scutch mill there is a
continuous risk upon the part of the farmer.
But I always thought that a great deal more
might be made out of the flax by skilful
scutching than has hitherto been done.
Mr. ARCHDALE: Hear, hear.
Mr. McGUFFIN: The Bill is making provision for that, and in that way is promoting
the interests and the well-being of the
farmers. I myself have heard farmers complain from time to time of the disappointing
yield there was in connection with the
scutching of flax. Where 30 stones, say, were
anticipated, the farmers have been told they
would only get 20 or 22 stones, whereas in
other mills neighbouring farmers were able
to get 35 and sometimes 40 stones. The
object of this Bill is to regulate the industry
in such a way that there shall be more
economic scutching, and that the yield shall
be greater than hitherto. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.)
There is the segregation of the tow-I call it
tow; I suppose that is the proper name for
it-into one, two or three classes; that is a
very important thing. What I approve of
most of all in this Bill is the restriction
that the tow shall form no part of the payment. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) I
remember being in a scutch mill during the
war, and I saw three large stacks of tow
there. I said "Of what value is this?"
""
What value is it?" said the man.
"Why
I am getting £45 a ton for that, and there
is a stack for which I am getting £50 a
ton." That works out at a higher rate than
was paid for Irish flax prior to the war. It
was a great injustice to the farmer that that
should be so. This Bill is going to prevent that, and I am only voicing the
opinion of several farmers with whom I am
acquainted, when I say that they have
long felt the existing conditions as a serious
disability in connection with their work. I
am very glad that the Minister, who is so
progressive in all his ideas in respect of this
matter, has seized the opportunity to introduce this Bill to provide against the serious
disability under which agriculturists suffer at
the moment.

Intoxicating Liquor Bill.
As amended, considered.
CLAUSE 1.—(Closing of Licensed Premises
on Sunday and Christmas Day.)
(1) It shall not be lawful for any person
at any time on Sunday or Christmas Day-
(a) to sell or expose for sale intoxicating liquor; or
(b) to open or keep open any premises
for the sale of intoxicating liquor:
Provided that nothing in this sub-section
shall apply to the sale of intoxicating
liquor in a hotel, where such liquor is sold
to a guest or traveller who has lodged for
the preceding night, or has in writing engaged a room for the succeeding night, in
the hotel, for consumption by him at the
same time as a substantial meal, in a portion of the hotel premises usually set apart
for the service of such meals.
(2) All drinking bars in hotels shall be
kept closed during the whole of Sunday and
Christmas Day.
(3) For the purposes of this section the
expression "hotel" means premises licensed
for the sale of intoxicating liquor by retail,
which are structurally adapted to be used
and bona-fide used for the purpose of the
reception of guests and travellers desirous
to sleep in the premises, and which contain
at least four apartments set apart and used
exclusively for the sleeping accommodation
of guests or travellers.
(4) The provisions of any Acts relating to
the sale of intoxicating liquor by retail,
which forbid the doing of any act, matter
or thing at any times during which such
sale is prohibited by those Acts, shall be
construed as if the times during which such
sale is so prohibited included the whole of
Sunday and Christmas Day; and the penalties in force under the said Acts shall be
applicable to cases in which any such act,
matter or thing is done in contravention of
the provisions of this section.
Mr. COOTE: I beg to move, in Sub-section

1341 Intoxicating Liquor Bill---

Report.
It does not require any second sight to
see what is going to take place. The four-
100med hotel may be, and no doubt will be,
an ordinary public-house. You will have one
of them in every village in Ulster in order
that this surreptitious drinking may be
carried on there. Four men will go in there
and order a room; they will register, and
then they can have anything they require.
What sort of supervision will you have over
these hotels? How is a policeman to know
what is going on? A policeman goes in and
asks those people what they are doing there,
but they are guests of the hotel; their names
are on the register. If they are apprehended
in this way it is very convenient for the
publican to keep them there all night. Men
resort to wonderful things in order to evade
the law and to have drink on Sunday. You
know how resourceful the publican is in
order to defeat the law in regard to the
sale of drink. Then a policeman having
heard that people were there may not find
them there, or they may not be drinking. You
cannot prove that they had been drinking.
Therefore I cannot see how you can effectively make the law respected by hotels of
this kind. The same will apply to every
hotel, if you like; the same will apply to
clubs. Am I right in saying that clubs will
have the right to supply drink to their
guests? I think so. I want to ask what you
are doing for the class of people who cannot
afford to be members of clubs or to spend
the week-end at hotels? What about the
man at the street corner who likes his glass
of beer just as much as the aristocrat who
goes into his club? You are dealing with
class legislation here: you are creating a
source of enmity in the community that will
lead to great exasperation: you are dealing
unfairly with the community as a whole.
any
I do not believe in Sunday drinking at
all. Therefore I say the only clean way is
to wash out the lot. Why should you allow
a club or a hotel to juggle with the trade
and to provide drinking facilities in
surreptitious way. I do not say they will
all do so. There are men who like to keep
the law, but they are very few. Why shou'd
you allow these people to get drink, and
prohibit the others? You are setting up a
different standard for the people who cannot
afford to go to those places on Sunday.
I read the statement here that when a man
is in his club or hotel he is in what is
equivalent to his own home, and, therefore,
he should have all the accommodation that
he would have in his home. I submit, in
reply to that statement, that, if a
man is
in his own home, and if he does not take the
trouble to lay in a store of drink on Saturday, he has no Sacilities for drinking on
Sunday; he cannot purchase drink. He can
do without the drink: so can the man in
his club. If the man in the club or hotel
must have drink then he ought to do what
the man in his home would do-lay in a
store on Saturday for Sunday. If the man
in a club must have drink on Sunday, if he
cannot live without it, he should have it
in his bedroom. That is the only place in
a club or in a hotel that is his own. The
only place of which a man can say "This
is mine" is the room that he has taken,
and if he has drink in his room then I say
the law should not touch him. It is quite
easy to solve the problem of a man having
the same rights in his hotel as he has in
his home. He can adopt the same procedure,
and arrive at the same result. If you can
see your way to delete the words that I
propose to omit you will have Sunday closing
in the only sense of the word that is Sunday
clesing. You will avoid friction; you will
not be pandering to one class more than
another; you will be giving everybody the
same treatment; you will not be differentiating against a man because he is poor.
If you do otherwise, you are resorting to a
procedure which is fraught with very great
danger of creating unrest in the minds of
the working classes and the poor of the
community. For these reasons I have no
doubt that this part of the section should
be deleted.

This is merely to enable the machinery with
