CLAUSE 3 (Restrictions as to the issue
of new licences).
The Licensing (Ireland) Act, 1902, is hereby repealed, and the following provisions
shall have effect, that is to say:-
(1) From and after the passing of this
Act no licence shall be granted for the sale
of intoxicating liquor, whether for consumption on or off the premises, except-
(a) for premises which are lawfully
licensed at the date of the passing of this
Act, or which were lawfully licensed at
any time since the first day of January,
nineteen hundred and twenty; or
(b) for a hotel, which expression means
a house containing at least ten apartments set apart and used exclusively for
the sleeping accommodation of travellers,
and having no public bar for the sale of
intoxicating liquor; or
(c) for a railway refreshment room.
(2) Where, by reason of the expiration of
a lease, a licence for the sale of intoxicating
liquor for consumption on the premises
comprised in the lease is extinguished or
surrendered, the licensing authority may,
notwithstanding anything in this section,
grant a licence for suitable premises in the
immediate vicinity of the premises to which
the licence so extinguished or surrendered
was attached.
(3) Where, owing to an increase of not
less than twenty-five per cent. of the population according to the last census, there
is a growth or an extension of any city or
Provided that such licence shall be
granted only for premises situate in the
ward or district electoral division in which
such increase in population has taken
place, and in substitution for at least two
existing licences held in respect of premises
situate within the city or town (as the case
may be) comprising such ward or district
electoral division.
(4) In the case of applications under subdivision (b) of paragraph (1), and under
paragraphs (2) and (3) of this section, the
premises shall be valued under the Irish
Valuation Acts at not less than-
Thirty pounds in the City of Belfast.
Twenty pounds in the City of Londonderry;
Twelve pounds in any town over ten

Ten pounds in all other places.
(5) Nothing in this section shall operate
to prevent the granting of new licences
where the licensing authority thinks fit,
to premises attached to or adjoining premises licensed for the sale of intoxicating
liquor at the date of the passing of

Provided always that such new licence as

licensed premises more suitable for the
business carried on therein.
(6) Nothing in this section shall be taken
to affect the law as to the transfer or
assignment of licences from one person to
another, or as to the renewal of licences.

CLAUSE 4 (Provisions as to Claims in
Respect of Abolition of Off-Licences)
(1) Compensation shall be payable, in
accordance with the provisions hereinafter
in this section contained and out of the
fund in this section mentioned, in any case
where, by reason of the foregoing provisions
of this Act with respect to the abolition of
certain off-licences, a licence for the sale by
retail of intoxicating liquor for consumption off the premises is not renewed at the
annual licensing sessions held next after
the passing of this Act.
(2) For the purpose of dealing with
claims for compensation as aforesaid, there
shall be established a tribunal (to be called
"the Claims Tribunal"), which shall be
constituted in accordance with the provisions of Part I. of the First Schedule to
this Act.
(3) The following provisions shall have
effect with respect to the powers and
duties of the Claims Tribunal under
this section:-
(a) The Claims Tribunal shall, in
dealing with claims for compensation,
be governed by the provisions of Part
II. of the First Schedule to this Act.
(b) The Claims Tribunal shall, in each
year, unless they certify to the Ministry
of Finance that it is unnecessary to do
so in any year for the purposes of this
section, impose, in respect of all licences
for the sale of intoxicating liquor by
retail, charges at rates not exceeding,
and graduated in the same proportion
as, the rates shown in the scale of maxi
mum charges set out in Part III. of the
First Schedule to this Act.
(c) Charges payable under this section
in respect of any licence shall be levied
and paid together with, and as part of,
the duties on the corresponding excise
licence, but a separate account shall be
1355 Intoxicating Liquor Bill HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Report.
kept by the Ministry of Finance of the
amount produced by those charges, and
that amount shall in every year be paid
over to the Claims Tribunal in accordance
with rules made by the Ministry of
Finance for that purpose.
(d) Any sums paid to the Claims Tribunal under this section shall be placed
to the credit of a fund to be called "the
Claims Fund."
(e) Any moneys expended by the Claims
Tribunal in the payment of claims under
this Act, or otherwise in the exercise of
their powers or the performance of their
duties, shall be paid out of the Claims
Fund.
(f) The Ministry of Finance may out of
the Consolidated Fund of Northern Ireland make advances to the Claims Fund,
to be repayable in accordance with rules
made by that Ministry for the purpose
of paying any claims arising or expenses
incurred by the Claims Tribunal under
this section.
(4) The Claims Tribunal shall continue
in existence for a period of three years
from the thirtieth day of September, nineteen hundred and twenty-three, or for such
longer period as the Minister of Finance
may determine; and after the Claims
Tribunal has ceased to exist this section
shall have effect with the substitution of
the Ministry of Finance for the Claims
Tribunal.
(5) The Ministry of Finance may make
rules for carrying into effect the provisions
of this section and may, in particular, by
those rules prescribe the procedure in connection with applications for claims, the
time and manner of making payments in
respect of claims and the manner in which
the accounts of the Claims Fund are to be
kept and audited.

sure how I stand I would like to say that
I am quite with him in my desire for temperance reform. I am most anxious to see this
measure carried through, and that it should
be a success, and I congratulate the Government on the firmness and courage with which
they have dealt with a very troublesome piece
of legislation. We have heard a great deal
about off-licences and spirit groceries in the
course of the discussions on this Bill, but
this class of trader is very largely confined
to the City of Belfast. In the country districts there is a very similar type of trader
who holds an on-licence. To all intents and
purposes, except that he has a licence for
the consumption of liquor on the premises,
he is in the same class as the off-licence
holder in Belfast. In every town and village
you find these men with a general business
with a licence attached. A great number of
these people will find difficulty in making the
structural alterations necessary to comply
with the requirements of this Bill, and I
find that a number of others are anxious
to get rid of the liquor trade, in which
sentiment I am entirely in agreement with
them. These men, under the Bill, get no
compensation, and I respectfully suggest that
if the Government could see their way to
accept this amendment they could reduce very
largely throughout the country the number
of places in which liquor can be obtained,
and assist the people in the struggle for
temperance. I believe that it is really a
temperance movement to eliminate as far as
possible these licences throughout the
country. I find that the publican, the onlicence holder, who proposes to hold on to his
licence is willing to compensate these men
in case they decide to give up their onlicences, and so it would not call for a great
demand upon the taxpayer. It is simply
a question of adjustment with the on-licence
holders. I hope the House will be able to
see its way to accept this amendment.

after the explanation I have given, the

affairs of which the hon. Member complains.
The Government made it possible for a licence
to be issued. An applicant comes forward
and makes his application for a licence upon
the good faith that it will be allowed to continue. But there is always a difference between a licence, as I take it, and a law. A

but all privileges, just as all laws, rest absolutely upon the will of the people. If the

pay, but the people who consume the liquor.

ing, there should be at least compensation

some of his speeches in this House. He indulges in language of the most extreme character. I do not think he always means to be
as strong and fierce in his language as he
really is. To-day he has denounced the Government and the friends of temperance in the
most unmeasured terms possible. I am proud
of the Bill. I am delighted with it, and feel
most grateful to the Government for the
splendid measure they have introduced, a
measure which I hope will shortly become the
law of the land, and which, I believe, will
satisfy ninety per cent. of the people of
Ulster, and especially those who proclaim
themselves temperance advocates.
My hon. Friend (Mr. Coote) touched mainly
upon the question of compensation, and that
is the only question with which I need to
deal, because I want to help the Government
to proceed with the remaining Clauses as
quickly as possible. I could not help noticing just one sentence, which I think will
dispose of the whole question of compensation as my hon. Friend has put it in this
House this afternoon. He told us he never
could see any objection to those that were exclusively in the trade if they were put out of
Mr. COOTE: On a point of order, I did not
say anything of the kind. I said I objected
to all spirit grocers. They were all included
in my objection to compensation, save the offlicence holders who have been living by that
trade exclusively.
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: That is just exactly what I have been saying, that he is
prepared to compensate the off-licence holders
who have been living exclusively by the
trade.
Mr. COOTE: The on-licence holder, I mean.
Sir RIBERT ANDERSON: The principle
and the logic are the same.
Mr. COOTE: No, no.
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: The position I
take up is, when you take away part of his
trade you compensate him for the part you
take from him. That is logical, and I cannot
for the life of me see where all the denunciation of the Temperance people and the
Government in the speech of my hon. Friend
comes in. There is the position in a sentence,
divested of all the trapping with which he
has invested his speech. Compensate the
man who has no other trade, but if you take
part of it you will not compensate him for
the part you take away. I cannot see the
consistency of my hon. Friend. It is an impossible position, and I leave it at that. I
think every right-thinking man will see at
once from the point of view of logic that the
hon. Member is in an untenable position. I
know there are folk who object to compensation, but I am one of those who want to see
a reasonable and fair measure of Temperance
reform. I even go so far on the compensation
question as to say that if I could compensate
every licence-holder in the country and get
him out of the trade, I would be prepared to
pay my share to do so, as it would be good
for the community.
But what are we doing in this case? I entirely dispute the argument that my hon.
Friend has used that the people of
the country are providing the compensation. They are doing nothing of the kind.
Absolutely not one penny of the public money
is going to be devoted to the compensation
of these people. The Government simply
raise a capital sum on the credit of the country that is all they are doing—and the interest and sinking fund to meet the capital
charge are provided by the increased licence
duty on the remaining licence holders. That
1373 Intoxicating Liquor Bill-

8 JUNE 1923
Report.
is the sum and substance of the whole thing.
In other words, the remaining licence holders
compensate those that have to go out of the
trade. I go further, and I say that if I can
see my way in coming years to get rid of 300
or 400 redundant public-houses throughout the
country-small, undesirable places that I believe the rest of the trade would be glad to
get rid of-I am prepared to adopt the same
principle of fixing compensation. This meaas it stands is a splendid measure of
temperance reform. It is a splendid step forward, one that will contribute to the happiness and prosperity of the country as a
whole, and will lessen temptation in every
direction. I do not wish to prolong the debate, but I desire to dissociate myself from
the position taken up by my hon. Friend. I
believe that in the position he has taken up
he will find himself, even amongst his temperance friends, in a hopeless minority.

Members of the House will recognise that
in many cases, particularly in the country,
a business of this kind is carried on by a
father and a daughter, or it may be by a
widow and her daughter, and to impose upon
such a person the obligation that a daughter
of, say, sixteen years of age should go away
and that another person should be employed
would create a very great hardship. I am in
absolute sympathy with the whole object of
this clause. I quite appreciate what is done,
and I am sure the House will consider that
in such a case as I have instanced, allowance
ought to be made. I take it the word
"employed" really means engaged, not
necessarily a contract of service, but the
actual carrying out of the work whether for
pay or otherwise. To meet a case such as I
have instanced, I think the clause in the
form in which it is in the Bill at the
moment is too drastic.

(1) Where any business, other than the

on the premises, is carried on in any premises licensed for such sale as aforesaid

for use and bona-fide used exclusively as a

for consumption on the premises.

court for the certificate required for the

of intoxicating liquor by retail, whether
for consumption on or off the premises, the
licensing court may require to be produced
before them, and to be deposited with their

which the application is made, and on
granting or confirming such certificate the
licensing court may by order direct that,
within a time fixed by the order, such

as the court thinks reasonably necessary
for the following purposes, namely:-
(i) for securing compliance with the requirements of sub-section (1) of this
section;
(ii) for securing that no part of any
room, which is used for consumption of intoxicating liquor on the premises is concealed or screened from
observation in such a manner as to
obstruct proper supervision, or contains
a back entrance likely to prevent such
supervision; and
(iii) for securing the proper conduct of
the business in accordance with the law
relating to licensed premises.

hundred and twenty-four, and before that

provisions of this section in such manner

Provided that the provisions of subsection (2) of this section shall come into
operation at the passing of this Act, so far

consumption off the premises.

Mr. HANNA: I beg to move in Clause 9, subsection 2, page 10, line 10, to leave out "shall”

I have made two or three speeches during the

it shall be recorded on the licence of the

1381 Intoxicating Liquor Bill-

Report.
amendment, that all convictions may be recorded on the licence. I do not say or suggest for a moment that there are not offences
against the licensing law that should not be
recorded against the licence, but in my experience I have come across a number of cases
where there were technical breaches of the
law, and if the House will allow me I shall
indicate one little instance. In Randalstown,
a licensed lady on a Sunday gave an old man
of 83 years of age a bottle of port wine. He
was an old-age pensioner. His brother was
also an old-age pensioner, and the brother
was dying. Dr. McMurtagh had directed
that some port wine should be got, and the
old man came in and pleaded with Miss
Macaulay, who was the owner of the licence,
for a bottle of port. She gave it to him, and
a policeman came up, and he brought her to
court. The lay magistrates found she had
committed an offence. Surely the discretion
of a judge should not be fettered in the way
that the word "shall " would do there.
Surely it can be left to a wise and discreet
resident magistrate to say what are offences
that ought to be recorded on licences and
ones that ought not. I ask the House to
adopt this.

is dismissed by the magistrates, but all they
have to do is to serve notice of appeal and
they need not bother their heads about it.
COMMONS.
They need not go near the court. I am reminded again that on this question they
would run the risk of costs. They run no
risk of costs. The total amount of costs
would not be 40s. Do we not know how it is
done? We know how licences are opposed at
the annual licensing session. A man of straw
is put up and represented by counsel, and for
the purpose of an offence here, for the purpose of making a case here, proceedings
would be taken in the name of the man of
straw. Why should the ordinary law be departed from in this case? That is the
question. The law has always been the common law of the country-no man can be convicted twice for the same offence. That is
very old. Why should it be departed from
in this case. I have raised this question
three times and I have not heard any answer
to it. I have seen books brought in and
sections of Acts of Parliament proposed to be
read and they never were read. I have
heard this question of costs brought up, and
I have denied it two or three times. I
would like to know what substance there is
behind it. I would like to know what earthly
reason there is why the ordinary law should
be departed from in this particular case.

Mr. MEGAW: The next amendment which
stands in my name is to sub-section (7)
of Clause 11 with regard to the sentence of
imprisonment applicable to a second offence
under the licensing laws. The criticism was
made that it is a terrible thing that one who
is convicted under the licensing laws should
be subject to imprisonment in any shape or
form. There are offences, no doubt, in which
it would be harsh to imprison, and I think
the resident magistrates might very well be
entrusted with the duty of deciding such cases
without any amendment, and I am quite sure
there would be no harshness exercised. But
there are technical offences, and it would be
a highly dangerous thing to entrust the resident magistrates with power to inflict sentence of imprisonment on a licence holder who
had offended through his servant and not
by himself. To make matters perfectly plain
we have decided to introduce a proviso that
stands on the Order Paper as follows:
1385 Intoxicating Liquor Bill—

Report.
"Provided that no sentence of imprisonment shall be inflicted except upon the person directly responsible for the act constituting the offence."
I beg to move.
Mr. DUFF: I want to make one or two
observations on this gathering up of subsections-as I call it-in Clause 11. The hon.
and learned Gentleman (Mr. Megaw) who has
moved this amendment has, in lawyer-like
fashion, confined his attention purely to this
section. I would like to draw attention to
the first sentence of this Clause and to make
a remark or two upon it. The phrase is:
"A person guilty of an offence under this
Act for which no special penalty is
provided."
That is the subject matter of the succeeding
part of the Clause, and I respectfully submit,
though I am not a lawyer, that it is the
subject matter of the subsequent imprisonment penalty. It is a very strange thing
that you ask leave to assume that the
offences under this Act for which no special
penalty is provided are much more serious
than the offences for which penalties are
provided. I would assume that during the
whole development of the Licensing Laws
the particular offences would be more or less
codified, and punishments adequate for the
crime inflicted. I may be wrong-I speak
subject to correction-but practically all the
offences that occur have only imprisonment
as an alternative to the non-payment of a
fine. If I am correct in assuming that what
I would call the uncodified offences-that is
the offences for which no special penalty is
provided are minor offences, if I have the
right to assume that, then we have this:
extraordinary situation that only on the
minor offences is this imprisonment clause
brought in. I speak subject to correction,
and I hope that when the hon. and learned
Gentleman (Mr. Megaw) is replying he will
reply to the question of fact, and not
wriggle out of it on lawyers' lines.
Again I want to make it perfectly clear.
I assume that the offences covered by this
Clause are offences for which no special
penalty has been provided, and, therefore,
they must be minor offences. I think I am
right in concluding that. If that is so here
you are instituting for the first time
imprisonment directed as the penalty subject to the discretion of the Court. I am
certain that those words "subject to the discretion of the Court" will be repeated to
the House in the reply of the hon. and
learned Gentleman (Mr. Megaw), but I
assume, and I think we have the right to
assume, that before imprisonment is
brought in as a direct punishment for a
certain offence, even though it is subject to
the discretion of the Court, it ought to have
stronger justification than has yet been put
before us. Just by way of comment I would
recall that the defence of the Government
against the amendment proposed by my hon.
and learned Friend the Member for Antrim
(Mr. Hanna) on sub-section (6) was that the
offence was not a criminal offence, and,
therefore, the police had the right to appeal,
or something like that; but here we have in
the very next sub-section a demonstration
that the offence is considered by the
Government to be a criminal offence; otherwise the justification for imprisonment has
yet to be made.
The PRIME MINISTER: My hon. Friend

into the point. I think there is a good deal
in what he says, but it is impossible for us
in a moment to decide on a form of words
to meet his objection.
Amendment agreed to.

FIRST SCHEDULE.
PART II.
PROVISIONS APPLICABLE TO CON-
SIDERATION OF CLAIMS.
In cases where the licence in respect of
any premises ceases, by virtue of this Act,
to be renewable, the following provisions
shall apply as respects the payment of
compensation to persons interested in the
premises :-
.-
(1) Compensation shall be paid in respect of the depreciation in the value of
the premises to an amount not exceeding
three times the difference between the
amount at which the premises were
valued under the Irish Valuation Acts immediately before they ceased to be
licensed premises and the sum which the
Commissioner of Valuation for Northern
Ireland certifies to be their annual value
immediately after they ceased to be
licensed;
(2) If the profits of the trade carried
on in the licensed premises bave for each
of the three years ending 5th April, 1923,
been brought into charge for assessment
under the Income Tax Act, 1918, or any
Act amending the same, compensation
shall be paid in respect of loss of profits,
either-
(a) to an amount equal to the part
of the aggregate amount of the profits
for the said three years so brought into
charge which was made by the trade
in intoxicating liquor; or
(b) if it is impossible to determine
what part of the profits SO brought
into charge was made by the sale of
intoxicating liquor, to an amount not
exceeding one-third of the aggregate
profits for the said three years
brought into charge of the total trade
carried on in the licensed premises.
SO
(3) If the profits of the trade carried
on in the licensed premises have not
for any year of the three years ending
5th April, 1923, been brought into charge
for assessment under the Income Tax,
Act, 1918, or any Act amending the same,
compensation shall be paid in respect of
loss of profits, to such amount, not exceeding two hundred pounds, as may be
determined by the Claims Tribunal.
(4) If the profits of the trade carried on
in the licensed premises have for one year
only, or for two years only, of the three
years ending 5th April, 1923, been brought
into charge for assessment under the Income Tax Act, 1918, or any Act amending
the same, compensation shall be paid in
respect of loss of profits either-
(a) to an amount equal to three times
the average profits made by the trade
in intoxicating liquor during the year
or years in respect of which the profits have been so brought into charge, or
(b) to such less amount as may be
determined by the Claims Tribunal.
(5) Notwithstanding anything in the
foregoing provisions of this Part of this
Schedule, if the Claims Tribunal is satisfied that during the three years ending
5th April, 1923, the trade carried on in
any licensed premises was adversely
affected by civil commotion to such an
extent as to render it inequitable that
the said three years or any of them
should be taken for the purpose of estimating the amount of compensation payable under this Part of this Schedule in
respect of loss of profits, the Claims Tribunal may take for that purpose the year
ending 5th April, 1919, or the year
ending 5th April, 1920 (or both of those

The PRIME MINISTER: I beg to move, in
the First Schedule, page 14, line 26, to leave
out the word "three" ("not exceeding three
times the difference") and to insert instead
thereof the word "five."
This amendment will call to mind the fact
that the hon. Member for North
Belfast (Mr. Lloyd Campbell)-whom I
do not see in his place at the moment
-along with a number of other
Members of the House, pressed me very hard
to stretch a point with regard to this compensation, and I threw out the hint that, if
it were at all possible, to add-I think I said
-a year or a year and a half to it the Government would do its best to meet the point.
We have very carefully thought it out, and
we have a suggestion made to us which I
think is a wise suggestion that if this were
made five years, instead of four or four and
a half, it might tempt a large number to
close their doors immediately, and to clear
up the whole business, and would leave no
uncertainty behind it. At all events my colleagues and I went very fully into the whole
matter, and we came to the conclusion that
sooner than have any dissatisfaction, or to
minimise dissatisfaction as much as possible,
we would increase it to five years all round.
That is the tenor of the amendments standing on the Paper, the first one of which I beg
to move.
Amendment agreed to.

6. The following provisions shall have
effect with respect to offences in connection
with premises licensed for the sale of intoxicating liquor by retail:-
(a) Any police officer or constable may
at all times enter any premises in respect
of which a licence is in force for the sale
of intoxicating liquor by retail, and every
person who by himself, or by any person
in his employment or acting with his
knowledge or consent, refuses, fails or unreasonably delays to admit any such
officer or constable demanding to enter
in pursuance of this paragraph shall be
guilty of an offence under this Act.
(e) It shall not be lawful for any person
to consume, or permit the consumption
of, intoxicating liquor on any premises
licensed only for the sale of intoxicating
liquor by retail for consumption off the
premises. This provision shall, as
spects any premises, have effect as from
the date when the licence for such sale
as aforesaid is first renewed after the
passing of this Act.

Mr. CRAWFORD: I would like to say just
a few words and I promise to speak with my
usual rapidity, so that I may not take up
the time of the House to any great extent.
. I feel I should like to say something this
evening in view of the attack which has
been made upon me. I stood it with patience,
and it took patience for me to sit in my chair
the whole time. I bore as patiently as 1
could the charges which were made. I
could have understood it if the hon. Member
my colleague for Antrim (Mr. Hanna) were
attacking me because he and I are like two
of George Birmingham's characters.
It was
said of them that they were good friends but
on occasions they fought bitterly and regularly, just like man and wife. I felt when
my hon. Friend, the Member for Tyrone and
Fermanagh (Mr. Coote) was speaking-I am
sorry he is not here now-that I would like
to say "save me from my friends
not from my enemies." I have read
recently of a gentleman who was exceedingly
anxious to get a concession from an Indian
tribe and he sent a legal friend to represent
him. The legal friend talked to the chief of
the tribe, a man called Red Cow, and after
the speaker had finished the chief got up,
and wrapping his mantle round him said:
"There has been a lot of big talk and high
wind and a heap of dust, but no water."
I would be inclined to use language of that
description to a great many of the things
said in this House this afternoon. Language
of that sort on behalf of the temperance
people has cut no ice in the past, and will
cut no ice in the future. It is wiser to look
at these things and realise them, and I hope
I will never hear of anyone of the
Temperance Party making use of language of
that description. I am not repentant of any
position I have taken up in the interests of
temperance. I have done the wisest and
right thing, and I will not be ashamed to
stand on any temperance platform and
advocate temperance principles in time to
come. I have said enough about that. I
want to congratulate the Prime Minister and
the Members of the Cabinet of Northern Ireland on the exceedingly useful measure, in
my opinion, they have been kind enough to
bring into this House. It has been a very
difficult problem, an exceedingly thorny
problem, and I am here to say that I believe
the Prime Minister, as he said in this
House, has held the balance fairly.
He has displayed a knowledge of the facts
that amazed me. I think he has shown
sympathy with all classes of the community.
He has been like the wise physician, he kept
his finger on the pulse of the people, and he
has tried to bring in a measure that might
be called legislation in deference to the
sympathies of the people. I believe this
measure is framed in such a way that it will
be based on the will of the people.
I know there have been great and conflicting views on this matter. Many meetings
have been held all through the country, and
all very important. I was at a number of
meetings myself. There were also a great
number of meetings held on the other
side. I rejoice to think now that
the war is over and this Bill is
being read the Third time, very little
in the way of ill-feeling was manifested
1397 Intoxicating Liquor Bill—

8 JUNE 1923
Third Reading.
in the whole thing. I attended meetings
in County Antrim, in County Down, in
County Armagh and in County Derry, and I
may say for myself that I believe in my heart
and soul I endeavoured at all times to use
courtesy to those who thought differently from
me, and I am not afraid to admit in this
House that I have little to complain of in
the way of the courtesy extended to me from
the other side. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
I personally rejoice at this thing. I have
further advanced views on the question of
temperance legislation than perhaps the
Prime Minister and the Members of the
Cabinet, but I am getting to be an old man.
It has been borne in upon me by experience
that wisdom runneth little risk of being
buried in the grave with me.
The question that faces me is that it is wiser
to take what temperance legislation we can
get than take no temperance legislation at all?
The Bill is not exactly the Bill that falls
in with my idea of things. I believe it is a
magnificent advance on anything we have
had in the past, and I believe if wisely administered it will be very helpful to the
people. On the whole I believe it is a good
Bill. It fulfils the promise made by the
Prime Minister to give us Sunday closing.
The Clause was greatly improved and we now
have Sunday closing we might say almost
altogether, the only exception being that if
a person makes a hotel a home he gets some
liquor along with a meal. We have the bonafide traveller knocked out of existence not
only for Sundays but week nights as well,
and for that we are profoundly thankful.
We have spirit grocers abolished. It is said
they have been a tremendous nuisance in the
past. We all sincerely hope that it will be
a helpful thing, especially to the women of
the city, that this source of temptation is
taken from out of their midst.
I am sorry that clubs have not been dealt
with in exactly the same way as other
places. All these clubs should have been
dealt with in the same way exactly as publichouses, and I am sorry the Government did
not see their way to do it. I sincerely hope,
whatever rivalry there may have been in the
past between these clubs and the people, that
rivalry in the future between them will be
as to which of them will try to keep to the
laws put into execution in Northern Ireland.
I hope that better administration, which my
colleague, the Member for Antrim (Mr.
Hanna) referred to, will result from the fact
that two resident magistrates will have
charge of these cases, and that they will
have the confidence of the people charged
with offences and those who make complaints.
I sincerely hope that the result of the whole
thing will be that the law will be SO
administered in Northern Ireland that it will
be respected and kept by the people as a
whole. I am delighted that the methylated
spirits clauses are so strong. I hope some
announcement will be made in this House
with regard to the illicit distillation of
spirits and dealing in poteen. I feel certain,
and I say it again, and I do not think I will
be afraid to say it on any platform in
Northern Ireland or elsewhere, that the
Prime Minister and the Cabinet have done
their best to try to satisfy both parties, an
exceedingly difficult thing to do. I rejoice
that the Bill is being read the Third time.

Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: I have no desire this afternoon to make a lengthened
speech in connection with the Third Reading
of this Bill, but I hardly think I would be
doing the right thing if I remained silent.
Ever since Parliament came into existence I
have constantly pleaded with the Government to bring in some remedial legislation
in regard to temperance matters. Time after
time I have perhaps strongly criticised
the Government in regard to their
hesitancy to deal with this whole
question, but seeing that we have
reached this stage in connection
this Bill I want now in my place in this
House to do what I am prepared to do on
every platform that I may stand on in the
Six Counties-to say that the Government
have honestly and faithfully carried out any
pledges they have given in regard to this
whole subject. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
I quite recognise, and I have recognised all
along, the difficulties that the Prime Minister
and his colleagues have had to contend with
on this matter. It is, and always has been,
a difficult subject to handle, and statesmen,
whether in Northern Ireland, or Great
Britain, or any other part of the world have
had enormous difficulties to contend with
trying to legislate, and legislate wisely.
As the hon. Member for Antrim (Mr.
Crawford) has told you there were three
things that those of us who were pressing
for temperance legislation in this Parliament
have contended for from the beginning. That
was Sunday closing, the abolition of spirit
grocers and the doing away with the bona-fide.
traveller. We claimed those three things,
While in some sense-a very small sensethere may have been a little extension in

and will be extremely grateful to them. I

in connection with temperance legislation. I

Northern Ireland has improved its licensing
laws in such a way that other countries may

The Government have done more than we
who may be classed as temperance people
have asked them for. They have recognised

the opportunity when they were bringing in

glad to think that on quite a lot of these

they have acted in harmony with the sentiment of what we may call the trade itself.
I think it is a marvellous advance to have
secured now what will be looked upon by
temperance people and the trade itself as a
tribunal to consider all licensing matters
that cannot come in for the criticism that
existed hitherto in regard to local justices.
The Court we have established will secure,
I believe, the confidence not only of
temperance people, but of the trade itself,
and will do away with abuses that have been

years. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) Then
I think it is a very in portant advance to have
secured that no ycang person under the age

public-house. The tightening up of the conviction for offences against the licensing laws
has been done with the consent, I take it,
both of the trade and all other parties interested. It may be considered an impertinence
on my part to say the trade itself, but I

those are most desirable things.
There are other very important matters in

I beg to thank very sincerely the Prime
Minister. I quite recognise the great difficulties with which he has had to contend,
but I am free to say in this House, as I am

the impression I have formed during my membership of this House-and I want to say it

the rising generation in this beloved Northern Ireland of ours, and those who are
going to rule in the future. It will take
temptation to a great extent away from those
who are easily tempted and liable to fall,
and it will make easier the pathway for
those who find it at times difficult to resist
these temptations with which they have
to contend. Even those who to-day

Mr. McGUFFIN: I would not like the
present occasion to pass without at least discharging the personal obligation of offering
to the Prime Minister and the Government
my hearty congratulations upon the Bill that
is now before the House for the Third
Reading. It is a good Bill. It was a good
Bill when it was first presented to the House,
but, perhaps, the Prime Minister
permit me to say that it has been
considerably improved in its passage through
Committee. 1 anticipate, like my hon.
Friend (Sir Robert Anderson), that there
will be a great moral advancement attained
in the operation of this Bill. In the course
of the Committte discussions I had to oppose
the opinions of the Prime Minister. I may
have done it heatedly, but I never speak in
opposition to the Prime Minister without
feeling at the same time the respect that is
due to him not only for the position which
he occupies in this House, but for the policy
and principles which he has maintained
throughout his life.
There is one thing I want to say in connection with this matter. The Temperance
party have been dragged in the gutter over
this matter, and have been made responsible
as it were, for all the ills that attend the
liquor people at the moment. The trade
have even gone so far as to say that the
introduction of this Bill was due to the
fanatical agitation of temperance faddists.
The trade should recognise, whether they do
or not, that there has been a persistent and
continuous effort for temperance reform, not
only in the city of Belfast but in the whole
of Northern Ireland, for a great many years,
and it cannot be pleaded that they have been
taken by surprise in respect of this matter.
The Bill represents the will of the people.
The trade allege that there was a no-pledge
election last time, but I would remind the
trade that the election that was conducted
when this House was returned was conducted
upon what was taken to be the most democratic principle upon which an election could
be conducted, namely upon Proportional Representation. Upon Proportional Representation this House was returned, with the result
that we have been able to achieve this Bill.
Laws are made at the instance of the
people, in the interests of the people, and can
only be cancelled or anuulled on the demand
of the people. That is all that has taken
place here. A licence was given to the
trade. That licence has been withdrawn. It
was only given as a licence, and if
it has ever been thought that it
was going to be given in perpetuity,
the nation would have hesitated to do
it. Then laws change, and must change, in
accordance with the people's experience.
The people have now learned to appreciate
the effect of temperance, and, moreover, they
have learned that the principles of
temperance are such as make for the wellbeing-both moral and social-of the people.
I do not think there is any person in this
House who will for a moment hesitate to say
that the trade in all probability has been
hard hit in this matter. We did not intend
that it should be so. So far as I am concerned I have always said that where
there was an interference or I should
say a confiscation of a right, the principle
of compensation should be admitted.
I still hold to that, and compensation has
been given, even though it be as alleged
through the trade. There are a great many
things in connection with the Bill that have
been a surprise packet to us. The Prime
Minister has not only implemented his
promise with regard to the three great conditions of the Bill, but he has gone a little
further and made very important amendments for which we thank him. I am sure
the right hon. Gentleman will find that the
course he has pursued in connection with this
Bill will be fully justified by the grateful
recognition of the people who have so long
looked forward to this measure of temperance
reform.

Local Government electors.
Whether his attention has been drawn to
the fact that this system is most cumbersome and costly, and very difficult for all
concerned to work.
Whether a form of register was submitted
by the County Council of Tyrone, and was
approved of by the Association of Clerks of

opportunity now offered by the revision of a

Ireland, under the Local Government Act,

SALARIES OF TEACHERS.
2. Dr. MORRISON asked the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Education
whether any explanation can be given with
regard to the delay in publishing the report
of the Departmental Committee upon
Secondary Education?
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY to
the MINISTRY of EDUCATION (Mr.
McKeown): The proposals made as to the
salaries of teachers in secondary and preparatory schools are still under consideration
as to their financial effects, and it is necessary before any definite scheme can be published that the Ministry of Finance should
examine the proposals which have been
made, but the matter is being expedited as
much as possible.
Dr. MORRISON: Arising out of that
answer, I would like to ask the Parliamentary Secretary if he could give us an approximate date on which this information will be
available?
Mr. McKEOWN: It is very difficult to give
an approximate date, but I can assure the
hon. Member that the Salary Scale will appear when the regulations come before
Parliament.

Since the 1st June, 1922, three appointments
have been made to the rank of District Inspector, two being filled by the promotion of
Head Constables, and the third by an officer
of the Special Constabulary. The service of
the two Head Constables at date of appointment to rank of District Inspector was as
follows:-23 years and 24 years respectively,
and that of the Special Constabulary officer
2 years. There were then forty-seven Head
Constables of over eighteen years' service.
The merits of these officers were fully considered by the Promotion Board, and the two
candidates whose qualifications were considered the most suitable were selected for
promotion.

R.U.C. REPRESENTATIVE BODY.
"
Mr. HANNA asked the Minister of Home
Affairs why a representative body" of the
Royal Ulster Constabulary has not yet been
constituted in accordance with the requirements of the Constabulary and Police (Ireland) Act, 1919, as applied to the said Constabulary by the Constabulary Act (Northern Ireland), 1922, and when such a representative body" will be set up and constituted.

Sir DAWSON BATES: Under Section 2 (3)
of the Constabulary Act (Northern Ireland),
1922, the representative body could not be set
up before the 1st instant. The rules in connection with the establishment of the representative body are already under consideration, and it is hoped that the election of
representatives in accordance with these rules
will take place at an early date.
PROMOTION IN R.U.C.
Mr. HANNA asked the Minister of Home
Affairs to state the number of persons appointed to the rank and position of District
Inspector in the Royal Ulster Constabulary
since the "appointed day" on which that
police force was established, other than
transferred officers of the R.I.C. How many
of these appointments were filled by promotion of Head Constables; what police service
each of the other persons so appointed had
before his appointment to such position; and
how many Head Constables having eighteen
years' service and upwards there were then
in the force already qualified by test or other
examination for promotion to the rank of
District Inspector?
Sir DAWSON BATES: On the 1st June,
1922, forty-six District Inspectors were required for the formation of the R.U.C. These
were obtained by transferring thirty-five
District Inspectors of the R.I.C., seventeen of
whom were cadet officers and eighteen of
whom had gained their promotion from the
ranks, and by appointing eleven officers of the
Special Constabulary, one of whom has since
resigned.

Public Records Bill (S.).
Order for Second reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed: "That
the Bill be now read the Second time."
Mr. BARBOUR: I am sure that hon. Members will appreciate the great value nowadays
of carefully collecting, compiling and preserving all documents of a public character.
Prior to the passing of the 1920 Government
of Ireland Act all deeds and public records
were kept in the Record Office in Dublin, but,
unfortunately, the destruction of that office
not only rendered it impossible for that office
to continue as the repository of such documents, but the passing of the Free State Act
removed that office from under the direct control of the Imperial Government. It was intended that the custody of public records
should still remain an Imperial service, but
under the 1920 Act it was made permissive
for the Government of Northern Ireland, if
it so desired, to set up its own public record
office, and it is with that intention that this
Bill is now promoted to enable us to establish here in Belfast our own repository for
these documents, to provide for their proper
collection, compiling and custody, and to
make the rules necessary in order that the
work in this department should be adequately
and efficiently carried on.
we
Hon. Members will see on reference to the
Bill that the effect of the first clause is to
divide all these records into two classes. The
first class relates to those of Northern Ireland over which we have absolute control,
and the second class refers to Imperial
records which may in the discretion of the
Imperial Government be harded over to us
for custody in this record office which
propose to set up. On page 2 the nature of
the records for which this office is to be provided is set out. The charge of the record
office and its management is vested in the
Ministry of Finance which has the power to
make all the regulations and appointments
that may be necessary in connection therewith. Clause 3 provides for taking over
from the different departments and Courts
of Justice those records which have ceased
to be of immediate value, but which it is desirable to set aside and store in case it is
necessary to make reference to them in the
future.
For the information of hon. Members I
may state that, generally speaking, records
remain within the department in which they
originated and are accumulated for about
twenty years, so that they may be available
for reference by that department in case of
necessity, but after that they are transferred
to this Public Records Office, where they are
carefully stored. Clause 5, we hope, will be a
convenience to individuals, and possibly may
also provide a means for accumulating documents which may prove of very considerable
interest and possibly utility in the future.
That is, it enables trustees or other
having
persons
of
the custody
deeds
and documents who may wish to provide for
their safeguarding to hand them over to
the Public Records Office for that purpose.
Clause 7 provides for a careful list of the

documents transferred to the Record Office
Clause 8 is a provision made to prevent
undue accumulation of documents which
obviously are not of such a character as to
be likely of further interest or utility. Hon.
Members can easily understand that very
careful precautions must be taken before a
document is finally destroyed. It will be
the duty of the Records Office to review
carefully the documents under its charge, and
if it thinks that a certain number of them
can be destroyed without any loss of anything of real value a list of those documents
shall be presented to this House and to the

may inspect them before the documents are
finally destroyed. In Clause 11 provision is
made for the transfer to this office of the
control of all parochial records. I think
these are the only points to which it is necessary to draw the attention of this House, and
I beg to move.

Mr. McGUFFIN: I have nothing but
praise and congratulation for the Committee
in respect of the way in which they have
discharged their duty with regard to the
Clauses generally in the Bill. Certain Clauses
have been withdrawn and others have been
amended which I would have preferred to
have seen in their original form; but I am
not going to raise any difficulty with respect
to that matter, nor do I propose to discuss it
in any way. But there was a Clause in the
Bill-namely, Clause 68, making provision for
pensions for the ordinary workers under the
Corporation. The Report of the Committee
with respect to that Clause says:-
"By the provisions of this Clause the Corporation asked for powers, with the consent of the Ministry of Home Affairs, to
introduce a non-contributory scheme granting to their workmen and servants a
weekly pension on retirement. Precedents
in the cases of Dublin County Borough and
Londonderry County Borough were quoted
on behalf of the promoters, but no evidence
was submitted as to the cost of these
schemes to the ratepayers of those places,
or the number of persons receiving benefit."
The difficulty really turns upon the next
paragraph:
"The actuarial report which was submitted by counsel on behalf of the Corporation indicated that a very heavy burden
would be thrown on the ratepayers if the
proposals contained in the clause were
passed.
"The two witnesses called on behalf of
the Corporation did not agree with the
findings of this report, but no further
expert figures were produced, and the Corimittee felt that they would not be justified
in recommending what appeared to them
to be necessarily a heavy burden to be
placed upon the community in order to give
special privileges to a small body of work-
Inen. The Committee, therefore, disallowed
the Clause."
It is upon this disallowance that I propose to
raise the question in the House this after-
Loon. It appears that the actuarial difficulty
was the burden that would be imposed upon
the rates, but there was a misconception on
the part of the Committee-due to the lack of
evidence, I suppose to the effect that the
proposal included a certain number of work-
I think they amounted to about 6,000.
men.
Mr. DONALD: No, 3,000.
Mr. McGUFFIN: There was a misconception with regard to it, because they were including quite a number of casuals, whom it
was not proposed to introduce to the privilege
of superannuation, and if that had been undersame
stood and it had been made perfectly plain, in
all probability the Committee might have
taken a different view of the matter. In discussing the thing in the general sense the
principle involved is the same whether
applied to salaries or wages, namely, the duty
of making provision for incapacitated workers.
I am just afraid that at the moment there
is too little regard had to the importance of
the worker. All thought seems to be concentrated upon the importance of the salaried
official. I do not want to take away from the
latter's importance, or from the difficult
nature, in some instances, of the duties
he is called upon to perform, but
the worker discharges his duties in
the
way precisely, to the extent
of his responsibilities, as the salaried
official does. The nature of the service
rendered hardly arises because, if a man
acts up to his responsibility, all workers in
that respect can be said to be on a par. I do
not think for one moment that there is any
reason why the working man, because of the
nature of his services, should be discriminated against, and when he comes to an age
that incapacitates him for work I do not see
why any Corporation should hesitate, because he is a working man and not a salaried
official, to recognise the services he has done
and to pay him a pension. Of course, where
distinguished service is performed it is a
very different matter, as, for instance, we
have Royal grants or Parliamentary grants
made to prominent men who have performed
distinguished services on land or sea. The
country feels under an obligation to those
men for the great services they have performed, in all probability in protecting our
very existence in time of war, but whenever
you come to the plain routine duty of service
there should be no distinction with respect
to pension. I think that is a proposition
that might very reasonably be entertained
by any person. If there is a distinction at
all I maintain it should be in favour of the
worker, who is paid so much less than the
salaried official, and on that ground is unable to make provision for old age or for the
incapacitation that comes through old age.
Ruskin had laid down a principle to which
the House will perhaps assent, and it is that
Honest work done in any capacity in life
fulfils the duty of the person concerned.
It does not follow that because a man is
sweeping the street or driving a cart in the
service of the Corporation he has no
claim. I say his claim is all the
greater, provided he has done his work well
and that his conduct entitles him to consideration. Therefore, I think it is very unfair to discriminate against the worker.
It appears that the financial difficulty,
which is the stumbling block in this case,
only arises for the first time in this
1423 Belfast Corporation Bill-

Third Reading.
[Mr. McGuffin]
connection. Did it not occur to those who
were initiating the principle of pensions for
salaried officials that the wider application of
it would ultimately lead to this difficulty?
Now the difficulty would appear to crop up
for the first time. Why was it not considered
long ago, and in relation to what might happen if in due time and in the development of
events it should come about that a similar
proposal was made on behalf of the workers?
There should be no discrimination against
the workers, and I am disposed to believe
that that discrimination is the ground of the
suspicion and the source of unrest in connection with present-day politics. I would think
it would be the duty of the Corporation to
press this matter and to see that the worker
is not discriminated against. I would go
further and say that I would favour the application of the principle industrially all
round, and I could not do that if in the case
of the Corporation I permitted them to be lax
with respect to that matter. I maintain that
the worker is entitled to the consideration of
his master, or the local body which he serves,
when he has reached that time of life when
it is impossible for him to discharge his duty.
I believe that if more regard were had to this
matter, so far as the worker is concerned,
there would be less chance of strikes and upheavals, such as at the present time are depressing and disturbing the industrial community.
The recommendation of the Committee is
going aside from their terms of reference a
little. The report says:-
It was not competent for the Committee
to consider any proposals alternative to
those contained in the Bill, but they think
that they ought to draw attention to the
fact that the general practice of local
authorities, for some time past, has been
to seek Statutory powers to adopt contributory pension schemes, and this has probably
led to the passing of the General Act by
the Imperial Government, viz., the Local
Government and Other Officers Superannuation Act, 1922, whereby municipal authorities in Great Britain are empowered to
adopt contributory schemes for the provision
of superannuation allowances to their employees."
It was not part of their terms of reference,
but they thought it wise to draw attention
to the fact. In view of the fact, I would
imagine, that they were appearing to do a
serious injustice to the workers, they then
come to the conclusion that they should
modify it to some extent by suggesting a contributory scheme. That is not new to anyone. It is in force in many boroughs at the
present time, and it would only require on
the part of this House an adaption of the
Act in order to make it applicable here. But
I say let us be fair all round. If a salaried
official is entitled to a pension by reason of
his services, then I maintain, and it is only
a matter of plain equity, that the worker,
who to the extent of his ability and opportunity fulfils the obligation of his position,
is entitled to like consideration. We are told
that such a scheme would contribute to a
further burden upon the rates, which at the
moment are heavy enough. We all admit
that; but I do not think that even the question of expense should be allowed to interfere
with the question of principle. The principle
involved is that of justice to the worker or
ordinary employe as compared with the
salaried official. There is no objection so far
as he is concerned, but in this particular
case, because it happens to be the poor man,
the hard worker, the toiler, who throughout
his life has never had the opportunity of
accumulating as much as would give him a
reserve against times of adversity, then it is
objected to. The principle is wrong in that
respect. We should not discriminate against
the worker in that way.
We are told that this will involve great
extra expense, and will throw a fresh impost
upon the rates. That may be the case, and
doubtless it will, though I am not so sure
that all that has been said with regard to
that is true or accurate. To my mind a great
deal of it may be taken with a pinch of salt.
We are told it may be anything from one
shilling to two shillings upon the rates. I am
not so sure that it would amount to that at
all, especially if you take into consideration
that there is not the number of workers
stated in this Report concerned at all, but a
very much smaller number-those who are
directly in the employment of the Corporation and as such are entitled to be considered.
Speaking for myself personally. I have no
money to spare and feel my limits financially
as much as any hon. Member of this House,
and yet I am prepared to contribute my
quota in order to see that justice is done to
the workers. I have nothing further to say
in respect to this matter only this, that if
the House is to be divided on it I hope the
Government will not put on the Whips and
so allow hon. Members to divide on this important principle according to their
consciences. If they do we will at any rate
have absolved ourselves in this matter from

We have preferred to call them the wageearning class, because I think we all belong

In this Clause we find a proposal to give

have worked this matter out, and I find that

The employees of the Corporation are at least

other workers under this scheme would be

The Corporation, under instructions from

Burn went very carefully into all the figures

funds the £1,807,000 can be spread over a

£91,000, involving charges on the rates of 1s
1d to 1s 7d in the £, according to the term of

cities for years past. Those contributory

scheme on the ground that it restricted his

not explain why the working men in English
cities-English cities are supposed to be
quite as intelligent as Ulster cities-did not
object to contributory schemes. The contributory schemes must have found favour in
England, for we find that inside the last two
years Liverpool, one of the most go-ahead
cities in the world, has taken powers for a
contributory scheme. We find three or four
other cities of the front rank have also taken
powers for contributory schemes. We have
heard no objections to those schemes, except
the vague objection on general principles
that the workmen do not like them.
much do these authorities in England-and

that, in order to save the trouble of applying

each city that desired to adopt such a scheme,
a Bill was brought in by the Home Department at Westminister last year to make it
legal to apply contributory schemes to any
authority in England and Scotland which
desired to use them, and so the Local
Government and Other Officers' Superannua-
So
tion Act, 1922, was introduced and passed.
Under that Act any authority in England
and Scotland, without the expense of having
to apply for an Act of Parliament, can apply
a contributory scheme to its employees both
on salary and weekly wage. Under that Act
those are entitled to benefit who have
had 10 years' service and who are rendered
incapable through ill-health or infirmity of
mind or body, employees who are 60 years
of age and have 40 years' service, or employees who have attained 65 years of age.
After 10 years' employment ten-sixtieths of
the average of the last five years may be
given as a pension, and so on up to fortysixtieths for 40 years. The contribution on
the part of the employee is 5 per cent., and
the contribution of the local authority is 5
per cent., and under certain circumstances
-apparently such circumstances as those to
which Alderman Boyd and Councillor Bradley
drew attention as a reason for the objection
of the working men to the contributory
scheme-the contributions are returned with
3 per cent. compound interest.
Your Committee, as I have said before,
approached this matter entirely with an
open mind and the desire to do what was
best both for the working men and for the
city. We would not permit even Labour
Members to claim that they have a greater
interest in the welfare of the labouring man
than we have. Every Member of this House,
I think, is of the same mind with reference
to the man who works for a weekly wage.
We all recognise that he has not the same
return for his labour as a man who is
engaged in operations which call for mental
work. At the same time we want to make
his lot as comfortable and happy as we can,
and so long as the economic questions can
be settled we are all glad that he should
have any advantages that we can give him.
But when we examined the great expense
to which apparently the City of Belfast
would be put should we agree to that clause
on your behalf, we felt it was too large a
proposition for us to accept. The risk of
enormous expenditure being imposed on the
city was too great. We felt that if anything
was to be done it should be done in the form
of a contributory scheme. Personally, I
think we
were all satisfied that a contributory scheme was desirable. We would like

tuberculosis officer, who goes down and in-
Belfast Corporation Bill- HOUSE OF COMMONS.
Third Reading.
[Dr. Morrison]
spects everything he does, and may overrule

I maintain that the general opposition to this
clause, which is a very serious thing, is due
entirely to a misapprehension of the Farmers'
Union. They thought that every farmer's
cowshed was about to be inspected, when, as
a matter of fact, it only referred to those
registered and who claimed the right of sending milk to Belfast. This is a very serious
thing, because the whole medical opinion of
Ulster is unanimous on this point, that it
has a great deal to do with the unfortunate
mortality that runs in Belfast and all industrial centres. I have here cut out what appeared in a paper-it appeared in a
paper in March, and I have carried
it in my pocket from then until now.
It says that the public health officer
in Belfast stated that during the week
ending 17th March 96 persons were diagnosed
as suffering from tuberculosis. That is, 96
new
cases were discovered suffering from
tuberculosis at the depot for examination. A
large number of people in Belfast suffering
from disease do not go through the depot,
and if that is so, think of the enormous number who do not come into the record.
In 1921 I secured from the Minister of
Home Affairs certain statistics.
The question I asked was as to the number of preventible diseases that occurred in Ulster, and
he gave me the figures for the Six Counties,
and also for the Borough of Belfast. I find
that in the Borough of Belfast in 1920 there
were 911 deaths from tuberculosis.
If you
add to that the other diseases which I think
are preventible, including 24 which were due
to gastric trouble very often originating in
milk, you have 965 deaths in the city of
Belfast recorded for that year. Every medical man knows that the children of Belfast
are exposed to very serious dangers from
tubercular milk, or from poison in the milk.
You have it in the joints, the kidneys, the
glands all over the body, and worst place of
all you have it in the brain. You have gastric
troubles, which cause many deaths, and all
these are due to dirty milk. You have the
Corporation Health Committee and the medical officer looking into these cases and reporting to the Health Committee. In Belfast
you are spending wisely. I think the Corporation in this respect has set an example
to all other Corporations in Ireland, and
after them I would say the Board of Guardians. They have done a great deal for the
prevention of tuberculosis. They come to
this Parliament with a Bill to enable them
to check the disease at its origin. That is a
bit of legislation that I think was absolutely
necessary. Power should be given with regard to this matter of the inspection of milk
at its source in order to get rid of the enormous suffering and the number of deaths that
in my opinion are preventible. The medical
profession have nothing to blame themselves
for in regard to this matter. One of my
colleagues in the representation of the University (Mr. Johnstone) had his name on the
back of this Bill, showing that he thought
it was necessary that it should be introduced, and he expressed the opinion on the
Second reading that the only Clause that was
of any particular value in the Bill had been
withdrawn, to his extreme regret.
The Ulster Medical Society passed a resolution, which was forwarded to every Member of Parliament, stating that in their
opinion it should be the right of every
public health authority to inspect the
food supply of their own area when they
thought wise and fit. Now this provision has
been wiped out, and nothing has been done
with regard to the matter. In connection
with the Ministry of Home Affairs there is a
Medical Advisory Committee. If that Committee had been asked to give an opinion on
this matter they would certainly have advised that the Clause introduced by the Corporation was a necessary, aye, a vital one.
But they were not asked to give any opinion
on the matter. As a medical man who has
had a fair experience, I look upon the elimination of this Clause not only as a scandal
but as a crime, and the consequences will be
very disastrous to many people who are now
perhaps in the enjoyment of good health.
We, as a medical profession, can do nothing
but protest. We can vote, and I will certainly vote, but largely our vote can only
end in protest. We make this protest, that
in the interests of the health of any great
industrial community, such as Belfast, it is
not only right and proper that the Corporation should do this thing, but it is the absolute duty, I would say, of the Government to
see that they have power for dealing with
this question. If the Government is going to
take up the question of a contributory pensions scheme for the workers who are unable
to help themselves, as I hope they will, I
hope they will also take up the question of
the right of every public health authority in
Ulster to examine the food supply at the
source and try if possible to see that it is
proper, and clean, and fit for human beings.

Mr. HANNA: I would like that the House

I confess that I do not understand it very

Mr. MARK: I thought my hon. and learned
Friend, the Member for Antrim (Mr. Hanna),
was likely to throw some light on this amendment to this section, and that he might have
told us what he thought it meant or what it

only thing is that it does open perhaps rather

HOUSE OF COMMONS. Prime Minister's Statement. 1160
Adjournment.
SUMMER RECESS
Adjournment.
STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER.
(Mr.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That this House do now adjourn."
Burn.)
The PRIME MINISTER (Sir James Craig):
Before the House adjourns I think it only
right to explain certain important matters
and to assure hon. Members and the public
outside that the Government will be vigilant,
active, and prompt in its dealings with such
outstanding affairs as demand attention
during the current year. Firstly, the House
will perhaps wish me to say something
regarding the state of trade in general and
the possibilities for the future. Taking a
broad view of the world's situation it becomes more and more evident that we can
get no real and enduring stability until
economic and financial equilibrium is restored on the Continent of Europe. These
are matters which we here can do little to
affect. We can, however, be patient, and
while we are waiting for the equilibrium to
be restored we can set our own house in
order, prepare ourselves for the better times
that are coming and develop our trade within
the Empire, where conditions are stable, to
the utmost of our ability. There is no
doubt that British trade is improving. The
curve is slowly but surely mounting upwards,
and so far as we in Ulster are concerned we
find in all circles a new confidence and a
feeling that the worst times have been left
behind. The Government, through the
Ministry of Commerce, are sparing no effort
to stimulate our export trade and to smooth
over the many difficulties that have been encountered. The House will see, therefore, how
imperative it is for Ulster as a part of the
United Kingdom to join whole-heartedly and
vigorously in the British Government's
policy of developing to the full the resources
of the great British Empire. Many steps
are being taken in this direction. I will
for the moment refer to two.
IMPERIAL ECONOMIC CONFERENCE.
In October of this year there will be a
meeting of the Imperial. Economic Conference, presided over by the President of
the Board of Trade. I can assure the House
that the interests of Ulster will be in every
way watched and safeguarded at this Conference, and I hope that as a result new
fields will be opened out for the enterprise
of our business community. In anticipation
of the Conference, the Ministry of Commerce
is exploring in great detail the possibilities
that lie before Ulster within the Empire, so
that when the Conference comes on we may
be able and ready to further our interests
as much as possible.
What I have said to the House will, I
hope, also have the effect of impressing upon
them the importance of the British Empire
Exhibition which is being held at Wembley
Park, in London, from April to September
next year.
The main object of the Exhi
bition is to demonstrate to the world the
degree in which the Empire is selfsupporting, and to bring together all parts
of the Empire, so that one part may not rest
in ignorance of the possibilities that lie
before them in another part. I am able to
tell the House that the Northern Government have decided to participate in this
Exhibition in the general industrial interests
of Northern Ireland. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.)
ULSTER PAVILION.
That participation will take the form of
an Ulster Pavilion in the Palace of Industry, and I am glad to say that I believe
that the site we have secured is without
question one of the best in the Exhibition.
That Pavilion will contain demonstrational
exhibits to illustrate the industrial greatness
of Ulster, and in the many preparations that
it is necessary to make, the Ministry of
Commerce has the assistance of a most
representative committee of the business
community of Ulster. We shall spare no
effort to make it a success, but it is essential
that we should have the hearty co-operation
of all sections of the commercial community
to enable us to do full justice to this great
project, which should be of great assistance
in developing Empire relations in company
with and as part of the United Kingdom.
ULSTER INTERNAL DEVELOPMENT.
So far as our own internal development
is concerned, as his Grace the Governor
announced in his Speech at the opening of
the present Session, the Government is
setting up a Commission on Development,
the composition of which will be announced
in the course of a few days and which will
hold its first meeting early next week. I
hope that as a result of the investigations
of this Commission, which I am glad to say
will be under the, chairmanship of Lord
Charlemont-who, by the way, is particularly
interested in matters of development and is
therefore an appropriate chairman-that
many new lines of development will become
apparent and that a great stimulus will be
applied to the matter of utilising to the
utmost the resources that lie untouched in
our midst, so that all classes of the comnunity may benefit thereby.
UNEMPLOYMENT.
The figures regarding unemployment are
interesting and instructive. For all Northern Ireland the unemployed on 24th June,
1921, numbered 63,507. To-day, after two
Adjournment.
Prime Minister's Statement.
15 JUNE 1923
years of our administration, the number is
38,402. The number of persons on short
time on 24th June, 1921, was 45,000, and today the number is 3,183. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) The Government are exercising
every effort to improve on this improvement.
We look upon the problem as the most important with which we are confronted, and
no stone will be left unturned to recapture
the position of pre-eminence in regard to
employment which we held before the war.
FX-SERVICEMEN'S HOUSING.
With regard to ex-Servicemen and the
housing problem, in order that the present
position in regard to ex-Servicemen's housing
may be fully appreciated, it is necessary that
I should again recount, briefly, the steps
which led up to the introduction of the Land
Trust Powers Bill recently before this
House. Under Section 4 of the Irish Land
(Provision for Sailors and Soldiers) Act,
1919. the Local Government Board for Ireland was empowered to provide cottages
for ex-Servicemen. The Local Government
Board for Ireland is no longer in being, and
to provide a successor the Imperial Government by Section 3 of the Irish Free State
Consequential Provisions Act, 1922, arranged
for the setting up of a Land Trust to consist of three representatives nominated by
the Imperial Government; one nominee of
the Northern Government and one nominee
of the Free State. To enable this Trust to
be established it was necessary that complementary legislation should be passed by
the Parliaments of Northern Ireland and the
Free State.
As hon. Members are aware, we have, so
far as Northern Ireland is concerned, taken
the necessary steps, but I would point out
that until complementary legislation on
similar lines has been passed by the Free
State Parliament, the Land Trust cannot be
established or function. In the meantime
we have been pressing the Colwyn Committee
to give a decision as to the allocation of
houses between Northern Ireland and the
Free State, as we estimate that on the basis
of soldiers recruited from Northern Ireland
and Southern Ireland
respectively the
number of houses which have thus far been
allocated to Northern Ireland is far short
of her proper share. We now await the
decision of the Colwyn Committee as to the
allocation of the sum of one-and-a-half
million pounds which is to be placed at the
disposal of the Land Trust for completion
of the housing schemes. Pending this decision, by an arrangement with the Imperial
Government, the Ministries of Finance and
Home Affairs are pressing forward, so far
as the powers at their disposal enable them,
the work of completing schemes actually
begun by the Local Government Board.
I would like to say emphatically that no
opportunity has been neglected either by our
representatives in the Imperial Parliament
or by this Government to press our claims,
but as the Imperial Parliament votes the
necessary money, and it is a large sum, we
are constrained to bear with patience the
delay caused by the regulations imposed by
the Free State and the Imperial authorities
respectively.
LAND PURCHASE.
With regard to Land Purchase in Northern Ireland, I am happy to be in a
position to state that, as a result of our
representations to the Imperial Government,
the matter is now making a definite move
forward, a committee having been appointed
by the British Government under the chairmanship of Lord Eustace Percy. The terms
of reference of this committee are
"to consider what should be the terms of
future land purchase in Northern Ireland,
and to make recommendations for legislation accordingly."
I have every confidence that the committee
will devise the most equitable and economic
means of bringing to a close this question
which has vexed the Irish people for so many
years. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) The
problem is most intricate, involving as it
does the interests of so many people, including this Government itself, but I am
confident that the committee will use all
expedition to arrive at conclusions which
will be the basis of what I hope to be the
final Land Purchase Act for Northern
Ireland. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
AGRICULTURAL RELIEF.
The House will have observed that in view
of the exceptional agricultural depression
resulting from the low prices of farmers'
produce the British Government has decided
to grant temporary relief to the farming
interest in Great Britain during 1923 and
1924. This relief takes the form of a reduction of the present assessment of agricultural
land from one-half to one-quarter. The
Local Authorities are compensated by the
Government for the loss of revenue sustained
through this relief, by grants from the Local
Taxation Account.
Uufortunately, similar conditions of depression are to be found in Northern Ireland,
and this Government feel it is equally urgent
and necessary that relief should be afforded
to this important industry, within the limits
of our financial capacity for a similar period.
But, in providing such relief, regard must
be had to the difference in the character of
the agricultural industry in Ulster as compared with that of Great Britain. In the
latter country the farms are large and highly
rated, whereas in our area the converse
conditions obtain.
