The Government has given anxious consideration as to how some real benefit can be
conferred on an industry which is admittedly
of foremost importance in the Province, and
in order that every avenue may be explored
we have decided that the best method of procedure is to appoint a small select committee
of experienced agriculturists whose report
would enable the Government to take some
practical steps in this matter. This will not
involve delay, as the committee will be
brought into existence immediately, and I
am happy to be able to announce to the
House that Viscount Pirrie has kindly consented to preside over the committee. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) It may not perhaps
be within the knowledge of the House that
Lord Pirrie is himself a great agriculturist
and is very much concerned as to the present
position of agriculture generally, and especially that of his own Province of Ulster.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
HOUSING SUBSIDY.
In view of the continued shortage of housing
accommodation, especially of the small house
class, the British Parliament is engaged in
considering a Bill directed to the provision
of a subsidy of £6 per house of a maximum
superficial area of 950 feet, for a period of
20 years. As the conditions of congestion in
Ulster, and especially in Belfast, are fully
as acute as those obtaining in Great Britain,
the Government feels that a measure of
relief is equally necessary in our own area.
To make provision for such relief it is proposed to introduce a Bill in the next Sitting
of the House, and in the meantime the
Government is engaged in prosecuting enquiries as to the particular form the subsidy
should take, whether by way of a yearly grant,
or an equivalent capital sum which would
go immediately to the reduction of the cost
of the House. It is contemplated that the
subsidy should be payable to urban authorities which undertakes the building of
houses, or to private builders, and that the
operation of the Bill should extend over a
period of two years.
LOANS GUARANTEE ACT.
Turning now to the operation of the Loans
Guarantee Act, hon. Members will be aware
that this measure concerns itself with one
main object, and that is to assist industry,
and at the same time to create employment
in our midst. With this object my right
hon. Friend was empowered to pledge the
credit of the Government in respect of loans
raised in the ordinary way by commercial
concerns in connection with undertakings of
a capital nature which were calculated to
promote employment in the Province.
As my right hon. Friend (Mr. Pollock) has
from time to time indicated, the facilities of
this measure have been largely availed of.
and in particular, as was only to be expected.
by our great shipbuilding industry. No
return has as yet been furnished to the House
regarding the guarantees which have been
given. A return will be submitted to this
House of the guarantees which have been
issued in respect of the quarter ending 30th
June, but as the House will not be in session
at that time I propose to refer briefly to
what is being done.
I am glad to say that guarantees have been
issued in respect of the completion of two
large ships, work in connection with which
had been suspended, and considerable em-

and I say further that when you have disregarded the law it is illegal to pay them.

applied all the law which applied to the old

I hope he has not forgotten that Act.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I can only repeat
that the hon. and learned Gentleman seems
to have forgotten that the Royal Ulster Constabulary was entirely a new force, and that
on the 1st June, 1922, the old Royal Irish
Constabulary ceased to exist. The men in
the old Royal Irish Constabulary ceased to
have any rights, except those which the
Imperial Government conferred upon them
by their pension rights. The Northern
Government were absolutely free to select any
member of the old Royal Irish Constabulary,
but there was no legal obligation, as the hon.
and learned Gentleman knows, on the
Northern Government to accept a single
member of the old Royal Irish Constabulary.
Furthermore, the older members of the Royal
Irish Constabulnary could, if they so chose,
come forward and offer their services. If the
hon. and learned Member thought for one
moment that the Government of Northern
Ireland were prepared to take over the Royal
Irish Constabulary, as he suggests, he is very
much mistaken. The Royal Ulster Constabulary, I repeat again, was entirely a new
force, a force which is being built up, and
which, I believe, in time to come, will be one
of the best police forces in the Three
Kingdoms.

The hon. and learned Gentleman (Mr.
Hanna) is also aware that the Police Committee was set up to assist the Government
in advising how best to form the Royal Ulster
Constabulary, and I would refer him to the
recommendations of that Committee. One
of the most important recommendations of
that Committee was that a due proportion of
the appointments in the police force should
be given to the Special Constabulary-(hon.
Members: Hear, hear) and I recollect that
when the Report of that Committee came
before the House, with this recommendation
that due recognition should be given to those
gallant men of the Special Constabulary in
our new police force, the hon. and learned
Member did not say a word in opposition to
it. Yet he comes here now and attacks the
Government for having had the audacity to
appoint those Special Constabulary officers to
be members of the Royal Ulster Constabulary.
The Government had a perfect right to
appoint those members of the Special Constabulary to be members of the Royal Ulster
Constabulary, and they stand by it.
In selecting the District Inspectors for the
new constabulary force, regard was had also
to the recommendations of the Police Committee, and as a result eleven appointments
to the rank of District-Inspector were given
to members of the Special Constabulary, and
thirty-five were given to old Royal Irish
Constabulary officers. But they came into
the Royal Ulster Constabulary as members of
the Royal Irish Constabulary, and not by any
right. They came in by virtue of their
appointment, and not by any right they
possessed to come in there. Out of those
thirty-five men, who were selected for appointment out of the Royal Irish Constabulary, I
find that eighteen were officers who had risen

(Mr. Hanna) suggest that, because those men

positions in the Royal Ulster Constabulary?

Condition of the Province.
STATEMENT BY THE PRIME MINISTER.
Motion made and Question proposed: "That
this House do now adjourn)" (Captain
Dixon)
The PRIME MINISTER: I think it will be
for the convenience of the House and of the
people outside our Parliament that on the
resumption of our Session, I should make a
few remarks dealing with matters of immediate
interest. As practically everybody is aware
I have, within the last few days, been visiting
the more outlying parts of Northern Ireland
for the purpose of meeting those who live
upon the borderland, and during that short
tour I had an opportunity of making several
speeches. I would like just to say a few
words about our position to-day. It is unnecessary for me to traverse the ground which
I have already covered, but the Horse will be
glad to know that so far as those who have
borne all the anxiety, grave danger, and inconvenience of living in those out of the way
places in Tyrone and Fermanagh are concerned, their courage is undaunted, and their
feelings remain, as ever they did, loyal to
our King and to our Constitution. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) And I re-assured
them, if re-assurance was necessary,
that not only so far as I was concerned
and my colleagues are concerned, but so far
as this House of Commons and Parliament
generally are concerned we were unchanged
and unchangeable regarding the views we take
in connection with the border question.
I would like to go on and point out that
we meet to-day under conditions vastly improved from any time that we have assembled
together, and that we must never forget when
we take comfort in that assurance that it is
almost entirely due to the magnificent
organisation of our new Royal Ulster Constabulary and our Special Constabulary.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear). What some
people would admire most about them, I
daresay, would be their fighting qualities, of
which there never has been any doubt, but
in the long run what has endeared them most
to my heart is the fact that during the most
provocative times they have managed to preserve law and order, to bring peace to the
1485 Prime Minister's Statement.

16 OCTOBER 1923 Prime Minister's Statement.
country, and at the same time to retain
friendly relations with all classes in their
midst. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear). Those
who study Ulster from the outside are blessing us every day for the magnificent result
that has been attained by those forces raised
in the hour of Ulster's danger-the Royal
Ulster Constabulary, and the Special Constabulary who are working so harmoniously
with them.
The peace and good feeling that now animate the hearts of all men inside our borders
are something to prize and to be proud of,
and I can only express the hope that, not only
in our own area, but throughout the whole of
Ireland, peace and prosperity will continue indefinitely. It may interest the House to know
that in the financial years 1913 and 1914 the
average daily prison population was 603 and
561 respectively-that is in the two yearsand the present prison population is now
only about 387. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
I think that speaks for itself. With regard
to the internees, there are at the present
moment 500 upon our hands. My right hon.
Friend the Minister of Home Affairs (Sir
Dawson Bates) has been able to release
some 200 under the restrictions which are
laid down, and he trusts to continue that
policy of gradually and slowly releasing these
men, provided that the conditions keep on as
they are at the present moment and other
circumstances permit.
It is interesting also as an impartial
pronouncement upon the state to which we
have now attained in Northern Ireland to
know that His Majesty's Judges at the
Spring Assizes congratulated the Grand
Juries of the different counties at the opening
of the Assizes on the marked improvement
in the state of their counties compared with
the previous spring, and at the following
Summer Assizes His Majesty's Judges'
charges show that they were greatly
gratified with the peace and good order prevailing throughout Northern Ireland.
If I may turn for a moment to trade and
commerce I would like to point out that it
is not good, but there is a slight improvement
from the time when we adjourned in the
early part of the summer. That improvement is bound to be slow. Our patience will
be taxed to the full probably before there is
a return of the old prosperity in our yards,
and certainly it will be some considerable
time before our looms and spindles are working at full strength; but the barometer of
unemployment is slightly better, and my
right hon. Friend (Mr. Andrews) has been
able cautiously throughout trying times to
co-operate with local authorities to bring
about a much better state of affairs. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear). Although no pessimist he has pictured from time to time the
very serious conditions that otherwise would
have existed, and by his advice and counsel
has improvised work which has been of inestimable value to those who otherwise would
have been practically upon the streets. Our
Trade Facilities Act has gone a long way
also to help in certain directions, and my
right hon. Friend the Minister of Finance
(Mr. Pollock) and the whole of his
colleagues are always prepared to take into
consideration further extensions of those
facilities where anything possible can be
done to help to revive trade and to bring
more work to the working classes.
Agriculture, we all know, has suffered a
terrible blow this year, not only in our own
counties but throughout Great Britain as a
whole, and I can only assure those who are
engaged in what, after all, is our greatest
industry-(hon. Members: Hear, hear)-that
we will take the utmost precaution to do
what lies in our power to help them through
the next two years at all events. The House
will bear in mind the setting up of the Committee under Lord Pirrie to inquire into this
matter, and will have read the report of that
Committee. The sum mentioned as an
equivalent grant to the grant that is made
in Great Britain is £128,000 for the year. I
have before mentioned it, but I think it is
well to reiterate in this House exactly how
we stand with regard to that £128,000. The
rates have been struck for this year, and,
therefore, it can only reach the outlying
counties in aid of next year's rates and not
of this year's. But it makes no difference.
So far as the Government is concerned the
full sum of money shall be spent in aid of
agricultural rates. The Committee went a
little further in suggesting that there were
many plans which might be carried out by
the Ministry of Agriculture to help that
great industry outside the question of the
alleviation of agricultural rates, and the
Cabinet have very cautiously considered a
scheme put forward by my right hon. Friend
(Mr. Archdale), in which he spreads over four
years a comprehensive scheme for agricultural education, which will amount to
£16,800, Cow Testing Associations £29,460,
poultry £2,000, improvement of pastures
£2,880, and the improvement of mountain
sheep £2,800, making a total of £53,940
spread over the four years 1924 to 1927.
am glad to say that we will be able to carry
that out in addition to the £128,000 for the
year, because we are most anxious to do
everything which our financial resources
will permit to help this industry in its very
serious depression. (Hon. Members: Hear,

I
Now, having reviewed that portion of our
affairs that relates to the prosperity of the
Province, I would like to answer a criticism
that has been made from one body of our
1487 Prime Minister's Statement. HOUSE OF COMMONS. Prime Minister's Statement. 1188
[The Prime Minister.]
people who feel they are somewhat aggrieved.
I refer to certain Benches of magistrates in
The
various parts of Northern Ireland.
Government have received, and are still receiving, a number of resolutions urging-to
use the terms of those resolutions---
"that the powers of which local Justices
have recently been deprived be restored,"
and they go on to say that the influence of
these men on behalf of good government in
their different localities should be increased
rather than diminished. The Government
would be the first to acknowledge the great
assistance which they have received from the
magistrates at all times in our Province. We
would be the first to acknowledge the good
work they have done, the pains they have
taken, and the great discomfort to which they
frequently have put themselves in attending
on the Bench in order to administer justice.
But we were not responsible, in the first
instance, for initiating the system whereby
certain types of cases are heard by Resident
Magistrates, because, without referring to the
Crimes Act of 1887, I can point out the Firearms Act of 1920, an Act passed by the
Imperial Parliament, in which the system was
introduced. When the Northern Government
had to stamp out the orgy of crime which
took place in the spring and summer of 1922
we followed this plan, and then subsequently
it was extended somewhat under the Intoxicating Liquor Act. But this House passed
that Act unanimously, and all sides, not only
those who were in favour of temperance reform but the trade-and I may say incidentally that I met very large deputations from
both were satisfied that the old system of
packing Benches should be done away with.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) Therefore, I do
not think that any reasonable-minded person
will feel in the slightest degree aggrieved
that, on the one hand, we have taken away
the responsibility-the much graver responsibility-from these unpaid J.P.'s throughout
the country and have put all the responsibility
--not alone the odium of trying the cases but
the responsibility of dealing with them on a
legal basis-on the shoulders of Resident
Magistrates. I think no reasonable person
would think we have gone far astray in
adopting that measure, and certainly in some
parts the scandal was so great that it would
be utterly impossible for the Government to
revert to the system under which from time
to time Benches were packed for a specific
purpose.
Now may I turn from that to one other
aspect of Ulster's prosperity and Ulster's wellbeing? Before I came down here I asked my
right hon. Friend (Mr. Pollock) if he would
be kind enough to let me know how his Ulster
Savings Certificates have been going on.
Everybody is aware that these Certificates
and Savings Bank savings are an indication
of the savings of the poorer classes. I am not
for a moment going to refer to what is occurring in our joint stock banks or other institutions showing what prosperity there may be
in that direction. I wanted, if I could, to get
some indication of the thrift of the workingclass community. I have here the annual
report of the Belfast Savings Bank, which
shows that it has now reached the state in
which there are over 30,000 accounts open in
that institution, and that the sum total of
their funds at the moment is £2,864,836 4s 10d
-nearly £2,900,000-and the increase for the
past ten months-that is the ten months to
30th September-alone amounted to £308,435
odd, whilst my right hon. Friend (Mr. Pollock)
informs me that there are now 13,922 investors in the Ulster Savings Certificates to
an amount of £899,000-nearly £900,000-and
I have no doubt whatever that within a
short time that total will reach a round
million. The number of investors spread
over the community is what strikes me, and
it shows there is considerable thrift among
the working classes when they have an
opportunity of laying by money towards a
rainy day.
May I just refer next to the Royal Ulster
Constabulary? The present strength of the
force is 2,750. Our recognised establishment
is 3,000, and we hope by carrying out the
policy that has been adopted so far not to
relax in any way the conditions of recruitment so far as efficiency is concerned, but to
take the same pains in getting the very best
type of men and officers into our force. We
do propose, however, to introduce a short
Bill enabling recruits from the Special Constabulary to be taken in at an increased age
limit. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear). I think
it will give general satisfaction throughout
the whole of our Six Counties to know that
this preferential treatment will be made towards the Special Constabulary. Of course
it is early to talk about next year. However,
I think it is fair to the House, and
particularly to the Special Constabulary
themselves, that they should know clearly
how we stand. Our financial year, of course,
runs us up to the beginning of April, 1924.
and therefore our next financial year goes
right up till 31st March, 1925. I have always
been urging the British Government that, so
far as their treatment of our Special Constabulary is concerned, they should give us
ample notice of their intentions. It is most
difficult to control and organise a force of
that size and responsibility without knowing
well beforehand where you stand, and I am
1489 Prime Minister's Statement. 16 OCTOBER 1923.
Prime Minister's Statement: 1490
pleased to be able to inform the House that
His Majesty's Government have, after careful consideration, agreed at my request to
grant a further £1,000,000 towards the
Special Constabulary for the forthcoming
financial year.
(Hon. Members: Hear,
hear). I think the House by its
acclamation has acknowledged that in
that matter the Imperial Government
has acted in a generous manner.
It is a relief to my mind. lt will mean
cutting down, of course; it will mean saving
here and there; it will mean a little reorganisation, but after consultation with my
right hon. Friend beside me (Sir Dawson
Bates) and our able Inspector-General, we are
able to assure ourselves that it will make but
little difference in the actual Force during
the coming twelve months. That, I think,
will be satisfactory to everyone, especially as
we are fully satisfied that the Force as it
will be then will be able to do anything they
may possibly be called upon to perform.
The next point I have to deal with is in
regard to a comparatively small item of
£17,000, to which I think reference has been
made outside. The Imperial Government has
paid the Free State a claim amounting to
£17,000 for expenditure incurred by the Free
State for the maintenance of individuals who
are said to have been refugees from Northern Ireland. In view of the fact that the
Imperial Government has made us such
generous grants for coping with our own
civil disturbances, I feel sure that the House
will agree with me that it is expedient that
we should consent to refund to the Imperial
Government this comparatively small payment, and a Vote accordingly will be submitted for your approval at an early date.
We shall, of course, on our behalf claim for
the sums paid by the organisation which my
right hon. Friend, the Chief Whip, got up
to meet the cases of the refugees who came
to Ulster from Southern Ireland. In other
words, he will put forward his claim, and 1
hope that that will be met in exactly the
same way that we propose to meet this claim
that has been pressed upon us by the British
Government, because they have paid it in all
good faith.
The next point to which I wish to refer is
perhaps the most important of all, and that
is the question of the Colwyn Committee Report. We will all have to exercise considerable patience on this subject, because 1
understand that having got through a certain amount of work up to the present
time they are now bending their energies
towards solving a problem that has caused
me grave anxiety since I took over the reins
of office and my right hon. Friend here
(Mr. Pollock) shares with me the task of
devising a way out of an extraordinarily
difficult situation. May I put it as plainly
as I can without going into any details? The
financial papers which were the basis of the
Act of 1920 have proved to be absolutely
false. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear). They
have not justified the optimism that was
entertained in regard to them by the
Treasury officials of the day. The point that
has always troubled us is that there was no
elasticity about the finances as outlined in
those White Papers to meet the case which
has cropped up since of a grant given by the
Imperial Parliament in aid of local affairs
of various kinds. There is no way in those
White Papers of making an equivalent
grant-and remember we are quite entitled
to it to us here in Northern Ireland; it
should flow naturally to us. But on the other
hand my right hon. Friend and myself and
others have to go over each individual
case to see that Ulster gets justice when these
particular grants are made. May I just take
an illustration, and my right hon. Friend
here (Mr. Andrews) will correct me if I go
wrong. Since we took over our work an in
crease of 3d was added on to the contribu
tion made by the Government towards Unemployment Insurance, for the purpose of
bringing in dependants. That was done in
Great Britain, and we have always held that
our conditions of labour shall be at whatever standard is pursued across the water.
If we once vary from that we get into extraordinary difficulties. It is a sum amounting
to £92,000, I think, for the ten months, and
to a hundred thousand and something in the
year. That burden is immediately thrown
upon the shoulders of the Ulster taxpayer,
without having any contribution coming
from Great Britain to correct it, because it
was never anticipated whilst the finances of
the Act of 1920 were being evolved. There
are other cases. There is the £6 per house
for so many years for building workmen's
houses, and there are various other grants in¹
aid which could be made by Great Britain,
and yet there is no provision whatever to
enable them to reach us in the normal¹ working out of the finances between the two countries. That is the problem that the Colwyn
Committee has now set itself to solve. It will
interest the House to know that at all events
they have come to this satisfactory conèlu
sion, that for the year 1923 and the year 19232
24 we are on very sound ground. Not only!
will my right hon. Friend (Mr. Pollock) have
no debt to deal with, but we trust that he
will have such a substantial surplus that he
will be able to meet out of that surplus the
various matters to which I have referred in
the course of my remarks.
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: Including the
financing of the Education Bill?
The PRIME MINISTER: Including the
financing of the Education Bill' and everything else that will fall upon us in the financial year ending 31st March next.

[The Prime Minister]
May I pass from that to the subject of
education? I asked my right hon. Friend,
the Minister of Education, the noble Lord
sitting in another place, if he would give me
a short note on the Education Bill for the
purpose of acquainting this House and the
country as to how we stand exactly. As the
House is aware,
"the Act passed last June has been brought
into operation at the earliest possible date,
His Grace the Governor having by Order
in Council appointed the 1st October as the
date for the assumption of all powers under
the Act by the Ministry of Education and
the other Ministries interested. By the

made with the scheme of local government
in public education foreshadowed by the
Act. Powers have been bestowed upon the
County Borough Councils which constitute
them local education authorities, and enable them in that capacity to set up the
necessary machinery for carrying out effectively those duties which will fall upon
them when the operation of the Act is further extended. In these matters the Government has been fully aware that the
utmost caution must be observed and that
all undue haste must be avoided. Every
consideration and assistance will be given
to the Councils in their new undertaking,
and the Government looks forward to a
steady advance along the lines laid down
in the Education Act with the full cooperation of the local authorities. The
question of the extension of the Act to the
Counties is receiving the earnest consideration of the Ministry.
"Steps have been taken to implement the
pledges of improved conditions of employment given to Secondary School teachers."
Dr. MORRISON: Hear, hear.
The PRIME MINISTER: I know that my
hon. and learned Friend will be very pleased
to hear that statement.
"Draft regulations containing minimum
salary scales for teachers in Secondary
Schools and their preparatory departments
have been published, and are to be laid
forthwith upon the Table of the House.
"In this connection it is felt that
Members will realise that, having regard to
the over-riding necessity for economy in
every department of public expenditure, the
Government has not been ungenerous. It
is the hope of the Ministry that a salarybasis has been discovered which will ensure
both an adequate reward for efficient service
and a constant flow of recruits of a high
standard to this branch of our system of
education."
Prime Minister's Statement.1492
May I turn to the question of unemployment? I can only say that we intend to carry
on. There has been a considerable amount of
work done. I am sure those who have stepped
aside to allow the tram lines to be repaired,
those who have been in some of the outskirts
of our city, and those who have been in other
parts, will recognise that a great deal is being
done by the local authorities with the assistance of the Government, and I cannot too
often reiterate that the harmony that exists
between those local authorities and ourselves
remains absolutely unimpaired. They have
right royally, in my opinion, tackled a most
difficult problem, and with the assistance of
the Government an immense amount has been
done to alleviate the grave state of affairs
that existed before this idea of undertaking
work instead of paying out large sums in doles
was adumbrated by my right hon. Friend
(Mr. Andrews). The greatest success has
attended our efforts. I do not propose to go
very largely into the matter to-day, because,
of course, we have from time to time in this
House interesting debates on this subject of
unemployment. But I am able to say this,
that these vast schemes could not have been
undertaken without the financial assistance of
the Government, and I wish to let it be known
now that assistance will be forthcoming
so long as the two Ministers concerned consider that they fall within the scope of unemployment work and so long as means are available. I do not think the Government could
do more. We are giving to the fullest extent
of the means at our disposal for assisting in
these matters, and therefore so long as the
schemes are put up to us by the local authorities throughout the Six Counties, and my
right hon. Friend the Minister of Finance and
my right hon. Friend the Minister of Labour
consider that these schemes fall properly
within the purview of the generous scheme
that was laid down, then we will go on and
help in every possible way.
Mr. DONALD: Is it not proposed to ask

The PRIME MINISTER: That matter has

that case,
you will get a percentage because
you are still inside the British Empire and

Well I would like also to say that there has
been of course a grant from the Imperial
Government of a million and a half in aid of
compensation for malicious injuries. They are
prepared to go further in helping us in this
way. Up to the present time the grant of a
million and a half covered awards in respect
of malicious injuries which occurred prior
to 14th January, 1922. In other words,
January, 1922, was the line drawn
and the million and a half was for compensation prior to that date. The proposal of
the Government now is to add a further half
million, making £2,000,000 in all up to 14th
October, 1922, by which time practically all
claims for malicious injury of the nature to
which this grant was intended to apply, will
have come in and been adjudicated upon.
To the best of our knowledge that two
millions will give in the aggregate 60 per
cent. of the total awards in connection with
the injuries. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
When one bears in mind the heavy rates that
are being imposed in consequence of some of
these dastardly outrages that have occurred,
it is a comfort to us to know, at all events,
that only the residue of the 60 per cent. will
fall upon the taxpayers of Northern Ireland.
I think that in this respect we have a right
to be very grateful to the Government, seeing
that they are backing Ulster up in these
very difficult times. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear).
I might refer to the Bills which are proposed to be introduced during the remainder
of our present Session. Amongst the Bills
proposed to be introduced this Session are
the following, and upon some of them I will
briefly touch in my remarks:
a Bill amending the Trade Boards Act,
a Housing Bill,
a Labourers' Cottage Bill,
a Local Government Bill, and
a Bill for the licensing of Charabancs.
I regret that we shall not be able to introduce a Bill in regard to the Rent Restriction Acts during the current session, as the
report of the Committee considering this
difficult subject was only received on the 6th
instant. The Reports are being laid on the
Table of the House, and will be printed
shortly, but as it is not a unanimous Report,
the Government will require time to consider the various representations that have
been made on this contentious problem. The
whole aim of the Government is to encourage
the resumption of building by private enterprise at the earliest possible moment.
Bill dealing with this subject will be the
first measure in the New Year. Meanwhile,
we are making provision for the continuation
of the existing Acts pending new legislation.
I am sorry that I have no further report to
make on the subject, but I read through
very carefully the principal report and the
minority reports, and I saw at a glance that
A
it was utterly impossible-that we should
probably commit many sins of omission if we
were to attempt it-to tackle such a very
delicate subject before next Session, when we
will have had ample opportunity between
now and then to bring forward a Bill which,
we trust, will satisfy the great majority of
those interested in the subject.
My right hon. Friend, the Minister of
Labour, has been considering the question of
Trade Board legislation, and with a view to
arriving at the considered opinion of the industrial community on the matter a committee composed of equal representation o
employers and workpeople was appointed
under the able chairmanship of my noble
After
Friend, the Speaker of the Senate.
careful consideration of this very controversial subject a unanimous report has been
produced. The Bill which it is intended to
introduce embodied the recommendations of

will be welcomed by all parties interested in

Then, besides that, there will be a Housin
Bill, in which it is proposed to give effect to
the promise made by the Minister of Home
Affairs for the payment of a lump sum subsidy of £60 for each small house built between October, 1922, the date on which the
loan subsidy ended, and 1st April, 1925.
The Bill also makes provision for empowering the local authorities to refund rates in
respect of such houses up to such proportion
and for such period as may be fixed by them
generally for their districts. A number of .
other important matters will also be included.
By the Labourers' Cottage Bill we are regularising by statute the system of payment
to rural district councils of portion of the

out labourers' cottage schemes.
Then there is the Local Government
Bill. These are only a few of those
that
is
will be introduced. Really there
not very much in the legislation
for the autumn excepting the Bills
that I have just enumerated to the House.
There is the question of road construction,
and I am pleased to announce that our Minister of Home Affairs has been able to grant
further assistance in Northern Ireland to local
authorities to enable them to carry out much
needed reconstruction works in connection

1495 Prime Minister's Statement. HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Adjournment.
[The Prime Minister]
I myself will take an early opportunity of
making a violent attack on the Minister of
Finance to endeavour to get him to allow us
to build two or three bridges at a very
awkward part of the Six Counties, in what is
known as the Triangle-(hon. Members: Hear,
hear) where I was astonished to find that it
was only by the courtesy of the Free State
that we were able to pass from one part of
Ulster to another. If I can possibly manage
it, I think that this House will not grudge it,
for after all it cannot be a very large sum of
money that will be called upon for these people
who have stood so firmly by us and who are
at extreme inconvenience, as I found to my
own cost when endeavouring to go round on
my visit. I am hoping to be able before the
end of the financial year to get this from my
right hon. Friend. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.)
I think I can hardly pass on without touching on some other matters. Our R.N.V.R.
scheme is proceeding apace, and the Admiralty
have granted us a fine ship on which to train
those who are desirous of preparing themselves for eventualities. She will, I hope, be
brought across, and anchored in a suitable
place the Belfast Harbour Commissioners will
point out to us. And here I should like to
pay a tribute to them for their courtesy in
every possible way, and for helping forward
this movement in which I personally take so
great an interest. She is called H.M.S.
Caroline. I have seen photographs of her,
and I think she will be in every way fitted,
and will be appropriate to a great maritime
centre like ours. I should like also to say
that the Boy Scouts, the Boys' Brigade, and
the Church Lads' Brigade are most thankful
to the House for the small sum of money
which enabled them to start a permanent
camp on the far side of Stormont. It has
delighted me beyond measure to see these
boys coming out of the narrow crowded
streets of this great City to enjoy in this
open space the fine air and the amenities of
a part of Ulster which is unsurpassable in
beauty of outlook, and in my opinion health
of soil. They are one and all most grateful,
and have from time to time made that very
apparent to me.
In conclusion, we have had an opportunity,
not always at the invitation of the Government, but at all events we have had an
opportunity of welcoming to Northern Ireland several very distinguished strangers.
We have had Lord Derby; we have had Sir
Philip Lloyd-Greame and Sir Montague
Barlow amongst others, each of them deeply
interested, as it is essential they should be,
in everything affecting the welfare of the
country. These distinguished strangers have
come and gone, and I have no doubt whatever that the kindly way they were received
and certain recollections of their meetings
held in Ulster will do them good for the rest
of their lives. I can recall one, at all events,
who when he was in the historic town of
Enniskillen had laid before him in terms
which I think no one could misunderstand
exactly what they thought and what they
intend to do in that place. Well, they have
come and gone, and I am perfectly certain
they will benefit by these journeys across the
water, and I think we will benefit by a better
understanding between them and ourselves.
Then we hope in a very short time to have
that great master of Finance, Mr.
Reginald McKenna, in our midst. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear). Everyone must
know that he is Chairman of, I suppose, the
largest joint-stock undertaking
in the
world, and that one of our leading banks, the
Belfast Bank, is incorporated with the bank
with which he is associated, and carrying out
in a private manner, in my opinion, one of
those good works that I only wish
could be extended in other directions.
In other words, you have a vast corporation
there with shareholders throughout the
world as well as in Great Britain, all of
whom are particularly interested in the prosperity of Ulster. We will welcome Mr.
McKenna when he comes, and I am sure he
will benefit from what he will see when he
is here.
Now, I come to a very distinguished visitor,
Lord Carson-(hon. Members: Hear, hear)-
and although it is perhaps an inopportune
moment to say much about our distinguished
leader of olden days, I would like to say that
Houses of Parliament have from time to time
paid this courtesy, that they have adjourned
in honour of a distinguished visitor. Therefore, although it is a hard thing to ask, I was
going to suggest to hon. Members that as
they will have an opportunity of criticising
anything I have said to-day, or of raising
any new matter, on Thursday or on any other
day on which we meet, and perhaps looking
through what I have said may help them to
decide what questions they intend to lay
stress upon, whether under these particular
circumstances they would be content, as there
is a very important function to be carried
out very shortly, to await criticism of what
I have said till another date, and allow the
House to adjourn now. (Hon. Members:
Agreed.)
Mr. LYNN: I am not rising for the purpose
of continuing the debate, but just to say that
all sides of the House agree with the Prime
Minister in the tribute he has paid to our
old leader. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Question: "That this House do now
adjourn," put, and agreed to.
Adjourned accordingly at Four
o'clock till Thursday next,
pursuant to the Resolution of
the House of this day.

Oral Answers.
Oral Answers.
18 OCTOBER 1923.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Thursday, 18th October, 1923.
The House met at Three of the Clock, Mr.
DEPUTY-SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
FINANCE ACT.
1. Mr. LYNN asked the Minister of Finance
whether the Government propose to take any
steps to repeal such parts of Section 4 of the
Finance (1909-10) Act, 1910, as are not repealed by Section 57 of the Finance Act,
1920 ?
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): The answer to the question of my
hon. Friend is in the affirmative. The Government consider it desirable to follow the
lead of the Imperial Government in this connection, and I propose to embody in the forthcoming Finance Bill a clause similar to
Section 38 of the Imperial Finance Act of
this year.
REGISTRATION OF TITLES.
2. Mr. LYNN asked the Minister of Finance
whether complaints have reached him about
the unjustifiable delays that are taking place
in connection with the registration of titles;
whether he is aware that grave inconvenience is caused to farmers and others; and
whether the Government will take steps with
a view to removing this grievance?
Mr. POLLOCK: I propose to reply simultaneously to the questions which have been
put by the hon. Members for West Belfast
(Mr. Lynn) and Queen's University (Dr.
Morrison) regarding delays in connection
with the registration of titles.
Mr. DEPUTY-SPEAKER: May I point out
to the right hon. Gentleman that there is no
question on the Order Paper in the name of
the hon. Member for the University? I think
the right hon. Gentleman is possibly anticipating a question for another day.
Mr. POLLOCK: Then I propose to reply to
the question which has been put by the hon.
Member for West Belfast (Mr. Lynn), regarding delays in connection with registration of titles. As members are aware, the
service of the Land Registry is a service
reserved under the Government of Ireland
Act to the Imperial Government, and, therefore, for any delays that may have occurred
my Ministry is in no way responsible. As
pointed out by me, however, in the reply
which I gave to the similar question put by
the Member for County Antrim on the 20th
June of last year, the work of the Central
Office was considerably hampered for many
months by the failure to transfer from Dublin
those records which escaped destruction in
the Four Courts. Coupled with this cause
of delay, which has now been removed, I
understand that the staff of the office has
only within the last month or two been
brought up to strength owing to differences
of opinion between the Judiciary and the
Imperial Treasury as to the actual staff required for the work. I, therefore, hope that
the delays, which, I am aware, have arisen
in the past, will gradually disappear as the
heavy accumulation of arrears is worked off,
and I am taking steps to impress on the
Imperial Government the necessity of providing an efficient service in respect of this
work.
PUBLICANS' EXEMPTION ORDERS.
3. Mr. LYNN asked the Minister of Home
Affairs whether the Police have informed
certain publicans that they are not to act on
exemption orders issued by Magistrates sitting
in Petty Sessions Courts, and whether he can
state who is responsible for the action of the
Police in this matter?
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): By the direction of the
Ministry the Police warned publicans who
had been granted exemption orders that they
would render themselves liable to be prosecuted if they acted under them. The whole
question has since become sub judice, and
pending the decision of the Courts I am not
prepared to make any further statement.
Mr. LYNN: Arising out of that answer,
may I ask my right hon. Friend whether it
is usual for the Executive to instruct publicans or other people that they are not to
pay any attention to orders that have actually
been given by regular Courts?

Ways and Means.
Considered in Committee.
(Mr. ROBB in the Chair.)
Motion made and Question proposed:
1. That it is expedient to amend the law
relating to certain duties of Inland Revenue
(including Excise), to alter other Duties,
and to make further provision in connection with Finance.
or
2. That where property situate out of
Northern Ireland is bequeathed to
settled on different persons in succession and
legacy duty or succession duty is payable
thereon, such duty shall, for the purpose of
Sub-section 2 of Section 2 of the Finance
Act, 1894, be deemed to be payable in respect of the property on the death of each
of those persons in succession, notwithstanding that the whole amount of the
duty is paid on one death only, as in the
case of a legacy to one person.
Mr. POLLOCK: The Finance Bill, of
which the Resolution I now submit to the
Committee is the precursor, is concerned
mainly with the question of financial administration. The most important department of
the measure relates to a change in the arrangement of a certain part of Death Duties.
I need hardly remind the Committee that
Death Duties form the most important department of our local tax revenue, and
any change which takes place on the other
side in respect of these matters has to be
carefully considered by us. Controlling this
source of revenue as we do, it is not absolutely necessary that we should follow Westminster, but I would suggest to the Committee that there is no part of our system of
taxation in which it is more incumbent upon
us to conform to the Imperial conditions than
Death Duties because of the wide distribution of assets with which they are concerned.
Therefore the object of this particular part
of the Finance Bill is really to assimilate our
own conditions to those that emanate from
the Imperial Parliament, following the
change that was made in the present Session.
I need also hardly remind the Committee
of the exceedingly complex and involved
character of this subject. Indeed I do not
know any department of taxation that is
more intricate in its character, and if I
attempted to analyse the whole subject
here I doubt very much if the Committee would be able to follow all
its intricacies. Therefore, I propose to
treat the subject generally, and I will begin
by asking those who are sufficiently old to
remember the dramatic change that was
made in Death Duties by the Monumental
Finance Act of 1894, introduced by Sir
William Harcourt, which revolutionised the
conditions of finance. It was a very
dramatic change, and entailed considerable
disturbance in so far as it affected the distribution of very many large assets. From that
time, in 1894, that measure of Sir William
Harcourt's has apparently remained unchallenged and unchallengeable, but, curiously
enough, there was one clause, which I will
read to the Committee, which has recently
formed the subject of contention. The
course of this contention has had a marked
effect on the measure itself and renders it
necessary that I should appear here to-day,
to propose this resolution which will be embodied in the Finance Bill that will follow.
or
The Finance Act, 1894, charges Estate Duty
in respect of all the property, real
personal, which passes in the case of every
person dying after the commencement of that
Act, and Section 2 of the Act, which defines
what property is deemed to pass, includes
the following words, and these are the contentious words:-
"Property passing on the death of the
deceased when situate out of the United
1501 Ways and Means.

Labourers' Cottages.
Kingdom (we read 'Northern Ireland') shall
be included only if, under the law in force
before the passing of this Act, Legacy or
Succession Duty is payable in respect thereof, or would be so payable but for the relationship of the person to whom it passes."
As I said, this particular Clause remained
unchallenged until some enterprising person,
possibly a lawyer who had been employed in
some particular case, challenged the interpretation of this Act as it had been understood in the past. The result of this appeal
to the High Court was that the Court agreed
with the contention of the applicant. This
introduced an anomaly into the taxation of
assets situated out of the United Kingdom. In our case it would be outside
Northern Ireland. It was therefore necessary for the Imperial Parliament to remove that anomaly. Following on this, the
Imperial Finance Act of the present Session
provided that in such circumstances as I have
mentioned, i.e., where the Legacy or Succession Duty has been paid in one sum on the
passing of the property on the first death, such
Duty shall be "deemed to be payable" on any
subsequent passing of the property. In this
way, Estate Duty can be charged on each
occasion on which the property passes, and
there is consequently no distinction between
the case in which Legacy or Succession Duty
has been paid in one sum and the case in
which such Duty is paid on each passing of
the property.
I do not know whether that is very illuminating to the Committee, but at any rate it
indicates to hon. Members, I have no doubt,
the necessity of removing the anomaly and
conforming our own law to that which now
exists in the Imperial Parliament. There are
other matters that will appear in the Finance
Bill, and I am pleased to say that one particular change relates to the relief of taxation
rather than to any imposition of additional
taxation. Hon. Members may recall that in
my Budget statement I referred to the intention of the Government to grant relief from
Entertainments Duty in the case of Agricultural Shows at which a band was present for
the purpose of varying the character of the
entertainment. It is now necessary to give
Statutory effect to the undertaking given at
that time, and it will be included in the
Finance Bill.
There is another matter which is only of
passing interest. It is necessary to make
provision for the taxation of a new type of
mechanically propelled vehicle, namely, a sixwheeled motor tractor, and this will have to
be done in accordance with the duties chargeable under the Schedule to the Finance Act
of 1920. These matters, as well as others
affecting administration, will be dealt with in
the Finance Bill which will be submitted in
the course of next week. I beg to move.

Motion made, and Question proposed:
That for the purpose of any Act of the
present Session providing for the making
of Grants in aid of the repayment of

(a) of an annual sum equivalent to

which the said Councils are liable to
provide in respect of the repayment of
certain outstanding Loans which were
made in connection with the provisions
of Labourers' Cottages before the commencement of the Labourers (Ireland)
Act, 1906.
(b) of an annual sum equivalent to
thirty-six pounds per cent. of the total
amount of the Purchase Annuities payable by the said Councils in respect of
Advances made by the Irish Land Commission or by the Land Purchase Commission, Northern Ireland, in connection
with schemes approved by the provision
of Labourers' Cottages and Allotments
subsequent to the commencement of the
Labourers (Ireland) Act, 1906.
Mr. POLLOCK: The Resolution now before the Committee has regard to a necessary
arrangement in connection with the
Labourers' Cottages Bill which will be submitted to the House in the course of next
week. It concerns itself with public funds
in connection with the erection of labourers'
cottages under the Labourers Acts. Hon.
Members are quite familiar with the
cottages which are scattered over the
country, and which form a very agreeable
outlook on the landscape, and have partially
removed, and I hope will continue to remove,
the hovels which were such an ugly feature
of Irish life. In the past it has been the
practice of the Government for a very long
period to subsidise Rural Councils to enable
them by borrowing money from the Board
of Works to build the cottages of which I
have spoken for the country labourers. I
should explain at the beginning that there
is no new charge involved upon the Northern

Committee.

[Mr. Pollock]
Government by the Resolution which I am
now submitting, nor by the Bill which will
be introduced, and it is merely for
the purpose of simplifying our financial
system which, as hon. Members
are aware, I have had to do in
SO many cases. I propose now to
explain very shortly to the Committee the
mode by which the assistance was given in the
past and that which it is proposed to adopt
for the future. It was in the year 1883 that
the Imperial Authority first undertook the
duty of contributing to the erection of cottages
in Ireland, and from that period forward to
1919 various Acts of Parliament were passed
making provision at different times and from
different funds for the same purpose. Prior
to 1906 a specific method was adopted, and
portion of the Exchequer contribution was
provided under the Land Purchase (Ireland)
Act, 1891, and paid through the Local Taxation Account, and the contribution, or subsidy,
or subvention amounted to 17 per cent. of the
annuities for which the Rural District Councils
were liable. That applied up to the year
1906. Following 1906 the assistance was
similarly given by a Government contribution
towards these annuities payable in respect
of the moneys borrowed for the purposes of
the Acts. These moneys, which had been
previously advanced through the Irish Land
Commission under the Land Purchase Acts,
are now advanced through the intermediary of the Northern Land Commission. I am speaking now of the period after
1906.
I have mentioned that 17 per cent. of these
annuities was contributed by the Government
prior to the period. Following the period 36
per cent. of the annuities for which the Rural
District Councils were liable was contributed
by the Government in order to assist and develop the erection of labourers' cottages. As
I have incidentally mentioned, the funds which
were applied to this purpose were derived
from four different sources, and each source
was ear-marked for the particular purpose in
view. As this to a man of ordinary business
capacity would seem to be a very cumbersome
and difficult method of making a contribution
to a specific object, we decided that when the
transfer was made and the matter came under
our control through the machinery of our
Parliament here, all moneys should accrue to
the Exchequer, and that all payments going
out of the Exchequer should come before
this House, so that the matter is greatly
simplified, and hon. Members will have
an opportunity of knowing how the money is
disposed of. If hon. Members would refer to
the Estimate which was submitted in the
early part of the Session they will find that
a sum of £16,470 was voted for the purposes
that I have indicated. This sum of £16,000
odd was the exact amount of all the different
grants that were made through the different
avenues to which I have referred. It comes
into one sum and is voted to the one object,
and hon. Members have there, as I say, an
opportunity of learning what the expenditure
is and its nature. But it is considered neces
sary that there should be a statutory enactment that provision should be made of a
permanent character, so that these Rural
District Councils who have undertaken
liability to the Board of Works based upon
the subventions they were given by the Imperial Authority should be assured of the permanence of this contribution, and toward that
end, in addition to submitting to the Committee an estimate of the amount year by year,
which does not vary, it is proposed now by
means of a Bill, and, I hope, an Act, that
the amount will be assured in permanence to
the Rural District Councils who have taken
the liability on the Government's suggestion. That is the object of the money resolution which is the forerunner of the Bill
which will be introduced probably next week.
As regards future loans that will be made,
the Government is prepared, subject, of
course, to the approval of Parliament, to

Councils will exercise the utmost economy in

This is, generally, the object of the Resolution which I hope the Committee will pass,
and the small Bill which will be presented
next week will give the terms on which the

Mr. LYNN: I am sure the Finance Minister will have no trouble in having this

It is a pleasure to one to go round the country and to see how neatly and well these
cottages are being kept. It is a credit to the

There is only one point regarding which I

We hear a good deal of talk nowadays about

There is nothing raises a firmer or stronger

and I do not see but I for one would approach the subject in a sympathetic spirit.

If I may take this opportunity I would like
to state why, in my opinion, and in the
opinion of those who sent me here, I am
sitting on this bench. I would like to make
it quite clear now. Outside it is understood,
but I know I will be made mincemeat of as
soon as I sit down, and will be
pulled to pieces and all that, but I cannot
help it. I must say what is in my mind.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) It is understood and believed outside that the Government which are in power now have exceeded
the mandate with which they were sent here.
They have made various mistakes. I
suppose it is quite a human thing to
make mistakes-and it is a big thing to
acknowledge mistakes when they are made.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) One of the
particular items which has given cause for
much annoyance, and-shall I say?-grorsing,
is that the administration is practically all
carried out by other than local people when
local people were available. This is no news
to the Government, I am sure, but there is a
very strong feeling on the matter outside.
Then lately a lot of the supporters of the
Government, men who went to considerable
trouble for and were staunch supporters of the
Unionist cause for years-since they were able
to think at all-have been annoyed, and feel
insulted and slighted by the fact that the
first time the Government had it in their
power to advise as to awards and honours
these were not given to them, but were
awarded to, in their opinion, outsiders, men
who had not been in the battle from the
beginning.
Then the people are suffering from various
restrictions which you, who understand the
Ulster people as well as I do, and perhaps
better, know that few independent Ulstermen
can stomach with calmness. For instance, we
have the Curfew Order. Well, many people
do not want to stay out after twelve o'clock,
but many of them have had experiences similar
to that which happened in my case. I, being a
very law-abiding citizen, had to run from the
top of the Crumlin Road, when I was too late
to catch the last car one night, up to this
district. I did it in twenty minutes, and I
am only getting better of it now.
If I were
a few years older I would not like it at all.
I think I would rather be arrested. The
Curfew restriction is irritating to a degree.
Then came the Licensing Act closing the
public-houses on Sundays. Now bona-fide
travellers, friends of the Government, who
go out on Sunday in motor cars, having been
short-sighted, like the foolish virgins, find
themselves in a part of the country where
they cannot get refreshment. Other people,
such as strangers coming from the country,
find it particularly dry and annoying, as do
people coming off the boats. I am not now
speaking about the Licensing Act in particular. When they come off the boat on
Sunday morning they cannot get a drink
unless by squaring someone. We do not want
the kind of law that makes a men a criminal
against his wish.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Then there is another thing that is very
irritating indeed to supporters of the Government and other people who have been always
loyal, always staunch and true to the flag
under which they live. That is Members of
this House going out into public and accusing
people who have criticised the Government
of being disloyal or Bolshevists. That, to my
mind, is an extraordinarily foolish thing to
do, because these men resent it. They are
not disloyal. They are perfectly loyal men,
and deserve every consideration from the
Government now, as they did from the same
men before they came here. It is deeply resented. One friend of mine put his case in
the form of a story. I do not know whether
it is true or not, but it sounds quite possible.
It is about an Orange Lodge which was
marching over the Crumlin hills when they
met the only Catholic in the district with a
donkey and cart. The man who was carrying
the flag at the head of the Lodge flapped it in
the donkey's face, and the donkey at once
kicked the whole cart into the ditch. One of
the members of the Lodge helped the old man
to get his donkey and cart on the road again,
and he said, Your donkey is an awful Sinn
Feiner. He is afraid of the flag," and the
old man said, "The flag is all right. It is the
beggar who is carrying it." That is how he
illustrated the thing. There is no disloyalty
to the flag, but to those who wave it.

Lord Carson, whom we all reverence, when
he was over here, said "Trust Sir James."
Well, we have trusted Sir James, and I hope
some time we will trust him again. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear). But another aspect
of the affair is why should that question have
to be asked? Is it because Sir James has not
trusted us inasmuch as the administration
has been taken out of the hands of the people
here? Is it because he cannot trust the
people here to have a drink on Sundays and
remain sober? There are various other
ways in which the men who live here are
at a disadvantage. I ask the Prime Minister
to consider that point of view, and I ask the
Government before it is too late to consider
the men outside, to see what can be done on
their behalf, and to think less of what can
be done on their own.

political principles of men who will only
With regard to Curfew, I am glad my hon.
and gallant Friend is a sprinter and was

make inquiries all over the North of Ireland,
as the Prime Minister is bound to do, and

of the maintenance of Curfew. (Hon. Mem.
bers: Hear, hear). We are very apt to for.
get the things that are behind; we forget the

that there is Curfew. I think if you took a

of maintaining the Curfew. Is there any
really great grievance at the present time?
As far as I know the police act with a good

I agree with my hon. and gallant Friend

Colonel Wedgwood is one of the most
bitter enemies of the Ulster people. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) Had Colonel Wedgwood's will prevailed we would have been in
the Free State now. Above all things the
Ulster people like people who are straight and

misleading statements made by that gentleman
to the public of Belfast. I went into his record in the Imperial Parliament, and I found

comes to the City of Belfast to try to stir up

claim the right to criticise our Government.
but when a Member of the Imperial Parlia
ment comes over here and tells deliberate
falsehoods against orr people it is time we
took steps to prevent any misunderstanding
creeping into the public mind. I want it to
be clearly understood that Colonel Wedgwood
is the bitterest enemy the Ulster people have,
and I hope those people who supported him
at that meeting succeeded in converting him,
and that when the Land Purchase Bill comes
before the Imperial Parliament he will not
take up the attitude he did on former occa
sions.
What did he say when you, Mr. Deputy-
Speaker, interrogated him on the Land Purchase question in the Imperial House? He

for building cottages for ex-Servicemen, and

intend to say more on this matter at a very

in regard. to the work that came

of-we are keeping in employment more

The PRIME MINISTER: I certainly cannot complain of the tone of the criticisms of
the statement I made on the re-assembling of

it on the day on which the statement was
made. I said:
Our Trade Facilities Act has gone a long
way also to help in certain directions, and
my right hon. Friend the Minister of
Finance (Mr. Pollock) and the whole of his
colleagues are always prepared to take into
consideration further extensions of those
facilities where anything possible can be
done to help to revive trade.
That covers the linen industry it covers all
industry inside Northern Ireland.
The second point of substance that he
raised was with regard to the question of the
remission of rates during a certain period
for the building of houses. These are the
words that I used:
There will be a Housing Bill, in which it
is proposed to give effect to the promise
made by the Minister of Home Affairs for
the payment of a lump sum subsidy of £60
for each small house built between October,
1922, the date on which the loan subsidy
ended, and 1st April, 1925. The Bill also
makes provisionthis is the pointfor empowering the local authorities to refund rates in respect of such houses up to
such proportion and for such period as may
be fixed by them generally for their districts.
That gives exactly the power that my hon.
and gallant Friend was asking for. It is permissory, and will allow local authorities to
adopt this system, or to leave it alone, or to
adopt it partially. It does not necessarily
mean carrying it out in full. Therefore, with
regard to the two points of substance that my

23 OCTOBER 1923.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Tuesday, 23rd October, 1923.
The House met at Three of the Clock, Mr.
SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
NATIONAL MILK CONFERENCE.
1. Dr. MORRISON asked the Minister of
Home Affairs if any medical man has been
deputed on behalf of the Government of Northern Ireland to attend the National Milk
Conference to be held in London on November
1st, and if he is aware that the whole question of the relation of milk to disease will be
discussed at this Conference by the most
eminent health officers of the Empire?
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): No arrangements have been
made for deputing a representative of this
Ministry to attend the Conference in question.
The Ministry have had before them full
particulars as to the scope and extent of the
Conference, and it appears that it covers the
milk question only to a limited extent. All
necessary information can be as easily ascertained from the reports of the proceedings of
the Conference, which will be duly obtained,
and unnecessary expense thus avoided.
Dr. MORRISON: Arising out of that
answer, I would like to ask the Minister if
the Corporation have decided to send a representative, and I would like further to ask him
if he has consulted his Advisory Medical Committee, or if he decides these things on his
own initiative, and without applying, as I
suggest, to the proper quarter?
Sir DAWSON BATES: In regard to the
first part of my hon. Friend's supplementary
question, I would like to have notice of the
query as to whether or not the Corporation
are sending a representative to the Conference. With regard to the other part, I
certainly do not claim to have any such experience as medical men have of matters of
this sort, and of course I consulted our own
medical inspectors.
REGISTRATION OF TITLES.
2. Dr. MORRISON asked the Minister of
Finance whether he is aware that delays in
the Registration of Titles in many cases extend over 12 months, and that this unreasonable and unaccountable delay which is causing serious injury to farmers and business
people and solicitors all over the Six Counties
has been the subject of protests by Chambers
of Commerce and other business organisations, and whether the Minister can give an
explanation and offer a remedy?
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): The information in possession of
the Ministry of Finance does not support
the contention that delays in Registration
of Titles have been so prolonged as stated by
the hon. Member.
For the causes of the delay and the
prospect of amelioration, I beg to refer the
hon. Member to the very full answer which
was given by me to the hon. Member for
West Belfast (Mr. Lynn) on the 18th inst.
Dr.
MORRISON: Arising out of that
answer I would like to ask if since June the
Minister has not had time to deal with the
complaint which is causing so much inconvenience. He gave an answer on this
question in June last, and it is a considerable time since then.
Mr. POLLOCK: I think I conveyed, in supplementing my answer on the previous day,
that the Service in question is an Imperial
matter over which we have no direct control.
But since June, the date to which the hon.
Member refers, my Department has been taking steps with a view to ameliorating the
delay which undoubtedly did exist, and which
we admit did exist. Quite recently we have
been able to reach an arrangement whereby
we hope that the cause of complaint will disappear. It cannot be expected, in view of the
great accumulation of work that naturally
exists, that a complete transformation can be
made at once, but I think the causes of the
trouble are removed.

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Electricity and Gas (Expenses) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made and Question proposed, “That
this Bill be now read the Second time."
Mr. ARCHDALE: The Electricity and Gas
Expenses Bill has been put forward by the
Ministry of Commerce in conjunction with
the Ministry of Finance for the purpose of
merging certain Funds known as 'The
Electricity Fund" and "The Gas Fund" in
the general accounts of the Ministry of
Commerce, and incidentally for adjusting
the basis of contribution to the Electricity
Fund from units generated to units sold.
I may explain at once that the Bill does
not propose to add to nor diminish the existing liability of the Municipalities and
Companies who supply electricity and gas
to the public. It is primarily a measure
for simplifying accounts.
The Electricity (Supply) Act, 1919, placed
upon authorised undertakers, that is to say,
undertakers having statutory powers to
supply electricity, the cost of the administration by the Electricity Commissioners of
electricity supply and the Electricity Fund
was set up to receive moneys payable to the
Commissioners in respect of fees for special
orders, and also the proceeds of the levy
made upon authorised undertakers to make
up the balance of the expenditure of the
Commissioners.
In Great Britain the Electricity Commissioners are a semi-independent body
employing a large staff. In Northern Ireland they are officials of the Ministry of
Commerce, who have many other duties to
perform, and no useful purpose will be
served by keeping a separate establishment
for the Commissioners and their staff.
Accordingly for as long as these conditions
apply in Northern Ireland, it is expedient
to merge the income and the expenditure of
the Fund in the general accounts of the
Ministry of Commerce.
At the present time there are only four
electricity undertakings liable to contribute,
viz., Belfast, Londonderry, Portrush and
Dunmurry, and the contribution will by the
terms of the Bill be based upon units of
electricity sold instead of units of electricity
generated.
With regard to the Gas Fund, the Gas Regulation Act, 1920, places upon statutory gas
undertakings the cost of the salaries, remuneration, pensions and gratuities of the
chief gas examiner and the gas referees and
their staff, together with any expenses of the
Ministry of Commerce attributable to the
execution of its powers and duties under the
Gas Regulation Act, 1920. That Act deals
mainly with the change over in the basis of
charge from measurement by the 1,000 cubic
feet of gas of a prescribed illuminating power
to the charge by reference to the calorific
value of the gas, otherwise known as the
charge per therm. The income of the Fund
arises from a levy upon all undertakers who
have adopted the thermal basis of charge. The
contributors to the Fund in Northern Ireland
are Londonderry, Omagh and Strabane, and
the annual contribution is limited to 3s per
million cubic feet of gas sold.
No useful purpose will be served by keeping
up a separate Fund, and the Bill accordingly
provides that the Gas Fund shall be merged
in the general accounts of the Ministry of
Commerce; and that the contributions from
the respective undertakers which would normally be paid into the Fund shall be brought
to account as Appropriations in Aid of
moneys provided by Parliament to defray the
expenses of the Ministry of Commerce.
Mr. LYNN: I would like to ask the right
hon. Gentleman two questions. The first
one is, what amount will be levied on these
bodies, and secondly, what services will the
Government give for the amount of money
that they receive?
Mr. ARCHDALE: There will be no change
in the amount paid by the bodies at the
present time. Heretofore they have had to
pay to Electricity and Gas Commissioners,
who are a separate body in Great Britain.
In Northern Ireland the Electricity and Gas
Commissioners are officials of the Ministry
of Commerce, and they have a great many
other duties to perform, so they do not want
a separate staff for this purpose. The best
way of dealing with these amounts is to
merge them in the Ministry of Commerce
accounts. This is proposed to be done with
the approval of the Ministry of Finance,
and the Appropriations in Aid will be dealt
with by Parliament.
Question put, and agreed to.
Bill committed to a Committee of the
Whole House for to-morrow.

The ATTORNEY GENERAL (Mr. Best):
This Bill is introduced for the purpose of
continuing certain temporary enactments
whether of the Parliament of the United Kingdom or of this Parliament, and annual Acts
which for certain reasons are only continued
from year to year. The date to which it is
proposed we should continue is the 31st December, 1924, but hon. Members if they will
look at the Bili will see that that is the date
"unless Parliament otherwise determines."
The reason why that provision is put in is to
meet Acts such as the Rent Restrictions Act
and the Workmen's Compensation Act, in reference to which legislation will probably be
introduced at an early date. I think I am
right in stating that the Prime Minister some
few days ago said that the Rent Restrictions
Act would probably be dealt with as one of
the earliest measures of next Session. It is
impossible to deal with it in this Session, because the report of Mr. Senator Greer has
just been received, and there has not been
time to base a Bill on it, but for the purpose
of preserving the rights of tenants and others
we are continuing for the moment the present
Rent Restrictions Act. However, that can
be made right in the early part of ext
Session. This Bill has been framed so as to
fit in with the Expiring Laws Continuance
Bill of the Parliament of the United Kingdom.
A provision of that Bill which has already
become an Act, is as follows: It applies to
Northern Ireland so far as it deals with any
enactment relating to subjects with respect
to which the Parliament of Northern Ireland
has not power to make laws. Of course, there
are many subiects on which this Parliament
cannot make laws, and if we cannot make
laws we cannot continue laws. As regards
that class of Acts which have been continued
by the Expiring Laws Continuance Act passed
by the United Kingdom, the present Bill
supplements this provision by applying it to
those Acts dealing with subjects in reference
to which we have powers of legislation. I beg
to move.
Mrs. CHICHESTER: When I first read
over this Bill I thought that it merely fulfilled a certain legal formality, as the right
hon. the Attorney-General has just said, and
that the Acts mentioned in it were perhaps
-certainly some of them-without very vital
interest to the community, but when I looked
through it more carefully I saw that I was
wrong. There are many Acts which it is
proposed to continue under this Bill that do
greatly concern us. There is particularly
one in which I am interested, because I think
that it vitally affects an industry in which
we are all interested. It is one which the
Prime Minister has referred to as the principal industry in the Six Counties-agriculture. I am now referring to the Summer
Time Act which it is proposed to continue
under this Bill. Those of us who represent
agricultural constituencies cannot let this
pass without a protest or without question.
I do not see very many of my colleagues from
the country here to-day, and I feel, perhaps,
I am rather treading on to a hornet's nest
when I bring this matter up, but the alteration of time, although perhaps to some may
seem very essential and to some may seem
very pleasant, is to the farmer both unpleasant and detrimental. There have been
many protests raised by the farmers in the
past, and the continuance of this Act under
this Bill will, I feel sure, be looked upon
with great alarm and great dismay. There
are many reasons which I could give against
the continuation of the Summer Time Act,
but I am not, perhaps, best fitted to put
those reasons in the most eloquent form
before this House, and I hope that the hon.
Member for Antrim (Mr. Crawford) may be
able to help me in this respect, as I am
sure he feels as I feel about it.
It is natural for the Irish farmers to suffer
urder a much greater disability than the
English farmers in this respect, because
they have a half-hour added on to the
time, so that they have a difference of
an hour and a half in the summer time.
am quite sure those who represent the cities

sure that everybody in the cities is in absolute agreement with the Summer Time Act,
and quite apart from any agricultural ques
tion I do not know that it is such a very good

In America, when I was there a year ago,
I know the big cities adopted summer time.
The railways of the country kept to the old

but it had also its advantages. It was clearly

I have listened to debates on this subject of

Lynn) for many years in the British House

the effects of bringing in summer time. Of

-comprise far more than half the population of the Six Counties, and, therefore, on balance it is really more important
to cater for their convenience and
health and prosperity than the other.
But far and beyond that where I join issue

is that the great cities like Belfast and other

Help all your cities and all your towns, and
if you do that you help yourselves.
There are many arguments on this subject.

parts of Great Britain, and we may not be
put to inconvenience consequent upon having
different times. There is only one point in it
in my opinion, and that is that by nature
we are twenty-five minutes or half-an-hour

HARBOUR AND COMMERCIAL
