Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That a supplementary sum not exceeding £12,000 be granted to His Majesty for
the service of the year ending 31st March,
1924, to provide for Harbour and Commercial Services, including certain fees
payable under the Companies (Re-constitution of Records) Act (Northern Ireland)
1923 and certain Grants in aid."
Mr. ARCHDALE: In introducing this
Supplementary Estimate for Harbour and
Commercial Services administered by the
Ministry of Commerce, I think it advisable,
in the first instance, to remind the Committee that the entire Estimate is in respect
of new Services which are not included in the
ordinary Estimate of the Ministry for the
current financial year. As hon. Members will
observe, the first sub-head in the Supplementary Estimate is in respect of the Reconstitution of Companies Records. The expenditure for which provision is now being
made is consequent upon the placing on the
Statute Book of the Companies (Reconstitution of Records) Act (Northern Ireland)
1923. Hon. Members will recollect that the
object of this Act is to provide for the reconstruction of the files of the Joint Stock
Companies in Northern Ireland, the records
of which were destroyed in the Dublin
Custom House fire in 1921. In order to
effect this necessary reconstitution of files, it
is laid down in the Act that the Registrar of
Joint Stock Companies in Northern Ireland
shall be furnished by the various companies
with certain particulars relative to their
constitution, capital and other matters, and
Section 6 of the Act authorises the payment
of fees to solicitors or professional accountants for professional services in prepar-
Supply-
23 ОСТОВЕЕ 1923.
Committee.
ing those particulars from the records in
possession of the companies. Under the
regulations made pursuant to that section
the fee payable for such services has been
fixed at one guinea, and approximately 1,300
companies are affected by the Act. The reconstruction of these files is now proceeding,
and it is. estimated that about 900 companies
will be dealt with before the close of the
current financial year. In some cases payment has also to be made for the cost of
providing copies of documents. This being
so, it is therefore necessary to present this
Supplementary Estimate for the sum of £1,000
for this service.
The second item in the Estimate (£11,000)
relates to expenses in connection with the
Ulster Pavilion at the British Empire Exhibition which is to be held in London from
April to October next year. I do not think
that it is necessary for ine to the more
than a passing reference to the importance
and magnitude of the British Empire Exhibition. As hon. Members are aware, it
will be the largest and most comprehensive
Exhibition of its kind in history. It is
going to be, I believe, the wonder of the
world. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear). I have
only to add that a total sum of about ten
million pounds is being spent on the erection
and equipment of the Exhibition, and that it
is anticipated that some twenty-five to thirty
million people will visit it. I am confident
that the Committee will realise that the holding of this Exhibition will constitute an outstanding event with which it is vital that
Ulster should be associated. The Government of Northern Ireland realising this
necessity has decided to erect an Ulster
Pavilion in which the natural resources and
industrial activities of Northern Ireland as
part of the United Kingdom will be represented side by side with those from all other
parts of our Empire. The expenditure from
Government Funds for the purpose referred
to will not exceed £12,000, of which it is
anticipated that £11,000 will be required in
the current financial year, and the remaining £1,000 next year. A site has been
secured in the Palace of Industry for the
Ulster Pavilion at a rental of £5,000. This
site, standing as it does at the junction of
two main avenues, may be considered as one
of the key sites of the whole of the Exhibition, and it is certain that no better position
could have been chosen for the Ulster exhibit.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.).
It is estimated that the erection and the
decoration of the Pavilion, which will be of
very handsome and arresting design, will
cost £1,500. The greater proportion of the
actual exhibits will be supplied by the various
trades, and good progress is being made towards the organisation of these exhibits. I
may say in this connection that a high
tribute has been paid by the Exhibition
authorities to the energy with which the
Government of Northern Ireland have
entered into this project, and of the advanced
stage to which they have brought their plans.
Hon. Members will realise that an undertaking of this nature involves a large amount
of responsible work and will in the future
involve several protracted stays in London,
which could not normally be undertaken by
the existing officials of the Ministry in addition to their ordinary work. To meet this
difficulty and to secure the successful handling of a matter upon which so much depends,
a manager has been appointed from June
last for a period of eighteen months at an
inclusive salary of £300 per annum. This
officer is responsible to the Ministry for the
general organisation of the Ulster exhibit, for
negotiations with the Exhibition authorities
in London, with the architect and the contractors, and he will also act as the intermediary between exhibitors and the Exhibition authorities. His work is carried on
under the supervision of the higher officers
of the Ministry, who have also the valuable
assistance of a representative Committee of
business men drawn from all quarters of the
industrial community and of the Six
Counties. This charge includes such items as
insurance, the cost, transit and care of official
exhibits; preliminary expenses in connection
with lighting, water and heating, and the
furnishing of the official office. There remains
a balance of £1,700 for Unforeseen Contingencies.". Hon. Members will readily appreciate that, in connection with an enterprise such as the one which we have undertaken, many small incidents of expenditure
are likely to arise which cannot be estimated
with any precision at the present time. Details of decoration, interior fittings and furnishings, which cannot be determined until
the Pavilion is in being; expenses in connection with stationery, printing, and the proper
advertisement of the Ulster Pavilion just
before the commencement of the Exhibition,
are such items as I have in mind. Moreover,
at this early stage, it is not possible to estimate exactly the cost of official exhibits, which
will include a large model in the shape of a
diagrammatic map of Northern Ireland in
relief, showing the location of its various
industries and its attractions for tourists.
There will also be a demonstration of the
agricultural resources of the Province.
Whereas the Government have entered into
this project with enthusiasm, believing that
it will be of the greatest benefit to Ulster, it
was manifestly their duty to set a limit, at
an early stage, to the expenditure which they
could authorise

I may say that I saw the Exhibition-the

I beg to move.
Mr. LYNN: I am in favour of exhibitions

CLASS IV. No. 2.
EDUCATIONAL SERVICES.
Considered in Committee.
(Mr. MOLES in the Chair.)
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That a supplementary sum not exceeding £30,000 be granted to His Majesty for
the service of the year ending 31st March,
1924, to provide for educational services,
including certain Grants in aid of the
Teachers' Pension Fund, Northern Ireland."
Mr. POLLOCK: In the absence of my hon.
Friend, the Parliamentary Secretary to the
Ministry of Education (Mr. McKeown), the
responsibility of presenting this educational
vote lies upon me. It is a very important
vcte because it raises the whole question of
the status of secondary teachers in Northern
Ireland, and, therefore, it is one to which
I have given a great deal of attention, because, I must admit, the responsibility to
a large extent for the figures lay upon me.
Hon. Members will recall that earlier in the
Session educational estimates for various
sums were voted by the Committee to provide for the wants of secondary education
generally, that is, so far as they could be
ascertained at the time. The present
additional estimate is intended to make the
necessary provision for payments to
secondary, intermediate, and preparatory
teachers to the end of the current financial
year. This liability is a consequence of the
Education Act which has just been passed
this Session.
I think it will be convenient if at this stage
I submit for the consideration of the Committee figures to show how this estimate of
£30,000 which I am presenting is made up.
The estimated amount of full salary, as per
scale, for this year, 1922-1923, for all eligible
teachers, of whom there are about 320. in
secondary schools, amounts to £90,000. However, there is a deduction from that amount
because of the non-incremental or basic
portion of the salaries which is provided by
the School Committees themselves. That
amounts to £62,000. Deduct that from
£90,000, and we reach a total incremental
grant of £28,000. But a further deduction
must be made on this estimate because of
money that has already been paid this year
to the teachers, and this amounts to £18,000.
Therefore the net sum payable is £10,000.
But there are some principal teachers in-
Icluded in the list who get special allowances,
and these amount to about £6,000. We therefore reach a total payable in respect of the
year 1922-23 of £16,000. There is a further
item of £14,000 in aid of teachers' salaries,
allowances, etc., to carry up to the 31st July,
1924. The full estimate is £40,000, but the
whole of it will not come into the present
year, as I am only making provision up to
the end of our financial year, and the proportion of that estimate will not amount to
more than £14,000, which, added to the
£16,000, makes a sum of £30,000, which
It
present to the Committee to-day.
Before entering upon a detailed explanation
of the Vote. I feel that it is necessary to offer
the Committee a short outline of the history
of Intermediate Education in Ireland.
was only when the last century was drawing
to a close that the British Government recognised any responsibility whatever for
Intermediate Education. Indeed, the
British Government recognised no Tesponsibility for secondary education
England prior to the year 1900. This class
of instruction was regarded as luxury education. The State undertook to provide
through the national schools sufficient inin
Committee-

Supply-
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Mr. Pollock]
struction for the average boy or girl to face
the ordinary battle of life, and therefore,
inferentially declared that if parents
desired their children to be educated for the
higher or professional standards, they were
entitled to pay for such education out of
their own resources. Indeed a good many
people to-day make the same assertion. I
do not mean to say that I necessarily agree
with them, but I hear it from time to time.
But the strength of public opinion forced
the Government to resile from this attitude,
and somewhat grudgingly, small grants were
made from time to time towards Intermediate education, although the basic
salaries of teachers during all this period
remained practically unchanged.
This condition of things continued unremedied so long as the Imperial Government exercised authority over local affairs
in Ireland. Even so late as 1919, a year
after the close of the war, the Intermediate
Board in their report made this statement:-
"Out of a total of 1,349 lay teachers in
Ireland only 100 are in receipt of £200 per
annum, and of these 31 are heads of
schools, while 30 per cent. of the whole
number of lay teachers are in receipt of
less than £100 per annum!"
It must be remembered that that condition
of things obtained until 1919, when the
Imperial Government, through their grants
to secondary education, however meagre
these grants were, committed themselves to
the principle of State recognition and aid
for secondary education. I regard it as little
short of a crime that such a state of affairs
as I have indicated should be permitted to
exist. But I have little doubt that had the
recent Constitutional changes not been
effected, secondary school teachers would
find themselves to-day in the same parlous
plight as they were in the year 1919. Let us
mark the transformation that immediately
ensued in their pecuniary circumstances.
From the first of February of last year, the
date on which our Government became responsible for education, they doubled the
interim grant then in existence. That was
the first acknowledgment of the position of
secondary teachers that was made by this
Government. It was only given, of course,
as a temporary palliative, and it was only
intended to be so pending the introduction of a general measure of education which
has been passed, as hon. Members are aware,
during the present Session.
If hon. Members will analyse the financial
arrangements which are the outcome of that
measure, they will find that those who have
received the greatest pecuniary benefits are
the secondary school teachers. I make this
comment because a good deal of animadversion has been made in the newspapers and
otherwise upon the action of the Government in respect of the scales of salaries of
secondary teachers. Under the Imperial
regime the primary school teachers had
been fully and generously provided for, but
as I have said, it remained for this Government to recognise the claims of secondary
education. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
In the past the basis of attack on the
Imperial Government was the charge that
the average salary of a secondary school
teacher in Ireland four years ago was £85,
surely a very miserable pittance.
Let us
see what the present Ulster Government proposes to do for them.
A young male teacher beginning his
career starts with a minimum basic salary
of £210, i.e., about 2 times the average
salary of many teachers of long service only
four years ago. For the first five years he
receives an increase of £12 yearly, and after
five years' service, he increases by £15 yearly
until he reaches £450. If he is a
University graduate with first
or second
class honours he has £50 added to that, and
therefore rises to £500 a year. That is the
position of male teachers. Women teachers,
similarly, begin at £200, reach £325 at
twelve years. and if University graduates,
they have £50 added, making an ultimate
total of £375. In the case of teachers in a
preparatory school or the preparatory department of a secondary school where
younger children are taught-who had not
been recognised in any way until the advent
of the Northern Government-young male
teachers start at £160 and rise to £100, while
female teachers begin at £150 and advance
to £300.
As I said, in the past no Government
grant of any kind was given to preparatory
schools, or the preparatory department of a
secondary school, so that in this department
of educational work the teachers have
leaped from penury to comparative comfort.
It must be clearly understood-and I hope
the Committee will realise it-that these are
minimum figures of salary. It is optional
with the authorities of any secondary school
out of their own resources to supplement the
basic salaries, if either on grounds of effeency or for any other reasonable cause, they
think fit to do so. If teachers reach the
position of principal, their emoluments increase by a maximum of £200 according to
the size of the school.
I have given this short outline of the
financial provision which the Government
proposes to make for secondary school
teachers.
There is an infinite variety of
detail in the regulations which I believe
have been circulated to the members
of the Committee, but I do not think
the Committee will expect me to enter
Committee-

Supply-
23 OCTOBER 1923.
into all the details which these regulations
contain. However, if hon. Members will
give close consideration to the figures I have
submitted, I can hardly believe that they
can form any other judgment than that the
Government has given very fair, and even
generous, terms to a body which has in the
past, in my opinion, been little cared for.
I have dealt with scales of salaries, but
there is another department which affects the
financial standing of teachers that I will speak
of for a few minutes, and that is the question of increments. The question is, are all
present-day teachers to have their salarics of
to-day based on the period in which they
have been engaged in the teaching profession? We cannot admit this contention. The
teachers entered the service with full knowledge of the conditions that were imposed,
and that they had no right to expect as
time went on that improvements in salary
or the institution of a pension scheme would
have any retrospective effect. Secondary
education was in effect, until recent times,
in very much the same category as any other
private business.
But although the Northern Government
has had no responsibility for the conditions,
it is admitted by us all that secondary
teachers have not been sufficiently paid in
the past. The national school teachers'
scales were made fully retrospective, but then
we must have regard to the different position of elementary teachers as compared with
secondary teachers. National school teachers
were State servants from the time they
entered the service, and have been contributing to the pension scheme for more than 40
years, and the improvement in their salaries
which was granted, as hon. Members may recall, a few years ago, was accompanied by
three years' "carry over."
The primary object of a salary scale is to
attract properly qualified teachers in future.
It is impossible for us in Northern Ireland,
with our limited resources, to go back to the
beginning of every teacher's career, and redress grievances-real or imaginary-from
which he thinks he has suffered, but for
which we had no responsibility whatever.
The Government, however, has no desire-I
state this deliberately-to stand on any
technical rights it may be supposed to
possess, and accordingly we have agreed to
give the teachers one increment of salary for
every two years' service, whether that service
may have been rendered in
Ireland, or outside of Ireland, if in
the opinion of the Ministry the nature
of the service warrants the increase.
Perhaps I may give the Committee an
example of how this would work out, as I
think it would be more illuminating
than merely quoting from the regulations.
Α teacher of twenty years' service, if
on our scale, would have begun at £210.
As I have already stated, he would
have five years increment added at £12,
which is £60. He has another five years' increment at £15, which is £75, a total of
£345. That is to say, a teacher at approximately 40 years of age would start with us
at £315. In seven years he would receive
£450, and if he happened to possess a University degree, would soon reach £500. This
salary is apart from any supplementary
grant from the governing body where he is
employed.
In view of the peculiar and exceptional
conditions under which this service Was
taken over, I cannot think that the provision made by the Government is ungenerous, while, by relation to our capacity, it is
liberal compared with the conditions of
secondary education in Britain. I need not
enter into the details of the conditions in
Great Britain, whether in England
or in
Scotland. If any discussion arises, and hon.
Members have any curiosity on the subject,
the information can be easily given or the
comparisions made, but I think I would be
only occupying the time of the Committee
unnecessarily in making these comparisons. I
make the statement deliberately that, in comparison with England and Scotland, our Government proposes to treat the secondary
teachers liberally and generously.
To provide the increments on the approved basis that I have discussed will rerequire a sum of £28,000 for the first year,
next year this will rise to £15,000, and a
gradual rise beyond this figure is inevitable
for some years to come. If the contention
that all past service is to count were conceded, a further sum of £20,000 would be
involved in the current year and a corresponding sum though in decreasing amount
in subsequent years. It is obvious that it
is necessary to cry a halt at some point and
I feel that the halt has been called at a
point beyond which it would not be
reasonable to expect the Government to go.
I sometimes ask myself where is all this
money for education to come from? The
question is not easy to answer at present,

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Wednesday, 24th October, 1923.
The House met at Three of the Clock, Mr.
SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
INTOXICATING LIQUOR ACT.
Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Finance what arrangements have been made
or are being made, to arrive at the amounts
of compensation claimed under the Intoxicating Liquor Act.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr. Pollock): I presume the hon. Member is familiar
with the provisions of the First Schedule to
the Intoxicating Liquor Act, which lays down
the basis upon which the settlement of claims
arising under that Act is to be arrived at.
The actual adjudication upon such claims is
a matter falling within the jurisdiction of
the Claims Tribunal, which body will
hold its first meeting on the 26th instant.
Colonel WOODS: Arising out of that
answer, I would like to ask the Minister of
Finance if he has considered the possibility
of local chartered accountants taking this
matter in hand at a cost possibly one-third
less than the expense involved in setting up
a new department to arrive at the proper
compensation to be paid in each case?
of my
Mr. POLLOCK: It is not contemplated to
set up an additional department for the
purpose of assessing the claims, except
so far as concerns the establishment of the
Claims Tribunal, which is composed of
Judge Thompson, Recorder of Belfast; W. D.
Scott, Esq., nominated by myself, a member
own department; A. Miscampbell,
Esq., J.P., Chairman of Antrim County
Council; and James Roche, Esq., Resident
Magistrate, both nominated by the Minister
of Home Affairs; and Thomas Brown, Esq.,
J.P.. chosen by the Justices of Belfast. In
reply to the latter part of the question, or
the comment of my hon. Friend, the arrangement in regard to the assessing of the
claims has not yet been determined, but I
have it in view to establish a panel of
accountants in Belfast, from which it will
be possible to select from time to time
certain names for the work in regard to the
value of establishments that will be
condemned.

ADMINISTRATION OF PUBLIC HEALTH.
Mr. JOHNSTON asked the Minister of
Home Affairs when he intends to appoint a
Committee of Inquiry into the administration of Public Health and of Medical
Benefit under the Poor Law, and what will
be the scope of the Inquiry?
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I am considering the
suggestion of the hon. Member in connection
with the contemplated Commission of
Inquiry, but I am not yet in a position to
announce the terms of reference.
Mr. JOHNSTONE: Arising out of that
answer, may I ask what date, approximately,
the House may expect the Committee to be
appointed?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am afraid I
cannot make a definite announcement in
regard to that. That particular Department
of the Ministry of Home Affairs has a great
deal of work in connection with two pending
Bills and the Rent Restrictions Bill, but I
hope to be able to make an announcement
certainly before the close of the year.

Mr. SPEAKER: I understand the hon.
Member refers to the Notice of Motion which
he put down dealing with certain features of
the Education Act. I have gone into the
matter and I have come to the conclusion
that that resolution is not in order because
it contravenes one of the oldest and most
strictly observed rules of Parliament. That
is that you cannot in the same Session ask
the House to reverse a decision which it has
already come to. Of course the Education
Act was passed in this Session and the
adjournment which has taken place since
the summer does not mean another Session.
It is merely a prolongation of the same
Session. The hon. Member's resolution seeks
to impugn the Education Act in so far as
it relates to the transfer of schools, the appointment of teachers, and to the financial
provisions of the Act.
Practically it impugnes the main features
of the Act, and that being so it is not per-

Bar Library.
Motion made and Question proposed:
"That in the opinion of this House a
Grant be made from public funds to the
Bar Council of Northern Ireland for the
purpose of providing an initial stock of
legal books, reports, etc., for the Library
of the Bar of Northern Ireland.
The PARLIAMENTARY AND FINAN-
CIAL SECRETARY TO THE MINISTRY OF
FINANCE (Mr. Barbour): On behalf of my
right hon. Friend the Minister of Finance I
beg to move this resolution, and in doing so
I have to refer very briefly to those reasons
which have induced the Government to move
that a vote of this kind be made for this
purpose. Hon. Members will remember the
disastrous conditions which prevailed in
Dublin which finally culminated, I may
almost say, in the destruction of the
Four Courts, and along with them the Bar
Library. The building, which was situated
within the Four Courts, was built out of
public funds in the year 1859, and the books
therein had been accumulated over a period
of upwards of 50 years, and had been provided partly out of annual subscription
by members of the Bar and partly by
donations and gifts. The books in the Library were the property of the members of
the Bar. On the division of the judiciary
in the year 1921, out of a total membership
of the Bar of about 500, 70 moved North and
joined the Bar of Northern Ireland, and
since then they have been very severely
handicapped in the transaction of their
duties by the absence of a suitable Library
to which they could refer.
A claim for compensation has been put
forward in Dublin for the destruction of the
Bar Library, but it is obvious that even if
such a claim was recognised and compensation was paid the proportion which would
be handed over to those members of the
Bar who moved to Northern Ireland would
be totally inadequate to supply a Library
of sufficient importance to enable the Bar
in Northern Ireland to continue to discharge
all its duties in the same high standard
in which the Bar of Ireland has always
Reprecarried on its professional work.
sentations were made to the Government
that a grant should be made in order to start
a Library for the use of the Northern Bar.
This, of course, will only be a skeleton
Library in the meantime, and will be added
to and built up in the same manner as
the Library which was destroyed in Dublin.
The Government have accordingly acceded
to the request, and they now ask this House
to agree to the sum of £4,000 being handed
over to trustees on behalf of the Northern
Bar for the provision of books of this
character. The amount of this estimate
was arrived at by the Bar Council, and
the House will be asked to vote this supply
along with the usual estimates, but owing
to this being non-recurrent and of a somewhat exceptional character it was thought
right to draw the attention of the House
to it, and not simply to have included it
in the estimates. You are, therefore, asked
to vote this amount. At the same time I
wish to remind you that it is a vote of an
unusual character, but I feel the best interests of the public generally are promoted
by having a suitable Library for reference
available for members of the Bar of
Northern Ireland. I beg to move.
Colonel WOODS: I was not prepared to
say anything about this, but it strikes me

would not care to be looked upon as objects
of charity. Surely they can afford to buy
their own Library. There is no precedent
for the Government supplying the Library,

Mr. BARBOUR: In moving the resolution
which stands in the name of my right hon.
Friend the Minister of Finance I do not
consider it necessary to go over again the
objects of the Bill which were so fully gone
into by my right hon. Friend the Minister
of Commerce in moving the Second Reading
of the Electricity and Gas (Expenses) Bill.
I merely wish to comment upon those
clauses which would appear to cast a burden
upon the public funds. I use the word
appear" advisedly, because I hope to be
able to explain to hon. Members that there
is no great burden on the public funds in
the carrying out of those duties. When the
electricity undertakings were first introduced
was intended that there should be

it
electricity commissioners appointed from the
outside public to undertake these duties, and
in order to meet the expenses which they might
incur or the cost of staff which might necesarily be employed by them an electricity fund
should be established and that fund should
receive contributions levied at a certain rate
from the various electricity and I may as
well bracket it-gas undertakings, so that
the expenses were met by that levy or contribution. Under that method of working
there was no charge upon the public funds.
In Northern Ireland we are a very much
smaller body than what obtains across the
water, and it has been felt that it is not
necessary, in the meantime at any rate, to
establish separate Commissioners and a
separate fund for carrying on this work or
to meet the expenses thereof in Northern
Ireland. The object of this Bill is to suspend
the working of these clauses which provide
for the setting up of a separate electricity
and gas fund. The work is being undertaken
in the meantime by certain officers of the
Minisry of Commerce who have been
appointed to undertake these duties. As
their salaries are borne by the vote of the
Ministry of Commerce it might be thought
that public funds were in some way
or another burdened with the amount of
the time which they devote to the discharge
of their duties. It will be their duty however to supply an annual estimate on the
basis of the amount of the expenses actually
incurred during the previous year in the
course of carrying out those duties. These
expenses will be met by a levy on the various
electricity and gas undertakings in the
manner described by my right hon. Friend
in moving the Second Reading. The levy
so raised will be treated as an appropriation
in aid of the cost of conducting the Ministry
of Commerce, when it will be seen that no
burden on public funds remains. I beg
to move.
Question put, and agreed to.
Resolution to be reported to-morrow.

RELIEF OF AGRICULTURE.
Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That
this House do now adjourn."--
(Captain Dixon.)
Mr. CRAWFORD: I would like to apologise to the House for detaining them at this
stage, but I wish to draw the attention of
the Members to a matter that I consider of
very great importance to the farming community of Northern Ireland. The Prime
Minister in this House on the 15th June said
he hoped the sum of £128,000 would be available for the purpose of assisting to relieve
the rates assessed on agricultural land in
Northern Ireland, and on several occasions
since then he has held out the hope that the
Northern Ireland farmers would get as good
+
treatment as the farmers in England and
Scotland. We all look upon ourselves as
members of the British Empire, and we think
that those in Northern Ireland are entitled to
as good treatment as those who live in Lanarkshire, Devonshire, or any part of England,
Scotland, or Wales. In 1896 a su n
of
£1,300,000 was passed by the Imperial Parliament on the assumption that it would pay
half the rates assessed on agricultural land.
Unfortunately for us that was standardised,
I understand, at the rates in existence, hut
although the rates have risen immensely we
never succeeded in getting half of the rates
that were in existence in 1896. I hope my
figures are correct. The proportion, I understand, available out of the £1,300,000 for Northern Ireland was £128,649. I am interested
in the farming people of the whole of Northern Ireland, but I am especially interested
in the farmers of the County of Antrim, the
constituency which I have the honour to represent. The proportion for County Antrim
of that £128,649 is £28,644. I want to point
out to the House that that £28,644 is very
far from paying half of the rates assessed
on agricultural land in County Antrim. In
the year 1900 the rates amounted to £79,000,
and we only got £28,644. We would have
required £39,500 to pay half the rates in
1900. We all know to our cost that rates went
up tremendously during the succeeding years,
and for the year ending 31st March, 1923,
County Antrim amounted to no less than
£126,000. We only got £28,000, and it would
have required £63.000 to pay half the
rates. In other words the ratepayers
of County Antrinm received £35,000
less than the amount that would have paid
half the rates last year. The amount we
got would not be one-fourth of the rates, let
alone the half to which we were entitled. As
the Members of this House know the
Imperial Parliament recently decided to increase the grant from £1,300,000 to £4,000,000
in order to pay 75 per cent, of the rates
assessed on agricultural land, and we are
only promised £128.000. My point is this, if
out of that £1,300.000 the Six Counties were
entitled to get £128,000, I say we should be
entitled to three times as much out of a
grant of £4.000.000. Instead of that we are
only promised an additional grant of £128,000
which would not pay half the rates let alone
the three-quarters to which we are entitled.
I do not know that I am putting the matter
as plainly as I might. The farmers in England are getting a grant of three-quarters
of the rates, and the farmers in Northern
Ireland are only getting what would not be
one-fourth, and a sort of promise that they
will get a very small proportion of the
additional grant made by the Imperial
Parliament. There is no doubt that the
farmers of Northern Ireland are suffering

I am in an awkward position. I am like the

I speak of the administration of this Fund.
I am told it is going to be divided over agricultural lands on the basis of the former
agricultural grant under Section 41 of the

Derry gets 1s 6d, Armagh gets 1s 51d, and

when the grant in relief of rates was given
the
by
Imperial Parliament it was
standardised, and, therefore, when the rates

teachers were kept in a state of semistarvation by the action of the Imperial

the farming interests had this relief

as time went on and the rates increased

different state of affairs obtained in Great
Britain, where, for some reason I cannot now define, the farming interests had
more influence with the Government. They
had their wants attended to from year to
year, and particularly recently, as the rates
advanced. We were not in that position.
Now when it came to the question of how
much relief we could give to the farmers
we considered how this could be put before
the Arbitration Board, which has within its
purview at present all financial matters between Northern Ireland and Great Britain.
There has been no opportunity to present it
as yet. It was a question with us what
arguments could be used, and how could we
secure an amount equivalent to this £300,000,
which I think my hon. Friend (Mr. Crawford)
said would be required to bring it up to the
British grant. On examination we found
that the grant in Great Britain was equal to
two shillings per head of the population,
whereas a similar grant in Northern Ireland
would amount to five shillings per head.
While I am not sure at the present moment
of the adjustment we may be able to make
with the Imperial Treasury, through the
Arbitration Board, on this subject, I feel we
could not, consistently with our position,
pledge ourselves to a greater expenditure
than a duplication of the amount which had
been paid in the past, that is to say that the
£128,000 should be raised to £256,000. That
is really the explanation of how the position
stands at the present time, and we have no

you

Now I would like to refer to the fiery indignation of my hon. Friend (Mr. Coote) in
respect of the non-provision of phosphates
for farmers. He drew a very lurid picture
of the ineptitude of the Northern Government for not throwing itself heart and soul
into a scheme, which the British Government
adumbrated, for importing phosphates
from a far away island in the
Southern Seas in order that cheap
phosphates might be distributed to the
farmers of Northern Ireland. The whole
proceeding in relation to that is something
like this. The British Government is possessed of an island, Nauru, on the Australian
coast, which has large phosphate deposits. The island was taken from the
Germans. There was an arrangement made
whereby Australia and New Zealand would
get a certain proportion, and the United
Kingdom would receive its fair share-1
forget the percentage; I think it was about
32 per cent. The fact is that the British
farmers can get phosphates of a higher constituent value from Africa much cheaper
than they can buy the phosphates which the
British Government own and which have to
be brought such a vast distance. The ocean
freight is so very considerable as to make it
more expensive than the near-by phosphates
which have a higher percentage of fertilising
matter.
Mr. COOTE: What are they selling it at?

because they are practically unused, and the

the British Government cannot take.

25 OCTOBER 1923.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Thursday, 25th October, 1923.
The House met at Three of the Clock, Mr
SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
VALUATION INQUIRY COMMITTEE.
Mr. LYNN asked the Minister of Finance
whether he can state when the Report of the
Valuation Inquiry Committee will be
published.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): In reply to the hon. Member, I may
say that I understand that a full report on
this highly controversial and technical
question, which has in the past formed the
subject of several protracted and fruitless
inquiries, cannot be made for some months;
but I am informed that an interim report
dealing with the most serious of the existing
anomalies will be made to me in the course
of a few days. The question of publication
is one for the Government to consider when
the report has been received.
REPORTS OF COMMISSIONS AND
COMMITTEES.

Finance whether a verbatim report of the
following will be placed in the Library of
the House for the benefit of Members of both

Boards, Committee on Cost of Living, Committee on Public Accounts.
Mr. POLLOCK: In reply to the hon.
Member, I am inquiring of the Chairmen
of the four Commissions and Committees
first mentioned whether they have any ob
jection to verbatim reports (if such exist)
being placed in the Library of the House.
If they see no objection, and if spare typewritten copies are available, I will take steps
to carry out the suggestion of the hon.
Member. There would, of course, be no
justification for incurring the large expenditure involved in having these reports
printed.
The report of the Committee of Public
Accounts, which is a Committee of this
House, is in a different category and it will
be for the Chairman of that Committee to
decide how far the reports of its proceedings
will be published verbatim. As the hon.
Member is aware, the Committee has not yet
reported to this House.
Col. WOODS: Arising out of that answer,
I would like to ask the Minister of Finance
if he will have these verbatim typewritten
copies circulated to the Members of this
House?
Mr. POLLOCK: You mean individual
copies ?
Colonel WOODS: Yes.
Mr. POLLOCK: My hon. Friend has
suggested a procedure which I am afraid
will involve considerable expense in having
these very voluminous reports typewritten.
He must remember that a verbatim report
means a report of every word of the
evidence which has been given in these
committees, and I think he will realise
that that is a very voluminous matter,
and will require an immense amount
of work. I think that if the reports are
placed in the Library they will give
sufficient information, as no Member is
likely to wade through all the proceedings of
these committees.
Colonel WOODS: Arising out of that
answer, I would like to ask the Minister

TAXATION OF MOTOR VEHICLES.
Mr. DONALD asked the Minister of
Finance if he will state the total amount of
revenue derived from taxation of motor
vehicles in Northern Ireland for the years
1921-22-23.
Mr. POLLOCK: As the hon. Member is
aware, the transfer of the control of financial matters to the Government of Northern
Ireland took place on the 22nd November,
1921. The total net amount of revenue
derived from the taxation of motor vehicles
in the Northern area for the portion of the
financial year, 1921-22-that is, from the 22nd
November, 1921 to the 31st March, 1922-was
as shown in the Finance Accounts for that
period, viz., £124,839. For the financial year
ended 31st March, 1923, the net receipts
amounted to £216,589.

THE UNMARRIED MOTHER.
Dr. MORRISON asked the Minister of
Home Affairs what steps he has taken with
regard to the unanimous resolution passed by
this House during the earlier portion of the
Session, calling on his Department to introduce legislation that would deal with the
problem of the unmarried mother.
Sir DAWSON BATES: Owing to the shortness of the present Session, which entails the
devotion of the whole time to Bills of imperative necessity, it has not been possible
for the Government to find time to deal
with this question. In any event, the Imperial Government have not completed their
legislation on the subject, as they have only
passed one of the Bills dealing with the
question of contributions.
The question of legitimization will not be
finally determined by the Imperial Parliament until the present Session. It will be
understood that it would be undesirable to
pass an Act dealing with legitimization in
Northern Ireland until it is possible to see
how the Imperial Government have dealt
with the question in Great Britain, as, of
course, important questions relating to property on both sides of the channel may
arise which will make it necessary to have
uniform legislation. This matter must,
therefore, stand over until it is possible to
deal with all aspects of the matter.
Dr. MORRISON: Arising out of that
answer, I want to ask the Minister of Home
Affairs if this question is going to be postponed indefinitely?
Sir DAWSON BATES: Certainly not. I
think my answer indicates clearly that the
Government intend to carry out the wishes
as expressed by the House in the resolution
passed last Session.
Mr. COOTE: Does not the right hon.
Gentleman feel that this is not a question
of legitimization, but a question of suing
for maintenance, and that this side of legislation is already in effect in Great Britain?
Therefore there is no necessity to wait. Is
the Minister of Home Affairs not also aware
that he promised legislation nearly two years
ago, at the beginning of the life of this Parliament, and that we are still just where we
started?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have already indicated that the intention of the Government is to introduce legislation in regard to
this matter, and I have explained that the
two questions of legitimization and contributions of course it may be a matter of
opinion are bound up the one with the
other.
Dr. MORRISON: May I ask if the Minister
of Home Affairs is fully conscious of the fact
that there are 1,300 unmarried mothers to
be dealt with in Northern Ireland every
year?
Mr. SPEAKER: I do not think you can
pursue this matter any further at this stage.
Resolved: "That this House, at its rising
this day, do adjourn until Tuesday next."-

Mr. COOTE: I wish to avail myself of the
opportunity afforded me under the Motion for
Adjournment to draw attention to certain inequalities and anomalies in the Education
Act, to which many people take very serious
exception, and I do so with very great regret
and with a sense of very great disappointment. After hearing the speech of the Minister of Education on the First reading of the
Bill, I had hoped that we were about to have
a very large, comprehensive and democratic
measure that would assimilate all systems
of primary education into one corporate body
and unify them, and make the consideration
of educational matters a delight instead of
making the position more serious than it ever
was before. Unfortunately this Act makes
provision for three grades of schools. There
are the transferred schools for which provision is made that they shall be conducted
by committes appointed by the County
Councils which are supposed to be the
education authority. They delegate their
powers to regional committees, and they have
all the powers in regard to the proper conduct of the individual schools in the counties
to which they belong. There is Grade 2,
which provides that a school need not necessarily transfer, but it may set up a committee
of two and four, which largely stamps that
school as a denominational school. This committee which can appoint and dismiss
teachers under the rules is to have half the
necessary cost of heating, lighting, and cleansing. No 3 Grade provides that a school may
be retained practically as it is, that the old,
almost antedeluvian system is yet to prevail,
and that the individual manager may appoint
and dismiss the teacher and may conduct
the school apart altogether from any control
either by the parents of the children attending the school or by the District Council or
County Council representing the ratepayers
of the particular district or county. There
is no redress in regard to his rulings, and he
is only subject to the over-riding authority of
the Ministry of Education. This last grade
is also to have half the cost of heating,
lighting and cleansing. I want to say in passing that I cannot for the life of me understand how you will reconcile these grades,
especially the last, with a democratic system
of education. It is a system which
probably commenced in the middle ages, and
it is about to be perpetuated by this Ulster
Parliament. It is one of the most unfortu
nate features that could be embodied in any
Act. You are discriminating. There is class
legislation. There is no uniformity.
All
people are not on the same plane, and there
is no fair treatment. If I may ask, why is
this Grade 3 put here at all? It is wellknown that it is put here for a purpose. It
is put here to allow the Hierarchy of the
Roman Catholic Church to maintain the
same grip upon education that they have
held, that they propose to hold, and that
they are trying to hold in every country in the
world where they have the power. What about
the poor teachers in those schools? Is
there to be no liberty for the teachers?
Have Roman Catholic teachers no rights?
Have they no feelings? Are they only
puppets to be kicked about as any church or
denomination may wish? Should they not
be as truly national as any other teachers?
As a democrat, I denounce this feature, and
I say that it alone destroys the Act. It is
not even a fair Act. It is dealing behind the
scenes with class legislation. This clause
was brought in for a purpose, and I am
sure the Ulster people will resent that purpose with all the strength in their power.
I want the House to understand that about
one-third of the schools in Ulster will re-

Stripped of all its verbiage, the question is
whether the public are to control the education which they pay for, or whether it is
going to be controlled by committees not
popularly elected. That is really the question.
My hon. Friend (Mr. Coote) talks about

the two representing the people who pay 100
per cent. of the cost, and the four representing the people who only indirectly pay the
cost, and he suggests that the rest of the
control should be left in the hands of my
noble Friend opposite (The Minister of Education). I have a good deal of confidence
in my noble Friend, but I am more of a
democrat than my Friend here (Mr. Coote),
because I want to find education controlled
by the people for the people. I think my
noble Friend would subscribe to that

education and help in many ways. Then
my hon. Friend says, "simply set up these
four and two schools and no other school."
It works out the same if you like. Two and
two and two make six, and four and two
make six, so that in the Act we have made
provision for four and two. The only
difference my hon. Friend wants to see made
is that we should have two and two and two.
Three twos make six, and two of the six he

the Act, but surely at this time of day no
man is going to get up in this House, or
indeed in Northern Ireland, before an
audience of intelligent people and suggest
that education should simply be put into the
hands of these four-and-two committees without any uniformity?

It cannot trust them. When it is handed

It cannot trust them to deal with the most

Ulster; it ties them down that they are not

when the Minister himself comes to deal

trust anybody. We have 1,948 schools, most
of which are voluntary and I believe, as the
hon Member for Tyrone and Fermanagh
(Mr. Coote) has said, that the county

Act. I was in England during the summer
and I went to Leicester which is a town in
the county of Leicester, equal nearly to
Belfast in population and area. The county
is a large, prosperous English county, and I
found that in that county and in that city
this whole question of education was dealt
with in a way that gave satisfaction to everybody. I beg the House to remember this, that
everybody was satisfied. I interviewed parents, I interviewed Roman Catholic priests,
I interviewed teachers, and the secretary of
the education authority of the city and of
the county, and they told me the Act was
working harmoniously and well. It was introduced in 1901 by Arthur James Balfour,
a statesman who even the Minister of
Education will admit was unrivalled in his
statesmanship and in his literary genius.
That Act is producing harmony-complete
and absolute harmony-and has gone on for 20
years. Under these four-and-two committees,
which we might have here, these schools get
100 per cent. We have the Prime Minister
here repeatedly telling us that we should
follow the pattern of English legislation.
If that English legislation which is working
so well there appeals to him, why should he
not introduce it here? So far as I can judge,
that Act would meet all the wishes and all the
different sections in Ulster and would be considered a satisfactory solution of the difficulty.
I do not think that in this Act and in the
proposals that are made by the clergy
any injustice has been done to the teachers.
They get a committee of six for the old
managerial system, and I think that any
man who is working under a committee of
six independent men is not likely to be subjected to any injustice. There is this,
further, that the Act itself provides against
any injustice. It makes it impossible that
any injustice can be done, for it gives the
teacher the right of appeal from a decision
of the Ministry, and it gives him the right
of being represented there by a legal adviser.
Not only that, but if the local committee
refuses to conform to the decision of the
Ministry in this matter the teacher may lose
his situation, but he is guaranteed by the
Act a salary for twelve months. That is a
complete cut from the old managerial system
and from the old vicious Star Chamber system
that dealt with the teacher in some compartment in Dublin and did not even let him
know what was being said against him or
the reports that were made against him. I
would readily agree to remove even an
imaginary grievance against an individual
if doing so did not inflict a greater evil
upon the community. I thought, and it
seems I was foolish in my thought, that this
Parliament would legislate in harmony with
Ulster ideals and seek to secure that religion
and education, knowledge and tolerance would
go hand in hand in promoting the peace of
the community. Personally, I am inclined to
fairly broad views, and have never been able
to inhabit the furnished lodgings of tradition
and dogmatism, but, in my opinion, this Act
in its spirit and in some of its clauses is

We are at this moment in an embryo state.
I need hardly say that when the Prime
Minister entrusted me with the duty of
framing an Education Bill I was fully aware
that we were laying very important foundations. With my advisers I studied every

assailed education in the past. I was well
aware that in the Six Counties we were confronted with a more acute religious problem
than existed in other parts of the kingdom,

through all those rocks with which I was

religions. I hope we have succeeded. I believe we have succeeded. I believe that when
a certain time has elapsed, and we have had
an opportunity of seeing the working of the
Education Act in the Borough of Belfast and
in Derry City, we shall realise that many of
those fears were entirely unfounded, and that
we have set up in this Province a system of
education which others in the future will
follow and find equally successful.

30 OCTOBER 1923.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Tuesday, 30th October, 1923.
The House met at Three of the Clock, Mr.
SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
STAFF OF BELFAST PRISON.
2. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Home Affairs if he will state the number of
ex-Servicemen on the Staff of the Belfast
Prison, with at least two years' prison
service, as Temporary Warders; how many
permanent appointments have been given to
these men, and how many permanent appointments have been given to non-ex-
Servicemen with less than two years' prison
service?
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): There are at present
five ex-Servicemen employed as Temporary
Warders in Belfast Prison who have over
two years' service in that capacity.
Since the Prisons Service was transferred
to this Government 12 Temporary Warders
have been promoted to the rank of Permanent Warders in Belfast Prison. These men
were all ex-Servicemen and one of them had
over two years' service as a Temporary
Warder.
No appointments as Permanent Warders
in Belfast Prison have been given to men
who have not served in His Majesty's
Forces.
A PRINCIPAL WARDER'S RANK.
3. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Home Affairs if he will state the reason why
Principal Warder Samuel George Willis, of
Belfast Prison, was reduced in rank from
Chief Warder of Belfast Prison to his present
rank.
Sir DAWSON BATES: Principal Warder
Willis was appointed on probation as Chief
Warder in August, 1921. As I was not satisfied that he was competent to enforce
discipline in the prison, I extended his period
of probation for another three months to
give him a further trial. Before this period
had expired he was found with some warders
inside the prison canteen at 11 p.m., although
the canteen should have been closed at 10
p.m. This satisfied me that he was not fit
for the post of Chief Warder, and I, therefore, could not see my way to confirm him
in that rank. I may state that shortly after
this occurrence wet canteens at the prisons
were abolished. (Hon. Members: Hear hear.)
I must deprecate these questions relating
to an individual officer, as it is hardly fair
to the officer concerned to make his shortcomings the subject of a Parliamentary
question and answer.
Colonel WOODS: Arising out of that
answer, I may say that this question was
put at the request of the officer concerned.
INSPECTORS OF PRISONS.
4. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Home Affairs if he will state if an Inspector
of Prisons has been appointed for Northern
Ireland?
Sir DAWSON BATES: The inspectorial
duties in connection with Prisons in Northern
Ireland are discharged by the Medical Inspectors and other permanent officers of the
Ministry as may from time to time be
specially deputed for the purpose under the
Ministries of Northern Ireland Act.
Colonel WOODS: Arising out of that reply,
is an officer who inspects Belfast prisons entitled under the Regulations to hear a complaint from one or a greater number of
warders?
Sir DAWSON BATES: Certainly, the
warders are entitled to bring the matter before the Inspector for the time being.
"CHELSEA HOSPITAL" PROJECT.
5. Colonel WOODS asked the Prime
Minister if he will state what progress has
been made with the local "Chelsea Hospital
project, as outlined by him in a public speech
on 1st June, 1923?
The PRIME MINISTER (Sir James Craig) :
The scheme is not a Government one, but is
being started by myself personally with the
object of providing a home for our ex-Servicemen in their old age, somewhat on the lines
of Chelsea Hospital. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear). Its success will depend upon the
measure of voluntary financial assistance received. I have made a good beginning, and
am confident of success, but, of course, the
need of such a hospital will not become pressing for some years.
CONSTABULARY SERGEANT'S OFFENCE.
6. Mr. COOTE asked the Minister of Home
Affairs if his attention has been drawn by the
Constabulary Authorities to the act of
Sergeant O'Brien, late of Castlecaulfield, now
of Omagh, in forging the name of a magistrate to a petty sessions summons, dated 25th
May, presented in court at Dungannon on
31st May, and admitted by the Sergeant on
10th June; is he aware that this is not a
disciplinary but a criminal offence, and what
Oral Answers.

[Mr. Coote]
course does he propose to take in the matter
in order to safeguard the honour of the Force?
Sir DAWSON BATES: It is a fact that
Sergeant O'Brien signed the name of a magistrate to a summons for allowing a horse to
wander on the public road. The magistrate
in question, who brought the matter to the
notice of the police authorities, adjudicateu
on the case.
Although the Inspector-General was afraid
that in country places sergeants of constabulary had sometimes at the request of magistrates signed summonses to save time and
trouble, he regarded this practice as most
irregular, and Sergeant O'Brien's act was a
very serious matter. He submitted the case
at once to this Ministry, and the papers were
immediately referred to the Attorney-
General who advised that a prosecution for
forgery could not be sustained. I, therefore,
directed the Inspector-General in the circumstances to deal with the case
a disciplinary point of view, and although
the Sergeant had a very good record, and had
been severely wounded in an ambush, the
Inspector-General felt he could not inflict a
less punishment than the award of an unfavourable record and the transfer of the
Sergeant at his own expense.

ERECTION OF PUBLIC ELEMENTARY
SCHOOLS.
7. Mr. COOTE asked the Minister of
Finance how much money has been granted
for the erection of Public Elementary Schools
in Northern Ireland since February, 1922,
and what proportion of this has been for
schools under Roman Catholic management?
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): This is mainly an educational matter, and, as such, should normally have been
addressed to the Minister of Education. As.
however, the Ministry of Finance is responsible for the technical aspect of school construction, I have consulted the Minister of
Education, and am prepared to supply the
information sought, prefacing my remarks
with the observation that with the exception
of one grant of extreme urgency, the whole
of the grants under review have been made
by the Ministry of Education in fulfilment
of undertakings given by the Commissioners
of National Education prior to February,
1922, when the service of public education in
Northern Ireland definitely passed under the
control of this Government. They partake of
the nature of liabilities under the Government of Ireland Act, 1920.
Honourable Members will appreciate that
neither the Minister of Education nor myself are concerned with the denominations of
the recipients of the grants, but only with
the educational necessity for such grants and
their economical disbursement.
The figures are as follows:-
The amount of money granted for the
erection of public elementary schools in
Northern Ireland, inclusive of works of
improvement in existing schools in excess
of £100, since February, 1922, is £13,550,
of which 85 per cent. has been made to
schools under Roman Catholic management.

My honourable and gallant Friend, however, I will realise that circumstances arise
in which it is impracticable at this stage

burden of the criticism was that the contract
was given to a firm who, at the time of
the awarding of the contract, were not

TRIBUTE BY THE PRIME MINISTER.
The PRIME MINISTER: With your permission and the leave of the House I think
I would be voicing the sentiment of all
shades of opinion if I intervened before we
proceed to the ordinary business to pay a
tribute to the late Mr. Bonar Law. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) If I may in the
first instance bring the memories of all those
who are here back to the early days of
that remarkable man's entry into public
life, I think I will be justified in saying
that those of us who came into close touch
with him recognised from the very outset
what a great man he was, and especially
what a great friend he was. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) Not only hon. Members of the
Imperial House of Commons, but some hon.
Members who sit here who were not members
of that assembly have had occasion from
time to time in days gone by to cross over
on business of a varied character in order
to interview him, and I am sure they will
agree with me-my hon. Friend the Member
for the North Division of Belfast (Mr.
McGuffin) is one of them-as to the way in
which he met those of us speaking on behalf
of Ulster from time to time. The cordiality,
the extraordinary interest that he took in a
particular question, the personal touch, his
rapier-like manner of getting to the bottom
of things, and, above all, the way in which
he sent us away confident will be borne
witness to by all those who have had
experience such as I have had. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.)
It is very difficult for any man who has
been a friend of one of England's Prime
Ministers-a close friend-to speak without
feeling and deep emotion. I can only say
that I had the opportunity on
more than
one occasion of being with him in great
trial, and nothing brings out a man's
character or allows another to understand
a man better than to work with him during
the times when the days were dark, when
our country was in danger, when the country
itself could only look to the leaders to carry
them through, and when the burden on a
man's shoulders was very heavy. I
experienced that. I can remember many a
time not only anxiety with regard to the
war but anxiety with regard to Ulster
bringing us together, and we were able to
discuss these things, as one man would with
another. Through it all there was outstanding the brilliancy of this great man
desirous to give of his very best, to spend
everything that was in him in order to
uphold the cause in which he believed. Then
from the personal point of view there was
his extraordinary susceptibility. We all
knew he was like a woman, he was like a
child so far as affection and the tenderer
sides of character are concerned, and yet
beneath it all were courage and firmness,
otherwise how could he exist so long as he
did in his country's service? What a debt
of gratitude we owe to him here when we
look back at Blenheim and when we think
of our own Balmoral, when we think of him
coming forward at a time when it was no
small thing for a great British statesman to
take his stand with little Ulster in her
difficulties. Unhesitatingly and unfalteringly he came along with us, and I believe
Ulster's memory of him will never fade nor
her affection towards him for the stand he
took. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Later on he became Leader of the House. In
modern times there was never such a Leader
of the House of Commons. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) He used to cast a spell not
over his friends alone, but over those who
were his political opponents, and he brought
debate in the Mother of Parliaments to a high
level by the simplicity of his character, and
by the honest, straightforward way in which
he attempted to lead that august assembly.
Then, later, he was tried and not found
wanting. He was offered the Premiershiphe could have had it for the asking-and in
the interests of his country, at a time of
peril, he sank all personal feelings and took
his stand beside Mr. Asquith in the first
instance, and Mr. Lloyd George in the second
instance, and only those two men can tell
what weighty counsels he was able to add,
what advice he was able to give to the
Cabinet of the day that carried us to success
during the great war. But we who came in
contact constantly with him were well aware
that by day and by night, without pausing
for a moment, he carried out his duties to
the State. We recollect him, always in the
House of Commons or in his room, always
accessible, ready to meet anyone who could
contribute to the common cause. That, in
my opinion, was one of the greatest times of
this great man's life-when he unselfishly
shouldered more than half of the burden by

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Trade Boards Bill.
Order for Second reading read.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): On rising as I do to-day at this
stage I cannot but feel prompted to say, with
the permission of the House, that I am sure
the heart of everyone in this building
is deeply touched by the gracious and appropriate tribute which our Prime Minister
has paid to the memory of a great statesman
and a great Christian gentleman whom the
whole Empire mourns to-day. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
As I rise to-day to ask this House to be
good enough to give a Second reading to the
Trade Boards Bill, Northern Ireland, I cannot help but feel that considerable responsibility rests upon me, especially when I remember that this Bill applies to 18 trades,
included in which trades are 6,000 firms,
giving employment to between 65,000 and
70,000 of our working people. There is an
old saying-I do not know whether it is true
or not-that if you touch a Scotsman's
pocket you touch his whole being.
Now, we
here in the North of Ireland have many
characteristics in common with our Scottish
friends, and the fact that this Bill very
closely affects the financial interests of both
employers and employed does not make my
part easier to-day. When I became Minister
of Labour, even before my department had
taken over its powers, I was approached by
many deputations asking me to abandon
altogether the Trade Board system in Northern Ireland. I was not able to agree to
do so. I would have been prejudicing the
position. I would have been taking from
our working people in those trades in which
there were Trade Boards, and are still, a
safeguard which the Imperial Government
felt that they required. I feel that our Government took the wiser course in setting up
a committee composed of an equal number
1655 Trade Boards Bill-

HOUSE OF COMMONS.
Second Reading.
[Mr. Andrews]
of workers' representatives and employers'
representatives in order to inquire into the
working of the Trade Board system in Northern Ireland. We were particularly fortunate in securing the services of the Speaker
of the Senate to act as neutral chairman of
that committee, and I feel that it was largely
due to his tact, judgment, industry, and
undoubted popularity with the whole committee that they were able to present me with
a unanimous report. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear). The result is that I am in a far
happier and less difficult position to-day than
I would otherwise have been.
That Committee decided at one of its earlier
meetings that the Trade Board system must
be retained in Northern Ireland, but at the
same time came to the conclusion that it
was necessary to amend the existing Acts in
several respects first, the principle upon
which the Trade Board will be brought in or
removed from the system, procedure for fixing or varying rates, provision for the substitution of voluntary machinery for Trade
Boards, extension of power of Trade Boards in
subsidiary activities, and last, the method of
the constitution of Trade Boards. This Bill
which I have the honour to ask should receive a Second reading to-day complies with
these general conclusions and is based upon
certain other recommendations contained in
the report which I will deal with when I
come later to explain the Bill itself. During
the war hon. Members will remember that
necessarily very drastic and far-reaching
control was established. It was willingly
submitted to by both employers and employees because they felt unitedly that it
was necessary to bring the war to a successful conclusion. But immediately after
the war the swing of the pendulum was in
the other direction. There was a general
demand that Government control should
cease altogether and that employers and employees should be left free and unrestricted
to settle their own affairs in their own way.
I think some people forget in making this
demand that before the war there was Government control in many directions. It may
astonish hon. Members to know that 500
years ago in certain parts of England wages
were fixed by the State in order to prevent
what they even then called sweating. Then
we had the Truck Act, the Factory Acts, laws
permitting workers to combine, Conciliation
Acts, Employers' Liability Acts, Workmen's Compensation Acts, Compulsory
Insurance Acts on
a contributory
basis
in relation to both health
and unemployment insurance; also we
had the Trade Board Act of 1909, amended
by another Act in 1918. Now, admittedly,
when our Government took over its powers
the Trade Boards were unpopular amongst
employers at any rate in Northern Ireland.
I think that was due to wrong impressions
that had been created through faulty administration as to what the duties, aims, and
objects of the Trade Boards were. I feel that
to-day Trade Boards are certainly more
popular than they were, and I am very hopeful that when this Bill passes-as I venture
to hope it will-Trade Boards will come to
be looked upon by both employers and employed as a blessing in the industries to
which they are applied. I would like to
make it clear, because I think there
is a wrong impression that a Trade Boards'
Act such as this is does not in itself
establish statutory rates. I saw in one of
our leading newspapers a statement somewhat to that effect. What a Trade Board
does is to set up machinery, to be drawn
from the trade itself, and composed of
workers' representatives and employers'
representatives with the help of a neutral
chairman to arrange wages for the trade
for the time being.
Now, I think that it is necessary that I
should prove two things, first, that in certain trades under present conditions Trade
Boards are necessary, and, secondly, that
the present Bill provides for the fairest,
safest, and most efficient form of Trade
Boards for dealing with the industrial problems that certain trades present. A
moment's consideration leads to the conclusion, I think, that in any civilised nation
a public sense of right and wrong must compel the State to concern itself with the conditions of the individual life of the people.
Obviously, work is the primary concern of
every nation, and history shows that in
proportion as a community becomes more
highly developed the State is increasingly
interested in maintaining in a healthy and
proper condition the industrial activities of
its subjects. A general conscience and intelligence develops-sometimes all too slowly
-which expresses itself in social legislation,
and nowhere is this more marked than in
the history of the United Kingdom.
It cannot be denied that wages must be
settled somehow. In days gone by an
employer simply said, "I am prepared to
pay such and such a wage; take it or leave
it." Very often the position was that might
was right. I think it will be generally
admitted that it is well that those days have
passed away. (IIon. Members: Hear, hear.)
We have now our Conciliation Acts.
have now Labour in many trades as well
as employers fully organised, and they can
come together in friendly negotiation across
the table in order to settle what wage an
industry can pay and what wage the worker
can reasonably be expected to accept. And
when on occasions they cannot agree they

Now, I come to the marrow of the case.
There are industries in which there is no
organisation worthy of the name either on
the one side or the other, and, therefore,
there is really nobody to negotiate with.
The parties themselves are only individuals
and are in a rather hopeless and unenviable
position, and the representative of the State
responsible for the time being for preserving
industrial peace is in a difficulty in which
I have felt myself on occasions-that there
was really no representative body to
approach. In these trades it is necessary
that the Government should endeavour to
arrange that representatives of both sides
should be brought together and should, with
as little Government assistance as possible
if you like, settle these matters for these
trades in some way similar to that which
I have endeavoured to explain.
I know that the workers in Northern
Ireland attach considerable importance to the
Trade Board system, a view which is now
shared by employers in many trades who rely
on statutory rates to secure them from unfair
competition on the part of individual firms
and sometimes unscrupulous employers.
Sweating admittedly is an evil and a menace
with which the Trade Boards have effectively
dealt, and they can prevent a recurrence of
it in trades to which the Bill applies or may
apply. In other words, when a Trade Board
is formed the representatives of the mployers and workers meet together under the
guidance of what is called an appointed
member. Prior to our taking over power
here there were three appointed members in
connection with each Trade Board. From
the standpoint of economy I think that was
unnecessarily many, but from another
standpoint as well I think it was wrong. I
think the fact that there were three of them
reinforced the appointed members in their
Own views that it meant they were
more or less independent of the trade
interests affected and, therefore, instead
of acting as conciliators they acted the
part of dictators. In fact, since we
took over our powers here we have
had only one appointed member, and we
have found that it works a great deal better
for the reasons which I have tried to
explain and for others to which it is not
necessary that I should refer.
I am now coming to the Bill itself, but
I think it is right that I should say at this
point that I cannot claim myself any credit
for the Bill, although, of course, I entirely
approve of it, otherwise I would not be
standing in the position to-day in which I
do. The credit is entitled to be shared by
the Parliamentary draughtsman, Sir Arthur
Quekett, the Permanent Secretary to the
Ministry, Mr. Dale, and Major McConnell,
who has acted as secretary to the Dufferin
Committee, and who is an expert in connection with Trade Board matters.

As regards the Bill, I come in the first
place, of course, to Clause 1, Sub-section (1).
It provides for the application of the Act
to any specified trade by Provisional Order
instead of by Special Order, as has been the
custom in the past. The Dufferin Committee
came to the conclusion that the Provisional
Order system was more in keeping with the
fitness of things than establishing Trade
Boards by means of Special Orders. The
difference, of course, is this: By a Special
Order the Minister of Labour can practically
establish a Trade Board himself and then
ask the permision of Parliament afterwards.
That was a position I did not seek, and,
therefore. I was quite pleased when the
Dufferin Committee proposed that the matter
should be dealt with in another way.
the Provisional Order system the Minister
of Labour has the right to ask Parliament
for permission to establish a Trade Board.
That can be threshed out by a Committee
of the House very much in the same way
as is done in the case of Private Bill legislation, and if Parliament approves of a
Trade Board being established for that
particular trade the Minister of Labour is
there and then empowered to do so. This
clause also continues the existing position
in regard to the application of the Act to
Trade Board trades. Sub-section (2) provides
for temporary suspension by Provisional
Order in cases where the Ministry, after
consultation with representative associations of employers and workers in
the trade, is satisfied that both sides
sufficiently organised to ensure collective bargaining. That means that
although the trade is placed under a Trade
Board to-day it is not necesarily kept under
a Trade Board for all time. If the conditions in the trade are changed the matter

Clause 2 provides for the confirmation,
amendment, or repeal of a Provisional Order.
Clause 3 enables the Ministry to establish
Trade Boards for the trades to which the
Act has been applied and to expand the
jurisdiction of a Trade Board over two or
more kindred trades.
Clause 4 is intended to give the Minister
an opportunity from time to time of ascerthe
taining the views of the Board as
representative trade body to advise the
State on matters connected with the trade.
Clause 5 imposes on a Trade Board the
obligation of fixing general minimum
time-rates and piecework-basis time rates
for piece workers. Everybody knows
what a general minimum time rate
means. It ensures to the worker of
average industry and average ability a fixed
rate, a time rate. Exceptions can be made
where the worker is either mentally or
physically feeble and where that worker
could not get employment if a particular
wage was absolutely adhered to. "Piecework-basis time rate," no doubt, sounds
somewhat complicated to hon. Members-
Mr. GRANT: Hear, hear.
Mr. ANDREWS: But it is really quite
simple. What it means is this, that a rate
shall be fixed for piecework which will be
in harmony with a time work wage.
