Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: Or vice versa?
Mr. ANDREWS: I now
Clause 6, Sub-section 1, which gives
power to
a Trade Board to fix general
minimum piece rates for in-workers. These
rates must be such
as will yield
the ordinary worker the equivalent of the
piecework-basis time rate. What that means
to
is this that a Trade Board may, if it thinks
it desirable, fix for any particular firm, or
in fact for the whole trade if it likes, a piecework rate which will apply to all piece
workers. Of course that is possible in some
instances, and in other instances it is not
possible, because the conditions in a trade
very often vary so much. Take the spinning
trade as an example, and it is the one I
know most about. One firm will be spinning
very fine yarns and another firm very coarse
yarns; one firm very good yarns and another
firm possibly very bad yarns. Of course
it makes a great difference to the workers
whether the yarns are good or bad, or
coarse or fine, and you can understand that
it will be very difficult in a case of that
kind to establish for the whole trade a piecework rate which would be applicable.
Therefore, it is left to the Trade Board to
do so if they find it is possible, but if they
do not do so at any rate the workers may
feel secure in possessing what is known as
the piecework-basis time rate.
This clause also gives power to fix general
minimum piece rates for out-workers.
These rates must be not less than the piece
rates paid for work done on the employers'
premises. It further gives power to fix
general overtime rates. Sub-section 2 provides that general minimum piece rates when
fixed shall apply instead of the pieceworkbasis time rate. Clause 8 deals with
rate-fixing procedure. Under the existing
Act a period of almost four months
-and this is important-must elapse
between the issue of notice of proposal
and the date when it becomes effective, whereas under the Bill a proposal to fix
rates can become effective in about six
weeks, and a proposal to vary a rate in about
four weeks from the date of issue of notice.
One of the complaints which were very frequent in reference to Trade Board procedure
was that it was so slow in its movements.
For instance, if it was considered by a
Trade Board that it was necessary to reduce
wages in order that more business would be
obtained, the employers naturally objected
when they did not get the advantage of
the fall in wages for four months after it
was actually agreed to, because their customers were of opinion that as wages were
actually to fall some time later they were
entitled to get the benefit in the cost of
the commodities produced, even before the
employer received the relief which it was
considered by the Trade Board that he
should have. On the other hand the workers
naturally felt that when wages were advanced
it was very unfair that they should be kept
waiting four mouths before they got the
advance which the Trade Board had decided
Therefore,
they were entitled to receive.
I think the quickening up of the procedure
will be acceptable to employers and workers
alike.

Probably every hon. Member understands
what all these clauses mean. If not he will
have a full opportunity of getting to understand all about them when the Committee
Stage is reached. As regards Clauses 17 and
18, I think it is necessary that I should
speak more fully about them. They are
very important clauses, and they deal with
the constitution and proceedings of Trade
Boards and the establishment of District
Trade Committees, and provide for the
limitation to one of the number of appointed
members on a Trade Board. That I have
already dealt with. There is another matter
to which I feel it is right that I should refer.
In regard to the laundry industry, the
Dufferin Committee came to the conclusion
that I am reading from the report of the
Dufferin Committee-
If it should be decided that a Trade
Board is necessary for this industry in
Northern Ireland the scope of the Board
should include workers engaged in all
laundries catering for the public and competing with a commercial laundry for the
trade.
I am sure the reason that influenced the
committee to come to that conclusion was
that they felt it was unfair to tie up one
section of the trade under a Trade Board
and leave another section free. They felt
that that would mean that one section of
the trade would be in a more favourable
position to compete for business than the
other section would be, and with that view
I was in entire sympathy. The practical
difficulty, however, is this-and, after all,
we live in a practical world-that the
institutional laundries, whether they be
under Catholic or Protestant auspices, are
really charitable institutions. They are
there for the purpose of providing a safe
refuge for those unfortunate women who are
not in a position to protect themselves.
Mr. COOTE: Will you let them be sweated
because they are unfortunate?
Mr. ANDREWS: Certainly not.
Mr. COOTE: How are you going to prevent
it?
Mr. ANDREWS: I was just going to deal
with that if the hon. Member will give me
a moment. The point is this-that this industry is divided into two sections, as I have
already said. You have got the institutional
laundries on the one hand and you have
got the commercial laundries on the other
hand. They are more or less competing bodies
and if you were to tie one and leave the other
free you would get an industrial condition
that would not be fair or reasonable.
We have had negotiations between the
institutional laundries on the one
hand, and the commercial laundries
on the other hand, and I am glad
to say that these conferences have resulted
in what I feel to be a happy way out
of the difficulty. An arrangement has been
agreed to between the parties concerned regarding charges that will prevent undercutting. It will prevent one section of the
trade being in a more satisfactory position
than the other section to compete for such
trade as is going.
Mr. McGUFFIN: Might I ask how the
Minister intends to provide for that supervision?
Mr. ANDREWS. I can answer my hon.
Friend quite easily-in fact I was going to
do so later, but he has anticipated what I
was going to say. This agreement between
the parties concerned, about which some hon.
Members seem to be a little bit uneasy, is
not an agreement for all time. It is an
agreement on the basis of goodwill between
the parties themselves. A joint committee
has been set up composed of representatives
of the institutional laundries and the commercial laundries which will review the
prices from time to time and will meet to
consider the problem as occasion may require.
I come now to another side of the same
problem which will interest the House. With
reference to the conditions under which persons work in these institutional establishments, I may say I have had an opportunity
of inspecting some of these institutions myself, including the Good Shepherd institution,
and I can testify that they conform to our
Factory Regulations and exceed these regulations in excellence in several respects. It
will, however, be open for our inspectors to
visit these establishments from time to time,
so that an old controversy which caused much
unpleasantness in the past can now be left
safely at rest. It is a settlement through
good-will displayed by both the representatives of the commercial and institutional
laundries, and I appreciate greatly the spirit
in which it has been made.
This Bill deals with a business problem
and I have tried to explain it in
a plain business way.
I appreciate
very much the patient way in' which
the House has listened to me for, I
fear, almost an hour, but I feel instinctively
that hon. Members are all agreed, as are
those whom for the time being they have the
honour to represent outside, that sweating
is a social evil-yes a social crime-and must
not be permitted in Northern Ireland.
Secondly, I think we are agreed as to the
desirability of preserving industrial peace
in every way possible. These are the two

Any officer appointed by the Ministry
under this Act shall have power for the
performance of his duties

•
to examine, either alone or in presence of

any person whom he finds in any such

been a worker in any trade within the

truth of the matters in respect of which

It is a principle of British justice that no
man shall be bound to convict himself, that
he shall not be bound to answer any question
that may be put to him which might lead to
his being involved in a criminal charge.
But an inspector of Trade Boards in this
Bill is given powers far beyond the powers
ever given to any policeman. He can go into
any place if he thinks there might be a trade
carried on there and examine any person,
employer, agent, sub-agent, foreman, worker.
He can compel him to answer any question
which he may put in the presence only of
the examinee, who is not entitled to be
protected by any person, and that examinee
is bound to sign a deposition which might
very easily lead to his conviction for a breach
of this Act. That is an absolutely new
principle in the jurisprudence of this
country, and I will never give my assent to
it unless some reasons are adduced that 1
cannot imagine. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) It does not appear in either of the
previous Acts that are applicable to Trade
Boards. It is a new provision in this Bill,
and no
reason has been given so far to
justify it.

Consequently, you have no agreement of
opinion regarding the adoption of Trade
Boards and the desirability of having them.
I do believe that Trade Boards performed
a very useful purpose when they were inaugurated under the 1909 Act. Prior to that
time, sweating was very prevalent. In fact,
I remember distinctly that there was a
regular propaganda with respect to it. It
was led in the British House of Commons
by the Nationalist Member for West Belfast
(Mr. Devlin). There was a furore in this
city in regard to it, and in all probability
it was induced by the fear of investigation.
Although I did not share the opinion of the
Nationalist member for West Belfast (Mr.
Devlin) with regard to everything he said in
respect of it, I saw evidence at the same time
that there was sufficient sweating going on
at that time to warrant the establishment of
a Commission to inquire into the subject. A
Commission was set up. It inquired into the
matter and reported that sweating was very
prevalent, and it proved a lead for legislation. Accordingly the Government introduced the 1909 Bill for the purpose of, as far
as possible, remedying the conditions then
existing. I might say that I am not one of
those who favour the principle of Trade
Boards. I cannot say that I am rigidly
opposed to them, for I doubt their
utility very much. The conditions which led
to the introduction of the Act of 1909 can
hardly be said to exist to-day, and they
would not be tolerated now if they did.
The Act was successful in remedying sweated
conditions of labour, and compelled employers
to recognise more just and merciful conditions and secure better remuneration for the
workers. I think that cannot be denied. The
pity was that it was through compulsion that
those conditions were recognised. Otherwise
the regrettable conditions that existed prior
to the introduction of that Act might obtain
to the present day.
Trade Boards may be necessary, but to my
mind they are undesirable institutions. They
never tend to bring employers and workers
together. That may be challenged. I have
taken the opportunity of interviewing both
sides on the Trade Boards, and I find that
while one side said it was a fairly good arrangement the other side said it was positively scandalous. They do not agree, and
discord, lack of unity and lack of sympathy
continue. Trade Boards are not effecting any
real good. I am not at all disposed to believe that wages would fall absolutely and
quickly if Trade Boards were withdrawn. I ask the right hon. Gentleman (Mr.
Andrews) to remember this, that the workers
have now got to understand that there is a
certain standard of comfort and a certain
standard of remuneration they must have.
That has been recognised, and they
will be slow to forego these things.
I do not think the lapse of Trade
Boards would in any sense affect the
condition of any industry or the remuneration of the worker. I contend this
--and I suppose the right hon. Gentleman
will sympathise with it-that mutual sympathy on the part of both sides with regard
to industrial difficulties is what is really
required. Trade Boards are much like the
law courts where litigants may submit to
but seldom concur in the decision. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) I think that after
the war all necessity for Trade Boards lapsed.
The late Prime Minister, who was responsible
for more enormities than any man I know,
told us we were going to have a new heaven
and a new earth, and we have had neither.
We have had a sort of hell upon earth, which
is the very opposite of his prophecy.
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: We have had
plenty of rain.
Mr. McGUFFIN: We were told we were
taught a lesson by the war. If we were
taught that lesson all I can say is, so far
as I can see up to the moment, the lesson
has been ignored. I am not speaking with
asperity; I only want to speak according to
experience. When employers have a particular purpose in view, when they have an
order to secure, and they think a cut in
wages would help to secure it, they seldom
scruple to make that cut. The unfortunate
thing is that they are oblivious to the effect
it has on the domestic conditions of those
concerned. That, to my mind, is the absolute
truth. What I maintain is this: that if
you bring in a new atmosphere and that
is what we are all hopeful for-by which
it would be possible for the employer on one
side and the worker on the other to meet
and adjust their difficulties you would be
furthering the social condition of the worker
much more than by a perpetuation of this
system. Tyranny in industrial relationship
always brings about re-action, industrial un-

Much of this thing called "ca' canny" in
connection with other industries, that is to
say, lowering the output in order to create
more employment, is nothing but revenge for
low-paid industry. What we really want in
connection with that is more of the human
element. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) We
want the employer to consider when he makes
a profit on wages with respect to the worker,
whether the worker can exist or is left in
destitution. We want him to take up the
human side of it. Depend upon it, where the
human element is absent in connection with
the regulation of any industry, either on one
side or the other, there is going to be no
success. Let me just quote the words of
John Ruskin, who is the despoiler of Ricardo
and Mill with regard to the shibboleths of
their
political economy, and who was
thought to have been the dominating thinker
upon the subject. This is what he says:
Since the industrial system exists for
man, every industrial process, whether of
production, distribution, or consumption,
must be weighed in terms of vital worth,
that is, human satisfaction, before its contribution to the wealth of the nation can
be determined.
It is not the piling up of wealth so-called.
Let me go on a little further. He illustrates
it:
The only wealth is life, life in all its
power of love, of joy, and of admiration.
That nation is the richest which nourishes
the greatest number of happy, contented
human beings, just as that man is the
richest who, having perfected the functions
of his own life to the utmost, has the
highest and widest influence personally and
through his position over the lives of
others.
There is the standard that I would commend
to you. While your Trade Board operates it
will never become effective. Men come there
to antagonise each other, and while that remains there will be a sort of ill-will. It
will present a sort of local difficulty. What
I would commend to the right hon. Gentleman is this: that he should, if possible, induce the unions to become more representative of the workers. He should ask the
workers to become members of their unions.
Let the representatives of the workers on one
side and representatives of the employers on
the other meet together to solve any particular difficulty or industrial problem that relates to the occasion. Let it be done in that
way rather than through the intervention of
any Government authority or any Government office.

Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: I have no intention of occupying the time of the House
for more than a few minutes, but I cannot
allow the opportunity to pass without saying a few words on the main-what I take it
is the main-feature of the Bill that was
presented to the House this afternoon by the
Minister of Labour. I do not intend to go
into any details whatever. That will be a
matter when we reach the Committee stage.
But there are some things suggested in the
speech of my right hon. Friend (Mr. Andrews)
to which I would like to refer. I was a little
bit nervous after the right hon. Gentleman
had proceeded to speak for five or ten
minutes, when he began to tell us what the
duties of the State should be in regard to
labour and to industry as a whole. He was
skating on very thin ice, and I was a little bit
nervous about him as to what he would eventually develop into. (Laughter.) He managed
to come out all right without venturing upon
either advocating the State coming into industry or treading upon any other dangerous
socialist theory. I think he has managed to
extricate himself tolerably well as far as
those points are concerned. Now the first
thing that struck me in regard to the whole
subject is this: is the Bill necessary or is it
not? That is the first thing that strikes me
in regard to the whole subject. Now I take
leave to say that the Minister of Labour
could do nothing else under the circumstances, as I understand them to-day, than
introduce a Bill on this subject into this
House. A committee, as he told us, was
appointed to consider this whole subject, and
they presented to the Government a unanimous report, and on the presentation of that
report I think it was absolutely necessary for
the Ministry and the Government to present
a Bill to this House on this subject. I think
I began to doubt whether it was necessary,
after the reply the Minister of Labour gave
to the question by my Friend for North
Belfast (Mr. McGuffin), when he told us that
the representatives of the employers and the
representatives of labour had agreed that
they had all these things that were essential

without the Trade Boards at all to fix up

Mr. ANDREWS: In one particular industry that agreement was come to.
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: In one particular industry Then probably if my right
hon. Friend had investigated the matter a
little further and invited the opinion of the

might have found out that the same answer
would have been tendered to him as well.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) However, that
is not the position in which we find ourselves now. We have got this Bill, and the
right hon. Gentleman asks the House to accept the main provisions here this afternoon.
And while I am not enthusiastic about these
Trade Boards I recognise that, as things are
at the moment, and in view of the recommendations he has received, we are bound to
have them in some form or other for some
time to come. The Bill is a considerable improvement, to my mind, upon what has
existed hitherto. The right hon. Gentleman
has told us very clearly that the Bill sets up
Trade Boards for two purposes-first of all,
to do away with sweating. Now I think,
although I am sure many hon. Members may
disagree with me, they have accomplished a
great deal in that direction, and there is no
employer to-day worthy of the name of being
an employer who will not be anxious to
see anything in the nature of sweating
abolished. The good employer in days gone
by was penalised on account of the sweating
that was done, and it was impossible for
him to compete with those men who were
sweating their workers, although those employers were willing and anxious to pay a
reasonable and good wage to their workers.
That point in the Bill is one that, so far as
I am concerned, appeals to me, and I think
it will appeal to every right-thinking person
in the community.
The second point that strikes me in connection with these Trade Boards is this: on
the same basis as I have laid down as to
wages paid in connection with industries that
were considered to be sweated employers are
anxious to see a uniform wage in all industries that are grouped together, because they
are then placed upon a basis of equality in
regard to wages, and consequently, as far as
finding markets for their wares is concerned,
they are on the same basis, and it makes for
efficiency and up-to-date methods if you are
carrying on trade in various parts of the
world.
Mr. McGUFFIN: What about the quality
of the work?
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: My hon.
Friend asks what about the quality of the
work. The quality of the work is essential,
and an employer who does not see to the
quality of his work is not doing a good turn
to himself, and he is doing an amazing
amount of harm to the workers. If a trade
cannot be carried on without the danger
that the hon. Member (Mr. McGuffin) fears,
then I think that that trade has in it the
elements of dissolution now or in the near
future. The other point that my right hon.
Friend (Mr. Andrews) referred to was the
question of industrial peace, and he said
that the Trade Boards had secured industrial
peace. I wish they had. They have done
something, I grant you at once, in the direction of bringing employed and employer together, and undoubtedly strikes have been
averted because Trade Boards have been in
existence. It is a good thing for the House,
after all, if we cannot secure the ideal
that we should all aim at, industrial
peace, when there is machinery that
can be brought into existence which
will lessen the evil, to adopt that
machinery and make it as adaptable to the
various trades as the wisdom and experience
of hon. Members will prompt them. There
is another point I like about this Bill in
regard to the changes that have been made.
The hon. and learned Member for the University (Mr. Robb) referred to the question
of appointed members. I do not think the
decision of these appointed members in a
great many cases gave satisfaction either to
one side or the other. Some of the men knew
more about philosophy and literature than
they knew about industry, and business, and
labour. They were not qualified for the
position at all.
Mr. McGUFFIN: A Professor of Latin.
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: I hope the
Minister of Labour, if he has anything to do
with the selection of these appointed members in the days to come, will select men of
wide outlook upon industrial matters, men
of some experience in business life, and men
who have some knowledge of labour problems
as well, and that men will not be put into
these positions because they happen to have
some learned qualifications but have nothing
else from the standpoint of either Labour or
Industry. There are various other matters
that will, I think, be more properly dealt
with when we come to the Committee stage.
The question of piece rate and the question
of time rate I understand thoroughly, and
the hon. and learned Member for the Uni-

should come under the piece rate. As soon as
a young person is qualified to take the piece
rate most employers are only too anxious to
put him on it and take him out of the
other category altogether. However, these
are matters that can be dealt with in the

The vexed question of these institutional
laundries has been referred to. I do not
intend to labour that point, but I do say this
much, that on broad principles any institution and any body of men
employing labour and paying for it, and going
into the labour market and competing for
trade, must be placed upon a uniform
basis. I understand from my right hon.
Friend (Mr. Andrews) that laundries are excluded from the scope of the Bill; they are
not in the enumerated trades, and it will
require a Provisional Order to bring them in.
I know cases throughout the country where
various institutions not only bring in laundry
work but engage in other trades. They compete with the ordinary manufacturer. I am
sure my right hon. Friend is familiar with
that too. This Bill has to do two things.
It has to protect the worker, to ensure that
the worker is paid a proper wage and works
under reasonably good conditions, and it also
insists that the employer has to pay such
reasonable wage as may be decided
upon by the Trade Board for the
work that is performed for him. If
there is going to be competition,
there is, and Trade Boards are going to
be set up to fix a certain standard of wages,
that principle must be insisted upon in connection with an industry that employs
hundreds of people throughout the country.
I think something will have to be done in
that connection, although it is not included
in the scope of this Bill, and, I suppose,
cannot be included in it now.
Mr. ANDREWS: No. 7.

Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: When we come
to that stage we will probably have something
further to say, although I am one of those
who recognise fully the difficulties of the

my right hon. Friend is in in regard to

These are the only remarks I have to make

My
right hon. Friend (Mr. Andrews) has outlined

and the House has listened to

Mr. DONALD: I will not detain the House
very long as I only want to make one or two
observations. My right hon. Friend (Mr.
Andrews) made a very lucid statement with
regard to this Bill. It is a Bill that is not
as simple as it looks. In the first place, we
had a lay-man who tried to interpret the law
at the beginning of this debate and we had
a lawyer who tried to interpret what was a
basis for piece work rate. I know something
about both these subjects, and I am not going
to enlighten the legal man with regard to any
of our secrets but I can tell him this and I
am voicing the opinions of 99 per cent. of
the people who do work on piece work-that、
they do not want any interference either by
Governments or Acts of Parliament as to
what wages they earn in the different industries. I know how the piece-work rate
was built up. Under ordinary conditions
when a piece worker has not sufficient to keep
him going he is simply transferred to time
rate at time and a half. That was a very
easy thing to do, but there is far more in
piece-work rates than I would like to disclose,
and in my judgment the law of contracts has
been and is being seriously interfered with
by Acts of Parliament. Like my hon. Friend
I can remember the propaganda that went on
from 1901 to 1911 with regard to the sweating
that was taking place in the different industries. I agree with him that the conditions have entirely changed between then
and now and that it is almost impossible
now, and that if there is sweating now or
underpaid workers the workers themselves
are more to blame than the employers.
There are one or two points that I would
like to be clear about. When my right hon.
Friend (Mr. Andrews) gets up to reply, will
he tell me what the meaning of the Provi-

sional Order is? I have a kind of idea of

Mr. ANDREWS: Quite right.
Mr. DONALD: It does appear to me that
in this age, instead of passing legislation,
we should, as far as possible, keep away from

some investigations into this matter I was
reminded-and I am speaking now in the
interests of the workers-that immediately
these Trade Boards were set up their effect
was to prevent an employer taking certain
persons into his employment. I have in my
mind two or
and
three old persons,
immediately these Trade Board rates were
introduced one old person was dispensed with
and then another was sent away.
The employers said, "We cannot afford to keep you.
We are compelled to do certain things and
we are going to manage our own affairs." I
deplore that state of affairs, because I know
of old people who, owing to these Trade
Board restrictions, are unemployed to-day. I
know the difficult problem the Minister of
Labour has to deal with. The committee was
supposed to present a unanimous report, but
I question its unanimity. Any employer I

Board. Thank goodness Trade Boards will
not interfere with the industry I had the
honour at one time to work in, because the
workers there would not allow it, and if this
Bill is intended to look after those who
cannot look after themselves
Mr. ANDREWS: That is it.
Mr. DONALD: If that is the object there
is probably something in it, but I would like
to know to what extent that is necessary in
any industry to-day? Nearly everybody is
organised in some shape or form. My right
hon. Friend says the Bill is not needed in
the rural areas where the employer works in
harmony with his workers and is not going
to join a Masters' Federation in order to be
tied down to this and other things. If it
does not apply there it does not require to
be brought into operation in the large industrial centres. It may be said by those
who read my speech that I am opposed to
Trade Boarde. I am opposed to certain
things, but what about the financial aspect
of the Bill? I took something like £19,000
to administer this Act in the whole of Ireland.
I want to know if we are going to increase
our expenditure by appointing inspectors who
will have certain powers at a time when we
cannot afford it. The Minister of Finance
has over and over again asked where he is
going to get the money from for certain
things, and the possibility of increasing
expenditure was one of the reasons why I
did not approach the Minister of Labour to
bring in this measure last year. We could
easily have brought it in last year, but the
view I took was that we were trying to find
employment for everybody, and we would
defeat that object if we told employers they
must pay certain wages. There are a great
many people who would be glad to get work
at any wage and to whom we are paying
unemployment money got on loan. I am not
sure whether we will not have to investigate
the whole financial resources of Northern
Ireland before very long. I am serious when
I say that. When we took the service over
the Prime Minister told us that we, unfortunately, had to pay an increase of 3d. in
unemployment insurance, but he did not tell
us that the unemployed people in Northern
Ireland were to-day receiving on an average
10s. a week less than the average unemployed
person in Great Britain. I take what I consider to be a broad commonsense view of
this question, and I want the Government
to be very careful that they do not overstep
the limits of their resources.
In connection with the administration of
this Act we are already practically two million
pounds in debt, and I do not see when we
are to begin to pay it off. I read yesterday
that our unemployment increased by nearly
1,000 within the past week or two. I know
that, and I know we are going to have a
very black winter. Only one employer in
this House has spoken on this Bill, but I
can assure him that two employers who sit
in this House have told me they do not like
the Bill. Then we are told there is
unanimity on the part of both the employers
and the workers in favour of this Bill. I
have the idea that the Minister of Labour
has been driven by a certain section of
workers who do not care twopence whether
anybody is unemployed. Who were the
Labour representatives on that Committee?
They were Socialists who will go to any
extremes and are demanding Government control of everything. No wonder they want
Trade Boards. But I hold a different view.
I always put a value on my own labour, and
I want no Government interference in fixing
my wages for I can fix them myself. A
similar view is held by most workers. Let
the employers and the workers come together
and keep the Government out of this business
altogether. I am sure this generation is not
going to put up with the conditions which
prevailed in the days of their forefathers.

They are very wide awake, and although they

Mr. LAVERY: I wish to congratulate the
Minister of Labour on the admirable manner
in which he has introduced this very
anomalous subject. At one time I was in
favour of Trade Boards, but to-day I am not,
As a matter of fact at one time I advocated
Trade Boards at meetings of the Association
which in justice to the business I follow, I
was bound to join, for the simple reason that
we were driven from pillar to post by the
trade unions. Now I have completely
changed my view. Give me back the trade
unions rather than the Trade Boards. The
workers do not want them any more than
the employers. They are tired of them. To
my
own knowledge, members who were
appointed on these Trade Boards resigned,
rather than continue to serve on them.
could never understand the system of voting
on the Trade Boards. I have read this Bill

have the opinion of a few. There may be ten

The whole decision rests with the appointed

In all my experience as a member of a Trade

Major SHILLINGTON: I do not intend to

The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY TO
THE MINISTRY OF LABOUR (Mr.
Gordon): The Bill submitted by my right
hon. Friend the Minister of Labour (Mr.
Andrews) has been so lucidly and clearly
explained that a chorus of approval has come
from quite a number of hon. Members on the
manner in which he has introduced the
measure. Trade Boards are but a continuation of the charter granted to the worker
under the Trade Board Act of 1909, mitigating the evils of sweating in industries where
there was no proper machinery for regulating
wages. Several speakers this afternoon, who
I thought would have supported a Trade
Boards Bill, have expressed their disapproval of and disappointment at the
Trade Boards Bill- HOUSE OF COMMONS.
Second Reading.
[Mr. Gordon]
measure. Among some of the expressions to
which utterance was given by some of the
previous speakers was that they saw no reason
or no necessity for the introduction of a
Trade Boards Bill, because the workers were
better organised to-day than they were when
Trade Boards were first introduced. 1
have no hesitation in saying that the
workers to-day are in a worse position than
they were when Trade Boards were first
introduced. Trades unions to-day have a lower
percentage of membership, and their financial
resources are nothing compared to what they
were in 1909. I am of opinion that it is
absolutely essential, not alone in the interests
of the organised trades, but more so in the
interests of the organised workers, that this
Bill should be received and passed by this
House. Many of the questions which have
been put before the House this afternoon are
questions which may be dealt with when the
Bill comes before the Committee, and consequently if I do not deal with every point
that has been raised by the various hon.
Members it is because I feel that the Minister
or myself can deal with them when the Bill
reaches that stage.
The hon. Member for North Belfast (Mr.
Grant) put a few questions to me. One important point he made was that I must not
say he knew nothing about the Bill, but he
himself said "I do not know anything about
the Bill." I am not going to say he knows
nothing about the Bill, but I am going to
endeavour to answer several very important
questions dealt with in the Bill, and to which
it is absolutely essential, when we come to
discuss the matter in Committee, we should
give a wider interpretation than probably
I am able to give the House to-day. The
hon. Member (Mr. Grant) asked what action
would we take to include a trade under the
Act. In replying to that question I am at
the same time replying to the hon. Member
for East Belfast (Mr. Donald). We would
include it by virtue of the Provisional Order,
which would be laid upon the Table of the
House, and to which effect would not be
given until we had received authority from
Parliament. If any exception were taken to
a particular trade being brought in under
the Act the representatives of that particular
trade could petition Parliament, and a committee representing both Houses would be
set up for the purpose of examining the
evidence that might be submitted to that
committee, and recommending to Parliament
the attitude it should adopt as to whether
effect should be given to the Provisional
Order.
The piecework-basis time rate is a complicated matter. The hon. and learned Member
for the University (Mr. Robb) attempted to
explain it, but I fear he adopted such a roundabout method that it was difficult to follow
him. The piecework-basis time rate is nothing
more or less than a rate given for piecework
that will yield the time rate in the trade,
so that the answer to the question raised by
the hon. Member for North Belfast (Mr.
Grant) is that when we refer to pieceworkbasis time rates we refer to rates given for
the performing of certain work which are
capable of yielding the time rate.
With reference to the District Trade Committees referred to in the Bill, and the
question put to me by the hon. Member (Mr.
Grant), it is, as he said, an adjunct of
the Trade Board. It is a district committee
which is appointed with a knowledge of
local conditions that obtain in a certain
district. Our experience in working the
Trade Boards was that many of the districts
felt that there were conditions imposed by
the Trade Boards, by virtue of their representatives from large industrial areas, that
were detrimental to the industry in smaller
or urban areas. Consequently we decided
to form district committees, which would
keep in close touch with the Trade Board
and make recommendations which would be
either accepted or rejected by the Trade
Board in existence.
With reference to varying or cancelling a
rate, under the old system of fixing a rate
under the Trade Board it required a period
of probably four months. Notice had to be
given, a certain time was allowed for the
purpose of receiving evidence, a meeting of
the Trade Board was called, the evidence
was submitted and examined, a certain
period was given for the Minister of
Labour to examine the evidence and to
determine what action he would take.
We have reduced the period now from four
months to eight weeks in the case of fixing
a rate, and for varying or cancelling
a rate from two months to something like
five or probably six weeks. That means that
if an application comes from an employer
to reduce a rate it is reduced in a shorter
period of time. If trade is good and an
application comes from the workers, and
the Trade Board agrees, the increased wage
is paid in a shorter time, so that both for
the employer and the worker it works
equally, and consequently is bound to give
satisfaction to the representatives of each
on the Board.
The hon. and learned Member for the
University (Mr. Robb) referred to juvenile

workers not being included for the piecework-basis time rate under the Bill. If he

The hon. Member for Fermanagh
Tyrone (Mr. Coote) raised an exceedingly
vexed question indeed, and I was surprised
that some of the Labour representatives did
not attempt to deal with it. He raised the
question of trades unions objecting to
trainees, consequently making it impossible
for them to obtain employment. A peculiar
position arises with reference to trainees.
A man is trained in a particular skilled
industry for a period of twelve or fifteen
months, and then it is expected that that
man should be accepted as a skilled industrial worker, while hundreds of thousands of better skilled men, who are more
capable of competing in the industry than
this man, are idle. It is hardly possible that
the trades unions are going to open up their
organisations and receive into their skilled
ranks the man to whom the hon. Member
(Mr. Coote) refers. It is really a matter for
the trades unions. It is not a matter for the
Trade Boards or for Parliament at all. It is
a question whether the trades unions will
discuss this question with the trainees themselves and open up their ranks for the purpose of diluting, as it were, the labour with
which they have been connected, or the
skilled occupation they have an interest in by
serving a period of seven or eight years.
Mr. COOTE: Are the trades unions
stronger than Parliament or the State?
Mr. GORDON: I should say that is an exceedingly debatable point. The State always feels that it is stronger than anything,
but at the same time the Minister of Labour
(Mr. Andrews) and myself are determined to
pursue the course which this House has
mapped out by the suggestions put before us
this afternoon, and that is that the State
should interfere as little as possible in all
sections of industry. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) Consequently we are determined to
interfere as little as we possibly can in any
action the trades unions may take with reference to the trainees. We may offer suggestions, and do our utmost to make the lot of
ex-Servicemen as easy as possible, but we will
take care not to dictate to the trade unions
within their own confines.
Institutional laundries were also referred
to by the hon. Member for Fermanagh and
Tyrone (Mr. Coote). A peculiar position
again arises in connection with the institutional laundries, and possibly we will be able
to discuss this matter in a wider sense and
take a broader view of it when we examine
it in Committee. My right hon. Friend and
myself have given considerable attention to
this matter. We have had deputation after
deputation, representing the institutional
laundries on the one hand and the industrial
laundries on the other hand, but we were
faced with this difficulty, that in the institutional laundries there are those employed
who are practically unemployable elsewhere.
They receive board and lodging and other
perquisites. The parties agreed to a pricelist, that there would be no competition between the two sets of laundries, and this was
perfectly satisfactory.
Mr. COOTE: Hear, hear; and the public
are fleeced.
Mr. GORDON: At the same time, when
this agreement was entered into, we got an
agreement made that there would also be a
reduction to those who patronise the laundries.
May I now refer to the speech of the hon.
Member for North Belfast (Mr. McGuffin)?
I regret that he is not in favour of Trade
Boards. He says that so far as he is concerned he does not favour Trade Boards, and
that to him they are disagreeable.
Mr. McGUFFIN: Undesirable.
Mr. GORDON: He also said that men go
to the Trade Boards for the purpose of antagonising each other. Our experience is different. Our experience with reference to
Trade Boards is that the best of feeling
exists between the representatives of both
sides, and very often agreements are arrived
at without a division between the members.
I should say that in the past few years few,
if any, strikes have taken place in Trade
Board trades.
The hon. Member for Londonderry (Sir R.
Anderson) sounded the right note when he
said that men are in greater need of protection in times of bad trade than when trade
is good, and in times of bad trade it is absolutely necessary that the Trade Boards
should be in operation. They are not
brought into operation for the purpose of
penalising the good employer, but for the
purpose of putting an end to the evil of lowpaid workers. Our experience in connection
with the carrying on of Trade Boards is that
the employers are satisfied. The hon. Member for Derry said that he was satisfied to be
connected with a Trade Board, and our experience is that the good employer is anxious
to become connected with a Trade Board for
the reason that it prevents unfair competition in his trade. Consequently those bad
employers who would be prepared to pay low
wages and to enter the field of competition in
an unfair way are prevented from doing so
by the Trade Boards Act.
Second Reading. 1692
Trade Boards Bill-
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Mr. Gordon]
One important point raised by the hon.
Member for East Belfast (Mr. Donald)
during the course of his speech was with reference to Trade Boards penalising old
people employed by a firm for a considerable
period of years. Let me say that the Bill
we have introduced gives these people exemption. Where an old person has been a
retainer, as it were, in a firm for a considerable number of years, or who is incapacitated
by virtue of ill-health or infirmity, he is
given a card of exemption and permitted to
work in that trade under the Trade Boards
Act, even though he is incapable of
earning the wages determined under
the Trade Boards Act. In conclusion,
I think that the Minister of Labour's
definite reply to a question put by
the hon. Member for North Belfast (Mr.
McGuffin) answered the point raised by the
hon. Member for County Down (Mp Lavery).
The hon. Member for County Down (Mr.
Lavery) said, "Give me back the trade
unions." We are prepared to give you back
the trade unions. If there is an agreement
amongst all parties, if the degree of organisation is such with the workers and the
degree of organisation is such with the enployers that they can confer with each other,
and a kind of wages board can be set up
between them, we are prepared to give back
the trades unions.
A deputation appeared before the Ministry
of Labour representative of the employers in
connection with the spinning trade and of
the workers in that trade. What was the
result? Let me say that I was deeply impressed with the strength of the arguments
put forward, not only by the employers'
representatives but also by the workers' representatives. After giving full consideration
to the matter, and after much give and take
on each side, they agreed that the Minister
of Labour should suspend the operation of
the Trade Board in connection with the
spinning trade, because they had sufficient
organisation amongst themselves to deal with
the question of wages. At the same time
they agreed to fix the wages between themselves for the succeeding twelve months. We
made some headway with reference to that
particular trade. I believe I am expressing
the sentiments of the Minister of Labour
when I say that we have no desire to take
any part in regard to the arranging of wages
in particular trades. We have no desire that
the Trade Board should operate only in the
interests of the low paid and ill-organised
worker. If employers connected with any
particular trade and the workers in that
trade have a degree of organisation amongst
themselves, and are in a position to settle
matters of this kind for themselves, we are
prepared to agree to the suspension of the
Trade Board from that particular trade.
I have endeavoured as far as possible to
answer as many questions as I could within
the short time at my disposal. As to any of
the more important questions raised by hon.
Members and not dealt with by me in detail
I may say that we will endeavour to deal
with them when they come forward again.
Mr. McGUFFIN: May I ask my hon.
Friend if it was not a fact that pressure
was put upon the trade union representatives
to accept the conditions set forth by the employers with regard to the textile trade? 1
made that assertion. I repeat it. I ask the
hon Gentleman, from his own knowledge,
whether that pressure was exerted or
whether the arrangement was mutually
agreed on?
Mr. GORDON: With the knowledge gained
by my experience I repudiate that assertion.
An arrangement was made between the representatives of the flax spinners and the
workers whereby wages were consolidated for
twelve months. An agreement was arrived
at, evidently, from all I can see, a most
amicable agreement for all parties.
Mr. McGUFFIN: Would you permit me
to ask another question? I want to know
was that agreement effected before they came
into the conference or was it the result of
the conference?
Mr. GORDON: I should say not a conference but several conferences in the
presence of the Minister of Labour and
myself.

the Northern Government. The certificates of

of the clause is to give statutory effect and

of that Act in respect of estate duty.
briefly to the objects and scope of the different clauses of the Bill. I think that it
will be found that there is not really any
controversial matter in this Bill, and that
some of the clauses are merely prompted by
expressions that have been made by hon.
Members themselves in this House. This refers more particularly to Clause No. 1.
Clause No. 1 is to relieve certain shows, such
as agricultural shows or shows promoted in
order to further the interest of any particular
industry, from the Entertainments Tax. It
allows of the inclusion of a band at these
shows. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) My
right hon. Friend (Mr. Pollock) in his budget
statement expressed his sympathy with legislation of this nature, and he explained to
hon. Members the great desirability of at all
times moving pari passu with the procedure
at Westminster in the administration
of this particular tax, because the
revenue is collected by the Imperial
Customs and Excise officers under
agency agreement with the Northern Government. The next clause is very similar in
character and provides for the exemption
from the Entertainments Tax of school
entertainments in cases where some of the
performers are over the age of
18 years.
It was felt that the participation of old boys,
that is former pupils of the school,
in a school entertainment should not o
itself render that entertainment liable to
the Entertainment Tax.
an
Clause 3 refers to taxation of a new type
of motor vehicle. It is a type, I believe,
that has not been used to any great extent
in this country as yet. It has been introduced in England and is in the form of a
six-wheeled vehicle in which the carrying
portion of the vehicle is attached or superimposed on the rear wheels of the part that
contains the motor. Doubt has arisen as to
whether this form of vehicle should be taxed
in respect of horse-power or in respect of
unladen weight. It has been decided now
that these vehicles should be treated as
single vehicles drawing a trailer. This is
the adoption of the ruling that prevails on
the other side of the water in respect of
such vehicles.
Clause 4 exempts from stamp duty any
documents that may be required in connection with savings certificates. When the
savings certificates regulations were made it
was not intended that the documents required to be executed in connection therewith should bear any stamp duty, but it was
not sufficiently clear whether legislation permitted that exemption, and so the present
clause is introduced to give statutory effect
to such exemption.
Clause 5 exempts from stamp duty the
certificates of whole-time officers employed by
Part III. Clause 7 repeals the last of the
land taxes. This particular section to which
reference is made required full particulars
to be given in respect of the sale of any
land or the granting of a lease for a term
exceeding fourteen years. This is the only
part of land values sections of the Finance
Act of 1909-1910 that has not been repealed.
Clause & merely provides the method by
which the Ministry of Home Affairs may
make certain refunds out of the Road Fund.
I will just illustrate this. For instance,
there is a rebate allowed in respect of motor
vehicles over a certain age. The permission
for making the payment of such refund was
not clearly expressed in the previous Act
and this will give statutory authority to
enable it to be made.
Clause 9 is in connection with the Loans
Guarantee Act. In the Act as it stands at
present no loan and no guarantee could be
given after 14th December, 1923, but during
the last Session of this House the amount
under the Loans Guarantee Act was increased
to 3 millions. It is considered advisable now
to extend the period during which guarantees
may be given under that Act.
Clause 10 refers to one of our own Acts
passed in the last Session, namely, Section 2
of the Exchequer and Financial Provisions
Act. I may explain to hon. Members that the
object of that clause as it stands at present
is to set up a maintenance and depreciation
fund in connection with public buildings.
Maintenance and depreciation are matters
which ought always to be borne in mind, and
as some of our buildings will in the course
of time be very substantial and very valuable
in character, it was thought that a charge
might arise which might be exceptionally
heavy for any one year to bear, and so it
was considered prudent to set aside a sum
each year.
However, on further reflection,

The second part of Clause 10 is an

Clause 11 is the usual construction clause,
and does not require any comment. I beg to

CONSTABULARY SERGEANT'S OFFENCE.
Mr. COOTE: I desire to explain at greater
length the circumstances arising out of the
question I put to-day to the Minister of Home
Affairs. It has reference to the case of
Sergeant O'Brien, lately of Castlecaulfiela,
and now of Omagh. On the 31st May, at a
Court of Petty Sessions held in Dungannon,
one of the magistrates-a Mr. Bennett-in the
course of his examination of the summonses
which were to come up, found that there was
a particular summons bearing his name, to
which he had not attached his signature at
all. When the attention of the districtinspector was drawn to the circumstances, the
district-inspector knew that Sergeant O'Brien
was in charge of the summonses, and it appears that Sergeant O'Brien tried to make
the district-inspector believe, and through
the district-inspector, to make the magistrate believe, that the summons was
signed by Mr. Bennett himself. Mr.
Bennett said that this could not be so,
and that it was not his signature. Accordingly he wrote to the district-inspector, and
a couple of letters passed between them. I
4K
Police Sergeant's Offence. HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Mr Coote]
will read the district-inspector's letters to the
House. The first one is dated 4-6-1923:-
Dear Mr. Bennett,
Reference summons handed by you to
me on the 28th ult., to which your signature
had, as alleged, been forged, I have to inform you that I instituted inquiries into the
matter, and as a result have elicited the
fact that Special Constable George Walker
was directed, on the 25th May, to bring
the summons to you for signature, and the
constable maintains that he complied with
the order, and that the signature is yours.
On the following day the district-inspector
wrote:-
Dear Mr. Bennett,
I am in receipt of your letter of the 4th
inst., and have noted its contents.
Not having heard from you, as promised
on the 31st ult., I wrote you yesterday
asking for favour of your further remarks
(on paper) following our conversation of
that date, so that our communications
crossed in the post.
I shall indeed be glad when this matter
is cleared up to the satisfaction of all concerned. Actions of the kind alleged cannot
possibly be tolerated in any police force.
I take a very serious view of your
allegation re Sergeant O'Brien's complicity
in the matter.
Naturally the magistrate felt very indignant
at the attempt to force down his throat-to
use a rough expression-the statement that
he had signed the summons, when he knew
he had not done so.
Mr. Bennett wrote:-
District-Inspector Walshe informed me
that Constables Beatty, Scriven, Magner,
Blancheflower, Boyd, Cochrane and Walker
had given him a written statement that
Sergeant O'Brien forged my name to the
summons in their presence. As Constable
Walker had made a written statement that
I signed the summons he states, when
questioned by the D.I. on the point, that
the sergeant coerced him to make the
statement.
I submit with great respect that that is
a condition of things that should not be
tolerated in any organised force, and that
the facts, if they can be proved, go to show
that this man is not a fit person to be in
charge of young constables coming into the
service. Not only did he forge a document
himself, but he went further and coerced the
constable into committing an act of felony.
It is a state of affairs that I hope does not
occur very often in the Force. I am sure
it does not. I submit that it ought to be
stamped out, and stamped out at once. That
is the reason why I bring it before you.
Police Sergeant's Offence.

You can easily understand the position of
a young constable going into the Force under
the influence of a very cute and seasoned
sergeant, who knows all the tricks of the
trade, so to speak. To allow that man to
have any influence of this kind over a young
constable is an atrocious thing. Presumably
that document stating that the summons was
served by the sergeant himself and that the
constable was coerced into saying he
brought the summons to the magistrate to
have it signed was sent to the districtinspector, then to the county-inspector, and
through him to the Inspector-General. I
want to ask the right hon. the Attorney-
General is this document in existence? Will
this man stand by the document? Will he
retain the services of a man who coerced a
young constable to do a thing he had no
right to do? That is my point. With regard
to the question of prosecution, in the Police
Code, at page 116, Courts of Inquiry, No. 490,
it states:-
Members of the Force offending against
the law will be tried before the ordinary
tribunals of the country, and the same
steps are to be adopted towards them as
would be followed in the case of persons
unconnected with the Constabulary.
I want to ask the Attorney-General if I
forge a man's name to a document will he
not order a prosecution against me? Why
screen a man because he is a policeman?
That is the point I wish to put before the
Attorney-General. If this man has done
wrong a course should be taken that is open
to all men. This is a free country. If we
are to condone these things in the beginning
of a great Force it spells badly for the purity
and dignity of that Force. I am not a lawyer
-I am sorry I am not-but I suggest to the
Attorney-General, and he will correct me if
I am wrong, that under 24 and 25 Vic., chap.
98, sec. 32, this man can be charged as a
felon. When the leaders of the Force do not
take disciplinary action this man ought to be
handed over and tried in the ordinary way.

for forgery could not have been sustained.
I so directed. What was the alternative?
The alternative was that this man should be
dealt with from the disciplinary point of view.
Accordingly the case was remitted to the
Inspector-General. Who is this sergeant?
He is a man who has done good service for
the country. He was wounded in an
ambush. He was for many months in hospital,
almost hovering between life and death. He
was, as I say, a sergeant in the old R.I.C.
When the call for recruits came he was one
of the very first to recruit. He has a splendid
record, and I may say this, and I think it
redounds to his credit, that both the districtinspector and the county-inspector pleaded
that he might be dealt with leniently having
regard to his splendid record, to the way he
had been wounded, and to his readiness to
volunteer for service in the R.U.C. Accordingly the Inspector-General dealt with the
matter, and while the way of dealing with
it is entirely in his discretion the punishment has been very severe. What is the
punishment? The punishment is the award
of a bad record, and also that the sergeant
should be transferred from the place where he
was to the place where he has gone to at
his own expense. People may say the
award of a bad record is a small thing. It
is not a small thing. It is a very great
thing, because it stands against the man for
five years, and if any disciplinary matter
should be alleged against him during those
five years a fresh period of five years starts.
He cannot get rid of that bad record unless
he is absolutely free from all disciplinary
fault for five years. Assuming he is not free
from it then it counts against him if he is
applying for promotion, and it counts against
him when his time of service is up in reference to the gratuity he gets. Therefore, I
say this man has been heavily punished,
severely punished, and I think it is a matter
of great regret that all the publicity that has
been given to this case should have been
given to it by the action of the hon. Member
for Tyrone and Fermanagh (Mr. Coote) and
by his friend, Mr. Bennett, the ex-R.I.C.
sergeant, now a magistrate in the county.

BRIDGES DESTROYED BY SPECIAL
CONSTABULARY.
1. Mr. COOPER asked the Prime Minister
if his attention has been called to the fact
that a number of bridges in Fermanagh and
Tyrone were destroyed by the Special Constabulary for the purpose of protecting the
whole of Northern Ireland against invasion
by Republicans from the Free State; and
if he is aware that the authorities have now
given permission to have the bridge at
Crockada repaired, and a broken culvert on
the road between Clogher and Gortnacarrow
rebuilt, both works being in the rural district of Lisnaskea, Co. Fermanagh, the estimated cost of these works being fifty-two
pounds; and whether the Government will
bear the cost of these and other similar
works rendered necessary through no fault
of the ratepayers in the aforesaid counties?
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I have been asked by
the Prime Minister to reply. The reply to
the first two paragraphs is in the
affirmative. As regards the last paragraph,
the Government will recoup to the local
authority the reasonable cost of repairing
any damage to bridges which may have been
done by its own forces for defensive purposes. The question as to the incidence of
the cost of repairing bridges which have
been destroyed by persons opposed to the
Northern Government, as in the case of
Crockada Bridge is under the consideration
of the Government.
PROTESTANT SOCIETIES IN NORTHERN
IRELAND.
2. Mr. COOTE asked the Minister of
Home Affairs if he can give the House the
result of the exhaustive inquiry which he
has caused to be made in the Six Counties
of Ulster as to the ramifications of Protestant societies, and if he can state the
number of societies found existing there,
and what were the reasons why such an
inquiry should have been made?
Sir DAWSON BATES: It is the duty of
the police to satisfy themselves as to the
bona fides of all new societies and associations which are formed in Northern Ireland, and in the normal course of their
duty the police made enquiries regarding
certain societies which, I presume, are the
enquiries referred to by the hon. Member.
It would be contrary to practice to make
any statement as to the contents of reports
furnished by the police for the information
of their superior officers.
Mr. COOTE: Arising out of that answer,
may I ask the Minister of Home Affairs if
ho is in any way nervous or afraid of these
societies and their ramifications through
Northern Ireland?
Sir DAWSON BATES: No. I am not.
Mr. COOTE: Then why does he inquire
about them?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have already
explained, I think, to the hon. Member (Mr.

4. Mrs. CHICHESTER asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether, in view of the
letter from the Ulster Society for Prevention
of Cruelty to Animals, which appeared in
the Belfast papers on October 26th, and contained grave allegations with regard to the
shipment of cattle from the port of Belfast,
he will make a statement regarding the
actual conditions prevailing, and if conditions are as appear in the aforementioned
letter, he will take immediate steps to
remedy this terrible state of affairs?
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (Mr.
Archdale): By permission I would answer
these questions together. The reply to the
first part of the hon. Member's (Mr.
Lynn) question is in the affirmative.
My Department has no official intimation as to how far the Press report
referred to accurately represents the conditions under which animals are carried
from Northern Ireland to ports in Scotland
and England, but I understand that a large
percentage of the casualties was due to the
gales at sea. At the same time, realising
how closely the question of the transit of
cattle is associated with the interests of the
farming community in Northern Ireland, I
at once entered into communication with the
Imperial Secretary, and the matter is now
receiving earnest consideration. The Ministry of Agriculture has, however, no statutory responsibility in regard to the transit
of animals.
Mr. DONALD: Arising out of that answer,

Trade requirements with regard to the
shipping of all cattle across the Channel,
similar to the Board of Trade requirements
in Great Britain are observed; and if he
has no representative in his Departmentthe sooner he has one the better-who can
see to it, because I myself know the regulations are not complied with?
Mr. COOTE: Might I ask further if there
are no inspectors in the port of Belfast-I
do not know whether they are employed by
the Imperial or by the Northern Government-who are entitled to see that the cattle
are put into proper ships and properly
attended in conformity with the statutory
conditions laid down by the Board of Trade;
and are these not carried out in the interests
of agriculture and in the interests of the
whole trade; and is there not some
of ending this appalling condition of things?

Mr. ARCHDALE: With regard to these

the Imperial Secretary, under whose control

at all to say to them. We hope to inquire

bruises, there are bound to be bruises to a
certain extent on the backs of cattle being
shipped. With regard to the deaths, I know
of two ships which went across on the same
night. One lost not a single beast, and the
other, which was forced ahead against the

Mr. ARCHDALE: I have no knowledge of
that.
Mr. LYNN: In view of the unsatisfactory
answers I beg to give notice that I will raise
this whole question on the adjournment.

Servants are to be placed in a category

Labourers Bill.

Mr. MOLES in the Chair.
CLAUSE I (Parliamentary grants in aid
of repayment of loans and advances)-
(1) There shall be paid in each financial
year out of moneys provided by Parliament
to the councils of the several rural districts
in Northern Ireland in which cottages were
provided under the Labourers Acts before
the commencement of the Labourers (Ireland) Act, 1906, being cottages in respect
of which loans are for the time being
outstanding, such sums as may be certified
to be payable in accordance with this
sub-section; and the sums so certified shall
be applied towards the repayment of those
loans.
The sum payable under this sub-section
in any year to the council of a rural
district shall be a sum equivalent to seventeen pounds per cent. of the sum which the
council is liable to pay or to set apart in
the course of that year in respect of the
repayment of any loan outstanding as
aforesaid.

In any event I do not think the amendment

operative, but it may become a very valuable

wording you will see that the amendment
proposes to leave the authority with any

formulating a scheme, and if that scheme
meets with the approval of the Minister
of Finance and the Minister of Home
Affairs it may come into operation.
I would
suggest to this committee
that notwithstanding the babbling that

Affairs. This proposal opens up what I

great question we have to deal with at the

this is not a digression-the new policy of
protection introduced across the water will
not bring any relief to us either.

matter is that these cottages were built for

it was one of the most creditable movements
ever made in connection with the Government control of agriculture. But do not forget the specific purpose for which these cottages were built. It is for the accommodation of the labourers, and my opinion is
absolutely in accord with that of the hon.
Member for Derry (Mrs. Chichester) in that

make an increment through the sale. Then
the cottages pass out of their hands and will
no longer be accommodation for the rural
labourer. That is the main point. That is
to say, we will have to begin and build new

in a vicious circle, building for one to sell to
another, which is not the purpose of the Act
at all.

These Labourers' Cottages Acts are now of
very long standing, and I dare say most of
the hon. Members present realise the motives
which prompted their introduction in the
first instance. It was at a time when
England began to realise the great detriment
that was being done to the physique and
stamina of our nation owing to the constant
lure of the town.
Mr. GRANT: Hear, hear.
Mr. BARBOUR: Our healthy yeomen were
leaving their country pursuits and going to
what might be more attractive from the
amusement point of view-but the far less
healthy environment of our great cities.
At that time sympathy was also entertained
for our farming population. The legislation
had undoubtedly all been in favour of our
great manufacturing centres with a desire
to provide cheap food and the cheapening
of the freights from far distant countries
where food stuffs could be raised much more
cheaply and to greater advantage than within

our own shores. That led to a complete

I quite agree with what has been said about
the agricultural labourer, in fact, I think it
may be said of our country-living population
generally that at a time of stress and sacrifice it bore forth some actual expression of
real sympathy, and that it was perhaps from
our rural districts that the more ready and
valuable response came. It was really out
of consideration for the labourer, and I may
say also for the farmer, his employer, but
I think also from a true sense of the interests
of the nation at large, that this legislation
was initiated to provide healthy dwellings in
the country for our agricultural labourers.
It was some consideration of this sort that
led the Government in the first Act that
was passed-for what we call the pre-1906
cottages to give such a large grant as 17
per cent. from the national funds towards
the annual cost of these houses. Then in
1906 the Government became more generous,
and that contribution of 17 per cent. of the
anuual cost was raised to 36 per cent. of
the annuity repayments arising from the
loans that were required in order to enable
these houses to be built. In regard to the
proposition of the hon. Member for the
University (Dr. Morrison) we have to look

or even from a rural district standpoint,

over our entire Province. The financial
aspect of the case attracts the attention of

runs to pretty nearly £250 each.
Mr. POLLOCK: Hear, hear.
Mr. BARBOUR: The total amount invested in these labourers' cottages for our
Six Counties is about one and a quarter
millions. If these houses were sold to their
present occupants at the figure of £30 instead
of this one and a quarter millions we
would realise the sum of about £275,000,
which would be distributed over these districts in the relief of rates, if we are to take
advantage of this amendment. The annual
contribution by rural district councils in
respect of loans granted them amounts
to £25,000 per annum, and there is
no suggestion on the part of the

sum is to come from. The annual
income in order to reduce these loans is derived from three sources. There is, first
of all, the grant of either 17 per cent. or
36 per cent., which comes from our Exchequer; then there is the actual rent paid by
the occupier of the house, and any difference
has to made up by rates collected by the
rural district council. Therefore, the annual
rental which is paid by the occupant is only
one portion of the annual cost. The rentals
paid by the agricultural labourers vary in
different districts. I do not know whether
some rentals go as low as 9d, but they run to
1s, 1s 3d, is 6d, and even taking 1s 6d the
annual rental paid by the labourer would
only amount to the sum of £4. Hon. Members who own their own houses will realise
that even in a modest house repairs would
probably reach that figure.

You cannot begin at £30 and go to £250,
because immediately you do that you have

Sir DAWSON BATES: I do not think anyone in this House will disagree with me when
I say that perhaps next to the unemployment problem the housing question is one
that presents the greatest difficulty to the
Government at the present time. In the old
days prior to the war the city of Belfast,
where the problem is felt in its most acute
form, was the best housed city in the three
Kingdoms.
Mr. LYNN: Hear, hear.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I think I would not
be going wrong in saying that at one period
there were at least 2,000 vacant houses, and
that at a time when the population was increasing rapidly. There is an absence of
slum areas.
There is also an absence of what
I regard as the most objectionable form of
housing, the flat system. Our houses were
self-contained. The causes which have led
to the present condition of affairs are not
far to seek. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Private enterprise in the old days had been
carried to the highest possible pitch of perfection in Belfast. Ground rents were low;
rates were low; and the small capitalists
were prepared to invest their savings in
artisan dwellings. I think it is only fair
that credit should be given to those pioneers
in the building trade in Belfast and to those
individuals who had sufficient courage and
belief in the future of this city to, in many
cases, invest their life savings. As a result
of all this the workers of the city enjoyed
the benefit of ample and cheap houses.
I have had some figures prepared showing,
for 1912, the comparative rents charged in
Belfast and other cities. Taking an index
figure of £100 for the City of London, I find
that the rent index of Belfast was as low as
.
£46; whereas in Dublin it was £75, Glasgow
£67, Liverpool £65, and in Newcastle-on-
Tyne £84, and this, I think, better than anything else, will give the House an indication
of the value to the community of private enterprise in building. The situation to-day is
completely changed. You are all familiar
with the causes of that change, just as well
as I am; therefore, there is no use going into
that aspect of the question. I have no reason to believe that the rents in Belfast have
increased disproportionately with the rents
charged in the other cities to which I have
referred. If the rents are high-and, of
course, they are higher than they were in
1912-they are correspondingly higher in
other cities, and I am satisfied that our
index figure to-day is not less small than it
was ten years ago. Instead of having empty
houses, from which a worker can select his
home, we are faced with the fact that to-day
in Belfast there is a shortage of something
between 8,000 and 10,000 houses. Anybody
who has studied the situation, or has gone
round the working-class areas in Belfast, will
realise the evils that must necessarily follow
from a congestion of the character I have
mentioned, and this Bill is an attempt on the
part of the Government, so far as within
their resources lies, to do something to abate
this evil. Private enterprise was responsible up till ten years ago for the advantageous position in which Belfast was situated
in regard to housing, and I believe it is only
by private enterprise that the existing situation can be relieved to-day. At the same
time, while I say this, I do not
for one moment mean to disparage
what has been done, and is being done,
by the local authorities to provide houses.
On the contrary, I would like to hear testimony to what they have done under extremely trying circumstances to relieve the
difficulties which have arisen. I would like
particularly to refer to the Belfast Corporation. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) Under
particularly trying circumstances, to which
I will refer hereafter, they have risen to the
occasion, and have helped materially to lessen
the housing shortage. Under this Bill we
Lope to relieve these local authorities from
some of the difficulties which they have encountered in administering former Acts.
There is one particular Act to which I
would like to refer, and that is an Act which
was passed in 1919 by the Imperial Government. The Government of that day undertook to pay an annual subsidy of 25s for every
pound of rent collected by the local authorities in respect of houses provided by them
under that Act. One of the conditions under
which that grant was made was that the
houses provided had to conform to a verv
high standard set up by the Local Government Board of that time. All I can say with
regard to this matter is that the framers of

have been built under that Act, and have

and I believe most of these cost round about
