like the rent he could afford to pay.
Members: Hear, hear.) I believe at the present time few of these houses are occupied by
the type of people for whom they were originally built, and, therefore, so far as the Act
of 1919 is concerned, it did not relieve the
housing shortage in Belfast to any appreciable extent. As regards the urban areas the
Act was availed of to a very small extent,
only 43 houses being built, owing to the huge
cost of construction necessitated by compliance with the Local Government Board
regulations to which I have referred.
Under the Housing (Additional Powers) Act,
1919, a scheme was provided under which
private builders received a lump sum varying from £230 to £260 in respect of houses of
a certain small category, built on or before
the 22nd of October, 1922, but under that
Fortuscheme only 533 houses were built.
nately, the Ministry of Labour were enabled
to make
the
unemployment grants to
extent of 60 per cent. of the cost of labour,
and under this a total number of 1,838 houses
of the artisan type have been, or are being,
erected in Belfast, of which 1,559 are being
erected by the Belfast Corporation, and 279
by private enterprise. In addition, 58 have
been built outside Belfast under the unemployment scheme. I would like here to
bear testimony to the practical help given by
the Ministry of Labour in doing so much to
solve the great problem with which we are
faced to-day.
It will, therefore, be seen that, notwithstanding all that has been done, much remains to be done to provide anything like
an adequate number of houses for the working classes, and, as I said before, this Bill
is an attempt on the part of the Government,
within their resources, to do something to
bridge the difference between an economic
rent and a rent which a working man,
having regard to the rate of wages and the
cost of living to-day, can afford to pay.
Let me deal with the various clauses.
With regard to Clause (1), hon. Members
who have followed similar legislation in
Great Britain will have observed that the
Imperial Government make provision for an
annual maximum subsidy of £6 payable for
20 years for each house erected under the
English Act. The subsidy is paid primarily
to local authorities who are empowered to
enter into agreements and give certain
financial assistance to private builders This
Government, however, have come to the conclusion, as a result of inquiries made and
representations which they have received,
that a lump sum paid down on the completion
of the house is a much more attractive proposition to the private builder in Northern
Ireland than the promise of £6 a year for 20
years. The Government has decided in lieu
of £6 a year payable for 20 years to pay a
lump sum of £60, which is comparable with
the actuarial value of £6 a year for 20 years
on an interest basis of 7 per cent. or 8 por
cent. In addition, and as a further inducement to private builders, the Bill empowers
the local authorities, if they so desire, and
by passing a special resolution to refund for
a period of 5 years the rates payable on new
houses erected.
Now, I will turn to the houses which will
qualify for these financial benefits, namely,
the State subsidy from the Government, and
the voluntary subsidy from the local
authorities. In the first place, the time
limit within which houses must be built s
between the 22nd of October, 1922, and the
1st April, 1925. Hon. Members will recollect
that under the Act of 1919 which I referred
to a private subsidy was granted to builders,
which ceased on 22nd October, 1922, and it
is felt that this Act should apply to houses
between those two dates.
The next point I would like to refer to is
the area within which houses should be
built to qualify for this financial help.
Hon. Members have heard a great deal about
labourers' cottages this afternoon, and 1
think, from what they have heard, they
have come to the conclusion that, as a rule,
ample provision has been made for labourers
in the rural areas. In addition to that, the
difficulty, so far as I can see, that we are
confronted with to-day is not so much congestion in the rural areas as congestion in
the urban areas; therefore, it is proposed
that this Bill should only apply to houses
built within a radius of 1 miles from the
boundary of urban districts. At the same
time there is this one exception-it is felt
that provision should be made for the development of industries which have sprung
up in some of our rural areas, and in regard
to which progress in development is hindered owing to the difficulty of providing
housing accommodation for the workers
engaged in those areas. It is felt that the
Labourers' Cottages Acts would not meet
the situation. Under these circumstances,
it is proposed by Clause 3, Sub-clause (d) (2)
Housing Bill-
Second Reading.
6 NOVEMBER 1923.
to apply the benefit of this Act to houses
built in the neighbourhood of industrial
centres which are required for the development of industries in Northern Ireland.
Now, dealing with the class of houses to
which it is intended that grants are to be
paid, under Sub-clause (4) of Clause 3, it will
be found that the concession will be confined
to houses of a class of what is known as
"kitchen" or small "parlour" houses. It
is felt here that the imperative need at the
moment is for low-rented houses, and,
accordingly, an upper and a lower limit of
floor space is specifically laid down; the
upper being 900 square feet, which would
correspond to a parlour house, and a lower
limit of 600 square feet, which would correspond to a kitchen house.
As a result of representations which have
been received from some of the local authorities to the effect that they could not afford
to build houses of greater floor space than
550 feet, power is taken by the Ministryif they are otherwise satisfied that a proper
house can be erected of these dimensionsto authorise.
In this Bill we have not attempted to
follow the extravagant proposals contained
in the Act of 1919, which I have referred
to, and the working of which has proved so
disastrous in Belfast. We feel that it is
possible, within the limits I have mentioned, to erect a good-even though smallhouse at such a price, that it can be
let at a rent which an artisan can afford to
pay.
Now, with regard to Clause (2), the effect
of this is to enable Local Authorities and the
Government to cut their losses in connection
with the houses erected under the Act of
1919. As I have already said, the houses are
not occupied by the people for whom they
were built, as, in order to avoid serious loss,
the Local Authorities to-day have had to
impose rents far beyond the reach of most of
the working class, and the Government feel
that in the days to come, when the rents
must necessarily fall, the charges on the
Local Authorities will be considerably high,
and, at the same time, the Government
will be faced with the problem of meeting,
for many years to come, a heavy annual
subsidy.
Various conferences have taken place of
representatives of the Government and the
Belfast Corporation, which is the body
mainly affected, and it is felt that the best
and the most courageous course to take is
for the Corporation to sell the houses at
the best possible price they can fetch, and
at the earliest possible date, and that the
Government should commute the annual
liability with which they are faced.
Mr. McGUFFIN: May I ask the right hon.
Gentleman is it a part of the arrangement
that they are to be sold? Is it a part of the
arrangement to pay the £127,000 that these
houses are to be sold?
Sir DAWSON BATES: The arrangement
entered into between my right hon. Friend,
the Minister of Labour, and the Belfast Corporation is that at a suitable time as soon as
possible the houses are to be sold. The
clause which is now before the House enables
the Ministry of Home Affairs, with the sanction of the Ministry of Finance, to enter into
the necessary agreements I have referred to.
Clause 3 deals with the case of houses
erected under the Housing of the Working
Class Acts, 1890-1908, and erected prior to the
passing of the Housing Act, 1919. Under the
Act of 1908 an Irish Housing Fund was estab
lished, out of certain capital sums, by the
Imperial Government. This was a Capital
Fund, and was invested by the Local Government Board, the income of the fund being
applied towards the reduction of the loan
charges payable by urban authorities in Ireland in respect of houses provided by them
under the Acts referred to. The income
which was derived from the fund was generally a fixed one, but as in the years following
the establishment of the fund the number of
houses provided increased, the amounts,
therefore, accruing to each local authority
naturally decreased. We find that for 1918
the grants payable to urban authorities in
Northern Ireland out of the Housing Fund
represent roughly 13 per cent. of the total
liability, and for 1919 the grants only represented 12 per cent., while for the year 1920
the grants were still further reduced to 11
per cent. Hon. Members will remember that
in the case of grants under the Local Taxation Account, which was abolished by the
Government of Ireland Act, 1920, it was decided by this Government to adopt the principle of taking an average of the grants payable during the years I have mentioned, and
if we were to adopt a similar basis the
equitable thing to do would be to
continue the grants formerly paid out
of the Housing Fund on a basis of 12 per cent.
However, as hon. Members will observe, under
the Bill we propose to go a little further and
to pay 12 per cent. They will find that the
share of the Irish Housing Fund which this
Government receives represents about 12 per
cent. of the total annuities falling to the Local
Government Board in Northern Ireland. As
has been done in the case of other capital sums
handed over to the Government of Northern
Ireland, which was formerly used as the payment of paying grants to the various local
authorities, the Northern Ireland share of the
Housing Fund has been applied to the General
Funds of Northern Ireland, and it is proposed

With regard to Clause 4, which extends provisions of the Small Dwellings Acquisition
Act with the view to making the existing
provisions more elastic and more attractive
to would-be builders, the first and most important provision is that advances may be
made by a local authority under the Acts
before the houses are completed. At present
the private builder before he can obtain an
advance under the existing Act has to wait
until he has the house finished. Under these
provisions it is proposed that the local authorities from time to time may make advances
as the result of valuation to the private
builder. Another provision in this clause
raises the limit of the market value of houses
which come within the scope of the Bill from
£800 to £1,200. In addition to that the restriction in regard to the three years'
residence qualification is removed, and the
local authorities are empowered to make
arrangements for having a valuation made
of the advances.
Clauses 5 and 6 are purely consequential,
and I commend this Bill to the House. I beg
to move.

step in again and carry on the work it did

pressing problem. The problem is not

:
only the extraordinarily high price of

I wish to direct my criticism to two points
only. One is the grant of £60, and the other
is the clause that deals with the free rating
or,
in other words, giving local authorities
power to refund rates up to a period of five
years. It used to be our proud boast that
building costs in Belfast were the lowest in
the kingdom; and perhaps it will surprise
the House to know that these costs are now
higher in Belfast than in many other parts
of the United Kingdom. You might naturally
ask "Why?" I will tell you. Some years
ago I, with others, on behalf of the Belfast
Corporation paid a visit to the large industrial centres of England and Scotland to
inquire into housing conditions prevailing,
and I found out that the rents of workers'
houses in Belfast were from 3s 9d to 7s 6d per
week, whereas across the Channel the rents
were from 8s 6d to 13s 6d per week. On
inquiring into the matter the difference was
easily explained. We had in Belfast large
tracts of building ground available; materials
were cheaper, bricks particularly were the
cheapest in the kingdom, being made within
the city boundary, free of cost of handling;
cement was no higher; timber, of which a
large quantity is used in the construction of
any house, was much lower than the cost
prevailing across the Channel; our building
by-laws were less stringent; and, above all,
we had an abundant supply of labour, which
gave a good output, and municipal rates,
generally speaking, were lower. All these
considerations combined made Belfast the
cheapest housed city in the kingdom.
Recently the Belfast Corporation sent 20
deputation across the Channel to ascertain
the cost of building prevailing, and in
January of this year the deputation issued a
report which was made public property.
It was there clearly set out that houses cou.d
be built in Nottingham and Leicester at
something like £300 per house, while the
same type was costing over £400 per house
here. On inquiry into the matter we found
that the materials in Belfast were much
higher in price, and labour across the water
was giving a larger output than in the City of
Belfast. I can give you figure after figure
which would illustrate what I am saying.
In Leicester bricks cost 68s 9d per 1,000 and
in Belfast they cost 105s, but there is a difference in the bricks. We in Belfast have to
use facing and common bricks, but across
the water there is a regulation or common
brick which might not suit here. We And
also that timber here costs £26 17s 9d per
standard against £22 13s in Leicester. Sand
in Belfast costs 5s 6d and in Nottingham
5s. During the past week I obtained the

In my opinion a grant of £60 is not going

As my right hon. Friend (Sir Dawson Bates)
has pointed out, in England they are giving

My capitalised figures are different from
those of my right hon. Friend (Sir Dawson
Bates). I make it out that on a five per cent.
basis it worked out at £75, and the Government of Northern Ireland are borrowing
money at 4 per cent., which on that basis
works out at £77. Therefore, I think the
offer of the Northern Government should be
at least as good as the payment made in England. You naturally ask me what subsidy I
would suggest would induce house building.
At the present time the Corporation of Belfast are building 1,559 houses with assistance given from the Belfast Unemployment
Relief Fund. The Government is paying
eighty per cent. of the wages. As far as I
can ascertain the Government contribution
will work out at £130 per house in the case
of the kitchen type, and £160 per house for
the parlour type, and as fast as we can get
these houses finished they are being sold, and
the people are glad to get them.
I now turn for a moment to Clause 8,
to
which I object. The right hon.

hon. Gentleman has been pressed to do this

consideration. But I do not know of one
qualified judge, a public accountant, or a
surveyor, or a treasurer, who has not condemned the system. It is opening up a dangerous principle, and there is no knowing
where it will end. Just fancy how it works
out. There are two men living next door to
each other, one paying rates and the other
exempt. The man who does not pay his rates
should not have a vote. I think the Minister
of Finance will agree with me when I say
that public authorities do not always represent the public. If you put a man in a house
and say, "For five years we will not ask
you for
any rates," he will not be
anxious about how the money is spent.
Let him pay his rates like any other individual, and he will take a keen interest in local
politics, and will certainly endeavour to return to the Corporation as the local authority
men who will help to keep the rates within
bounds. There are many things against such
a clause, and I do not know one solitary
reason why it should be in this Bill. It is
most objectionable. I am not going to say
Wipe it out" without offering a substitute.
Let the authorities determine what amount

was put in, a clause on the lines I suggest :--
(a) A lump sum grant per house.
The lump sum grant may take the form

houses.
and so on, on those lines. I think it is only

SHIPMENT OF CATTLE.
Mr. LYNN: Earlier in the sitting to-day,
I gave intimation to my right hon. Friend
opposite (Mr. Archdale) that I would raise
this question with regard to the shipment
of cattle across the Channel and the conditions under which they are shipped. I have
no desire to occupy the time of the House.
They have sat long and patiently to-day.
(Hon. Members: "Hear, hear.") But this
is really a very serious matter. I know
exactly that the responsibility does not rest
on my right hon. Friend. Indeed, if it did,
I fancy he would have had it made right at
once. But, still, we cannot shut our eyes
to the fact that a terrible condition of affairs
exists. My right hon. Friend to-day, in
reply to a question, pointed out that it was
often owing to very stormy weather.
little over a month ago I had occasion to
cross to Glasgow. It must have been a very
calm night, because I was not sick. When I
got up the Clyde I discovered that about
twelve fat bullocks had died or had been
killed during the passage across. As I saw
those animals being taken off I could not
help thinking what the casualties would
have been if there had been a stormy night.
There is no doubt whatever that sufficient
care is not being taken in regard to the
treatment of these animals by the shipping
companies or the railway companies.
A
I do not know what the remedy is or how
we can apply it; but I do say that, as
humane persons, our business is to protest
-if we can do nothing else. But surely we
can do something else? Surely we can put
an end to the condition of affairs that has
been described by people who have examined
very carefully, over not one day or two, but
over a very long period. The situation has
become very serious, so far as Northern
Ireland is concerned, and, on behalf of this
House, I would like to enter the strongest
protest I can against the conditions under
which cattle are being shipped at the present time.

something wrong somewhere. I am not an

It has been stated that there were terrible
storms at the time mentioned in this letter

more.

Dr. MORRISON: There is one point I
would like to refer to which has been overlooked or forgotten, and it is the thing
which in this report horrified us so much.
I desire to associate myself with what the
previous speakers have said, and I think
we should be very grateful to the hon.
Member for West Belfast (Mr. Lynn) and
the hon. Member for County Derry (Mrs.
Chichester) for having brought this matter
before us. The Minister of Agriculture
mentioned, and I think he has no intention
of deceiving the House, that a number of
these cattle fell and were killed. Any man
who knows anything about fat and heavy
cattle going across the water knows they are
fatigued by the long journey and want to
lie down, and once they lie down they are
trodden on and destroyed. The men use
their utmost efforts to keep those cattle on
their feet. While I recognise that an
accident like that might happen or that
the rough sea might put them down, the
report which horrified us all so much pointed
to the fact that the backs and loins of these
cattle were so abused and blackened that
they were unfit for use and had to be cut
off before the carcases were sold. A moment's
thought will show that if an animal is lying
on its side, as it would be if it had fallen,
the treading of the others on it would injure
its ribs and not its back. Once a beast
leaves the hands of its owner it is put into
the hands of professional drivers. I have
watched them frequently. The cattle are
driven before them slowly and steadily to
their journey's end, but the moment a beast
falls behind the man rushes up and as soon
as he gets within reach welts it for all he
is worth. I am afraid he must injure its
tissues and make effusions of blood, and that
the carcase when the skin is taken off will
be blackened. I believe we have power
enough to prevent that and for the Ministry
of Home Affairs to take action. I am glad
to know they have done it. There should
be effective supervision of cattle going from
this area, from the railways to the boats
and when they are being put on the boats,
to see that they are not subjected to abuse,
because if an animal on the ship shows the
least tendency to lie down it is welted by
a man with an ash plant and submitted to
the utmost violence and torture to keep it
on its feet. I think if this were carried
out we would prevent this disgrace for all
time. It is a most extraordinary thing to
say we have no responsibility in this matter,
because under the ordinary laws that govern
us we have the right to protect birds and
fishes and all dumb animals from cruelty.
We have officers for that purpose, and we
have courts of law into which we can take
trespassers. As that is so I think we could
bring an action against the trader in cattle
for putting too many cattle into a waggon.
I have seen prosecutions for overcrowding
fowls or carrying them with their heads
down, and why should we not prosecute in
the case of the overcrowding of cattle? If
there is overcrowding in the harbour surely
we have the right of supervision in our own
harbour. I think we have ample power for
dealing with this question, and there is no
good saying we are not responsible. It is
a disgrace to Ulster that this should go on,
and I am glad to be able to raise my voice
in protest against it.
Mr. McGUFFIN: I would like to associate

Northern area. I am not at all disposed to

My hon. Friend, the Member for the

and I may point out that they go in batches

Why did the inspectors of the Society for

I
ate enormously the value of the cattle.
would like to say it is not now only we are

Imperial Secretary here, and I may say he

cruelties. We have been in constant communication ever since trying to find out
whether these things really happened, and

The hon. Member for Derry (Mrs.

the worst casualities occurred. That steamer
was not one of the ordinary vessels trading
from the port of Belfast. She ordinarily
trades from Dublin, but at the time of the

I forget which.
The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of Home Affairs (Mr. Megaw) has told
the House about the police patrol being put
on. I have seen the reports of those police
patrols, and in no case since they went on
have they seen any cruelty. As regards a
bullock or a cow falling when a ship is rolling, I say of course that would not occur
in a properly-fitted ship.
Mr. DONALD: That is the secret of the
whole trouble.
Mr. ARCHDALE: In a very heavy gale a
beast may come down by accident, and I can
assure the hon. Member for the University
(Dr. Morrison) that not only would his ribs
be bruised, but his head and back, indeed
every part of him would suffer. I have seen
it in a steamer crossing the Atlantic. I have
not the slightest doubt that if proper precautions are taken many of these dreadful
occurrences will not take place. I hope that
in a very short time those precautions will
be taken in all cases. As I said before the
owners are going about with the cattle. I
really am astonished, when these dreadful
tales are going about, that no prosecutions
have occurred. I have crossed a good many
times by these steamers, and in every case
I have seen an inspector standing on the
gangway watching the cattle going into their
pens. I have been very careful to watch if
they were battered with sticks. Several times
I have seen them getting a heavier clout than
was necessary, but it was with a very small
switch. I have never seen anything but a
small switch in use. I have seen the owner
going over to the man who did that and preventing any further incidents of that kind.
I do not think the cases, bad as they have
been, have been quite so bad as some of the
lurid reports would lead one to believe. No
one with any humane feelings would permit
such things to happen, and certainly the
Ministry of Agriculture will do everything
they can to see that things are right in
future.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Wednesday, 7th November, 1923.
The House met at Three of the Clock, Mr.
SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answer to Question
SALARIES OF MEDICAL OFFICERS OF
BELFAST CORPORATION.
Dr. MORRISON asked the Minister of
Home Affairs if his Department proposes to
hold an inquiry with regard to the salaries
of the medical officers of the Belfast Corporation; at whose request has this matter
been taken up by the Ministry, and if it is
proposed to confine the inquiry to salaries
of medical officers only, and the reason for
this attitude on the part of the Ministry?
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): The answer to the first part
of the question is that we propose to hold
an inquiry into the proposals of the Belfast
Corporation to increase the salaries of certain
officers, including medical officers connected
with the Public Health, Tuberculosis, and
other Committees of the Belfast Corporation,
which salaries and increases thereof are
subject to the approval of the Ministry. The
inquiry is being held in the ordinary exercise
of the powers of the Government with a
view to their being satisfied as to the
propriety of the proposals.
Dr. MORRISON: Might I ask if the powers
of the Home Office are limited to the salaries
of the medical officers, or have they any
supervision over the whole Corporation
salaries?
are
Sir DAWSON BATES: No. We
specially limited to the public health side.

Mr. LYNN: During the course of the debate yesterday a good deal was said by the
right hon. Gentleman (Sir Dawson Bates)
and by my hon. Friend the Member for South
Belfast (Sir Crawford McCullagh) with regard to the condition of housing in Belfast
some years ago as contrasted with the condition that unfortunately exists to-day. In
trying to reach a solution of this very difficult question it is important that we should
try to study and examine carefully and dispassionately the causes that have led up to
the present shortage of houses. Most of the
Members of this House, especially those who
are citizens of Belfast, know that prior to
1910 the supply of houses in this city was
much larger than the demand. I do not
like to tax myself with saying the exact
number, but certainly there were thousands
of vacant houses in this city, and the
Minister of Home Affairs was fully justified
in saying yesterday that Belfast was one
of the best and most cheaply housed cities
in the Kingdom. He gave figures which
showed conclusively that we occupied a
very enviable position, but unfortunately
that position has not been maintained. One
might ask why the change has come about.
I think it has largely come about from two
causes, the first legislative interference, and
the second an attitude of mind, which has
grown up, that it is as easy to repeal the
law of supply and demand as it is to repeal
any Act of Parliament. Mr. Lloyd George in
his wisdom introduced a Bill in the Imperial
Parliament in 1909 which caused a good deal
of trouble, and which was to settle the agricultural question. By the way, I notice in
passing that he is now making inquiries into
that subject which he was supposed to settle
in 1909 and 1910. The first result of that
action of his was to destroy confidence in
building, and capital that had naturally
flowed into the building industry was taken
elsewhere, with the result that by degrees
building began to ease off in Belfast, and
then the situation became worse owing to the
war. Then, in our attempt to make the world
fit for heroes to dwell in, we undertook a
housing scheme in 1919. As a matter of fact
I think there is scarcely a Member of this
House who would say that that scheme has
been a success.
My right hon. Friend (Sir Dawson Bates)
referred to what the Belfast Corporation had
done, and as I might be disposed to be somewhat biassed in any opinion I would give regarding that body, I would only say that the
other day my hon. Friend the Member for
South Belfast (Sir Crawford McCullagh), who
was more impartial in his treatment of the
Belfast Corporation than I might be, declared that the Belfast Corporation had not
spent a shilling of the ratepayers' money in
carrying out the scheme, so that anything
that really has been done so far as the city
of Belfast is concerned has been carried out
by this much-abused Parliament and by its
ancient parent the Imperial Parliament.
Even that scheme did not work out well.
You may ask me why it did not, and I will
tell you. Every interest connected with the
building industry seemed to lay itself

out with the object of fleecing the unfortunate

am not going to apportion blame on one side

whether it was the bricklayer, whether it was

or the gentleman who sold the slates-it does
not matter who it was-every one was out
with the object of seeing how much he could
make. That was the first result of trying to
repeal the ancient law of supply and demand.
What did it result in? It resulted in houses
being built for the working classes in the city
of Belfast the economic rent of which was 45s
a week. Imagine a working man in Belfast
being asked to pay 45s a week! But I shall
be told, of course, that he really had not to
pay that. Of course he had not, because
Parliament came in and guaranteed fiveninths of the actual sum; but, even when you
take five ninths of it, you discover that these
houses were being let at something from £1
to 22s, at any rate at a rent which made it
impossible for an ordinary working man with
a wage of say £2 or £2 10s a week to take
them, so that, so far as that scheme was concerned, for the working man it proved a
failure.
Now I think I am right in saying, and
I know the difficulties my hon. Friend
behind me (Sir Crawford McCullagh) has
had, and I give him credit for the personal
efforts he has made-(hon. Members: Hear,
hear) because he was fighting against forces
against which it was really difficult for any
ordinary man, to fight, but I think I recollect
--and he will correct me if I am wrong-that
at one period he was going to give us 5,000
houses at a cost of £2,000,000. As I understand it we have got 500 houses at a cost
of something like £600,000, so I do not know
what the 5,000 houses will cost us when
500 have cost us £600,000. That brings me to
a clause in the Bill which deals with the
commutation of the five-ninths that was to
be paid to the Corporation. I hope before
this debate is ended we will get some fuller
information than we have yet had with
regard to the sum of, I think, £228,000 that
the Government is going to pay to the Belfast
Corporation. I congratulate my hon. Friend
(Sir Crawford McCullagh) on being able to
say that they have carried out this costly
experiment-because it has been a costly
experiment--without a shilling expense to
the ratepayers, but I am sorry I cannot
congratulate the Government on the way it
has defended the taxpayers, who after all
have to pay this £228,000. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) If the rumours that reach me
are in any way accurate, I understand that
at one time the Government refused to budge
beyond £150,000. Well, of course, as a ratepayer of Belfast I ought to be pleased that
they did not go beyond £150,000, because
I would have had to pay as a taxpayer, but I
would like to know on what principle the
Government did move from the £150,000 to
the £228,000? I think as taxpayers, not only
of this city, but of the whole of Northern
Ireland, we should get some fuller information regarding this sum that is to be paid
and for which you are making provision
in the Bill. That, of course, is more a
Committee point, and I hope will be raised
and fully debated.
The larger question of housing remains.
My right hon. Friend (Sir Dawson Bates)
yesterday emphasised the fact and rightly
emphasised the fact-that one of the causes
of the shortage of houses was that we had
killed private enterprise. I look on it myself
as if we had deliberately killed private
enterprise in building. Take the Belfast
Corporation and I want to be quite fair
to the Corporation-it has been building most
of the houses in the city, and the cost, as
my hon. Friend (Sir Crawford McCullagh)
pointed out yesterday, of building houses in
this city is much higher than in any city
on the other side of the water. Surely we
ought to know why that is so. Surely the
Government should institute an inquiry as
to why the Corporation was paying double
the amount for something that was being
paid by cities in a similar position on the
other side of the Channel, (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) That is a matter, I think,
that calls for very serious consideration.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) Of course, my
hon. Friend (Sir Crawford McCullagh) very
carefully skidded over the question of direct

Bates) also did not touch on it yesterday,
but it might interest the House to know
that in the direct labour scheme that the
Corporation are carrying out-and I am sure
they are doing their best-the men employed

by private builders. Is that the sort of
thing to encourage? If my figures are wrong
I am sure my hon. Friend (Sir Crawford
McCullagh) will challenge them. I wish he
would challenge them, because I say that
the Belfast Corporation are not getting 350
bricks a day laid, whereas private builders
are getting 800 laid. We ought to know why
there is this difference.

local
matters
in Belfast are dragged

The other suggestion made to meet the

give relief in the way of remission of rates

proposal in the Bill is for the grant of a
lump sum of £60. The proposal of the Imperial Government is £6 yearly payable over
a period of 20 years.
I now want to deal with the very able
speech of my hon. Friend, the member for
South Belfast (Sir Crawford McCullagh),
yesterday. He quoted from the report of a
deputation appointed by the Belfast City
Council last December to visit England, and
I have in my hand the report from which he
quoted. He made a comparison, and he told
us that the houses built in Belfast cost £100
more than the houses built across the water
under similar conditions. But he did not tell
us the wages that were being paid, and this
is a very important point. For skilled
labourers the rate in Belfast is 1s 7d per
hour, in Nottingham 1s 8d, and in Leicester
1s 8d. That means that skilled labourers in
Belfast are paid 1d per hour less than the
skilled labourers in the two towns across the
water. The unskilled labourer in Belfast is
paid 1s 1d per hour, in Nottingham 1s 3d per
hour, and in Leicester 1s 3d per hour. I
want that point brought out, because it is
only fair to say that the whole fault for
the difference of £100 in the cost of the
houses in Belfast and the English towns
named does not rest with labour. The wages
of the Belfast workmen are lower than the
wages of the workmen across the channel.
He also referred to the output, and on that
question the hon. Member for Derry (Sir
Robert Anderson has just touched the spot.
There are three things to be done to solve
the housing problem. If the fault lies with
labour, then I suggest to the Government
that they should call the labour representatives of the building trade together, and they
should also call together those who are holding
up building materials, and who are known as
rings. Then the Government will get at the
truth of the whole situation. Break the rings
and you will get houses. If the fault lies with
labour, let the labour representatives come
together and realise that this is a question
of national importance. We heard a great
deal about that during the war, and I maintain that this is a question of national importance and a very urgent question. If the
fault is due to the output, then something
should be done with a view to getting a
greater output. I am not going to dwell further on that question. I want to give the
House some idea of where the trouble lies.
There are several cities which have just as
much trouble as we have here in connection
with this question. Let me refer to the
troubles they have under the Scottish Board
of Health. In 1922 the Secretary for Scotland said: :-
"I am informed that the total number of
unemployed workers in the building trades
in Scotland was 10,121 in April, 1922, the
latest date for which figures are available.
I have no information about the cost of
house building in 1910, but the average
costs under the State Assisted Housing
Schemes during 1919, 1920, and 1921 are as
follows:-Three-apartment flats in 1919
cost £700, in 1920 £900, and in 1921 £850.
Three-apartment cottages in 1919 cost
£750, in 1920 £950, and in 1921 £950."
Further he said:
66 The Scottish Board of Health have not
had a sufficient number of housing tenders
to enable adequate comparison to be made
with these figures, but tenders submitted
last month by the Town Council of Glasgow give some indication of present-day
building costs, the improved cost of four
types of houses specified being £504, £612.
£634, and £699 respectively."
So you see that other cities have their
troubles as well as ours. The hon. Member
for West Belfast (Mr. Lynn) dealt with the
question of the cost of materials. I happen
to have the honour of being a member of the
Cost-of-Living Committee, and it was very
interesting to me when the representatives of
the merchants dealing in the different materials used in house building came before us.
I am not going to give you their names, but
I will quote the evidence given by them to
the Cost-of-Living Committee. I will take
timber first. All the timber coming into Belfast is imported from Canada and Russia, and
the freight on timber brought to the port of
Belfast is 20 per cent. higher than the
freight to other ports, such as Liverpool and
Glasgow. That in itself is one of the things
that has helped to raise the cost of the
building of houses in Belfast. Dealing with
the different timbers, the witness said that
in regard to the timber used in the carcassing

These are all important matters in the

worst case of all, and that is cement. Another witness told us that the present cost
of cement in Belfast is 67s, and in pre-war

He was asked if that was the retail price,
and his answer was:
"Yes, either in ton lots or 20 ton lots.
Perhaps I should explain that cement is in
the hands of a ring at the present time,
the Manufacturers' Federation, and they
deal only with those who buy cement from
them. They do not handle foreign cement.
If you handle foreign cement, or buy outside any of the makers of the Federation,
you are cut off their list and do not get
the discount which they give to those who
support them only; so that at the present
time cement, so far as Belfast is concerned,
is more or less in the hands of a ring."
Does that not prove conclusively that if we

authority is being examined and exposed.
Up to the present it has been clearly shown
that for four solid years the local authority
in Belfast has not spent one penny to share
the burden that was duly theirs, and, further
than that, it can be shown that not only did
they not spend one penny, but they burdene;'

those houses with charges they had no right

The Hon. Member for South Belfast (Sir

the people in about one-fifth of the total cost.

Sir CRAWFORD MCCULLAGH: There is

Mr. COOTE: I know there is not, but there

I would like, if I may, to try to discuss

said that private enterprise would not solve

the problem, if you make it popular. There
are hundreds of people in the city who have
small sums of money, and who, if they could
borrow the remainder of the money at
popular rates of interest to build houses for

private builder, and it is the private builder
who will break the ring. The profiteer will
soon disappear if you encourage the private
builder to build his own houses. I have been
spoken to since I came to the city by numbers of people, who say: Can you not do
something when this discussion comes up to
secure money on loan to the citizens on safe
security, on popular terms, and thus enable
us to build our own houses, and not wait for
this unfortunate Corporation, with all the
juggling that goes on amongst the rings that
control that body?" That is the question you
have to face. I submit it is one of the most
popular ways in which you can face it so as
to break these rings and bring some relief to
the congestion in the city.

under a system of letting. If the Government
was to be responsible for the loss, which apparently was obvions, it was clearly necessary
that they should have some say in the
arrangement as to the realisation of the
property. The Corporation agreed with that,
and on the question of the capital sum which
was required to indemnify the Corporation for
that possible loss it was not unnatural that a
difference of opinion should arise as to the
amount that would be necessary to reach that
result. I did mention in this House and elsewhere that I thought £150,000 would have
been a sufficient capital sum for this Government to pay to the Corporation in
exchange for the liability. That, of
course, did not include the sum of £25,000 or
£27,000, the year's contribution for which this
Government was liable. Several discussions
took place, and it was difficult to reach a conclusion; but finally my right hon. friend, the
Prime Minister and myself decided, as it was
a very complex matter, and as the opinion of
the legal advisers of the Corporation was that
the liability of this Government was a continuing liability for a very long period, it
would be better in the interests of all parties
even at the sacrifice of a small additional
sum of £50.000-if that can be regarded as a
small sum-that the transaction should be
closed, and that the Corporation should be
free and untrammelled in their realisation of
the property. That transaction, as I calculate, did enable the Corporation to proceed
immediately to the realisation of the houses
in question. How far they have succeeded in
that up to the present I do not know, but I
certainly do claim that it was better for the
Government by the payment of this capital
sum to settle with the Corporation than that
a contentious and very disagreeable matter
should be allowed to continue without
limit, probably causing difficulties between
the two bodies. That is the history of the
transaction in regard to the payment of the
£227,000 for which statutory authority is provided in this measure that we are now discussing.
I come now to the question of the subsidy,
and as I had some hand in the settlement of
the subsidy possibly I should not be standing
here and defending it. It is very well known
that the British method of subsidising local
authorities and private individuals is £6 per
year for a period of 20 years. The question
arises then, what would be the equivalent of
that by our own method of paying a capital
sum rather than a continuing yearly liability? Naturally the first inquiry is-Why
did we select a capital sum? Because of the
local conditions, because private builders and
Second Reading. 1802
Housing Bill-
7 NOVEMBER 1923.
others who are interested in the covering of
land with houses greatly prefer a sum of
money in hand rather than a yearly contribution for twenty years. They have very
little interest in what becomes of the houses
at the end of twenty years, because, as is
well known, private builders do not build
houses for retention and for letting, but
rather for sale. We thought, and I still believe it is right, that if private builders were
offered an inducement of a capital sum of
£60 rather than a continuing 20 years' contribution of £6, it would be an inducement to
them to provide houses. (Hon. Members:
"Hear, hear.") What has been my experience? It was obviously my business to discover whether a £60 capital grant would or
would not be an attraction to private
builders, and I found, undoubtedly, that it
was. I have it from different private
Owners of land and from speculators
that the £60 contribution on the part
of the Government was recognised as something that would induce them to build.. On
this very day two of the largest owners of
land and builders in Belfast are making arrangements to continue under the £60 subsidy to put up a large number of houses. That
is the practical proof I offer as to the value
of the £60.
Mr. McGUFFIN: Is the right hon. Gentleman aware that the firm of private builders
to whom he refers have for a long time been
putting up houses irrespective of the subsidy?
Mr. POLLOCK: I am.
Mr. McGUFFIN: Then what is the justification for the proposal to give a subsidy of
£60?
Mr. POLLOCK: I do know that private
builders have been building houses and selling them in large numbers without any subsidy, but inasmuch as the housing problem
is acute it is obviously to the advantage of
the community that some stimulus should be
given to the operations, and it is in order
that a stimulus should be given that the Government decided to follow the example of
Great Britain, and the housing question is,
perhaps, more acute here than it is across
the Channel. But I go further and I say
that up to the present the Corporation has
not lived up to its responsibility in this matter. Under the unemployment scheme the
Corporation has been provided with large
sums of monev as the hon. Member for South
Belfast (Sir Crawford McCullagh) admitted
yesterday, to the extent of £130 per house.
which was provided through the activity of
the Prime Minister, who succeeded in securing a large sum of money in order to
help unemployment. That, however, is a different subject, but I make the point that the
Corporation has been relieved of a large liability by this sum. I am very glad, indeed, to
welcome the suggestion made by the Member
for South Belfast, on behalf of the Corporation, that that body is willing now, as I understand, to begin a contribution scheme so as
to supplement whatever grant the Government may give, and, therefore, expedite, so
far as they can, the building of houses in
Belfast.
I suggest that if the Corporation do carry
out that scheme and are willing to contribute a sum of £40 to supplement the Government's £60, there will be such enthusiasm to
build on the part of private builders and on
the part of those who wish to build a house
to live in themselves, that it will be very
difficult for the labour in the city to keep pace
with the work. I have no doubt that during
the next two years one will see a wonderful
transformation in regard to the condition of
the housing question in Belfast.
If I may
say so, it would not impose a very heavy burden on the Corporation to follow this course,
even taking 5,000 houses as the number that
would at least partially remove the present
acuteness. If the Corporation gave a subsidy of £40 per house, it would represent a
capital sum of £200,000, which at 5 per cent.
would be a yearly payment of £10,000. 2d in
the pound would provide £16,000, SO that
with a rate of 2d in the pound the Corporation could provide 5,000 additional houses and
a Sinking Fund that would extinguish the
£200,000 in a comparatively limited period. I
throw this out in order that the Member for
South Belfast may understand the point of
view from which I approach this question.
Let me say that I have made my calculations
as I sat here, and they developed entirely out
of the discussion I have heard here.
As I said, the question of profiteering and
the other matters that have been discussed at
such length have very little bearing upon the
question, except in so far as the cost of housing is concerned. They have not any bearing
on finance, except in so far as a reduction in
the cost per house will necessarily help the
financial aspect of the question. But I would
remind my hon. Friends that you cannot
interfere with economic laws. You cannot change economic laws as readily
as you can change an Act of Parliament, and
I wish to emphasise the point that under no
conditions can you successfully interfere with
the economic laws, because they will ultimately assert themselves under every condition,
however much you may endeavour to break
through them. Therefore, we have to recognise economic conditions as they are and not
as we would like them to be under the ideal
conditions in our minds. These are the facts
in regard to the financial position of this subject and perhaps my hon. Friend who has
charge more particularly of the technical
aspect, may touch on the other matters.

Local Government Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made and Question proposed: That

Sir DAWSON BATES: As I have already
indicated, the Government propose to set up
a Commission to inquire into Local Govern-
Inent administration, including Poor-law and
medical administration. I think it is obvious
to hon. Members that the question involved
will require protracted consideration at the
hands of such Commission, and following the
recommendations which the Government may
receive from such Commission, some time-a
considerable time-must necessarily elapse
before statutory effect can be given to such
recommendations as may be ultimately
adopted by the Government. In the meantime the experience of the Ministry has been
such that certain immediate amendments in
the existing Local Government administration should be carried into effect, and these
amendments, while to a certain extent they
are of a minor character, will go a
way to make the wheels of Local Government administration run more smoothly.
They are of necessity of a long and controversial character, but are generally
in conformity with the views of the
Local Government authorities as expressed by
the Association of County Councils and other
bodies.
long
I propose to take the clauses of the Bill
separately and endeavour to explain shortly
the origin and effect of these amendments.
Now with regard to Clause 1, which deals with
county infirmaries, these infirmaries were established under an Act so far back as 1765,
and were originally designed to be administered on a voluntary basis. They were not
brought into county administration until the
Grand Jury Act of 1836, and under that Act
the amount which the Grand Jury could contribute to the maintenance of these county infirmaries was limited to a sum of £1,400 per
annum. Although the Local Government Act
of 1898 incorporated the county infirmary system with the whole system of county administration the limitation of £1,400 still
mained. The insufficiency of that annual contribution which the county councils could
contribute to the maintenance of these
county infirmaries was realised by the Imperial Government, and under the Local Government Act of 1902 a clause was inserted
under which it is possible for the County Infirmary Committee to obtain a refund from
the county of any deficit that might arise
after a certificate is given by the auditor. Of
course that arose after the money had been
spent, and it was felt here that it would be
much more satisfactory that the county
council should have power to say beforehand
how much money they have that can be devoted to these county infirmaries.
re-
I think hon. Members will agree with me
that although nothing should be done to affect
the incentive on the part of private individuals and people who are anxious to contribute to these institutions, at the same time
it is undesirable that these institutions, which
carry out such important work in the counties, should live from hand to mouth in the
way they have done up to the present time.
They are the only general hospitals in the
counties and in many cases the only hospitals in which the poorer individuals can
get proper medical and surgical theatment,
and in which major operations
be
carried out. Now it is proposed that the
limitation of the yearly contribution to
£1,400 should be done away with. It might
be left to the County Councils to say how
much they are prepared to contribute in the
future to the maintainance of these institutions. The clause is entirely an administrative one.
can
I would like now to refer to the question
of doctors' salaries. Under the existing law
the salaries of the doctors of these county
infirmaries can only be contributed to by
the counties to the extent of £94 per annum.
I think hon. Members, while they have different views as to what an adequate salary
is for a doctor, will agree with me that the
chief doctor of an institution of this character
is certainly inadequately paid by the sum
of £94 per annum.
Local Government Bill-
Second Reading.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
Mr. LYNN: Can my right hon. Friend
give us an indication of how much of his
time is spent.
Sir DAWSON BATES: My experience,
from what I know of the work of the
doctors in these institutions, is that they devote a large amount of their time to looking
after the patients. They are not whole-time
doctors, but the chief medical superintendent
usually performs all the operations necessitated in that institution. However in this
case also we propose that the county council
may, if they so desire, contribute a larger
amount than £94 per annum to make up the
salary of the doctor.
With regard to fever hospitals under the
existing law the county council is limited to
paying a sum of £500 per annum to the
maintenance of these institutions. Here
again we propose to allow the county councils, if they so desire, to contribute a larger
amount per annum.
The next matter I would like to touch
upon is the question of the superannuation of
the medical officers attached to these institutions. I think they are the only class of
Local Government officials that is not entitled to receive superannuation allowance.
Here again we propose to allow the county
councils if they so desire, in conjunction
with the County Infirmary Committee, to
fix superannuation allowance on the same
lines as the ordinary Local Government
officials.
With regard to Sub-clause 3 we propose
here that the accounts of the County Infirmary Committees should be audited by the
Local Government Board auditor. At the
present time they are not so audited.
I
think it is the only committee in the county
whose accounts are not audited by the Local
Government auditor. I think hon. Members
will agree with me that the county councils
have a right to see that the money contributed is properly spent.
Clause 2 is of a temporary character and
is intended to meet the abnormal conditions
caused by the fact that we have had no census
taken since 1911. Under the Towns Improvement Act, 1854, no place can become a town
within the meaning of the Towns Improvement Act or become an urban district within
the meaning of the Public Health and Local Government Acts unless it has a population of
1,500 at the last preceding census. Representations have been made to the Government
by one district, Whitehead. It has been represented to us that although the population
in 1911, the date of the last census, was something like 1,209 inhabitants, as a matter of
fact it has at the present time a population
of over 1,500. It is a very important seaside
residence, and the inhabitants down there
feel that they should be put in a position to
look after the public health of their own district, and that they should become an urban
district. Therefore we propose that the
Minister of Home Affairs should have power
if, after investigating all the circumstances,
he is satisfied that the population is 1,500 and
otherwise that the district is suitable to take
the necessary steps to put into force the existing law as if the population was 1,500 on
the date of the last census.
to
Clause 3 empowers the Minister of Home
Affairs to sanction justifiable expenditure not
exceeding £100 in any one case which has
been incurred by the Local Government
authority although there is no specific authority for that purpose. In England the
Ministry of Health, which corresponds to our
Ministry of Home Affairs here, has the right
authorise expenditure on the part of
any local authority up to any amount.
While it is perfectly true that up to the present time no such power has been placed in
the hands of the Ministry of Home Affairs or
the old Local Government Board, our predecessor, at the same time it is felt that in
many cases it is most advisable that some
such power should be placed in the hands of
the Ministry. Several cases have been brought
to the notice of the Ministry where hardship
has arisen by the absence of such power. I
will give you one example. It is the case of
the driver of a steam roller who has been in
the employment of the County Council for a
considerable number of years. In driving
this roller, which had got out of control, in
an effort to prevent the roller dashing into a
wall, and perhaps destroying property to the
extent of a couple of hundred pounds he was
thrown from the vehicle and broke his false
teeth. That meant a considerable sum of
money to a man
The
in that position.
County Council found themselves in the position that they could not make any compensation. It did not come under the Workmen's
Compensation Act. They were faced with
doing an injustice to the man or being surcharged.
Mr. CRAWFORD: Could they not have increased his pay a little bit?
Sir DAWSON BATES: That may be perfectly true, but if you increased a man's
wages every time he suffered some slight injury, the scale of wages would rise very
high.
Mr. LYNN: Could it not be covered, as it
is in any private firm, by insurance.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The County Council
is obliged to insure under the Workmen's
Compensation Act, but, as I explained to the
hon. Member (Mr. Crawford), I do not think
I ever heard of a breakage of false teeth coming under the Workmen's Compensation Act.
Lloyds, or some other underwriters, might
do it.

Sir DAWSON BATES: Clause 4 deals with
the fixing of election expenses for an urban
area. Under the existing law the County
Council has to fix the rate of expenses
urban areas in its county, and it has been
found in practice that it is very unsatisfactory that the County Council should have the
duty of fixing the expenses of an urban district. After all, the Urban District Council
is the rating authority, and if it is fit
to carry on the affairs of the district it
is certainly fit to fix the election expenses.
Under Clause 5 we propose to enable the
Rural District Councils to contribute an
annual sum of £5 towards a new Association
of Rural District Councils which is being
formed. At the present time there is an association representing the County Councils.
The County Councils are entitled to contribute a sum of £10 to that association, and I
think it is only right that the Rural District
Councils should have an opportunity also of
contributing to their central body. These
central bodies are extremely useful in expressing the concrete views of the community on
any particular subject affecting the Rural
District Councils or the County Councils.
With regard to Clause 6 it is proposed there
to increase the fee charged for holding a
Local Government Board inquiry from three
guineas to five guineas to meet the present
additional cost.
Clause 7 empowers local authorities to take
over and maintain such War Memorials as
may be vested in them from time to time. At
the present time local authorities can take
over ancient monuments and statues, and we
think it right that the same power should
be placed in their hands in regard to War
Memorials.
With regard to Clause 8, at the present
time local authorities have the right to strike
a rate not exceeding 1d in the pound for the
purpose of advertising the beauties of their
particular districts. It is felt that 1d is not
sufficient, and we propose to allow local
authorities, if they so desire, to strike a rate
not exceeding 3d in the pound for this purpose. Of course, that again, is entirely permissive.
Clause deals with the question of dispensary districts. It is a clause which naturally
follows the recent revision of the electoral
areas in Northern Ireland, which has been
carried out in accordance with the promise
given to the House during the passage of the
Local Government Bill last year. The Poor
Relief Act of 1851 requires that dispensary
districts must comprise complete district
electoral divisions, and the recent alterations
in these district electoral divisions have cut
across the boundaries of some of the existing
dispensary districts. We now propose to ask
the House to allow us either to retain the old
districts as dispensary districts, where considered suitable, or else form new divisions.
Clause 10 deals with the Local Taxation
Account. The object of this Clause is to
carry into statutory effect the principles
which have been adopted by this House for
making grants to local authorities. Hon.
Members are aware that the old Local Taxation Account has been done away with, and
the money from it transferred to the Northern
Government and put into the general funds.
This Clause is to enable the Government to
pay out to these local authorities the necessary
grants from time to time. I do not think
there is anything else to which it is necessary
to draw the attention of the House. I beg to
move.
Mr. CRAWFORD: I desire at the earliest
possible moment to enter a protest against one
or two of the Clauses in this Bill. If I had
not had an opportunity of seeing the Bill a
few days ago, and had only been forming an
opinion of it from the speech of the right hon.
Gentleman (Sin Dawson Bates) I would have
thought it was perhaps a harmless sort of
Bill, and calculated to do good, but I am
afraid that I can only describe it as a Bill intended to increase the taxation of the people
in a very marked degree. The only specific
reason given by the right hon. Gentleman (Sir
Dawson Bates) for doing that is that some one
who was driving an engine was unfortunate
enough to get his false teeth broken. No
other specific reason was given for anything
in the way of the increases which he has foreshadowed to such an extent in the Bill. I
recognise that it would be very difficult to
bring in a Bill that would be applicable to all
the local authorities of the whole Six Counties
of Northern Ireland, but I want to point out
as briefly as I possibly can the injustice this
Bill would do to the county which I have the
honour to represent.
The right hon. Gentleman (Sir Dawson
Bates) spoke of these County Infirmaries, to
which the County Councils were obliged to
contribute an annual amount of from £600 to
£1,400. He spoke as if there were no other
such places in the County of Antrim-I take
it as the one I know. It is interested in one
County Infirmary-and that was the reason
why we should contine to give not only the
amount we were compelled to give in times
past, but that power should be given to the
County Council to increase that contribution
as far as they pleased. Now I am perhaps
not as skilled as I ought to be in what Acts
of Parliament should be, but I am one of
those who think that an Act of Parliament
should not only not put fresh burdens on the
people but should remove at least some of the
burdens that exist at present. The very first
words in the first Clause of this Bill are:

Board laid upon our shoulders, and kept on

Gentleman (Sir Dawson Bates) says "Give
more power to the Ministry of Home Affairs,

little finger is going to be thicker than his
predecessor's loins in this matter. We must
not decrease our payments but we can increase
them if we wish. I would like to point out
that the County Council of Antrim, in April,
1922, sent to the right hon. Gentleman (Sir
Dawson Bates) a resolution on the subject of
the Lisburn County Infirmary. May I say in
passing that Lisburn County Infirmary has
served the County of Antrim in a magnificent
way, and I am not here to find fault with it
in any shape or form. The hospital has
served a good purpose in the past, but it no
longer serves that purpose to County Antrim.
The resolution reads:
"That as Lisburn County Infirmary has
ceased to serve the purpose for which it was
established we strongly urge upon the
Government the necessity of passing a Bill
to repeal the law that makes an annual
contribution by the County Council compulsory."
That resolution was sent by the County
Council of Antrim to the right hon. Gentleman (Sir Dawson Bates) and to the Government, and the reply is the Bill laid on the
Table to-day. We asked for bread and they
have given us a stone. Instead of doing what
was asked they say to the people responsible
for striking the rates in County Antrim,
"Keep silence, and do as you are told, continue to pay as you paid in the past, and we
will give you permission to pay more." We
have to increase salaries and give superannuation to people for whom we are not responsible. Has the Government considered the
position of County Antrim as compared to
what it used to be? In olden times when the
burden was put on our shoulders-and it
was right we should bear the burden-there
was only one place to send our poor people
to apart from the workhouse, and those who
did not want to be tainted with pauperism
had to be sent to the County Infirmary at
Lisburn, We have now excellent institutions throughout the county. Recently the
Government gave power to Boards of Guardians to dissociate the infirmaries from
workhouses, and they have no longer the taint
of pauperism.
We have not only the County Infirmary but
a splendid institution in the town of Lisburn
itself, which is supported by the rates of the
people, and is as well equipped as the County
Infirmary and as well able to look after the
interests of the people. In addition to that
we have one in Larne which is either supported by the rates or by voluntary contributions.
We have one in Antrim, we have one in
Ballymena, we have one in Ballymoney, we
have one in Portrush, we have one in Ballycastle, and we have one in Cushendall. These
are supported either by the rates of the people
in the rural district in which they are situated
or by voluntary contributions, and yet the
Government says to us in County Antrim,
"You must continue not only to support these
various establishments, which are doing the
work better than in Lisburn, but you must
continue to contribute to Lisburn." If the
Government carry this out they will treat the
county most unfairly. Something must be
put into the Bill which should exempt a
county like Antrim, that has taken such an
interest in its poor people, and established,
in various districts, hospitals that are doing
excellent work. If we had been neglecting
the poor and had no other place to send them
to but the workhouse, I would be the last
man to say a word against it, but in nearly
every town we have provided a place that has
not the taint of pauperism for the people. If
the return of patients treated in Lisburn is
looked into, it will be found that it is
impossible to send them from the
northern portions of the county. It
would be unreasonable to expect a poor
person to be sent fifty miles to be
treated in the infirmary at Lisburn when
there is one at his own door, and it would be
unreasonable to ask us to pay anything when
we are not sending patients to that place.
I intend to bring this forward in Committee, and will put in amendments which
I hope the Government will see their way
to agree with, so as to do away with this
thing. Section 3, page 4, gives power to the
Ministry of Home Affairs to allow the
auditor not to surcharge a public body up
to £100. I have been a member of a great
many Boards, and I do not think it is fair
for the Government to put upon those people,
who are trying to discharge their duties on
the various boards, the burden of refusing
these things. It simply means that any
person with a peculiar fad for getting something done, and can bring influence to bear
on a Council, will go to the Minister of
Home Affairs, who is a soft, kind-hearted
sort of gentleman, and get him to allow the
thing. Whole lots of things could be done,

in consequence of the overlapping and waste

is another Standing Order. I do not think
I need read it all.

The infliction of fines by the Governors
shall be discontinued. The scale of punishment by the Governor will be as follows:-

8 NOVEMBER 1923.
HOUSE OF COMMONS

Thursday, 8th November, 1923.
The House met at Three of the clock, Mr.
SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions
RELIEF SCHEMES.
1. Mr. DONALD asked the Prime Minister
whether it is the intention of the Government to facilitate further relief schemes for
the relief of unemployment, seeing that poor
people are undergoing real hardship, including those in receipt of only 20s per week
benefit, with no further relief to maintain
the heads of the family and five children?
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): I have been asked to reply to my
hon. Friend. I would refer him to the statement made by the Prime Minister in this
House on the motion for the adjournment on
the 16th October. The Government certainly
intends to continue to give every possible
facility to schemes of public utility undertaken for the relief of unemployment. The
local authorities throughout Northern Ireland have hitherto rendered invaluable help
in the matter, and as the Prime Minister
stated, so long as they continue to submit
schemes of permanent public utility the
Government will give financial assistance to
the fullest extent of the means at its disposal.
REFUSED UNEMPLOYMENT BENEFIT.
2. Mr. DONALD asked the Minister of
Labour if he will state why Robert Carson,
53 Lord Street, Belfast, has been refused unemployment benefit; whether he can find
grounds for refusing benefit, and whether
benefit with arrears due will be paid?
Mr. ANDREWS: Mr. Robert Carson, 53
Lord Street, Belfast, first lodged a claim to
unemployment benefit on 17th February,
1921. Between that date and the 18th
August, 1923, Mr. Carson was paid 488 days'
unemployment benefit, the greater part of
which was uncovenanted benefit. On the
latter date payment of further uncovenanted
benefit was suspended pending a review of
his claim by the Local Employment Committee. On the 10th September, 1923, a Rota
Committee had the claim before them, but
they were not satisfied that Mr. Carson was
making consistent efforts to obtain employment. The Committee took into consideration the fact that Mr. Carson, who is a single
man, had done no work for 2 years, and recommended that further benefit should be
Committee's recommendation.
Mr. DONALD: Arising out of that answer,
in view of the fact that there are hundreds
of people, who like this young man, have
been trying to get employment and have
failed, will the right hon. Gentlemen reconsider this case?
Mr. ANDREWS: It will be remembered that
my hon. Friend was one of those who most
strongly urged the appointment of these local
Employment Committees and Rota Committees, and having appointed them, hon.
Members will appreciate that I am extremely
reluctant to overrule their decisions, which
I find are taken, after very exhaustive
inquiries, in the public interest. I would
like to say that I feel I have got to look at
this matter in a double capacity. I have in
the first place to endeavour to see with the
help and guidance of these Local Employment Committees that benefit is paid where
it ought to be paid, but on the other hand
it is my duty as the trustee of the fund
to see that it is not abused.
This young man has had two and a half
years to find work, and has not found it.
The Rota Committee came to the conclusion
that he was not consistently endeavouring
to find work, and by that decision I have
been bound, unless some fresh information can
be brought before my notice which would
justify me in referring the matter back to
the Rota Committee.
Mr. DONALD: In view of the fact that this
young man is an ex-serviceman, and that the
Minister has been mis-informed, I beg to give
notice that I will raise the matter on the
motion for the adjournment .
REFUND OF CONTRIBUTIONS.
3. Mr. DONALD asked the Minister of
Labour if he will state the statutory conditions relating to a refund from the
Unemployment Insurance Act, under Section
25, that is, the number of weeks the insured
contributor must have paid, having regard
to the age, before a refund can be made.
Mr. ANDREWS: There are two conditions
which our contributors must satisfy before
they become eligible for a refund of
contributions under Section 25 of the
Unemployment Insurance Act, 1920, i.e.:-
1. They must have reached the age of 60,
and
2. They must have paid a minimum number of contributions depending on
their age when they entered insurance.
For example, if a person is under 55 when
he first becomes insured, the minimum number of contributions required is 500. But,

DUTY CHARGED BY FREE STATE.
Mr. MILLER (for Mr. Cooper) asked
the Minister of Commerce if he is
aware that a small parcel stamped
ninepence, containing tea and tobacco,
was posted at Willowfield Post Office,
Belfast, on 12th October, 1923, addressed
to Mrs. Armstrong, Clonshannagh, Drummully, Clones, and then taken to Dundalk, where it was opened, and duty amounting to 3s 7d assessed by the Free State
Authorities, and charged to Mrs. Armstrong,
on delivery at her home in Clonshannagh,
Co. Fermanagh, on 16th October, and if
similar cases have occurred in other parts of
Fermanagh, and if the 3s 7d will be refunded
to Mrs. Armstrong, and by what authority
are parcels for citizens of Northern Ireland
taken to Dundalk, opened and taxed?
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE (Mr.
Archdale): I have carefully examined this
case. It is evident that confusion has arisen
through the fact that the parcel, although
destined for a place in County Fermanagh,
was addressed to a postal district lying in
County Monaghan, and in the circumstances
it is open to the addressee to make application to the Postmaster-Surveyor, Belfast, for
the refund of the duty charged by the Free
State Authorities. In reply to the second
part of the hon. Member's question, I would
inform him that no cases similar to the one
to which he refers have been brought to my
knowledge. I am, however, taking this
matter up with the Post Office Authorities
with a view to securing, if possible, a reorganisation of their distributing system,
whereby Clonshannagh and places similarly
situated will be brought within postal districts situated in Northern Ireland.
