Dr. MORRISON: I should like, if it were
possible, to raise the debate on this subject
into a somewhat different atmosphere to
that in which it took place yesterday. We
were subjected, I think, in the main yesterday, to destructive criticism, but what we
want if possible is constructive criticism.
I understand I shall be followed by my hon.
Friend on my right (Mr. Lynn), who I think
is a constructive statesman, and an opportunity is now presented to the House to do
something constructive with regard to the
treatment of people in the Six County area.
The county infirmaries were established in
1765, that is 158 years ago. The salary then
fixed for the infirmary surgeons was £100,
and in 1836 it was reduced to £94.
There was also £100 given for the maintenance of the infirmary, for food for the
patients, for medicine, and for other necessary supplies. You heard here graphic pictures of men who were drawing large
salaries and who were practically in a Land
of Canaan, a land flowing with milk and
honey. I happen to know something about
the conditions that prevail in these infirmaries and the opportunities that they offer
to medical men. I have a son who was appointed to one of these infirmaries, and the
conditions were such that after six months'
trial he gave it up as a hopeless venture.
Local Government Bill- 8 NOVEMBER 1923.
Second Reading.
He
No man who wanted to progress and make
a decent living would accept the position
conferred by this infirmary appointment.
He had a friend who was a good surgeon,
and he recommended him to try it.
went to this infirmary and tried it, and
stayed for a year. He secured the support
of a large number of people connected with
the shipbuilding industry, and when he tired
of the hopelessness of doing any effective
good, he also threatened to resign. A deputation came to him asking him to stay, hut
he found the position impossible, and he
turned his back on this rich plum that a
speaker here endeavoured to convince the
House was the most valuable position a
medical man could get in a county. Now,
the peculiarity about this thing is that it
was dependent on these two small items of
support, £94 and the £100 local grant, for
its maintenance. The money was voted by
the grand jury, and it was found after a
time that the local people, the people in
the vicinity of these infirmaries, took an
interest in them and subscribed in order to
help to provide the funds that the State was
not able to provide. And so 133 years afterwards, by the Local Government Act of 1898,
there was established what is called the
joint system of management, by which the
local interests and the local people who were
contributing to its funds were associated in
the management that hitherto had been done
by the Grand Jury. They secured in this
way a joint system of management, and I
think it was recognised as a great advantage. The same happened with
regard
to the dispensary system in Ireland, which
is now universal. It also had in each district a certain number of philanthropic
people who contributed to the relief of the
poor before the State recognised its responsibilities. People in the olden time who
gave a subscription of £1 were entitled to
vote in the selection of a dispensary doctor,
but afterwards the whole control was taken
over by the local poor-law guardians, as it
was recognised that these people should have
local knowledge and know what the wants
of the district were. But they had the right
to vote at the selection of an officer in just
the same way as the joint committee of
management did in the selection of an
infirmary surgeon.
That to my mind is a very interesting
evolution. In the first instance you have
centralization, you have the county council
or the grand jury administering these things.
You then find that it is insufficient, that
you want to try to secure local interest, and
that was done by calling in these people and
giving them a share in the appointment of
the officer. That is the second stage, and the
third stage, what we find prevailing at the
present time, has a tendency to go back to
centralization. That is, the whole management is put into the hands of the county
council. The treatment of tuberculosis, the
treatment of venereal disease, the inspection
of school children, and the midwives also come
under the control of the county council by
the Local Government Act of 1898, also contagious diseases of animals and the diseases
of trees and fruit-all these things are
handed over to the county council. You see
the last stage in this evolution is that we
are going back to local control. The union
has in many cases been abolished, and in
place of the union hospital has been developed
the cottage hospital. This cottage hospital
is administered by the local people, by the
guardians, and by the representatives of the
public, who will be expected to assist in the
management and contribute to the funds.
It will be under the control of the central
body, the county council. This shows-and I
think we should profit by this lesson, but I
am afraid that in one respect this Parliament
has forgotten this lesson-that these great
changes that are working out evolving
the true and proper method of dealing with
this question, point to the fact that you
cannot ignore local influence if you wish to
run any undertaking successfully. You may
have the administration by the county council, but it will never become effective unless
you can secure local interest, and so I think
we are coming back to a central contributory system which will co-ordinate and take
advantage of the essential interests that can
only be furthered by local help. I would ask
the House to remember the conditions that
prevailed in Ulster when these infirmaries
were established 158 years ago. We were dependent on stage coaches; we had no railways. Belfast was a little village on the
banks of the Lagan. Lisburn was the central
place in Co. Antrim, it was even then an
important town and had its cathedral. It
is still an important town, and has contributed to the State affairs of this great
Empire of ours very important and valuable
assistance. Any one who reads the history
of Lisburn shou'd be proud of it, and I think
there are indications that the great men
associated with it in the past are still represented, that they, too, will be an influence
in the Empire that no one can estimate.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
Derry city was even at the time the most
prominent place in Ulster. You had Downpatrick, in County Down, which was then
a cathedral city and is still an Assize town.
In these central towns of the counties they
planted the infirmaries, and anyone who
looks at the thing will see that they had
obvious disadvantages. These local and chief
centres are now dominated by other influences.
For instance, Belfast with its phenomenal

growth dominates the whole Six Counties.
I am speaking from the surgical standpoint.
(Laughter). From the surgical standpoint
Belfast dominates the whole Six Counties,

(Hon. Members: Hear, hear). In Belfast we

Obviously infirmaries situated in the chief
towns of particular counties were inconvenient to the great bulk of the inhabitants
of those counties. You have Lisburn here
with its infirmary, and you go away north
to Ballycastle. It is impossible to get
patients to go from Belfast or Ballymoney,
or even from Ballymena to Lisburn. You
have Derry City Infirmary, situated in the
extreme north of the county, and it is impossible to get patients to go from the
southern end of the county so far away from
home as to Derry Infirmary. I had charge
of a large dispensary district for twenty-eight
years, and I think in all that time, although
we were country people, we never sent a
patient-perhaps one or two were sent-to
Derry Infirmary. The result of that was
that people did not take an interest in it,
and they objected to pay rates-naturally
objected to pay rates-and so we formed in
Coleraine and in another place cottage
hospitals, because people objected to what is
called the taint of the poor-law, and
naturally objected. I am proud to be able
to say I was one of the original founders of
the cottage hospital in Coleraine. We spent
a very considerable sum, and we have carried
it on successfully from then till now. The
spirit that animated me in helping that
movement was to get a decent place where
we could attend and look after our own
patients, and, secondly, where a deserving
poor man, who was willing to make a little
effort on his own behalf, could go without a
loss of self-respect to the cottage hospital
and be treated by his own doctor. By contributing a certain sum of money for his
attendance he would be saved the disgrace
that attached to any man who was receiving
relief from the poor law. In Ballymena you
have a cottage hospital, and in Larne, by the
generosity, by the wonderful generosity that
is seen in Larne, you have a magnificent
hospital, presented by a citizen. I have been
through these places. I know them, and I
know the wonderful work they are doing.
They help the deserving poor and give the
doctors an opportunity of performing an
operation under safer conditions than those
under which it could be done in a workman's
house.
A Vice-Regal Commission was appointed in
1906 to examine into the whole relations of
the
these infirmaries. The support for

I would like to tell the House of an incident which I know happened in this hospital
in Omagh, because there are two sides nearly
to every picture. Before we knew anything
about anti-diphtheritic serum there was no
treatment for diphtheria. The House will
remember how Princess Alice went to kiss
one of her children, contracted the disease
by the mere act of kissing him, and died. A
child was brought into Omagh Infirmary, and
the only operation that could be done was
by making an opening in the wind-pipe and
putting in a tube. That tube was blocked by
mucus and did not give the patient the relief it was intended to, because the whole
breathing apparatus was stopped. The infirmary surgeon, who was spoken of so disparagingly here yesterday, sucked the mucus
out himself. He took his life in his hands.
He got the gold medal for an heroic
attempt to save life, and I think he was
worthy of it, and he was worthy of the best
and most honourable traditions of the
medical profession. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear).
One thing that struck me with regard to
this House, and especially during the time
we were discussing the Intoxicating Liquor
Bill, was the fairness of the Members. Some
of us thought that some of the privileges for
which these people that is the trade-were
being compensated had grown up and were
somewhat irregular, and there was really no
moral or reasonable claim for compensation.
But the House, for moral or legal reasons,
no matter what it was, said, "We do not
think it is fair that the men who have enjoyed the privileges should have them
suddenly cut off without giving them compensation," and they gave them compensation. Now you have in these infirmaries,
and there are not very many of them-there
are only six-men who have served their
country and filled these posts, and have done
their duty according to their lights as well
The cottage hospital system will soon be developed all over Ulster. I welcome it. It
will bring relief to the people and will give
them a place near home where they can have
minor operations done, where they can have
major operations done if they wish to bring
a big surgeon from Belfast, and where their
parents can go to see them. It will be a
great boon. I think the policy this House
should adopt with regard to these hospitals
is that they should all be on an equality. I
do not advise that liability should be incurred that will be handed over to the ratepayers. I think the ratepayer has a burden
now sufficiently heavy, and I would wish to
guard against that. We have pressed for the
last twenty or thirty years for a contributory
scheme of pensions. I think if a scheme of
pensions were adopted by which all officials
appointed in future would be compelled to
pay towards the scheme it would prevent any
burden being put on the ratepayers.
Now equipment is necessary for all these
things. It is a fact that sometimes the
county councils and other public boards are
hardly able to distinguish between what is
necessary equipment and what can be done
without. Sometimes, I regret to say, money
is spent unwisely, on the recommendation of
a local doctor, on equipment that turns out
to be practically useless. For instance, you
can easily understand that in the advance of
medical science an X-ray apparatus is sometimes needed, but I do not say that local
cottage hospitals have any necessity for a
valuable and costly piece of apparatus like
that. They have it in some places. I think
it costs more than it is worth for the comparatively few times it is needed. They have
it, I know, in some of the county infirmaries,
but that should be left, I think, to a central
body like one of the great hospitals in Belfast. But, while I would like to guard
against unnecessary expenditure, I would also
point out that if you wish to advance science,
or if you wish to keep shoulder to shoulder
with the advances science is making, money
is necessary, and these things cannot be done
without. The University made a big claim
on the Minister of Finance yesterday. I was
present along with my colleagues pressing for
a big expenditure of money in reference to
the advancement of science. There is a
matter here in connection with scientific
advance in which I think the State should
help. I maintain that the State has no right
to do for people what they can do themselves,
but there are some cases in which individual
1839 Local Government Bill-

effort is not sufficient. There are even some
things sometimes which a whole class cannot
do. On a recent occasion a distinguished
surgeon from Belfast, one of the most
distinguished men I suppose in the city, discussing the newest discoveries of science, told
me that he had two cases of cancer that in
his opinion were inoperable. From what he
said and from what I know, they were inoperable. They were in difficult, inaccessible
places, and the disease had extended from
its original starting point and had affected
other organs. There was no use in attempting to use the knife. He sent those people
over to London and had them subjected to
the new system of intensified X-ray treatment, and he told me that a month afterwards the tumours had disappeared and the
two people were practically well. Now that
intensified X-ray apparatus probably cost
£6,000, and I think it would be very well today if this Parliament would take the
necessary steps to see that it was installed
somewhere in Belfast, so that the people of
Ulster might obtain the benefit that science
has put within their reach.
I beg the House to-day to approach this
question in a proper, kindly spirit, to
approach it with the object of trying to help
to rectify these abuses, and to help the medical profession in reducing sickness and in
saving life. There was no great necessity, 1
thought, for any heat over the introduction
of this Bill. There was no great necessity
for describing it as a stone for people who
were asking for bread. The Bill only gives
powers to the county councils to do certain
things. It is practically optional with them
whether they do them or not. What I would
say to the House is: "Let this Bill go into
Committee, and let us see if we can evolve
some practical measure that will be helpful
to the people of Ulster and just to the men
who occupy positions in these infirmaries."
For my part I back the Ministry of Home
Affairs. I think they have done a wise thing
and a necessary thing. They have introduced
a Bill that was long overdue, and a Bill that
it will be possible to work in a way that will
be very valuable indeed to the sick and
suffering people of the Six Counties. Under
it we will get rid of an old worn-out system,
that has served a great and useful purpose,
and arrangements will be made by which it
will fit in with a great scheme of Poor Law
reform, which I think the Minister of Home
Affairs (Sir Dawson Bates) has in his mind,
that will abolish the taint of the workhouse,
and do something worthy of a great people
for the deserving poor in our midst. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear).
Mr. LYNN: I do not rise for the purpose
of indulging in any captious criticism, and I
do not want to embarrass the Government,
but I want to say this that I think the
Government is pursuing a wrong policy in
giving us an overdose of legislation, whereas
the greater part of the time ought to be
spent in trying to make the new administration more effective. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear). The one thing that the country is
suffering from at the present time is an overdose of legislation, and I am very sorry to
see that this young Parliament, that ought
to set an example to--
Mr. ROBB: To its parent.
Mr. LYNN: To its older Parliament, is
pursuing that same foolish policy that has
been pursued on the other side of the
Channel for the last twelve or fourteen years.
I think the most popular thing that could
happen either here or in Great Britain would
be, if it were possible, to do without a single
Bill for the next ten years. If such a policy
was pursued I believe you would have an
opportunity of recovering from the bad effects
of the legislation that has been imposed
upon us in past years. If I wanted a single
argument in favour of the rejection of this
Bill I would find it at once in the opening
statement of the right hon. Gentleman, the
Minister of Home Affairs. He informed the
House yesterday that he was going to appoint
a commission to deal with the whole question
of Local Government. That really is a
question the solution of which is long over
due (hon. Members: Hear, hear)—and why
the Government on the eve of revolutionary
legislation because we know it will
be revolutionary legislation-come now
and offer a Bill of this character I
for one cannot understand. There is
not a single clause in this Bill that is
really needed except Clause 10, which confirms the grants made to local authorities.
I do suggest to the Government that they
would act wisely, and they would not hurt
their dignity if they would withdraw this
Bill in the meantime and wait until we have
had the result of the commission that is going
to be set up.
I am not going into the question raised by
my hon. Friend the Member for Antrim (Mr.
Crawford), with regard to cottage hospitals

that I am sure in this House he never got

would convince me that it was quite unnecessary to go on with this Bill, because, as
he points out to us, cottage hospitals have
grown up all over the country. In County
Antrim fifty and sixty years ago you had

nothing but the Lisburn Infirmary.

Clause 3 is simply slackening the control that
the Home Office at present keep over local
authorities. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
The one thing that we have got to complain
of is that the control is not strong enough
at present. Some of the most important
councils in Northern Ireland are spending the
ratepayers' money in a most outrageous and
scandalous fashion, and there is no control
over them. Of course, you may say there is
the control of the ratepayer, but the ratepayer only gets exercising that control now
and again, whereas the Local Government
Auditor, who has to go through the accounts
if he has got proper control and proper
power, is able to keep a restraining hand on
extravagant local bodies that cannot be exercised by an unorganised body of ratepayers.
Swift was right when he said on one occasion that one man in armour could always
defeat twelve men clothed only in their
shirts. In the same way, a small public
body which is more or less organised, can
be extravagant without being brought to
book unless you have got the control of a
Central Authority over it. I am sure if I
asked my right hon. Friend the Home Secretary he would tell me with regard to the
extravagance that has been carried out by
some bodies more or less under his control-
I should say less under his control-that he
has no power to prevent them from doing
very foolish things. For example, what
would you think of a local body that discovers that its own roads are very bad, and
not kept in order, and that goes to Spain
for information as to how the roads can be
made worse, certainly not to find out how
the roads can be improved? (Laughter).
This is no laughing matter. It has become an exceedingly serious thing for the
ratepayers in the Six Counties. One of the
troubles that this House and this community, and, indeed, the whole country is
confronted with at the present time is unemployment.
Mr. McGUFFIN: Hear, hear.
Mr. LYNN: And one of the causes of unemployment is high taxation. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) Should it not be the
business of this Parliament, if it wants to
get at the root of unemployment, to try to
reduce taxation at every possible point?
There is not a single clause in this Bill, except the one which deals with the Short
Title, Construction and Repeal, &c., that
does not aim at increasing the burden on
the ratepayer. I wonder has the Government
stopped to think that if this Bill is passed
it is going to increase the cost of local government in the country, whereas the demand
all over the country is to have the cost of
local government reduced? I do appeal most
strongly to the Prime Minister-and no
Member of this House is more anxious to
help than I am-to take a strong attitude
with regard to these policies that are going
to land us into unnecessary extra expenditure. I do say, in the interests of Northern
Ireland, to say nothing of the interests of
the Government, that we should aim at the
cutting down of expenditure at every possible
turn, that we should aim at increasing the
control of the Central Body over extravagant
expenditure. I do not say for a moment that
the Local Government Board should have an
absolutely deciding power as to what the
local council should do, but it ought, where
there is wilful mismanagement of public
funds and where there is wilful extravagance, to have the power to come in and
check these things. If it does, it will be
doing much better service to the community
than it is doing by this Bill. I think this
Bill is wrongly framed. The policy it enunciates is a bad policy, and I do appeal to the
Government to withdraw it.

My hon. Friend (Mr. Lynn) in

Government to withdraw this Bill. I take
it that he has really at the back of his mind
the possibility at an early date of our being
able to introduce a comprehensive measure
dealing with the whole question of the reform of Local Government and our Poor
Law system. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
That was the intention of the Government,
as I announced some time ago, but the more
went into this intricate question the
more certain we became that it covered
such wide field, that it opened up in
every corner of administration in Northern
Ireland issues of really great importancethe more we felt inclined to deal with the
immediately pressing smaller points and

a
On one occasion I had the honour in the
Imperial House of Commons to introduce
upon a Friday, and to get through its Second
reading, a Bill dealing with the reform of
the Poor-law system in Ireland. In the preparation of that measure I had to thank, and
have thanked on many occasions, the present
Lord Justice Moore, who, with several of my
colleagues representing Ulster in the Imperial House, spent long and weary days in
debating the subject, which is one of such
intricacy that the ordinary individual seldom
understands it. I cannot conceive even the
most industrious and learned committee
coping with such a vast question in less than
nine months or a year. Thereafter there
must be framed a Bill, which takes a considerable time, and thereafter it must be
discussed in this House and the Senate before it becomes an Act. Consequently the
Government felt that with that view before
them it was much better to deal with
what I call more or less unimportant matters, but still pressing matters,
to carry us over until the larger measure
is produced. I may say at once that there
is nothing in this measure to in any way
interfere with the larger one when it comes
under jour purview. The matters dealt
with here, moreover, do not constitute a
charge upon public funds to the extent
of one
penny. Clause 10 in the Bill is
printed in italics, which indicates, as my
hon. Friend (Mr. Lynn) and other Members
of the Imperial House will understand, a
charge upon public funds, but even that
clause is only a readjustment and adds nothing to the cost of Local Government.
Then my hon. Friend (Mr. Lynn) objects
to giving more powers to the County Councils. That is really what it come to. He
charges us with over-confidence in the
County Councils and trusting them too
much. I do not believe myself that that
trust will be abused, and I do not believe
that it is good for the community to keep it
too tightly in strings. It is only by responsibility that you will get people with the best
brains in Our Province to come forward and take part in local affairs.
All that this Act does is to give permission
to county councils to make certain provision
if they, as trustees of the ratepayers of the
county, are satisfied that it would be for the
benefit of the community amongst whom they
live. Although we might possibly extend
that proposition too far I hold that by the
moderate scheme which is now before us we
have done what is reasonable and fair, and
we have not held out to county councils any
great temptation to squander public money.
My hon. Friend, I think, said that every
clause meant more money. There is one
clause over which my colleagues and I spent
considerable time, and that is with regard
to giving permission to watering places to
advertise more widely, and the popularity
that might be given to Ulster if they were
all to combine together. I cannot remember
at the moment, and I do not suppose any of
my colleagues can help me, but I think that
at the present moment Portrush only realises £75 by the penny in the £ which it
is permitted to raise for advertising purposes. If one takes Portrush, Bangor,
Whitehead, Newcastle, and so on, and
allows them to advertise individually to the
extent of a penny in the £ they really can
do nothing as compared with the advertisements that are to be seen in favour of the
Isle of Man, in favour of Wales, and in
favour of what is called the Cornish
Riviera. Anyone who travels much across
the Channel will have observed the most
magnificent and picturesque posters in
almost every important railway station
throughout England, Scotland and Wales,
advertising not so much individual places as
a locality as a whole. I have for some
time past been urging these watering-places
in Ulster to combine together to advocate
Ulster as a holiday resort, and let them
pool the visitors when they arrive. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) Although this does
give additional power to raise the rate from
a penny to threepence, that power is confined to the area itself. think the Bill excludes the rural area, and only allows the
urban district to raise a rate for this purpose. It applies only to those who have to
spend the rates and those who have to pay
the extra amount, such as lodging-house
keepers, hotel managers, and so forth, who
will reap the whole benefit by the increase in
visitors whom it is hoped to attract by some
wider scheme of advertising.
That is one

defence, at all events, which I think is a good

Then there is the question of Urban Councils' expenses, which, I think, everybody is
agreed should be paid. The County Councils
have power, and there is no reason why the
others should not have the power, to pay for

Then we had in any case to alter the local

hon. Friend in moving the Second Reading of
the Bill. That is done in one of the other
clauses.
There is also a matter in connection with
Whitehead, which I think was left in a very
difficult position when they are so desirous of
going on with their improvements and being
granted the same privileges as a town. They
have been prevented up to the moment,
simply by the accident that no recent
statistics have been taken of the population
of Ulster.
There are other matters in the Bill which
we are all quite ready to deal with when we
go into Committee. I can only say, in conclusion, that the Government, by introducing
the Bill, far from shelving the larger question,
are only temporarily dealing with these
matters to prepare the road for what I believe
will be the grandest measure of reform that
this House will be asked to pass.

The PRIME MINISTER: It is impossible

The PRIME MINISTER: But I can assure

years if it were possible to do so. (Laughter.)
It does not really much matter when one is
talking about these smaller Bills, but I can
assure the House that there are many things
that will have to be done in Ulster, not in
order to surfeit people with legislation, but
in order that Ulster may be brought up to
the proper standard which it has not yet
reached owing to the blocking of legislation
in the Imperial Parliament for so many years
past.

necessary.

an opportunity to leave one of these county

be pensionable at 65, and can spend the rest

is a condition that ought to hold in any properly run and properly managed institution.
When you take a man you ought to take
him in under the good old Civil Service rule
that he retires at 65. Put him out at 65 and
let somebody who is younger and fresher
have a chance. If these county infirmaries do
in any way fall short of the highest possible
ideals it is simply because in many cases
the men who are in charge of affairs keep

course they should have retired to settle

I think when a man is approaching 65-and

rest. These men all have to do a very large
amount of surgery, which is extraordinarily

Superannuation Bill.
Order for Second reading read.
Motion made and Question proposed :
That the Bill be now read a Second time."
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr. Pollock): This Superannuation Bill, which I now
present for second reading, is a very small
and unpretentious measure, and I hope I will
not incur the censure of my hon. Friend, the
Member for West Belfast (Mr. Lynn) as to the
general surfeit of legislation which is presented to this House. Perhaps hon. Members
may regard this measure as being couched
in somewhat professional and technical
language, because it refers to a number of
Bills that have been passed, repeals
various sections, and may be regarded as
strictly technical in its expression. I think,
therefore, it will be convenient if, in my own
simple and non-technical language, I offer an
explanation of the general character of the
measure. I would remind the House, in the
first place, that this Parliament, in the early
part of its history, passed two other small
Acts regularising the superannuation of
officers in the employment of the Northern
Government. But developments have taken
place since then which render it necessary
to make statutory certain arrangements
which have been arrived at in conference
with the Imperial Treasury.
There are two classes of officers included in
the superannuation measure. The first are
specially-appointed officers, that is to say
those officers who came from the Imperial
service to this side and were specially appointed. Under our own Superannuation Acts
of 1921 and 1922, to which I have made incidental reference, the position of these
officers was regularised as regards superannuation. The Imperial Treasury agreed to
pay its share, whilst we provided for the
period during which the officer was in the
employment of the Northern Government,
which seemed a very fair and equitable arrangement. No arrangement, however, was
made for the re-transfer to Great Britain
of Northern Ireland Civil Servants, if they
elected to return, or were recalled for any
purpose, nor for the members of our
staff who came to us automatically under
the Government of Ireland Act. I have
mentioned that we had negotiations with the
British Treasury, and as a result of those
negotiations it was agreed that, regardless of
the period of service of the officer, whether
in Great Britain or in Northern Ireland,
continuity of service would be observed, and,
when the period arrived for the officer
to be superannuated, proper allocation
and division would be made of the separate
liabilities of the two parties. This arrangement is embodied in Clause 2 of the Bill.
There is another class of servant to which
it is necessary that I should make reference,
-a very small number, but still they require
to be dealt with. When the segregation of the
whole Civil Service was being carried out
under the Government of Ireland Act, there

were certain Civil Servants who made application to come to the North, and who desired
to come to the North. These servants were
then under the Imperial Government in
Dublin. At that time it was not possible to
absorb all the applicants who were anxious
to come to the North, but since that period
it was found necessary to call upon the services of some who had so applied, but who in
the meantime had been automatically
allocated to the Provisional Government.
They only number six or seven, but
as they were technical officers and required for technical purposes in the North,
they were established here as Civil Servants.
The point then arises, what arrangement
should be made for the continuity of their
pensions, having regard to the fact that
they were engaged with the Provisional
Government for a few months? The
amount is comparatively trifling, and
the Free State Government will, it is expected, assume the pension charge for the few
months during which these gentlemen have
been in their employment. As I said, the
amount is so trifling that it is hardly worth
considering, but I think we are under
moral obligation to see that continuity of
service is maintained in calculating their
superannuation when their period of
service comes to an end. These are
the two points contained in this short
Bill, and I have no doubt they will be
regarded as non-contentious, because they
simply conform to the general regulations
which have been in existence for many years
in the Imperial service, in connection with
Colonial servants, and over which we have
control as a matter of course in this
service of ours. I think that fully explains
the nature of this whole measure, and I beg
to move.

The PARLIAMENTARY AND FINAN-
CIAL SECRETARY TO THE MINISTRY
OF FINANCE (Mr. Barbour): On behalf of
my right hon. Friend (Mr. Pollock) I should
like to take this opportunity of refreshing
the memories of hon. Members in connection
with the various developments that have
taken place leading up to the introduction
of the particular clause in this Bill which
seems to have attracted the criticism of hon.
Members. I refer to the grant of housing
loans to Civil servants. I think the other
clauses in the Bill have all been accepted
and approved of in principle. We should
cast our memories back as far as eighteen
months ago when the estimates were presented, on the 14th March, 1922, in which a
sum not exceeding £5,000 was voted for the
purpose of making loans to Civil servants
transferred from Dublin or London to enable them to provide themselves with housing accommodation in the city of Belfast,
accommodation I think which was even more
difficult to get then owing to the large number of servants who had been brought to this
district within a comparatively short space
of time.
This amount was duly passed in the Estimates. These advances were to be repayable
by instalments with interest at Local Loans'
rate. Under the conditions under which these
advances were made the amount of the loan
was limited to one-third of the purchase
price of the house and was repayable in
a period not exceeding twelve years. As
the arrangements developed it became
evident that advances of this kind were not
so much a Revenue charge as the use for
the time being of the capital in the hands
of the Northern Government, and conse
quently were not proper charges to be voted
on the Estimates. In the Exchequer and
Financial Provisions Act, which received the
Royal Assent on the 29th March of this year.
provision was made to transfer such issues
from Votes to the Consolidated Fund and in
accordance with the principles already ap
proved by the House in voting the money
the making of such advances was confined to
transferred Civil servants. While, however,
the Bill was proceeding through the House
private Members pressed that an amendment
should be introduced so that loans might be
made to all Civil servants employed by this
Government, and not only those transferred
from Dublin or London. In deference to the
views of this House the Government introduced an amendment into the Exchequer
and Financial Provisions Bill SO as to
enable loans to be made to all such
Civil Servants. In other words, at
that time hon. Members took a more
generous view of this policy of the
Government than the Government had at
first proposed to the House.
After the Act was passed, that is to say,
enabling these loans to be made from the

Colonel WOODS: This clause is against the
whole policy of the Government, because it
is creating a privileged class. The Civil
Servants are remarkably well off in these days
when both employers and employed are feeling the effects of bad trade. If the Government is prepared to extend this privilege to
the general public there will be nothing
wrong with it, but they are confining the
privilege to Civil Servants. I have nothing
against the Civil Servants. They are all very
decent fellows, and they treat me very well,
but on principle I object to this clause, because it will deprive the Government
money which could be used for the benefit of
the people who pay the taxes. The hon. and
charming Member for Derry (Mrs. Chichester)
drew attention to the fact that there is mistrust of the Parliamentary representatives.
I do not think that this clause will add to
the confidence of the constituents in the
different representatives in this House. The
hon. Member for East Belfast (Mr. Donald)
said that it was a principle of government
to keep abreast of public opinion. I do not
think that the Government has seriously considered whether this will meet with the
approval of public opinion. I know that I
am but a voice in the wilderness. Sometimes
notice is taken of what I say and sometimes
not, but I would like to ask the Minister of
Finance to consider again the question of
extending this principle. If he would extend
it in some degree it would take away to some
extent the feeling that outside people have
that this is a privileged class. From that
point of view it is unreasonable. I just want
to register my opinion in this matter. I know
that no notice will be taken of it, but still I
have to say what the people outside are
thinking.

13 NOVEMBER 1923.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

TUESDAY, 13th November, 1923.
The House met at Three of the clock, Mr.
SPEAKER in the chair.
Oral Answersto Questions,
THE CURFEW ORDER.
1. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Home Affairs if he will now consider the
desirability of withdrawing the Curfew Order
in peaceful areas?
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): As the hon. and gallant
member has already been informed, the
Curfew will be withdrawn as soon as it is
considered safe to do so. To differentiate between areas would raise considerable difficulties. The hon. Member must be aware
that if the Curfew were withdrawn from
areas which are peaceful at present criminals
from other areas would resort to those where
the Curfew was withdrawn, and where as a
consequence their movements would be less
restricted.
GOVERNMENT CONTRACTS.
2. Sir ROBERT ANDERSON (by private
notice) asked the Minister of Finance
whether his attention has been called to the
statement made at the monthly meeting of
the Executive Committee of the Belfast and
District Chamber of Trade, on the 12th inst.,
that in awarding contracts the Ministry of
Finance conferred preference on cross-Channel firms tendering for Northern Government contracts, by refunding to them the cost
of freightage?
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): My attention has been called to the
statements appearing in the public Press to
which my hon. Friend refers. There is
absolutely no foundation whatever for the
allegation that local traders are prejudiced
in regard to tenders for supplies for Governnucnt Departments by reason of the condition
under which a refund of freightage is allowed
in one or two cases.
I may explain that in the great majority
of contracts tenders for goods supplied must
be for delivery at the point where the goods
are to be used. In a few exceptional cases,
however, as in the case of furniture, following on the method adopted by the Imperial
Government, purchases are made at the
works, and when the freight is paid by the
contractor it is refunded; but as this expenditure is always taken into account in
determining the placing of the contract,
certainly no question of preference to the
Cross-Channel firms is involved in the
ariangement.
The criticisms, to which considerable publicity has been given, convey an entirely
erroneous impression, and, as I have stated,
are based on a misapprehension of the position. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)

1871 Local Government Bill-
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Committee.
Mr. BARBOUR: In moving this resolution
I should at once explain that no additional
charge on public funds is contemplated,
The object is to give statutory effect
to the practice which has been followed
during the last two years in regard
to the payment direct from voted
moneys of certain grants to local authorities.
In this connection I would refer honourable
Members to Page 75 of the Estimates, Subhead "J"-Grant in Relief of Rates on Agricultural Lands; Sub-head "K"-Workhouse
Officers' Salaries Grant; Sub-head "Q"—Exchequer Contribution; and to Page 73 of the
Estimates, Sub-heads "M," "N," "O," and
"P," dealing with the Union Medical and
Educational Expenditure Grant, the Sanitary
Salaries Grant, the Maintenance of Lunatic
Poor Grant, and the Railway and Harbour
Guarantees Grant, I may say that all these
grants were formerly paid out of what has
been called the Local Taxation Account.
It will be within the knowledge of hon.
Members that the provisions relating to the
Local Taxation Account no longer apply to
Northern Ireland, and it consequently became necessary for these grants to be made
out of voted moneys instead of being paid as
hitherto out of the Local Taxation Account.
1 may remind hon. Members that this is a
further consequence of our legislation
whereby all moneys accruing to the Northern
Government are paid into our Northern Exchequer, and then the grants are paid out
of the Northern Exchequer instead of being
drawn from certain funds and certain
accounts, as in the past.
The object of this is to stereotype the payments which have been made up to date, and
also to place local authorities in the position
of knowing that payments will continue on
the same basis until a new basis has been
arrived at. The amounts in the case of the
two grants first mentioned, i.e., the old Agricultural Grant and the Exchequer Contribution, are fixed grants, but the amounts of
the other grants, which were formerly
the Estate Duty Grant and the Local Licence
Duty Grant, and which are now comprised
under six sub-heads in the Vote for Grants
to Local Authorities, are based on the average
of the payments made to local authorities in
the three financial years ended 31st March,
1918; 31st March, 1919; and 31st March, 1920.
The stereotyping of these amounts in the
present Bill is merely a temporary arrangement which it is considered advisable to
make until it is possible to remodel the existing system governing the payment of grants
to local authorities. It will be necessary,
however, to carry out a thorough investigation of the Local Government and Poor Law
system of administration, a Committee to go
into which was alluded to by my hon.
Friend the Minister for Home Affairs, and it
will undertake an investigation of the entire
matter. Until this is done, it is not possible
to place these grants on a permanent basis;
but meanwhile the present Bill will stabilise
and give statutory effect to the grants which
have been voted in the Estimates for the past
two years which we have completed. I beg
to move.
Mr. COOTE: I should just like to ask a
question, because of my own want of knowledge and not of any wish to oppose this
resolution. Now that the Taxation
Account is done away with do I understand
the hon. Gentleman (Mr. Barbour) to say
that, therefore, accounts that were passed
by this House, accounts that are perennial
accounts, such as in connection with our
Local Government Board, will now be voted
by Parliament every year, and if so will the
Ministry then not have the right to pay in
the interval through the year such moneys as
have been passed ? What I mean is will the
new system be so ordered that there will be
no hitch in the payment of moneys to public
bodies heretofore paid out of the Taxation
Account ?
Mr. BARBOUR : The object of this Bill is
to give greater security to local authorities
in that respect. They had a statutory right
to these grants in the past, and this is to put
them on a statutory basis in the future.

Considered in Committee.
(Mr. MOLES in the Chair.)
Motion made and Question proposed :
"That for the purpose of any Act of the
present Session giving the force of Law to
certain arrangements made by the Treasury
of the United Kingdom with the Government of Northern Ireland, pursuant to subsection 2 of section seven of the Irish Free
State (Consequential Provisions) Act, 1922,
and amending the Superannuation Acts
(Northern Ireland), 1921 and 1922, it is expedient to authorise a charge upon moneys
provided by Parliament in respect of
amounts apportioned by the Treasury or
determined by the Joint Exchequer Board
to be paid out of the Revenue of Northern
Ireland under the arrangements aforesaid."
Mr. BARBOUR: This Bill deals with
the pension rights of Civil Servants who, at
the time of the passing of the 1920 Act. were
already in the Civil Service and since then
have been transferred to the Northern
Government, or, to look a step further, who
Superannuation (Money)-
Committee.
13 NOVEMBER 1923.
may at present be in the service of the
Northern Government and may at some time
in the future re-enter the Civil Service of
the United Kingdom. The object of this
Resolution, briefly, is to provide that their
service, under whichever Government they
may have served, may be regarded as continuous, so far as pension rights are concerned,
and to provide for the proper apportionment
between the different Governments of the
payment of the pensions to which they would
become entitled. The matter has been referred to by my right hon. Friend the Minister of Finance (Mr. Pollock) in introducing
the Bill. The object, of course, is to give
statutory effect to arrangements recently
concluded with the Treasury in connection
with the transfer and re-transfer of officers
between the Northern Government and the
Imperial Government. The Superannuation
Acts of 1921 and 1929 made provision for
reckoning the Imperial service
"specially-appointed officer" as service with
the Northern Government and for abating
the superannuation allowance payable by the
Northern Government to such officer on retirement by the amount which was payable
from Imperial funds in respect of his
Imperial service.
of
a
It was felt, however, that some reciprocal
made with the
arrangement should be
Treasury, whereby specially-appointed
officer, or one whose original appointment
was with the Northern Government, could
transfer to the Imperial service, and, by so
doing, could have his continuity of service
maintained. The resolution, therefore,
authorises a charge on moneys provided by
this House of the amount apportioned by
the Treasury or determined by the Joint
Exchequer Board as being so payable. The
retiring allowances are calculated on the
retiring salary in accordance with the law
and regulations of the service from which
the officer ultimately retires, and the
Treasury apportions the amount to be paid
by each employer on the length of service
rendered to each employer and the emoluments received by the officer on transfer.
An equitable contribution, therefore, will be
mado by both Governments, having regard
to the service rendered and to the emoluments received in each period of employment, and this contribution will be determined, in the first instance, by the Treasury,
but may be reviewed by the Joint Exchequer
Board if the Northern Government so desire.
I beg to move.
Mr. McGUFFIN: I would like to ask is
this a reciprocal arrangement between the
British Treasury and the Northern Government? Does it mean that one of our servants being transferred to the Imperial service would come under precisely the same
conditions as one of their servants being
transferred here?
Mr. BARBOUR: Yes. That is just the
object of the Bill.
Mr. DONALD: I think the whole thing is
to bring all the Civil Servants, including
Cvil Servants who have been transferred,
together, and, for the purpose of continuity
of service, to put them in a position as if
they never had been transferred. Is that the
meaning of the Bill?
Mr. BARBOUR: Yes, that mere transfer
does not constitute a break in the continuity
of service.
Mr. COOTE: I should like to know if we
are in any way responsible for the pre-existing service of these officials who have been
transferred from the service of another Government to ours? Assuming for the sake of
argument that the other Government breaks
down-I hope it never will break down-are
we responsible for the superannuation of
these servants? I take it-I hope I am
right-that there is only provision here for
the respective service which is given to this
Government being put into our quota, and
that we only contribute on our part for the
services rendered to us. Another question I
should like to ask is: Have we now reached
the limit of the compulsory transfer of these
servants from the Free State to us?
Mr. POLLOCK: I explained when I introduced the Superannuation Bill that there
were two different sets of servants, namely
those who came from the Imperial Government to ourselves-those are the specially
appointed officers-and those who came by a
more circuitous route from Dublin, and were
segregated or separated, therefore, from the
servants who came to us here after the
passing of the Government of Ireland Act.
I would invite the attention of hon. Members
to the fact that this is not the Bill itself;
it is only the Money Resolution, and I would
endeavour to impress on the Committee the
fact that Money Resolutions are only the
preliminary to the Bill. In respect of the
Civil Servants coming from Dublin, their
service under the Imperial authority and
with us is continuous, and when the pensionable period arrives their pensions are separated the Imperial Government pays its
share and we pay our share, as the case may
be. That is the essence of the whole thing.
I think there were some five, six or seven
Civil Servants who were automatically transferred to the Provisional Government against
their will, and as those gentlemen had made
application to come to Northern Ireland they
were afterwards brought North. Apart from
those five or six-it is quite a negligible
number-the other Civil Servants are in the
position I have just indicated.

Trade Boards Bill.

(Mr. MOLES in the Chair.)
Clause 1 (Application of the act.
1.--(1) The Ministry of Labour for
Northern Ireland (in this Act referred to
as "the Ministry") may make a provisional
order applying this Act to any specified
trade, if the Ministry is satisfied that the
rate of wages prevailing in any branch of
the trade is unduly low as compared with
the rates in other employments, and that,
having regard to the degree of organisation
in the trade, and to the other circumstances
of the trade, it is expedient that this Act
should apply to that trade:
Provided that this Act shall apply to the
trades mentioned in the Schedule to this
Act (being trades in Northern Ireland to
which the Trade Boards Act, 1909, applied,
or to which the said Act and the Trade
Boards Act, 1918, were applied by virtue of
provisional or special orders) but without
prejudice to the powers of the Ministry by
a provisional order to suspend temporarily
the operation of this Act as respects any
such trade, to withdraw any such trade
from the operation of this Act, or to alter
or amend the definition of any such trade.
(2) If there exist at any time, in the case
of a trade to which this Act applies,
organised associations of employers and
workers respectively, the Ministry may,
after consultation with those associations,
and on being satisfied that a trade council
or other voluntary body consisting of employers and workers is, or is about to be,
constituted for the regulation of the wages
to be paid throughout that trade, make a
provisional order suspending temporarily
the operation of this Act as respects that
trade.

CLAUSE 2 (Provisions as to Provisional
Orders).
(1) The Ministry may submit to Parliament for confirmation any provisional
order made by it in pursuance of this, Act,
but no such order shall have effect unless
and until it is confirmed by Parliament.
(2) If, while a Bill confirming any such
order is pending in Parliament, a petition
is presented against any order comprised
therein, the Bill, so far as it relates to that
order, may be referred to a joint committee
of both Houses and the petitioner shall be
allowed to appear and oppose as in the case
of local Bills.
(3) Any Act confirming a provisional
order made in pursuance of this Act may be
repealed, altered or amended by any subsequent provisional order made by the
Ministry and confirmed by Parliament.

CLAUSE 4 (Duties and Powers of Trade
Boards as to reports and recommendations).
A Trade Board for any trade shall consider, as occasion requires, any matter
referred to them by the Ministry with reference to the industrial conditions of their
trade, and shall make a report upon the
matter to the Ministry.
A Trade Board may also, if they think it
expedient, make recommendations to the
Ministry, with reference to the industrial
conditions of their trade.

CLAUSE 5 (Obligation of Trade Boards to
fix general minimum time rates and piecework-basis time rates).
5. Every Trade Board shall fix, for timework in their trade, minimum rates of
wages (in this Act referred to as "general
minimum time-rates") to apply respectively
to men, women, and juvenile workers.
General minimum time-rates shall be fixed
with reference to the general body of
ordinary time workers, being men, women
and juvenile workers respectively, engaged
on the least skilled operations in the trade.
Every Trade Board shall fix, for piecework
in their trade, minimum rates of wages on a
time basis (in this Act referred to as
piecework-basis time rates") to apply respectively to men and women workers.
Piecework-basis time rates shall be fixed
with reference to workers of ordinary
skill and experience employed on the
general classes of piece-work operations
carried on in the trade, and shall be at
least equivalent to the general minimum
time-rates fixed for men and women respectively in that trade:
Provided that if a Trade Board report
to the Ministry that it is unnecessary or
impracticable in any case to fix a general
minimum time rate or a piecework-basis
time-rate, the Ministry may, so far as respects that case, relieve the Trade Board
of their duty.

Mr. GRANT: I want to support this

the man who goes on piecework to increase

operation of this Clause will very much depend on how the Trade Boards cater for
what is called minimum rates. I do not
know what method of procedure is adopted
in connection with the Trade Boards in
determining what a minimum rate should
be. Do they fix it as a sum that will be
adequate to the proper standard of living?
We know that there has been some difficulty
upon that matter, because a Committee of
the National Industrial Conference in 1919
confirmed the principle of a national minimum rate, and a Bill was introduced to set
up a Commission to inquire and decide what
a minimum rate should be, regard being
had to the cost of living and other matters.
Would it not be possible for this House to
regulate in some degree the procedure of
these Boards so as to ensure that what is
called a minimum rate would be something
approximate at least to what is necessary to
give a decent living to the worker?
You ask what the minimum rate is? In
England some Boards have based the sum or
amount on the cost of living, while others
have taken into account the value of the
work done and the charge upon the industry.
I do not know whether they proceed on that
method here. Listen to this:
Other Boards fixed it as the lowest wage
possible to the least skilled worker in the
cheapest living area covered by the rate.
They could not get it lower if they tried.
Is that the principle upon which you
operate here? But a more interesting definition than that has been given:
It is a wage sufficient to provide a young
woman of 18 years of age with means
sufficient to enable her to maintain herself
without assistance, or to enable a young
man of 18 years of age to contemplate
marriage.
That is a thing he would think of independent of his income. All the same I am quite
convinced of this that it is very important
to ascertain what is the definition of a minimum rate. If you are going to leave that
entirely in the control and at the decision
of the Trade Boards, I cannot for the life of
me see how your intervention in connection
with the adjudication of those Boards is
going to be of any material value. Really
it will all turn upon that. Then as to the
question of piece rates. I have never
favoured the principle of piece rates. The
Clause provides for it here, and therefore I
am going to subscribe to it, but my
experience in connection with piece ratesan experience going back a considerable
number of years-is that you went into
competition in order to find what was the
highest possible output, and having
attained that, you made it a standard for
the reduction of wages.
I do not know that
piecework is carried out in that way to-day,
but it was one of those conditions that made
me an opponent of piecework wherever it was
possible to establish what was called a time
rate.
Another thing, too, in connection with
what you call piecework, you have as an
hon. Member stated in the House to-day,
workers of unequal skill. You have to remember this that it frequently happens that
the worker who is least skilful strives most
and the remuneration is not in accordance
with their effort at all. It is in all probability in accordance with the result, but
not in accordance with the effort. Am I
wrong in thinking that there is always in
connection with piecework an
implied
suspicion with regard to the worker? You
say: "You cannot possibly do a day's work,
and I will introduce a system by which I
will try whether I will pay you or not."
That is to say, you put them on at piece
rate and say, "Your wages will depend on
your effort." It would be far better if it
were possible to encourage a time rate with
regard to all industries, and to secure by
Trade Boards Bill-
Committee.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Mr. McGuffin]
mutual sympathy that the worker would
give of his best and the employer would pay
a fair rate. John Ruskin, whom I have
more than once quoted in connection with
this question, has said:
"The best results from a worker are
going to be obtained by sympathetic consideration of the worker."
Let a worker see that you are going to be
cheeseparing in this respect, that you are
not going to treat him or her liberally, handsomely, aye, and even generously, and the
production will correspondingly fall away.
Give them the impression that you are going
to trust them to do their best work, and that
you are going to pay them not necessarily
in respect of what is produced, but in respect of what is necessary at home, then you
are going to produce mutual confidence
between workers and employers and you will
obtain far more. I am of opinion-I may be
wrong or I may be right-that the day is
approaching when we will have to have that
reciprocal confidence if we are going to have
success in business. In proportion as distrust grows there is a reduction of output,
and in proportion as sympathy is extended
to the worker you will have increased output as a result of their encouraged efforts.
This is a defect in the Clause. I am sorry,
but I for one will not oppose the Clause in
the hope that we will have better times in
the future than we are experiencing at the
present time.

Mr. ROBB: I beg to move in page 10, line
7, after the word 'shall" ("shall be liable
on conviction") to insert the words unless
he proves that he acted under the orders of
the employer." The object of this amendment is to extend to an employee the same
sort of exoneration as is extended to an employer. Sub-section (5) reads as follows:-
Where an offence, for which an employer is under this Act liable to a fine,
has in fact been committed by some agent
of the employer or other person, that agent
or other person shall be liable to be proceeded against for the offence in the same
manner as if he were the employer, and
either together with, or before or after the
conviction of, the employer, and shall be
liable on conviction to the same punishment as that to which the employer is
liable."
Now the next sub-section deals with an agent
of the employer having committed the act,
but it turns it round the other way. It
says:-
"Where an employer is charged with an
offence against this Act, he shall be entitled, upon information duly laid by him,
to have any agent or other person whom
he charges as the actual offender brought
before the court at the time appointed for
hearing the charge; and if, after the commission of the offence has been proved, the
employer proves to the satisfaction of the
court-
(a) that he has used due diligence to
enforce the execution of this Act; and
(b) that the said agent or other person
had committed the offence in question
without his knowledge, consent or connivance,
that agent or other person shall be summarily convicted of the offence, and the
employer shall be exempt from any fine in
respect of the offence, without prejudice,
however, to the power of the court under
this section to adjudge him to pay any sum
which appears to the court to be due to the
person employed on account of wages. The
agent or other person so convicted shall, in
the discretion of the court, be also liable
to pay any costs incidental to the proceedings."
That is the agent shall be punished and the
employer shall get off. I think it is only
fair that, where you are giving power to
prosecute an agent of the employer or other
person, that agent of the employer should
get off if he can prove that he did the act
under the orders of his master. Supposing,
for instance, a foreman or a cashier has paid
an illegal rate of wages, under this section
as it stands you could prosecute the
employee, although he might only have been
doing what his employer told him to do. I
think it would be only fair that, where you
find a case of a. man acting under his
employer's directions and orders, you should
not be entitled to prosecute the employee
but only the employer, but I would put upon
the employee the onus of proving that he
acted under his employer's directions in
doing the act for which he might be
prosecuted.
Mr. ANDREWS: In order to safeguard the
wording of the Bill in this connection we
have to be careful that neither employer
nor employee does an illegal Act. An employee who commits a crime knowing that he
is doing so ought not to be allowed to shelter
himself behind his employer. Of course, I
am quite certain that the judge who would
be called upon to deal with the matter would
gauge the sentence in relation to what he
thought was the guilt of the person after he
had heard all the evidence connected with
the particular case that was being considered.
I think it is safer to leave it as it is.
Mr. McGUFFIN: I am very glad that the
Minister is going to resist this amendment,
and I will tell you why. An illustration has
been drawn by the hon. and learned Member
for the University (Mr. Robb) of the cashier
paying over the wages. It is more the duty
of the cashier than of the owner to know the
rates payable and to determine the amount
to be paid. To exonerate him would, in my
opinion, be a very great mistake, because he
might be the accomplice of his master. That
is not what we want. We want to, see the
Bill equitably carried out, and to exonerate
the paymaster would be, in my opinion, a
great mistake, for he might be cognisant of
the whole affair and yet might shelter himself behind the employer.

Mr. COOTE: By some mistake an Amendment that I handed in was put down in reference to Clause 8 instead of Clause 18. On
the question of the appointment of District
Committees in an area such as the Six
Counties, I want to ask is there any necessity
for adding to the expense in this way-an
expense that will be gone into very fully
when the time for dealing with the Estimates
comes round. This expense is very much
objected to by the public. Are you wise in
creating further expense by starting District
Boards to create trouble in districts where
everything at present is peaceable and quiet?
I submit there is no necessity for these District Boards. According to the next two
clauses, 19 and 20, you are appointing inspectors, and you are rightly arming those
officers with very drastic powers. The wage
of the trade is settled at the headquarters
of the trade, wherever that is, and as it is
applied to the whole trade, what do you want
District Committees for? Is not it the work
of the inspectors to go round the various
districts where the trade operates, and to
see that everything that is binding on
employer and employed is carried out.
Otherwise what is the use of the inspectors,
and what are you paying them for? We will
have very much to say when we come to discuss these matters on the Estimates. For
very many reasons we did not discuss the
Estimates last year, but we will be very
chary in passing the expense of a number of
inspectors when you are going to set up District Boards and pay men and women for
attending them. The only inference we can
draw from that line of action is that these
District Boards will be a means of getting
money out of the taxpayers. You propose to
set up these Boards at the cost of the taxpayers to do work that is already done. This
work ought to be carried out by the inspectors. I suggest that District Boards
are very objectionable and interfering
bodies. If you persist in giving effect
to this clause it will lead to trouble
and expense. It will be simply
covering ground that has been already
covered by the inspectors. The creation of a
new batch of officials is most reprehensible, so
far as the public is concerned, whether employer or employed. That is what we object
to, and that is what the taxpayers of this
Province must set their faces against.
Mr. ANDREWS: I would point out to my
hon. Friend that I think he is under a misapprehension. The District Committees are
necessary for this reason, that the rate fixed
by the Trade Board for the whole of the
industry, apart altogether from the area over
which the industry is spread, is not necessarily uniform. In other words, the Trade
Board may come to the conclusion that
a lower rate should be fixed for a country
district than for, we will say, the city of
Belfast, the reason being that employers in
the country districts suffer from disadvantages that the employers in Belfast do not
suffer from. I need not go into what those
disadvantages are, because I am perfectly sure
they are obvious to my hon. Friend.
As regards the actual cost of these District
Committees, the hon. Member is under the
impression that the members are paid. The

THE CURFEW ORDER.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That this House do now adjourn."-(Captain Dixon).
Colonel WOODS: I chiefly wish to bring up
the question of the Curfew Regulation in
order to give some hon. Members of the
House a chance of expressing their views and
those of their constituents. It appears to me
extraordinary-a thing, indeed, not equalled
anywhere else in the civilised world-the
amount of freedom we enjoy here under Curfew and under various other items. I would
like to ask the right hon. Gentleman, the
Minister of Home Affairs, whether he considers it a good thing to have no better
regulations for doctors who have to go out
at night? I have had complaints from various doctors, who have gone out at midnight
and after it, that they are stopped every five
or ten yards-or hundreds of yards. I have
heard, also, of two cases where fatal consequences followed. The father of a sick child
was afraid to go out. There was no telephone
in his house, and the result was fatal to the
child. I would like to ask the Minister if
there is any place he can imagine in Europe,
or in the British Colonies, where there is
such freedom enjoyed as we have here-a
place we hear so much about of civil and
religious liberty?
Mr. McGUFFIN: If it is the intention of
the right hon. Gentleman, the Home Minister to retain the present Curfew Regulation,
I, for one, will support him most cordially in
doing so. I do not think it is for any Member of this House to determine whether or
not this is an opportune moment to abolish
it. That is governed by the Minister, who
regulates it. It has been cited here that there
are specific grievances. Those adduced by
the hon. and gallant Gentleman (Colonel
Woods) do not appeal to me. There may have
been one or two cases which proved fatal, but
I do not think any man going out to summon a doctor to attend his child will run
grave risk in meeting a policeman on the
street if he shows him that it is a case of
vital importance. I do not think there would
be the slightest possibility of the man being
apprehended and put in prison. I have not
heard of such a case. With regard to complaints they seem to be very numerous,

so peaceable and free from

There is another point I would like to
bring before the notice of the Minister of

Folice themselves. The House will remember

time and all the times that have

The CHAIRMAN OF WAYS AND MEANS
(Mr. Moles): A number of amendments to
Standing Orders relative to Private Bills are
set down in the Order Paper. Most of them
are drafting amendments, and others of them
merely technical. I propose to call the attention of the House to four of these Orders,
the only ones which require any explanation.
The general principle of them is that we
should bring our Standing Orders into strict
conformity with the Standing Orders at Westminster. The advantage of this procedure is
so obvious that I do not labour it.
The first Standing Order I wish to
draw the attention of the House to
is No. 10, in which there are four amendments proposed. These amendments will
relieve promoters from the necessity of making application to owners, lessees and occupiers as to whether they assent, dissent or are
neuter in respect of taking houses or lands
compulsorily. Notices will of course have still
to be given, but at Westminster it has been
found that the replies to the application have
never been made any use of, and these amendments were made in the Westminster Standing
Orders last year. The next is No. 30. The
Board of Trade as the custodian of Crown
rights in foreshores and also as the authority for navigation desire to see the plans and
sections, and as a matter of courtesy, if for
no other reason, it is desirable to provide by
this amendment that these plans are 60
lodged.
The third Amendment is No. 41. To explain
this Amendment I must refer to an Amendment further down on the paper, viz.-leave
out Order No. 65. This Order provides that
in the case of a Railway or Tramway Bill
authorising the construction of works by a
non-statutory company a declaration may, in
certain cases, take the place of the deposit of
5 per cent. on the amount of the estimate
which is insisted on by Standing Order No.
64. At Westminster this Standing Order has
been found practically useless, and has
hardly ever been relied on, and was struck
out last year.
The next Amendment to which I call attention is No. 105. This Amendment is framed
so as to make it somewhat easier to nominate
a Joint Committee to consider the provisions
of an opposed Bill-for instance, the Corporation Bill of this year. The words which we
propose to leave out, "Locally or otherwise
interested," if interpreted widely make it
very difficult indeed to pick out a Committee of the two Houses in the case of a Bill
such as the Belfast Corporation Bill of this
year. In other words, a situation might conceivably arise in which we could not set up
a Committee at all. I beg to move.

CLAUSE 19 (Appointment of Officers).
The Ministry may appoint such officers
as it thinks necessary for the purpose of
investigating any complaints and otherwise
securing the proper observance of this Act.
Any officers so appointed shall act under the
directions of the Ministry, or if the
Ministry so determine, under the directions
of any Trade Board, and any such officers
may be appointed for the purpose of making such special investigations as may be
required from time to time, or carrying out
ordinary inspections in the interests of
unorganised workers.

means the loss of wages, the loss of trade
union funds, confusion in the industries of
the country. I rather think it would be
well-spent money if we expended a few
thousands of pounds for the purpose of carrying on these Trade Boards, so that we can

if you only employ twenty-three or twentyfour you get off. This clause would not meet

remedy for the difficulty I would be only too
delighted.
Mr. JOHNSTONE: I rise for the purpose of
asking information. These District Committees have been mentioned in connection
with this matter, and they certainly seem, at
first view at any rate, a very good way of
escaping from the difficulty, which I think
every hon. Member sees in regard to industries in the country. May I ask how is a
District Committee to be formed, supposing
you have a village or small town where there
is a particular industry with only one employer and fifty or sixty employees? I understand the Committees are to consist of equal
numbers of employers and employed. There
would be only one employer, assuming that
there is nobody else carrying on exactly the
same industry. Is he to meet with one
representative of the employees and an
assessor sent down by my right hon. Friend
the Minister of Labour? Are the three of
them then to fix the rate of wages? The
same difficulty, as far as I can see, applies
also in the case of District Committees in
connection with an established trade. If you
take an outlying country town where a
factory has been established, you have only
one employer there and whatever the number
of employed may be. Are they to meet
together and say, "We recommend that our
wages be so-and-so?" I want to know what
the position of the District Committee will
be in such a case.
Mr. ANDREWS: My hon. and learned
Friend, the Member for the University (Mr.
Robb), asked for some remedy to meet a difficulty which he sees very clearly. These district committees are really intended to be the
remedy. It is rather strange that the hon.
Member who has moved this clause is the
man who very strongly opposed these district
committees yesterday on the ground of expense. I said yesterday they would be well
worth any small expense there would be in
connection with them, and I think the feeling of the Committee undoubtedly is that I
was right in taking that view. My hon.
and learned Friend, the Member for the
University, who is sitting opposite to me (Mr.
Johnstone), asked how a district committee
could be formed in a small town where there
might be only one employer. I would say
the district committee in that instance would
not be confined to the small town; it would
embrace a larger area and would bring together representatives of the employers and
workers in that area.
Mr. COOTE: And they would cut out the
new industry in the small town.

Mr. ANDREWS: There is one large ropeworks in Belfast, and I understand there are
two or three smaller concerns scattered

the District Committee in Enniskillen report
