"
For the purposes of this Act the expression "juvenile means a person who has
ceased to be a child, and who is fourteen
years of age, but has not reached the age
of eighteen years.


The expressions men and women
mean persons of the age of eighteen years
or upwards.-(Mr. Donald).
Brought up, and read the First time.
Motion made, and Question proposed,
That the Clause be read a Second time."
Mr. DONALD: This is purely a drafting
Clause and does not require much explanation from me. The right hon. Gentleman
(Mr. Andrews) touched upon this matter
yesterday. In my judgment the Bill would
not be perfect if we had not an explanation
of the meanings of the expressions. During
the discussion yesterday the principle was
laid down that a juvenile meant a young
person of the age of fourteen years, and then
the Bill also laid down the principle that
after a working period of six months, if they
were qualified to earn a certain wage, they
would not be debarred from earning the
maximum, or the wage set down. The proposed clause reads:-
"For the purposes of this Act the expression ‘juvenile' means a person who has
ceased to be a child, and who is fourteen
years of age, but has not reached the age
of eighteen years,"
and then further
"The expressions 'men' and 'women'
mean persons of the age of eighteen years
or upwards."
I can see no harm in the clause, and, furthermore, I can see no reason for any heat such
as we had in the last discussion arising out
of this new clause. I beg to move.
Mr. McGUFFIN: It is purely a legal question, I suppose, to determine what the expression "juvenile" really conveys. I would
remind the hon. Member for East Belfast
(Mr. Donald), who is responsible for this
clause, that in last night's proceedings in the
Imperial House of Commons on the Workmen's Compensation Act a clause was submitted which limited the thing so that up
to eighteen years of age any individual was
considered a child. If you will look at the
clause as submitted to the House you will
find that there is no necessity for the expression "juvenile" there, for all young
people concerned up to the age of 18
years are considered children. It was submitted that way in the Imperial House, and
I am sure for good reasons, and on that
account I would not think it is necessary to
alter it here. I contend that the definition
"child" applies up to the age of eighteen,
and that "juvenile" has no status whatever
in connection with the question, nor would it
have in law.
Mr. ROBB: The objection to the proposed
clause is that when a Trade Board comes to
fix rates of wages it fixes them for men and
women, and for those who are not men and
women. From a Trade Board point of view
a juvenile is a person of an age such that in
that industry he or she cannot earn the
adult rate of wages. The difficulty about
putting in a clause of this sort is that that
age varies in different trades. Under some
Trade Boards you will find the juvenile rate
ending as low as sixteen or sixteen and a
half, while in others you will find it runs
up as high as twenty, and even twenty-one
in one instance of which I know. Below
that age a person is treated for Trade Board
purposes as a juvenile. "Juvenile" in Trade
Board legislation means a person who cannot
earn the adult rate of wages. A person who
is able to earn the adult rate of wages can be
of different ages in different trades, and it is
not possible, consistently with the working of
a Trade Board, to lay down in the Bill what
you shall mean by juveniles. You might
have to fix the ages up to nineteen or twenty
in one trade and only up to seventeen in
another, and, if you are going to compel, as
you do in the Bill, a Trade Board to fix minimum rates for juveniles, you cannot say that
means eighteen, because it might not apply
to that particular trade at all. It is far
better to leave it as it is now so that each
Board decides for its own trade.
Mr. McGUFFIN: On a point of order, I
do not think the House is entitled to pass
this without a specific understanding as to
what is implied in it. The hon. and learned
Member (Mr. Robb) has not enlightened us
in the slightest degree. He says the definition
of a juvenile will very much depend upon
the industry in which it is engaged.
Mr. ROBB: Is rot that quiet clear?
Mr. McGUFFIN: It is not clear at all,
because we do not deal with juveniles. We
are making certain legal conditions with
regard to children under eighteen. We
speak of them as children, and up to
eighteen they are children, and there is
nothing which applies in connection with
juveniles that would not be equally appropriate if applied to a child if it were under
18 years of age.
Mr. DONALD: I put this new clause down
with the best intentions, and if it has done
nothing else it has enlightened me, and, I
am sure, other hon. Members. My reason
for putting it down was that the word
"juvenile' was used throughout the Bill,
and I thought a definition of the word necessary, but my hon Friend (Mr. McGuffin) has

second day of November, nineteen hundred and twenty-one, for the purpose of
the Housing of the Working Classes (Ireland) Acts, 1890 to 1921,
THE PARLIAMENTARY AND FINAN-
CIAL SECRETARY TO THE MINISTRY
OF FINANCE (Mr. BARBOUR): It is not
my duty in putting this Resolution before the
Committee to touch on the objects of the Bill
or on the other Clauses. I am confining my
remarks purely to those which are considered
to have a financial bearing, and consequently
it will not be necessary for me to detain hon.
Members very long in moving this Resolution. I presume hon. Members will have
observed that on the Paper to-day, on page
5, there is a new clause which will be moved
in due time by my right hon. Friend the
Minister of Finance (Mr. Pollock). It will
necessitate as a consequence an alteration
in those clauses which are printed in italics
in the Bill which is in the hands of hon.
Members. They will find that there is really
very little change. It is better drafting as it
brings all the financial clauses within one
clause, instead of having them scattered in
three places through the Bill as at present.
The object in moving that new clause is, as
hon. Members will see at once, that, while
the effect of those clauses as they stand might
have been that any of these grants made to
encourage the building of houses might be
chargeable in the one year in which they
were made against moneys voted by
Parliament, these grants, which necessarily
will be made within a very short space of
time, should for the purpose of easier financing be spread over a longer period. The Bill
provides that they shall be repaid within a
period of twenty years from the making of
the grant.
If hon. Members will turn to the Resolution
on the Paper they will find that sub-section (a)
defines the area within which houses must be
built in order to qualify for the bonus which
is to be granted. They will see that within
the area of a local authority the sum fixed is
the flat sum of £60 per house, and in certain
industrial centres in rural districts a sum not
exceeding £60. Reference has already been
made in the course of the discussion which
has taken place this afternoon to the differences in the costs of buildings and the various
conditions which prevail in urban districts
as compared with rural districts. It was felt
that, while £60 might be an adequate inducement to offer to encourage building in dense
centres of population, possibly in other districts a somewhat less sum might be offered
and be equally successful in attaining the
object of the Bill.
The next Sub-section refers to the organisations of people who may qualify for receiving this bonus-that is to say, it may be paid
to any persons or bodies of persons constructing houses, or to local authorities carrying
out schemes for the provision of houses for
the working classes under the Housing of
the Working Classes (Ireland) Acts, 1890 to
1921. These govern the amount of the grant
to be made, the areas and the persons or
organisations to whom the sum may be paid.
The Minister of Home Affairs (Sir Dawson
Bates), in introducing the Bill, said that he
had had a report made to him that in the
city of Belfast alone it was estimated that
there was a shortage of nearly 10,000 houses.
Now, while the main object of this Bill, of
course, is to encourage the building of houses
as much as possible, I am afraid that even
the most sanguine of us must realise that
there are many conditions which will
probably operate against anything like the
number of 10,000 houses being built within
the period contemplated by this Bill. I am
afraid that will prove to be so, but from the
money point of view we have to contemplate
the greatest liability to which we may be
subjected by reason of these grants which it
is proposed shall be paid. If this entire number of 10,000 houses were to be built and qualify for the grant the total sum involved would
be £600,000. That could be paid off under the
conditions provided in this Bill by an annual
sum of £47,000 spread within the limit of the
twenty years. Therefore, I believe that hon.
Members will see and believe that, large as
the sum may be in comparison with the benefit to be derived by securing that extra houses
will be built, it is not a sum that is incapable of being borne by our Northern area.
As to the houses which may be built in the
rural districts, there the same inducement
does not exist to build as in the centres of
denser population, and so it is hard to form
an estimate as to the number of houses that
may qualify for these grants outside the
urban districts, but it is not felt that they
would amount to any very large sum.
Sub-section (b) hon. Members will observe,
refers to the commutation or compounding
of any grants which we have to pay to local
authorities in respect of losses resulting
from schemes approved under Section 1 of the
Housing (Ireland) Act, 1919. Reference to
this liability has been made on many
occasions in this House, and hon. Members
will, of course, be aware that in the current
Estimates the sum of £27,000 was voted in
respect of this liability for the present year.
It was felt that this Government would do
well, if it could, to commute its liability in
this respect. The amount of the liability is a
very difficult thing to compute, as it is based
on a sum which may vary from year to year,
and as the period in respect of which we
were liable to pay this subsidy is the long
period of 60 years it is quite obvious that conditions probably will vary very much indeed
during that long time. Therefore, power was
taken under this clause to compound those

Sir DAWSON BATES: When the Bill was
first introduced it was proposed that in addition to the State subsidy of £60 power should
be given to local authorities to remit rates
for a fixed period of years. There was a
general feeling amongst Members that that
was an undesirable course to take, with the
result that after consultation with various
local authorities and those in a position to
judge, the Government have come to the conclusion that, in addition to allowing the local
authorities to pay a fixed grant of £40 out of
the rates for every house qualified, which is
in addition to the 260 the State proposes to
pay, they should be given an alternative.
They can either pay a lump sum of £40 out
of the rates, or, at the option of the builder
of the house, the local authority can advance
100 to the builder free of interest for a
period of twenty-five years.
I think that in many ways that is the most
desirable course to take. After all, we want
to get houses built, and I hope that when the
Bill leaves this House the action the local
authorities will take will be the passing of
a resolution under which this £40 will be
paid, or in the alternative, that these loans
free of interest will be granted to builders.
In that way the builder will know exactly
what he is going to get, and he will know the
cost of the house, and we hope that before
long the effect of this Bill will be seen in
the number of houses built in Belfast and
elsewhere.
Mr. DONALD: Will it be optional whether
local authorities grant this £40 or not?
The CHAIRMAN: I think it will be better
if I read the amendment in the form in
which it will now stand.

Sir DAWSON BATES: I am afraid the hon.
Member has not quite appreciated the effect
of the Bill. There are two subsidies, the
subsidy granted by the State, and the subsidy
which, I hope, the local authority will grant
to the builder. It is entirely optional for
the local authorities to give that subsidy, and
if they do so they can do it in two formseither by granting a lump sum of £40, or a
loan of £100 free of interest for twenty-five
years. If local authorities refuse to give the
grant or loan the only thing a builder will
get will be the State subsidy of £60.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Sir Crawford McCullagh].
I am speaking now on behalf of the Corporation of Belfast, and I will leave the representatives of the counties to speak for themselves. As far as the Corporation of Belfast
is concerned I believe they will give the maximum grant of £40, making, with the Government grant of £60, a total subsidy of £100 to
a person who will build a house in the city of
Belfast. I also congratulate the Government on the further proposal they have
introduced. We all know the value of money
to a builder, and I am sure it will be found
that a builder would rather have £100 down
than £40, and the Corporation are taking
powers to advance him £100 instead of giving
him a grant of £40, and he will pay it back,
free of interest, in 25 years. In the meantime he will have £100 instead of £40 with
which to go on building his house.

Mr. McGUFFIN: In so far as this amendment will facilitate the building of houses
I am in accord with it. I think it would meet
the objection of the hon. Member for East
Belfast (Mr. Duff) if the alternative to the
grant of £40 was abolished, and there was
only a subsidy of £40 from the local
authority, in addition to the State grant of
£60. That is what should be. As I understand them, the object of these subsidies is
to promote building. Is it not going to result
in increased profits to the builders and that
only? Is there any evidence up to the
moment that these subsidies are going to
give us more houses? We are told it is going
to encourage the builders. The Minister of
Finance told me so the other day, but the
point is this, and it was emphasised by the
Member for South Belfast, that the number
of bricklayers available is limited. You cannot build beyond your capacity. We know
there are houses being built which require
half a dozen bricklayers and only one is
engaged. You are now going to give a subsidy which will mean increased profits for
the builder and will not produce the houses
required. The ratepayers have a right to
look into this matter. No builder is complaining that he is not making enough out
of the building of houses. Some of them
have been building with profit without the
subsidy and now we are going to superimpose on their ordinary profit an extra £100.
Now if you are going to pay that amount
surely it is the duty of the House to consider
whether we are going to get facilities for
paying so much more. My impression is that
we are not. It has been stated here in the
House by the hon. Member for West Belfast
(Mr. Lynn) that we are only getting 350
bricks laid here whereas they are getting 900
laid in Liverpool.
Mr. POLLOCK: Is it the desire of the hon.
Member that we withdraw the question of
subsidy?
Mr. McGUFFIN: No, I am coming to that
point. I do not suggest that you withdraw it,
but are you likely to encourage the production of houses? That is within the power
of the workmen if they wish to lay more than
350 bricks, and give, for instance, the quantity quoted as being laid in Liverpool, namely
900.
Sir CRAWFORD MCCULLAGH: 700.
Mr. McGUFFIN: 900 was quoted. It
does not matter what number the hon. Member (Sir Crawford McCullagh) advocates, I
am quoting the figures mentioned here. If
we could get the workmen to lay more brick
we would have more houses.
Mr. FOLLOCK: Hear, hear.
Mr. McGUFFIN: But you will not have
more houses, I maintain, by simply piling on
this subsidy in addition to the profits being
made at the present time. Surely no hon.
Member in the House would maintain for a
moment that houses built without the subsidy
are being built without profit? And yet you
are going to encourage them by giving £100
more for the building of houses, while you
have no assurance that it is going to work.

That is not the proposal. The proposal is to
give the builder £100 of aided money. There

Mr. POLLOCK: As this matter touches on
finance, I think I am entitled to clear it up.
The power which it is proposed to confer upon
the Corporation is of a two-fold character.
They may give a subsidy of £40 in a lump
sum to the builder of the house, making
with the Government grant of £60 a total
subsidy of £100. As an alternative to that,
they may give to the ultimate buyer of the
house a subsidy of £100 in the nature of a
loan free of interest for 25 years. The hon.
Member (Mr. Duff) asks how that is going to
affect the buyer of the house. It affects the
buyer only to this extent. When he purchases
the house he takes on that liability of £100,
and any money over that £100 he pays to the
builder. He himself carries on with the £100
and makes his annual payments during the
25 years, but the builder gets so much less for
the house. I think that that is perfectly
clear. The buyer is not prejudiced in any
way, but is advantaged from the fact that
he has not the money himself. He has the
bonding of £100 free of interest for 25 years.
That is the contribution that is offered to the
buyer to acquire his house under the Small
Dwellings Acquisition Act. In regard to the
question asked by my hon. Friend the Member for Tyrone and Fermanagh (Mr. Cooper)
as to how local authorities will get the money.

Mr. DONALD: I would liked to have intervened before my right hon. Friend (Mr.
Pollock) spoke. I am not against any method
whereby we can get houses, but I must say
that it does appear to me that these subsidies
are only supporting the profiteering that is
going on with regard to the cost of material.
It is quite evident that there will be no reduction in the cost of material. During the
Second reading debate in this House, I quoted
evidence that was given about the cost of
material. It is quite evident from this section
that a bargain has been entered into between
the Government and Belfast Corporation, but
my hon. Friend has given us to understand
that it has not the authority of the Corporation as a body. However, let it be right or

reduce the cost of materials.
Mr. McGUFFIN: Or build more houses.
Mr. DONALD: And it will not induce
people to build more houses. It would have
been far better if the Government had
adopted my suggestion of trying to break up
these rings that are keeping up the cost cf
material. That would have been the proper
course for the Government to adopt. They
are simply shelling out the money, no matter
where it comes from. There are rings in
connection with building and with
materials. I do not like this method of voting out money; it is only encouraging these
people to keep up the high cost of materials.
Mr. JOHNSTONE: In connection with this
proposed loan for 25 years free of interest,

a bad comparison.

Mr. DONALD: For the first time.

The PRIME MINISTER (Sir James Craig) :
I rise on this occasion because I think I am
justified in intervening for a few moments.
When the Bill was first produced, it was
thought by the Government that it would
facilitate the building of this small type of
house by granting to local authorities the
power of foregoing the whole or part of the
rates for a certain number of years. That
is, something on the same lines as the facilities the railway companies have been
accustomed to granting along the main arteries of traffic if people will erect houses within
a certain circle of the various stations on the
line. The matter gave the Government a
very considerable amount of thought. That
was our idea in the first instance.
Subsequent to the introduction of the Bill,
the question was raised as to whether some
convenient alternative to that plan could be
devised, and here I would like to pay a personal tribute to the hon. Member for
South Belfast (Sir C. McCullagh) and
the officials of the Belfast Corporation
for the courteous manner in which they met
my colleagues and myself in conference on
this subject. I think, perhaps, my hon.
Friend the Member for East Belfast (Mr.
Duff) has gone a little far in attributing
some sinister design behind that. I am sure
neither my hon. Friend (Sir Crawford
McCullagh) nor myself, in a matter of such
public importance, would agree to anything
if there were a sinister object behind it. Our
sole object is to really hasten on this question
of the building of houses. All sorts of suggestions and plans are put forward. Many of
them are really magnificent on paper, but
very few of them fulfil the function of getting
to work at once before the winter sets in, not
only in order to supply houses, but also to
help the unemployed. I repeat that our informal conversations, if I may put it that
way, with the great City Corporation have
been on most cordial and friendly terms, and
the result is that we have practically an
agreed clause, which I would ask the House
to allow to be put into the Bill at this stage.
I should say that it is to be deprecated that
amendments are not put on the Paper, and
that the Government especially cannot put
an amendment on the Paper the day before,
but still it is better to have an agreed amendment put in in manuscript, and then on the
Report stage the whole House can study it
carefully. In the meantime I commend this
amendment to the Committee, and hope it
will meet the difficulties which have been toc
leng in the solving.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.
Thursday, 15th November.
The House met at Three of the clock, Mr.
SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
FLOODING IN FERMANAGH AND
TYRONE.
1. Dr. MORRISON (for Mr. Cooper) asked
the Prime Minister if he is aware that very
grave losses have been sustained by farmers in
Counties Fermanagh and Tyrone this year
owing to flooding from the Sillies, Minyburns,
Ballinamallard, Arney and other rivers, and
whether the Government is prepared to empower the county councils in Northern Ireland
to undertake minor works in rivers, such as
the clearing of fords and shoals, which would
give immediate partial relief, and to charge
the cost to the areas benefited, and whether
the Government intends to set up a Committee to consider the larger question of
drainage in Northern Ireland, and when.
men-
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): I have been asked by the Prime
Minister to reply to this question. My attention has been called to the fact that heavy
floodings have occurred in the areas
tioned, although I have no information as to
the seriousness of the losses to which the hon.
Member refers. Under existing statutes
county councils can obtain powers by Provisional Orders taking over the duties of
drainage boards, though, I understand, that
no attempt has been made to obtain such
Orders. The whole question of the administration of the Drainage Acts is at the present
time being carefully considered by the several
Departments interested, and pending such
consideration I feel that no useful purpose
would be served by setting up a special committee to deal with the subject.
The Committee now sitting on the development of the industrial resources of Northern
Ireland may possibly regard this as a matter
which comes within the scope of their inquiries.
WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BILL.
Mr. GRANT (by private notice) asked the
Minister of Labour whether the Government
intends to introduce a Workmen's Compensation Bill similar to that now before the
Imperial Parliament in order that our industrial workers may receive the same industrial benefits as their fellow-citizens in
Great Britain?
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): Yes, sir, certainly. The Government is most anxious that the provisions relating to workmen's compensation should be
the same in Northern Ireland as those in
Great Britain, and they will take the earliest
opportunity next Session of seeking the
authority of our Parliament for this purpose.
Pending the introduction of this measure the
existing provisions will continue as provided
by the Expiring Laws Continuance Bill which
has recently been before our Parliament.
Mr. DONALD: Arising out of that answer,
I should like to ask the Minister of Labour if,
as the Bill before the Imperial House may become law in the course of a week, the workmen of this Province will be put in a similar
position, as this Bill could not be introduced
until next year.
Mr. ANDREWS: Of course, I do not yet
know what the final form of the Imperial
measure will be, but I think I am correct in
saying that the Bill as it stands at the
moment gives somewhat more generous treatment in the case of death and somewhat less
generous treatment in the case of injury.

sidered unnecessary. That is, if the Lisburn
Hospital is considered unnecessary you can
close that hospital and rebuild in a central
place in the county, or if the Derry Infirmary
is unnecessary you can close it, and the county
council can open a new one in the centre of
the county. This opens up a very important
question. One thing which I think every hon.
Member of this House would like to guard,
and guard jealously, is the rights which belong to the poor, and the weak, and the helpless in the community. Everyone will admit
that that is the first claim on every assembly
like ours.
The rich and the middle classes
can provide for themselves, but someone must
look after the poor. If you wish to avoid,
as I maintain many of them do, anything in
the form of a poorhouse, you must provide
some institution in the county where the poor
can get surgical and medical relief from a
specially qualified man.
If you close an infirmary, or if you divert
funds from it to the cottage hospitals or any
other institution in the county, you are giving money to institutions that have no obligation on them to admit poor patients free.
That is the great point I would like to impress on the Committee. To all these public
infirmaries the poorest in the county have a
right to go and get treatment from a man
who is supposed to be specially qualified for
the purpose, and to get special treatment as
long as it is considered necessary. These are
rights I would like to conserve for the poor,
and I think that any man who looks into the
question will see that it must be done, or if
this is reduced and taken from them they
must be safeguarded in some other way
that appeals to and satisfies every reasonable
man. My object in moving this amendment
is that as the clause clearly contemplates a
new infirmary or the re-opening of an infirmary, the Minister with the approval of
the council may close any hospital that is
not considered necessary. The one follows
the other, and is necessary if you are going
to re-build. It is entirely a matter for the
county council, and I am sure when my hon.
Friends from Fermanagh and Antrim come
to approach this question they will get rid
of some of the heat that they have appeared
to develop in this matter, and will approach
it in a broad, generous spirit, thinking only
of the welfare of the community and
especially of the welfare of the poor.

I take it that in the case of future appointments contribution to the pension scheme
should be compulsory. I think that is a very
wise provision. There has been a good deal
of friction in rural councils and county councils about granting superannuation to poor
law officers who are engaged in administering
affairs in Ireland, and their brethren in the
medical profession feel this is a grievance,
or has been a grievance, that they were denied
the right of entry into the pensions scheme.
It would enable them to contribute to their
own pensions, and they could say they were
earning their pensions the same as the schoolmasters and other men engaged in the public
service: I think if we adopted this system,
under this new Act it would be a wise thing
and a step in the right direction. It would
avoid friction. The serious objection to lack
of pension is this-In many cases it is apparent that the professional man is compelled
-through poverty he can make no provision
for old age to hang on to office when he is
long past service. Now in one of these
county infirmaries before the House I know
as a matter of fact one man who held office
as county surgeon for 50 years. Obviously
that could only be done in injury to the
patients that came under his care. The present man in that office has 40 years' service
and I think any man who knows anything
about surgery will be able to tell that a man
forty years in a post like that is not qualified
for those delicate operations on which the
life of a patient may depend. For these reasons I would wish this clause introduced into
the Bill to serve in a measure to relieve the
friction that sometimes arises in granting
superannuation that would enable these men
to retire and live a little bit in comfort in
their old age, and would also prevent ineffi
cient officers hanging on to office where their
presence is an injury to the public service.

Antrim to state that there is more than one
representative for the county. I do not
know if it has been entrusted to any one of
the six members to speak in the House as
the sole representative of that county on this
point. I have no authority vested in me to
speak for any other part of the county in respect of this matter than that with which I
am immediately associated. I may say that
any statement I make in connection with
County Antrim Infirmary is founded upon
intimate personal knowledge and acquaintance with that institution now extending
for-I regret to say-more than 25 or 30
years.
That institution does receive the support
of the county at large. I may illustrate
the point in connection with my own property in the townland of Kilmakeen which
is most unfortunately situated. But there

I am rated for no fewer than three different

(Hon.
What brought me to my feet on the present occasion was that the hon. Member for
County Derry (Mrs. Chichester) presupposed
a condition which is so far from the actual
fact and thereupon was beginning to found
a case that I really thought many hon.
Members might be under a very wrong impression of the true state of affairs. You
can naturally understand-it must obtain in
the case of any county-that greater advantage will be taken of that institution by
people in its immediate vicinity. But on the
other hand, we do have patients from the
most remote parts of the county. We endeavour to serve to the utmost capacity everybody that comes within our doors. The
greatest part of the support of this institution
comes from those round about, and I think
the hon. Member for the University (Dr.
Morrison) has said that these institutions
exist really for the poor who are not able to
do so very much for themselves.
Members: Hear, hear.) I think there is no
greater tribute to the usefulness of these institutions than that only within the last two
or three years the workpeople in the town of
Lisburn and immediate neighbourhood outside the urban district have formed themselves into a workers' committee, and have
raised-I am only speaking from memory,
and I hope hon. Members will realise I am
only giving the impression I have-I think
these workers have contributed between £400
and £500 a year to this institution. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear). After all, I regret
myself that I am speaking from this standpoint on a general measure which deals with
the provision of infirmaries throughout the
whole area. I regret that what brought me
to my feet was to address the committee on
this particular standpoint. We are entitled
to speak for our own constituencies. Still
our duty here as Members of Parliament is
to consider these things from the broad standpoint of the thing that is best for the whole
area of the Six Counties. Are we going to
say that these institutions should be liable to
be wiped out? Or do we consider it really
necessary for the suffering poor or for cases
of accident thoughout the area, that there
should be some institution in each of the
counties to which these people should have
access?

Mr. COOTE: On a point of order, will you
allow me to revert to a decision you have
already given on Clause 1?
I feel very
strongly on this point, although I do not
attach any blame to you. You will see that
on the Order Paper I had an amendment to
leave out Clause I, and I always assumed,
and am I not right in assuming, that you
call out my name when you come to dealing
with Clause 1 as a clause. What you did, if
I remember rightly, was to put the clause,
but you did not call out my name as objecting to the clause. I was talking to other hon.
Members at the time, and I suppose I was
waiting to hear my name called out, but I
did not hear it. I deplore the fact very
much, because I intended to divide the Committee, and if I had done so I should have
been satisfied. I submit to your ruling because you have a varied and extensive knowledge, and I do not for a moment cavil, but
I do ask you if I have not the right to have
my name called?
The CHAIRMAN: The point which the hon.
Member submits is a simple one. I can deal
with it in a strictly technical way and point
out that to leave out Clause I would not have
been a competent amendment, the clause
having been amended, but I put the specific
question that the clause as amended stand
part. The technical effect of that is that
if the House had decided contra Clause 1
would have been defeated. The hon.
Member has had as long an experience of
Parliament as anyone in this Committee, and
he knows perfectly well that has
happened hundreds of times in the
Imperial House and scores of times even in
this House. It is the technical method, when
a clause has been amended, to invite the
committee to determine whether the clause
shall or shall not be added to the Bill.
Having put that specific question the hon.
Member had his opportunity. I can quite
see that in his conversation with other hon.
Members he may not have heard the question.
I regret that as much as he, but I put the
question with the utmost plainness and the
entire committee heard it. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) I am sorry the hon. Member
lost his opportunity, but the committee
having decided that Clause I stand part of
the Bill I could not invite them to reverse
that judgment.
Mr. COOTE: I may be wrong, but it was
my experience in the British House of
Commons that when an amendment was
down on the Order Paper in the name of
a Member that Member's name was called
before his amendment was disposed of.
The CHAIRMAN: The hon. Member is
taking me upon the technical point. I have
indicated to him as clearly as I can that the
clause having been amended the form in

Sir DAWSON BATES: The object of this
Bill is to enable members of the Special
Constabulary who are over the statutory
limit of age to be admitted to the Royal
Ulster Constabulary if they are otherwise
deemed suitable. Hon. Members are aware
that under the Constabulary Bill—
Mr. McGUFFIN: May I ask if that applies
to those who have already been demobilised?
Mr. SPEAKER: The hon. Member must
let the Minister make his explanation first.
Sir DAWSON BATES: Hon. Members are
aware that under the Constabulary Act of
last year the age limit for candidates joining
the Royal Ulster Constabulary was fixed at
35 years, but it was felt at that time, in
order to give an opportunity to members of
the old R.I.C., and members of the Special
Constabulary who were over the age of
35 years but who otherwise would make very
suitable constabulary officers in the new
force, that that period should be extended
and that these men should be admitted to
the Force up to the age of 40 years for a
period of twelve months. It was then hoped
at the end of that time we would have our
full quota. As a matter of fact we are short
of the quota 250 men at the present time,
and this Bill now proposes that all existing
members of the Special Constabulary, notwith.
standing the age, and who are otherwise suitable, should be allowed into the Royal Ulster
Constabulary. We feel, now that we are
entering on a period of peace, that these men
who have done such good work as members
of the Special Constabulay Force should
have an opportunity of joining the Royal
Ulster Constabulary even although they are
over the age of 35 years. I beg to rove.
Mr. McGUFFIN: I only intervene to emphasise the question I addressed to the
Minister. I am sorry to hear, and I hope
this is not his final decision, that this will
apply only to those who were members of
the Special Constabulary at a special time.
Some very estimable men, and very eligible
men too, have been demobilised, and I presume on that account are not going to have
the opportunity of taking advantage of the
offer made through this Bill. I am rather
at a loss to understand how this Bill is
being introduced at the moment. Is it because the right hon. Gentleman has absolutely failed to secure the number?
Sir DAWSON BATES: Certainly not.
Mr. McGUFFIN: Was it because of the
too rigid examination of those who presented themselves? In many instances admirable men have been turned down owing
to questionable reasons. I suppose this has,
moreover, been introduced as a concession
and measure of justice to the men who have
served in a very important crisis in our
city and who have done very effective work.
If that is the consideration leading up to
this I would like to ask how it comes about
that in last September 20 per cent of the
force W2S demobilised with four days'
notice, and that on the first of this month
40 per cent of the existing members got a
month's notice that they were being demobilised. If it is a matter of doing justice to
these men, I would ask the right hon. Gentleman to consider their claims. These men
have served us well, and have received on
the whole such ungrateful treatment on the
part of the Ministry that they are to be
demobilised after four days' notice, and yet
they are excluded from the benefits of this
Bill. I have no objection in the wide world
to men being specially selected, or that
they should in every instance conform to the
terms laid down in the Constabulary Bill:
but I question very much if the men feel
that they have been dealt with justly in
respect of the administration up to the
moment.
Constabulary Bill- 15 NOVEMBER 1923.
Second Reading.
We should not forget our obligations to
these men. If justice is going to be meted
out by giving an opportunity to some to become members of the R.U.C., I think it
should also be given to those who have been
and are about to be demobilised. This is all
the objection I offer to the Bill at the
moment. I would like the Minister to say
something as to why in one instance 20 per
cent. of the Constabulary are demobilised
on four days' notice without any remuneration, and why in the second instance men
to the extent of 40 per cent. received a
month's notice on the first of this month
that they were being demobilised?
Mrs. CHICHESTER: I have endeavoured,
as far as possible, in this House not to speak
on any Bill either on the Second reading or
in Committee, about which I had not a suitable amount of knowledge, and I feel particularly nervous about speaking on this one
after the rebuke which was administered to
me a short time ago in Committee by the
hon. Member for Antrim (Mr. Crawford),
when I spoke on something about which,
perhaps, I had not as much knowledge as
other hon. Members. However, I would just
like to support to a certain extent what has
been said by the hon. Member for North
Belfast (Mr. McGuffin) when he asked the
Minister of Home Affairs to consider, when
removing the limitation of age which is imposed on members of the Special Constabulary who wished to join the Royal Ulster
Constabulary, the case of the men who were
demobilised through no fault of their own
because of the limitation of age under the
old restrictions. I would like to go still
further, and ask whether it would not be
possible to consider the case of men who have
been or may be turned down after they have
done excellent service, because their height
was possibly a fraction under the standard
laid down or their chest measurement was
a fraction less than the standard laid down?
Mr. McGUFFIN: Hear, hear.
Mrs. CHICHESTER: These men were good
enough for the Special Constabulary when
every man was needed. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) They came forward when danger
threatened. They took their lives in their
hands so as to protect us and in order that
we might lie safely in our beds. They
stood the strain-the terrible strain-all the
time, more particularly in the last year.
They did their duty gallantly and faithfully.
I have heard of hard cases in this connection.
Men were turned down simply because they
were a fraction under the necessary height,
and yet those men not only served in the
Special Constabulary but also in the war,
and have gallant records. I wonder when
the Bill is being brought in later would it not
be possible to consider their case? (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) I consider, of
course, they should have had such service
as may be specified by the Minister of Home
Affairs in Clause I of the Bill, but these
men have done excellent service. I would
ask the Minister to consider the advisability
of withdrawing some of the other limitations.
and to remember that it is not always the
largest frames that contain the most gallant
spirits. It is not always the case because
a man's chest measurement is narrower than
another man's that he has a narrower or
smaller sense of the duty he owes to his
country and to the force to which he belongs.
1 would remind him also that Nelson was
not a big man nor a strong man. If I have
spoken on a subject which does not really
belong to those which I have a particular
right to speak on I hope, at any rate, the
Minister will consider the question I have
put to him.
Colonel WOODS: I am particularly
fortunate in having two supporters in what
I have to say, because I have put down a

(Mr. McGuffin), and I have also put down

have had considerable experience of men

the standard also for height and chest
measurement. It would be only fair.

Friday, 16th November, 1923.
The House met at Three of the clock, Mr.
SPEAKER in the Chair.
Resolved: That, notwithstanding anything
contained in Standing Order No. 8 (2), Questions be taken at this day's sitting. (Captain
Dixon.)
Oral Answers to Questions.
POST OFFICE TEMPORARY SORTERS.
1. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Commerce whether he is aware that twentysix ex-servicemen are at present employed as
temporary sorters in the Belfast Post Office,
with periods of service ranging from 1 to 9
years; that eight of these men are now
under notice of dismissal on the 20th inst.
Will he give the reasons for their dismissal
at this stage, when the Christmas pressure is
about to commence, and will he ask the Imperial Government to postpone the notices,
and afford these men an opportunity to
qualify at a limited examination for permanent appointments?
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE (Mr.
Archdale): The matter to which the hon. and
gallant Member refers is not one in which,
as he is aware, the Northern Government
have any jurisdiction. My Department have,
nevertheless, been in communication with the
Postal Authorities on the question of the dismissal of the eight ex-Servicemen to whom
he refers. I am glad to be able to inform
the hon. and gallant Member that their notices have been temporarily withdrawn. He
will remember that my Department approached the Postal Authorities some months
ago, at his instance, on this same subject,
and that a full explanation was obtained of
the terms under which the ex-Servicemen
were appointed in the Postal Service, and
communicated to him.
DEMOBILISED SPECIAL CONSTABLES.
2. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether it is a fact that a
considerable number of special constables
were demobilised in September, 1922, with
only four days' notice, and if he will state
whether they received any compensation or
other consideration.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): It is a fact that a considerable number of Special Constables were demobilised in September, 1922, consequent
upon their contracts having expired. This
course was necessary in view of the financial
stringency, and also to the fact that conditions were more peaceful. Each "A"
Special Constable on leaving the Force receives a bounty in lieu of Pension.
UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF SCHEMES.
asked
3. Sir CRAWFORD McCULLAGH
the Minister of Labour whether local
authorities engaging in schemes for the relief of unemployment, including housing
schemes, which receive the approval of his
Ministry, will receive the monetary assistance provided in such cases, although the
schemes may not have been completed on or
before the financial year ending 31st March,
1924.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): All the obligations which I have
undertaken on behalf of the Government
will be met, whether or not the schemes are
completed before March 31st next.
THE UNMARRIED MOTHER.
4. Mrs. CHICHESTER asked the Minister
of Home Affairs if he will give an assurance
that he proposes to introduce a Bill early
next Session dealing with the question of the
unmarried mother?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I regret to find
that, owing to the difficulties of the problem involved, the Legitimacy Bill, which
has been before the Imperial House of Parliament has been suspended in its progress.
I am, in the circumstances, faced with the
problem of introducing a Bill next Session
dealing with the limited matter covered by
the Bastardy Act, 1923, viz.: making the
putative father responsible for the maintenance of a bastard child.
As the hon. Member is aware, the law in
force in this country on this subject has, for
the last half century, been different from
that in England, and as this House has passed
a resolution suggesting the passing of legislation on this point, I will be prepared to introduce a Bill for this purpose in the next
Session of our Parliament on the lines of
the Bastardy Act.

the consequence is that I think that is one

The second reason is because the Government failed to accept what was a necessary
and mild amendment which would have relieved the county of Antrim, of which I have
the honour to be one of the representatives,
in a way which I believe it is absolutely
entitled to. They refused to accept this
amendment which would exempt any county
council that could satisfy the Ministry that
suitable and sufficient infirmaries and hospitals existed within its area from compulsory
yearly contributions. I endeavoured yesterday to convince this House-I am sorry I did
not succeed in doing it, and I feel that if
someone else had had the case I had they
could easily have done it-that a grave injustice was being done to County Antrim by
this Bill which the Government propose
should be read to-day the Third time.
It was mentioned yesterday in the House
that a great many patients were admitted
from various parts of County Antrim outside the Lisburn area to the Antrim County
Infirmary. I have to-day in my hand a return showing there were 370 intern patients
in the County Antrim Infirmary for the year
ended October, 1922, and that only 26 of them
were from outside the Lisburn area, and all
those not sent by the guardians who have
charge of the poor. The hon. Member for
the University said my idea would be to
interfere with the poor. I had no idea of
that description, and the hon. Gentleman
was quite wrong in attributing any such
idea to me. I have a great interest in the
poor and a great desire to see them well
looked after. I would be sorry to say anything that would look like interfering with
the treatment of the poor. There were only
26 from outside Lisburn, and there were 40
from outside County Antrim treated in the
infirmary. Yet you ask County Antrim to
continue giving yearly subscriptions towards
them. From the Ballymena rural district
there was only one patient sent in 1922, and
one in 1923 by the guardians. From Antrim
rural district, the one lying next to it, there
were none at all sent in, and from Lisburn
rural district there were none sent. I may
say to-day what I was not in a position to
say yesterday-I was not exactly sure, and I
do not want to say anything of which I am
not sure that is, that the Lisburn Rural District Council itself sent a resolution to Antrim
County Council asking that steps should be
taken to exempt the County Council from
contributing to the infirmary situated in Lisburn. This was from Lisburn Rural
District Council itself. Larne sent one
patient three years ago, and if you
take the contribution that the district
of Larne is compelled to rive towards
the infirmary it was expensive treatment that
that one patient received. There were only
two patients from the Ballymoney district,
and I am not sure whether the Guardians
sent them or not, and in the case of Ballycastle also I cannot say whether the Guardians sent or not, but there were only three
from the whole rural district.
The Antrim County Council has received resolutions from every rural district council in
the county asking to be exempted, and yet
the Government cannot see their way to accept an amendment which would not wreck
their Bill but would relieve County Antrim
of this injustice. I am aggrieved that the
Government were not willing to do as they
were asked in this simple amendment. I
had no desire to wreck the Bill. I have no
desire to make myself a nuisance in this
House, but I have a strong desire to see fair
play given to every county, and especially
to the county which I represent. These councils are loyal to this Government. If I could
in my person epitomise their feelings I might
use the very strongest language in regard to
the respect which they have for the Government. I can say if they allowed me to
express their feeling that
Fame, could fame be mine that fame were
thine,
And shame, could shame be thine that
shame were mine.
The councils are loyal to this Government,
and I warn the Government against turning
their friends into enemies. There is such a
thing as taking away faith and putting unfaith in its place. I remind hon. Members
that
Faith and unfaith can ne'er be equal
powers;
Unfaith in aught is want of faith in all.
And when fair things, straight and honest
things, are brought up before this Government, and they have not gone into them, I
say they have taken away the faith of the
representatives on the rural district councils
and the county council in County Antrim.
You know what Tennyson said about
unfaith?
It is the little rift within the lute
That by and by will make the music mute,
And, ever widening, slowly silence all.
If this Government should put unfaith in
the place of faith I would regret exceedingly
to see such a thing come to the county
which I have the honour to represent.
I speak against the Third Reading of this
Bill, and I will vote against the Third Reading of it, and I hope the Government will
see their way to treat the people of County
Antrim with more consideration in future
than they have done in the past.

for Antrim (Mr. Crawford) has said, I would

it will help to remove a great many of the
anomalies that exist. I have no doubt whatever that the hon. Member is perfectly sincere
in his desire that the Government should
meet the wishes of the people in this matter
as expressed through their representatives on
the county and local councils. In my opinion
what he proposes to do would perpetrate a
much greater injustice than the system that
already exists. Lisburn Infirmary is a very
old institution. The late surgeon of that
infirmary was a distinguished Ulsterman
who for many years carried on a beneficent and beneficial work in that institution.
He had in a marked degree the respect of all
the medical profession, but he held that post
when he was long past the age when a man
could perform efficiently the duties for which
he was appointed, with the result that the
infirmary itself was not used for the purpose
for which it was intended. I suggested
amendments to the Government which ohviously, perhaps, are difficult to introduce at
the present moment. I have received statements from the Government that they will
consider these amendments favourably before
remodelling the whole poor-law system of
Ulster. These amendments contemplated
putting into these infirmaries men with
special surgical qualifications, and without
that we fail to secure the confidence of the
doctors in the counties. Secondly, you give
them superannuation and retire them at a
time when they are able to perform their
duties, but also when they are approaching
the borderland that they cannot perform
their duties.
I think if these regulations had been in
force during the last twenty or thirty years
a great many of these complaints would not
have arisen. It is obviously open to the Government when introducing a new measure
dealing with all these questions to bring in
amendments that will rectify this matter.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
I would go
a great deal further. I agree that an institution such as this, which is placed at the end
of a very large county and which owing to
its position is never able to satisfy the necessities and wishes of the people of the county,
should not be closed and demolished, but
that it should be sold to the people of Lisburn and established as a cottage hospital.
The County Infirmary of Antrim should be
placed in a central position in the county,
with a properly qualified surgeon in charge,
so that it would be within easy reach of all
the unions in the county. In that way I
believe you would meet-and this is the crux
of the whole question-what are the undoubted rights of the working people as regards these infirmaries. I maintain that for
150 years the working people of our different
counties have had this right conferred on
them, a right which this Bill, in my opinion,
takes from them. It is, in my opinion also,
the only blot in the Bill. I do not wish to
say that the Government is doing it intentionally. I know they are desirous of
doing what is fair and just, but I should like
to say to this House that what they have
done is an injury, and a serious injury, to
the rights of the working people of Ulster.
I may quote a few lines of poetry:-
"Evil is wrought by want of thought,
As well as want of heart."
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear). It occasionally
happens that an injustice is done, not because people want to do it-they are even
anxious to prevent it-but simply because
they do not know.
I want to impress this fact on the House
that for 150 years the poor people of Ulster
-the working classes-on whom half of the
prosperity of agricultural Ulster depends,
had this right-the right of going to the
county infirmary and being treated free by
a specially qualified man, who had a special
knowledge of surgery. That was a valuable
concession that the working people had. Any
dispensary doctor in the whole county could
have his patients sent there, and the infirmary doctor was glad to have them. If
the infirmary was wrongly situated, away,
as in County Derry at the extreme end of the
county, or as in County Antrim where it
ceased to perform the function for which it
was intended owing to the difficulties I have
mentioned, the people lost confidence, and the
patients were sent either to Belfast or for
minor operations to the cottage hospital
which they had to establish, and which we
had to do in Coleraine out of the pockets of
the people themselves. Look at Section 1,
Sub-clause 2, of the Bill:
The joint committee for the management of a county infirmary or fever hos
pital may, at their discretion, with the
consent of the Ministry of Home Affairs
for Northern Ireland (in this Act referre]
to as "the Ministry of Home Affairs ") and
of every contributory council, close their
infirmary or fever hospital if they think it
unnecessary, and may dispose of the buildings and devote the proceeds of same and
of any endowments to the maintenance of
other institutions doing similar work in the
county.

[Dr. Morrison]
There are similar institutions in some counties. In County Antrim the workhouses have
been abolished, and the infirmary attached to
the workhouse has been turned into a county
hospital, but I maintain that the stigma of
the workhouse system attaches to this place.
Mr. CRAWFORD: No.
Dr. MORRISON: In the opinion of some
it may not, but in the opinion of others it
does. What I want to point out is that in
these local infirmaries you have no specially
qualified men. For instance, you may not
have in the vicinity of a union infirmary
transformed into a special hospital a man
who is qualified to do surgical work. It is
a special thing. For the workhouse infirmary
with a specially qualified surgeon you substitute a cottage hospital and you tell the
poor, "You must go there." I maintain that
that is an injustice to the poor. That is
all very well in County Antrim, where they
have abolished their workhouses, but in
County Derry we have not abolished our
workhouses. We have not even these cottage
hospitals. We have one cottage hospital in
Coleraine. There is no other in the county.
The whole poor-law system in County Derry
is working to-day in the same way as when
it was established. And when you come to
deal with dispensary patients from County
Derry, where are you going to send them?
If the county council takes upon itself to
abolish the county infirmary, which is situated close to Derry and is practically a cottage hospital for the Derry people, and
utilised by them, although built at the expense of the county, I maintain that we cannot send our patients and devote the money
to hospitals doing similar work, as the Act
declares, in other parts of the county. We
have no provision for all these patients in
Coleraine Cottage Hospital. Although we are
making big extensions there we are not able
to meet the want that exists.
I want the House to understand and
recognise the difference between a transformed infirmary under the Poor Law and a
cottage hospital.
The guardians may send patients to the
transformed infirmary and contribute to their
support, but we have no system in the cottage
hospital by which we will take in patients.
and if we do take in patients, there must
be an elaborate scheme arranged and a
system of audit established so that the
accounts may be audited carefully, and we
will be able to strike a balance. I do not
know whether the cottage hospital would be
willing to undertake the treatment of these
patients. There were difficulties with regard
to the treatment of disabled soldiers;
in fact, the cottage hospital was not able to
make provision for them. I can hardly conceive that men representing rural Ulster will
say the poor are to lose a statutory right and
be handed over to the care of this Infirmary
Committee.
When I raised this question yesterday, the
Minister of Home Affairs said that the poor
were protected by the Infirmary Committees
and by the county councils. If the poor have
a statutory right, established by law for 150
years for special treatment, is that right to
be handed over to a county council or to any
committee without very serious consideration? What I maintain is that if the
County Antrim suffers through this system of
having its infirmary at the end of the county,
the proper remedy is for the county council
to abolish the infirmary and build
one in the centre of the county, but to
shift over the claims the poor have
had on the workhouse infirmaries is, I think,
unfair and unjust. County Derry has no
means of shifting them over. We have not
got the length of abolishing our workhouses.
If they are to be shifted on haphazardly to
cottage hospitals which cannot provide for
them I think it should be obligatory on the
county council to sell the infirmary to
the Derry people, who could use it as
a cottage hospital, and build a central
infirmary in County Derry with these
cottage hospitals, which perhaps had no
special equipment, no X-rays, and no
special men capable of performing serious
operations. In the central infirmary you
could have special men with special qualifications and proper equipment for carrying out
the work which was carried out under very
serious disadvantages but in a splendid manner by some of these infirmaries, such as
Omagh and Enniskillen.
I suggest this to the consideration of the
Home Office. As I said before, I am perfectly certain they are desirous of doing
everything that is right and just. I am sure
that these things will be taken into consideration when they are framing that new
scheme of reform, and I leave it with confidence in their hands, but I would like to
know in the meantime if County Derry
abolishes its infirmary under the powers
granted by this Bill-because they have the
power-what is to become of the poor people?
You can quite understand the feeling that
exists in County Antrim after the speech of
such a moderate, genial, and benevolent man
as the hon. Member for Antrim (Mr. Craw
ford), who put forward his case so strongly
here. If County Derry does as Antrim has
done, you see what happens to the poor
people. I have made this protest, and I have
done SO in the interests of the poor

CLAUSE 1 (Temporary Suspension of Age
Limit for Certain Appointments to Royal
Ulster Constabulary).
(1) So long as this Act continues in force,
a special constable, belonging to any such
class of special constabulary and having
such service as may be specified by the
Minister of Home Affairs for Northern
Ireland, may, notwithstanding any limitation of age imposed by any enactment, be
lawfully appointed as an officer or constable of the Royal Ulster Constabulary.
(2) This Act shall continue in force until
the thirty-first day of Devember, nineteen
hundred and twenty-six, and no longer.
Colonel WOODS: I beg to move in Clause
1, sub-Clause (1), line 9, after the word "age"
("notwithstanding any limitation of age
imposed by any enactment") to insert the
words "height or chest measurement."
It is only in order to bring the clause
into some uniformity that I move this
amendment that height and chest measurement shall also be affected by its operation.
The alteration of the age limit must
necessarily mean the alteration of the height
and chest measurement for the same reason.
I have heard it suggested outside that the
reason for this Bill is to include some one
who is a friend of the Government, but I
said that could not be so for the friends of
the Government are all in already. The
Clause is to meet the case of men who have
served particularly well, and who may be
over the age limit, but there may be men who
have also served particularly well and who
may be a quarter of an inch below the
necessary stature or a quarter of an inch
short of the necessary chest measurement.
At any rate it is a hardship to make an
alteration in one physical regulation and not
in another. It is a hardship to those who
are cut out. During the Second reading the
Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of
Home Affairs (Mr. Megaw) asked where would
we stop if we included height and chest
measurement. Where do we stop at the age?
The same argument applies there. It is quite
conceivable that there may be ancients who
are hale and hearty at seventy years of age
and who would look very well in the King's
uniform.

must have uniformity on parade, but all the
members of the Police Force do not go on

uniform as possible, but the difficulty is not

ORDER OF THE DAY.
Workmen's Compensation Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That the Bill be now read a Second time."
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr. Andrews): I know that I am leaving myself open
to be accused of unduly rushing legislation
in asking this House not only to give a
Second Reading to this important measure
to-day, but also to pass it through all the
remaining stages. I can assure the House,
however, that the Government has no desire
of the kind, but we were faced with a great
difficulty in having to choose the lesser of
two evils. If we had decided that we would
not proceed with this Bill we undoubtedly
would have left our workers in Ulster in a
less favourable position than those of Great
Britain until next Session, when the matter
could have been dealt with, and I know the
whole feeling of this House is that a course
The
of that kind should not be pursued.
Government, therefore, decided to ask the
House to treat this as a non-contentious
measure, and to allow it to proceed through
all its remaining stages to-day. I may say
that even at Westminster a somewhat similar
course was adopted. In the early stages of
the Bill's progress through the Imperial
House it is perfectely true that it got a
great deal of very careful consideration, but
when the General Election was decided upon
very suddenly, the question of what was to
be done as regards this measure came to the
forefront. It was felt that as it was a
measure which was most important and farreaching, and as it had already got a great
deal of consideration and thought, it would
be a pity that all that labour should be lost,
and, therefore, the Government entered into
an arrangement with the opposition by which
the remaining stages of the Bill would be
taken with great rapidity As an example
of that, I would like to tell the House that
it passed through all its stages in the House
of Lords in less than two hours, without
amendment. The Government have very
carefully considered the various provisions
of this Bill, and they are to-day submitting
it to this House in the form in which it
was passed at Westminster.
I may say that prior to 1880 workers had
to depend upon the Common Law for any
compensation which they got owing to injury.
In 1880 the first Employers' Liability Act
was passed, and it also gave very inadequate
compensation to workers in case of injury.
In 1897 the first Workmen's Compensation
Act was passed through the exertions and
energies of the late Right Hon. Joseph
Chamberlain. (Hon. Members. Hear, hear.)
It undoubtedly stabilised and improved the
workers' position very much. That Act was
followed by an Amending Act in 1906, and
later on-in 1917 and 1919-we had what are
known as the two War Addition Acts.
This Bill that I have the honour to ask
the House to consider to-day has 29 Clauses,
and I do not think that it is at all necessary
that I should take up time by dealing with
very many of these important provisions.
Hon. Members have had the Bill in their
Workmen's Compensation Bill— HOUSE OF COMMONS.
Second Reading.
[Mr. Andrews]

who will continue to obtain compensation,
notwithstanding that this Bill will come
into force on 31st December, until such time
as they have recovered and are able to
return to work.
Mr. McGUFFIN: May I ask the right
hon. Gentleman if the review of those cases
would come under this Bill?
Mr. ANDREWS: Anyone who has been
injured prior to the 31st December will come
under the 1906 Act, plus the War Addition
Acts. Any accident that may occur after the
31st December next-provided that this Bill
passes to-day-will come under this Bill.
Clauses 2 and 3 increase the minimum
amount of compensation from £150 to £200.
and for the first time account is taken not
only of the pre-accident wages but also of
the amount of responsibility which the
person killed had in respect of his dependants. In other words, for the first time
provision is made which will allow of compensation being fixed having regard to the
number of dependants which the deceased
had. In addition to that the total amount
of compensation which may be awarded is
raised to £600.
I come next to Clause 4, which increases
the maximum weekly payment from £1 to
£1 10s., and gives the lower paid worker
an advantage in the way of enabling him
to obtain a larger percentage of his preaccident wages than it is proposed to give
to the higher-paid worker.
Clause 5 deals with the waiting period.
As hon. Members know, before any claim
could be made under the existing law a week
had to elapse, and unless the worker was
out of employment through accident for at
least a fortnight the compensation for this
waiting period would not be paid. It was
found that that had obvious disadvantages,
and the present Bill substitutes for a week
three days, and on the other hand provides
that compensation cannot be obtained for
those three days unless the worker has been
out of work for at least four weeks.
Clause 6 simply deals with the setting up
of certain administrative machinery, and
Clause 7 deals with the inclusion of certain
accidents arising outside the scope of employment. What that means is this, that
workers sometimes feel called upon to do
work which may not be directly held to be
their legitimate employment, and if they did
were
that work in the past and if they
killed or injured in the doing of it there
was no compensation payable. A very good
example of the injustice of that was cited
to me a day or two ago. A locomotive
engineer, who felt that there was something
wrong with the front part of his engine,
left the footplate, and risking his life for
the sake of the passengers behind him, went
out on to the front of the engine to see what
was wrong with it. He fell off and was
killed, and the Courts held that the next-ofkin was not entitled to compensation. This
Act will bring in cases of that kind, and
removes what was obviously a very great
hardship, which could occur under the Act
of 1906.
Clause 8 is an extension of the principal.
Act to certain share fishermen. What is
meant by that is: Share fishermen were not
included in the Act of 1906, but as share
fishermen are very often
paid partly
by getting a share of the catch. and also by
getting wages, it is thought that they ought
to come under this Act.
can
Clause 10 deals with the question of notice.
At the present time a worker has to give
notice to his employer in writing. Sometimes workers fail to do that. Some of them
do not care very often to write to an employer telling him that they are going to
make a claim, and this clause provides that it
will be sufficient for an employee to give
verbal notice to the foreman, who in turn
pass it
on to the employer-(hon.
Members: Hear. hear)-and so relieve the
worker from what some of them felt was
a rather embarrassing position-to have to
make a claim upon their employer very often
before they knew actually whether the
injury which they had received was serious
or not. They naturally felt that some employers might think they were making a
claim without justice, and might resent their
doing so. This clause removes the worker
from that embarrassing position.
Clause 11 provides that either party can
apply for a medical referee instead of, as
at the present time, both. I think the House
will feel that is as it ought to be.
Mr. McGUFFIN: Hear, hear.
Mr. ANDREWS: Clause 12 deals with the
question of registration, and Clause 14, which
is the next one I think I need refer to, dealwith the ending or diminishing of weekly
payments on doctor's reports. What that
means is that the employer under the 1901
Act could notify his worker that the weekly
payment would no longer be made, and the
worker had to take proceedings against the
employer. In the meantime no weekly pay
2097 Workmen's Compensation Bill- 23 NOVEMBER 1923.

Second Reading.
ments were made. Now, if a worker obtains
a doctor's certificate to the effect that the
worker in his opinion is entitled to continue
to get weekly benefit, the employer is bound
to continue to pay until the Courts have
decided whether or not he is entitled to pay.
Clause 15 deals with the question of the
fluctuation of wages. If wages fluctuate to
more than the extent of 20 per cent. either
up or down an application may be made
to have the weekly payments on account
of partial or total incapacity reviewed. 1
think that is a reasonable and proper clause.
Clauses 17 and 18 again deal with the
question of machinery for the administration
of the Act, and Clause 19 safeguards the
worker in the case of the bankruptcy of a
firm in which he is employed. Under the
1906 Act if a firm went into bankruptcy the
debentures reckoned before compensation.
Now compensation is reckoned as wages and
must be paid in the same way as wages
are paid in priority to any other charge
upon the firm, whether it be in the form
of debentures or not.
The next clause I ought to refer to is
Clause 26. It provides that first aid and
ambulance arrangements must be provided
in all classes of factories.
Mr. McGUFFIN: Does that mean, irrespective of the size of the factory, there will
have to be an ambulance provided?
Mr. ROBB: Not an ambulance.
Mr. ANDREWS: Ambulance arrangements;
but, of course, in a smaller concern
I do not suppose as complete an arrangement would be insisted uupon as in a
larger concern. Still, a worker who is
employed in a small concern has just the
same right to get first aid as a worker who
may be employed in a larger one. It is on
the principle that prevention is better than
cure, and that sometimes a stitch in time
saves nine. Before I come to the end of
these few remarks I would like to tell the
House that I do not think they need look
upon this Bill, when it becomes an Act,
as a permanent Act. Mr. Bridgeman, when
the Bill was passing through the Imperial
House, stated that he intended to bring in
a Bill later on, if the Government was again
in power, to consolidate the various Acts
dealing with workmen's compensation. This
Bill is really legislating by reference, which
is always objectionable. However, I think
it is a useful forerunner of a consolidated
Bill which it is proposed to introduce during
the early years of the new Parliament. I beg
to move.
Mr. DONALD: I rise to congratulate my
right hon. Friend on the speedy way in
which he has introduced this very important
measure, and on the steps he has taken on
behalf of the Government to have this Bill
passed through this House. I want to
facilitate the passing of this Bill to-day,
but there is no reason why we should not
embrace this opportunity of saying what we
have to say with regard to this important
measure. I want later on to offer one or
two suggestions, which will not alter the
Bill in any way, with regard to the administration. My right hon. Friend (Mr.
Andrews) has clearly pointed out the steps
taken under the original Acts with regard
to compensation. Compensation means
making provision for the industrial warrior.
I have had some little experience in regard
to the administration of the Workmen's
Compensation Act, especially since the 1906
Act. My right hon. Friend (Mr. Andrews)
stated quite clearly that the War Additions
measure was brought in in 1917. That increased the amount by one quarter above
the 1906 Act, and the reason was quite
obvious. The cost of living had something
to do with it, notwithstanding the risks that
workers were running at that time in the
manufacture of munitions and so forth.
A further amending Bill was introduced in
1919, and this increased the amount to threequarters above the 1906 Act for the same
reasons, I take it. This Bill that my right
hon. Friend (Mr. Andrews) has introduced
to-day is a very important measure embodying 29 clauses, and there is a great
principle underlying it. I would like my
right hon. Friend (Mr. Andrews) to notice
that the Bill was not rushed through the
Imperial House. If our Bill is the same as
the Imperial measure the House is responsible. I had not time to go into the details
of the Bill, but I want to see the measure
becoming law to-day. At the same time it
took eleven days to go through the Standing
Committee of the Imperial House with all
parties represented. My hon. Friend for
West Belfast (Mr. Lynn) was on that
Committee.
Mr. ANDREWS: On a point of order,
what I did say was that in its latter stages
the Bill was hurried through the House, but
in its earlier stages it got a great deal of
careful consideration, and it was because of
that careful consideration that it was felt

should become law.
Mr. DONALD: If I misunderstood my
right hon Friend (Mr. Andrews) I accept
his explanation. What I want to point out
is that the measure was deliberated upon
clause by clause for eleven days in Committee.
and those of us who have experience know
that that is where the work is done. When
it came before the House all parties agreed,
owing to the dissolution, to its becoming

as
law. I quite understand that. Clauses

matter, there is one feature which I fail to
understand. It is, that out of every £100
really only £48 goes towards compensation,
