much of this money for that purpose.
I want to make one or two suggestions to
my right hon. Friend (Mr. Andrews), if he
turns his attention to Clause 26. sub-Clause
3, on page 22. That is a very important
clause. It reads:
any
Where it appears to the Ministry of
Labour that, in view of the number and
nature of accidents occurring in
factory or class of factories, special provision ought to be made at that factory or
at factories of that class to secure the
safety of persons employed therein. . .
Here is where I want to make a suggestion
to my right hon. Friend. There are Safety
Committees set up in Great Britain, and I
think it was in 1911 that I submitted evidence with regard to the prevention of
accidents. I think a committee of that description would be very useful in this
is
country. There
a Shipbuilding Committee, for instance, to make suggestions to
the Minister for the prevention of accidents,
a very useful committee indeed, and I am
sure my right hon. Friend will give this
matter some consideration. When I submitted my evidence I am not putting it
that way, but I want to show my right hon.
Friend the necessity of such a thing-I submitted it on actual facts as they occurred to
me working in the shipyards. On three
occasions I very nearly lost my life as the
result of accidents. I pointed out remedies
to the factory inspector whereby these could
to some extent be prevented in the future.
I will give you an illustration. I remember
one day going on board ship. One end of
the gangway was on the graving dock and
the other end was on board the ship, but the
handrail was only attached to the gangway
and not to the ship. There were a large
number of men on the gangway, and it broke
in the centre. The gangway came down at
an angle, and we would every one have been
killed but for the fact that it jammed in the
graving dock. I pointed out as a remedy that
in all future cases the handrail should be
attached on board the ship instead of to the
end of the gangway, and that it should, if
possible be a wire rope. These and other
precautions have helped.
At this juncture I should like to pay a
tribute to the Factory Inspector, Mr. Eraut.
He is a gentleman we do not hear very much
about, but he is a very useful man in this
country, and he has brought out several
suggestions and patents for the better ventilation of factories. I think it is only right
to say that a gentleman like Mr. Eraut
should be encouraged by a Safety Committee
such as I propose, and I would suggest to my
right hon. Friend (Mr. Andrews) that he
should offer a prize for the best paper in
any industry on the prevention of accidents
in workshops and such places as the shipyards. Working men as well as employers
have given a very great deal of time to the
introduction of patents to prevent accidents,
and many a time I have remarked that the
workmen themselves have laid traps for
themselves. But such things as patent
slings have been introduced whereby when
you are slinging plates they will not slip,
and then there are patent staging hooks.
These things all tend to the safety of the
working people, the question of gangways,
the covering of dangerous holes, and all
that---

Committee.

Mr. McGUFFIN: I do not intend to delay

the justice of the Bill in view of the fact

APPOINTMENT OF A SPECIAL
CONSTABLE.
Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Home Affairs, whether it is the fact that
Special Constable Bartlett was sent to Headquarters, Special Constabulary, Omagh, as a
wireless mechanic, and whether, having no
knowledge of wireless he was retained in the
Police Force as a constable; and if he will
state what appointment he now holds, and
what is his remuneration?
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): I have been asked by my right
hon. Friend the Minister of Home Affairs
(Sir Dawson Bates), to reply to this question.
Special Constable Bartlett joined the Force
on 19th June last as a fitter in the Wireless
Section, and was posted to Omagh for duty.
Bartlett, who is a most proficient fitter, was
not employed as an operator. Owing to reductions in the staff of fitters in the Wireless
Section he was transferred to ordinary duty
in August last, and is now performing duty
with a platoon as a special constable, receiving the usual remuneration as such.
Colonel WOODS: Arising out of that
answer, I would like to ask the Minister of
Labour if Constable Bartlett is not manager
of a canteen, and if he can say he is an ex-
Service man?
Mr. ANDREWS: I regret that I cannot
furnish this information, but I am sure if
my hon. and gallant Friend would apply to
the Minister of Home Affairs he will furnish
him with the information required.
Royal Assent.

Governor, in the name of and on behalf of
his Majesty the King, had been pleased to
give his assent to the following Acts agreed
upon by both Houses:-

Mr. McGUFFIN: Would I be in order in
addressing the House at the moment?
Mr. SPEAKER: No.
Mr. McGUFFIN: There is a question I
I would like to ask.
Mr. SPEAKER: The hon. Gentleman should
have asked his question at the close of questions. There is always a moment after the
questions on the Paper. I am afraid now he
is too late. There is no Question before the
House and question time is over.
Mr. McGUFFIN: I might point out that
this is a question that perhaps could not
have been included in the Orders. It is
one-
Mr. SPEAKER: I am sorry. We are only
waiting now for the summons to the Senate
for prorogation. If the hon. Gentleman had
come to me before and asked me, certainly
he could have asked his question at question
time. It would be quite out of order to allow
it now. I am sorry.
PROROGATION.
Message from the Senate.
A message was delivered by the Gentleman
Usher of the Black Rod, as follows:-
Mr. Speaker, his Grace the Governor
of Northern Ireland commands this
Honourable House to attend immediately
in the Senate.
The House went, and having returned,
Mr SPEAKER (standing in the Clerk's
place at the Table): I have to inform the
House that the House has been to the Senate.
where his Grace the Governor communicated
his Speech to both Houses as follows:-
2111 The King's Speech.
The King's Speech.
HOUSE OF COMMONS

KING'S SPEECH,
Members of the Senate and of the
House of Commons:
I have to congratulate you upon a
fruitful Parliamentary Session, the outstanding feature of which has been the
placing upon the Statute Book of Acts dealing
with Education, Housing and Licensing
Reform.
I have observed with satisfaction the
energetic and sympathetic manner in which
the problem of unemployment has been faced
and the cordial co-operation between Parliament and Local Authorities in promoting
schemes to provide work for those who,
through no fault of their own, are suffering
hardshihs consequent upon the continued
depression in trade, and I rejoice to know
that so long as the proposals put forward
by the Local Authorities are considered by
your Ministers of Finance and Labour to
fall properly within the purview of the
general scheme that has already been laid
down, and within the limits of the financial
resources of the Province, they will continue
to help in every possible way.
Equally diligent consideration has been
devoted to the problem of agricultural
depression, and I trust that the financial
arrangements proposed will materially assist
that great industry throughout the hard
tines now prevailing.
The association of your Ministry of
Commerce with the Economic Conference
has proved of great benefit, which will
become more apparent when the world'
visitors to the great Empire Exhibition next
year have an opportunity of inspecting the
Ulster Pavilion and judging of the merits
of our Exhibits.
Members of the House of Commons:
thank you for the provision of supplies
For the public services.
The Committee engaged upon the task of
adjusting the financial relations between
Great Britain and Northern Ireland having
had to postpone its Report places you in a
difficulty regarding the future, but I am
glad to know that so far as the years 1922-3
and 1923-4 are concerned an arrangement has
been come to which will enable you to meet
all known charges upon your Exchequer for
those years.
Members of the Senate and of the
House of Commons:
I am glad to learn that substantial progress is being made by the Commission
established to inquire into the natural and
industrial resources of Northern Ireland
and trust that as a result of its deliberations
there may be opened up new avenues of trade
and commerce.
It is a cause of disappointment that the
Committee established to inquire into the
subject of rent and mortgage interest
restrictions found it impossible to present
a unanimous report, but a Bill dealing with
this subject will be prepared in time to take
a place in the forefront of your legislation
in the ensuing Session.
I express myself as fully satisfied with
the existing conditions of law and order
throughout Northern Ireland. and congratulate the Government and also all ranks
of the Royal Ulster and Special Constabulary, with which bodies I have come
in close personal contact during the past
year, for the part played by them in maintaining this happy state of affairs.
I pray that the blessings of Almighty God
may rest upon your labours.
Afterwards the Speaker of the Senate read
the Proclamation proroguing Parliament as
follows:-
BY HIS GRACE THE GOVERNOR OF
NORTHERN IRELAND.
A PROCLAMATION
Proroguing the Present Parliament of
Northern Ireland.
WHEREAS it is provided by Section eleven
of the Government of Ireland Act, 1920, as
modified by and in pursuance of the Irish
Free State (Consequential Provisions) Act,
1922, that the Governor of Northern Ireland
shall, in his Majesty's name, summon, prorogue, and dissolve the Parliament of
Northern Ireland:
AND WHEREAS it is desirable that this
present Parliament of Northern Ireland
should be prorogued to the eleventh day of
March, One thousand nine hundred and
twenty-four,
NOW I, JAMES ALBERT EDWARD,
DUKE OF ABERCORN, Governor of
Northern Ireland, by this Proclamation do
Prorogation.
End of Session.
27 NOVEMBER 1923.
publish and declare His Majesty's pleasure
that the said Parliament be, as from the
reading of this Proclamation in the Parliament of Northern Ireland, prorogued to
Tuesday, the eleventh day of March, One
thousand nine hundred and twenty-four.
AND I DO HEREBY FURTHER DECLARE
His Majesty's Royal will and pleasure to be
that the said Parliament shall, on the said
eleventh day of March, One thousand nine
hundred and twenty-four, assemble and be
holden for the despatch of divers urgent and
important affairs, and the Senators and
Members of the House of Commons of
Northern Ireland are hereby required to give
their attendance accordingly.
Given at Belfast this twenty-seventh day
of November, One thousand nine hundred and
twenty-three.
(Signed by his own hand)
ABERCORN.
GOD SAVE THE KING.
End of the Third Session (opened

Tuesday,
27th February, 1923) of the First Parliament
of Northern Ireland, in the Fourteenth year
of the Reign of His Majesty King George
the Fifth.
